records.title: Coupled physicochemical and microbial recovery of aged premise plumbing following water-supply interruption.
records.abstract: Water-supply interruptions can cause pronounced deterioration of premise-plumbing water quality, yet the coordinated responses of bacterial communities, antibiotic resistance, bacteriophages, and microbial functional potential during water-supply resumption remain poorly resolved. Here, a full-scale 24-h water-supply interruption in an approximately 25-year-old cast-iron premise-plumbing system was investigated by integrating physicochemical measurements, quantitative PCR, metagenomics, virus-host prediction, and functional analyses. At 1 min after water supply resumption, residual chlorine was undetectable, whereas turbidity and total iron ranged from 149.9 to 155.3 NTU and 13.4 to 13.8 mg/L, respectively. By 40 min, residual chlorine reached 0.52 to 0.56 mg/L, while turbidity and total iron declined to levels of 0.56 to 0.61 NTU and 0.028 to 0.041 mg/L, respectively. Concurrently, Legionella pneumophila decreased from 4.12 to 0.83 log10 (gene copies/mL), and mexA from 5.55 to 1.77 log10 (gene copies/mL). Metagenomic analyses revealed pronounced succession of bacterial communities, putative human pathogen-associated taxa, and the resistome. Caudoviricetes dominated the viral community and showed coordinated temporal changes with predicted bacterial hosts. Biofilm-associated functional genes, extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), and putative phage-encoded auxiliary metabolic genes were more abundant in the initially discharged water and generally decreased following water supply resumption. The elevated EPS may have reflected both microbial production and detachment of pre-existing biofilm-associated material. Collectively, the results identify the initially discharged water as a distinct post-stagnation physicochemical and microbiological state. Water-supply resumption represents a rapid ecological transition in which restoration of disinfectant residual and displacement of stagnant/pipe-associated material jointly restructure the microbiome, resistome, and virome.

records.title: Genomic detection of domoic acid biosynthesis uncovers expanded toxigenic diversity across  Pseudo-nitzschia  diatoms
records.abstract: Domoic acid (DA) production by diatom genus  Pseudo-nitzschia causes recurrent harmful algal blooms with major consequences for marine ecosystems, fisheries, and human health. Predicting DA risk remains challenging because toxin production varies across morphologically similar and cryptic lineages. Consequently, morphology or single marker genes often fail to resolve toxigenic potential. Here, we expand genomic resources for  Pseudo-nitzschia by generating and compiling high-quality genomes spanning diverse species and biogeographic origins, establishing a genus-wide phylogenomic framework to investigate the distribution and evolution of the DA biosynthesis (  dab ) gene cluster. Among chemically characterized strains, the  dab pathway was detected in species only with confirmed DA production. While the cluster exhibits a conserved core structure, several lineages display signatures of ongoing evolution, including intronization, locus rearrangement, and pseudogenization. One striking example of  dab variation occurs in toxigenic  P. australis strains, in which its biochemically validated isodomoic acid A synthase-encoding gene  dabC is located outside the  dab locus. Metatranscriptomic surveys reveal widespread environmental  dab expression across size classes and species, implicating taxa not typically associated with environmental DA events, such as  P . cf.  obtusa and  P . cf.  plurisecta . To connect  dab expression with chemical output, nutrient limitation experiments in the historically inconsistent DA producer  P. pseudodelicatissima combined transcriptional profiling and nontargeted metabolomics demonstrating coordinated  dab expression across distinct co-expression modules and DA accumulation in response to silicon limitation. Together, these results refine the phylogenetic scope of DA production and provide a genome-resolved basis for improved molecular monitoring of toxigenic diversity.

records.title: Isolation and genomic characterization of a Teetrevirus phage infecting Klebsiella quasipneumoniae with a putative SAMase gene.
records.abstract: Phages regulate bacterial populations in engineered ecosystems. However, wastewater associated phage lineages remain uncultured and poorly characterized. Here, we describe vB_KquP_T1, a bacteriophage infecting Klebsiella quasipneumoniae and exhibiting a lytic growth phenotype, isolated from urban wastewater. Genome-based phylogenomic analyses revealed that vB_KquP_T1 represents a distinct species-level lineage within the Teetrevirus of the Autotranscriptaviridae, closely related to uncultured viral genomes. Metagenomic recruitment from 234 global wastewater datasets reveals that vB_KquP_T1-like phages are widespread, with pronounced regional variation. Notably, the vB_KquP_T1 genome encodes a putative S-adenosyl-L-methionine hydrolase (SAMase)-like protein. Structural modeling and comparative analysis revealed a conserved structural architecture, while molecular docking predicted potential interactions with SAM-related ligands. These findings link an uncultured viral lineage to a cultivated representative and support the conservation of SAM metabolism-related auxiliary genes across tailed phages.
records.authors: Chen K, Li J, Zhou L, Ge R, Zheng K, Xu C, Su Y, Sun S, Liang Y, Xing J, Wang M.

records.title: Characterization and Genome Analysis of a Novel Vibrio Alginolyticus Phage and Its Biocontrol Efficacy in Pearl Oyster Aquaculture.
records.abstract: A novel lytic bacteriophage, designated vB_ValS-L9, infecting the potentially pathogenic bacterium Vibrio alginolyticus L4, was isolated from a coastal aquaculture area in Beihai, China. Transmission electron microscopy revealed that vB_ValS-L9 possesses an icosahedral head (56.50 ± 4.19 nm in diameter) and a long tail (143.03 ± 5.32 nm in length), exhibiting a typical siphovirus-like morphology within the class Caudoviricetes. The phage demonstrated stability across various temperatures, pH levels, and salinities. Genomic sequencing showed that vB_ValS-L9 has a circular double-stranded DNA genome of 44,025 bp with a G + C content of 43.56% and 61 predicted ORFs. No tRNA, virulence, or antibiotic resistance genes were identified. Genomic and phylogenetic analyses, including ANI, VICTOR, VIRIDIC, and conserved protein phylogenies, identified vB_ValS-L9 as a novel species that, together with Vibrio phages Artemius and VapS30, forms a new genus in the class Caudoviricetes, for which the name Artemiovirus is proposed. Furthermore, in vivo trials using juvenile pearl oysters (Pinctada martensii) revealed that vB_ValS-L9 provides substantial prophylactic and therapeutic protection against V. alginolyticus L4 infection, especially when the phage was administered before bacterial challenge. Collectively, these findings suggest that vB_ValS-L9 shows potential as a safe, environmentally robust, and promising biocontrol candidate for managing vibriosis in aquaculture.
records.authors: Chen X, Li X, Zhu Y, Liang Y, Ren X, Zhang S, Tao J, Zou K, Lu L.

records.title: Jestvirus, a Novel Genus in the Family Autotranscriptaviridae Infecting Aeromonas.
records.abstract: Aeromonas species are ubiquitous, aquatic, opportunistic pathogens; however, their viral predators remain underexplored. Here, we isolated and characterized Aeromonas phage vB_AsaP_JS1, a dsDNA phage with a short non-contractile tail that infects Aeromonas salmonicida. Comparative analyses indicate that vB_AsaP_JS1 diverges from representative T7-like phages, with gene content similarity below 50% and a maximum amino acid identity of 70% or less. It forms a supported monophyletic clade in both phylogenomic and protein-based trees. Gene-sharing network analysis further shows that vB_AsaP_JS1 and its closest relatives form a distinct, isolated cluster, clearly separated from all currently recognized genera within the family Autotranscriptaviridae and related lineages of Caudoviricetes. Collectively, these features satisfy ICTV criteria for genus demarcation and support the establishment of a novel phage genus, tentatively designated Jestvirus. Functional annotation highlights a compact transcriptional module containing a single-subunit T7-like RNA polymerase and a streamlined replication packaging operon. Several putative host-interaction-related genes, including a deoxycytidine kinase homolog, a PelC-like protein, and a putative glycosidase, are encoded in the genome; their possible roles in nucleotide scavenging or host interaction during infection represent hypotheses that require experimental validation. Metagenomic read mapping reveals sequence-level signals related to vB_AsaP_JS1 in wastewater datasets from multiple geographic regions, suggesting a potentially wider environmental distribution for this phage lineage than previously recognized, though confirmation of phage identity and prevalence will require further investigation. Together, our results expand the known genomic diversity of T7-like phages and provide taxonomic, functional, and ecological evidence for a new phage lineage within Caudoviricetes.
records.authors: Chen K, Li J, Chen J, Zheng K, Zhou L, Su Y, Sun S, Chen X, Wang W, Liang Y, Shao H, Liu Y, Zou X.

records.title: CnidoSite: A Multi-Omics Database for Cnidarians
records.abstract: The phylum Cnidaria, encompassing reef-building corals, sea anemones, hydroids, and jellyfish, includes both ecological keystones of the marine biosphere and indispensable models for reconstructing early animal evolution. However, escalating ocean warming, recurrent mass coral bleaching events, and intensifying jellyfish blooms have underscored the urgent need to dissect the molecular underpinnings of cnidarian thermal tolerance, symbiosis, and environmental adaptation. Progress in cnidarian research is hindered by the lack of centralized, high-quality multi-omics resources. To address this, we present CnidoSite (https://CnidoSite.org), a comprehensive, analysis-ready multi-omics platform dedicated to Cnidaria. Spanning 327 species across 120 families, 23 orders, and 7 classes, it integrates 147 full-annotated genomes, 15,642 bulk transcriptomes, 50 single-cell datasets, 46 proteomes, 723 epigenomes, 1,650 metagenomic samples, and 180,652 phenotype records. Complemented by advanced toolkits for multidimensional functional and comparative analyses, CnidoSite provides extensive functional genomic resources, including genome assemblies, phylogenies, fossil entries, functional annotations, BUSCO assessments, and mitochondrial annotations. Key features include 29 co-expression networks with cross-tissue visualization and single-cell atlases to map developmental trajectories and stress responses. In summary, CnidoSite serves as a centralized platform that bridges cnidarian biology, marine conservation, and evolutionary genomics to investigate coral bleaching, symbiosis breakdown, jellyfish blooms, and the mechanisms driving environmental adaptation.
records.authors: She J, Jiang C, Fan J, Qian P, Wu L.

records.title: Contrasting edaphic and land-use signatures of microbial phosphorus mobilisation and accumulation genes.
records.abstract: Phosphorus (P) is an essential nutrient that constrains productivity across many terrestrial ecosystems. Soil microorganisms regulate P transformation through distinct functional strategies, yet how these strategies vary with land use and environmental conditions across chronically P-impoverished landscapes remains poorly understood. Here, we combined 268 soil metagenomes from natural, pasture, and cropland systems across Australia with genome-resolved analyses of 1,077 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). Results revealed contrasting genomic distributions among P-cycling strategies. P accumulation genes were widely distributed across bacterial phylogeny, whereas mineralization gene and solubilisation gene were concentrated within specific lineages. Land-use-associated differences were most evident in the relative abundances of mineralisation and solubilisation genes, whereas accumulation genes showed comparatively little variation. Soil properties were stronger predictors of relative P-cycling gene abundance than climatic variables. Among these variables, soil pH was the strongest predictor of both the combined relative abundance of P-cycling genes and mineralisation genes, whereas accumulation genes were negatively associated with the mineral-associated organic carbon fraction. Continental predictions further suggested higher combined relative P-cycling gene abundance in wetter south-western and coastal eastern regions. These analyses reveal contrasting microbial P-cycling gene strategies across Australian soils and provide a genome-resolved framework for understanding their phylogenetic distributions and environmental associations at the continental scale.

records.title: Whole-genome characterization and genomic stability of Mastadenovirus F40 and F41 in pediatric gastroenteritis.
records.abstract: BackgroundHuman adenovirus types 40 and 41 (HAdV-40 and HAdV-41), belonging to the species Mastadenovirus faecale, are among the leading viral causes of acute gastroenteritis in children. Despite their clinical importance, whole-genome data on circulating strains remain limited. This study investigated the epidemiological and genomic characteristics of enteric Mastadenoviruses detected in children with acute gastroenteritis.MethodsA total of 632 stool specimens collected from hospitalized children with acute gastroenteritis were screened using a multiplex gastrointestinal real-time PCR panel. Five representative Mastadenovirus-positive samples underwent shotgun metagenomic sequencing followed by genome reconstruction, phylogenetic analysis, pairwise sequence identity comparisons, genome-wide variant analysis, amino acid substitution profiling, and recombination analysis.ResultsMastadenoviruses were detected in 60/632 (9.5%) children, with the highest positivity observed among those aged 1-3 years. Co-infections occurred predominantly involving bacterial pathogens. Complete or near-complete genomes were recovered for all five sequenced isolates with high sequencing depth (2,806 × -34,120 ×), genome coverage (94.8%-100% at ≥ 10 ×), and nucleotide identity (99.19%-99.78%) relative to genotype-matched reference genomes. Phylogenetic analyses identified two HAdV-F40 and three HAdV-F41 isolates. Gene-specific phylogenies of the hexon, penton base, fiber, and DNA polymerase genes consistently confirmed genotype assignment. Pairwise sequence identity analysis and recombination analysis further supported classification with no evidence of intergenotypic recombination.ConclusionsThe sequenced enteric Mastadenovirus isolates exhibited high genomic conservation with limited within-genotype diversity and no detectable evidence of recent recombination. The concordance between gene-specific phylogenies, sequence identity analyses, and whole-genome comparisons supports the robustness of current molecular typing approaches and expands the limited genomic data available for circulating HAdV-F40 and HAdV-F41 strains.
records.authors: El-Shahidy SM, Zakaria AM, Ibrahim MA, Diab AM.

records.title: PhytClust: Efficient and Optimal Monophyletic Partitioning of Rooted Phylogenetic Trees.
records.abstract: Phylogenetic trees play a fundamental role in elucidating evolutionary relationships among taxa. Clustering taxa remains a major challenge across diverse biological domains such as cancer genomics, microbial systematics, and phylogenomics. Several methods partition taxa in phylogenetic trees into clusters, but these approaches face key limitations. Many rely on user-defined distance thresholds, whose choice often depends on prior knowledge and may be difficult to justify consistently across datasets. More broadly, existing methods often differ in how clusters are defined and commonly rely on heuristics or user-specified criteria to make the search space tractable for large trees. Here, we present PhytClust, a threshold-free algorithm that partitions trees into monophyletic subtrees (clusters) by identifying groups of taxa with low within-cluster dispersion. For a fixed number of clusters, PhytClust finds the exact global optimum under this objective and then selects the optimal number of clusters using a cluster-validity index. The resulting partitions are reproducible and reflect both tree topology and branch lengths. In simulated datasets, PhytClust outperforms existing methods in accuracy and remains competitive in speed while scaling to trees with more than a hundred thousand taxa. We apply it to viral and bacterial phylogenies, single-cell cancer phylogenies, archaeal and avian phylogenomics, gene family evolution, and plant conservation genomics. By providing a standardized method for partitioning phylogenetic trees, PhytClust yields partitions that are reproducible, exactly optimal under a stated objective, and computable on large trees.
records.authors: Ganesan K, Billard E, Kaufmann TL, Strange CB, Cwikla MC, Altenhoff AM, Dessimoz C, Schwarz RF.

records.title: Metagenomic insights into the avian gut microbiome: novel viruses, antimicrobial resistance, and beyond.
records.abstract: Birds play crucial roles in shaping ecosystems, and their gut microbiomes significantly influence host physiology and pathology. Understanding the composition, functions, and dynamics of avian gut microbiomes is therefore essential. Recent advances in metagenomic and metatranscriptomic sequencing have greatly increased our ability to characterize the avian gut microbiome. This review presents a systematic summary of the current knowledge regarding the composition of the avian gut microbiome as revealed through high-throughput sequencing technologies. It provides a statistical overview of the predominant bacterial and viral taxa present in the gut microbiomes of 195 bird species, revealing a persistent trend toward the discovery of novel viruses, and gives insight into the gene functions of these taxa. Interestingly, in terms of both antimicrobial resistance and multidrug resistance, wild birds harbor a greater diversity of resistance types than poultry. This review also presents a discussion of the relationships of avian life stages and the living conditions of birds with the gut microbiome and highlights practical applications of microbiome regulation in poultry production. Building on this foundation, future research priorities are outlined, such as the study of archaea, fungi, protists, and novel viruses, ways of improving methods to reduce costs and standardize protocols, and the development of more extensive metagenomic and metatranscriptomic data resources. Ultimately, these efforts could provide a holistic understanding of the avian gut microbiome.
records.authors: Xu Y, Zhang C, Wu Y, Zhuo J, Shen X, Zhou Y, Jin J.

records.title: Earl Grey ParTEA: scalable, consistent transposable element annotation from pangenomes to deep phylogenetic scopes
records.abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) are major drivers of genomic diversity, yet understanding their mobility and functional impact requires their accurate description in genomes. TE annotation is still typically performed genome-by-genome. TEs are often shared between some members of the same or closely related species. Hence, TE annotation with a library from a single reference misses families absent from that assembly, whereas building independent per-genome libraries fails to consistently surface shared TEs, hindering comparison. Here, we present Earl Grey ParTEA, a fully automated Snakemake pipeline extending the functionality of Earl Grey for comparative TE annotation across genome panels. ParTEA builds a single non-redundant TE library from all input genomes, resolves chimeric consensus sequences, and uses this shared library to annotate every genome, enabling direct comparison of TE family diversity, abundance, shared and private content, and activity landscapes. Optional modules provide TE library saturation analysis, BUSCO-based assembly quality control, and phylogenetic ordering of outputs. We applied ParTEA to sets of genomes spanning evolutionary scales: ten  Arabidopsis thaliana accessions, ten  Drosophila species, and ten species spanning the fungal kingdom. The  Drosophila TE library expanded from 343 to 1,852 curated families including a previously missed rolling circle element with over 6,000 copies in  D. miranda . The proportion of TE families shared across all genomes was highest within  A. thaliana (97.3%), 37.7% across  Drosophila species and only 0.5% across the set of fungi. ParTEA is available through Bioconda and represents a computationally efficient reproducible framework for comparative TE analysis in the era of large-scale genome analyses.
records.authors: Baril T, Feurtey A, Croll D.

records.title: The YjfJ protein is the effector of a second PspA/VIPP1 system that is widespread in the Gammaproteobacteria
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Maintaining the integrity of the cytoplasmic membrane is essential for bacterial cell survival. Unsurprisingly, prokaryotes have evolved conserved mechanisms by which they sense, maintain, and repair membrane integrity in response to stress. The phage shock protein (Psp) is one such system, understood primarily through work undertaken in the Gammaproteobacterial species  Escherichia coli and  Yersinia enterocolitica . The system utilises an effector, PspA, alongside accessory proteins that sense stress and recruit PspA to damaged membranes. Homologues of PspA - part of the PspA/VIPP1 family - are found in a variety of bacterial phyla. Although most work in the Gammaproteobacteria has concerned the canonical Psp response, there have been descriptions of non-canonical PspA/VIPP1-containing systems that warrant further genomic analysis. By analysing the PspA/VIPP1 content of a diverse selection of Gammaproteobacterial genomes, we reveal the existence of two phylogenetically distinct subtypes of PspA/VIPP1 proteins, PspA- and YjfJ-like, which are found at similar frequencies. The YjfJ-like proteins are not only a novel subtype of PspA/VIPP1, having their own unique set of accessory proteins, but in some species, such as the ESKAPE pathogen  Pseudomonas aeruginosa , comprise the only PspA/VIPP1-containing system. Our study positions the YjfJ-like containing systems on equal footing with the PspA system in terms of their conservation and distribution in the Gammaproteobacteria. This suggests that studies into the biological functions of YjfJ-like proteins would be well-justified from their unique presence in some important human pathogens.  DATA SUMMARY  The authors confirm that the supporting data have been provided within the article or in the supplementary material. IMPACT STATEMENT  The discovery of bacterial homologues of mammalian ESCRT-III proteins that remodel membranes stimulated renewed interest in the function of these PspA/VIPP1 family proteins at the bacterial membrane. The first identified bacterial system, discovered over 30 years ago, was the Psp system of the Gammaproteobacterium  Escherichia coli , and while the regulation of expression of the  psp genes is well understood, the molecular function of the effector protein PspA at the membrane is still unclear. In this work, using microbial genomics analysis, we find that Gammaproteobacteria contain a second PspA/VIPP1 protein, named YjfJ in  E. coli , which is widespread and is the only system in the ESKAPE pathogen  Pseudomonas aeruginosa . Its accessory proteins, which are likely involved in the sensing of stress and activation of the effector, are entirely different to the PspA system which suggests that these are two independent pathways of membrane stress response. In fact, the YjfJ-containing systems appears to be as widespread as the canonical PspA system, suggesting that the study of YjfJ function would shed light on membrane repair systems across the Pseudomonadota (Proteobacteria).
records.authors: Game DR, Livsey HC, Van der Woude MW, Thomas GH.

records.title: Comparative multi-omics of host genome, metabolome and associated rhizosphere microbiota across karst-endemic and widespread Rhododendron species
records.abstract: Abstract    Background  To examine how classically calcifuge plants persist in phosphorus-poor, high-Ca  2+  karst bare-rock habitats, we compared genome, leaf-metabolome and associated rhizosphere-microbiome patterns in the karst-endemic  Rhododendron bailiense  Y.P.Ma, C.Q.Zhang & D.F.Chamb. with those in the widespread  R. delavayi  Franch. and allopatric  R. ambiguum  Hemsl. We integrated a multi-omics investigation across three natural microhabitats to decode these inter-kingdom interactions, combining whole-genome comparative analysis, UHPLC-MS/MS non-targeted leaf metabolomics, fungal internal transcribed spacer (ITS) amplicon profiling, and deep rhizosphere metagenomic sequencing. Results  Comparative genomics revealed significant expansion of secondary metabolism gene families in  R. bailiense  . Metabolomics showed a distinct chemical profile rich in specific flavonoids and polyacetylenes, such as luteolinidin and safynol. These species-specific metabolite profiles co-varied with microbial hubs, including  Piloderma  ,  Streptomyces  ,  Pseudorhodoplanes  and  Candidatus Sulfotelmatobacter  , whose reported or predicted functions are relevant to phosphorus mobilization, rhizosphere defence, recalcitrant-carbon turnover and mineral-associated sulfur cycling. In contrast, the  R. delavayi  and  R. ambiguum  rhizospheres were enriched in saprotrophic taxa, including  Mortierella  , consistent with broader nutrient-turnover potential. Conclusions  R. bailiense  showed a species-specific leaf-metabolite profile that co-varied with a distinctive rhizosphere microbiome. Together, these coordinated patterns suggest a potential functional link between species-specific host chemistry and rhizosphere-community organization, and highlight microbial and metabolic candidates relevant to karst persistence and conservation.
records.authors: Wen S, Leng Y, Yao H, Zhou K, Min Y, Peng L, Ou J, Qiao G, Wen X, Ding G.

records.title: Metagenomic and metabolomic analysis of a bryozoan-associated microbial complex from the Hanjiang River, China.
records.abstract: BackgroundBryozoans are ancient colonial animals that have existed for over 470 million years and are widely distributed across aquatic environments. Recently, many spherical colloids (average diameter≈1 meter in diameter), containing bryozoans and diverse microorganisms, were found in the Hanjiang river in China. In this study, we investigated these bryozoan-dominated microbial complexes using metagenomic sequencing, metabolomic profiling, and complementary approaches.ResultsThe results revealed that the microbial structure dominated by bryozoans included eukaryotes such as fungi, microalgae, as well as prokaryotes such as bacteria, and acellular entities such as viruses. All members form a highly integrated consortium that collaboratively maintains community function and stability, which displayed the shape and structure of a regular microbial complex and increased in size. Additionally, the results suggested the predominately presence of Proteobacteria were particularly abundant and are known to produce bryozoans in response to bryozoan signals. Interesting, it was implied that a decrease or even a loss in virulence occurs when pathogenic microorganisms become members of the complex. This is the first study focusing on the composition and metabolites of the unusual microorganism complex. The results discovered the close and intriguing connections within the microbial communities dominated by the ancient organism bryozoan through multi-omics technologies. It showed that both eukaryotes and prokaryotes can coordinate, thereby forming a stable composite structure.
records.authors: Zhu H, Lin X, Wang R, Zhang T, Xu W, Gao W, Fang F, Huang J, Sun Y.

records.title: Genomic and ecological specialization of Methanobrevibacter species shape human methane emission and overall gut ecosystem function
records.abstract: Abstract  Methane is a unique archaeal metabolite that links gut microbial ecology to host physiology. Although intestinal methane production varies by several orders of magnitude between individuals and has been associated with gastrointestinal transit and disease states, the ecological and functional determinants underlying this variation remain poorly understood. Here, we integrate breath methane phenotyping with shotgun metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, comparative genomics, cultivation and stable-isotope tracing in 80 deeply characterized individuals to determine the species-level and functional basis of human gut methanogenesis. Breath methane levels strongly reflected archaeal abundance but could not fully explain methane emission; species-resolved profiling revealed that methane emission represents distinct archaeome states rather than differences in methanogen quantity alone. High methane emitters were dominated by Methanobrevibacter smithii and M. intestini, whereas low emitters harbored a previously uncharacterized Methanobrevibacter lineage (M. sp900766745), for which we propose the name Candidatus Methanobrevibacter hominipaucus sp. nov. Comparative genomics revealed that M. sp900766745 represents a metabolically streamlined lineage lacking several methyl-compound utilization pathways and displaying reduced substrate acquisition capacity. Communities of low-emission individuals exhibited reduced microbial transcriptional activity and accumulated incompletely processed dietary metabolites, indicating lower fermentative turnover and altered hydrogen flux.

records.title: Hologenomic Analysis of Anopheles plumbeus Reveals Genomic Complementarity with Its Endosymbiont Candidatus Tisiphia sp.
records.abstract: Anopheles plumbeus is a widespread forest mosquito species and an effective vector of human, animal, and avian malaria pathogens. In this study, we sequenced and assembled the genome of female An. plumbeus mosquitoes obtained from a laboratory culture. The mosquitoes were collected at the larval stage in the vicinity of Sochi (Black Sea coast of the Caucasus) and reared to adulthood on an artificial diet. The genome was generated using Oxford Nanopore Technologies long-read sequencing. The resulting hologenome comprises 1,449 contigs with a total length of 188,457,274 bp. It has been deposited in the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) and is publicly available as a metagenome-assembled genome. The high quality of the eukaryotic metagenome-assembled genome (eMAG) assembly was confirmed by BUSCO analysis, demonstrating 97.5% complete BUSCOs. A single intracellular bacterial symbiont, Candidatus Tisiphia sp., was identified within the hologenome. The symbiont genome was assembled via a Whole-Genome Shotgun (WGS) approach using the Flye assembler (v. 2.9-b1774), yielding a size of 1.7 Mb. The registered assembly of Candidatus Tisiphia sp. was designated as a 'reference sequence'. Genome annotation revealed 1,761 genes, including 1,525 protein-coding genes, 4 rRNA genes, and 38 tRNA genes. A distinctive feature of this novel Candidatus Tisiphia genome is the high abundance of IS DNA transposons belonging to several families. In total, 361 IS elements were identified in the Candidatus Tisiphia sp. genome. Eight identified IS transposon families—IS6, IS701, IS4, IS630, ISNCY, IS110, IS5, and IS1634—are multicopy. Crucially, we identified for the first time in this bacterial species the biosynthetic genes for folic acid (vitamin B9), biotin (vitamin B7), and thiamine (vitamin B1), as well as a gene cluster for heme biosynthesis, which is essential for the functioning of mitochondrial cytochromes in the mosquito's respiratory chain. These data provide a foundational framework for developing biocontrol strategies against this potentially dangerous malaria vector.
records.authors: Andrianov B, Bega A, Vasilenko O, Goryacheva I, Gorelova T, Moskaev A.

records.title: Longitudinal Multiomics Reveals Core Microbiome Disruption and Potential Keystone-Associated Recovery Following Pesticide Exposure.
records.abstract: Pesticides have become indispensable in modern agriculture, serving as a primary tool to minimize crop loss amid increasing human population pressures. While the negative effects of pesticides on the soil microbiome have been reported, the temporal dynamics of soil microorganisms under pesticide use remain underexplored. Specifically, limited knowledge exists regarding how the soil microbiome responds to pesticides before and after the manufacturer-labeled 'safe period' of 21 days after application. We conducted a longitudinal microcosm study to investigate the temporal impacts of herbicide, fungicide, and insecticide on soil microbial diversity, composition, network complexity, and functional pathways across five time points. Our results show that soil microbial communities are negatively impacted by pesticide applications, but there is a trend of recovery after 21 days. We found a significant impact of the temporal persistence of pesticides on both bacterial and fungal community composition, with a stronger effect on fungi. Network analysis revealed that core microbiome networks were negatively impacted by pesticide applications, with the core microbial nodes, raw associations, and modularity declining in pesticide-treated soils, and this negative effect was particularly strong for pyrethroid insecticides. We identified several differentially abundant taxa, including Xanthobacteraceae and Vicinamibacteriales among bacteria, and Mortierella, Mytilinidales among fungi, which could serve as useful biomarkers for pesticide-affected soils. Results from microbial co-occurrence network analysis revealed that one ASV assigned to the Methyloligellaceae family consistently emerged as a keystone taxon in pesticide-treated soils. Using genome-resolved metagenomics, we assembled the genomes (MAGs) of Methyloligellaceae members and found these taxa harbor putative genes associated with pesticide degradation and antimicrobial resistance, suggesting their possible role in community recovery. Given the remarkably dynamic nature of soil microbial communities, our findings bridge an important knowledge gap regarding the short-term dynamics of microbial structures and functional pathways in response to major pesticides.

records.title: Microbial and antimicrobial resistance signatures differentiate healthy and inflamed ileal pouches in patients with ulcerative colitis.
records.abstract: Background and aimsFecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from healthy donors with a normally functioning colon has limited clinical effect in the treatment of chronic pouchitis. However, a normally functioning ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA) physiology differs from individuals with a healthy intact colon. We aimed to investigate the microbial characteristics of patients with a normally functioning IPAA (HealthyPouch) compared with chronic pouchitis (SickPouch), ulcerative colitis (UC), and a healthy intact colon microbiome (NormalGut). Furthermore, we investigated how repeated antibiotic use influences antimicrobial resistance on a bacterial genome level.MethodsFecal samples from 190 participants were collected; HealthyPouch (n = 38), SickPouch (n = 37), UC (n = 23), and NormalGut (n = 92) and sequenced with Illumina and taxonomically profiled. Samples from HealthyPouch, SickPouch, and NormalGut were also long-read sequenced using Oxford Nanopore Technologies for reconstruction of 12 282 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). DNA methylation motifs were used for plasmid-host association.ResultsThe HealthyPouch microbiome is distinct from both the UC, NormalGut, and SickPouch microbiome. Escherichia coli MAGs in the SickPouch (n = 21) microbiome had significantly higher co-occurring ciprofloxacin resistance mutations in the gyrA and parC genes, compared to both HealthyPouch (n = 26; BH adjusted P ConclusionsHealthyPouch microbiota differs from NormalGut microbiota, and could therefore be more appropriate for FMT treatment of chronic pouchitis. The association between E. coli and resistance gene-carrying plasmids underscores the importance of integrating plasmid analysis into metagenome-based approaches for personalized antibiotic treatment and resistance monitoring.

records.title: Public Goods Supply Structure Shapes Microbial Network Organization during Full-Scale Anammox Reactor Start-Up.
records.abstract: Key public goods (KPGs) are metabolites or functions produced at a metabolic cost by microbial populations but potentially benefiting the community. In engineered anammox systems, such functions may underpin interdependencies between anaerobic ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (AnAOB) and associated microorganisms, yet their supply-side organization and temporal dynamics remain poorly understood. We integrated genome-resolved metagenomics and metatranscriptomics to quantify relative transcriptional contributions to 33 KPG biosynthesis pathways during start-up of a full-scale anammox reactor. Across 42 high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), these transcriptional contributions were used to infer supply structure and temporal evolution. Inferred KPG supply structures were highly uneven across stages (Gini = 0.74-0.98), with the top 20% of populations accounting for up to 98.7% of total transcriptional contribution. Three resource-specific trajectories emerged: progressively concentrated, persistently concentrated, and dynamically fluctuating supply. AnAOB dominated contributions associated with low-cost amino acids, acetate, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, coenzyme A, oxidative-stress defense, and extracellular polymeric substance export potential, but showed apparent dependence on non-AnAOB populations for vitamins, cofactors, and high-cost amino acids. Restructuring was driven mainly by redistribution among retained populations rather than supplier turnover, with the strongest reorganization occurring during early start-up. These findings reveal a structured, resource-dependent, and dynamically reorganized KPG landscape during reactor establishment.
records.authors: Zhu D, Gong H, Zhou S, Yang J, Xie L, Azari M, Zheng M, Dai X.

records.title: A portable C-terminal rheostat calibrates RecE/Redα exonuclease activity for enhanced bacterial recombineering
records.abstract: Recombineering enables precise genome engineering across diverse bacteria, yet efficient tools for large DNA integration remain underdeveloped for Streptomyces and other biotechnologically relevant bacteria. Here we identify a panel of highly active RecET recombinase pairs from actinobacteriophages that mediate efficient homologous recombination in Streptomyces. The lead candidate, Che9cRecET, supports genomic integration of kilobase-scale DNA with only 50bp homology arms and enables accurate insertion of 79kb biosynthetic gene clusters, far outperforming conventional genome editing approaches. Structural and biochemical analyses reveal Che9cRecE as a distinct C3-symmetric toroidal homotrimeric 5′-3′ exonuclease, whose extended C-terminal loop acts as a tunable rheostat calibrating exonuclease activity to an optimal window for recombination. We further show this portable C-terminal loop enhances recombineering efficiency across phylogenetically diverse exonucleases including Escherichia coli Redα/RecE and Pseudomonas A. Our work uncovers a conserved regulatory mechanism of the RecE/Redα exonuclease family and delivers a generalizable strategy for advancing bacterial genome editing.
records.authors: Luan J, Jiang C, Guo R, Wang C, Wang S, Stewart AF, Fu J, Zhang Y, Wang H.

records.title: Exiguobacterium sargassi sp. nov., a novel seaweed-associated bacterium isolated from Sargassum henslowianum with a glycoside-hydrolase-enriched CAZyme repertoire
records.abstract: Abstract    Marine macroalgae are rich in complex polysaccharides, making them ideal habitats for finding undiscovered bacterial lineages with unique metabolic capabilities. A novel Gram-variable, facultatively anaerobic bacterium, designated strain RM11  T  , was isolated from the internal tissue of  Sargassum henslowianum  collected in Quang Ngai province, Vietnam. Growth occurred at 10–45°C, pH 7.0–10.0 and 1–12% (w/v) NaCl. Phylogenetic analysis of the 16S rRNA gene placed strain RM11  T  within the genus  Exiguobacterium  , with the highest sequence similarity to  E. qingdaonense  S82  T  (99.82%). Average nucleotide identity (ANI) values ranged from 86.46 to 90.92% and digital DNA–DNA hybridization (dDDH) values from 30.5 to 41.7%, both well below species-delineation thresholds (95–96% ANI; 70% dDDH). The genome (2,859,837 bp; G + C 47.79%) encodes genes for heavy-metal transport, ammonia assimilation, and oxidative and osmotic stress responses. Annotation of carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) revealed a glycoside-hydrolase-dominated repertoire enriched in GH13 family members predicted to participate in α-glucan metabolism, together with a candidate secreted GH16_3–CBM4 β-glucanase, whereas no polysaccharide lyase genes were detected. Based on the combined phenotypic, chemotaxonomic and genomic evidence, we propose  Exiguobacterium sargassi  sp. nov., with the type strain RM11  T  (= KCTC 43930  T   = InaCC B1791  T  ).
records.authors: Han HL, Vuong TQ, Nguyen TDP, Kim S, Dang MN.

records.title: Machine Learning based Classification of Ocular Pathogens using Host-transcriptomic Signatures: a proof-of-concept
records.abstract: Abstract  Background.  Diagnosis of infectious keratitis, uveitis, and endophthalmitis is constrained by the scarcity of pathogen-derived material in small-volume ocular specimens. The host transcriptome is an abundant alternative signal: infection elicits pathogen-class-specific transcriptional responses that may permit pathogen identification without direct detection. We tested this premise as a proof of concept using publicly available in-vitro infection RNA seq. We assembled 330 human RNA-seq samples (177 infected, 153 mock) spanning six pathogens (Herpes Simplex Virus-1, Human Cytomegalovirus Virus, Aspergillus Fumigatus, Candida Albicans, Pseudomonas Aeruginosa, Mycobacterium Tuberculosis) across 36 BioProjects and 24 host cell types. Results.  Per-study differential expression yielded a robust-gene feature matrix. Pathogen classification was evaluated with Random Forest under leave-one-study-out (grouped) cross-validation and contrasted against random cross-validation to quantify study-level information leakage. Under random (non-grouped) cross-validation, balanced accuracy reached 0.85–0.92 across gene panel sizes (8–700 + genes). Under honest, leakage-corrected leave-one-group-out validation, balanced accuracy was lower than random cross-validation and remained stable across panel sizes and gene-selection strategies, peaking at 0.70 (60–100 gene panel) and averaging 0.519–0.60 across the full range of gene sets tested (8 to 9,942 genes; chance level = 0.14 for 7 classes). Unsupervised UMAP visualization of the robust gene set showed distinct clustering by pathogen and by pathogen class (viral, fungal, bacterial), with cross-kingdom pathogen pairs showing more distinct separation than within-kingdom comparisons. Conclusions.  Beyond established diagnostics such as PCR and metagenomics, host transcriptomic signatures analyzed via machine learning offer a promising alternative approach to pathogen classification, achieving balanced accuracy substantially above chance under rigorous, study-independent validation. These findings support the feasibility of host-transcriptome-based diagnostic classification, with dataset provenance as the primary current limitation to clinical translation.
records.authors: Plumber¹ MT, Kumar R, Yadavalli T.

records.title: A life-history axis of resource acquisition in bacteria: depolymerisation versus uptake
records.abstract: Microbial decomposition of complex organic matter is a major control on the global carbon cycle, and its efficiency hinges on how microbes acquire resources. Decomposition requires costly extracellular enzymes to break down complex polymers, whereas the resulting soluble products are captured far more cheaply through membrane transporters. How microbes balance investment between these two processes is a fundamental axis of microbial life history, yet it has remained difficult to quantify across their vast diversity. Using genomic repertoires for carbohydrate depolymerisation and uptake, we developed a simple ratio distinguishing depolymerisation-optimised from uptake-optimised strategies, and applied it to more than 249,000 environmental and host-associated bacterial genomes. These strategies were strongly phylogenetically structured and differed by habitat, with uptake-optimised bacteria unexpectedly more prevalent in diffusion-limited soils than in aquatic environments. In an 18-month field-scale plant litter decomposition experiment, uptake-optimised bacteria dominated during early decomposition, when fungi were more abundant and strongly expressed hydrolytic enzymes, shifting towards depolymerisation-optimised bacteria at later stages. A simple genomic ratio therefore captures ecologically meaningful resource-acquisition strategies that vary with phylogeny, habitat and successional stage. The balance of these strategies could shape community-level extracellular enzyme investment, with consequences for decomposition and carbon cycling.
records.authors: Fu Y, Rodriguez LC, Ramoneda J, Shek K, Martiny JB, Allison SD, Luo Y, Malik AA.

records.title: Transposable element content is associated with total genome size and host taxonomy in sulfur-oxidizing bacterial endosymbionts.
records.abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) are mobile genetic sequences that can disrupt, relocate, or create genes and regulatory elements, thereby contributing to genome evolution. Their potential role in shaping adaptation, including symbiotic relationships, has drawn increasing attention. Most research on TEs to date has focused on terrestrial environments, while less is known about TE function and prevalence in marine habitats. This study investigates the presence and distribution of TEs in marine chemosynthetic symbioses, specifically among the genomes of sulfur-oxidizing Gammaproteobacteria associated with animals living in a diversity of chemically reducing environments. Our data reveal that factors such as phylogenetic relationship and habitat type have no demonstrated association with TE abundance, while factors such as genome size, host family, and lifestyle are significantly correlated. Almost all vesicomyid clam symbionts lacked TEs likely because of reductive genome evolution, while mytilid symbionts had the highest TE abundance possibly due to increased rates of homologous recombination or TE proliferation related to adaptive genome streamlining. Transposase family diversity varied considerably among symbiont groups but was not associated with genome size, indicating that other factors influence transposase composition. Notably, a large fraction of transposase genes was flanked by genes involved in DNA replication and repair, membrane transport, and prokaryotic defense systems, implying a possible role in environmental or host adaptation. This study highlights the dynamic nature of TE content in symbiotic bacteria and allows for the formulation of hypotheses on TE function for the evolution of bacteria in diverse, chemically reducing environments.ImportanceTransposable elements are key drivers of bacterial genome evolution and environmental adaptation by creating new gene functions and altering existing ones, yet they remain comparatively understudied in marine microbes. In this study, we assessed TE content and the function of flanking genes in symbiotic and free-living sulfur-oxidizing bacteria from a variety of aquatic environments. Our analyses show that genome size, bacterial lifestyle, and host association have a significant impact on TE abundance, but not necessarily transposase diversity. Transposases were often flanked by DNA replication and repair genes, membrane transporters, and prokaryotic defense systems, which likely represent transposition cargo that might be relevant for habitat adaptation. The patterns observed within these data further our understanding of the distribution and function of transposases and lay a foundation for future studies investigating the role of transposases in bacterial genome evolution.

records.title: The impact of strain heterogeneity on genomic profiling accuracy in mixed-strain  Escherichia coli  metagenomes
records.abstract: Metagenomic sequencing is increasingly used for surveillance of bacterial populations, enabling simultaneous characterisation of antimicrobial resistance, virulence, and epidemiologically relevant strain markers. However, the ability of commonly used bioinformatic tools to recover these features from heterogeneous populations remains incompletely understood. Here, we developed a controlled benchmarking framework based on simulated single-species  Escherichia coli metagenomes generated from genomes with PCR-determined annotations. Assembly-based and read-based tools were evaluated for antimicrobial resistance gene (ARG) detection, virulence gene (VG) detection, multilocus sequence typing (MLST), and serotype prediction. In addition, datasets with varying strain compositions were used to assess the effect of population complexity on strain-level characterisation.  We found that recovery of individual genetic determinants of interest (7 ARGs, 3 VGs) was consistently more successful than recovery of strain-level markers. ARG detection achieved high recovery rates across all evaluated tools (84.3–90.0%), while short read sequencing typer SRST2 achieved the highest virulence gene recovery rate (100.0%). In contrast, MLST and serotype prediction were strongly affected by strain composition. None of the evaluated MLST tools correctly assigned the dominant sequence type in the multi-strain log-normal dataset, despite successful partial recovery of MLST alleles, while complete serotype recovery remained uncommon across all methods. Decreasing the complexity of the simulated metagenome by increasing the abundance of the dominant strain improved both MLST and serotype prediction performance, while long-read analyses indicated that increased read length was insufficient to overcome the challenges associated with mixed-strain communities. These findings demonstrate that performance estimates derived from gene detection do not necessarily translate to strain-level characterisation. While individual resistance and virulence determinants could often be recovered reliably, accurate reconstruction of sequence types and serotypes remained strongly constrained by strain heterogeneity. More broadly, the results highlight current limitations in resolving strain composition from metagenomic data and provide a framework for investigating the abundance thresholds and population structures required for reliable strain-resolved surveillance. Contribution Statement  This study quantifies how strain heterogeneity influences recovery of clinically relevant genomic features from low-complexity  Escherichia coli metagenomes. We show that gene-level characterisation remains largely robust, while strain-level markers such as MLST and serotype are substantially more sensitive to mixed-strain populations. These findings highlight strain heterogeneity as a major barrier to linking clinically relevant genes to their epidemiological background in metagenomic surveillance.
records.authors: Shridar VD, Engblom S.

records.title: Hybrid genome assemblies of Bacteroidota isolates uncover mobile genetic elements, antimicrobial resistance genes, and novel antimicrobial peptides.
records.abstract: Members of the phylum Bacteroidota dominate the mammalian gut microbiota and represent promising candidates for next-generation probiotics. However, the resolution of complete Bacteroidota genomes is often hindered by extensive repetitive sequences and mobile genetic elements, a technical challenge further exacerbated by high intraspecies diversity and strain-level variants that drive assembly fragmentation and preclude the recovery of contiguous scaffolds. We recently isolated 18 strains that belonged to the Bacteroidales order of Bacteroidota from mouse ceca, human feces, and tortoise stool, which we now sequenced using both Illumina and Oxford Nanopore platforms. We developed a specialized assembly workflow to reconstruct high-resolution genomes and characterize their extrachromosomal landscapes. The hybrid pipeline yielded 2 fully closed, single-contig chromosomes, 10 almost closed genomes, and 6 draft assemblies. Genomic integrity was exceptionally high, with completeness scores ranging from 99.6% to 100% and contamination levels below 2%. A total of 12 circular plasmids were detected across 10 isolates; eight isolates harbored a single plasmid, while two isolates (241163E and 241171E) each carried two distinct circular plasmids. Seven of these plasmids were experimentally confirmed through isolation and sequencing, and five were classified as viral contigs. Functional annotation revealed a diverse repertoire of antimicrobial resistance genes and identified several predicted antimicrobial peptides in the assemblies through machine-learning analysis, of which two selected ones were experimentally verified. Overall, the resulting assemblies provide a reliable foundation for tracking mobile genetic elements, assessing resistance potential, and mining bioactive peptides in Bacteroidota species intended for therapeutic development.ImportanceBacteria in the phylum Bacteroidota are essential to mammalian gut health and are currently being developed as advanced probiotics. However, their complex DNA often prevents scientists from mapping their complete genetic blueprints, which can leave hidden traits like antibiotic resistance undetected. In this study, we combined two advanced DNA sequencing methods to create highly accurate and complete genetic maps for 18 Bacteroidota isolates from humans, mice, and tortoise. We successfully uncovered small, elusive DNA rings (potential plasmids) and confirmed their physical presence in the laboratory. Furthermore, we identified genes responsible for antibiotic resistance and used artificial intelligence to discover new antimicrobial peptides. This research provides a crucial foundation for the scientific community to accurately track mobile genes, rigorously evaluate the safety of potential gut therapeutics, and discover novel molecules for medical applications.
records.authors: Tufail MA, Bethge H, Chibani CM, Ladewig L, Schmitz RA.

records.title: gcPathogen 2.0: an expanded multi-omics database advancing global pathogen surveillance and One Health research.
records.abstract: Launched in 2024, gcPathogen established a critical foundation for the genomic surveillance of human pathogens. Here, we present gcPathogen 2.0, a major multi-omics update designed to address key analytical bottlenecks, including the integration of genomic and transcriptional profiles, systematic tracking of cross-habitat distribution, and large-scale discovery of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). This release expands coverage from 1134 to 1506 pathogenic species, spanning 557 bacteria, 508 fungi, 258 viruses, and 183 parasites, and increases total genomic records past 2.3 million. By incorporating 12 597 transcriptomes across 148 species, gcPathogen 2.0 bridges the gap between gene carriage and functional expression for risk assessment. Furthermore, the platform integrates 285 925 pathogen metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) spanning human, animal, and environmental niches. Mapped across 68 Environment Ontology (ENVO) habitat categories, these MAGs enable comprehensive tracking of cross-habitat distribution of pathogens, antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), virulence factors (VFs), and mobile genetic elements (MGEs). Leveraging a nonredundant reference set curated from seven public databases, we identified over 77 million AMPs belonging to >55 000 families across 438 bacterial pathogens. Finally, pan-genome analyses of 440 bacterial species map intraspecies functional distributions across core, accessory, and unique gene repertoires. gcPathogen 2.0 is publicly accessible at https://nmdc.cn/gcpathogen/.
records.authors: Chen Q, Guo C, Wang L, Fan G, Qu X, Li S, Feng M, Ma J, Tong Z, Song H, Wu L.

records.title: Genomes2Genes: A Progressive Cactus Gene Analysis Pipeline
records.abstract: Whole-genome alignments are fundamental resources in comparative genomics, because they place genes and their surrounding sequences in a shared evolutionary context. Progressive Cactus aligns large numbers of genomes without a reference genome and reconstructs ancestral sequences along the input phylogeny. However, its Hierarchical Alignment Format output has mainly been used for visualization, phylogenomics, and pangenome studies, and gene-level analyses of these alignments remain difficult. Here, we present Genomes2Genes, a pipeline that converts Progressive Cactus graph-based alignments into validated coding sequence alignments of extant species and their reconstructed ancestors. The pipeline extracts exon alignment blocks, handles atypical genomic jumps, stitches exons into transcripts, and reports start codons, stop codons, and frameshifting indels across species, with validation steps throughout and a base-by-base audit of the final alignments. It catches both biological and technical artifacts and can be run on any part of the genome. We anticipate that this pipeline will be useful in identifying and removing problematic regions used in the potential reconstruction of species or gene phylogenies. We developed and tested the pipeline on a whole-genome alignment of 21 Brassicaceae species and 2 outgroups and found that, among 45,491 lineage-specific genes, the pipeline supported 22,376 candidate de novo genes, of which 1,811 had complete evidence of enabler mutations. Genomes2Genes is publicly available and extends whole-genome alignments to gene-level questions in comparative genomics and evolutionary biology.

records.title: Contig-Resolved Genetic Context of Antimicrobial Resistome in Sediments of Two Contrasting Wastewater-Impacted Rivers
records.abstract: River sediments harbor diverse antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants; however, gene abundance alone provides limited insight into their genomic context, mobility potential, and associated bacterial hosts. This study employed an assembly- and read-mapping metagenomic framework to surface-sediment metagenomes (40.78 Gb clean data) from two contrasting wastewater-impacted Indian rivers, Adyar (Chennai) and Musi (Hyderabad), retaining sample-, contig- and open reading frame level provenance. ARG-carrying contigs (ACCs; n = 2,402) were annotated for mobile genetic elements (MGEs), biocide/metal resistance genes (BMRGs), virulence factor genes (VFGs), nitrogen-cycling genes (NCycGs), and putative host taxonomy. The resistomes exhibited substantial diversity (264 ARG subtypes) and spatial heterogeneity, with subtype richness in the Adyar (up to 171 subtypes) than in the Musi, where richness progressively declined downstream. Rank IV determinants dominated ARG abundance (77.82%), whereas Rank I determinants accounted for only 9.89%. MGEs were detected on just 3.12% (75/2,402) of ACCs, predominantly comprising plasmid-like contigs and proximal ARG-MGE associations. Co-occurrence with BMRGs was observed on 386 ACCs, whereas VFGs were uncommon (26 ACCs) and primarily represented dual-annotated efflux and envelope-integrity determinants rather than independent virulence loci. NCyc annotations were sparse (12 ACCs), with no evidence of complete nitrification or denitrification pathways. Taxonomic classification resolved 217 ACCs to the species level, with no matches to curated human pathogenic bacteria. Only two Acinetobacter-assigned ACCs exhibited both genus-level pathogenicity and mobility evidence. These findings highlight the importance of integrating mobility and host-taxonomic information to distinguish baseline environmental resistance from potential priorities for AMR surveillance.

records.title: Antimicrobial Peptides in Marine Bivalve Mollusks: Family Diversity, Immune Expression, Mechanisms of Action, and Biotechnological Translation.
records.abstract: Marine bivalves encounter high microbial loads in seawater and depend on humoral innate defenses, including antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). This review brings together evidence on bivalve AMP families, evolutionary diversity, expression responses, and mechanisms of action. The synthesis connects these biological findings with peptide preparation, production research, and biotechnological development. Genomic studies associate family diversity, including defensins, mytilins, and myticins, with duplication, recombination, and selection. The functional consequences still require peptide-specific validation. AMP transcripts in immune and barrier tissues vary with development, pathogen exposure, and environmental conditions, while mature-peptide abundance and activity have been studied less extensively. Studies of characterized bivalve AMPs identify mechanisms beyond membrane permeabilization. These include inhibition of lipid II-dependent cell-wall synthesis, teichoic acid-associated nanonet formation, bacterial DNA interactions, and changes in reactive oxygen species homeostasis. Some members also inhibit biofilms or regulate host immunity through chemotaxis and phagocytosis. The evidence supports several antimicrobial and immune-regulatory roles for bivalve AMPs, but endogenous defense, exogenous efficacy, and production feasibility have been validated to different extents. A major gap remains between candidate sequences, verified mature-peptide functions, and reproducible production under use-relevant conditions. Research should therefore connect functional validation with folding, stability, scalable preparation, safety, and application-specific testing.
records.authors: Shen C, Wang Y, Huang Q, Cai X, Guo Y, Zuo Q, Lin X.

records.title: Identification of ebastine and ceritinib as effective inhibitors of Fusobacterium nucleatum FtsZ.
records.abstract: The role of microorganisms in cancer is not a new concept-bacteria, parasites, and viruses have all been implicated in cancer development. Fusobacterium nucleatum, a member of the oral microbiota, has emerged as an important cancer-associated bacterium. Unbiased global genomic analyses have demonstrated that F. nucleatum is enriched in human colorectal cancer (CRC) tissues compared with noncancerous colorectal tissues, underscoring the urgent need for specific antimicrobial agents targeting F. nucleatum for CRC prevention and treatment. In this study, structure-based virtual screening successfully identified ebastine and ceritinib as antimicrobial agents targeting Fusobacterium nucleatum FtsZ (FnFtsZ). Their potent anti-F. nucleatum activity was confirmed through in vitro assays, including minimum inhibitory concentration determination and microscopic observation of filamentous morphology. Both ebastine and ceritinib exhibited significant antibacterial effects. Enzyme activity and polymerization assays demonstrated that their mechanism of action involves inhibition of FnFtsZ GTPase activity and disruption of FnFtsZ polymerization. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and light microscopy further confirmed that these compounds effectively disrupt cell division, leading to abnormal or halted division and inhibiting F. nucleatum proliferation. Overall, our findings identified ebastine and ceritinib as potential drugs against F. nucleatum proliferation, although further structural optimization is required. Additionally, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of an integrated computational-experimental approach targeting bacterial cell division in microbiome-associated pathologies.ImportanceColorectal cancer (CRC) is strongly driven by the enrichment of the oncogenic bacterium Fusobacterium nucleatum in gut lesions. However, the lack of targeted anti-F. nucleatum drugs significantly limits microbe-related interventions for CRC. In this study, we repurposed two clinically approved drugs, ebastine and ceritinib, as highly effective inhibitors of FnFtsZ, the key protein responsible for bacterial cell division. We demonstrated that both drugs inhibit bacterial proliferation by suppressing FnFtsZ function and disrupting the cell division process. Our work offers safe, readily available candidate agents for controlling CRC-associated pathogenic bacteria and establishes a reliable computational-experimental workflow to screen division-targeted antimicrobials for microbiome-related cancers.
records.authors: Fang H, Shu Y, Zhou Z, Li Y, Gong T, Yang M, Zhang B, Jin Y, Liu Y, Wang C, Zhao L, Liu Y, Chen P.

records.title: Assembly of host-specific bacterial and fungal communities from soil by diverse subaerial green algae
records.abstract: Green algae recruit microbes from their environment to the phycosphere, a region closely surrounding algal cells which is analogous to the rhizosphere of land plants. Recent work showed that subaerial green algae can recruit and assemble their phycosphere microbiota from soil-derived bacteria. However, how widespread this ability is among diverse green algae, whether host identity shapes community composition, and whether soil-borne fungi can be recruited to the phycosphere remained unclear. Here, we show that subaerial green algae spanning Chlorophyta and Streptophyta assemble distinct phycosphere communities from soil-derived bacteria and fungi, with host identity as the primary driver of phycosphere composition, both in natural soil and in a liquid mesocosm. In soil, bacterial communities were strongly reshaped by algal hosts, whereas the fungal communities responded more weakly and less consistently. In liquid system, bacterial community composition was correlated with host phylogeny. Phycosphere communities included taxa known to associate with land plants in the rhizosphere, supporting the finding that some microbial taxa associate with a wide range of photosynthetic hosts. Our findings demonstrate that the green algae capacity to assemble distinct phycosphere communities possibly predates the divergence of Chlorophyta and Streptophyta. The stronger effect of host identity on bacterial than fungal community mirrors patterns observed in land plant microbiota, suggesting that principles of host-microbe interactions are conserved across evolutionarily distant photosynthetic hosts.
records.authors: Slawinska MW, Melkonian B, Melkonian M, Flores-Uribe J, Durán P, Garrido-Oter R.

records.title: Microbial lineages and metabolic capacities associated with mercury methylation in supraglacial cryoconite.
records.abstract: Supraglacial cryoconite concentrates mercury (Hg), but the transcriptionally active putative Hg-methylating lineages and their metabolic organization remain poorly resolved. We combined an 8 h in situ HgCl2 perturbation with metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, expression-based functional prioritization, and genome-resolved analyses. Initial post-dose total Hg (THg) was positively associated with endpoint methylmercury (MeHg) after controlling for sampling site (within-site ρ = 0.749, permutation P = 0.0002). hgcA transcripts were detected in 29 of 30 treatment units across all six treatment levels, with prominent contributions from Bacteroidota and Desulfobacterota. We recovered 512 HgcA-like sequences, including 258 with conserved cap-helix motifs. Among 34 candidate metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), 26 had same-contig HgcAB support and 32 reached ≥ 90% genome breadth in at least one 2023 DNA sample. Functional prioritization highlighted corrinoid, heme/siroheme, and amino-acid/C1 metabolism. Their recurrence in candidate MAGs, together with model-predicted cobalt, iron, and amino-acid uptake, defines cofactor, methyl-donor, and cellular redox capacities relevant to established HgcAB biochemistry. These findings resolve transcriptionally active putative Hg-methylating lineages and their metabolic organization in glacier-surface ecosystems.
records.authors: Xu Y, Chen Z, Capo E, Kang S, Guo J, Wang S, Zhang W, Liu G, Chen T, Zhang B.

records.title: Transmission risk and mechanism of antibiotic resistance genes driven by glacier melt: Insight from Asian water tower to global significance.
records.abstract: Accelerated glacier melt due to climate change is increasingly releasing sequestered antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). However, ARG transmission risk and driven mechanisms that are associated with glacier retreat remain poorly understood. We employed genome-resolved metagenomics along a 246.5 km sampling transect spanning two distinct hydrological seasons and multiple habitats to track the dissemination of ARGs along the hydrological continuum of the Kuoqionggangri Glacier on Tibetan Plateau. Our results demonstrate that hydrological connectivity facilitates the physical transport of antibiotic resistant bacteria. Specific microbial lineages, particularly pathogenic Ralstonia pickettii were traced continuously from glacial sources to downstream rivers, disseminating both ARGs and virulence factors. Beyond host-mediated transport, glacier-derived ARGs can spread into downstream indigenous microbial communities via horizontal gene transfer. Genomic evidence confirmed that sulfonamide and β-lactam determinants transfer across taxonomic boundaries, disseminating from upstream environmental taxa (e.g., Novosphingobium) into downstream opportunistic pathogens. Finally, integrating 156 global glacier metagenomes revealed that the Tibetan Plateau yields an exceptionally high absolute ARG concentration (8.85 ± 0.07 log10 copies/L). Surpassing > 99% of the surveyed regions globally, the sheer magnitude of this genetic discharge identifies glacial melt as a critical emission hotspot, overwhelming downstream aquatic systems with severe ecological resistance risks.
records.authors: Zhang H, Zhang S, Zhuang W, Huang M, Mao D, Tong Y, Wang X, Luo Y.

records.title: Microbiome-derived proline dipeptides underpin improved nitrogen utilization efficiency in dairy cattle.
records.abstract: Dairy production is constrained by low nitrogen utilization efficiency (NUE; milk N/intake N), leading to nitrogen losses and environmental pollution. Although the rumen microbiome is central to nitrogen turnover, the role of small peptides, a critical nitrogen pool, remains poorly understood. Here, we constructed a genome-resolved atlas of predicted small-peptide metabolism and integrated high-performance chemical isotope-labeling metabolomics with metagenomics in 30 dairy cows. Among 349 detected small peptides, proline-containing dipeptides were associated with higher NUE, together with an S15 peptidyl-peptidase with Xaa-Pro dipeptide-generating activity. In vitro rumen fermentation, metatranscriptomics and targeted quantification showed that proline-dipeptide accumulation coincided with transcriptional patterns consistent with nitrogen assimilation and amino acid biosynthesis. Bacterial incubation and heterologous expression confirmed that S15.001 hydrolyzed Xaa-Pro substrates. These findings identify a microbial proline-dipeptide axis associated with NUE and provide a basis for precision nutrition strategies targeting ruminal peptide metabolism.
records.authors: Qi W, Chen X, Guo H, Zhu S, Zhou Z, Xu L, Yan Q, Gu FF, Liu JX, Sun HZ.

records.title: DoriC 14.0: an updated database of prokaryotic replication origins with significantly expanded plasmid oriV annotations.
records.abstract: Replication origins are essential for both chromosome duplication and plasmid maintenance; however, their annotation remains challenging across different replicon types and across diverse phylogenetic lineages. DoriC 14.0, the latest update of the database of replication origins in prokaryotic genomes, restructures and greatly expands this resource, with particular emphasis on plasmid replication. The latest release contains 530 178 computationally derived origin records, associated with 432 232 distinct sequence accessions, including 434 060 chromosomal and 96 118 plasmid records from bacteria and archaea. For bacterial plasmids, OriV-Finder was applied with RNA II-based refinement, whereas a customized OriV-Finder pipeline was employed for archaeal plasmids, which relies on archaeal replication-associated proteins and origin recognition box motifs. DoriC 14.0 combines literature evidence with computational predictions, maintains traceable record identifiers, and offers versioned data with release history. New features include comparative sequence support, related-origin links, interactive candidate replication initiation protein (RIP) sequence-similarity networks, plasmid-level analyses of origin recurrence, RIP profiles, and RNA II variation. The updated website provides filter-based browsing, record-level views, BLAST searches, and standardized downloads, and is freely accessible at https://tubic.org/doric/ and https://tubic.tju.edu.cn/doric/ without registration.
records.authors: Li Y, Dong M, Geng Y, Luo H, Gao F.

records.title: Prokaryotic homologs of the major vault protein form engineerable vault nanocapsules
records.abstract: Vaults are the largest ribonucleoprotein particles in eukaryotic cells, built from 78 copies of the major vault protein (MVP), yet their function remains unknown four decades after their discovery. MVP homologs occur in prokaryotes and bacteriophages, but whether they form vaults is unknown. Here, we show that prokaryotic and bacteriophage MVP homologs assemble into vault particles. We surveyed approximately 15 billion proteins, found MVP homologs in 29 bacterial and 4 archaeal phyla, and used size-exclusion chromatography to rapidly screen and isolate vault particles of eight homologs expressed in  Escherichia coli . Cryo-electron microscopy structures of the phage homolog L05 at high resolution reveal a shell of 96 MVP chains enclosing a volume ∼25% larger than human vaults, among the largest protein shells of defined size outside virus capsids. Prokaryotic MVPs typically carry seven wall repeats and eukaryotic MVPs nine, and adding wall repeats to L05 yields larger vaults. Prokaryotic vaults expand the known diversity of vault architecture and offer a tractable system for studying vault assembly and a size-tunable scaffold for cargo encapsulation.
records.authors: Athukoralage JS, Yoon PH, Shanehsazzadeh A, Kauderer-Abrams E, Perry NT, Durrant MG.

records.title: A large, distinct family of RNase H fold nucleases associated with numerous defense systems in prokaryotes
records.abstract: During the last decade, systematic efforts aimed at the characterization of prokaryotic immunity resulted in the discovery of several hundred distinct defense systems in bacteria and archaea. This suggests that the common defense systems were already known and only rare ones remained to be identified. Here we present a genomic census and analysis of a vast family of bacterial and archaeal proteins (known as Domain of Unknown Function, DUF3800) that contain a distinct variant of the RNase H fold and are encoded in a striking 15% of the available complete prokaryotic genomes. Most of these proteins are encoded in defense islands, often in a close association with known defense systems, hence the designation WARD (  W eaponized  A ntiphage  R Nase-dependent  D efense). The WARDs display a broad variety of protein domain architectures and genomic contexts, including a strong link to restriction-modification, CRISPR-Cas, retrons, and non-coding RNAs, suggestive of a substantial diversity in defense mechanisms. We experimentally tested 10 WARDs, mostly, encoded by standalone genes, and found that 9 of these conferred robust protection against diverse phages in  Escherichia coli . Therefore, WARDs appear to represent the third most abundant defense system type in prokaryotes.
records.authors: Wolf YI, Arshad K, Kannatey-Asibu K, Theisen RQ, Kitzinger KA, Jain PV, Koonin EV, Makarova KS, Ledvina HE.

records.title: MicrobeRT: A Framework and Suite of Fine-tuned Language Models for Genomic Sequences
records.abstract: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on mutable reference databases, and high computational cost.  To combat these challenges, we introduce MicrobeRT, an integrated suite of genomic language models fine-tuned to classify metagenomic sequencing reads across three tasks: (i) species level taxonomic identification, (ii) antibiotic resistance gene detection, and (iii) pathogenicity assessment. The framework builds on three pre-trained genomic language models - Nucleotide Transformer (Dalla-Torre et al 2025), DNABERT (Ji et al 2021, Zhou et al 2024), and HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al 2024) - leveraging their large-scale genomic pre-training, adaptability to downstream tasks, and, in the case of HyenaDNA, ability to capture long-range sequence dependencies. The models are fine-tuned on large, curated datasets spanning microbial, viral, fungal, and human genomes, including more than 500,000 genomes and 250,000 antibiotic resistance gene sequences.  To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned genomic language models across classification tasks, we developed a benchmarking framework that compares MicrobeRT against state-of-the-art (SOTA) bioinformatics tools. Across both simulated and empirical datasets, the models achieve strong performance while reducing computational overhead. MicrobeRT is released as open-source software, enabling further fine-tuning and reproducible integration of alternative models and classifiers. We also demonstrate seamless, drop-in integration by incorporating our fine-tuned taxonomic classification models as an optional add-on within the open-source TaxTriage pipeline (Merritt et al 2026). MicrobeRT demonstrates the feasibility of three clinically relevant multi-label analyses, offering a practical path to scalable, reproducible metagenomic diagnostics and enabling broader deployment of AI/ML-enhanced infectious disease testing.
records.authors: Narayan V, Merritt B, Choudhery S, Jimenez D, Ta S, Berman DS, Ratcliff J, Gallagher ME.
