records.title: Complete genome sequence of Pseudomonas sp. gA1, a metabolically specialized deep-sea bacterium from abyssal sediment of the Western Pacific Ocean.
records.abstract: The abyssal seafloor, exposed to extreme pressure, near-freezing temperatures, and severe carbon limitation, remains one of the least understood microbial habitats on Earth. Branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) are an abundant but underexplored carbon source in abyssal sediments, yet the genomic basis for their use by deep-sea heterotrophs remains uncharacterized. Here, we report the complete genome of Pseudomonas sp. gA1, isolated from 6,000 m sediment in the Western Pacific Ocean by anaerobic enrichment with amino acids under 40 MPa. The 7.27 Mb circular chromosome encodes 6,827 protein-coding genes. Polyphasic taxonomy-including average nucleotide identity of 94.15% to P. yamanorum and digital DNA-DNA hybridization of 55.5%-confirmed strain gA1 as a novel species within the P. fluorescens group. We compared gA1 against 16 reference genomes from the P. fluorescens group and the marine Halopseudomonas and Stutzerimonas lineages. Under elevated hydrostatic pressure at 10 °C, which approximates selected aspects of the abyssal environment rather than the in situ pressure and temperature of the 6,000-m collection site, BCAAs accounted for 49% of total amino acid consumed, and growth increased by 50% at 40 MPa. Genome analysis revealed a largely represented BCAA degradation pathway (11 of 14 KEGG Orthology identifiers) conserved across the P. fluorescens group and a complete arginine deiminase (arcABC) pathway supporting anaerobic ATP generation by substrate-level phosphorylation. Denitrification and anaerobic respiratory genes were not detected, a trait shared with the marine Halopseudomonas lineage. Its most distinctive feature is expanded amino acid and peptide acquisition: 44 expanded orthogroups, including families involved in dipeptide, oligopeptide and amino acid acquisition, alongside a chaperone network and 17 biosynthetic gene clusters, including one similar to those associated with viscosinamide A/pseudodesmin A biosynthesis. These findings establish gA1 as a metabolically specialized deep-sea bacterium whose genomic architecture couples amino acid acquisition to piezotolerance.IMPORTANCEThe abyssal seafloor is the largest and most energy-limited habitat on Earth, yet how its resident bacteria sustain growth where several canonical respiratory chains are not detected remains poorly understood. This study shows that a cultured abyssal isolate grows under elevated hydrostatic pressure on amino acids, and that its genome encodes a complete arginine deiminase pathway as a potential route to substrate-level phosphorylation, the contribution of which to energy metabolism remains to be measured. Through direct comparison with 16 related genomes, the same genomic configuration is shared across the sampled Halopseudomonas genomes rather than being confined to this isolate. The work carries a broader methodological message for deep-sea genomics: pathway-completeness scores and the presence or absence of individual genes are weak proxies for physiological capacity, and adaptation in these organisms appears to proceed through expansion of existing uptake systems rather than acquisition of novel functions. Because strain gA1 is both cultured and experimentally tractable under high pressure, it offers a testable model for linking genome content to function in the deep biosphere, and it identifies amino acid and peptide acquisition, rather than catabolism, as a point at which lineages adapted to cold, organic-poor sediments diverge.
records.authors: Zain Ul Arifeen M, Zhou X, Hussain S, Mahtab N, Jiang H, Hou S.

records.title: Temperature effects on life history strategies for rapid growth potential of leaf epiphytic bacteria.
records.abstract: Phyllosphere bacteria, occupying both epiphytic and endophytic habitats, constitute a critical plant-atmosphere interface. However, their community assembly and life-history strategies (LHSs) in response to temperature increase remain poorly understood. Here, we compared leaf phyllosphere bacterial communities with those in other plant compartments across four representative plant species from an alpine meadow on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. By combining observations along an elevational gradient with a controlled warming experiment, we found that temperature was closely associated with the deterministic assembly of leaf phyllosphere bacterial communities. Elevated temperature corresponded to shifts in taxonomic composition, diversity, assembly process, cross-compartment bacterial source, and co-occurrence network. Furthermore, elevated temperature was associated with a shift toward r-strategists in leaf phyllosphere bacterial LHSs, evidenced by higher ribosomal RNA operon (rrn) copy numbers for rapid growth potential and corroborated by genome assemblies of four warming-responsive epiphytic isolates and metagenomic sequencing. Based on 880 public 16S rRNA gene datasets from 45 locations on six continents, we identified a global increase in the rrn copy number in leaf epiphytic bacterial communities across diverse plant species, which was associated with elevated temperatures and enhanced diurnal fluctuation. Finally, we proposed a concept of four LHSs (growth, stress tolerance, competition, and resource acquisition) based on functional inference from 16S rRNA data, supported by the assembled epiphytic bacterial genomes and metagenomes. Collectively, our findings established a trait-based framework for understanding responses of leaf phyllosphere bacteria to future warming.
records.authors: Wang Q, He X, Han B, Shi L, Hu H, Liu F, Nie J, Chen Y, Zhou J, Li Y, Zhao K, Ni K, Zhang L, Jia S, Shao X.

records.title: Polyphyletic origins and lineage-specific expansion of chemosensory systems in phylum Actinomycetota
records.abstract: Phylum Actinomycetota (syn. Actinobacteriota or Actinobacteria), one of the largest well-studied bacterial phyla, is renowned for complex morphology, non-motility, ecological versatility, and secondary metabolite production. Chemosensory systems (CSS) are among the most sophisticated prokaryotic signal transduction architectures, yet their evolutionary distribution in this phylum remains poorly understood. Here, a comparative genomic analysis of 693 high-quality genomes spanning the phylum resolves the diversity, distribution, and evolutionary trajectories of CSS. Despite extensive genomic complexity and ecological versatility, only 6.9% of genomes encode complete CSS clusters, confined to a subset of lineages within a few classes, indicating lineage-specific retention or loss. In contrast, two-component systems (TCS) are ubiquitously abundant, with hybrid kinases enriched in CSS-deficient classes, suggesting functional compensation for the absence of dedicated chemosensory pathways. Basal lineages retain simplified CSS (F1 or F5), whereas Actinomycetes show lineage-specific expansion into multiple classes (F5, F8, F9, and ACF), often co-occurring, indicative of enhanced sensory complexity. The phylogeny of CheA homologs shows a polyphyletic distribution, supporting a mosaic evolutionary history shaped by multiple independent acquisitions, diversification, and gene loss. Collectively, our findings show that, unlike motile bacteria, Actinomycetota members rely predominantly on TCS-driven regulatory networks, with CSS retained only in select lineages where ecological demands require enhanced environmental sensing. This work provides a phylum-wide evolutionary framework for the emergence, diversification, and functional specialization of CSS in non-motile bacteria. Importance  Bacteria rely on sensory signal transduction systems to detect and respond to environmental changes. Chemosensory systems typically control movement along with alternate cellular functions, but their role in non-motile phylum Actinomycetota has remained unclear. By analyzing approximately seven hundred Actinobacterial genomes, we report that these systems are rare and restricted to specific lineages, suggesting they are retained only where they confer ecological advantages. In contrast, most Actinomycetota depend on alternative signaling pathways, particularly two-component systems, for environmental adaptation. These findings highlight how different bacterial groups evolve distinct strategies for sensing and responding to their surroundings, providing new insights into microbial evolution, ecological specialization, and the emergence of complex adaptive traits.
records.authors: S SN, Brighty S, Sharma G.

records.title: Decoding horizontal transposon transfer across plants through a comprehensive HTT atlas.
records.abstract: IntroductionHorizontal transposon transfer (HTT) plays an important role in genome evolution; however, its prevalence, evolutionary patterns, and potential mechanisms in plants remain poorly understood due to limited taxonomic sampling and challenges in distinguishing HTT from vertical inheritance.ObjectivesThis study aimed to systematically identify HTT events across major plant lineages, investigate factors potentially associated with HTT, and assess the possible evolutionary significance of HTT in plant genomes.MethodsA total of 558 high-quality plant genomes representing 352 species spanning algae to angiosperms were analyzed. A conservative phylogeny-informed framework integrating transposable element (TE) annotation, orthology inference, sequence similarity analysis, and lineage distribution filtering was developed to identify putative HTT events. Co-transfer relationships, host gene enrichment, transport-related pathways, and exosome-associated sequences were further analyzed to investigate candidate factors associated with HTT.ResultsIn total, 1,548 putative HTT events involving 684 TE families were identified across diverse plant lineages, indicating that both RNA- and DNA-mediated transposons contribute extensively to HTT in plants. Co-transfer analyses revealed widespread associations among TE superfamilies, whereas functional enrichment analyses highlighted chromatin-related and transport-related host genes frequently associated with HTT regions. HTT-related TE sequences were also detected in publicly available plant exosomal sequencing datasets, and several hotspot TE families showed homology to viral-associated sequences, suggesting potential involvement of vesicle-mediated transport and viral interactions in HTT processes. In addition, genes associated with cold acclimation and stress responses were enriched near several HTT regions, suggesting that HTT may contribute to environmental adaptation in some plant lineages.ConclusionThis study provides a comprehensive atlas of HTT across plants and establishes a scalable framework for HTT detection in large-scale comparative genomics analyses. These findings generate candidate hypotheses regarding the mechanisms and evolutionary significance of HTT and provide a resource for future functional and experimental investigations.
records.authors: Huang Y, Sahu SK, Wang H, Lin Z, Hu J, Zhao Y, Varshney RK, Liu X.

records.title: Horizontal Gene Transfer from Fungi to Myxozoa: Genomic Evidence and Evolutionary Implications.
records.abstract: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is increasingly recognized as an important mechanism driving evolutionary innovation in eukaryotes, yet its functional significance in parasitic lineages remains poorly understood. Myxozoans are obligate cnidarian parasites characterized by extreme genome reduction and complex two-host life cycles, making them an intriguing system for investigating the evolutionary role of HGT. We conducted a comparative genomic and transcriptomic analysis to identify and characterize candidate genes putatively transferred from fungi to myxozoans. Phylogenetic reconstruction, sequence composition analyses, and functional annotation provided multiple lines of evidence supporting ancient HGT events retained across diverse myxozoan species. Candidate transferred genes encode proteins putatively involved in carbohydrate metabolism, defense, and regulatory processes. Exploratory codon-usage analysis revealed compositional differences between candidate genes and the sampled reference sets, a pattern that may be consistent with partial amelioration following ancient transfer, although broader quantitative comparisons will be required to evaluate codon adaptation more rigorously. Molecular clock analyses place the inferred fungi-to-myxozoan HGT events within a time interval that overlaps with the major diversification of myxozoans, around 300 Ma. Collectively, these findings suggest that candidate horizontally acquired genes may have contributed to functional innovation during myxozoan evolution, expanding our understanding of the evolutionary impact of HGT in these highly reduced parasites.
records.authors: Ibrahim AGA, Adriano EA.

records.title: Linking geography, isolation source, and genomic diversity in a global Candida albicans phylogeny.
records.abstract: Candida albicans is a common commensal species in the human microbiome at multiple sites and an opportunistic pathogen. Previous phylogenomic analyses identified major clades but often relied on imprecise genomic methods, limited geographic and ecological sampling, and non-standardized strategies for phylogenetic resolution. Here, we address these gaps by reconstructing a whole-genome phylogeny to examine how geography and site of isolation contribute to phylogenetic structure in C. albicans. We analyzed phased genomes from 945 global isolates obtained across diverse clinical and ecological contexts and applied an agnostic, threshold-based clustering approach to systematically define cluster boundaries and quantify intraspecific genomic features. Our analyses preserved previously defined major clusters while identifying six novel clusters, predominantly composed of highly admixed Asian isolates. Although geographic origin and isolation source were each significantly associated with cluster membership, these associations were confounded because isolates from specific regions were disproportionately derived from particular sources. However, an analysis of environmental isolates alongside a diverse strain collection from Winnipeg, Canada, highlights the potential for frequent local transmission. More than 95% of isolates were heterozygous at the mating-type locus, while aneuploidy was present in 8% of isolates distributed across the phylogeny. Analysis of the AGO1 PAZ domain involved in RNAi interference identified both known and novel RNAi variants, predominantly in a heterozygous state. Intra-host analysis of isolates from 95 individuals revealed predominantly clonal colonization, though fourteen individuals harbored isolates from different clusters. Together, these findings refine the phylogenetic structure of C. albicans and provide insights into genomic plasticity and strain transmission in this common fungal species.
records.authors: Adamu Bukari AR, Opulente DA, Hittinger CT, d'Enfert C, Cuomo CA, Gerstein AC.

records.title: Novel Biomarkers for Bacterial Meningitis and Other Central Nervous System Infections.
records.abstract: Purpose of reviewTimely and accurate diagnosis of central nervous system (CNS) infections remains challenging because of nonspecific clinical characteristics and limited diagnostic accuracy of conventional tests. Novel cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers may improve early diagnosis and facilitate differentiation between infectious aetiologies. This review summarizes established and emerging CSF biomarkers for the diagnosis of CNS infections, with a focus on bacterial meningitis, and discusses their potential clinical application.Recent findingsSeveral novel CSF biomarkers have demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance for bacterial meningitis. Among these, CSF C-reactive protein (CRP) has recently been implemented in clinical practice, while heparin-binding protein and combinations of CSF CRP with inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-1β show similarly high diagnostic accuracy. Pathogen-specific biomarkers, including CXCL13 for neuroborreliosis and β-D-glucan and galactomannan for fungal CNS infections, further expand the diagnostic repertoire. In addition, multi-omics approaches, including metabolomics, lipidomics, and proteomics, have identified promising candidates such as pyruvate and phosphatidylcholines, although these require further validation. Untargeted techniques, including metagenomic next-generation sequencing and phage immunoprecipitation sequencing, further enhance pathogen detection and may complement microbiological testing. Novel biomarkers have the potential to substantially improve the diagnosis of CNS infections. Several biomarkers for bacterial meningitis are already available for clinical implementation, particularly in patients with intermediate CSF leukocyte counts, where diagnostic uncertainty is greatest. For viral and other CNS infections biomarkers remain scarce. Future studies should focus on validation of emerging biomarkers and on integrating biomarker panels with advanced molecular diagnostic techniques to enable rapid, accurate and clinically applicable diagnostic strategies.
records.authors: Nieuwenhuijsen BL, Olie SE, van de Beek D, Brouwer MC.

records.title: Characterization and Functional Analysis of the Oropharyngeal Microbiome in ICU staff via Metagenomic Sequencing
records.abstract: Abstract  Background  ICU staff face an elevated risk of colonization by drug-resistant bacteria, potentially associated with persistent occupational exposure to hospital environments. The oropharynx, as a key ecological niche at the interface of the respiratory and digestive tracts, serves as an important reservoir for opportunistic pathogens. This study employed shotgun metagenomic sequencing to systematically characterize the composition and functional profiles of the oropharyngeal microbiota in ICU staff. Methods  A cross-sectional study was conducted, enrolling 10 full-time ICU staff (with ≥ 5 years of clinical experience) and 10 healthy non-medical controls with no history of medical-related employment. Oropharyngeal swabs were collected for metagenomic sequencing. Multi-dimensional comparative analyses were conducted between the two groups, covering community structure, taxonomic composition, KEGG metabolic pathways, virulence factor profiles, and antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) profiles. Results  Compared with the control group, ICU staff exhibited significantly reduced genus-level richness (Chao1 index) but elevated community evenness, resulting in higher Shannon and Simpson indices, with a clearly distinct overall microbial community structure. The abundances of potential pathogenic genera including Pseudomonas, Streptococcus, Escherichia, Mycobacteroides, and Helicobacter were significantly enriched, whereas core oral commensal genera such as Prevotella were depleted. Functionally, ICU staff exhibited significant enrichment in bacterial biofilm formation, drug metabolism–cytochrome P450, and ABC transporter pathways; marked upregulation of virulence factors associated with adhesion, immune evasion, and endotoxin biosynthesis; and elevated abundances of five resistance genes primarily derived from Streptococcus and Haemophilus species (mel, patB, mdtG, hmrM, and rlmA(II)). Conclusion  ICU occupational exposure is associated with systematic remodeling of the oropharyngeal microbiota, characterized by depletion of core oral commensals and enrichment of opportunistic pathogens. Functionally, this remodeling supports the formation of a potential synergistic resistance system of "biofilm barrier–P450 metabolic inactivation–ABC active efflux," providing novel metagenomic evidence for microbiome-based surveillance and occupational health protection of healthcare workers.
records.authors: Zhou k, Li j, Ling B, Fan z, Xiu g.

records.title: Context-dependent and shared responses of the zebrafish gut microbiome to KH<sub>2</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> enrichment.
records.abstract: Anthropogenic phosphorus (P) enrichment is widespread in aquatic ecosystems, yet its effects on the functional potential of fish gut microbiomes remain poorly understood. We conducted a replicated 42-day experiment with zebrafish (Danio rerio), combining shotgun metagenomics with genome-resolved analyses to examine how sustained KH2PO4 exposure reshapes the gut microbiome in water-only and sediment-associated systems. Evidence for sediment-dependent modulation of microbial diversity and community composition was primarily observed during early exposure, indicating that these effects varied over time. Despite context-specific differences in functional profiles, both environmental backgrounds showed enrichment of genes or modules associated with P acquisition and turnover, selected carbon utilization pathways, energy transduction, and biosynthesis, accompanied by reduced potential for certain aromatic compound degradation and nitrate assimilation processes. Genome-resolved analyses further identified a Mycobacterium population that exhibited positive abundance responses to KH2PO4 addition in both environmental backgrounds. Its genomic traits related to P homeostasis, substrate utilization, and cellular biosynthesis provide candidate mechanistic explanations for this shared response. These findings reveal sediment-dependent responses of the zebrafish gut microbiome to extreme KH2PO4 input and identify microbial functional shifts that warrant further investigation as potential indicators of P-associated environmental disturbance.
records.authors: Zhu W, Yu X, Niu S, Ge K, Liu H, Zhang S, Li M, Ming Y, Li T, Zhao Z, An X, Niu M, Wu K, Xie W, He Z, Yan Q.

records.title: Sourmash accurately profiles strains from long-read metagenomes preserving gene content
records.abstract: Background  Metagenomic strain-level profiling remains challenging because closely related bacterial strains often share more than 99% average nucleotide identity (ANI). However, they can differ substantially in gene content and functional potential. Sourmash uses k-mer sketches with FracMinHash to compare sequencing reads against reference databases, which makes it an interesting approach for strain-level profiling. Because it compares sketches rather than full alignments, it enables fast searches against large reference databases. However, its ability to recover biologically relevant strains and preserve community gene content has not been specifically assessed. Here, we evaluated the performance of sourmash for strain-level identification abundance, functional gene content recovery, and abundance estimations using five mock communities of increasing complexity with known composition. Results  We first assessed whether nucleotide similarity reflects functional similarity between strains. Gene content similarity was generally consistent with ANI but revealed important divergences between closely related strains. For example,  Escherichia coli strains sharing more than 98% ANI showed gene content similarities ranging from 20% to 57%, highlighting that nucleotide similarity alone is insufficient to assess functional proximity and consequently the accuracy of strain identification. Above sufficient genome coverage, sourmash identified strains either exactly or with closely related strains sharing highly conserved gene content. These closely related strains provided a biologically relevant representation of the expected functional potential of the mock communities. Gene content recovery was highly accurate, with F1 scores ranging from 0.942 to 0.998 across the five mock communities. Genome abundances estimated against sourmash-identified genomes closely matched the expected community composition: Pearson correlation coefficients ranged from 0.823 to 1 at strain level and from 0.978 to 1 at species level.  Conclusions  Our results show that sourmash provides a biologically relevant approach for strain-level characterisation in microbial ecosystems. Even when the exact strain could not be identified, closely related strains retained most of the expected gene content and abundance estimations were accurate, supporting the use of sourmash for downstream functional profiling or metabolic network reconstruction.

records.title: A new  Serratia  taxon found in a trombidiform mite shows genomic evidence of host adaptation but is phylogenetically distinct from  Serratia symbiotica
records.abstract: The evolutionary transition from free-living bacteria to host-adapted symbionts is typically accompanied by substantial genomic changes. Within the genus  Serratia , this transition has so far been documented only in the aphid-associated species,  Serratia symbiotica , whereas all other  Serratia species are free-living. In this study, we identify a putatively new  Serratia taxon using metagenomic approaches in the trombidiform mite,  Halotydeus destructor . We provide genomic evidence for a possible transition to a host-adapted lifestyle in this new  Serratia sp., which sits phylogenetically within a clade of free-living  Serratia species. The genomic signatures of evolving toward a host-adapted lifestyle include a reduced genome size and coding capacity, an elevated transposase fraction, and detectable chromosomal rearrangements, relative to other free-living  Serratia species. However, the species does not show the same structure of genome reduction as  S. symbiotica . Functional gene content analyses including COG categories and virulence factor repertoires also showed that our new  Serratia sp. had a distinct gene profile from both free-living  Serratia and  S. symbiotica . Additional genomic screening suggests that infections of the new  Serratia sp. are common in wild populations of  H. destructor across its invasive Australian range, warranting future investigations on the possible role this symbiont plays in the evolutionary ecology of its mite host. Our work not only highlights a potential parallel transition to a host-adapted lifestyle in the  Serratia genus, but also represents the first characterisation of a possible host-adapted  Serratia taxon in a trombidiform mite.
records.authors: Chang J, Hoffmann AA, Young ND, Sumanam SB, Schmidt TL, Thia JA.

records.title: Metagenomic analysis of tomato rhizosphere microbiomes detects Ralstonia phage sequences in Kenyan agricultural soils.
records.abstract: Bacterial wilt caused by Ralstonia solanacearum species complex is a major constraint in tomato production in Kenya, resulting in yield losses of up to 100% in heavily infested fields. This study used high-throughput shotgun metagenomic sequencing approach to characterize the rhizosphere microbiomes of tomato plants in three of the major production areas in Kenya (Kirinyaga, Kiambu, and Laikipia counties) focusing on detecting Ralstonia phage sequences. Soil samples were collected from the rhizosphere of bacterial wilt-infected tomato plants, and microbial DNA was extracted using a modified phenol-chloroform protocol and sequenced using Illumina NovaSeq platform. Taxonomic profiling revealed diverse microbial communities dominated by Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria. Four Ralstonia species were confirmed (R. insidiosa, R. pickettii, R. mannitolilytica and R. wenshanensis). Sequences similar to the R. solanacearum species complex were also detected but were too short for species-level confirmation. Metagenomic analysis detected sequences matching four previously described Ralstonia phages (RSL1, RSIBR3, Anchaing, and Cimandef). Functional annotation demonstrated abundant metabolic pathways, energy production systems, and stress response mechanisms, indicating highly adaptive microbial communities in the tomato rhizosphere. This study provides baseline data on rhizosphere microbiome composition in Kenyan tomato production systems and identifies Ralstonia phage sequences that could guide future isolation and host-range studies. If future work shows that these phages are active against Ralstonia, they could contribute to locally adapted biocontrol approaches that reduce reliance on chemical pesticides.
records.authors: Mogire DB, Neondo J, Muhonja C, Awuor C, Mureithi D, Ogada S, Wekesa TB.

records.title: Extracellular polymeric substances drive Curvibacter host adaptation and cospeciation with Hydra.
records.abstract: The interactions between hosts and their microbial symbionts play a crucial role to host physiology. Bacteria can adapt to specific host environments over evolutionary timescales, leading to cospeciation and the formation of specialized host-microbe relationships. Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying these adaptations provides key insights into the evolution of symbiosis and the stability of microbial communities. This study investigates the cospeciation and molecular adaptations of Curvibacter to its host Hydra, a well-established model for the study of host-microbe interactions. We provide strong evidence of cospeciation, as demonstrated by phylogenetic congruence between different Hydra species and their corresponding Curvibacter symbionts, along with preferential recolonization of germ-free Hydra by their native Curvibacter strains. Comparative genomic analyses reveal that host-associated Curvibacter strains exhibit distinct metabolic and biosynthetic adaptations compared to their free-living relatives. Specifically, the enrichment of proteins linked to host glycan interactions, extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), DNA metabolic processes, ABC transport, sugar metabolism, and bacterial chemotaxis highlights specialized adaptations of Curvibacter symbionts within the Hydra glycocalyx. Importantly, some of these signatures are only detectable within the Hydra vulgaris-associated Curvibacter subgroup, emphasizing the need to examine host-specific adaptations at a finer taxonomic resolution. Functional experiments identify a symbiont-specific EPS operon as a factor for host colonization, thereby establishing its role in facilitating symbiont specificity and stability. These findings provide insights into the molecular mechanisms driving host-microbe coevolution and highlight the evolutionary forces shaping microbial specialization within host-symbiont relationships.
records.authors: Becker L, Fürbach L, Minten T, Bathia J, Karbach M, Foret S, Winterfeldt NM, Usadel B, Pauly M, Axmann IM, Fraune S.

records.title: Expanding the range of habitats colonized by the Verrucomicrobiota: Description of three novel Oleiharenicola species thriving in a co-culture with methanotrophic bacteria.
records.abstract: In this study, we characterize five strains of ultra-small verrucomicrobia, which affiliate with the genus Oleiharenicola, the family Opitutaceae, and develop in trophic associations with methanotrophic bacteria due to the ability to utilize organic acids excreted by methanotrophs and their exopolysaccharides. First representative of these bacteria, strain Vm1ᵀ, was isolated from a laboratory bioreactor with a Methylococcus-dominated methane-oxidizing consortium. Four additional isolates, strains 1P4, E5ᵀ, A3, and T2ᵀ, were further retrieved from Methylocystis, Methylosinus, and Methylomonas-dominated methanotrophic enrichment cultures obtained from freshwater habitats. Cells of these strains were Gram-negative cocci, 0.35-1.6 μm in size, which reproduced by binary fission and formed micro-colonies on media prepared with semi-solid gellan gum. These aerobic bacteria utilized a variety of mono- and disaccharides, organic acids, yeast extract, peptone, and grew at 15-42 °C and pH 5.0-9.0. Their closest phylogenetic relative was Oleiharenicola alkalitolerans NVTT (97.4-98.3% 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity). The genomes determined for strains Vm1ᵀ, E5ᵀ and T2ᵀ were 4.5-5.0 Mb in size and contained gene clusters involved in the degradation of recalcitrant sugars, such as L-rhamnose and L-fucose, including an array of genes encoding planctomycetal-type bacterial microcompartments. The latter were expressed in L-fucose-grown cells. Phylogenomic analysis revealed that these isolates constitute three novel Oleiharenicola species, for which the names Oleiharenicola thermotolerans sp. nov. (type strain Vm1ᵀ = VKM B-3854ᵀ = BIM B-2222ᵀ), O. aggregatus sp. nov. (type strain E5ᵀ = VKM B-4035ᵀ = BIM B-2221ᵀ), and O. mucosus sp. nov. (type strain T2ᵀ = VKM B-4036ᵀ = BIM B-2220ᵀ) are proposed.
records.authors: Salova VD, Danilova OV, Gorbunov AM, Dedysh SN.

records.title: ArchaeaHQ: a curated reference database of archaeal genomes.
records.abstract: Archaea have proven to be major players in biogeochemical cycles across diverse ecosystems, yet we still see an underrepresentation of archaeal genomes in the datasets used by popular computational biology tools. Here, we present ArchaeaHQ, a quality-controlled, systematically curated reference database of 25,584 archaeal genomes compiled initially from 43,045 assemblies from all four archaeal kingdoms retrieved from NCBI: Methanobacteriati (Euryarchaeota), Thermoproteati (TACK), Nanobdellati (DPANN) and Promethearchaeati (Asgard). All genomes in the database passed standardized quality control, requiring ≥70% completeness and ≤10% contamination. A total of 44.0% of genomes in ArchaeaHQ achieved ≥90% completeness, while 92.7% exhibited ≤5% contamination. ArchaeaHQ comprises 18,701 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs; 73.1%) and 6,883 isolate genomes (26.9%). Approximately 76% of MAGs are assigned to 17 ecologically meaningful categories based on sampling origin, and around 65% of genomes include geographic metadata. ArchaeaHQ is available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.32266599 for download and at https://vee-lab.eu/archaeahq for online browsing. This resource was designed to provide an analysis-ready reference set for metagenomic, biogeochemical and ecological studies, comparative genomics analyses and the development of archaeal-specific bioinformatic tools.
records.authors: Bespiatykh D, Leão P.

records.title: Tenacibaculum profundi sp. nov., Tenacibaculum aquaeponti sp. nov. and Tenacibaculum profundicola sp. nov. isolated from seawater samples of the western Pacific Ocean.
records.abstract: Three Gram-staining-negative, rod-shaped, yellow-pigmented, strictly aerobic bacterial strains, designated C7A-26P2T, ZS6-P6T and C14-20M1T, were isolated from seawater samples of the western Pacific Ocean. All strains were able to grow in the presence of 1.0-6.0% NaCl, at pH 6.0-8.0 and at 10-37 °C. Phylogenetic analysis based on 16S rRNA gene sequences indicated these strains belong to the genus Tenacibaculum, with strain C7A-26P2T closest to Tenacibaculum xiamenense Wj-1T (97.9% sequence similarity), ZS6-P6T closest to Tenacibaculum jejuense CNURIC013T (98.7%) and C14-20M1T closest to Tenacibaculum mesophilum NBRC 16307T (96.4%). Genome sizes were 3.8 Mb (G+C content 30.8 mol%) for C7A-26P2T, 4.0 Mb (G+C content 30.1 mol%) for ZS6-P6T and 4.6 Mb (G+C content 33.0 mol%) for C14-20M1T, with average nucleotide identity and digital DNA-DNA hybridization values with other Tenacibaculum species below 87.9 and 34.8%, respectively. Cellular fatty acid profiles identified C15 : 0 iso, summed feature 3 (C16 : 1  ω7c/C16 : 1 ω6c), C18 : 0 and C15 : 1 iso G as the predominant fatty acids for C7A-26P2T; summed feature 3 and C16 : 0 as the major fatty acids for ZS6-P6T; and C15 : 0 iso and summed feature 3 as the major fatty acids for C14-20M1T. The respiratory quinone detected was MK-6 for all strains. The major polar lipids of these three strains were phosphatidylethanolamine, glycolipid, aminolipid and phospholipid. Based on phenotypic, chemotaxonomic and genomic characteristics, strains C7A-26P2T, ZS6-P6T and C14-20M1T were identified as three novel species within the genus Tenacibaculum, for which the names Tenacibaculum profundi sp. nov., Tenacibaculum aquaeponti sp. nov. and Tenacibaculum profundicola sp. nov. are proposed; the type strains are C7A-26P2T (=MCCC M21464T=NBRC 117451T), ZS6-P6T (=MCCC M21515T=NBRC 117453T) and C14-20M1T (=MCCC M24271T=NBRC 117450T), respectively.

records.title: A domesticated totivirus-like tandem array undergoes interspecific transfer and asymmetric evolution.
records.abstract: Functional genes derived from nonretroviral RNA viruses are generally expected to evolve more slowly following integration into host genomes. Here, we characterize Scheffersomyces totivirus-like open reading frame repeat module (STORM), a tandem array of four totivirus-derived ORFs (TLC1 to TLC4) maintained in wood- and insect-associated yeasts for at least 15 My. STORM has nevertheless accumulated greater amino-acid divergence than sampled exogenous totiviruses. Host-calibrated rate analyses estimated that STORM evolved approximately 7-fold faster than related exogenous viral lineages. Evolution within the array was asymmetric. RELAX identified strong gene-wide relaxation in TLC4 (K = 0.29), whereas BUSTED detected no episodic positive selection. Despite this relaxation, TLC4 retained predicted decapping-associated residues, with evidence of purifying selection at several positions. Structural predictions indicated that STORM proteins retain a totivirus-like architecture, and RNA-seq comparisons revealed paralog-specific expression. Among 3,527 complete nuclear gene trees, none recovered all relationships defining any of the three STORM discordances with strong support, indicating that these patterns are exceptional relative to the nuclear genomic background. Local synteny and preservation of the four-copy array further support three interspecific transfers. In the best-supported transfer, STORM was flanked by an ATP10 pseudogene and a transposase pseudogene from yeast endogenous element transposon (YEET), a newly identified Tc1/mariner-like transposon family. Both pseudogenes grouped phylogenetically with the inferred donor clade, and YEET1a-like terminal inverted repeats at the locus were characteristic of that clade. STORM therefore illustrates the selective maintenance, rapid asymmetric evolution, and horizontal mobility of a nonretroviral paleoviral array.
records.authors: Taylor DJ, Tringali DA.

records.title: Environmental constraints reveal condition-dependent advantages of a defined benzene-degrading consortium.
records.abstract: Benzene-contaminated soils remain difficult to remediate because bioaugmentation strategies often rely on selecting individual strains with high degradation activity, while their long-term performance under environmental constraints is uncertain. Here, we show that a defined three-member consortium sustained benzene removal more effectively than the strongest degrader alone under environmental constraints. By integrating field microbiome analysis, 13C-benzene DNA stable isotope probing, genome-resolved metagenomics, cultivation, defined consortia, isotope labeling, and long-term soil incubation, we identified and reconstructed a functional benzene-degrading consortium. Field profiling identified a limited set of taxa associated with benzene contamination. DNA-SIP, genome-resolved metagenomics, and isolate assays further differentiated the roles of the focal lineages. Stutzerimonas showed the strongest benzene degradation, Rhodococcus encoded additional aromatic-catabolic potential, and Rhizobium exhibited nitrogenase activity. Although Stutzerimonas showed the highest degradation efficiency in monoculture (approximately 78%), the three-member consortium displayed a stronger advantage under environmental constraints. When the exogenous nitrogen source was omitted, corrected degradation reached approximately 73% in the three-member consortium, compared with approximately 38% in the Stutzerimonas-Rhodococcus consortium. At 700 mg L-1 benzene, the three-member consortium retained approximately 86% corrected degradation, whereas Stutzerimonas alone declined to approximately 44%. During 6 months of repeated benzene amendment in soil, the consortium maintained rapid benzene removal together with continued detection of all three focal bacterial lineages. These findings show that the benefit of the consortium depended on environmental context and provide a basis for evaluating candidate inocula for benzene remediation.
records.authors: Zhang B, Li Y, Du C, Xiong Y.

records.title: Effects of chemical fertilizer application on soil properties, banana (Musa paradisiaca) yields, and soil microbiomes in a long-term cultivation field.
records.abstract: Due to climate change and increasing food demand, conventional agriculture relies heavily on chemical fertilizers. This study investigated the effects of chemical fertilizer application on soil properties, banana (Musa paradisiaca) yields, and soil microbiomes in a long-term cultivation field. Metagenomic analysis of the 16S rRNA gene provided a comprehensive overview of soil microbial diversity and functional potential. Nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (NPK) fertilizers at 0, 119, 238, and 476 kg ha-1 were applied monthly for one year. Fertilizer application significantly altered soil properties and microbial community dynamics but had no significant effect on banana yields. Higher fertilizer rates reduced soil pH and increased available phosphorus and exchangeable potassium, while total nitrogen and organic matter remained relatively unchanged. Elevated NPK inputs increased the abundance of specific microbial taxa, including Bacillus, Streptomyces, uncultured bacterium JG30-KF-AS9, and Nitrospira, while Xanthobacteraceae, bacteriap25, Micromonosporaceae, Nocardioides, Subgroup 6, and Gemmatimonadaceae consistently represented core taxa across all treatments. Pearson's correlation analysis revealed that soil total nitrogen and exchangeable potassium were positively correlated with the abundance of key plant growth-promoting and nitrifying taxa, including Pseudomonas and Nitrospira, whereas soil pH was negatively correlated with Acidothermus, Nitrospira, and Bacillus, but positively correlated with Subgroup 6. Functional gene profiles further indicated enhanced anaerobic processes associated with carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur cycling. The findings suggest that long-term nutrient accumulation resulting from repeated fertilization and crop residue inputs may sustain banana crops throughout the 10-month production period without additional fertilization. Together, these findings highlight the need for fertilizer regimes tailored to long-term soil nutrient status, contributing to both sustainable agriculture and microbiome-informed crop management.
records.authors: Pruksangkul S, Termsaithong T, Mhuantong W, Limpiyakorn T, Sonthiphand P.

records.title: A novel nudivirus from the Jonah crab (Cancer borealis: Brachyura).
records.abstract: Nudiviruses are double stranded DNA viruses known to infect arthropod hosts. Around 20 different nudiviruses have been identified from crustacean hosts alone. In crustaceans, the hepatopancreas is the primary target of infection, where nuclei appear hypertrophic under histological preparation due to a growing intranuclear viroplasm. The Jonah crab, Cancer borealis, is the target species of an emerging fishery located in the New England (USA) region. Histological and metagenomic tools were used to characterize a new nudivirus, including pathological characterization and sequencing of the 97,677 bp genome, which encoded 93 open reading frames. The genome housed a genetic synteny that was similar to other gammanudiviruses. The virus also phylogenetically clusters with other members of the Gammanudivirus genus based on a 17-protein concatenated phylogenetic tree. Comparative genomics revealed up to 66 conserved genes across all Gammanudivirus species, including a putative deneddylase that appears not to be present in all other nudivirus lineages. Discovering and identifying this nudivirus provides greater detail on a new pathogen that poses a potential risk to the emerging fishery.
records.authors: Conover G, Behringer DC, Clark F, Montague AM, Jennings L, Scro A, Goldstein J, Bojko J.

records.title: Abundance-weighted analysis and deep functional metagenomic selection reveals unrecognized diversity of soil-derived streptothricin acetyltransferases
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Streptothricins (STCs) are broad-spectrum antibiotics under investigation for their therapeutic potential against antibiotic-resistant Gram-negative pathogens. However, the extent and diversity of genes that confer resistance to STCs, or their environmental resistome, remains largely unknown and is essentially limited to a handful of STC acetyltransferases. Here, we used a deep functional metagenomic approach to uncover previously unrecognized STC resistance determinants. A functional metagenomic library containing  ca. 700 Gigabases of soil metagenomic DNA was selected for resistance to nourseothricin (NTC), a mixture of STC congeners, resulting in collection and sequencing of nearly 30,000 resistant clones. An abundance-weighted sequence analysis identified 265 acetyltransferase-like candidates spanning broad phylogenetic, taxonomic, and genomic diversity. Re-cloning and experimental testing of 18 candidates chosen to cover acetyltransferase sequence space confirmed that 10 conferred significant NTC resistance in  Escherichia coli . Phylogenetic analyses identified three previously uncharacterized STC acetyltransferase lineages, designated as SatC, SatD, and SatE. Despite substantial sequence divergence from characterized streptothricin acetyltransferases (maximum amino acid identities of approximately 31% for SatC and SatD and up to 47.5% for SatE), these enzymes largely retained key residues associated with streptothricin binding and catalysis. In addition to strongly increasing NTC resistance, expression of the SatC construct in  E. coli also significantly decreased susceptibility to the aminoglycoside antibiotics amikacin and kanamycin. Together, these findings reveal a substantially broader than previously known environmental repertoire of STC acetyltransferases and demonstrate how deep functional metagenomic selections, combined with abundance-weighted hit calling, phylogenetic analysis, and structural prediction, can uncover novel resistance functions.

records.title: Ancestral state inference at an uncertain trifurcation: What colors of light could the common ancestor of the fungi "see"?
records.abstract: Reconstruction of the traits of extinct ancestors is a central challenge in evolutionary biology. This reconstruction is especially difficult in lineages such as fungi, whose extraordinary ecological, biological, and morphological diversity is underserved by a sparse fossil record. In fungi, therefore, this limitation makes phylogenetic comparative approaches essential for inferring traits at key ancestral nodes. Because the deepest fungal ancestors appear to be aquatic-and because extant aquatic fungi appear to retain several ancestral sensory systems, photoreception provides a compelling system for investigation of early fungal ecology and evolution. Yet modern fungi harbor a much broader diversity of light-sensing pathways, leaving unresolved which components were already present in the most recent common ancestor of fungi. Accurate assessment of the apparati for light sensing in the ancestor of all fungi is the very first step to understanding the evolution and divergence of fungal "eyes": receptors that are sensitive to specific spans of the wavelengths of visible light. Here, using recent fungal genome sequencing, annotation and phylogenomics, with particular emphasis on flagellated lineages, we reconstructed the ancestral presence or absence of all known fungal light-sensory genes. To account for uncertainty in early fungal relationships, we evaluated two competing phylogenetic hypotheses that differ with regard to the controversial placement of Blastocladiomycota. Across these analyses, the CyclOp and the White Collar light-sensing systems were consistently inferred to have been present in the fungal ancestor, whereas phytochromes were likely absent, providing a phylogenetically explicit foundation for understanding the early evolution of fungal photoreception.
records.authors: Wang YW, Hassler HB, Wang Z, Townsend JP.

records.title: Full-length genomes evolve in parallel in a long-term evolution experiment with phage φX174.
records.abstract: The study of evolution in organisms with high mutation rates requires detailed data on the genomic composition of the population. Here we report on an innovative use of high-throughput sequencing technology combined with rapid experimental evolution that allowed us to follow the genetic diversification of four independent bacteriophage populations for 412 generations in extraordinary detail. One of our goals was to assess phylodynamic methods that use genetic information to infer key parameters of the population history. Because phylodynamic methods assume neutral evolution, we did not actively impose any selection pressures in our evolution experiment (in addition to those inherent in the bacterial cell environment). Tracing over 80'000 bacteriophage genomes, representing 884 distinct genotypes, we find that the patterns of viral diversification result in largely non-congruent genotype distributions, but also document multiple instances of parallel evolution. Unlike previous observations of parallelism in viral evolution, we do not just see the parallel evolution of mutations at single sites, but on the level of full-length genomes. Computer simulations that recapitulate our experiments in great detail show that this degree of parallelism is inconsistent with neutral evolution. We further show that the observed extent of parallel evolution biases phylodynamic analysis of migration rates, and wrongly estimates significant migration between the independent evolution lines. Our approach is applicable to many other viruses and paves the way to advanced population genetic investigations that aim to shed light on phenomena that relate to genetic linkage across the genome.
records.authors: Bons E, Chabas H, MacDonald H, Escalera Ledermann A, Ösze S, Dunstan J, Ochsner N, Angst DC, Bonhoeffer S, Regoes RR.

records.title: BacPath: A Rapid Metagenomic Workflow with a Curated Reference Database for Species-Level Detection of Bacterial Plant Pathogens
records.abstract: The emergence of plant pathogens through geographic spread, host shifts, and climate change threatens disease management and global food security. Detection of emerging pathogens without prior genomic information is critical for preventing widespread outbreaks and enabling timely management to reduce economic impact. Accurate and reliable detection of infecting organisms using metagenome-based bioinformatic pipelines is therefore essential. To address this, we have developed and validated BacPath pipeline and a highly accurate complete genome database, BacPathDB. Raw read files obtained from Oxford Nanopore sequencers (MinIon and Flongle) were processed, quality-scored, and mapped against a curated database. The expandable BacPathDB contains high-quality genomes with accurate metadata and currently includes 317 genomes, representing species, within the genera Dickeya and Pectobacterium, including most type strains. The pipeline accurately detected all 32 species within these two genera in silico, with no false positives or false negatives. In vitro analyses with both Pectobacterium and Dickeya species further confirmed the accuracy of the developed pipeline for detecting pathogens from complex plant tissue samples infected with single or multiple pathogens. Detection can be achieved with as little as a single read, however, analyses based on five or more reads provide higher confidence in the results. The pipeline is rapid, enabling detection in approximately one minute, and can be performed on a 16 GB laptop without requiring high computational resources. This makes it well suited for field applications, while the curated reference database enhances its reliability for routine diagnostics, epidemiological investigations, disease surveillance, regulatory programs, biosecurity, and microbial forensics.
records.authors: Arif M, Montesinos S, Maurya N, Alvarez AM, Dobhal S.

records.title: Expanding the Repertoire of Associations Between Antibiotic Resistance Genes and Putative Mobile Genetic Element Carriers Using Metagenomic Long Reads
records.abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and the mobile genetic elements (MGEs) that mediate their horizontal transfer are central to understanding the mechanisms, evolution, and dissemination of antimicrobial resistance. Although thousands of ARGs have been documented and numerous ARG–MGE associations have been reported, broader questions about the diversity and distribution of these associations remain underexplored. How comprehensive are the current catalogs of ARG–MGE associations? Are certain MGE families preferentially associated with particular ARGs, and vice versa? How are ARG–MGE associations distributed across microbial taxa? Is the environmental abundance of an ARG related to the diversity of its MGE associations? Do ARG–MGE association patterns vary across environments? Here we address these questions by analyzing multiple publicly available long-read metagenomic datasets from various environmental settings, leveraging the ability of long reads to capture ARGs along with their genomic contexts within individual reads. We identified numerous potential ARG–MGE associations not found in existing databases. A few MGE families were putatively associated with nearly all identified ARGs. ARG–MGE associations were unevenly distributed across taxa. ARG abundance was positively associated with both MGE association diversity and the taxonomic spread of those associations. Furthermore, ARG–MGE association patterns varied across environments. Overall, our findings reveal an extensive diversity of ARG–MGE associations that remains largely underrepresented in current knowledge bases. Importance  Antibiotic resistance is a growing global concern, in part because mobile genetic elements facilitate the spread of resistance genes across bacterial populations, taxa, and environments. Characterizing the associations between resistance genes and mobile genetic elements, and assessing their distribution across taxa and environments, can provide insights into the mobilization and dissemination of antibiotic resistance. Although these associations have primarily been investigated using assembled genomes, our findings demonstrate the potential of unassembled long-read metagenomic data to uncover previously uncharacterized gene–element associations. Our results reveal a substantial reservoir of such associations that remains underrepresented in existing knowledge bases.
records.authors: Go DJL, Shrestha AM.

records.title: Genomic Insights into the Pathogenicity and Host Adaptation of Pseudomonas amygdali pv. mori, the Causal Agent of Mulberry Bacterial Blight.
records.abstract: Mulberry bacterial blight (MBB), a devastating disease of mulberry (Morus spp.), causes substantial losses in yield and quality. This study isolated and characterized the highly virulent strain MYC18 from diseased tissues and identified it as Pseudomonas amygdali. The MYC18 genome comprises 6.39 Mb across a single chromosome and three plasmids, encoding 5,979 predicted coding sequences. Comparative genomic analysis indicates an open pan-genome and significant structural diversity among phylogenetically related strains. Genome annotation revealed 322 virulence-associated genes and 21 multidrug resistance determinants, along with a highly conserved type III secretion system (T3SS) encoding 29 predicted effectors. qRT-PCR analysis of eight representative T3SE genes revealed temporally partitioned expression patterns: early transient induction (hopF1, hopR1, hopD2), sustained high expression (hopI1, hopM1), and late-peaking (hopG1, hopX1, avrD). As the first high-quality reference genome for P. amygdali pv. mori, the MYC18 assembly provides a critical genomic resource for elucidating the pathogenic mechanisms of mulberry bacterial blight and developing targeted disease control strategies.
records.authors: Dai X, Tang Q, Wang S, Liu Y, Zhao W, Wang Z, Sheng S, Wu F, Li P.

records.title: Scaling laws link conserved gene-abundance distributions to adaptive expression in diatom communities worldwide.
records.abstract: Marine microbes sustain Earth's major biogeochemical cycles, yet how they maintain stable ecosystem functions across diverse environments remains unclear. We analyzed metagenomic and metatranscriptomic data from diatom communities sampled during the Tara Oceans global expedition. While gene abundance distributions remain statistically similar across sample, gene expression varies systematically across geographical locations, a global pattern we show reflects predictable scaling laws. Global distributions, scaling relationships, and variability among sampling stations are captured by a stochastic model linking gene abundance dynamics to gene expression. While colder waters are associated with higher transcriptional activity and warmer regions show more selective gene usage, we find that transcript abundance increases nonlinearly with transcript richness. This general scaling is captured by our model and suggests that diatom communities balance high expression of core genes with specific functional diversity. These scaling relationships hold consistently across ocean basins, with temperature, used as an effective large-scale environmental descriptor whose signature cannot be fully disentangled from spatial structure, sufficing to predict transcriptional patterns from genetic composition. Our findings reveal how the stability of gene-abundance structure in diatom ecosystems coexists with transcriptional variability, enabling flexible functional responses.

records.title: Morphogenomic description of Cranifera cranifera (Chitwood, 1932) Kloss, 1960 from captive Blaptica dubia Serville, 1838 cockroach.
records.abstract: Nematodes of the superfamily Thelastomatoidea are found in the digestive system of various arthropods, feeding on their host microbiome. They are sometimes considered to be ecologically intermediate forms between free-living rhabditids and parasitic Spirurina, while phylogenetically they are nested within the latter. In addition to new morphological data on the male morphology, this manuscript presents the first nuclear genome assembly of a thelastomatid species, Cranifera cranifera, using a long-read sequencing approach, making a total of three nuclear genomes available for superfamily Thelastomatoidea. The C. cranifera nuclear genome assembly presented here is 243 Mb long, consists of 7563 contigs, has an N50 of 43 kb, and includes 94% of the BUSCO nematoda_odb12 genes. The mitochondrial genome is 24644 bases long, includes a complete set of protein-coding, rRNA, and tRNA genes, and a repetitive region 9731 bases long, which includes multiple copies of tRNA-Asn(gtt) and tRNA-Lys(ttt). The nuclear assembly also contained two sequence variants of the 28S rRNA and two of the 18S rRNA genes, highlighting the presence of intragenomic variation within the rRNA operon. The newly generated assemblies (nuclear and organelle) will add to a growing body of genomic resources for underrepresented and understudied animal parasitic nematodes from Clade 3, enabling comprehensive studies in their phylogeny and trait evolution in the future.
records.authors: Morffe J, Guiglielmoni N, Wassey N, Gueddach K, Schuster A, Becker K, Bast J, Schiffer P, Holovachov O.

records.title: ArthroVerse: mapping protein family diversity across arthropod-associated microbiomes.
records.abstract: Metagenomic studies of arthropod-associated microbiomes have generated vast amounts of sequence data, yet the functional and structural organization of these proteins remains largely unexplored. Here, we present ArthroVerse, the first comprehensive database of protein families derived from arthropod-associated metagenomes. Non-redundant protein families were generated after rigorous filtering, deduplication, and clustering. The protein families were further annotated with microbial taxonomy, host associations, protein structural information, and carbohydrate-active enzymes predictions. The resulting dataset integrates both metagenomic and reference genome-derived proteins, enabling systematic exploration of functional diversity, evolutionary relationships, and host-microbe interactions in insect microbiomes. ArthroVerse provides a valuable resource for the study of microbial ecology and arthropod physiology, offering unprecedented insight into the protein landscape of insect-associated microbial communities. ArthroVerse is publicly accessible at https://envofams.org/arthroverse/.

records.title: Beneficial microbes in plant salt stress tolerance: mechanisms, antioxidant defense, and multi-omics insights.
records.abstract: Salinity stress represents a significant environmental challenge that affects plant growth, resulting in adverse impacts on crop productivity and overall yield. Salt accumulation in plants affects cellular homeostasis and provokes osmotic and ionic imbalance. It stimulates higher reactive oxygen species (ROS) production leading to oxidative stress damage and eventual cellular dysfunction. Beneficial microorganisms like plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria, arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, endophytic fungi, and rhizosphere-associated microbes have recently emerged as resources for sustainable solutions to enhance plant resiliency against salinity stress. Their effects can involve osmotic adjustment, ion sequestration, oxidative-stress mitigation, phytohormone regulation, and rhizosphere-mediated stress buffering. The mechanisms to impart such benefits may include improved nutrients acquisition, assist in osmotic regulation, modulation of phytohormones signaling, and maintenance of cellular ion homeostasis. Often, beneficial microorganisms carry the potential to trigger both enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant defense mechanisms. These responses contribute to oxidative-stress mitigation, yet, their interpretation requires contemplation of fine balance between oxidative damage and plant responses. For example, selected microbial inoculation studies have reported changes in the activity of crucial antioxidant enzymes, like superoxide dismutase, ascorbate peroxidase, catalase, and glutathione reductase. However, the magnitude and the direction of these responses are context dependent. Multi-omics approaches, including amplicon and shotgun metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, host transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, have expanded our understanding of the taxa, genes, transcripts, proteins, and metabolites associated with plant-microbe interactions under salinity. Therefore, here an effort has been made to present the evidential support for reported microbial effects and their proposed mechanisms of salt tolerance, with a focus on enzymatic and non-enzymatic defense mechanisms and the learnings of multi-omics studies. Frontier integrative mechanisms, including microbiome engineering, synthetic microbial consortia, and systems biology frameworks, are discussed for cultivating climate-resilient crops and sustainable agricultural systems in the salt-affected environments.
records.authors: Shree S, Chaudhary A, Kumar S, Singh K, Dubey N.

records.title: Compound microbial intelligent membrane fermentation reshapes the bacterial community and reduces antibiotic, metal, and biocide resistance genes and virulence factors in duck litter.
records.abstract: BackgroundContaminated duck litter is a leading cause of flock disease and a bottleneck for the sustainable development of large-scale dry-rearing systems.MethodsWe applied shotgun metagenomics to litter from four positions within each of three independent compound microbial intelligent membrane fermentation beds, with unfermented litter from the same three batches as the control. We investigated the bacterial community alongside the abundance of antibiotic, metal and biocide resistance genes (ARGs, MRGs and BRGs) and of virulence factor genes (VFGs).ResultsFermented litter was consistently enriched in thermophilic and thermotolerant taxa and in beneficial genera such as Paenibacillus and Bacillus, while opportunistic pathogens including Streptococcus, Mycobacterium and Escherichia were clearly reduced. The total burden of the ARG and VFG classes fell in every fermented position, and representative determinants were consistently depleted: floR, qacEdelta1 and sul2 among the ARGs, ruvB among the MRGs, mexF, ideR and sodA among the BRGs, and htpB, clpV and katA among the VFGs. A small number of genes, tet(L), fexA and bacA among them, rose in the most active zones, indicating structural remodeling of the resistance reservoir rather than uniform removal. Fermentation was not spatially uniform: the upper and edge layers were more active, and the center-lower layer remained closest to the unfermented control.ConclusionIntelligent membrane fermentation reduced the overall abundance of resistance and virulence determinants in the litter microbiome, and spatial uniformity is important for the process. Because these data are DNA-based, they describe the abundance of resistance and virulence determinants and not resistance or virulence phenotypes.
records.authors: Sun T, Mei G, Li M, Mo J, Zhang C, Ma Y, Zhao J, Peng S, Lin F, Chen JL, Li Z.

records.title: Ecological and metabolic signatures of biofilm viromes across a national river surveillance network
records.abstract: Benthic biofilms are biogeochemical hotspots in rivers, yet their endogenous viral communities remain poorly resolved at national scales. We analysed 447 biofilm metagenomes from 146 sites within England’s River Surveillance Network (RSN), sampled in spring and autumn from 2021 to 2023, integrating viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), water-quality gradients, predicted host associations and auxiliary metabolic genes (AMGs). We recovered 38,534 vOTUs, revealing extensive viral novelty, where 93% of the vOTUs could not be assigned to a known family. Viromes were dominated by Caudoviricetes and unclassified lineages and were extremely heterogeneous: no vOTU occurred in more than 8.3% of samples. Season, but not sampling year, structured virome composition (family-level PERMANOVA R  2 = 0.050, p = 0.001; year p = 0.08), and within-site turnover between spring and autumn exceeded turnover between years. Bray–Curtis ordination linked virome structure weakly to pH, dissolved organic carbon, conductivity, nitrate-N and dissolved oxygen (envfit R  2 ≤ 0.066), while threshold indicator taxa analysis (TITAN) identified vOTUs with abrupt change points along alkalinity, dissolved oxygen, nitrate-N and temperature gradients. Predicted host associations were concentrated in Pseudomonodota, Cyanobacteriota and Bacteroidota, with  Microcoleus ,  Chamaesiphon and  Flavobacterium among the dominant host genera. Virus–host networks were modular, and module abundances correlated with water quality variables (dissolved oxygen, pH, nitrate etc.), suggesting that environmental filtering acts partly through host ecology. Predicted virus–host associations formed a sparse network organised around a few highly connected viral lineages. Functional profiling showed that the biofilm virome was dominated by nucleotide metabolism, DNA methylation, phosphate-stress, glycan-modification and photosynthesis-related AMGs, with  nrdA /  nrdB ribonucleotide reductase as the dominant AMG signal. Few vOTUs (1.2%) were detected as proviruses, although provirus fractions were higher in selected host-linked lineages. Collectively, these results show that river biofilm viromes are seasonally structured ecological communities whose composition, host associations and metabolic potential reflect the physicochemical and biological state of rivers. We propose that biofilm viromes provide a complementary layer of information for understanding river health, microbial ecology and the propagation of anthropogenic pressures in freshwater systems.

records.title: Structure, function, and evolution of topoisomerase modulatory proteins in bacteria.
records.abstract: SUMMARYDNA topoisomerases are essential for maintaining the integrity and functionality of the genome. By homeostatically controlling the genome topology in bacteria, these enzymes influence essential cellular processes such as gene expression, replication, recombination, and chromosome segregation. Although DNA topoisomerases were initially considered to act as stand-alone enzymes, they are now being recognized as integral components of dynamic protein complexes that perform diverse functions in vivo. The discovery of several proteinaceous modulators of DNA topoisomerases has expanded the understanding of their functional versatility. These are encoded either by the bacterial chromosome or extrachromosomal elements like plasmids and bacteriophages. Chromosomally encoded modulators are engaged in fine-tuning topoisomerase activity, enabling them to carry out specialized cellular functions beyond their canonical enzymatic roles. Crucially, they prevent genomic instability that may arise from dysregulated topoisomerase activity. By altering DNA topology, modulatory proteins can influence transcriptional bursting, leading to epigenetic heterogeneity within the bacterial populations, crucial for bacterial stress adaptation. In contrast, topoisomerase interacting proteins encoded by plasmids and phages have dedicated roles in facilitating plasmid maintenance and phage propagation by suppressing host defenses and promoting horizontal gene transfer. We present a comprehensive analysis of the topoisomerase modulatory proteins discovered so far, offering insights into the mechanisms by which DNA topology and homeostasis are maintained within the intracellular environment. We project the potential of topoisomerase modulator-based drug design as a promising strategy for combating multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens.
records.authors: Biswas P, Nagaraja V, Sengupta S.

records.title: Type III effector repertoires as a window into Pseudomonas syringae pv. actinidiae evolution and Actinidia defense responses.
records.abstract: Kiwifruit bacterial canker, caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. actinidiae (Psa), represents a complex disease system in which closely related bacterial populations differ in host association, pathogenicity, genomic composition, and geographic distribution as evidenced by pandemic spread of biovar 3 after 2008. Closely related Psa lineages differ in host association, virulence, and distribution, yet these differences arise largely outside the conserved core genome. Mobile genetic elements remodel accessory regions, and acquisition, loss, and redundancy of type III effectors shape whether a lineage colonizes or is restricted by a given Actinidia genotype. Virulence is therefore a host-dependent property, not a fixed lineage rank. On the host side, genome assemblies, QTL mapping, and infection transcriptomics indicate that resistance reflects the timing and persistence of immune signalling rather than receptor presence alone, although few candidate receptors have been validated in planta. Durable resistance is most likely to derive from recognition of non-redundant effector functions and from immune hubs, such as RIN4, that multiple effectors target. Integrating pathogen population genomics, effector biology, and host immune genetics is the route to predicting which lineages will emerge next.
records.authors: Asif M, Zhao Z.

records.title: Metagenomic insights into microplastic micro-interfaces: Transforming pollutants and spreading resistance.
records.abstract: Microplastic micro-interfaces (MPMI) in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) serve as critical hubs for microbial colonization, pollutant transformation, and antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) dissemination. In this study, a large-scale genome-resolved metagenomic approach was employed to reconstruct 463 quality-filtered metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from biofilms established on polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polyethylene (PE), and polypropylene (PP) within a municipal WWTP. Taxonomic profiling revealed that MPMI selectively enriched strict anaerobes and uncultured taxa, driving a profound ecological shift relative to the surrounding water and indicating the formation of localized hypoxic micro-niches. Functionally, the MPMI microbiome constructed a highly integrated metabolic network. Dominant lineages were found to synergistically couple aromatic hydrocarbon degradation (via the shikimate pathway and β-oxidation) with complex carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur cycling, while deploying energy-efficient nucleotide salvage strategies to ensure biofilm stabilization under nutrient stress. Crucially, horizontal gene transfer (HGT) emerged as a fundamental mechanism for functional diversification, facilitating the active cross-genomic exchange of key adaptive traits associated with pollutant metabolism and biofilm regulation. Furthermore, MPMI harbored a highly diverse resistome comprising 36 ARG categories and 289 subtypes, highlighted by the critical genomic co-localization of mobile elements and clinical resistance markers (e.g., mcr-5.1, mupA) in core colonizers. Ultimately, these genomic insights identify the MPMI as a major ecological hotspot driving the concurrent adaptation of metabolic networks and the resistome, thereby exacerbating the risk of ARG dissemination in aquatic environments.
records.authors: Tian H, Liu J, Zhang Y.

records.title: Reconstructing skin microbiome of G. Clemenceau (1929): paleoproteomic analysis of his bath sponge.
records.abstract: Paleoproteomic analysis of a bath sponge belonging to Georges Clemenceau explores the possibility of reconstructing the skin microbiome of a historical figure from a preserved personal item. Using high-resolution mass spectrometry and a cascade proteotyping strategy, several microorganisms were identified, dominated by environmental bacteria of the genus Pseudomonas and opportunistic fungi such as Aspergillus and Exophiala. Traces of Escherichia coli, human proteins, marine organisms, and plants were also detected. Overall, the results suggest that the sponge does not accurately reflect Clemenceau's stable skin microbiome, as microorganisms typically associated with human skin are absent, likely due to taphonomic biases and preservation phenomena. On the contrary, the object appears as a complex microenvironment that has accumulated contamination over time related to humidity, the domestic and coastal environment, as well as the conditions of use and storage. The presence of opportunistic microorganisms, notably Exophiala sideris, even suggests a potential risk of skin infections in an elderly diabetic individual. This study thus demonstrates that everyday objects can constitute unique biological archives for paleopathology, not for precisely reconstructing an individual microbiota, but for documenting dermatological hygiene practices, microbial environments, and the infectious risks associated with reusable, damp objects at the beginning of the 20th century.
records.authors: Charlier P, Armengaud J, Gebelin M, Lhortolary S.

records.title: A functional two-pore-domain K<sup>+</sup> channel from a large DNA virus.
records.abstract: The evolutionary history of proteins helps to understand their structure/function correlates and suggests on how functional complexity evolved from primitive precursors. In the superfamily of K+ channels, functional features of complex eukaryotic inward rectifier (Kir) channels and voltage-dependent (Kv) channels could be understood in terms of an increase in structural complexity of their prokaryotic precursors. K2P channels, which are made from tandem repeats of two pore domains, are not found in prokaryotes and their evolutionary origin is still unknown. In searching for primitive K2P channel precursors, we screened the genomes of nucleocytoplasmic large DNA viruses (NCLDVs) for genes coding for K2P channels. This was motivated by two reasons: NCLDVs are already known for coding primitive Kir type channels, and they play important roles in the evolution of eukaryotes. Here, we report that the NCLDV Pyramimonas orientalis virus codes for K2P-like K+ channels. With only 178 amino acids and no cytosolic domains, this Kpov protein is much smaller than any eukaryotic K2P channel, but still functional as K+ selective channel in lipid bilayers. Phylogenetic analysis suggests that Kpov is not the product of molecular piracy from the host but may result from fusion of primitive viral K+ channel pore domains.
records.authors: Rauh O, Mach S, Clarke O, Toews J, Van Etten JL, Althaus M, Moroni A, Thiel G.

records.title: Novel putative PETase candidates from metagenomic mining of Ebrié lagoon and Kassembié lake, Côte d'Ivoire
records.abstract: Plastic pollution threatens aquatic ecosystems in Côte d’Ivoire, yet their microbial potential for polyethylene terephthalate (PET) degradation remains poorly characterized. We applied shotgun metagenomics to five samples from Biétry bay, an urban site in the Ébrié lagoon, and Kassembié lake, a low-impact reference site. MetaPhlAn4 detected 131 site-specific, uncharacterized species-level genome bins, including 76 found only at Biétry. Functional annotation of the non-redundant gene catalogue identified 15,860 hydrolase genes and 195 genes assigned to the CE1 carbohydrate esterase family, used here as a proxy for general ester-cleaving potential. Structural prediction with ColabFold (AlphaFold2) and comparison with IsPETase using TM-align prioritized four novel PETase-like candidates, BietPETase1–4. These findings reveal under-explored microbial and enzymatic diversity in Ivorian aquatic ecosystems and provide candidates for experimental validation in PET-bioremediation research.
records.authors: Anderson HK, Nouho OK, Ines Estelle KA, Olivier YK.
