records.title: Phage-directed precision microbiome medicine: engineering pathobiont depletion, synbiotic succession, microbial-function editing, metabolite host signaling, neurophagomics, and durable ecological state control in gut dysbiosis associated diseases.
records.abstract: Bacteriophages are being investigated as strain-selective tools for modifying intestinal microbial communities, but the evidence supporting ecological reconstruction is substantially less mature than the evidence supporting targeted bacterial depletion. This review separates current knowledge into three domains: established and emerging experimental evidence, human translational evidence, and hypotheses proposed for future testing. Human studies show that orally administered natural or engineered phages can be recovered from the gastrointestinal tract and can alter selected bacterial populations without antibiotic-like loss of overall community diversity. Preclinical studies further demonstrate targeted suppression of inflammatory Klebsiella pneumoniae in inflammatory bowel disease models, cytolytic Enterococcus faecalis in alcohol-associated liver disease, evolutionary steering of Escherichia coli, in situ bacterial genome editing, local therapeutic-protein production, and phage-probiotic cooperation. These findings do not yet establish that an integrated phage-successor-prebiotic sequence can durably reprogram a human gut ecosystem. To organize this translational gap, we use Subtract-Seed-Feed-Lock as an explicitly proposed design framework. A phage or phage-derived platform first depletes, weakens, or edits a disease-relevant bacterial strain or function; a niche-matched successor is then introduced; a selectively utilized nutrient supports that successor; and durability is assessed after treatment withdrawal. Related terms used in this review-Functional Phageability, Minimum Ecological Dose, Ecological Vacancy Window, nutrient-conditioned phagogram, ecological pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (Eco-PK/PD), ecological pharmacovigilance, neurophagomic reverse translation, and microbiome-state digital twin-are hypothesis-generating operational concepts rather than validated clinical methods. Host signaling is likewise framed as predominantly indirect: phage-induced changes in bacterial abundance or function may alter lipopolysaccharide, short-chain fatty acids, indoles, bile acids, and other metabolites that subsequently engage inflammatory, barrier, hepatic, or neural pathways. The gut-brain application remains especially preliminary; targeting urdA-positive imidazole-propionate producers has not been validated with therapeutic phages. Clinical development will require reproducible good manufacturing practice, control of endotoxin and host-cell contaminants, product stability, resistance and immune-neutralization monitoring, environmental-shedding assessment, and regulatory strategies for genetically modified, dynamically updated, and multi-component products. The immediate opportunity is therefore precise microbial perturbation with evidence-matched endpoints; durable programmed reconstruction remains an experimentally testable objective.
records.authors: Saeed U, Piracha ZZ.

records.title: Comparative Genomics Analyses of Bacterial tRNA Modification Protein Families Using Clusters of Orthologous Genes (COG) and KEGG Orthology (KO) Classification Systems
records.abstract: Accurate identification of bacterial tRNA modification enzymes is essential for understanding translation, physiology, and genome evolution, yet annotation remains complicated by paralogy, multifunctionality, functional divergence, and non-orthologous replacement. We compiled an experimentally supported catalog of bacterial tRNA modification proteins and linked them to 71 Clusters of Orthologous Groups (COG) and 74 KEGG Orthology (KO) families. Their distributions, conservation, and copy-number patterns were examined across 1,322 bacterial genomes represented in both annotation systems. Comparison of COG and KO assignments revealed strong agreement for one-to-one family relationships but substantial discordance for broad COG families that encompass functionally distinct paralogs. Genome-scale profiling identified a conserved core repertoire of tRNA modification systems that was supported by both phylogenetic conservation and retention in bacteria with highly reduced genomes. Phylogenetic distribution patterns highlighted known and candidate cases of non-orthologous replacement, including alternative solutions for m5U54 and xm5(s2)U34 biosynthesis, and identified Actinomycetota as a promising source of currently uncharacterized tRNA modification enzymes. Gene-duplication analyses revealed that most core tRNA modification pathways were maintained as single-copy genes or highly conserved single-copy modules, whereas only a limited number of families, displayed substantial expansion. Predicted tRNA modification repertoires increased with genome size, but the relationship was weak, lineage dependent, and better described by log-linear than linear models, indicating diminishing gains in modification capacity with increasing genome complexity. Finally, phylogenetically informed analyses identified a small number of associations between specific tRNA modification pathways and physiological traits. Together, these results provide an updated COG-KO reference framework for bacterial tRNA modification systems, clarify the strengths and limitations of commonly used orthology resources, and highlight evolutionary processes shaping the diversification of bacterial tRNA modification pathways.

records.title: Biological characterization of the lytic Pseudomonas aeruginosa phage BUCT980 and its therapeutic efficacy in a murine lung infection model.
records.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an important opportunistic pathogen whose increasing multidrug resistance limits conventional antimicrobial treatment options and underscores the need for alternative antibacterial strategies. In this study, we isolated and systematically characterized a novel lytic phage, BUCT980, and evaluated its antibacterial activity and therapeutic potential. Transmission electron microscopy showed that BUCT980 is a myovirus. One-step growth analysis indicated an apparent latent period of approximately 60 min and a burst size of approximately 173 PFU per infected cell. The BUCT980 genome is 60,697 bp in length, and comparative genomic and phylogenetic analyses support its placement within the class Caudoviricetes. No known lysogeny-associated genes, virulence factors, or antibiotic resistance genes were identified by genomic analysis. In vitro, BUCT980 markedly suppressed the growth of P. aeruginosa PAO1 across the tested multiplicities of infections (MOIs) and inhibited biofilm formation. In 10-fold serial-dilution spot assays, BUCT980 formed clear plaques on 4 of 29 clinical isolates and produced visible inhibition in 13 additional isolates representing multiple sequence types. In a murine model of acute P. aeruginosa pneumonia, intranasal administration of BUCT980 significantly improved survival, reduced pulmonary bacterial burden, and alleviated lung injury. No overt histopathological abnormalities were observed in the liver or kidney during short-term observation. These findings support further evaluation of BUCT980 as a candidate therapeutic phage for acute P. aeruginosa lung infection.IMPORTANCEPseudomonas aeruginosa is a major cause of difficult-to-treat respiratory infections because of its antibiotic resistance and biofilm-forming capacity. Here, we characterized BUCT980, a lytic phage that suppressed P. aeruginosa growth, inhibited early biofilm formation, and showed activity against clinical isolates from multiple sequence-type backgrounds. Genomic screening identified no known lysogeny-associated genes, virulence factors, or antibiotic resistance genes. In a murine acute pneumonia model, intranasal BUCT980 treatment improved survival, reduced pulmonary bacterial burden, and alleviated lung injury. Bacterial regrowth during prolonged exposure and limited activity against established biofilms indicate that combination strategies may be needed for sustained treatment. These findings support further preclinical evaluation of BUCT980 for acute P. aeruginosa lung infection.
records.authors: Yu X, Chen J, Zhang W, Tong Y, Xie L, Li M, Yao M.

records.title: Systematic mapping of the prokaryotic noncoding sequence space with a genomic language model
records.abstract: Prokaryotic genomes encode a vast repertoire of noncoding elements such as ribozymes, riboswitches, and CRISPR RNAs. The sequence-level diversity of these intergenic elements precludes alignment-based clustering that would enable annotation and discovery of novel noncoding RNA families. Here, we show that a genomic language model fine-tuned on prokaryotic intergenic sequences learns representations of noncoding elements from DNA sequence. We used these embeddings to organize 376 million intergenic regions from 1.3 terabase pairs of prokaryotic genomes and metagenomes into 5.14 million clusters. This approach nominated 20,149 clusters of putative structured RNAs with a candidate protein partner. Periodicity in token entropies revealed internal architecture, recovering CRISPR, TIGR and VIPR arrays together with their cognate effector proteins from sequence alone. Targeted clustering of bridge recombinase-adjacent sequences identified bridge RNA variants with longer guide recognition sequences than any characterized ortholog. Finally, we directed teams of AI agents to mine the database under researcher-defined criteria, uncovering divergent riboswitches, ribozymes, and other structured RNAs with biological hypotheses for their function. We release a publicly available database that transforms the dark matter of prokaryotic genomes into an explorable resource for human-agent molecular discovery.
records.authors: Sun G, Hudelmaier T, Gilligan JC, Gonzalez GA, Yin P, Wan F, Ma Z(, Durrant MG, Ricci-Tam C, Pawluk A, Puschnik AS, Konermann S, Hsu PD.

records.title: From assembly to yield: kingdom-specific rules, keystone networks and a Bayesian structural equation framework for the maize rhizosphere microbiome
records.abstract: Abstract    Background and aims.  The rhizosphere microbiome is an extension of the crop genome, yet the rules governing its assembly and its statistical links to yield remain unresolved. We asked whether bacteria and fungi follow kingdom-specific assembly rules across genotypes and stages (RQ1), which taxa form network backbones (RQ2), and through which statistical pathways microbial features connect to measured grain yield (RQ3).  Methods.  Bacterial and fungal communities of seven maize cultivars were profiled at seedling (V6) and tasseling (VT) stages, integrating diversity analyses, robustness-validated co-occurrence networks, FAPROTAX/FUNGuild annotation, BSEM, and machine-learning signature identification; grain yield was measured and no forecasting was attempted.  Results.  Bacterial assembly was dominated by developmental stage (ANOSIM R = 0.90), shifting from copiotrophic Proteobacteria toward oligotrophic lineages, whereas fungi retained stronger genotype structure at tasseling (R up to 0.74). Phenotypic and community distances were decoupled at the genotype level. Proteobacteria and Ascomycota formed network backbones whose removal eliminated 81.5% and 93.6% of edges. BSEM reproduced 68–69% of yield variance and resolved coherent phyla → functional guilds → agronomic traits → yield pathways (β = 0.55 for agronomic traits → yield), with cultivar effects ranging from + 0.50 (Nonghua 106) to − 0.49 (Dr. King 825). Machine learning confirmed complementary yield-associated signatures (Rhodanobacter ASV1138, ρ = 0.91).  Conclusion.  Bacteria and fungi obey kingdom-specific assembly rules; Proteobacteria and Ascomycota are structurally indispensable network backbones; and a Bayesian structural equation framework traces interpretable pathways from microbiome features to measured yield, offering testable hypotheses for microbiome-assisted maize breeding.
records.authors: Ban Y, Zhao G, Feng S, Han X, Lü Q, You Y, Huang T, Wang G.

records.title: Bioprospecting the Cultivable Bacteria Associated with Trididemnum maragogi from the Saint Peter and Saint Paul’s Archipelago (Brazil) for Bioactive Metabolites
records.abstract: Abstract    Ascidians and their associated microbiota represent one of the most prolific sources of novel bioactive compounds with application in marine biotechnology. This study investigates the pharmacological potential and metabolic diversity of the bacterial microbiota associated with the ascidian  Trididemnum maragogi  , collected at Saint Peter and Saint Paul’s Archipelago (SPSPA), Brazil. A total of 45 bacterial strains were taxonomically identified via 16S rRNA gene sequencing into 11 distinct genera, with a predominance of  Bacillus  and actinomycetes such as  Micromonospora  ,  Salinispora  , and  Streptomyces  . Crude organic extracts from bacterial cultures were evaluated for antiproliferative activity against human cancer cell lines (501-Mel and HCT-116). Extracts from  Micromonospora  spp. (BRB-810, BRB-814, BRB-832) and  Salinispora  spp. (BRB-803, BRB-808) exhibited potent cytotoxic activity. Metabolomic profiling via HPLC-MS/MS and Feature-Based Molecular Networking (GNPS) enabled the annotation of staurosporines, rifamycins, diketopiperazines, and other bioactive classes, while revealing that approximately 95% of detected features remain unannotated. Furthermore, whole-genome sequencing of  Micromonospora aurantiaca  BRB-832 unveiled 20 biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) related to macrolides, alkylresorcinols, anthracyclines, and novel uncharacterized pathways. These findings highlight  T. maragogi  and its microbial symbionts as a valuable, underexplored source of novel bioactive natural products with biotechnological potential.

records.title: Pathogen profiling of inflammatory eye diseases with metagenomic deep sequencing in a tertiary referral center
records.abstract: Abstract    Background  Intraocular inflammation is a leading cause of blindness globally, but the precise etiology may be unknown in many cases due to challenges with traditional diagnostic modalities. Metagenomic deep sequencing (MDS) is an unbiased method for pathogen detection and may provide advantages over conventional diagnostic methods. Methods  Patients with possible infectious eye diseases were enrolled at the Emory Eye Center from January 2018 to March 2021 for MDS analysis of intraocular fluid samples in addition to standard-of-care conventional testing, including polymerase chain reaction and bacterial and fungal cultures. Samples were sent to the Proctor Foundation at the University of California, San Francisco for analysis. Pathogens were identified through a rapid computational pipeline that analyzed non-host sequences. Data were collected on patient demographics, medical history, ophthalmic exam, and conventional diagnostic results and summarized with respect to MDS findings. Results  Forty-one patients were included in this study with 25 females (61.0%) and a mean age of 55.3 years (SD:±16). The anatomic distribution of uveitis included anterior uveitis in 13 patients (31.7%), anterior/intermediate uveitis in 7 patients (17.1%), posterior uveitis in 4 patients (9.76%), panuveitis in 15 patients (36.6%), and scleritis in 2 patients (4.9%). Intraocular fluid was collected from 25 aqueous humor samples (61.0%) and 16 vitreous samples (39.0%). MDS identified pathogens in 11 of 41 samples (26.8%). The MDS positivity results by the site of sampling were 20.0% (5/25) from the anterior chamber and 37.5% (6/16) from the vitreous cavity. Pathogens identified included bacterial species such as  Klebsiella pneumoniae  ,  Serratia marcescens  , and  Streptococcus pneumoniae  ; viral pathogens including Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) and Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV); fungal organisms such as  Candida parapsilosis  and  Cladosporium  species; and parasites including  Toxocara canis.  Seven patients had an infectious etiology determined by MDS that was not detected by conventional diagnostics. Intraocular and systemic testing was concordant with MDS results in 4 patients. Conclusion  Infectious organisms associated with inflammatory eye diseases presenting to a tertiary referral center are diverse and include fungi, bacteria, parasites, and viruses. The unbiased nature of MDS may be advantageous in these tertiary settings, assisting in diagnostics and guiding appropriate therapies.

records.title: Perspective: Evolutionary Genetics Is the Backbone of Genomic Epidemiology in Fungal Pathogens.
records.abstract: Genome sequencing is rapidly becoming a routine component of outbreak investigation and pathogen surveillance. In human fungal pathogens, however, the analytical framework has often remained centered on a single tree built from variants called against one reference genome. While that representation has been and will continue to be useful, epidemiological inference can also benefit from other approaches drawn from evolutionary genetics. Here, I review the transition from multilocus sequence typing to genome-scale epidemiology in human fungal pathogens, summarize representative successes in Coccidioides, Cryptococcus, Candida auris, Aspergillus fumigatus, Histoplasma, Sporothrix, Pneumocystis, and other fungi, and identify biological and technical sources of error that are still inconsistently addressed. More than a critique, this piece is a call to action. I argue that we need to start treating phylogenetic trees as one layer of evidence within a broader population-genetic framework and not as a stopping point. From a data collection point of view, we need a more robust epidemiological metadata collection scheme. From an analytical point of view, analyses of gene-tree discordance, demographic inference, ancestry, and structural variation can reveal features that a single tree derived from concatenated markers cannot. The amount of public sequence data is no longer the only limiting factor. The next pressing challenge is to translate the data generated by genomic and phylogenetic analyses into reproducible evolutionary inference while preserving and communicating the uncertainty that matters for public-health decisions.
records.authors: Matute DR.

records.title: On the Distribution of Synteny Block Lengths in Prokaryote Genomes under a Neutral Model of Genome Dynamics.
records.abstract: In bacterial and archaeal genomes, functionally linked genes often cluster in operons that enable coregulation of expression of these genes and production of their protein products in stoichiometric amounts. Many operons are shared by genomes of distantly related bacteria and archaea due in part to evolutionary conservation and in part to horizontal gene transfer (HGT). In contrast, similarity between species in their gene order along the chromosome can be merely a result of evolutionary closeness such that synteny has not yet been disrupted by genome dynamic events occurring during evolution. In general, however, accurate differentiation of operons from spurious gene clusters is a non-trivial task that depends on an underlying model of neutral genome evolution. Here, we employ a recently developed stochastic model of genome rearrangement ("jump model") that accounts for HGT across prokaryote species evolving along a phylogenetic tree to infer the size distribution of shared gene strings (synteny blocks) under neutral evolution. Analytic expressions are derived for the expected number of synteny blocks of a given size (or of maximal size) depending on the evolutionary distance between the genomes and the rates of different types of evolutionary events. This analysis is related to the well-studied family of stick-breaking problems, but the discrete structure and stochastic nature of the evolutionary process provide for the development of a simple, independent model. We demonstrate the predictive power of this model by computer simulations of synthetic data as well as by simulating genomes on real trees obtained from the Alignable Tight Genome Clusters database.

records.title: Phylogeography of clinical Burkholderia pseudomallei isolates in Cambodia demonstrates diversity, broad dispersal, and novel genes.
records.abstract: Burkholderia pseudomallei, the causative agent of melioidosis, is ubiquitous in Southeast Asia but remains understudied in many endemic countries. The species' high genetic diversity necessitates large-scale sampling to resolve fine-scale population structure. In countries bordering the Mekong River, the geographic range of B. pseudomallei strains may be increased by water-mediated dispersal. Between 2021 and 2023, we collected and sequenced 253 clinical B. pseudomallei isolates from patients admitted to six Cambodian hospitals and geotagged isolates by patient village. Isolates were genetically diverse and grouped into 11 clades, including one characterized by a chromosomal genomic island containing unique genes absent from other isolates, consistent with local evolution. Comparison with 3,234 publicly available global genomes revealed intermixing between Cambodian and other Southeast Asian isolates but clear distinction from Australian strains. Phylogeographic analyses further demonstrated spatial localization along major waterways, suggesting that river systems, including the Mekong, may contribute to bacterial dissemination in Cambodia. Taken together, these findings demonstrate the importance of localized data sets for contextualizing the population structure and evolution of this diverse pathogen in Southeast Asia.IMPORTANCEBurkholderia pseudomallei is a highly diverse bacterial species with genomic features that vary based on geographic sampling location. Existing data predominantly from Thailand show that isolates from Southeast Asia may be closely related to each other. Here, we sequenced isolates associated with human disease in Cambodia and compared these against genomes from public sequence repositories. We identified many distinct bacterial strains and found that some of these were localized either to the south or in the north of the country. We identified a unique group of genes in one cohort strain with putative roles in bacterial metabolism and genomic recombination. Finally, in a global phylogeny constructed from publicly available genomes, we found that Cambodian isolates intermixed with other Southeast Asian isolates. Our study is the largest genomic study of B. pseudomallei in Cambodia to date, with findings that contribute to the global understanding of the bacterium's diversity and evolution.

records.title: Exploring antimicrobial resistance in wild and domestic animal populations: combining publicly available data with BV-BRC resources to introduce bioinformatics in an undergraduate classroom.
records.abstract: Bioinformatics blends the fields of biology, statistics, computer science, and information technology for the processing and analysis of genomic data. Despite the growing demand for trained bioinformaticians and a positive job market outlook, most undergraduate institutions struggle to integrate bioinformatics into their life science curricula. Educators face numerous barriers to incorporating bioinformatics into their classes, including technical issues and expertise. To address this need, we are developing web-accessible, course-based materials for general microbiology, infectious disease, genomics, and other similar undergraduate and graduate classes that use bioinformatic workflows within the Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center (BV-BRC), one of three National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID)-funded Bioinformatics Resource Centers. Here, we present one such activity: a three-part exercise focused on antimicrobial resistance and metagenomics that uses six publicly available metagenomic samples collected from wild and domestic animal populations to explore the distinctions between their gut microbiomes and their respective antibiotic resistance genes. To analyze community composition and identify antibiotic resistance genes, students use two end-to-end services offered by the BV-BRC: Taxonomic Classification and Metagenomic Read Mapping. This assignment was developed to introduce students to core competencies in the field of bioinformatics and to highlight the BV-BRC as an educational resource for integrating bioinformatics without requiring students and instructors to possess the technical proficiencies and computing resources traditionally needed. We successfully implemented this exercise in an upper-level undergraduate microbiology course, demonstrating the feasibility of using the BV-BRC for bioinformatics education in the classroom.
records.authors: Sheriff J, Capria A, Bowers N, Wattam AR, Poretsky R.

records.title: Biosurfactant production under cold-saline stress is a strain specific trait independent from phylogeny and biosynthetic gene content
records.abstract: Microbial genomes code for far more biosynthetic potential than a single cell typically expresses, but the environmental and cellular controls that determine whether the latent capacity is realised remain poorly understood. Biosurfactants, surface-active metabolites proposed to aid survival in cold and saline habitats, exemplify this gap: capacity is often inferred from genomes or detected chemically, but is rarely linked to the specific conditions that stimulate its production in the same organisms. Here we combine whole-genome sequencing, untargeted LC-MS/MS metabolomics, and quantitative surface-tension assays across 25 bacterial isolates isolated from the cold, hypersaline Qaidam Basin (a terrestrial analogue for ancient Mars) and contrasting marine environments. We show that biosurfactant production is not a fixed lineage trait but a regulated, strain-specific response that emerges under combined cold and salt stress. This response is structured into three tiers: genomic capacity defines the accessible chemical space; the genomic complement of pathway-regulator genes tracks responsiveness; strain-level physiological state determines realised output. Regulatory-gene content, rather than biosynthetic-cluster count, predicted surfactant production across strains. Production was amplified by low temperature and high salinity and showed little phylogenetic signal, with near-clonal strains differing in their stress-response. These findings reshape biochemical adaptation in extreme environments as a problem of conditional activation, not only of genomic potential, but of cellular systems that permit its expression, which requires looking beyond biosynthetic-gene content to the cellular factors that determine whether that potential is expressed.
records.authors: Ullah H, Han Z, Lau Vetter MCY.

records.title: Detection of merbecoviruses in Danish bats using a novel broad-range RT-qPCR assay
records.abstract: Bat-associated merbecoviruses comprise a genetically diverse group of coronaviruses with variable receptor usage and host range, highlighting the need for efficient tools for their surveillance. Here, we developed and optimized a broad-range reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) assay for the detection of bat-associated merbecoviruses, including the lineage previously identified in brown long-eared bats (  Plecotus auritus ) in Denmark.  In silico analysis predicted detection of 898 of 941 (95.4%) merbecovirus sequences, and the assay detected all bat-associated merbecoviruses included in the experimental panel. The assay was applied to 33 bats sampled through the Danish national bat surveillance program in 2025. Merbecovirus RNA was detected in two samples, one from a  P. auritus and one from a Nathusius’ pipistrelle (  Pipistrellus nathusii ), representing the first detection of a merbecovirus in  P. nathusii in Denmark. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing recovered a complete merbecovirus genome from the  P. nathusii sample. Phylogenetic analysis assigned the virus to the MOW clade and showed that it was closely related to the Russian MOW15-22 virus, sharing 98.67% nucleotide identity across the complete genome and 99.85% amino acid identity in the spike protein. Limited sequence data obtained from the  P. auritus sample was consistent with the merbecovirus lineage previously identified in this species in Denmark. Together, these findings demonstrate the utility of broad-range RT-qPCR combined with metagenomic sequencing for surveillance and genomic characterization of bat-associated merbecoviruses.
records.authors: Johnston CM, Moreno A, Lelli D, Marving EL, Baagøe HJ, Elmeros M, Fjederholt ET, Lohse L, Rasmussen TB.

records.title: Metagenomic Characterisation of Antimicrobial Resistance Gene Profiles in Shrimp Farm, Pond Microbiomes From the Southern Coastal Areas of Kerala, India
records.abstract: Abstract  Aquaculture is the fastest growing animal protein production sector in worldwide and Asia contributing annually with about 90% of the global seafood production. Penaeus monodon commonly known as the giant tiger prawn is a marine crustacean that is widely reared for food. The global rise in antibiotic resistance vitalised by indiscriminate antibiotic usage presents a significant public health challenge. The detrimental impact of antibiotic resistance includes the persistence of antimicrobial residues in fish and the surroundings. It gradually leads to the accumulation of resistance genes with the consequent contamination of the environment and the human food chain. There is a scarcity of data regarding the antibiotic resistance of shrimp aquaculture farms and ponds in Kerala. In the present study the metagenomic analysis revealed the occurrence of AMR genes across the southern coastal areas of Kerala, India. The pooled shrimp gut, water and sediment samples were subjected to metagenomic analysis. The antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes were determined by various databases like RGI (Resistance Gene Identifier) and the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD).In addition to this, KEGG and COG databases revealed the important biochemical pathways, cellular functions and specific protein ortholog of bacterial and archaea genomes of the studied locations. The outcomes imply noticeable regional differences in presence of AMR genes in the shrimp gut, sediment and water samples of the different southern coastal areas of Kerala.
records.authors: S DCCSDCC, Sabu KKSDKK.

records.title: Lineage-specific metabolic transcription across environmental gradients in geothermal microbial communities.
records.abstract: Understanding how environmental heterogeneity shapes microbial metabolism remains a central challenge. While metagenomics has revealed extensive metabolic potential, how these functions are transcriptionally represented across environmental gradients and microbial lineages remains unclear. Here, we integrated genome-resolved metagenomics and metatranscriptomics with co-expression network analysis to examine metabolic transcription across geothermal environments. Across Tengchong hot springs, metabolic transcription varies with pH, temperature, and organic matter. Acidic, organic-rich springs show prominent heterotrophic and sulfur-metabolism-related transcription, with Mesoaciditogales primarily associated with coenzyme and purine biosynthesis and Thermoplasmatales with sulfur reduction and central carbon metabolism. In contrast, non-acidic thermal springs show carbon fixation transcripts from Aquificales and Cyanobacteriales and sulfur oxidation transcripts from Aquificales and Deinococcales. Under more extreme conditions, carbon-fixation pathways become less diverse and increasingly biased toward energetically efficient strategies, while nitrogen-cycling transcription remains restricted. These findings reveal how microbial functional programs and their lineage associations reflect environmental heterogeneity across geothermal habitats.
records.authors: Chen XX, Xie QJ, Qu YN, Tang Q, Cai C, Chen LX, Hua ZS.

records.title: Northern palsa and peat ecosystem microbiomes are potentially supported by hydrogen and carbon monoxide metabolism
records.abstract: Northern peatland and permafrost ecosystems are facing rapid changes, with increasing temperatures, permafrost thaw and shifts in hydrology. Characterizing microbial communities and metabolic potential from the soils and associated water bodies is crucial to understanding the changes in biogeochemical cycling in these ecosystems. For this, samples were collected and sequenced from subarctic palsa and peat soils, along with samples from associated thaw ponds and streams. Metagenomics was utilized in describing the microbiome and its metabolic potential in these environments. Palsa soils hosted microbial communities that were distinct from the peatland soils, ponds and stream waters. Soils and their adjacent ponds shared taxa, and peat soils and ponds also shared taxa with the streams, unlike palsa soils which were likely more hydrologically isolated. Based on metabolic marker gene ratio for denitrification [(nirS+nirK)/nosZ], palsa soils had the strongest potential to be a source of nitrous oxide (N2O) out of all the sample types. Marker genes for hydrogen gas (H2) and carbon monoxide (CO) utilization were abundant across soil environments and metagenome assembled genomes, suggesting that trace gas oxidation is likely one of the key energy sources for microbiomes. In the palsa ponds and peat soils pmoA, marker gene for methanotrophy, was the most abundant compared to the other sample types.
records.authors: Tuomela N, Thomas DN, Kaartokallio H, Välikangas T, Hultman J.

records.title: Isolation, genomic and comparative proteomic characterization of three lytic Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteriophages from wastewater in Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso
records.abstract: Abstract    Background.  Pseudomonas aeruginosa  is a leading cause of opportunistic and healthcare-associated infections and is listed by the World Health Organization among the pathogens for which new therapeutic options are most urgently needed. Lytic bacteriophages are one of the few alternatives that can be deployed rapidly and at low cost, but phage collections and phage genome sequences remain very unevenly distributed geographically, and West Africa is particularly under-represented. Wastewater, which combines high bacterial densities with continuous inputs of faecal, hospital and industrial effluent, is the most productive environment for recovering phages that are locally adapted to circulating clinical strains. We therefore set out to isolate lytic phages active against clinical  P. aeruginosa  isolates from wastewater in Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso, and to characterize their genomes. Results.  Twenty-eight lytic phages were isolated from five wastewater sites using six  P. aeruginosa  host strains, and screened against a panel of eleven clinical and reference strains. Host ranges were broad: eleven isolates lysed at least ten of the eleven strains and three lysed all eleven, while only two isolates were restricted to four strains. Five phages were selected for whole-genome sequencing and three yielded complete, high-quality assemblies. All three belong to the class  Caudoviricetes  . vB_PaeM_CM0001 (57,614 bp; 63.5% GC; 88 CDSs) is a member of the family  Mesyanzhinovviridae  , subfamily  Bradleyvirinae  , genus  Abidjanvirus  . vB_PaeP_CM0002 (43,491 bp) and vB_PaeP_CM0003 (43,177 bp), each encoding 65 CDSs with 62.3–62.6% GC, belong to the family  Autographiviridae  , subfamily  Krylovirinae  , genus  Phikmvvirus  . Intergenomic similarities indicate that vB_PaeM_CM0001 is a new isolate of an existing  Abidjanvirus  species, whereas vB_PaeP_CM0002 and vB_PaeP_CM0003 represent two new  Phikmvvirus  species. The two  Phikmvvirus  genomes share 91.9% nucleotide identity and 62 orthogroups and are fully collinear with each other and with their closest relatives; their divergence is confined to nucleotide substitution and to a single 2.0 kb region spanning the tail fibre locus. vB_PaeM_CM0001 shares no detectable orthogroups with them. Conclusions.  These three genomes are the first  P. aeruginosa  phage genomes reported from Burkina Faso. Two of them represent new species. Their broad host ranges, strictly lytic gene repertoires and absence of resistance determinants make them credible starting points for a national phage bank and for future therapeutic evaluation.
records.authors: Gnada K, Silga EW, Essoh CY, Yao RK, Sanou AQ, Ouangraoua A, Gomgnimbou MK.

records.title: DIA quantitative proteomics reveals the regulatory mechanism of aroma-producing yeast on the formation of Xuanwei ham flavour: microbial fermentation and protein degradation.
records.abstract: To clarify the regulatory effects of three aroma-producing yeasts (Rhodotorula mucilaginosa, Yamadazyma triangularis, and Debaryomyces hansenii) on microbial community structure and muscle protein expression during Xuanwei ham fermentation, this study used Xuanwei ham inoculated with the three yeasts as the research material. High-throughput sequencing was applied to analyze changes in microbial community composition and diversity. Data-independent acquisition (DIA) quantitative proteomics was used to identify differentially expressed proteins, combined with Gene Ontology (GO) functional enrichment, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway, and protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analyses. The results showed that inoculated yeasts significantly reshaped the bacterial and fungal communities of ham, markedly inhibited the overgrowth of Aspergillus, and enriched functional microorganisms such as Staphylococcus and Serratia, with significant differences among groups (P < 0.05). A total of 3401 proteins were identified, were screened. These proteins were mainly enriched in pathways including carboxylic acid metabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, myofibril depolymerization, mitochondrial energy metabolism, and regulated muscle protein degradation and flavour precursor formation through the core protein interaction network. These findings indicate that aroma-producing yeasts improve the quality of Xuanwei ham by optimizing microbial community structure and regulating muscle protein metabolism, providing a scientific basis for the development of starter cultures suitable for dry-cured ham and precise quality control.
records.authors: Ren R, Zhou N, Xun W, Li J, Du Y, Yang Y, Tan J, Tang S, Yang K, Weng C, Dong H, Pu E, Liao G, Wang G.

records.title: A validated low-abundance uterine microbial signature associated with chronic endometritis.
records.abstract: BackgroundChronic endometritis (CE) is a persistent inflammatory endometrial disorder associated with infertility, recurrent implantation failure, and pregnancy loss. While previous microbiome studies have focused on Lactobacillus depletion and common genital tract bacteria, low-abundance microbial lineages remain poorly characterised.ObjectiveTo identify reproducible low-abundance microbial signatures associated with CE and evaluate their robustness through external validation and complementary analyses.MethodsUterine lavage specimens from infertile women with CE (n = 29) and non-CE controls (n = 16) were analysed by 16S rRNA sequencing in a discovery cohort. An independent cohort of 58 participants was used for external validation. CE was diagnosed by hysteroscopy and CD138 immunohistochemistry (≥5 stromal plasma cells/10 high-power fields). Multiple negative controls were included, and contaminants were assessed using decontam. Prespecified analyses included cervicovaginal source tracking, shotgun metagenomics in a subset, cytokine profiling, and post-treatment follow-up.ResultsCE samples exhibited increased richness and modestly higher diversity. Presence/absence-based beta diversity demonstrated clearer separation between CE and controls. CE was associated with enrichment of Patescibacteria, Planctomycetota, Bdellovibrionota, and selected archaeal-lineage signals. After contaminant filtering, major rare-lineage features remained enriched. Patescibacteria and Bdellovibrio-related signals correlated with CD138-positive plasma-cell counts and inflammatory cytokines. A nested discovery model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.84, and the locked marker panel achieved an AUC of 0.81 in external validation.ConclusionsCE is associated with a reproducible low-abundance microbial signature in uterine lavage samples. These findings highlight candidate microbial lineages for further investigation but do not establish causality or uterine residency.
records.authors: Ha S, Lv C, Cui J, Yu H, Sun L.

records.title: Host control and regulation of human anellovirus persistence
records.abstract: SUMMARY  Anelloviruses are the most abundant and diverse eukaryotic viruses known to infect humans and can persist throughout our lifetimes. Despite their ubiquity, the host factors governing their physiologic distribution and abundance remain poorly understood. Here, we construct a viral pangenome of 2,023 strains to quantify anellovirus DNA in >1.1 million participants spanning three genetic biobanks. Genome-wide association studies identify 121 loci linked to viral persistence, predominantly via immune regulation by NF-κB signaling. Further, we associate variable anellovirus detection with conditions characterized by immune dysfunction, including lymphoid malignancies. By screening 3.2 petabases of human single-cell sequencing data, we identify myeloid progenitors in the bone marrow as a prominent site of anellovirus transcription in vivo. Finally, Perturb-seq of anellovirus proteins reveals that anellovirus ORF2, particularly from Alphatorquevirus, attenuates TNF-α-induced NF-κB signaling, connecting host genetic variation, cellular context, and viral immunomodulation to characterize the persistence of the eukaryotic human virome’s most abundant component.

records.title: Investigations into the Virome of Grasses Growing in the Environment of Sugarcane in Florida.
records.abstract: Samples of 26 plant species and the aphid Melanaphis sorghi were collected in the Everglades Agricultural Area (South Florida) from 2017-2019 to investigate the virome of grasses growing in the environment of sugarcane. Leaf samples were obtained from cultivated as well as from wild species. Detection and identification of the viruses present in 388 plant and 11 aphid samples were performed using the virion-associated nucleic acid (VANA)-metagenomics approach. Twenty-four viruses were identified, and 12 plant species and the aphid were infected by at least one virus. Fourteen of these 24 viruses were known viruses whereas 10 were putatively new virus species, including an alphaendornavirus (family Endornaviridae), an alphanucleorhabdovirus (Rhabdoviridae), an amalgavirus (Amalgaviridae), a marafivirus (Tymoviridae), a mastrevirus (Geminiviridae), and a sobemovirus (Solemoviridae). The highest number of viruses was detected in Columbus grass and sorghum (10 and 11, respectively). Sugarcane mosaic virus (SCMV; Potyvirus sacchari, Potyviridae) and maize chlorotic dwarf virus (Waikavirus zeae, Secoviridae) were the most widespread viruses, occurring in nine and seven plant species, respectively, and were also detected in the aphid. In a phylogenetic tree constructed with partial genome sequences (4,000 nt) of SCMV obtained from GenBank and herein, virus isolates from eight plant species were distributed in three different lineages, thus suggesting significant diversity of this virus in Florida. Only two Saccharum-infecting viruses, SCMV and sugarcane yellow leaf virus (Polerovirus SCYLV, Solemoviridae) were detected in sorghum and other grasses. These plants may, therefore, serve as putative reservoirs for the causal agents of two sugarcane diseases in Florida.
records.authors: Rott PC, Filloux D, Daugrois JH, Fernandez E, Julian C, Galzi S, Beiriger R, Odero DC, Sood SG, Roumagnac P.

records.title: Genomic and phenotypic characterization of four foodborne Vibrio harveyi: Insights into antimicrobial resistance, secretion systems, and ecological fitness.
records.abstract: Vibrio harveyi is a prominent marine and seafood-borne pathogen that poses a significant threat to global aquaculture and public health. To better understand its adaptive evolution, four V. harveyi isolates recovered from Chinese seafood markets were comprehensively characterized using an integrated framework of whole-genome sequencing, comparative genomics, and phenotypic profiling. The genomes ranged from 5.7 to 5.8 Mb and exhibited high overall genomic conservation, with ANI values exceeding 98%, but substantial variation was observed in accessory genomic regions. Phylogenomic analysis separated the isolates into three major lineages, with Vh1067 showing the greatest divergence from the other isolates. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing revealed widespread resistance to β-lactams, while Vh1067 displayed a multidrug-resistant phenotype associated with blaVEB-1, tet(C), sul2, floR, ereA, and multiple aminoglycoside resistance determinants within a Tn3-type transposon. All isolates exhibited optimal growth at 2-3% NaCl and retained both swimming and swarming motility, whereas biofilm-forming capacity varied substantially among strains. Comparative analysis identified extensive diversity in T6SS, T3SS, Rhs-associated systems, toxin-antitoxin modules, and other virulence-associated determinants. All isolates exhibited bactericidal activity against Escherichia coli, with Vh2287 and Vh2376 showing the strongest competitive effects. This study highlights substantial genomic variation among the four seafood-associated V. harveyi isolates and underscores potential associations between secretion system features, antimicrobial resistance, and environmental adaptability.
records.authors: Hui M, Li B, Huang X, Ding F, Liu H, Wang X, Jiang X, Lu P, Chen K, Zeng P, Dong N, Chen S, Cheng Q.

records.title: Massive inter-animal horizontal gene transfer contributes to stress tolerance in the fungus gnat Bradysia coprophila
records.abstract: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in animals is thought to be rare and largely restricted to transfers from non-animal sources. In contrast to this expectation, we discovered that 9.2% of the protein-coding genes in the genome of the dark-winged fungus gnat Bradysia coprophila (order: Diptera, family: Sciaridae) are of potential HGT origin. Most of these genes have phylogenetic affinity with sequences from other distantly related arthropods that inhabit a shared soil-dwelling niche with B. coprophila. We show that these findings are inconsistent with genomic contamination or widespread gene loss and instead suggest a level of inter-animal HGT that is, to our knowledge, unprecedented. Consistent with their potential functional importance, ~75% of putative B. coprophila horizontally transferred genes (HTGs) are transcribed, and nearly all are shared across multiple sciarid fungus gnat species that diverged tens of millions of years ago. Further, domain annotations suggest that HTGs participate in diverse processes potentially important to B. coprophila ecology. We tested the functions of eight putative B. coprophila HTGs through transgenic expression in the fly Drosophila melanogaster and the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and found evidence that HGT has likely endowed B. coprophila with the novel capability to biosynthesize NAD+, as well as enhanced capacity to withstand stressors imposed by arsenic, cyanide, alkylating agents, and reactive oxygen species. Our findings reveal a previously underappreciated contribution of inter-animal genetic exchange to the evolution of genomic, physiological, and ecological novelty.

records.title: Physiological, behavioral, and genetic factors that shape interactions in the plant growth-promoting maize rhizosphere synthetic community.
records.abstract: Profiling microbiomes is an important way to understand the function and composition of communities in the wild, but natural microbiomes are often highly complex and often unamenable to experimentation to reveal cause-and-effect relationships. By using a small group of cultivable strains to represent those found in the wild, synthetic communities are one solution to this problem. Here we describe the maize rhizosphere synthetic community (MARSc), a genome-enabled 31-member bacterial community representative of the diversity found on the roots of maize grown in Iowa soils. This community is built around Pseudomonas putida KT2440, a model maize rhizosphere colonist and synthetic biology chassis. We characterized microbe-microbe interactions and biofilm formation of MARSc members in a variety of environmental contexts, finding that both behaviors are broadly controlled by nutrient levels. Genomic analysis and microbiome profiling of these organisms revealed that annotated biofilm genes (such as surface attachment and exopolysaccharide production) were significantly correlated with rhizosphere abundance, but neither trait correlated to in vitro biofilm formation. In vitro interaction assay findings were surprisingly consistent with co-correlations of rhizosphere abundance among MARSc members on roots. Finally, we found that when applied to the roots, MARSc can increase maize biomass (dry weight) by up to 40%-50% under varying nitrogen fertilization levels. Altogether, MARSc is a useful tool for identifying some of the factors influencing rhizosphere microbiome assembly and will be a strong foundation for further work in this area.IMPORTANCEThe microbiome surrounding the roots of plants can play an integral role in plant health and growth, and it is composed of thousands of species of microbes that are specific to the plant and environment it is grown in. However, due to this complexity, little is known about the means by which microbiomes form. In this study, we developed the maize rhizosphere synthetic community (MARSc) to gain a better understanding of the formation and function of microbiomes on the roots of plants. This consortium consists of 30 bacterial isolates plus Pseudomonas putida KT2440, a model maize root colonist. In this study, we investigated the interactions between these organisms, their genomes, cultural characteristics, and growth on the roots of maize. We show that MARSc increases maize growth under low nitrogen fertilizer, suggesting it will be a useful tool for identifying the mechanisms behind microbiome formation and plant growth promotion.
records.authors: Paulsen AA, Roghair Stroud MN, Halverson LJ.

records.title: An Enzyme-Mediated Duplex Exponential Amplification Assay for Rapid Detection of Plasmodiophora brassicae.
records.abstract: Clubroot, caused by the soilborne obligate biotrophic protist Plasmodiophora brassicae, substantially reduces the yield and quality of cruciferous crops worldwide. In this study, an enzyme-mediated duplex exponential amplification (EmDEA) assay was developed for rapid detection of P. brassicae in extracted DNA. By comparing the P. brassicae strain 3A genome with representative bacterial, fungal, and oomycete genome assemblies, we identified 157 candidate regions that showed no detectable matches in the selected non-target genomes under the specified alignment criteria. Pbspec1, a fragment within the annotated locus PBTT_08698, was selected based on computational non-target screening, within-species conservation, and suitability for assay design. PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing were used to validate the target fragment. Six forward primers, six reverse primers, and six RNA probes were screened, and F2-R4-RNA2 was selected for subsequent EmDEA experiments. Using serial dilutions of purified recombinant plasmid DNA, the F2-R4-RNA2 combination consistently detected template concentrations of 1.0 × 103 copies/μL and above. No amplification was observed from the 12 non-target fungal or bacterial organisms. The assay detected P. brassicae in DNA extracted from four infected root samples and three naturally infested soil samples. All tested positive samples produced detectable fluorescence during a programmed 20-min run on a portable isothermal fluorescence instrument. These results support the potential use of EmDEA for rapid preliminary screening of P. brassicae following DNA extraction.
records.authors: Zhang Y, Qian K, Chang S, Chen Y, He M, Hu J, Zhao J, Mao Z, Ling J.

records.title: Dual-Track Genome Evolution in Curvularia muehlenbeckiae Suggests Host Jump to Pecan via Putative Mini-Chromosome Acquisition and Zn2Cys6-Centric Coadaptation.
records.abstract: Curvularia muehlenbeckiae (P-6) is an emerging fungal pathogen responsible for severe leaf spot disease in pecan (Carya illinoinensis); however, the genomic mechanisms underlying its host jump remain elusive. Here, we present the first near-complete genome assembly of P-6 (33.77 Mb), revealing a karyotype of 14 chromosomes, including two putative mini-chromosomes (Chr13/Chr14) that harbor 17 and 22% of the pathogen's candidate virulence factors, respectively. Notably, Chr14 contains a transposase-flanked secondary metabolite biosynthetic gene cluster, a configuration often associated with horizontal gene transfer in fungi. Pan-genome analysis exposed a conserved Curvularia virulome (99.55% of P-6 virulence orthogroups) alongside lineage-specific expansions of major facilitator superfamily (MFS) transporters (299 genes) and Zn2Cys6 transcription factors (126 genes) that facilitate adaptation to woody hosts-a signature distinct from graminaceous-infecting Curvularia species. Time-resolved transcriptomics revealed a Zn2Cys6-centric biphasic infection strategy: an early phase (0.5 h postinoculation [hpi]) governed by Zn2Cys6 hubs regulating MFS transporters and reactive oxygen species detoxification genes, and a late necrotrophic phase (72 hpi) mediated by distinct Zn2Cys6 factors inducing carbohydrate metabolism (AMY1 and INV2) and toxin production (PKS7 and NRPS3). Weighted Gene Coexpression Network Analysis confirmed stage-specific modules associated with these Zn2Cys6 transcription factors. Ecological profiling indicated optimal growth at 28°C and pH 5.0 to 6.0, consistent with subtropical disease epidemiology. Our findings support a dual-track evolutionary model where putative mini-chromosomes may facilitate virulence gene acquisition, while correlated expansions of Zn2Cys6 transcription factors and MFS transporters form a coregulated network associated with a biphasic infection strategy. The identification of these hubs will provide promising targets for eco-friendly management of pecan leaf spot.

records.title: Dehalobacter-mediated reductive dechlorination of the organophosphorus insecticide chlorpyrifos in mangrove sediments.
records.abstract: Mangrove sediments are important sinks for organic contaminants, including the widely used chlorinated organophosphorus insecticide chlorpyrifos (CPF). Although CPF degradation under oxic conditions has been extensively studied, its anaerobic transformation in reducing coastal environments remains poorly understood. Here, a mangrove sediment-derived anaerobic enrichment culture achieved nearly complete transformation of 10 mg L-1 CPF within 10 days. Ultraperformance liquid chromatography-Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometry (UPLCOrbitrap-HRMS) revealed the formation of a mono-dechlorinated CPF product, which was tentatively assigned as O,Odiethyl O-(3,5-dichloro-2-pyridinyl) phosphorothioate based on tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) evidence and density functional theory (DFT) calculations of C-Cl bond dissociation energies. The enrichment culture also reductively dechlorinated 3,5,6-trichloro-2-pyridinol (TCP), a common CPF transformation product, primarily to 5,6-dichloro-2-pyridinol, with Ecological Structure-Activity Relationships (ECOSAR) modeling predicting lower aquatic toxicity for the dechlorinated products than for their parent compounds. 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and metagenomic analyses revealed marked enrichment of Dehalobacter during active CPF transformation, strongly implicating this organohalide-respiring lineage in CPF dechlorination. A high-quality Dehalobacter metagenome-assembled genome harboring 39 rdhA homologs was recovered. Integrated metatranscriptomic and metaproteomic analyses further prioritized four candidate reductive dehalogenases (CPF-RDH1/2/3/9), with CPF-RDH2 showing the strongest proteomic support. Together, these findings uncover an overlooked anaerobic transformation route of CPF through direct reductive dechlorination and highlight the potential role of Dehalobacter-associated organohalide respiration in the environmental fate of chlorinated organophosphorus contaminants in mangrove sediments.
records.authors: Li J, Zhong Y, Yang S, Wu J, Zhang Y, Zeng Y, Song J, Zhu X, Li D, Ling J, Yu Z, Häggblom MM, Peng P.

records.title: A generic residue-numbering system for microbial rhodopsins.
records.abstract: Microbial rhodopsins are photoreceptors with a conserved seven-transmembrane core architecture that use the chromophore retinal-a vitamin A derivative-to convert light absorption into ion transport, signaling, and enzymatic activity. Since their discovery half a century ago, genome sequencing has uncovered thousands of these proteins across archaea, bacteria, eukaryotes, and viruses, revealing a diverse functional repertoire that includes ion pumps and channels, transducer activators, and enzyme/channel regulators. Although the structure of the seven-transmembrane bundle core and the retinal-binding pocket is highly conserved, the sequence identity across major classes is low. This low sequence identity, combined with the rapidly expanding number of microbial rhodopsins identified by metagenomics, makes direct comparisons across the superfamily increasingly difficult. Here, we introduce a generic residue-numbering system for microbial rhodopsins (MO numbering system), a structure-guided framework anchored to the retinal-binding pocket that enables consistent residue comparison across even the most divergent family members. Analyzing 129 structures and approximately 40,000 sequences, we demonstrate its utility by analyzing sequence-structure-function relationships across the superfamily, including previously uncharacterized members. The MO numbering system provides a common language for organizing the growing repertoire of microbial rhodopsins, integrating structural, spectroscopic, and electrophysiological data, and engineering next-generation optogenetic tools.
records.authors: Hidber FS, Tajima S, Kishi KE, Nishimura Y, Yoshizawa S, Deupi X, Kato HE.

records.title: Discovery of Molecular Factors in the Non-CYP51A Route for Tebuconazole Resistance: An Adaptive Laboratory Evolution Research.
records.abstract: Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a well-established model organism for studying antifungal responses and resistance mechanisms. Its well-characterized genetics and conserved cellular processes provide a useful framework for investigating responses to azole fungicides such as tebuconazole. The present work aimed to discover molecular factors underlying tebuconazole resistance in S. cerevisiae. For this purpose, genetically stable, tebuconazole-resistant S. cerevisiae mutants were obtained by adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) and were investigated at the physiological and genomic level to determine molecular factors responsible for the tebuconazole resistance. ALE analysis showed that tebuconazole-resistant mutants could be developed without using any physical and chemical mutagens prior to the selection, demonstrating a potential mutagenic effect of tebuconazole. The resistance analyses showed that the mutants could still survive at tebuconazole levels up to 40 μg/mL (130 μM). The cross-resistance and cell wall degradation analyses revealed that the selected three mutants exhibited resistance to cell membrane disruption (0.006% SDS), acid stress (30 mM acetic acid), lignocellulosic hydrolysate stress (8 mM vanillin), antifungal stress (100 μg/mL prochloraz), oxidative stress (1 mM H2O2), and cell wall disruption (lyticase), compared to the wild-type strain. Whole genome sequencing (WGS) analysis indicated that three mutants possessed 16 common nonsynonymous variations, and they were distributed into eight genes (Q0182, FLO9, FIT1, COS8, YHL008C, HSP150, YMR057C, and YMR306C-A) independent of the CYP51A pathway. Biological process annotation analysis by STRING revealed that the mutant proteins and their interacting partners were associated with cell wall-related functions (Hsp150p), iron metabolism (Fit1p), flocculation (Flo9p), and largely uncharacterized biological processes (Cos8p and Q0182). According to YEASTRACT analysis to determine the potential transcription factors responsible for tebuconazole resistance, Yap1p, Pdr3p, and Rpn4p were identified as common transcriptional regulators of the six mutated genes found in the three mutants, suggesting that these transcription factors may contribute to the development of tebuconazole resistance. The findings of this study suggested that FLO9, FIT1, COS8, HSP150, YHL008C, Q0182, YMR057C, and YMR306C-A were novel genes whose genetic variations were associated with tebuconazole resistance through a non-CYP51A (ERG11)-mediated mechanism.
records.authors: Kurt H, Altan H, Taş F, Yurdagül H, Velioğlu HM, Sürmeli Y.

records.title: A  Staphylococcus  phage recombination cassette that enables recombineering across distant bacteria
records.abstract: Modifying bacterial genomes with phage recombinases, a process termed recombineering, has enabled precise genome editing, but its reach is limited by host specificity: each new organism generally requires its own recombinase to be identified and optimized. Using known phage recombination genes as synteny anchors, we mined  Staphylococcus genomes and recovered a diverse collection of phage recombination cassettes, spanning the RAD52-like annealase superfamily (Sak, Erf) and the RAD51/RecA-like Sak4 family. Functional testing of representatives in  S. aureus identified several highly efficient systems that support recombineering. We engineered the most efficient of these into a single-plasmid tool that yields markerless editing in  S. aureus in four days. Notably, where other recombineering systems rely on host-specific factors for nuclease evasion and ssDNA loading, this cassette encodes both activities itself: a predicted broad-spectrum nuclease inhibitor and a dedicated single-stranded DNA-binding protein. We therefore tested the cassette across phylogenetically distant hosts, and observed recombination in  Streptococcus pyogenes, Enterococcus faecium, Francisella novicida , and  Escherichia coli . These results identify a self-sufficient class of phage recombination systems and provide a portable tool for genetic manipulation in bacteria that lack established recombineering methods.
records.authors: Maguin P, Aghahosseini M, Brodmann M, Chen V, Zhu J, Szenkiel K, Marraffini LA, Varble A.

records.title: Exploring the wild soybean derived cross-kingdom SynCom for mitigating continuous cropping obstacles: potential links to fungus-associated bacterial dispersal and root exudate reprogramming.
records.abstract: Continuous cropping obstacles severely constrain global soybean productivity, yet scalable biological solutions remain limited. While continuous monoculture typically causes yield decline in cultivated soybean, its wild relative persists in the same soils for decades without apparent decline, suggesting the presence of a protective native rhizosphere. By integrating long-term field surveys, metagenomic profiling, and stress-directed cultivation, we established a multi-tiered rational design framework to construct a functionally complementary, cross-kingdom synthetic community from wild soybean rhizospheres. Using a reductionist hydroponic model to isolate direct microbial effects from the complexities of the soil matrix, a simplified bacterial-fungal consortium successfully mitigated CCO-associated stresses. Specifically, SSC mitigated the growth inhibition caused by continuous cropping obstacles, enhanced disease resistance, and reduced the accumulation of phenolic autotoxins in the rhizosphere. Regarding the mechanism of action, compartmentalized experiments suggest that fungal hyphae can act as bacterial carriers, facilitating bacterial dispersal and increasing the accumulation of beneficial bacteria in the plant rhizosphere, thereby promoting rapid root colonization. SSC reprograms root exudates, significantly upregulating the biosynthesis of flavone and flavonol biosynthesis, which may act as chemotactic inducers to recruit beneficial microorganisms to soybean roots. Our research reveals that the wild soybean microbiome is an exploitable reservoir, providing a practical framework for translating the resilience of the native microbiome into sustainable agricultural solutions.
records.authors: Song W, Wei Y, Tang L, Wong FL, Lam HM, Prasad R, Zhang S.

records.title: Unprecedented urban freshwater microviral survey highlights shift from sewage to river water communities
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Microviruses are abundant yet still poorly resolved components of virosphere, particularly across urban freshwater continua. Here, we investigated complete microvirus genomes recovered from sewage water (SW), treated wastewater (TW), and river water (RW) along an urban SW–TW–RW continuum, providing an extensive genomic dataset of 18,449 complete genomes grouped into 825 genera. This catalog enabled a high-resolution assessment of microvirus diversity, taxonomy, and ecological distribution across anthropized aquatic compartments. All currently described microvirus orders were detected, with  Gokushovirales dominating the dataset and  Betagokushoviridae emerging as the most prevalent family in TW and RW samples. In contrast,  Alpavirales were enriched in SW but strongly depleted after treatment, consistent with their association with gut-related bacterial hosts. Alpha- and beta-diversity analyses showed that water type was the main driver of microvirus community structure, whereas seasonal effects were weak and not robust under the hydrological conditions of the sampling year. Wastewater treatment plants thus acted as strong biological filters, reshaping viral assemblages and selecting compartment-specific microvirus populations. Finally, the pronounced and reproducible shifts observed across the continuum suggest that selected microvirus groups may serve as promising bioindicators of anthropogenic influence in freshwater systems.
records.authors: Langlais A, Dumont C, Mougin J, Rechdaoui-Guérin S, Roose-Amsaleg C, Enault F, Quaiser A.

records.title: RubisCO-encoding methanotrophs elicit a coordinated transcriptional response to carbon dioxide limitation
records.abstract: The methanotroph  Methylococcus capsulatus encodes the carbon dioxide (CO  2 )-fixing enzyme ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RubisCO), which, along with CO  2 and methane (CH  4 ), are required for growth of this bacterium. This unique, dual one-carbon metabolism is present in phylogenetically diverse methanotrophs and is likely widespread in nature, but the connection between organic and inorganic carbon metabolism in these methanotrophs is unclear. Here we used a systems approach to investigate the requisite role of CO  2 in  M. capsulatus metabolism and physiology. We show that atmospheric CO  2 levels are sufficient for  M. capsulatus cultivation, and that CO  2 assimilation is linked to cellular redox balance. In the absence of CO  2 ,  M. capsulatus elicits a global transcriptional response that includes induction of RubisCO- and other inorganic carbon assimilation-encoding genes with a concomitant decrease in ribosome biogenesis and nitrogen assimilation genes typical of a bacterial stringent response. This CO  2 starvation response balances biosynthesis with carbon availability. Genetic and biochemical evidence show that a LysR-type transcriptional regulator (CbbR) activates RubisCO and other CO  2 assimilation gene transcription via direct promoter binding in response to elevated intracellular RubisCO substrate, ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, in CO  2 -starved cells. These results offer insights into the essentiality of CO  2 for  M. capsulatus metabolism and establish a function for CbbR-family regulators in methanotrophs beyond their canonical association with CO  2 fixation in autotrophic bacteria.  Significance  Methanotrophic bacteria are the primary biological sink of atmospheric methane and represent candidates to develop methane mitigation biotechnologies. Several methanotrophs encode the carbon dioxide-fixation enzyme, RubisCO, enabling them to use carbon dioxide and methane, but the role of carbon dioxide in their metabolism and physiology is not understood. Here, we identified how a RubisCO-encoding methanotroph,  Methylococcus capsulatus , responds to carbon dioxide starvation. The methanotrophs alter their gene expression to produce proteins that facilitate carbon dioxide capture, a phenotype like that observed in carbon dioxide-starved autotrophic and phototrophic bacteria. These findings show how methanotrophs adapt to changing environmental conditions and emphasize evolutionary relationships between methanotrophs and autotrophs. This knowledge can also guide the use of methanotrophs for reducing climate-active atmospheric gases.
records.authors: Lee SA, Henard JM, Yu Y, Henard CA.

records.title: Beyond the CaCl₂ Brine: Transient Microbial Communities at the Edge of Habitability in lifeless Don Juan Pond, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Antarctica
records.abstract: Abstract    Background  Don Juan Pond (DJP), located in the McMurdo Dry Valleys of Antarctica, is one of the most extreme aquatic environments on Earth due to its CaCl₂-rich brines, low water activity, exceptional chaotropicity, subzero temperatures, intense solar radiation, and recurrent desiccation. Although the central DJP brine has long been considered largely inhabitable, the surrounding basin seasonally harbors temporary streams, ponds, and sparse microbial mat. Here, we investigated the diversity, ecological organization, and environmental factor chaping the structure of microbial communities inhabiting these peripheral habitats by integrating hydrochemical analyses, in situ reflectance spectroscopy, DNA metabarcoding, and ecological network analysis.  Results  No DNA suitable for PCR amplification was recovered from the central CaCl₂ brine. In contrast, peripheral streams and ponds supported diverse prokaryotic, microeukaryotic, and fungal communities, with the highest alpha diversity consistently observed in the hydrologically heterogeneous S1 stream system. Prokaryotic assemblages were primarily associated with salinity-related variables, including chlorinity and Mg/Ca ratios, whereas eukaryotic and fungal communities were more strongly correlated with hyperspectral indices indicative of photosynthetic biomass. Transient habitats also hosted micro-metazoans, including rotifers, tardigrades, and nematodes, indicating ecological refugia capable of sustaining complex trophic interactions under polyextreme conditions. Hyperspectral indices successfully discriminated active microbial mats from inactive sedimentary crusts and were significantly associated with the distribution of multiple bacterial, fungal, and microeukaryotic taxa. Network analyses revealed highly interconnected multi-domain communities composed of bacteria, fungi, algae, protists, and microbial grazers.  Conclusions  The presence of life in the Don Juan Pond basin appears to be largely restricted to temporary habitats supported by seasonal meltwater inputs rather than the central CaCl₂ saturated brine itself, which is anathema to all life forms due to a number of strict physicochemical constraints imposed on life. The contrasting responses of prokaryotic and eukaryotic communities suggest that adaptation and persistence represent distinct ecological strategies in this polyextreme ecosystem. These findings indicate that environmental stability may be as important as salinity/chaotropicity in determining habitability limits and demonstrate the value of integrating molecular and hyperspectral approaches to investigate life in extreme terrestrial and exo-planetary analogous environments.

records.title: Genomic convergence and geographical divergence: multi-scale salinity adaptation mechanisms of microbiomes in shale gas flowback and produced water.
records.abstract: Shale gas flowback and produced water (FPW) represents a spatially heterogeneous artificial hypersaline ecosystem, in which the salt‑tolerance‑related genetic repertoire of indigenous microorganisms and the mechanisms shaping in‑situ community salinity adaptation patterns remain poorly clarified. Here, we collected metagenomic data from major shale gas-producing regions worldwide, encompassing 68 FPW samples from five basins: the Sichuan Basin, Anadarko Basin, Denver-Julesburg Basin, Western Canadian Sedimentary Basin, and Permian Basin. Based on these data, we constructed a genomic dataset comprising 699 high-quality MAGs to unravel the multi-scale salt adaptation mechanisms of the FPW microbiomes. Genomic results revealed that over 80% of FPW microbes encoded salt-in and salt-out pathways, demonstrating widespread genetic functional redundancy across geographically isolated basins. Despite convergent genomic potential, FPW microbiomes exhibited basin-specific adaptive differentiation, with Sichuan and Permian Basins favoring the salt‑in pattern and Anadarko Basin favoring the salt‑out pattern. Given the high conservation of gene repertoires and the physicochemical differences across basins, such salinity adaptation patterns decoupling between genomic repertoire and community adaptation may be driven primarily by environmental filtering. Machine learning identified trehalose metabolism genes (e.g., K00697, K17311 and K17313) and K⁺ uptake genes (e.g., K03498) as the biomarkers governing salt‑out and salt‑in pattern biases, respectively. Metabolic cross-feeding mediated by trehalose public metabolites, supported by keystone taxa of Thermotogota and Bacillota, potentially further enhanced community-level salt tolerance via interspecific metabolic synergy. This study elucidates the hierarchical adaptation mechanism coupling intrinsic genomic potential and local environmental filtering, providing novel ecological insights into microbial salinity adaptation and theoretical support for hypersaline wastewater biological treatment.
records.authors: Shi X, Duan S, Zhang Y, Hou B, Zhang L.

records.title: Gut microbiome-associated adaptability of suckermouth catfish inhabiting the polluted Buriganga River: insights into heavy-metal-remediating microorganisms
records.abstract: The suckermouth catfish (SMCF), known for its pollutant tolerance and high invasiveness, is prevalent in the heavily contaminated Buriganga River in Bangladesh. This waterway, contaminated with a variety of pollutants, including heavy metals, has experienced the near-complete disappearance of native fish populations; however, the suckermouth catfish demonstrates remarkable adaptability in this environment. One objective of this study is to elucidate the role of the gut microbiome in SMCFs’ adaptation to this severely polluted habitat. We performed next-generation sequencing (NGS) of gut contents from SMCFs to analyze the gut microbial profiles of the fish samples. The results indicated that the suckermouth catfish’s gut is enriched with microbial communities, including  Paraclostridium ,  Klebsiella ,  Staphylococcus ,  Bacillus , and  Pseudomonas , which have the potential to remediate pollutants, including heavy metals. The subsequent aim of this research is to isolate and identify bacteria from the SMCF gut capable of remediating multiple heavy metals. We isolated three isolates with the potential to remediate multiple heavy metals and identified them as  Staphylococcus pasteuri SD,  Morganella morganii SAS1, and  Sporosarcina saromensis SAS using partial 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and conventional techniques. All isolates showed distinct capabilities for remediating multiple heavy metals. Notably,  S. pasteuri showed the highest lead (Pb) bioaccumulation (36.28%), S. saromensis showed the highest chromium (Cr) uptake (39.22%), and  M. morganii showed the highest nickel (Ni) uptake (35.90%). Furthermore, these isolates exhibited remarkable metal-tolerance profiles, with maximum tolerable concentrations ranging from 125 ppm to 1000 ppm, and sustained healthy growth under metal-supplemented conditions throughout a 48-hour incubation period. This validates their potential to remediate multiple heavy metals. Collectively, the results underscore the ecological adaptability of suckermouth catfish in polluted aquatic environments, which is associated with their gut microbiome, and highlight the bioremediation potential of these gut-derived microbes as effective agents for mitigating heavy metal contamination.
records.authors: Dey S, Sikder SA, Rahman Epa M, Das SK, Alam MZ.

records.title: Isolation, characterization, and therapeutic potential of a novel phage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 infecting Klebsiella pneumoniae.
records.abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae (K. pneumoniae) is an important opportunistic pathogenic bacterium that is often characterized by a multidrug-resistant phenotype, which can lead to the failure of antibiotic treatments. The emergence of multidrug-resistant K. pneumoniae, including carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae (CRKP), poses a significant threat to public health security. Bacteriophages, which are viruses capable of lysing bacteria, represent a promising alternative for treating infections caused by highly virulent K. pneumoniae and other antibiotic-resistant pathogens. In this study, we used K. pneumoniae 32b as the host bacterium and isolated the bacteriophage vB_KpiP_JZBo1. The optimal MOI of this bacteriophage is 0.01. And phage exhibited high activity across a wide range of temperatures (20°C - 50°C) and pH (4 - 11) following 1 h of incubation. Whole genome analysis revealed that the bacteriophage was a double-stranded DNA virus, encoding a total of 91 open reading frames (ORFs). Notably, genetic evolutionary analysis and BLASTN results indicated that phage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 shares the closest evolutionary relationship with K. pneumoniae phage KP8. However, genome-wide comparison revealed that they only exhibit 88% coverage and 93.03% nucleotide homology. This suggests that phage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 may be a novel species of phage. No genes associated with antibiotic resistance, virulence factors, and tRNA were found in the phage genome, and it belongs to Kaypoctavirus genus of the Schitoviridae family. Additionally, higher phage doses resulted in greater inhibitory and bactericidal effects against K. pneumoniae in LB medium. In model of G. mellonella, bacteriophage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 can effectively eliminate the infection of K. pneumoniae 32b and increase the survival rate of G. mellonella. These findings suggest that the bacteriophage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 has potential for the treatment and prevention of K. pneumoniae, and they also provide a theoretical basis for clinical applications.
records.authors: Peng D, Cao R, Sun X, Jia C, Huang L, Yao X, Han Y, Liu Y, Yang Y, Yang G, Wang Y, Li H.
