records.title: Phylogenomics of "Candidatus Rickettsia mendelii" reveals a distinct early-diverging lineage with small genomes within the genus Rickettsia.
records.abstract: The genus Rickettsia comprises obligate intracellular bacteria belonging to the class Alphaproteobacteria. Although Rickettsia species have traditionally been classified into several phylogenetic groups, recent genome-based studies have revealed greater diversity within the genus and related Rickettsiaceae lineages than previously recognized. Here, we isolated six rickettsial strains from Ixodes turdus ticks collected at various locations across Japan and performed whole-genome sequencing. A closed-genome sequence was obtained for one of the isolates. The six isolates shared highly similar genomic features and were identified as "Candidatus Rickettsia mendelii" on the basis of conserved rickettsial marker gene sequences. The genomes of "Ca. R. mendelii" were smaller (1.05-1.06 Mb) and had lower GC content (29.2-29.3%) than most analyzed rickettsial genomes and were comparable in these respects to those of Typhus Group rickettsiae. Family-wide phylogenomic analysis using a quality-filtered Rickettsiaceae genome data set placed "Ca. R. mendelii" in a distinct early-diverging lineage within the genus Rickettsia. Chromosome-level comparisons with many other Rickettsia species revealed stretches of conserved synteny distributed across the chromosome of "Ca. R. mendelii." Genes encoding major secretion-related and host interaction-associated components were detected, whereas no hits meeting the detection criteria were obtained for the F-type IV secretion system (F-T4SS) proteins encoded by Rickettsiales-amplified genetic elements (RAGEs). These results provide the first genome sequences from cultured "Ca. R. mendelii" isolates and expand our understanding of genome diversity and evolution within the genus Rickettsia.ImportanceGenome-based studies have expanded the known diversity of the genus Rickettsia and related Rickettsiaceae lineages, but genome information from cultured isolates remains unavailable for some poorly characterized taxa. Here, we report the first whole-genome sequences from six cultured isolates of "Ca. R. mendelii" and show that this taxon represents a distinct early-diverging lineage within the genus Rickettsia. The genomes of "Ca. R. mendelii" were smaller and had lower GC content than most analyzed rickettsial genomes and were comparable in these respects to those of Typhus Group rickettsiae, despite the distinct phylogenetic placement. This indicates that similar genome characteristics can occur in phylogenetically distant rickettsial lineages. The low genomic diversity among geographically separated "Ca. R. mendelii" isolates suggests broad dispersal of closely related strains, which may be facilitated by infected ticks carried by migratory birds. These findings improve our understanding of the genome characteristics and geographic distribution of "Ca. R. mendelii."
records.authors: Gotoh Y, Kasama K, Yamamoto S, Yoshino S, Kawabata H, Ando S, Hayashi T.

records.title: Genomic Characterization and Environmental Adaptability of Burkholderia cenocepacia Isolated from Commercial Liquid Soap in Bangladesh
records.abstract: Abstract    Commercial liquid soaps may harbor opportunistic pathogens such as  Burkholderia cepacia  complex (BCC), yet genome-scale characterization of soap-associated BCC isolates remains limited in South Asia. In this study, a bacterial isolate, designated DG4, was recovered from a commercial liquid detergent and characterized using phenotypic, biochemical, whole-genome, and comparative genomic approaches. The isolate exhibited substantial growth under alkaline conditions, with optimum growth observed at pH 8 and detectable growth up to pH 10, while growth was severely restricted at pH 11–12. The isolate was catalase and lipase-positive and its crude supernatant demonstrated surface-active properties, producing a 1.08 ± 0.10 cm oil-displacement zone and an emulsification index (E24) of 53.07 ± 0.11%. The strain also exhibited strong biofilm-forming ability, with an OD570 of 0.508 ± 0.00. Whole-genome sequencing revealed a 7.89-Mb draft genome comprising 459 contigs, with 67.16% GC content and 40× sequencing coverage. Genome-based taxonomic analyses, including ANI and phylogenetic analysis, identified DG4 as  Burkholderia cenocepacia  , with an ANI of 98.28% against the reference strain  B. cenocepacia  J2315 genome. Multilocus sequence typing revealed a potential novel allelic profile not assigned to a previously recognized sequence type. Genome annotation identified 7,964 coding sequences, including genes associated with stress adaptation, membrane transport, biofilm formation, antimicrobial resistance, virulence, and diverse metabolic pathways. The genome contained multiple resistance determinants, including  adeF  ,  amrA  ,  qacG  ,  OXA-1142  ,  PEN-B1  , and a  vanF  -associated  vanH  gene. PathogenFinder predicted a human pathogenicity probability of 0.9819. In addition, numerous genes involved in hydrocarbon degradation, aromatic compound metabolism, desulfurization, and biosurfactant-associated functions were identified, supporting considerable bioremediation potential. AntiSMASH analysis detected 21 biosynthetic gene clusters, while prophage, mobile genetic element, and CRISPR-Cas analyses demonstrated substantial genomic plasticity and defense capacity. Comparative orthologous analysis revealed a conserved core genome of 5,243 gene clusters and only 14 DG4-specific clusters among six  B. cenocepacia  genomes. Commercial liquid detergent can harbor environmentally adapted  B. cenocepacia  with clinically relevant resistance and virulence determinants. These findings emphasize the importance of microbiological quality control and AMR surveillance of personal care products while highlighting the strain's potential for bioremediation research.

records.title: Baltic Sea microbial cohorts exhibit catabolic specialization and anabolic interdependencies across environmental gradients.
records.abstract: Microbial communities are structured by environmental gradients and metabolic interactions, making the study of co-occurring populations essential for understanding emergent ecological properties. Here, we investigated microbial cohorts, recurring groups of co-occurring microorganisms shaped by shared environmental preferences and potential biotic interactions, across the Baltic Sea, a well-characterized region where microbial community composition and metabolic functions vary strongly across salinity, temperature, and oxygen gradients. We used a genomic catalog consisting of 701 species-representative genomes to recruit reads from 112 metagenomes and infer cohort structure, environmental distributions, and metabolic potential. We identified nine microbial cohorts that showed strong associations with environmental gradients, indicating deterministic assembly. Cohorts differed markedly in their genomic and functional characteristics. The most abundant and prevalent cohorts were dominated by taxa with smaller, streamlined genomes, whereas the low-oxygen cohort contained larger genomes and contributed disproportionately to nitrogen and sulfur transformations. Within cohorts, different biosynthetic pathways were consistently associated with different taxonomic groups. Complete amino acid biosynthesis pathways were common among individual genomes, whereas complete B-vitamin biosynthesis pathways were rare. The six biosynthetic pathways with the lowest completeness were consistently associated with different taxonomic groups across all cohorts, with individual genomes encoding only a subset of these pathways, consistent with widespread metabolic interdependencies. Together, these results show that Baltic Sea microbial cohorts are ecologically structured assemblages whose genomic repertoires reflect catabolic specialization and anabolic interdependencies.
records.authors: Pacheco-Valenciana A, Milke F, Wienhausen G, Garcia SL.

records.title: Pantoea agglomerans T6SS effectors reside in hotspots with combinatorial antibacterial and antiviral arsenals.
records.abstract: Gram-negative bacteria deploy type VI secretion systems (T6SSs) to mediate interbacterial competition. Although numerous T6SS effectors have been identified, their pan-genomic repertoires and evolutionary dynamics remain poorly understood. Here, we combine proteomics and comparative genomics to map the T6SS effector landscape across Pantoea agglomerans, a species that includes pathogenic and beneficial strains. We uncover an extensive pan-genomic arsenal in which most effectors are encoded outside the T6SS gene cluster, within dynamic hotspots distributed across the chromosome and megaplasmids. Analysis of these hotspots reveals combinatorial arrangements of shuffled genetic cargo. Remarkably, these loci act as versatile "genomic armories" that co-localize offensive antibacterial weapons with protective anti-phage defense systems. By investigating uncharacterized genes within these variable regions, we discovered and validated a novel T6SS effector and a previously unknown anti-phage defense system, named Juno. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that bacterial warfare arsenals are highly modular and reside in dynamic genomic hubs that alternate or combine interbacterial aggression with viral defense. This evolutionary association reveals a functional blurring between offensive and defensive strategies within the bacterial accessory genome.IMPORTANCEBacteria inhabiting competitive environments must simultaneously contend with rival bacteria and bacteriophage predators. Here, we show that Pantoea agglomerans, a species with both pathogenic and biocontrol lifestyles, meets this challenge through dynamic genomic loci we term "genomic armories." By mapping the type VI secretion system (T6SS) secreted effector arsenal of P. agglomerans, we uncover the largest T6SS effector arsenal associated with a single T6SS described to date. Strikingly, nearly all effectors reside in variable genomic regions, most of which are hotspots that cycle through diverse genetic cargoes across strains. These hotspots combinatorially co-localize antibacterial T6SS effectors with anti-phage defense systems, providing bacteria with integrated offensive and defensive capabilities within a single locus. These findings reframe our understanding of how bacteria organize and diversify their arsenals, with implications for bacterial competition and phage-bacteria co-evolution.
records.authors: Leo K, Fridman CM, Haldar A, Mahata T, Qimron U, Bosis E, Salomon D.

records.title: Comparative genomics reveals expanded cell-surface signaling and siderophore scavenging repertoires in Pectobacterium.
records.abstract: Iron acquisition in gram-negative bacteria relies on TonB-dependent receptors (TBDRs), some of which initiate cell-surface signaling (CSS) by activating extracytoplasmic function (ECF) sigma factors that induce cognate transport pathways. Although well characterized in Pseudomonas, CSS systems remain poorly explored in plant-associated bacteria. Surveying 6,847 plant-associated bacterial genomes revealed near-ubiquitous CSS systems in Pseudomonas and Pectobacterium, with markedly lower strain-to-strain variation in the latter. In 902 high-contiguity Pectobacteriaceae genomes, Pectobacterium averaged 5.03 CSS modules per genome, compared with 0.67 in Dickeya, despite their shared soft-rot lifestyle. De novo clustering identified 14 distinct CSS systems across the family, with nine found in Pectobacterium. The ferredoxin receptor gene fusA was conserved in 572 of 586 Pectobacterium genomes; however, only 126 carried fusA under CSS regulation. These strains were phylogenetically dispersed but formed a single fusA clade, a pattern consistent with co-acquisition of the receptor and regulator as a transferable module. Pectobacterium also encoded a more diverse repertoire of siderophore receptors than related taxa, suggesting broader potential for siderophore utilization across bacterial lineages. Notably, the predicted amonabactin-like biosynthetic gene cluster and its putative cognate TBDR were highly conserved within Pectobacterium but rare elsewhere in the family, supporting its potential role in the endogenous siderophore system in the genus. These findings reveal an expanded genomic repertoire of CSS systems and siderophore receptors in Pectobacterium, providing a framework for investigating their roles in environmental sensing and iron acquisition.IMPORTANCEBacteria often use cell-surface signaling systems to sense environmental cues and coordinate the uptake of substrates that cannot freely cross the outer membrane, including siderophores and host-derived proteins. Through comparative genomic analysis, we demonstrate that Pectobacterium harbors one of the richest and most diverse repertoires of these cell-surface signaling systems among plant-associated bacteria. Despite similar lifestyles, its repertoire far exceeds that of other Pectobacteriaceae and reveals extensive predicted siderophore producer-scavenger relationships within the genus and across the family. These expanded signaling and siderophore acquisition systems in Pectobacterium may contribute to its environmental adaptability and ecological versatility by broadening opportunities for nutrient acquisition and interactions with surrounding microbial communities.
records.authors: Seo J-Y, Park DH, Lee JH.

records.title: Genome-based reclassification of Streptosporangium sandarakinum Kämpfer et al. 2013 as a later heterotypic synonym of Streptosporangium nondiastaticum Nonomura and Ohara 1969 (Approved Lists 1980).
records.abstract: A comparison of 16S rRNA gene sequences between Streptosporangium sandarakinum GW-12028T and Streptosporangium nondiastaticum IFO 13990T revealed a sequence similarity of 98.8%. The genus Streptosporangium includes 33 species with validly published names. The type strains S. sandarakinum GW-12028T (=DSM 45763T=LMG 27062T) and S. nondiastaticum IFO 13990T (=ATCC 27101T=DSM 43848T=JCM 3114T=KCTC 9434T=NBRC 13990T=VKM Ac-1299T) were both isolated from soil. Whole-genome data were used to clarify the taxonomic assignment of these two closely related Streptosporangium species. Overall genomic relatedness index analyses indicated that S. sandarakinum GW-12028T and S. nondiastaticum IFO 13990T shared average nucleotide identity and digital DNA-DNA hybridization values >95% and >70%, respectively, exceeding the thresholds for bacterial species delineation. Additionally, S. sandarakinum GW-12028T and S. nondiastaticum IFO 13990T displayed near-identical phenotypic and chemotaxonomic profiles. Based on the 16S rRNA gene phylogenetic tree and the core-genome phylogenomic trees, S. sandarakinum GW-12028T and S. nondiastaticum IFO 13990T phylogenetically form a separate, tight cluster apart from other Streptosporangium species. Based on this combined evidence, S. sandarakinum Kämpfer et al. 2013 is proposed as a later heterotypic synonym of S. nondiastaticum Nonomura and Ohara 1969.
records.journal: International Journal of Systematic and Evolutionary Microbiology
records.authors: Cruz A, McLaughlin RW, Elshahed MS, Lawson PA, Miller SL.

records.title: Elevation Amplifies Carrier-Type Differences in Nitrogen Cycling and N2O Dynamics in Lake Biofilms.
records.abstract: Lake biofilms are microbial habitats for nitrogen transformation, but how carrier type and elevation influence N2O dynamics remains unclear. We examined abiotic- and biotic-carrier biofilms from 12 lakes spanning 4-4272 m using anoxic incubations, 15N tracing, selective inhibition, isotopocule analysis, and metagenomics. Net N2O emission potential increased with elevation in both carrier types, with the largest carrier contrast at high elevation, where biotic-carrier biofilms showed the highest net N2O emission potential. 15N partitioning showed a marked shift in emission sources. At low elevation, heterotrophic nitrification dominated abiotic-carrier biofilms (∼91%), whereas denitrification contributed ∼57% in biotic-carrier biofilms. At high elevation, denitrification accounted for 67-97% of net N2O emission across both carriers, and bacterial denitrification dominated the total denitrification rate potential. Metagenomic profiles provided mechanistic support: high-elevation biotic-carrier biofilms showed higher relative representation of genes for dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium and nitrogen fixation, but had few nosZ-carrying genomes, indicating weak terminal N2O reduction capacity. Overall, carrier type and elevation jointly shape nitrogen transformation pathways. High-elevation lake ecosystems, particularly those with abundant biotic substrates, may harbor disproportionately important biofilm N2O hotspots under global change.

records.title: Characterization of household microbiomes from three unique cities around the world.
records.abstract: Characterizing the household bacterial microbiome allows for a stronger understanding of the various microbes to which a person is exposed every day in their home. Exploring household microbiomes in different countries around the world increases our understanding of the impact human behaviour might have on niche microbial communities in the house. The goal of this study was to use shotgun metagenomics to characterize the microbiome from ten locations around the house in ten different houses from three countries (Mysuru, India; Dubai, United Arab Emirates (UAE); and Tucson, USA). There was a significant difference in alpha diversity between the three countries (ANOVA, PP=0.001] and, within cities, by household location (PERMANOVA, P=0.001), with geographic location explaining 5.3% and household location explaining 7.3% of variation. Household location was a strong driver of diversity within each of the three cities individually, accounting for 14-18% of microbiome variation. The highest levels of bacterial diversity across the three cities were found underneath the toilet rim and within bathroom and kitchen sinks. A core microbiome of classes Actinomycetota and Gammaproteobacteria was found in all homes in all three cities. Within each city, a core microbiome was identified at the species level within specific household locations. Many bacterial taxa found in the homes were a part of the human-associated phyla Actinomycetota (e.g. genera Brevibacterium, Mycolicibacterium and Rhodococcus), Pseudomonadota (e.g. genera Acinetobacter, Moraxella, Paracoccus and Pseudomonas) and Bacillota (genus Streptococcus), which is comparable to previous studies. The household microbiome is variable across different locations within the house and on a global scale. Factors such as human activity, cultural practices, climate and surface type and use may drive this diversity. Characterizing the household microbiome on a global scale allows for a better understanding of what drives microbial diversity, increasing our understanding of how microbial communities are shaped by the environment and how humans influence their dynamics, as well as any risks to human health that the built microbiome may potentially pose.

records.title: Targeting the Skin Microbiome in Dermatology: Translational Hype or Emerging Therapeutic Modality?
records.abstract: The human skin microbiome is a complex network of microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, viruses, and archaea, that exist in a mutualistic relationship with the host. These microorganisms play important roles in maintaining skin homeostasis, defense against pathogens, regulation of immune response, and antimicrobial peptide synthesis. Dysbiosis, defined as an imbalance of microbial communities, has been linked to dermatological conditions including atopic dermatitis (AD), acne, psoriasis, and chronic wounds. Despite compelling mechanistic insights, the translation of microbiome science into clinically effective therapies remains inconsistent and prematurely optimistic. Emerging therapeutic strategies aim to restore and modulate the skin microbiome with precision, thereby moving beyond conventional broad-spectrum antimicrobial approaches. These encompass probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, live biotherapeutic products (LBPs), bacteriophage therapy, microbiome engineering, postbiotics, microbial consortia treatment, and antimicrobial peptides that selectively target microbial communities instead of eliminating them. While these strategies are biologically plausible and have initial-phase evidence, their clinical stability, reproducibility, and scalability are uncertain. Major limitations include inter-individual variability of microbiomes, transient colonization, methodological limitations in functional profiling, and regulatory uncertainties surrounding them. This review article critically evaluates microbiome-directed dermatologic therapies at the crossroads of real therapeutic potential and translational overextension. The field is not just hype; its clinical application has advanced more rapidly than the supporting evidence base justifies. Progress in this domain requires a shift from descriptive and associative research toward mechanism-driven, precision-based interventions. Such interventions must be validated against robust clinical endpoints. By critically assessing biological plausibility, clinical evidence, and translational barriers, this review provides a balanced perspective on the field and outlines realistic pathways for its evolution into a viable therapeutic paradigm.

records.title: Importance of rumen ciliated protozoa and current research techniques for their analysis.
records.abstract: Rumen protozoa are an integral component of the ruminant foregut microbiome, with a profound influence on feed digestion, microbial ecosystem dynamics and enteric methane emissions. Although they represent only a small proportion of species richness, protozoa contribute significantly to microbial biomass and functions in fibre degradation, volatile fatty acid production, microbial protein turnover, pH modulation and hydrogen-mediated methanogenesis. In addition to highlighting their importance to rumen function, this review summarizes classical and contemporary methodologies for enumerating, identifying and characterizing rumen protozoa. These methodologies include microscopy, fluorescent staining, flow cytometry and molecular approaches such as 18S rRNA, ITS and 28S rRNA amplicon sequencing. All major rRNA primers widely used over the last two decades are catalogued and their coverage is evaluated against current databases, highlighting the superior taxonomic resolution provided by ITS-based markers. The integration of single-cell sequencing and long-read platforms with multi-omics approaches (metagenomics, metatranscriptomics and metaproteomics) and advanced bioinformatic tools enables genome-resolved and functionally informed analyses of rumen protozoa. Methodological advances are integrated with functional insights to elucidate the contributions of protozoa to rumen ecology, feed efficiency and methane output. Key research gaps are also identified, including the need for improved microscopy techniques, automated image analysis, optimized cryopreservation protocols and robust culturing systems. This synthesis provides a comprehensive resource for researchers in microbial ecology, animal nutrition and environmental science, enabling precise protozoal profiling and informing strategies to enhance livestock productivity while mitigating environmental impacts.
records.authors: Maloney S, Folliard NT, Karakaya G, Waters SM.

records.title: Benchmarking nanopore-based strategies for antimicrobial resistance prediction.
records.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) presents a pressing need to ensure that the right antimicrobials are used to target the right microbes at the right time. Ideally, the appropriate antimicrobial is selected after patient samples have been cultured and assessed with antimicrobial sensitivity testing (AST). However, the time needed for culture-based diagnosis leads to immediate empirical treatment, often with broad-spectrum and/or high-tier antimicrobials. Direct nanopore metagenomic whole-genome sequencing to identify pathogens and predict their AMR is a rapid and patient-side alternative. A limitation of this approach is potential inconsistencies in i predicted AMR phenotypes. Here, we benchmarked the current performance of in silico AMR prediction strategies for nanopore-generated long-read data. Using real-world nanopore data paired with AST phenotyping for 201 samples representing 27 bacterial species, we assessed the impact of basecalling mode, data volume and assembly strategy and compared the performance of eight in silico AMR prediction tools with seven AMR databases. We found that basecalling accuracy mode does not significantly affect the overall accuracy of in silico AMR predictions but assembly strategy and data volume both do. Prediction tools using the ResFinder database scored best for balanced accuracy (0.80±0.02 for both ResFinder and ABRicate), whilst DeepARG scored best for sensitivity (0.65±0.03); predictions were more accurate for some antibiotic classes and genera than others. However, even the best-performing in silico AMR prediction strategy missed some resistance identified by lab-based AST. We conclude, therefore, that currently in silico AMR prediction can supplement lab-based AST but cannot yet replace it.
records.authors: Ring N, Low AS, Evans R, Keith M, Paterson GK, Gally D, Nuttall T, Clements DN, Fitzgerald JR.

records.title: Fungal-bacterial interactions.
records.abstract: The study of fungal-bacterial interactions is an emerging field of biology with relevance for environmental health, medicine, and agriculture, among other sectors. The frequent co-occurrence of fungi and bacteria in many habitats has facilitated the evolution of their symbioses. Both groups are key players in host-associated microbiomes and in nutrient cycling, and these roles often intersect in dynamic ways. Interactions between fungi and bacteria can be mutualistic, commensal, or pathogenic, and they can vary in a context-dependent manner. In mutualistic interactions, fungi and bacteria can exchange nutrients, ameliorate each other's stress, enhance growth, enable dispersal, and facilitate novel niche exploration via metabolite exchange. In contrast, antagonistic interactions frequently involve competition for limited nutrients, such as iron, and active chemical warfare with secreted and bioactive compounds. Bacteria associated with fungi can occur inside of fungal cells (endosymbiotic) or on the surface of fungal hyphae (exosymbiotic). Endosymbiotic bacteria can be further differentiated into facultative symbionts, which retain the ability to enter fungal hyphae but also live independently, and obligate endosymbionts, which are always intracellular and not capable of independent life outside of hyphae. Whereas free-living bacteria can be pathogenic or mutualistic, endosymbiotic bacteria are often regarded as commensals or mutualists, although some can exhibit parasitic attributes in some conditions. A combination of molecular genetics, genomics, and microscopy has been used to study free-living bacteria. In addition to these approaches, fluorescence and electron microscopy have been used as the gold standards to study and differentiate endosymbiotic bacteria based on their intracellular location. More recently, researchers have started using systems-biology approaches to study fungal-bacterial interactions including high-throughput -omics assays. These methods produce expansive datasets that are ideally suited to artificial intelligence (AI)-based approaches to tackle long-standing questions about the basic biology and evolution of fungal-bacterial interactions. In this primer we give an overview of fungal-bacterial interactions, including their diversity, community structure, and symbiotic evolution. We highlight two research systems in particular: the intracellular endosymbionts of Mucoromycota fungi and the free-living bacteria associated with edible fungi. We focus on these systems because fungi remain understudied relative to other groups, and only a handful of fungal taxa with their bacterial symbionts are backed by large enough data sets to explore these concepts in detail. Our aim here is not to be comprehensive, but instead to use the most well-understood systems to illustrate emerging principles. We then discuss advances in using AI to infer new aspects of microbial biology and provide suggestions for how these technologies could advance research on fungal-bacterial interactions utilizing existing genomic datasets.

records.title: Biosynthetic Pathways and Regulation of Antibacterial Compounds From Endophytic Fungi: From Chemistry to Genomics and Biotechnology.
records.abstract: Endophytic fungi are non-pathogenic symbionts that represent a rich source of structurally diverse bioactive secondary metabolites. However, genome-mining studies reveal that most of their biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) remain transcriptionally silent under standard laboratory conditions, leaving much of their chemical diversity unexplored. This review examines antibacterial natural products from endophytic fungi by integrating three complementary aspects: metabolite chemistry, biosynthetic pathways, and strategies for activating cryptic BGCs. Endophytic fungi produce polyketides, non-ribosomal peptides, terpenoids, phenylpropanoid-derived compounds, and hybrid metabolites with antibacterial activities mediated through inhibition of ribosomes, cell wall and membrane biosynthesis, and bacterial resistance mechanisms. Their genomes encode diverse PKS, NRPS, TPS, and hybrid biosynthetic systems, many of which remain cryptic. Advances in chemical elicitation, co-cultivation, epigenetic modulation, CRISPR-based engineering, genome mining, and machine learning are accelerating the activation of silent clusters and the assignment of BGCs to their metabolites. Several fungal metabolites exhibit potent activity against multidrug-resistant pathogens, including MRSA, and some enhance the efficacy of existing antibiotics. This review highlights current progress, identifies remaining challenges in metabolite production and BGC annotation, and outlines future directions for translating endophytic fungi into a sustainable platform for next-generation antibacterial drug discovery.

records.title: Haplotype-phased assemblies of the two poplar rust fungi species: Melampsora larici-populina and Melampsora allii-populina.
records.abstract: Dikaryotic rust fungi maintain 2 distinct haploid nuclei for most of their life cycle, making their large, repeat-rich genomes difficult to assemble and phase. Here we present haplotype-phased, near chromosome-scale genome assemblies for the poplar rust pathogens Melampsora larici-populina 98AG31 and Melampsora allii-populina 12AY07, generated using PacBio HiFi sequencing and Hi-C-guided scaffolding. For each species, we resolved 18 chromosomes per haplotype, providing the first near chromosome-level representations of poplar rust fungal species. M. larici-populina diploid assembly spans ∼203 Mb, while M. allii-populina reaches ∼416 Mb, with high completeness and strong collinearity between haplotypes. Compared with previous fragmented or collapsed references, these assemblies greatly improve contiguity, recover centromeric and telomeric features, and support the transposable element-driven genome size expansion in M. allii-populina. The haplotype-aware annotations of genes and predicted effectors derived from these resources will enable detailed analyses of genome architecture, repeat dynamics, and key loci such as avirulence genes. Together, these assemblies provide a robust genomic resource for investigating host adaptation, virulence evolution, and population diversity in poplar rust fungi.
records.authors: Corre E, Morin E, Sperschneider J, Abdalrahem A, Pernaci M, Grigoriev IV, Frey P, Duplessis S, Lorrain C.

records.title: Genomic characterization of the endangered medicinal polypore agarikon (Laricifomes officinalis syn. Fomitopsis officinalis).
records.abstract: Agarikon (Laricifomes officinalis syn. Fomitopsis officinalis) is an endangered fungus belonging to a unique lineage in the Polyporales (Basidiomycota) with a growing body of evidence supporting its medicinal value. In this study, we report the hybrid de novo assembly and annotation of the nuclear and mitochondrial genomes of L. officinalis, with a nuclear genome size of 28.76 Mb assembled across 66 contigs (51.96% GC content; BUSCO completeness of 99.4%) and a complete core mitochondrial genome size of 197.67 kb. Structural and functional annotation of the nuclear genome yielded 8,717 predicted genes including 8,604 protein-coding genes, with 287 genes in 27 candidate biosynthetic gene clusters. We characterized the mating type loci matA and matB, consistent with a tetrapolar mating system, and identified genes encoding key enzymes involved in triterpenoid and polyketide biosynthetic pathways that lead to the production of a diverse array of secondary metabolites. Additionally, we conducted maximum likelihood phylogenomic analysis to confirm the taxonomic position of L. officinalis among other species in the Polyporales using protein sequences for 730 shared BUSCO genes. This high-quality annotated genome of L. officinalis will serve as a foundation for further investigations into its evolutionary history, provide a reference for future population genomic analyses, and elucidate mechanisms underlying the synthesis of the bioactive compounds responsible for agarikon's wide-ranging medicinal benefits.
records.authors: Bennett PI, Bair ZJ, Bradshaw AJ, Stamets P.

records.title: Gut microbiota composition of India's Baiga tribe: Insights from an indigenous particularly vulnerable tribal group.
records.abstract: The transition from traditional foraging lifestyles to modernized urban environments is associated with reduced human gut microbiome diversity. To examine this shift within the Indian subcontinent, we used shotgun metagenomics to compare the gut microbiota of 50 adults: 25 from the indigenous, foraging, and particularly vulnerable Baiga tribe and 25 from an urban population in Bhopal, Central India. The Baiga maintained a diverse ecosystem enriched with fiber-degrading bacteria such as Roseburia and Faecalibacterium, forming networks suited to complex carbohydrate fermentation. The urban microbiome showed lower phylogenetic diversity and evenness, with higher relative abundance of Prevotella copri and dairy-adapted taxa. Functionally, the tribal gut retained pathways for environmental sensing and complex plant metabolism, whereas the urban gut was enriched in pathways associated with potential inflammation. These findings identify the Baiga as a reservoir of preserved human microbial diversity relevant to metabolic health.
records.authors: Kallapura G, Prakash AS, Prasad R, Josphine I, Maurya M, Dhar D.

records.title: Halophyte-derived rhizosphere microbiome transplantation improves physiological homeostasis and salt tolerance in alfalfa.
records.abstract: Halophyte-associated microbiomes are promising reservoirs of stress-adapted microorganisms, yet the consequences of transferring whole rhizosphere communities to phylogenetically distinct crops have remained unclear. Here, we evaluated rhizosphere microbiome transplantation (RMT) from Suaeda salsa to alfalfa (Medicago sativa) in a 2 × 2 factorial experiment comprising control and RMT treatments at 0 and 300 mM NaCl. Plant physiological responses were integrated with metagenomic profiling, community assembly analysis, microbial association networks, and functional gene analyses. Under salinity, RMT increased plant height, leaf area, and both shoot and root biomass, reduced shoot Na+ accumulation, and increased the shoot K+/Na+ ratio. RMT also reduced H2O2, malondialdehyde, and relative electrical conductivity while increasing antioxidant enzyme activities and osmolyte concentrations, whereas gas-exchange parameters showed no significant recovery. RMT altered rhizosphere community composition and assembly and was associated with greater network connectivity and simulated robustness. Metagenomic KO profiles showed higher relative representation of functions correlated to osmoprotection, ion transport, redox protection, and cell-envelope processes. These microbial functional shifts coincided with the physiological domains most strongly improved by RMT but did not establish direct causal microbial mechanisms. Overall, halophyte-derived RMT improved alfalfa performance under salinity, with coordinated physiological recovery accompanied by substantial reorganization of the recipient rhizosphere, supporting further evaluation of whole-community microbiome transplantation for crop production in saline soils.
records.authors: Hu J, He Y, Cui W, Wei L, Li L, Wang L, Alwathnani H, Rensing C, Zhang J.

records.title: A synthetic microbial community derived from the roots of Kalidium gracile enhances its salt tolerance by modulating gene transcription and reshaping the rhizosphere soil microbiota.
records.abstract: Soil salinization and alkalinization are severe environmental problems in the desert-oasis transition zone of the Hexi Corridor, China. Rhizosphere microbial communities are key regulators of plant adaptation to saline-alkali environments. However, the functional microbial resources and ecological mechanisms underlying the contribution of the rhizosphere microbiome associated with Kalidium gracile to its saline adaptation remain poorly understood. In this study, we characterized the rhizosphere microbiome of K. gracile inhabiting severely saline-alkali soil and isolated two Bacillus strains with strong plant growth-promoting potential, which were subsequently used to construct a synthetic microbial community (SynCom). Inoculation experiments under salt stress demonstrated that SynCom increased plant biomass and chlorophyll content and modulated host transcriptional responses associated with the "growth-defense trade-off." Shortly after inoculation, plant growth-related pathways were suppressed, while CAT and POD activities surged by 45% and 213%, respectively. At later stages after inoculation, the expression of growth-related pathways was significantly upregulated. Metagenomic sequencing revealed that SynCom reshaped the rhizosphere microbial community, with the relative abundances of the halophilic bacteria Halomonas and Marinobacter increasing by 317% and 1162%, respectively. The abundances of functional genes involved in soil carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur nutrient cycling were all significantly increased. Collectively, these findings indicate that SynCom enhances plant salt tolerance through a multi-layered regulatory mechanism by coordinating host physiological responses and rhizosphere microbial functions. Collectively, these findings reveal a multi-level regulatory mechanism through which SynCom enhances plant salt tolerance by coordinating host physiological responses and rhizosphere microbiome functions.
records.authors: Yue Y, Yuan M, Fan Z, Shan L, Zhao Y, He C, Ma Q, Zhang L.

records.title: Diversity-generating retroelements enable phages to expand their host range in the human gut
records.abstract: Diversity-generating retroelements (DGRs) are genetic elements that use error-prone reverse transcription to hypermutate specific target genes, most often the receptor-binding proteins of phages. They are enriched in human gut viruses, where they are hypothesised to enable phages expand their host range. Yet DGR-mediated host-range expansion across bacterial species has so far only been predicted  in silico and has not been examined directly within complex microbial communities. To test this hypothesis  in situ , we tracked phage-host interactions in the human gut, combining bulk metagenomic, virus-like particle (VLP), and Hi-C sequencing of longitudinal faecal samples collected over a five-week period. This culture-independent approach identified 380 interactions between 97 phages and 76 bacterial hosts. Nearly a third of these phages (31 of 97) encoded a DGR, and DGR-encoding phages were more likely to interact with multiple bacterial species. Moreover, nucleotide diversity in DGR-targeted genes increased with the number of hosts a phage interacted with and was concentrated in the surface-exposed, DGR-targeted variable region of its receptor-binding proteins. Together, these results provide  in situ evidence that DGRs enable phages to expand their host range in the human gut.

records.title: Proteomics reveals conserved features of histone biology in dinoflagellates
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Current knowledge of DNA packaging in eukaryotic nuclei largely centers on its basic unit, the nucleosome. Multiple lineages have, however, diverged from this paradigm, most notably dinoflagellates. Among other molecular oddities, these enigmatic protists have enormous genomes, permanently condensed chromosomes and a foreign gene encoding Dinoflagellate Viral Nucleoprotein (DVNP), which is used for packing DNA. Some dinoflagellates also have Histone-like Proteins (HLPs) acquired from bacteria via lateral gene transfer. Dinoflagellates were long thought to lack histones entirely, but canonical histone genes have been identified by transcriptomics. Here, we performed proteomics on purified nuclei and confirmed the presence of all four core histone classes, along with variants, and DVNP in the dinoflagellates  Oxyrrhis marina and  Amphidinium carterae and HLPs in  A. carterae . We also identified putative histone post-translational modifications found in canonical eukaryotes. Comparative genomics of dinoflagellates revealed histone-handling and modification machinery alongside an apparent reduction in, or diversification of, machinery responsible for replication-dependent nucleosome deposition (CAF-1), consistent with a predominantly transcription-associated role for nucleosomes. Furthermore, proteomics revealed modifications of DVNP and HLP, raising the possibility of machinery co-opting. These observations support a new model of a dinoflagellate chromatin that includes the localization of canonical nucleosomes to “insulated chromatin territories” (INTs).
records.authors: Brask N, Haro R, Archibald JM, Stairs CW, Slamovits CH.

records.title: The large conjugative plasmid pAB3 integrates into the chromosome of  Acinetobacter baumannii  ATCC 17978
records.abstract: ATCC 17978 is one of the most utilised lab strains of  Acinetobacter baumannii . Current literature suggests ATCC 17978 can have either a sulfamethoxazole-resistant phenotype or have the type VI secretion system (T6SS) switched on depending on the presence/absence of the large conjugative plasmid pAB3, which encodes the antimicrobial resistance gene (ARG)  sul2 and T6SS repressors  tetR1 /  tetR2 . Here, we show that pAB3 integrates into the ATCC 17978 chromosome, which enables a large inversion resulting in the chromosomal arrangement labelled GS2.24 by Socru. This integration has no transcriptional impact on nearby genes or  tetR1 /  tetR2 . We find several instances were a portion of integrated pAB3 containing  tetR2 is lost but the rest of the sequence, including  sul2 , is maintained, suggesting pAB3 integration may serve to make further rearrangements more tractable, enabling a putative T6SS+ sulfamethoxazole-resistant phenotype.  Impact statement  Acinetobacter baumannii is a major cause of hospital infections and is often resistant to antibiotics. The strain ATCC 17978 is one of the most widely used laboratory strains, underpinning research on how this bacterium competes with other microbes, causes disease and resists treatment. Its original genome assembly placed a plasmid, pAB3, within the chromosome, which was later considered an error. We show that pAB3 is genuinely integrated into the chromosome in just over half of the ATCC 17978 strains studied. This integration enables a large chromosomal inversion but does not alter the activity of nearby genes under standard conditions. We also identify strains in which a region of pAB3 encoding a repressor of the type VI secretion system, a bacterial weapon, is missing while a sulfamethoxazole resistance gene is retained, with implications for trade-offs between bacterial virulence and antimicrobial resistance. These findings reveal that the ATCC 17978 chromosome is more variable than previously recognised, a significant advance for researchers using this strain, and contributes to understanding of bacterial chromosome structural variation, plasmid integration and resistance evolution, of interest to microbiologists, clinicians and evolutionary biologists.  Data summary  Sequencing data is available on the sequence read archive (SRA) under BioProject PRJNA1544396.
records.authors: Neil M, Langridge GC, Evans BA.

records.title: Proinflammatory strains of Mediterraneibacter gnavus are enriched during spondyloarthritis and bolster disease severity in animal model.
records.abstract: ObjectivesSpondyloarthritis (SpA) is a chronic inflammatory rheumatism with osteoarticular and extra‑articular manifestations. Intestinal dysbiosis has been implicated in SpA, notably the expansion of Mediterraneibacter gnavus (MG), a gram-positive coccus associated with several inflammatory disorders. We aimed to determine whether distinct MG strains were associated with SpA and contributed to disease pathogenesis.MethodsMG strains from patients with SpA and healthy controls (HCs) were identified based on metagenomic analysis, isolated and whole‑genome sequenced. Pathogenicity of selected strains was compared by mono-associating curdlan-treated germ‑free SpA-prone SKG mice. Putative strain selection under inflammatory pressure was examined by culturing MG in the presence of nitric oxide (NO). Functional effects were assessed by exposing monocytes from patients with SpA to MGstrains.ResultsPhylogenetic analysis separated MG strains into 3 main clades/subclades, using both metagenomic data and sequencing of 46 MG strains (39 from SpA and 7 from HCs). SpA-derived strains were significantly enriched in 2 clades/subclades, whereas the third clade was dominated by strains from HCs, suggesting clade-specific disease association. MG-mono-association of curdlan-treated SKG mice induced SpA, in which SpA-derived strains induced stronger colonic inflammation and arthritis. Consistently, MG DNA of these strains persisted in the inflamed colonic submucosa and SpA-derived strains showed enhanced resistance to NO. In vitro SpA-derived strains were enriched in toxic and proinflammatory properties.ConclusionsSpA is associated with a distinct repertoire of MG strains characterised by increased adaptability to inflammatory stress and heightened proinflammatory and toxic potential. These findings establish a link between strain‑level microbial diversity and disease susceptibility.

records.title: RDAR biofilm formation and in silico analysis of putative amyloid proteins in Azospirillum baldaniorum Sp245.
records.abstract: Azospirillum baldaniorum Sp245 is a plant growth-promoting rhizobacterium (PGPR) whose ability to benefit host crops depends on robust root colonization, a process driven by the transition from a planktonic state to a sessile, biofilm-associated lifestyle. This study investigated the capacity of A. baldaniorum Sp245 to form Red, Dry, and Rough (RDAR) morphotype biofilms. Through macroscopic evaluation and confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM), we visualized the presence of exopolysaccharides, putative amyloid proteins, and extracellular DNA (eDNA) within the RDAR biofilm matrix using Calcofluor White (CFW), Thioflavin S (TS), and Propidium Iodide (PI) fluorescent probes, respectively. Furthermore, formic acid treatment of extracellular matrix proteins extracts suggests the presence of resistant, putative amyloid proteins. Because genomic screening revealed the absence of homologs of a canonical curli-dependent amyloid system, we performed a genome-wide in silico analysis to identify genes encoding alternative biofilm-associated proteins. Using the Staphylococcus aureus Biofilm-Associated Protein (Bap protein) as a reference, we identified 20 candidate proteins characterized by extensive domain reiteration and diverse architectures, including bacterial immunoglobulin (Ig-like) domains, VCBS repeats, SWM motifs, DUF4347, PKD domains, and RTX β-roll structures. Three-dimensional modeling indicates that these candidates possess elongated, filament-like conformations with repetitive β-strand motifs typical of amyloid-like assembly and calcium-dependent adhesion. These findings suggest that in the absence of traditional curli machinery, A. baldaniorum Sp245 could be using a diverse, domain-rich repertoire of alternative matrix proteins to facilitate cell surface interactions, coordinate structural stability, and establish the RDAR biofilm morphotype. Ultimately, this study establishes a foundation for understanding the role of amyloid proteins in Azospirillum biofilm matrix formation and offers new insights into the potential mechanisms of bacterial persistence and ecological fitness in the rhizosphere.

records.title: A bacterial chaperone–usher pathway links interkingdom association to antimicrobial protection of a fungal partner
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Antimicrobial compounds (AMCs) influence species-level composition of microbial communities, governing beneficial and pathogenic interactions with plant and mammalian hosts. Phenazine-1- carboxylic acid (PCA) is a bacterially produced, redox-active AMC abundant in the rhizosphere. A recent study discovered the PCA-susceptible fungus  Aspergillus calidoustus can grow in PCA- abundant environments by associating with phenazine-tolerant bacteria, including the novel species  Paraburkholderia edwinii .  P. edwinii’s protection response is characterized by adherence to its fungal partner, bacterial aggregation, and sequestration and reduction of PCA, rendering PCA less toxic. Deletion of the bacterial transcriptional repressor HrcA generates a constitutively active protection response and enhanced protection of  A. calidoustus . Here, we use the Δ  hrcA strain to determine whether fungal protection uses bacterial self-protection machinery or dedicated interkingdom mechanisms. We identified a divergent archaic chaperone–usher pathway (CUP) operon encoding a predicted periplasmic chaperone, outer membrane usher, putative major pilin-like subunit, and putative adhesin-like tip protein. While many archaic CUP operons are annotated in diverse bacteria, their functions remain largely unexplored. We show these  f ungal  a ttachment  c omplex (  fac ) genes promote bacterial-fungal attachment, are required for  P. edwinii to sequester and detoxify PCA, and contribute to full fungal protection from PCA stress, despite not being required for  P. edwinii ’s own tolerance of PCA. We further identified the transcription regulator, FacR, that influences expression of the  fac system. Understanding the functions of divergent archaic CUP systems may illuminate protective interkingdom partnerships and inform how pathogenic and beneficial microbes gain entry to AMC-replete environments, shaping microbial communities in agricultural and clinical contexts.  IMPORTANCE  Some species of fungi can be opportunistic pathogens, while others promote rhizosphere stability. Antimicrobial compounds help govern the composition of microbial communities by excluding susceptible organisms and selecting for microbes with intrinsic resistance. However, susceptible fungi can gain entry into microbial communities containing antagonist compounds by partnering with protective bacteria, and it is unknown whether bacteria are extending the mechanisms of self-tolerance to fungal partners, or if there is dedicated machinery for interkingdom protection. Here, we show that  Paraburkholderia edwinii uses a divergent chaperone–usher system to associate with its fungal partner,  Aspergillus calidoustus , and protect it from phenazine stress. This system promotes fungal attachment, antimicrobial sequestration, and maintenance of a reducing environment, yet is dispensable for the bacterium’s own survival. These findings demonstrate that bacteria can deploy dedicated machinery to protect partners across kingdoms, revealing that antimicrobial tolerance can emerge from microbial interactions rather than intrinsic resistance alone.
records.authors: Gonzalez A, Dahlstrom K.

records.title: Genomic Dissection Explains Temporal Dynamics of Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans.
records.abstract: Bacterial spot of tomato caused by four taxonomically diverse Xanthomonas pathogens is one of the main seed-borne constraints of the tomato industry worldwide. Among the four bacterial spot xanthomonads, Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans has a particular importance in terms of competitive aggressiveness and global distribution. Bacterial spot of tomato was observed for the first time in Iran in 2015, where X. euvesicatoria pv. perforans was identified as the causal agent. While occurrence of this disease appeared to have subsided in the following years, a resurgence of the disease in the main tomato-growing areas of Iran has raised serious concerns since 2023. In this study, we assessed the range of new bacterial spot outbreaks in the country during 2023-2024. Our data showed that the disease is currently present in five Iranian provinces, including the two provinces where it had originally been reported in 2015. Whole genome sequence-based phylogenomic investigations suggested that the causal agent of tomato bacterial spot in Iran is still X. euvesicatoria pv. perforans, while genetic diversity was observed in the recently emerging population of the pathogen compared to the old population. The bacterial strains isolated in 2023-2024 surveys were phylogenetically distinct from those isolated in 2014-2016 surveys. Furthermore, type III effector repertoires varied significantly among the strains isolated in this study, regardless of their geographic origin. We provide novel insights into the ever-changing nature of tomato bacterial spot pathogens, highlighting the impact of seed-borne lineages of X. euvesicatoria pv. perforans in the population dynamics of the bacterium.
records.authors: Hajian-Maleki H, Briand M, Dittmer J, Koebnik R, Shams-Bakhsh M, Jacques MA, Chen NWG, Osdaghi E.

records.title: Graph-based pangenome analysis uncovers structural and functional impacts of allopolyploidization events.
records.abstract: The emergence of graph pangenomes has advanced the study of structural variants (SVs) across diverse species, yet the impact of complex ploidy on SV landscapes remains poorly explored. Brettanomyces bruxellensis, a yeast shaped by multiple allopolyploidization events, offers a compelling model due to its well-characterized genomic and phenotypic diversity. Here, we integrated subgenome-resolved assemblies with population-scale genomic and transcriptomic datasets to characterize SV distribution and functional impact at the species level. Leveraging a reference graph pangenome, we detected 5972 unique SVs across 1060 isolates. Allopolyploid genomes harbored significantly more SVs (320 on average) than diploids (116), reflecting hybridization's extensive impact on genome architecture. Functional association analysis revealed that 27.5% of SVs locally influence gene expression. Furthermore, a subset of SVs originating from ancestral divergence between subgenomes (hybridization-associated SVs) formed hotspots of structural diversity and disproportionately affect gene expression, with larger effect sizes than other SVs. These findings underscore allopolyploidization as a driver of structural and functional genomic diversification, highlighting the value of graph-based approaches in dissecting complex genome evolution.
records.authors: Loegler V, Friedrich A, Schacherer J.

records.title: Ecological role of the heterotrophic protist Aurantiochytrium (Labyrinthulomycetes) as a key consumer of viral-induced dissolved organic matter following the lysis of the red tide-forming microalga Heterosigma akashiwo.
records.abstract: Marine algal blooms play a vital role in oceanic carbon cycling. However, the ecological consequences of the organic matter released following bloom collapse via viral infection are poorly understood. Recent studies have shown that viral infection dramatically alters the intracellular metabolite composition of the host, and that the resulting viral lysate selectively promotes the growth of specific prokaryotic populations. This study aimed to elucidate the effects of organic matter derived from healthy and virus-infected cells of the bloom-forming alga Heterosigma akashiwo on the growth of heterotrophic eukaryotes, specifically labyrinthulomycetes. These marine protists are primarily saprotrophic or predatory and contribute to dissolved organic matter (DOM) decomposition and nutrient cycling. Field monitoring conducted in Osaka Bay over a 12-month period revealed that, although the overall Labyrinthulomycetes community showed no clear seasonality, specific populations of these protists co-occurred with Heterosigma akashiwo. To mechanistically investigate the potential trophic linkage suggested by these field observations, a co-culture system comprising H. akashiwo, its specific virus (HaV53), and Aurantiochytrium sp. NBRC102614, used as a model labyrinthulomycete, was established. In co-culture experiments, viral lysis of H. akashiwo led to a significant increase in the cell density of Aurantiochytrium sp., demonstrating that Aurantiochytrium can thrive on substrates derived from virus-infected algae, including viral-induced dissolved organic matter (vDOM). These findings highlight that heterotrophic Labyrinthulomycetes are key consumers of virus-modified organic matter, playing a pivotal role in carbon cycling following the collapse of harmful algal blooms and influencing carbon transfer within coastal microbial food webs.ImportanceMarine ecosystems are shaped by interactions among microalgae, viruses, and heterotrophic eukaryotes, although the ecological roles of heterotrophic protists remain poorly understood. This study investigated the dynamics of oceanic microalgae and heterotrophic eukaryotes, namely Heterosigma species and Labyrinthulomycetes, and examined the effects of viral infection of Heterosigma akashiwo on the growth and proliferation of Aurantiochytrium species, members of the heterotrophic Labyrinthulomycetes. Our results revealed the dynamics of several Labyrinthulomycetes associated with Heterosigma populations and suggested that Aurantiochytrium species can redistribute carbon by utilizing the vDOM released during Heterosigma bloom termination induced by viral infection. These findings also reposition Aurantiochytrium from a passive heterotrophic component to an active ecological agent associated with Heterosigma viral infection, thereby influencing microalgal community dynamics. Overall, this study provides new insights into the fate of virus-infected Heterosigma in coastal marine systems, mediated by heterotrophic Labyrinthulomycetes, particularly Aurantiochytrium species, thereby filling an important knowledge gap in microbial ecology.
records.authors: Chen S, Aoki M, Sano K, Yamamoto K, Takao Y, Kamikawa R, Nagasaki K, Yoshida T.

records.title: Diversity and Taxonomic Classification of Plasmids in Pantoea.
records.abstract: Plasmids play a key role in prokaryotic evolution by providing adaptive traits that may facilitate colonization of new ecological niches. Members of the genus Pantoea harbor diverse plasmids, several of which carry metabolic and phytopathogenicity functions relevant for the interactions with plants and other eukaryotic hosts. Pantoea species harbor mobile plasmids that are able to transfer between cells, as well as domesticated plasmids that are vertically inherited, similarly to chromosomes. Although knowledge of Pantoea plasmid function and evolution is expanding, a general framework for their classification is still lacking. Here, we propose a framework for classifying Pantoea plasmids into plasmid taxonomic units (PTUs). By analyzing 797 publicly available Pantoea genomes, we identified 5,320 plasmids, of which 1,925 were classified by plasmid gene content similarity into 82 prevalent clusters of homologous plasmids. Integrating the clusters with plasmid backbone gene phylogeny, we recovered three previously described PTUs-LPP1, LPP2, and pOnion-across a broader taxonomic range than previously recognized. Additionally, three novel PTUs-LPP3, pPLD, and pINT-with distinct functional traits and pangenomic characteristics are proposed. We show that phylogenetic placement can assign previously unclassified plasmids to the plasmid groups defined here. Our analysis supplies a unified framework for plasmid classification in Pantoea and provides a foundation for future comparative studies of plasmid diversity and evolution in this taxon. records.title: Identification and genomic characterization of the nitrifiers in a full-scale municipal wastewater treatment plant with efficient, year-round nitrogen removal.
records.abstract: Effective nitrogen removal from wastewater is crucial for environmental preservation. However, wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) often experience decreased nitrogen removal rates during winter months when water temperatures decrease. This study investigated the microbial community of a full-scale WWTP that maintains efficient nitrogen removal even at temperatures as low as 7 °C. The nitrifying community was primarily composed of Nitrosomonas and Nitrospira, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and fluorescence in situ hybridization. Metagenomic analysis revealed a nitrifying community affiliated with Nitrosomonas cluster 6a and cluster DK-WWTP, comammox Nitrospira clade A, as well as canonical Nitrospira lineage I. A large-scale metagenomic screening showed that these nitrifiers are widespread in WWTPs worldwide across a broad temperature range. Furthermore, a pangenome analysis identified putative genetic traits which are potentially involved in adaptations to lower temperatures. These findings not only demonstrate the potential for maintaining high nitrification rates at lower temperatures, but also provide genomic evidence for adaptive traits that support stable nitrogen removal at lower temperatures. The presence of these nitrifiers can serve as an indicator of temperature-independent efficient nitrogen removal. Engineering strategies aimed at obtaining or maintaining these nitrifying microorganisms might lead toward year-round efficient wastewater treatment.

records.title: Thiamphenicol residues promote dark ammonia assimilation over oxidation in up-midstream of Jiulong River estuarine waters.
records.abstract: Estuaries receive large amounts of pollutants, including nitrogen nutrients and antibiotics, discharged by human activities. Ammonium (NH4+)/ammonia (NH3) is a preferred inorganic nitrogen nutrient utilized by microorganisms and an energy source for ammonia-oxidizing microorganisms. Nevertheless, the impact of residual antibiotics on NH3 transformation in estuary is not clear. So we investigated how thiamphenicol (TAP) - a ribosomal-targeting antibiotic widely used in aquaculture - alters dark NH3 transformations in the Jiulong River Estuary (JRE, 15NH4+ isotope tracing with metagenomic analysis. We found that tributaries are sources of antibiotics for JRE and single antibiotic concentration less than 0.1 μg/L, although the concentration varied with the seasons. In up-midstream dark zones, environmentally relevant TAP concentrations (0.01 μg/L) disproportionately stimulated NH3 assimilation over oxidation and the maximum stimulation was 118.6 ± 18.2% and 19.0 ± 1.1%, respectively. This made NH3 assimilation's contribution to total NH3 transformation maximally increased by 13 percentage points at upstream in winter and 15 percentage points at midstream in summer. Meanwhile, TAP had no directly significant effect on NH3 transformation in the downstream. Metagenomic analysis revealed that ammonia-oxidizing bacteria might be more sensitive to TAP exposure than ammonia-oxidizing archaea. Especially the ammonia-oxidizing bacteria community was composed of Betaproteobacteria. Our findings confirm that the hormetic effect of low-concentration antibiotics manifests in the NH3 transformation processes. The significant enhancement of NH3 assimilation by environmentally residual levels of TAP strengthens the flow of NH4+ to particulate nitrogen throughout the estuary, thereby potentially prolonging the residence time of NH4+ in aquatic systems. This provides a new perspective for understanding estuarine water eutrophication.

records.title: Whole-genome Mining of a Lead-resistant Bacterial Strain (Bacillus cereus).
records.abstract: BackgroundHeavy metals cause neurotoxicity/neuroinflammation in animals, including humans, and heavy metal contamination of soil/water is one of the major factors in neurodegenerative diseases. Soil bacteria that persist in metal-impacted environments often carry genomic determinants for metal detoxification alongside biosynthetic pathways for the production of structurally diverse secondary metabolites. We combined phenotypic identification, whole-genome sequencing and annotation-based genome mining to characterise a soil Bacillus cereus isolate (designated as VLR6) recovered alongside five additional bacterial isolates (VLR1-VLR5) from the same sample set.PurposeAnnotation-based mining to identify heavy-metal resistance genes involved in metal transformation, which is essential for understanding metal detoxification mechanisms and their potential implications for neurodegenerative diseases.MethodsIsolates were identified by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionisation-time-of-flight mass spectrometry (Bruker Biotyper). The VLR6 genome (5,411,809 bp, single contig) was annotated with Bakta v1.12.0 (database v6.0) and screened for acquired antimicrobial resistance determinants with the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database Resistance Gene Identifier (CARD-RGI). Biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) were predicted using antiSMASH v8.0.4 (default rules; Minimum Information about a Biosynthetic Gene Cluster 3.0 KnownClusterBlast comparisons) and identified through systematic keyword screening of the Bakta functional annotation.ResultsVLR4-VLR6 were identified as B. cereus, VLR1 as Escherichia coli, VLR2 as Citrobacter braakii (within the C. freundii complex), while VLR3 yielded no interpretable spectrum. The sequenced isolate (VLR6) genome encoded 5,504 coding sequences, 108 tRNAs, 39 rRNAs and one clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats array (35.3% GC). CARD-RGI identified 14 antibiotic-resistance-associated loci, dominated by glycopeptide-resistance gene cluster components (vanT/vanW/vanY homologues) and B. cereus class A/B1 beta-lactamases. antiSMASH identified 12 complete BGC regions, including an NI-siderophore region matching petrobactin (BGC0000942) independently corroborated by annotation keyword screening of the asb/fpu/fat loci, non-ribosomal peptide synthetases-metallophore region matching bacillibactin and an azole-containing RiPP region matching the thiopeptides thiocillin I/micrococcin P1; six regions returned no significant known-cluster match. Annotation-based mining additionally identified a heavy-metal-resistance gene set including a zntA-annotated Pb(II)/Cd(II)/Zn(II)-class P-type ATPase homologue, a complete ars operon (arsRBC) and two czcR-family regulators.ConclusionThe VLR6 genome carries a genomically confirmed set of BGCs, most confidently a petrobactin siderophore cluster corroborated by two independent methods alongside an annotation-supported heavy-metal-resistance gene set. Phenotypic lead-MIC determination and metabolomic or transcriptomic validation are still required before any bioactivity, neuroactive or otherwise, can be attributed to this strain or its predicted metabolites.

records.title: Microbiology Galaxy Lab: a community-driven gateway for reproducible and FAIR analysis of microbiological data.
records.abstract: The explosion of microbial omics data has outpaced the ability of many researchers to analyse it, with complex tools and limited computational resources creating barriers to discovery. To address this gap, we present the Microbiology Galaxy Lab (MGL): a free, globally accessible, community-supported platform that combines state-of-the-art analytical power with user-friendly accessibility. Supported by the Galaxy and global microbiology communities, this platform integrates over 315 tool suites and 115 curated workflows, enabling comprehensive metabarcoding, (meta)genomic, (meta)transcriptomic, and (meta)proteomic data analysis within a FAIR-aligned environment. It also supports research in the health and infectious disease sectors, as well as in environmental microbiology. The platform's utility is exemplified through various use cases, including antimicrobial resistance tracking, biomarker prediction, microbiome classification, and functional annotation of key microbes. Built on reproducibility and community engagement, it supports the creation, sharing, and updating of best-practice workflows. Over 35 tutorials and learning paths empower scientists, fostering an ecosystem that keeps resources at the forefront of microbiological data analysis. The MGL enables collective analysis, democratising research, thereby accelerating discovery across the global microbiology community ( microbiology.usegalaxy.org , .eu , .org.au , . fr ).

records.title: Whole-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analysis of Anolis adenovirus 2 reveals conserved genome organization and gene-specific evolutionary patterns.
records.abstract: Adenoviruses, which infect vertebrates, have a rich history of evolution that includes both host switching and coevolution, particularly within Barthadenovirus, a genus that infects squamate reptiles, birds, and mammals. Potential host-switching events can be identified by comparing the evolutionary histories between viruses and their hosts; however, many Barthadenovirus phylogenies have been inferred based on a limited number of easily-amplifiable gene segments. Whole-genome sequencing of novel strains of Barthadenovirus can provide greater phylogenetic confidence, and therefore more accurately identify host-switching when it occurs. Here, we present the coding-complete whole-genome sequence, annotation, reconciled species tree, and molecular evolution analyses of two isolates of Anolis adenovirus 2, a member of Barthadenovirus. Our two isolates of Anolis adenovirus 2 are sister lineages with very high sequence identity. Our results support existing hypotheses regarding the ancestral hosts of Barthadenovirus (squamate reptiles), and proposed host switching events within and between squamate reptiles and other vertebrate classes. We leverage our novel genome annotations to perform comparative synteny analyses, identifying a set of shared genes across Barthadenovirus whose gene order is largely conserved within the genus. Finally, our molecular evolution analyses highlight trends in evolutionary pressures on individual genes: Genes associated with viral replication and structure have experienced slower rates of evolution than those encoding proteins involved in host interaction. Our two sequenced isolates of Anolis adenovirus 2 add to an expanding number of adenovirus genomic resources and facilitate future investigations into the patterns and processes shaping adenovirus diversification.

records.title: Gut microbiome and metabolomics reveal the role of thioproline in attenuating colorectal cancer-associated inflammation.
records.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the top three cancers globally in terms of both incidence and mortality, and its development may be influenced by an inflammatory environment in the intestines, often associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis. Food bioactives could modulate gut microbiota through anti-inflammatory and epigenetic mechanisms. Given the significant role of thioproline as a food bioactive with antioxidant properties, its potential to modulate gut microbiota and mitigate CRC remains largely unexplored. This study aims to understand the effects of thioproline on gut microbiota community and investigate the mechanisms through which thioproline regulates gut microbiota and exerts its anticancer effects. Fecal and intestinal tissue samples were collected from health, CRC, and thioproline-treated CRC mice. The metagenome and metabolome data revealed that thioproline treatment significantly altered the gut microbiota community composition and metabolism in CRC mice. These CRC-associated gut microbiota and bacterial metabolites returned to normal levels. Moreover, under thioproline treatment, the microbial-metabolite interactions in CRC mice shifted toward patterns more closely resembling those observed in healthy mice. Thioproline treatment increased linoleic acid levels in mice, indicating its role in promoting linoleic acid metabolism to therapeutically restore homeostasis and alleviate inflammation in CRC. This was further supported by hematoxylin and eosin staining, which demonstrated that thioproline alleviated inflammation in CRC mice. Our study highlights thioproline's dual role in regulating the gut microbiota community and bacterial metabolism, modulating bacteria-host interactions, and ultimately reducing inflammation in CRC. These findings offer valuable insights for future research and therapeutic applications.IMPORTANCEColorectal cancer (CRC) is associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis and intestinal inflammation. While food bioactives can modulate the microbiome, whether thioproline exerts inhibitory effects against CRC through microbial regulation remains unknown. Using integrated metagenomics and metabolomics, we show that thioproline treatment restores the gut microbiota composition and bacterial metabolites disrupted by CRC to near-normal levels. Importantly, thioproline remodels microbial metabolite interaction networks, elevates linoleic acid levels, and alleviates intestinal inflammation. This study provides a systems-level perspective on how a single dietary bioactive compound reshapes the gut microbial ecosystem and its metabolic landscape to reduce inflammation in CRC. Our findings suggest a potential role for microbiome-targeted nutritional strategies in protecting against CRC progression through modulation of the gut microbiota and intestinal microenvironment.

records.title: Genomic and functional characterization of compost-derived bacteria identifies a candidate bioinoculant that influences tomato physiology and leaf metabolism
records.abstract: Soil biodiversity is increasingly threatened by anthropogenic activities, with intensive agriculture having a particularly detrimental impact on soil microbial communities and potentially disrupting plant-microbe interactions that contribute to plant growth and resilience to environmental stresses. Biofertilizers based on Plant Growth-Promoting Rhizobacteria (PGPR) and organic amendments represent promising strategies to restore microbial diversity and promote crop health. Although compost is widely used as an organic fertilizer, its potential as a reservoir of culturable beneficial bacteria for the development of bioinoculants remains largely unexplored. In this work, we isolated and identified six bacterial strains from commercial compost derived from municipal organic waste and screened them for plant growth-promoting traits. Two representative isolates, Kocuria rhizophila and Glutamicibacter arilaitensis, were subjected to whole-genome sequencing and comparative analyses to investigate their taxonomy, functional potential, rhizosphere competence, secondary metabolism, plastic degradation associated features, and predicted human pathogenicity. K. rhizophila was subsequently tested as an inoculant on tomato plants grown in soil, compost-amended soil, or sterile compost-amended soil. Five of the six isolates exhibited many of the plant growth-promoting traits tested. Genomic analyses of the two strains supported several of the observed phenotypes and revealed functions potentially associated with nutrient metabolism, plant-root interactions, environmental adaptation, and degradation of plastic polymers. Neither strain was predicted to be pathogenic to humans, indicating a potentially low safety risk for their application as bioinoculants. Upon inoculation with K. rhizophila, plant responses were influenced primarily by substrate type, although the bacterium produced specific, substrate-dependent effects at 33 days post inoculation. Inoculation resulted in a trend towards increased dry biomass in plants grown in sterile compost and influenced leaf metabolic profiles at 33 days. These results support the potential of K. rhizophila as a compost-derived bioinoculant and indicate that enriching compost with beneficial strains isolated from the same matrix could be a useful approach to complement its effects on plant growth.

records.title: Illuminating phage dark matter beyond the reach of structural alignments with PhageFlare
records.abstract: Many phage proteins remain functionally uncharacterized despite advances in structural-similarity-based annotation. We introduce PhageFlare, a deep learning framework for predicting phage protein functions lacking significant structural matches to annotated references. Across three structure-disjoint benchmarks, where no significant Foldseek match was detected between training and test proteins (E-value thresholds of  10  − 3 ,  10  − 4 , and  10  − 2 ), PhageFlare achieved macro-averaged  F 1 scores of 0.871, 0.889, and 0.738 outperforming the strongest baseline (0.789, 0.814, and 0.732). Systematic evaluations demonstrated that protein language model selection critically influences performance, with ESM-C achieving stronger overall performance than ESM-2 and ProtBert. Embedding-guided case studies revealed local structural correspondences among proteins with limited global similarity. Applied to the efam and Metagenomic Gut Virus datasets, PhageFlare annotated 38.0% and 51.8% of proteins unresolved by Fold-seek, respectively. Furthermore, PhageFlare identified lysogenic potential in 1,866 prophage-designated genomes misclassified as lytic by BACPHLIP. These results show that PhageFlare complements structural-similarity-based annotation and expands functional discovery across viral dark matter.
records.authors: Wang C, Xu Y, Li Z, Zhang L, Zhang L.
