records.title: Microbiome-targeted strategies for Alzheimer's disease: multi-omics signatures, mechanistic links, and intervention evidence.
records.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is increasingly studied in relation to gut microbial mechanisms because microbial metabolism, mucosal barrier function, and peripheral immune activation may influence neuroinflammation and host metabolic stress. This review evaluates microbiome-linked evidence in AD with emphasis on studies that combine metagenomics, metabolomics, inflammatory markers, neuroimaging, cerebrospinal fluid or blood biomarkers, and cognitive phenotyping. Current data support several recurring but not yet causal axes, including bile acid transformation, short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), bacterial product-related inflammatory signaling, and barrier dysfunction. We also review microbiome-targeted interventions, including diet and prebiotics, strain-specified probiotics and synbiotics, oligosaccharide-based agents, gut-restricted antimicrobials, and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT). The strength of evidence differs substantially across these strategies: sodium oligomannate has been tested in a phase 3 trial, whereas many probiotic, antimicrobial, and FMT approaches remain early clinical, preclinical, or mechanism-generating. Future trials should define a priori microbial, metabolite, immune, and brain biomarker endpoints; control diet, medication, and comorbidity confounding; and validate candidate signatures across independent cohorts before using microbiome profiles for screening or treatment selection.
records.authors: Huang X, Zhang X, Zhu Q.

records.title: Chromosome-level assembly of Lemnamoeba sinaloensis gen. nov. et sp. nov. (Apofilosa) reveals dynamic genome evolution in Rhizaria.
records.abstract: BackgroundRhizaria is a eukaryotic supergroup including many amoeboid protists. Despite harboring a large diversity and many ecologically important species, the genomes belonging to this supergroup remain poorly explored. With only a handful available genome sequences, most of low contiguity, little is known about overall architecture, characteristics, and evolution of rhizarian genomes.ResultsWe provide a highly contiguous genome assembly of an undescribed marine rhizarian amoeba formerly known as M6MM. The assembly revealed a small (27 Mb; 8704 genes) and compact genome (84% genes, 10% repeats, 6% intergenic regions), and was almost fully captured in six contigs confirmed cytologically to represent chromosomes. The genome contains a very large amount of simple-sequence repeats (SSRs), particularly of the AC:GT dinucleotide class (206 loci/Mb), in total covering almost 2% of the assembly. We also obtained the complete mitochondrial genome, which is reduced and devoid of ribosomal protein genes similarly to some other rhizarians. Some of these "missing" mitochondrial-encoded genes are found in the nuclear genome and are predicted to be targeted to the mitochondrion. In our 18S rDNA phylogenetic analysis, M6MM loosely groups with environmental sequences and the amoeboflagellate Viscidocauda repens. However, this amoeba is phylogenetically distant from any described species and expresses a unique pseudopodial morphology, prompting us to erect the novel genus and species Lemnamoeba sinaloensis gen. nov. et. sp. nov. Environmental data show that L. sinaloensis has a wide marine distribution and can mostly be found between the surface and 100 m depths.ConclusionThis study adds another genus to the hitherto taxonomically poor Apofilosa, provides one of the highest-quality rhizarian genome assemblies to date, and reveals an abundance of SSRs in the genome, highlighting the complexity of eukaryotic genomes in underexplored parts of the tree of life.
records.authors: Hiltunen Thorén M, Onuț-Brännström I, Zlatogursky V, Pardasani Y, Pecková H, Karlíková A, Holzer AS, Burki F.

records.title: The pangenome of the human fungal pathogen  Cryptococcus neoformans  reveals that subtelomeres are hotspots for gene content variation
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Cryptococcus neoformans is a human fungal pathogen that causes cryptococcal meningitis, primarily in individuals with advanced HIV disease. The  C. neoformans species is composed of four unique molecular types: VNI, VNII, VNBI, and VNBII, with thousands of global isolates within these groups. While previous descriptions of these molecular types have focused on nucleotide divergence between shared genes, there has been limited examination of variation in gene content between isolates. Here, we define the genome content diversity within a collection of 383  C. neoformans isolates spanning all four molecular types. To do so, we constructed a pangenome through  de novo assembly and annotation of short-read Illumina sequences. We defined 6,564 representative ortholog groups of the predicted proteins leveraging high-quality data from reference strain H99. We classified ortholog groups as either core (93.8%) or accessory (6.2%) based on their presence across the species. We next used long-read assemblies for a subset of our isolates to define the predicted accuracy of our classifications and account for errors in assembly or annotation of short-read sequences. We determined that while a subset of accessory genes are segregating across the entire species, many accessory genes are found only within specific molecular types, suggesting limited gene flow between groups. Additionally, we found many accessory genes are poorly conserved within the  C. neoformans species but share high sequence similarity to genes found in related Cryptococcaceae species, suggesting horizontal gene transfer. We also found that accessory genes were enriched within subtelomeric regions, implicating the subtelomeres in gene content variation between isolates. We show examples of accessory genes located within subtelomeres of  C. neoformans isolates that were conserved with subtelomeric proteins of other Cryptococcaceae species. Our pangenomic analysis of  C. neoformans gives species-level insights into its biology, potentially illuminating genetic contributions to pathogenesis.
records.authors: Reichardt CE, Billmyre RB.

records.title: Cross-kingdom metabolic regulation by a symbiotic virus: Transient viral microRNAs coordinate host metabolism and immune responses.
records.abstract: Symbiotic microorganisms and endogenous viruses play fundamental roles in shaping host physiology, yet the non-coding RNA-mediated mechanisms underlying viral-driven metabolic reprogramming remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate a novel mechanism of cross-kingdom metabolic manipulation mediated by symbiotic viral microRNAs. Using the tobacco cutworm Spodoptera litura, its endoparasitoid wasp Snellenius manilae, and the wasp-associated bracovirus SmBV as a model system, we identified two virus-derived microRNAs, SmBV-miR-2733 and SmBV-miR-3772, that target the host lipogenic genes encoding AGPAT and lipin, leading to the suppression of glycerolipid biosynthesis and reduced lipid accumulation. Functional analyses revealed that these symbiotic viral miRNAs concurrently attenuate host innate immune signaling pathways (Toll and JAK/STAT) and cellular encapsulation, establishing a mechanistic link between viral metabolic coercion and host immunomodulation. Crucially, this viral microRNA-mediated regulation is transient and highly dynamic; miRNA expression declines during later stages of infection, coinciding with an intermediate recovery of host lipogenic gene expression and lipid reserves, which may help sustain the developing parasitoids. Prolonged experimental maintenance of viral miRNAs disrupted host energetic homeostasis and compromised symbiotic success, underscoring the evolutionary necessity of temporally coordinated metabolic regulation. Comparative genomic analysis identified miR-2733- and miR-3772-like candidate loci with miRNA-precursor-like structures that are unevenly distributed across related bracovirus lineages. Together, our findings provide significant mechanistic insights into how symbiotic viral effectors post-transcriptionally rewire host metabolic and immune networks, offering a broader conceptual framework for understanding homeostasis in diverse host-microbe symbioses.
records.authors: Lin YC, Tseng YK, Chen P, Lin CY, Tang CK, Wu YL.

records.title: Divergent transcriptional responses of conserved cellular machinery to warming and phosphorus limitation in freshwater phytoplankton
records.abstract: Lakes are simultaneously warming and becoming phosphorus limited, but whether phytoplankton taxa of the same phylum respond through similar molecular mechanisms remains unclear, challenging a common assumption underlying predictions of ecological responses to environmental change. We cultured four freshwater phytoplankton species, including two diatoms (  Fragilaria crotonensis and  Nitzschia palea ) and two cyanobacteria (  Microcystis aeruginosa and  Synechococcus sp. ), across factorial gradients of temperature (20, 24 and 28 °C) and phosphorus (P) limitation, and characterized gene expression using RNA-seq, differential expression analysis and signed gene set enrichment. We generated predictions for expected responses for categories of gene functions derived from the growth rate (GRH) and temperature-dependent physiology hypotheses (TDPH). Warming and P limitation engaged largely the predicted functional categories in all species, however the direction of the response was not conserved, even within phyla—the two cyanobacteria regulated photosynthesis, ribosomal and chaperone genes in opposite directions. Ribosome- and translation-related genes gave the strongest warming response and, in  N. palea , reversed direction within the species, increasing between 20 and 24 °C and decreasing between 24 and 28 °C, below the strain’s thermal optimum estimated under moderate P limitation. Ribosomal allocation thus supported each hypothesis in different species and temperature ranges and was not predicted by thermal position alone. Where the interaction effects could be tested, P limitation rarely recruited novel pathways but modified existing warming responses, suppressing them in  F. crotonensis and amplifying and redirecting them in  M. aeruginosa . Molecular responses to combined drivers therefore diverge among related taxa, cautioning against aggregating species into functional groups when forecasting phytoplankton responses to global change.

records.title: Longitudinal Skin Bacterial Cluster Associated With Protection Against Allergic Co-Morbidity in Pediatric Atopic Dermatitis.
records.abstract: BackgroundAtopic dermatitis (AD) is an inflammatory skin condition that often portends the development of allergic comorbidities. Despite evidence supporting the role of the skin microbiome in AD, its temporal patterns and associations with risk or protection for allergic co-morbidity remain unclear. Our objective is to characterize core species of the pediatric AD bacterial microbiome, assess microbial networks and clusters, and identify global microbial changes relevant to AD and the atopic march.MethodsWe performed metagenomic shotgun sequencing on 353 non-lesional skin samples from children in the Mechanisms of Progression of Atopic Dermatitis to Asthma in Children (MPAACH) cohort across 5 annual visits. We assessed taxonomic composition and analyzed longitudinal skin microbial patterns with progression to allergic co-morbidities.ResultsWe identified 436 distinct species. Shannon diversity and richness declined with age, and socioeconomic factors explained the variance in species composition. Staphylococcus aureus (SA) was more abundant in severe AD. Cluster 5, comprised of typically gut-associated microbes, was more abundant in non-sensitized children who did not develop allergic co-morbidities over time.ConclusionsOur analyses revealed key patterns in core taxa, diversity and abundance of the skin microbiome over time in early life and highlighted previously unexplored factors such as socioeconomic status as key contributors to the variability in species composition. Abundance of SA confers risk, while gut-associated microbes may offer protection, influencing the clinical trajectory of AD and the atopic march. Thus, these results provide a novel and comprehensive understanding of the temporal dynamics of the skin microbiota in pediatric AD.

records.title: Comparative genomics of seven Tenacibaculum maritimum isolates from farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar), Atlantic halibut (Hippoglossus hippoglossus), and lumpfish (Cyclopterus lumpus) in Canada and Norway reveals conserved features.
records.abstract: Tenacibaculum maritimum is a major bacterial pathogen of marine fish responsible for ulcerative disease outbreaks and high mortality in numerous fish species and represents an important challenge in aquaculture worldwide. In this study, we characterized seven newly sequenced T. maritimum isolates recovered from farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar), Atlantic halibut (Hippoglossus hippoglossus), and lumpfish (Cyclopterus lumpus) in British Columbia (Canada) and Norway, including the first complete genome of T. maritimum isolated from Atlantic salmon in Norway. Comparative genomic analysis revealed the presence of a complete Type IX secretion system (T9SS) and the canonical gliding-associated machinery. We also identified a largely conserved repertoire of candidate T9SS substrates and several major host-interaction proteins. Phylogenetic analysis placed the isolates in several well-supported clades comprising strains from different geographic origins and host species. Characterization of the O-antigen gene clusters identified three different types (1-0, 2-1, and 4-0), whose distribution was not congruent with the phylogenetic relationships among isolates. Colony development of the four Norwegian isolates on agar was strongly influenced by incubation temperature, with rapid growth at 20-24°C, slower growth at 12-16°C, and only limited growth at 8°C. This study expands the available genomic resources for T. maritimum and highlights the importance of integrating genomic and environmental surveillance to improve tenacibaculosis management in aquaculture systems.
records.authors: Lagadec E, Gulla S, Småge SB, Pino-Martinez E, Solheim K, Handeland SO, Nylund A.

records.title: VenusGenome: Genome-Aware Masked Autoencoding for Microbial Genome Representation Learning
records.abstract: A  bstract   Genomic-context models have shown that contextualizing protein embeddings can improve predictions of microbial function. We observe that a gene’s protein embedding is partially predictable from the embeddings of neighboring genes in the genome, motivating high-ratio masking that requires reconstruction from sparser genomic context. Genomic modeling must also distinguish biological relationships from assembly conventions, since the ordering of separate contigs does not imply adjacency and strand labels depend on the reference orientation. We therefore introduce VenusGenome, a gene-resolution masked autoencoder that combines visible-only encoding with genome-aware attention incorporating contig boundaries, relative strand orientations, and gene positions. We pretrain this model on a curated corpus of over 1.7 million microbial genome assemblies from isolate and metagenomic sources, using frozen protein embeddings as gene-level inputs. Across genome-level phenotype prediction and gene-level tasks, the resulting frozen representations achieve the highest mean performance among the evaluated models on nine of eleven primary metrics. An exploratory gene-input perturbation analysis further links representation sensitivity to experimentally measured fitness defects. Ablations support the contribution of genome-aware attention and show the benefits of masked autoencoding over BERT-style masked modeling, with further gains from higher masking ratios.
records.authors: Zhang L, Zhang Y, Tan Y, Jiang F, Zhong B, Cheng X, Hong L, Li M, Yu Y.

records.title: Heptyl prodigiosin from estuarine Zooshikella sp. RANM57 induces caspase-dependent apoptosis and suppresses clonogenic survival in androgen-independent prostate cancer cells
records.abstract: Abstract    Estuarine microbiomes are rich ecological niches for discovering novel secondary metabolites with therapeutic applications. This study focuses on the isolation, purification, structural elucidation, and antineoplastic evaluation of a red pigment from a marine microbial isolate. The bacterium  Zooshikella  sp. RANM57 was isolated from the Netravathi River estuary. Biomass was recovered using an alum-induced flocculation technique and solvent extraction, after which the primary pigment was purified via flash chromatography and structurally characterized using HRLCMS-QTOF and NMR spectroscopy. Anticancer potential was evaluated against human PC-3 prostate cancer cells using MTT and clonogenic assays. The underlying apoptotic mechanism was delineated using Annexin V/PI staining, Caspase-3 quantification, and TUNEL assays. The purified pigment was identified as the tripyrrole alkaloid heptyl prodigiosin based on HRLCMS-QTOF, UV-Vis/FT-IR profiling, and 1D NMR spectral concordance with reported prodiginine features.  In vitro  evaluations revealed significant dose-dependent cytotoxicity against PC-3 cells (IC  50   = 9.00 µg/mL), demonstrating high anticancer efficacy relative to cisplatin. Mechanistic profiling confirmed that cell death occurred exclusively via an intrinsic apoptotic cascade, as evidenced by significant phosphatidylserine externalization (17.60%), executioner Caspase-3 activation (52.45%), and terminal DNA fragmentation (21.25%), without inducing primary necrosis. Furthermore, treatment also reduced clonogenic survival after 24 h exposure and 8-day outgrowth. The successful isolation and characterization of heptyl prodigiosin from  Zooshikella  sp. RANM57 underscores the value of estuarine bacteria in natural product discovery. Our biological evaluations demonstrate that the compound functions as a precise, potent inducer of caspase-associated apoptosis, positioning this tripyrrole scaffold as a highly promising candidate for further anticancer pharmacological development.
records.authors: Madtha RS, Balakrishna K, Deen KR, Rithick S, Ignacimuthu S, Pandikumar P, Chirakkara SP, Abraham A.

records.title: Metagenomic and thermodynamic mapping of Ny-Ålesund, Arctic microbiota: harnessing low temperature biohydrogen production.
records.abstract: Biohydrogen produced by psychrophilic dark fermentation has lower energy requirements than conventional methods. In this study, kinetic, thermodynamic, and functional metagenomic analyses were conducted to determine the profiles of microbial consortia from Ny-Ålesund, Svalbard, incubated at 4°C and 20°C in the presence or absence of the methanogenic inhibitor 2-bromoethanesulfonate. Biogas potential values derived from volumetric analyses indicated that pure biohydrogen (>95.6%) was produced, while also confirming the presence of these consortia adapted to operate with lag phases of 4-7 days and exhibiting temperature sensitivity coefficients (Q10) Clostridium, Enterobacter, and Klebsiella) harboring the genetic potential for the pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR) and formate hydrogenlyase (FHL) pathways. Metagenomic enrichment for the genes encoding cold-shock defense (cspA, dnaK) and putative electron-bifurcating complexes (rnf, ech) highlights the combined genetic potential to sustain viability and overcome thermodynamic limits at all incubation temperatures. Overall, the biochemical characteristics of native Arctic consortia provide evidence of their potential to serve as viable biocatalysts for biohydrogen production, currently under laboratory batch conditions at low temperatures.IMPORTANCEBiohydrogen production is a potentially sustainable energy source that offers new options for generating carbon-neutral renewable energy. Traditionally, biohydrogen production methods require substantial, continuous heating energy input. This publication describes the examination of the "underutilized" biohydrogen production potential of microbial communities in the Arctic region (Ny-Ålesund, Svalbard) that have separately evolved genetic adaptations necessary to maintain metabolic functions at sub-zero temperatures. Psychrophilic dark-fermentation experiments, combined with thermodynamic modeling and metagenomic analyses, show how unique cold-adapted microorganisms can produce high-purity biohydrogen gas at extreme ambient temperatures under laboratory batch conditions, highlighting a fundamental baseline that could inform future efforts to reduce the energy footprint of biofuel production. While long-term reactor stability and scalability remain to be validated, this work bridges the divide between observational Arctic microbiology and foundational green energy research, demonstrating that the discovery of extreme microbial environments holds promise for developing low-energy biological processes.
records.authors: Mishra S, Mutnuri S.

records.title: Seasonal community structure and environmental associations of putative pathogenic microorganisms in the Shelf-Margin Sea of the Northwestern South China Sea.
records.abstract: Marine pathogenic microorganisms are crucial to ecological health and fishery aquaculture. However, the composition and influencing drivers for pathogenic microorganisms in the Shelf-Margin Sea of the Northwestern South China Sea (SMS-NWSCS) are still unclear. This study applied 16S rRNA and ITS gene high-throughput sequencing combined with multiple bacterial pathogen detection (MBPD) and FUNGuild database to explore putative pathogenic microorganisms in the SMS-NWSCS and to investigate the main environmental associations of the composition, diversity, complexity and stability of putative pathogenic microbial communities. Results showed that Escherichia coli (31.77%), Pseudomonas fluorescens (16.25%) and Sphingomonas paucimobilis (6.90%) were dominant putative pathogenic bacteria, while Pseudozyma sp. (48.36%) and Malassezia globosa (48.34%) dominated the putative pathogenic fungal communities. The putative pathogenic bacterial community exhibited higher alpha diversity in winter, while the fungal community showed greater alpha diversity in summer. Beta diversity analysis revealed significant seasonal dynamics in both putative pathogenic bacterial and fungal communities (bacteria: R2 = 0.12, p = 0.001; fungi: R2 = 0.08, p = 0.007). Spearman's correlation analysis suggested that a suite of environmental factors, including temperature, pH, DO, Chla and nutrients, played significant roles in influencing putative pathogenic microbial community structure. PLS-PM analysis demonstrated that bacterial alpha diversity was positively associated with community complexity (R2 = 0.10, p 2 = 0.45, p 2 = 0.10, p 2 = 0.21, p < 0.001) showed positive correlations with the stability of the putative pathogenic fungal community. Our study reveals the seasonal patterns of putative pathogenic microorganisms in the SMS-NWSCS and enhances the understanding of their community maintenance mechanisms.
records.authors: Deng X, Chen Q, Ferdoush J, Huang C, Tang Y, Zhang G, Zhu Y, Jiang G, Dong K, Li N, Huang L.

records.title: A Specific Ancestral Sequence Reconstruction of Flagellin Can Drive Motility in  Salmonella enterica  but not  Escherichia coli
records.abstract: The bacterial flagellar filament, built from thousands of flagellin subunits, is essential for flagellar motility. Here, we aimed to use ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR) to generate conservative, ancestral flagellin sequences that surround the divergency point between  Escherichia and  Salmonella species and tested their ability to restore motility in flagellin deleted  Escherichia coli and  Salmonella Typhimurium. Only one (N131) out of three candidates restored motility in  S. Typhimurium but not  E. coli , despite high structural similarity to native FliC/FljB.  S. Typhimurium expressing N131 showed reduced motility relative to wild-type  Salmonella FliC, alongside increased tumbling frequency. Serial passage across swim plates produced a derivative, N131.10, containing a single flagellin mutation (M144I), with a larger swim ring diameter but also increased tumbling frequency. Comparison of structural interaction networks among the residues of  S. Typhimurium LT2 FliC with those of other filament proteins showed that non-motile candidates (N132 and N134) carried substitutions that disrupted key core-domain atomic interactions. These results demonstrate that flagellar filament assembly tolerates only limited sequence variation and that this capacity for tolerance differs between  E. coli and  S. Typhimurium despite their close phylogenetic relationship.  Importance  Bacteria swim using long, rotating filaments assembled from thousands of copies of a protein called flagellin. We reconstructed likely ancestral versions of this protein to investigate how evolutionary changes affect swimming. Of three versions tested, only one restored swimming in  Salmonella unable to make its own flagellin. The same protein did not work in the closely related bacterium  E. coli . After repeated selection for better movement, a single additional change helped the  Salmonella spread farther and also altered its swimming behaviour. These findings show that closely related bacteria differ in the changes that their flagellar assembly machinery can tolerate. Understanding these limits helps explain how flagella evolve while retaining their function and provides a foundation for studying the role of flagellar variation in immune recognition and evasion.
records.authors: Scadden J, Philip JS, Ridone P, Sowa Y, Baker MA.

records.title: Insights Into The Early Diversification of  bla  NDM-1  Genetic Contexts Following its Emergence in  Acinetobacter  species and Spread to Enterobacterales
records.abstract: Since its emergence, the New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM) has become a major global antimicrobial resistance threat, enabling bacterial hosts to resist most β-lactam antibiotics, including carbapenems, and spreading widely across bacterial species and geographic regions. Believed to have originated in  Acinetobacter spp.,  bla NDM subsequently spread to Enterobacterales through mobile genetic elements, despite barriers to lateral gene transfer between these phylogenetically distant taxa. To investigate the genetic diversity and mechanisms underlying this interspecies transfer and subsequent global expansion, we sequenced and characterized 13  bla NDM-1 -positive Gram-negative bacterial isolates collected in India in 2007, among the earliest known isolates harboring  bla NDM-1 . Clonal diversity was observed among both  Escherichia coli and  Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates. Comprehensive genomic analysis revealed that  bla NDM-1 was consistently embedded within a conserved multidrug resistance region, often associated with mobile genetic elements involved in lateral gene transfer. Notably, the insertion sequence IS  Aba14 was identified in 6 of the 13 sequences, suggesting a potential role in the early dissemination of  bla NDM-1 among diverse bacterial hosts. These findings contribute to our understanding of the evolutionary origins and early genetic context of  bla NDM-1 , highlighting the importance of continued genomic surveillance and functional studies to better understand the persistence and dissemination of carbapenem resistance.  Impact Statement  This study characterizes 13 previously undescribed genetic contexts of the New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase-1 gene (  bla NDM-1 ) in Enterobacterales isolates collected in India in 2007. These isolates represent some of the earliest known  bla NDM-1 -positive Enterobacterales and are the earliest collected  bla NDM-1 -positive Enterobacterales for which whole-genome sequences are now available. Their genetic contexts include diverse combinations of antibiotic resistance genes and associated mobile genetic elements. Notably, the insertion sequence IS  Aba14 was identified in 6 of the 13 sequences, highlighting its frequent association with  bla NDM-1 during the early stages of its dissemination. Together, these findings reveal substantial genetic diversity surrounding  bla NDM-1 early in its emergence and suggest that diverse arrangements of mobile genetic elements may have contributed to its early dissemination across bacterial hosts and the subsequent spread of carbapenem resistance.
records.authors: Allard N, Touati D, Faille N, Grenier F, Beauchemin-Lauzon E, Lévesque S, Rodrigue S, Haraoui L.

records.title: First Report of Vibrio harveyi From Starry Flounder (Platichthys stellatus) With Phenotypic, Pathogenicity and Whole-Genome Characterization.
records.abstract: Vibrio harveyi is a prominent bacterial pathogen of marine aquaculture. Vibrio harveyi has not previously been reported in starry flounder. In this study, phenotypic and genotypic characterizations and pathogenicity assessments of V. harveyi isolated from starry flounder in South Korea were conducted. Phylogenetic analysis identified strains VH-SF-1, VH-SF-2, VH-SF-4 and VH-SF-5 as V. harveyi . Motility assays showed that VH-SF-2 displayed the highest activity at 27°C. In pathogenicity tests, VH-SF-2 caused 100% mortality within 16 and 48 h at doses of 3 × 108 and 3 × 107 CFU/fish, respectively, whereas a 10% mortality rate was observed at 3 × 106 CFU/fish. The lethal dose (LD50) was estimated to range from 3 × 106 to 3 × 107 CFU/fish, providing the first evidence of the pathogenicity of V. harveyi in starry flounder. These findings suggest that V. harveyi may emerge as a novel pathogen of this species. To investigate genomic characteristics and virulence factors, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was conducted. Strain VH-SF-2 harboured multiple virulence-related mechanisms, including outer membrane proteins, motility, quorum sensing, bacterial secretion systems, iron uptake and regulation and virulence regulators. The study aimed to elucidate the biological and pathogenic characteristics of V. harveyi isolated from starry flounder.
records.authors: Park JH, Kim SW, Kim JO.

records.title: Chromosome-scale nuclear and mitochondrial genome assemblies reveal extreme genome compartmentalization in the hazelnut pathogen  Anisogramma anomala
records.abstract: Anisogramma anomala is an obligate biotrophic ascomycete and the causal agent of Eastern filbert blight, the most economically important disease of hazelnut in the United States. Here, we generated a chromosome-scale reference genome for  A. anomala isolate OR-Ennis-d and characterized its nuclear and mitochondrial genome architecture. The 344-Mb nuclear genome was resolved into 9 predicted chromosomes and is repeat-rich, with transposable elements comprising 88.8% of the assembly. Although transposable elements are abundant, their divergence landscape and low retention of conserved protein domains support a history of past extensive transposon proliferation followed by widespread degeneration. Repeat accumulation was highly uneven and generated pronounced genome compartmentalization. Approximately half of predicted genes occur in compact, TE-poor regions with short flanking intergenic regions that are enriched for conserved BUSCO orthologs. In contrast, genes in TE-rich, gene-sparse regions with long flanking intergenic regions are enriched for carbohydrate-active enzymes, secreted proteins, and candidate secreted effector proteins, consistent with a two-speed-like genome architecture. The 462-kb mitochondrial genome is among the largest reported for ascomycetes and contains 117 introns, including an intron adjacent to  cob codon 143 that may prevent acquisition of the p.G143A substitution associated with resistance to quinone outside inhibitor fungicides. Finally, we identified mitochondrial DNA insertions at 20 nuclear loci totaling at least 616.9 kb, an unusually extensive amount for a fungal genome. This chromosome-scale genome resource reveals the extreme nuclear and mitochondrial genome architecture in  A. anomala and provides a foundation for investigating genome evolution and adaptation to hazelnut resistance.
records.authors: Zaccaron AZ, Søndreli KL, LeBoldus JM, Weisberg AJ.

records.title: Comparative Genomics of Multidrug-Resistant and Extensively Drug-Resistant Acinetobacter Baumannii Clinical Isolates from an Intensive Care Unit in Northeastern Brazil
records.abstract: Abstract    Acinetobacter baumannii  is an opportunistic pathogen linked to healthcare-associated infections and the dissemination of multidrug-resistant phenotypes in critical hospital settings. In this study, we performed a comparative genomic analysis of clinical isolates identified as  A. baumannii  by routine hospital microbiology, obtained from an intensive care unit in Northeastern Brazil and classified as susceptible (SEN), multidrug-resistant (MDR), or extensively drug-resistant (XDR). Fifteen isolates were subjected to whole-genome sequencing; after quality control, 14 genomes were included in the main comparative analyses. Genome assembly metrics, functional composition, pangenome, resistome, virulome, Pasteur MLST, core-genome phylogeny, phenotype–genotype concordance, and FastANI-based taxonomic refinement were evaluated. MDR and XDR isolates carried a higher burden of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes than SEN isolates. Pangenome analysis revealed a conserved core genome combined with variable accessory content, whereas the virulome was relatively conserved across phenotypic groups. Quinolone resistance-determining region (QRDR) mutations in  gyrA  and/or  parC  were detected in ciprofloxacin-resistant isolates, supporting the role of chromosomal mechanisms in fluoroquinolone resistance that may not be captured by analyses restricted to acquired resistance genes. FastANI analysis further revealed taxonomic discrepancies in two susceptible isolates, highlighting the complementary value of WGS for hospital surveillance and taxonomic refinement within the  Acinetobacter calcoaceticus–baumannii  complex. Overall, our findings indicate that antimicrobial resistance in these clinical isolates is a multifactorial phenomenon shaped by clonal diversity, accessory genome variation, AMR gene burden, chromosomal resistance mechanisms, and taxonomic complexity within the ACB complex.

records.title: Ultra-deep HiFi sequencing reveals rare structural-variant subpopulations in multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa from an LVAD-associated infection.
records.abstract: BackgroundPseudomonas aeruginosa is a Gram-negative opportunistic pathogen frequently associated with multidrug-resistant infections in clinical settings. The rise of antibiotic-resistant strains and their genomic complexity necessitate advanced tools for comprehensive genetic characterization, particularly in the context of resistance to antibiotic and phage therapies.MethodsHere, we use ultra-deep high-fidelity (HiFi) sequencing to analyze strain NRD619, a multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa isolate that had colonized the driveline of a left ventricular assist device of an 82-year-old male who was identified as a phage therapy candidate. Through HiFi long-read sequencing and bioinformatic analysis, we identified low-frequency heterogeneous structural variants (SVs) and investigated their potential phenotypic consequences through functional annotation and literature-based gene-function analysis.ResultsSmall variants in known resistance-associated genes, including an early frameshift in mexZ, were consistent with components of the multidrug-resistant phenotype, whereas several other genotype-phenotype associations remained uncertain. Ultra-deep long-read sequencing identified five low-frequency heterogeneous SV signals. A reciprocal 31.7-kb deletion and duplication of a phage-rich region were supported by 3 and 95 reads, respectively; three multi-kilobase insertion candidates were each supported by a single HiFi molecule. Observed variant allele frequencies ranged from 1.2119% to 0.0122%. The insertions intersected genes involved in type IV pili, transport, and stress response, providing plausible hypotheses for effects on biofilm-related behavior, device colonization, and other phenotypes.ConclusionsThis study demonstrates how ultra-deep sequencing can uncover cryptic genetic heterogeneity in bacterial pathogens, offering insights into P. aeruginosa population structure in a clinical isolate that are inaccessible to conventional-depth sequencing. Because sequencing followed single-colony recovery and laboratory expansion, the origin and in vivo frequencies of the rarest SVs cannot be established. The detected diversity may reflect structural states accessible in vivo or variation arising during ex vivo propagation; the latter remains relevant because culture-based genomic and phenotypic characterization interrogates the expanded population. Future applications could refine our understanding of multidrug resistance, phage susceptibility, and adaptations influencing host colonization.SignificanceChronic bacterial infections are usually represented by a single genome, even though clinicians and microbiologists know genetically diverse subpopulations can coexist within a patient. Using ultra-deep, high-fidelity long-read sequencing of a multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa clinical isolate from a left ventricular assist device-associated infection, we reveal structural heterogeneity distinguished by phage and mobile-element architectures and associated small variants. Coverage-based modeling shows that several of these rare structural states would be poorly sampled at standard sequencing depths, yet they occur in loci linked to virulence, surface interactions, transport, and stress response. Because the isolate underwent single-colony recovery before sequencing, the study cannot determine whether individual rare variants arose in vivo or during ex vivo propagation. Either possibility is informative: the former represents hidden within-host diversity, whereas the latter can alter the population used for culture-based genomic and phenotypic characterization. These findings establish ultra-deep long-read sequencing as a strategy for revealing hidden adaptive potential in chronic and device-associated infection isolates.
records.authors: Bosco A, Luong T, Jeshvaghane MA, Fallahpour M, Modlin SJ, Roach D, Valafar F.

records.title: RNA viruses as drivers of rapid diatom succession within a single bloom event.
records.abstract: Diatoms frequently dominate seasonal phytoplankton blooms and contribute ~40% of marine primary production. Viruses drive phytoplankton mortality and bloom collapse, yet how viruses regulate diatom bloom dynamics is not well resolved. Here, using quantitative metatranscriptomics, we tracked temporal patterns of diatoms and associated viruses at near-daily resolution during the spring bloom in the Gulf of Aqaba, Red Sea. We captured distinct phases and rapid restructuring within both the diatom community and cell-associated virosphere. Diatom transcriptional profiling indicated activation of stress and death pathways prior to taxon-specific demise. RNA viruses emerged as dominant players within the bloom, with fluctuations of putative diatom-infecting RNA viruses across intracellular and extracellular fractions revealing sequential waves of active virus infection that were consistent with virus-mediated diatom mortality. Correlation and codon usage analyses further implicated specific diatom taxa as putative hosts for the identified RNA viruses. Rather than a uniform 'boom and bust', the spring diatom bloom comprised a mosaic of overlapping successional waves of diatom and viral taxa unfolding on daily timescales. These findings support RNA viruses as drivers of diatom turnover, advancing our understanding of how viruses temporally structure diverse diatom assemblages and the biogeochemical trajectory of diatom blooms in marine systems.
records.authors: Mellijor JL, Tennenbuam-Azulai Y, Spungin D, Avrahami Y, Vardi A, Frada MJ, Kranzler CF.

records.title: Molecular and morphological characterization of nine new Gnomoniopsis species (Diaporthales, Gnomoniaceae): Genomic insights into evolution and phylogeny.
records.abstract: Gnomoniopsis comprises parasitic, endophytic, and saprophytic fungi. Since its establishment, this genus has presented considerable taxonomic challenges owing to extensive morphological overlap among species, rendering traditional classification systems that rely predominantly on phenotypic characteristics no longer applicable. To resolve the current taxonomic confusion and clarify the species diversity, phylogenetic relationships, and genomic adaptive characteristics of Gnomoniopsis, the present study was carried out. In this study, the internal transcriptional spacer (ITS), translation extension factor 1-α (tef1), and partial beta-tubulin (tub2) were analyzed and combined to observe morphological characteristics of Gnomoniopsis. The isolates were identified from chestnut (Castanea), Embelia vestita, tea (Camellia sinensis), and other hosts in Sichuan Province, as well as from Quercus species and partial leaf rot from Fujian Province. Nine new species, namely G. xiaoheijiangensis sp. nov., G. embeliae sp. nov., G. yunvfengensis sp. nov., G. quercus sp. nov., G. ledongensis sp. nov., G. yonganensis sp. nov., G. conghuaensis sp. nov., G. loropetali sp. nov., and G. qixiensis sp. nov., were obtained. Phylogenomic analysis based on 7,942 orthologous proteins' clusters revealed distinct species boundaries within Gnomoniopsis. Phylogenomics has thus effectively resolved the ambiguous phylogenetic relationships in this genus. This work identifies nine previously undescribed Gnomoniopsis species, clarifies the species diversity and conserved genomic characteristics within the genus, and lays a foundation for subsequent taxonomic analyses of Gnomoniopsis.
records.authors: Wang X, Jiang Y, Liu W, Yan X, Sheng J, Ai C, Liu X, Zhang X, Meng Z, Wang S.

records.title: Archaea are more hospitable hosts for mobile inteins than bacteria.
records.abstract: Intervening proteins, or inteins, are mobile genetic elements characterized by their ability to rearrange peptide bonds through a post-translational, self-splicing reaction. Here, we expand the scope of a prior investigation to reexamine the distribution of inteins across archaea and bacteria. This update represents 20- and 50-fold increases in archaeal and bacterial genomes, respectively. In accordance with previous findings, inteins are enriched in DNA replication, recombination, and repair (RRR) proteins, but they are substantially more prevalent in archaea than bacteria, a difference twice that previously reported. Moreover, mini-inteins lacking homing endonucleases (HENs) are more common in bacterial inteins, suggesting bacterial inteins undergo HEN domain loss more frequently than archaeal inteins. This reduction in the prevalence of HENs, the drivers of intein mobility, offers a potential explanation for the lower density of inteins in bacteria than in archaea. Furthermore, certain classes of bacterial intein-containing proteins primarily contain mini-inteins rather than full-length inteins. The enrichment of mini-inteins within certain bacterial protein classes suggests that HEN domains may impose a greater functional cost in these proteins, creating selective pressure for HEN domain loss and resulting in reduced intein mobilityIMPORTANCEInteins are translated within host proteins and removed via a self-mediated splicing reaction. Prior comparative genomic analysis established that inteins are abundant in both bacteria and archaea, and that their distribution is strongly biased toward proteins involved in DNA transactions. Utilizing genomes made available over the last decade, this work increases the number of putative inteins by over twenty-fold. By investigating the distribution of inteins that can spread throughout/between genomes compared to those that have lost their ability to act as mobile elements, we provide a possible explanation for the higher abundance of inteins in archaea than bacteria. This work not only highlights that archaea are more hospitable intein hosts than bacteria but also serves to update the catalog of known prokaryotic inteins, which will function as a resource to the communities interested in inteins as mobile elements, tools in protein engineering, antimicrobial targets, and post-translational regulatory elements.
records.authors: Ariagno TM, Winkelman JD, Belfort M, Lennon CW.

records.title: Microdiversity drives resilience and niche partitioning in the bloom forming cyanobacteria  Limnospira platensis
records.abstract: The intraspecific evolutionary mechanisms of adaptation in blooming cyanobacteria, particularly those occurring on small spatial and temporal scales, remain poorly understood. Here, we used the unique properties of Lake Dziani Dzaha, which hosts a persistent population of  Limnospira platensis inhabiting distinct macro-habitats, to explore the spatial and temporal dynamics of microevolution. The Lake Dziani Dzaha (Mayotte), very stable at least since 2010, has experienced a seismo-volcanic crisis from May 2018 to November 2019, characterized by CO₂ outgassing that led to the mixing of the initially seasonally stratified water column, as well as changes in numerous physicochemical parameters. Phylogenomic analysis of 108 strains isolated during sampling campaigns in 2010, 2014, 2022, and 2024 revealed a population that remained highly phylogenetically cohesive over time. In 2022, genomic expansion was observed, characterized by an increase in genome size due to the proliferation of insertion sequences and a subsequent loss of adaptive genes. By 2024, a rapid recovery of the 2010-2014 genetic content took place through multiple independent events of horizontal gene transfer. At the spatial scale, although no significant differences in gene content were detected, distinct subpopulations were identified based on allele frequencies. Some alleles were specifically fixed and subject to different selection pressures among the subpopulations, suggesting the existence of distinct ecotypes. Overall, this study highlights the role of microdiversity in rapid resilience of blooming cyanobacteria populations within dynamic environments and in their adaptation through niche partitioning.
records.authors: Le Vern A, Duval C, Frère J, Bouly J, Troussellier M, Hugoni M, Agogué H, Jézéquel D, Marie B, Bernard C, Halary S.

records.title: Accretion of novel genetic elements reverses genome erosion and enables host-switching in the deep sea
records.abstract: Endosymbiont genome erosion is driven by relaxed selection and isolation from free-living relatives’ gene pools, and can be stalled by horizontal transmission events, but it remains unknown whether genome erosion can be reversed. The chemosynthetic gammaproteobacterial symbionts of deep-sea clams in the family Vesicomyidae offer a useful test case for whether eroded symbiont genomes can acquire novel functional content. Despite having some of the smallest genomes among marine endosymbionts, several lines of evidence, including divergent 16S rRNA variants within hosts, host-switching in sympatry, and phylogenetic signatures of repeated host transitions, suggest these symbionts retain more environmental exposure and evolutionary flexibility than expected under strict vertical transmission. Here, we use comparative genomics across the vesicomyid symbionts to test for evidence of functional gene gain. We find that three lineages have each independently expanded their genomes by approximately 25% relative to close relatives, with some expansions driven by insertion sequence (IS) or phage acquisition. The genomes that contain IS elements have disrupted genome synteny genome-wide, suggesting that these elements mediated structural rearrangements through ectopic recombination. Most strikingly, the symbiont of a thyasirid clam host,  Thyasira sp. Haima SOB, harbors four unusually large (∼24–40 kb), highly repetitive genes with structural homology to adhesins found broadly across prokaryotes and eukaryotes. These genes show hallmarks of horizontal acquisition and IS-mediated mobilization, and their predicted export via a Type I secretion system suggests a role in mediating attachment to, or exchange of metabolites across, host cell surfaces. Considering that this symbiont lineage switched from a vesicomyid host to a thyasirid host relatively recently, and thyasirids typically host extracellular symbionts, these adhesins may have been instrumental in this host-switch. Together, these findings provide evidence that genome erosion in intracellular symbionts is not strictly unidirectional, and mobile genetic elements can serve as vectors for functional innovation, potentially enabling adaptation to new hosts and environments even after substantial genome reduction has occurred.
records.authors: Morey CN, Corbett-Detig R, Russell SL.

records.title: Transgenerational immune priming (TGIP) and its potential association with EGR1 in Penaeusvannamei.
records.abstract: Acute hepatopancreatic necrosis disease (AHPND) caused by Vibrio parahaemolyticus remains one of the most serious bacterial diseases affecting Penaeus vannamei aquaculture. Immune priming has recently emerged as a promising strategy for enhancing disease resistance in aquatic animals. However, the molecular basis of immune priming and its potential effects on offspring remain poorly understood. In this study, UV-inactivated V. parahaemolyticus (V160807) was used to induce immune priming in P. vannamei. Primed F0 female shrimp were subsequently bred to obtain F1 offspring, and disease resistance, histopathology, cellular immunity, humoral immunity, transcriptome profiles, and DNA methylation patterns were evaluated. Both the F0 and F1 generations exhibited higher survival rates, lower bacterial loads, enhanced hemocyte-bacteria binding capacity, and stronger immune-related enzyme activities following bacterial challenge. Transcriptome analysis revealed significant enrichment of genes associated with pathogen recognition, melanization, and immune signaling pathways. In particular, pattern recognition receptor (PRR)-related genes, including CLEC4G and DSCAML1, were markedly upregulated. Whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) showed that histone H3 genes were hypomethylated, whereas ATP synthase-related genes displayed hypermethylation. These changes were accompanied by suppression of several energy metabolism pathways. Integrated transcriptomic and WGBS analyses identified EGR1 as a candidate regulatory gene. In F0 shrimp, EGR1 exhibited promoter and gene-body hypermethylation accompanied by reduced expression. Similar methylation changes were detected at the EGR1 locus in F1 offspring, including a conserved 61 bp hypermethylated region within the promoter. Pyrosequencing and RT-qPCR were further used to evaluate the methylation and expression patterns of EGR1. These findings demonstrate that prior exposure to UV-inactivated V. parahaemolyticus induces immune priming in F0 shrimp and is associated with enhanced disease resistance and immune response in F1 offspring. The EGR1 DNA methylation and gene expression changes may contribute to the establishment of maternal TGIP.
records.authors: Zhu Z, Liu Y, Zhang H, Luo K, Wang Y, Mu C, Yan M, Wang X.

records.title: Detection, characterization, and evolutionary inferences regarding a novel virus identified in Amblyomma dissimile Koch, 1844 (Acari: Ixodidae) from the Amazon, Pará, Brazil.
records.abstract: Ticks are among the primary vectors of infectious agents of medical and veterinary importance, second only to mosquitoes in the number of pathogens transmitted to humans. These arthropods are capable of transmitting a wide diversity of microorganisms, including protozoa, bacteria, and viruses. Notable among tick-borne viruses are those associated with viral encephalitis, which cause severe acute and chronic neurological infections in humans. This study aimed to characterize the RNA virome of an Amblyomma dissimile specimen collected from a Boa constrictor rescued in the municipality of Ananindeua, Pará state, in the Brazilian Amazon, using an RNA metagenomic sequencing approach. A total of eleven viral sequences were identified, distributed across five families: Chuviridae (n = 2), Rhabdoviridae (n = 2), Orthomyxoviridae (n = 5), Nodaviridae (n = 1), and Orthototiviridae (n = 1). A key finding was the identification of Dissimile tick rhabdovirus a potential new member of the Rhabdoviridae family described here for the first time, with no prior records in the scientific literature. Additionally, segments of Granville quaranjavirus were detected in Brazil for the first time, expanding the known geographic distribution of this virus. These results highlight the underrepresentation of viral diversity associated with Brazilian ticks in reference databases, underscoring the need to expand metagenomic surveillance and virological characterization efforts in the country, particularly given the potential impacts of climate change on tick distribution and virus circulation dynamics.

records.title: Purification of filamentous phage ssDNA genomes using Chaotropic salt/silica methods
records.abstract: Filamentous phages play important roles in molecular biology and bacterial pathogenesis. There is therefore great interest in the genomes of the phages, including M13 and Pf, which infect  Escherichia coli and  Pseudomonas aeruginosa , respectively. However, efficient methods for purifying single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) from filamentous phages are scarce and rely mainly on repurposed commercial kits developed for dsDNA. These kits yield variable amounts of ssDNA, varying considerably from one phage to another, their solutions are proprietary and troubleshooting, and customizing the protocol to improve purification is not possible. Here, we developed and optimized two protocols based on ssDNA binding to silica columns in the presence of guanidine hydrochloride and potassium iodide chaotropic salts, for filamentous phages M13KO7 and Pf4. The protocols achieved 60 to 100% recovery, equal to or higher than the Monarch Spin gDNA Extraction and DNeasy Blood and Tissue kits, with similar A  260/280 and A  260/230 ratios, intact DNA in agarose gels, and no detectable host genomic DNA by PCR. Recovery depended critically on the chaotropic salts and on ethanol, and did not increase at lower pH, consistent with a water-exclusion model in which hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonding dominate over electrostatic repulsion. Phage-specific differences in recovery indicate that optimization may be needed for some phages, which the fully customizable nature of these protocols facilitates. Comparing the virion ssDNA with the double-stranded replicative form (RF) revealed genome variants in both phages, including a shorter M13KO7 form lacking the kanamycin resistance-p15A insert, and illustrates the value of analyzing both RF and ssDNA forms to study filamentous phage biology. Implementing these protocols in routine filamentous phage workflows should facilitate their characterization and engineering.
records.authors: Perez-Rodriguez S, Khosravi A, Milla C, Bollyky PL.

records.title: Early-life core microbiota are associated with postlarval survival of  Penaeus vannamei  : A meta-analysis
records.abstract: Larviculture is critical to the production of  Penaeus vannamei , the world’s leading farmed shrimp species, but remains constrained by erratic postlarval survival. Although early-life microbiome establishment is increasingly recognized as essential for larval health and survival, microbiome-based hatchery interventions are hindered by limited understanding of larval core microbiota. Here, we synthesized publicly available and self-generated 16S rRNA gene amplicon datasets of larval and rearing-water microbiota from 13 studies encompassing seven major producing regions worldwide to characterize shrimp larval core microbiota, their assembly processes, and their associations with larval survival. Although larval prokaryotic communities exhibited stronger geographic variation than developmental-stage succession, a conserved set of dominant bacterial families, including  Roseobacteraceae ,  Vibrionaceae ,  Flavobacteriaceae ,  Moraxellaceae , and  Pseudoalteromonadaceae , consistently prevailed across developmental stages and regions. By integrating occupancy, persistence, and ecological network centrality analyses, we demonstrated that common, temporal, and ecological core microbiota differ substantially in composition, diversity, stage specificity, and ecological roles in network stability. Compared with non-core taxa, core taxa were generally assembled more deterministically, irrespective of core category, suggesting stronger host selection and/or more rapid dispersal during microbiome establishment. Core microbiota also generally showed stronger associations with postlarval survival than total communities or non-core taxa, although contrasting survival associations among core members indicated that core microbiota are not ecologically homogeneous. Our work provides the first systematic categorization and characterization of larval core microbiota throughout the shrimp larviculture cycle, offering new insights into the ecological significance of core microbiota and identifying potential universal targets for microbiome-based intervention in shrimp larviculture.
records.authors: Chen R, Zhang W, Yu J, Song H, Zhou Y, Chen C, Huang X, Zhang D, Yan M, Wang K.

records.title: Estimating Gene Prevalence with Incomplete Genomes: Application to the Prochlorococcus Pangenome
records.abstract: Gene prevalence is an essential statistic in population genomics, defined as the proportion of a population carrying at least one ortholog of a given gene family. Common approaches to estimating gene prevalence either assume complete genomes or exclude genomes below a completeness threshold, resulting in biased and high variance estimates that fail to take advantage of all available data. Here we developed a maximum-likelihood framework that explicitly models genome completeness in order to estimate gene prevalence and associated confidence intervals from collections of complete and incomplete genomes. We applied the methodology to marine Prochlorococcus, a globally abundant photosynthetic bacterium for which the majority of available genomes are incomplete. Our methodology produced gene prevalence estimates with associated confidence intervals for a total of 52,500 gene families, more than 4 times the number quantifiable using complete genomes alone. We find a core of 714 genes are likely universal to the Prochlorococcus genus and a substantial majority of 49,828 gene families occur at low prevalence. Our results reveal a Prochlorococcus pangenome dominated by rare flexible genes and provide a general framework for incorporating incomplete genomes into quantitative analyses of microbial genomic diversity.

records.title: Isolation, characterization, and biocontrol potential of a novel lytic phage vB_VpaS_R27Z against Vibrio parahaemolyticus for mitigating seafood contamination.
records.abstract: Vibrio parahaemolyticus is a critical seafood-borne pathogen that poses substantial risks to food safety and public health. Effective mitigation of this bacterium in fresh and minimally processed seafood remains challenging, since conventional antimicrobial treatments induce antibiotic resistance and degrade the sensory quality of seafood products. As natural antimicrobial agents, lytic bacteriophages represent a targeted alternative to antibiotics for suppressing V. parahaemolyticus in seafood. In this study, we isolated and characterized a novel lytic bacteriophage, vB_VpaS_R27Z (R27Z), targeting V. parahaemolyticus, and further assessed its biocontrol potential against this pathogen in seafood matrices. Phage R27Z exhibited siphoviral morphology, featuring an icosahedral capsid and a long non-contractile tail. It possesses a short latent period of 20 min and a burst size of approximately 58 PFU per infected cell, reflecting its high lytic replication efficiency. R27Z is stable at a broad temperature range of 4°C to 50°C and a pH range from 5 to 10, suggesting tolerance to conditions relevant to seafood handling and storage. Genomic analysis revealed that the genome size of R27Z was 51,052 bp and it contained 64 open reading frames. Notably, no genes associated with lysogeny, bacterial virulence, or antibiotic resistance were detected within its genome, which is essential for food applications. In vitro growth inhibition assays demonstrated that R27Z inhibited V. parahaemolyticus growth at multiplicities of infection (MOIs) of 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, and 100, with the strongest early-phase inhibition observed at MOIs of 10 and 100. Furthermore, R27Z markedly suppressed V. parahaemolyticus on both fish flesh and fish skin, with maximum reductions of 3.62 log10 and 2.84 log10 units at an MOI of 1 alongside rising recoverable phage titers throughout treatment, confirming host-supported replication in these food matrices. Collectively, these results highlighted that R27Z could act as a potential alternative natural biocontrol agent against V. parahaemolyticus in seafood products.

records.title: Dynamic changes of chicken gut microbiota and resistome during enrofloxacin treatment against multidrug-resistant Salmonella based on metagenomics.
records.abstract: Antibiotics are widely used to treat and prevent bacterial infections in human and animals. However, the impact of antibiotic dose on bacterial burden and diachronic changes and transfer of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in gut bacterial infections remains unclear. Here, we used enrofloxacin (ENR) at sub-inhibitory (1 mg/kg b.w.), prophylactic (3.03 mg/kg b.w.), and therapeutic (10 mg/kg b.w.) doses to treat infections with Salmonella harboring plasmid pJX-4, with infected but untreated groups as controls. We found that subtherapeutic ENR may pose potential risks to the gut ecosystem. Specifically, sub-inhibitory ENR led to persistently high Salmonella and its carried resistance gene qnrS1 levels; under this dose condition, preliminary evidence suggested that intestinal Escherichia coli was a potential host for in vivo transfer of plasmid pJX-4. The prophylactic dose group showed significantly higher relative abundances of human bacterial pathogens and ARGs, especially during treatment. Furthermore, this group was enriched in genes related to oxidative stress, cellular signaling, and secretion systems, and these functional genes were primarily associated with ARGs. Overall, different ENR doses shaped distinct evolutionary trajectories of the gut microbiome and resistome. This study provides a theoretical basis for the rational use of antibiotics in treating bacterial infections.
records.authors: Chen Y, Chu J, Guo Y, Farhan MHR, Lu X, Wei H, Xie C, Wang X, Huang L, Cheng G.

records.title: Microbial volatile humulene orchestrates plant-microbe alliance to establish disease-suppressive rhizosphere.
records.abstract: Microbial volatile organic compounds (mVOCs) suppress growth and virulence traits of soil-borne pathogens, yet their ecological roles in disease suppression remain unclear. Here, we show that the sesquiterpene humulene from Streptomyces acts as a multifunctional regulator that suppresses bacterial wilt through coordinated inhibition of Ralstonia solanacearum, plant metabolic reprogramming, and rhizosphere microbiome modulation. We combined in vitro pathogen assays, pot experiments, microbiota transplantation, rhizosphere 16S rRNA profiling, root-exudate metabolomics, and plant and pathogen transcriptomics to investigate the direct and microbiome-mediated effects of humulene. Humulene reduced disease severity and pathogen abundance via a microbiome-dependent mechanism. Microbiota transplantation confirmed that the humulene-conditioned microbiome retains transferable disease-suppressiveness. Humulene also selectively enriched antagonistic Streptomyces, not by direct growth promotion, but by reprogramming tomato root exudation to produce lipid-derived petroselinic acid, which promoted Streptomyces growth, humulene production, and pathogen suppression. Root transcriptomics further revealed activation of lipid metabolic pathways involving alternative fatty acid desaturation and oxylipin signaling. Together, humulene functions as an ecological signal that integrates pathogen suppression, host lipid metabolism, and microbiome assembly to establish a disease-suppressive rhizosphere, enabling microbiome-informed control of bacterial wilt.
records.authors: Huang Y, Zhang F, Zhang J, Zhang W, Wang N, Wang X, Wei Z, Jiang G, Raza W.

records.title: Core bacterial and host fruit-specific yeast microbiota in a polyphagous fly pest.
records.abstract: Holometabolous polyphagous insects undergo metamorphosis and exploit multiple host plants, exposing them to highly variable ecological conditions across both life stages and host plants. Whether these insects harbor a stable core microbiota, a life stage- or a host plant-specific microbiota remains open questions. Here, we characterized fungal and bacterial communities associated with Drosophila suzukii across life stages (larvae, pupae, and emerging flies) and host fruits (cherry, blackberry, and strawberry) using 16S and ITS metabarcoding. We tested the relative influence of life stage and host fruit on microbiota composition using community and network-based analyses. First, we identified that yeasts, but not bacteria, were strongly structured among host fruits. Bacteria and filamentous fungi were shared across fruits, constituting a fruit core microbiota dominated by Gluconobacter cerinus, Tatumella sp., and Cladosporium spp. In contrast, yeast were rather fruit-specific: the genera Hanseniaspora and Pichia were mostly associated with cherries and strawberries, contrary to Metschnikowia with blackberries. Second, we found that fungal, but not bacterial, communities of D. suzukii were structured among host fruits. D. suzukii harbored a core bacterial microbiota composed of G. cerinus and a niche-specific (host plant-specific) microbiota composed of yeasts: Hanseniaspora was typical in individuals related to cherry and strawberry, whereas Metschnikowia to blackberry. We also verified that individuals from artificial laboratory infestations and natural field infestations harbored similar microbial communities when they developed under the same laboratory conditions. Components of both core and niche-specific microbiota were most likely horizontally acquired by D. suzukii from host fruits. Taken together, our results underline the importance of metacommunity approaches to investigate tripartite interactions among insects, host plants, and microbiota.IMPORTANCEThe role of microbiota in mediating interactions between phytophagous insects and their host plants has been well illustrated in specialist species. However, it has been less comprehensively studied in polyphagous species, which infest multiple host plants, and across life stages in holometabolous species that experience separate ecological niches through development. We tested the existence of a core, a niche-specific, and a stage-specific microbiota in a polyphagous holometabolous species, D. suzukii. We examined both fungal and bacterial communities in larvae, pupae, and emerging flies infesting three host fruits. Our results showed, first, that the assembly of bacteria, filamentous fungi, and yeasts on fruits is driven by different ecological processes. Second, D. suzukii harbors a core bacterial microbiota, a niche-specific microbiota constituted by yeasts and no stage-specific microbiota. Our study emphasizes the importance of considering jointly the assembly of host plant and polyphagous insect microbial communities to better understand insect-microbe interactions.
records.authors: Dunis S, Lapègue M, Deschamps C, Cesari L, Loiseau A, Facon B, Rode NO.

records.title: Genome-wide conservation and locus-specific coding variation in  Teratoramularia rumicicola  , a candidate microbial herbicide for  Rumex  weeds
records.abstract: The  Rumex pathogen  Teratoramularia rumicicola is a candidate microbial herbicide, but its functional genomic repertoire and variation among isolates remain poorly characterised. We generated a PacBio HiFi reference and evidence-supported gene annotation for TR4 and a short-read assembly for GR1, then compared the isolates using assembly- and read-based analyses. The TR4 and GR1 nuclear assemblies comprised 22.34 Mb (13 contigs; N50, 2.90 Mb) and 21.23 Mb (486 contigs; N50, 0.350 Mb), respectively. The TR4 annotation predicted 8,898 protein -coding genes, and the representative protein set was 96.7% complete in the Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologues assessment. Functional annotation identified 593 putatively secreted proteins, 258 candidate effectors, 355 carbohydrate -active enzyme (CAZyme) candidates and 20 predicted secondary-metabolite biosynthetic regions. Seven secreted CAZymes were prioritised as potential host-barrier-associated factors based on predicted activities and homology to virulence -related entries in the Pathogen–Host Interactions database. Despite 99.81% average nucleotide identity across aligned regions, read-based comparison identified 28,040 high-confidence isolate-fixed differences. Of 158 reconstructed candidate GR1 alleles, 147 showed strong assembly support. Notable differences included predicted truncations of two Zn(II)₂Cys₆ transcription factors, one adjacent to an intact nonribosomal peptide synthetase-like core gene, and a separate gene showing a localised repeat-induced point mutation (RIP)-like substitution pattern and predicted premature termination. Together, these resources and candidate loci provide a foundation for investigating pathogenicity and strain variation relevant to microbial herbicide development.

records.title: ARG-PASS v2.0 expands global resistome surveillance to reveal previously unrecognized antibiotic resistance genes reaching the human gut
records.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a significant global public health threat, and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) that bacteria depend on to withstand treatment are its molecular basis. How ARGs move from environmental reservoirs into the human microbiome, and eventually into human pathogens, remains one of the most important unresolved questions in AMR research. The environmental reservoir remains poorly described and the routes connecting it to human microbiomes are largely inferred rather than observed. Describing that reservoir requires computational methods able to recognise ARGs that share little similarity with known enzymes, yet retain accuracy after experimental validation to enable scalable applications. Dietary exposure through unprocessed ferments offers a tractable setting in which such a route can be observed directly. Here we introduce ARG-PASS v2.0 and first apply it to a lake metagenome from Kolkata, India, where 10 of 11 tested candidates across diverse ARG classes were functionally confirmed after expression in  Escherichia coli . Given their clinical relevance, we then predicted 918 class B1 metallo-β-lactamases (MBLs) from MGnify and the PLSDB, with most diverging from characterized enzymes, but as widely distributed. Often tracking their hosts’ distribution, we find that most class B1 MBL diversity lies outside human-associated microbiomes. Cross-referencing against the Unified Human Gastrointestinal Protein catalogue identified a carbapenemase, an ANT, and class A β-lactamases from  Bacillus sonorensis and  Bacillus licheniformis , detected in South Korean fermented soybean paste (  doenjang ) as well as gut isolates of populations consuming these foods. Together, these results point to a largely chromosomal reservoir of ARG diversity that reaches the human gut through both resident and generalist hosts. Once in the human microbiome, treatment may be compromised directly if the host is an opportunistic pathogen, or after transfer to a clinical pathogen.

records.title: Glowing pathogenic bacteria discovered in the Aral Sea – a harmless evolutionary feature or a hidden threat?
records.abstract: Abstract  Bioluminescent bacteria are widespread in marine ecosystems, yet whether they can establish stable populations in long-isolated inland saline lakes has remained unknown. Here we report species-level identification and comprehensive characterization of the first isolated bioluminescent bacteria from the Aral Sea, a formerly extensive inland water body that has remained isolated from the world ocean since its Holocene formation while experiencing extreme fluctuations in salinity, temperature and water level. We show that the luminescent microbiota comprises two marine species, Vibrio cholerae and Vibrio vulnificus. V. cholerae isolates displayed enhanced tolerance to low salinity and possessed a thermolabile luciferase. In contrast, isolated V. vulnificus strains grew and emitted light over an exceptionally broad elevated salinity range (5–70‰) and retained luminescence at temperatures exceeding 40 °C, indicating remarkable adaptation to the highly variable physicochemical conditions of the Aral Sea. Phylogenetic analyses place isolates close to contemporary type strains, and the retention of virulence-associated genes indicates limited evolutionary divergence, suggesting a relatively recent colonization rather than long-term independent evolution. Together, these results demonstrate that bioluminescent bacteria from pathogenic species can successfully colonize ecological niches in isolated inland saltwater ecosystems typically occupied by other Vibrio species in the open sea.

records.title: Identification of Soybean Bush Dwarf Disease Associated with Coinfection of a Phytoplasma and Cowpea Mild Mottle Virus in Guangxi, China.
records.abstract: Phytoplasmas and viruses are important pathogens of soybean (Glycine max) and other legumes, posing a severe threat to global legume yields. In this study, three soybean plants exhibiting severe bush dwarfing, stem necrosis, leaf deformation, and wrinkling were collected from Nanning, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, China. High-throughput sequencing coupled with reverse transcription-PCR (RT-PCR) was employed for virome analysis, while nested-PCR and conventional PCR with 16S ribosomal RNA (16S rRNA) universal and tuf gene-specific primers were used for the specific detection of phytoplasmas. All three samples were confirmed to be coinfected with Cowpea mild mottle virus (CPMMV) and Candidatus Phytoplasma. The complete genome sequence of CPMMV was determined, which showed the highest nucleotide identity with the CPMMV isolate GX NiuDaLi, and the putative new isolate was named CPMMV GX-NN. Biological inoculation assays showed that CPMMV GX-NN could infect Glycine max, Vigna sinensis, and Nicotiana benthamiana, inducing typical viral symptoms. Phylogenetic analysis based on 16S rRNA sequences and virtual restriction fragment length polymorphism via iPhyClassifier was further conducted, and the phytoplasma was classified into the 16SrII Group. This is the first report of coinfection by CPMMV and a phytoplasma in soybean plants in Guangxi, China, providing critical insights for diagnosing and managing soybean diseases caused by these pathogens.
records.authors: Liu J, Chen Y, Tang Z, Xu X.

records.title: Earthworm-assisted enrichment of specific indigenous soil microbes for the preferential degradation of hexaconazole R-enantiomer.
records.abstract: This study examined the influence of earthworm addition on the enantiomer-specific degradation of the chiral triazole fungicide hexaconazole, focusing on the associated functional bacterial communities in soil and earthworm casts. S-hexaconazole was preferentially degraded in soil, whereas R-hexaconazole strongly inhibited soil microbial activities. Earthworm addition preferentially accelerated R-hexaconazole degradation and eliminated its inhibitory effects. Two soil bacterial families, Sphingomonadaceae and Xanthomonadaceae, and two biodegradation genes, p450 and ppo, were associated with the preferential degradation of S-hexaconazole. Two bacterial strains, HEX1 and HEX2, which belong to Sphingomonadaceae and Xanthomonadaceae, respectively, degraded R-hexaconazole but preferentially degraded S-hexaconazole in pure culture. In the R-hexaconazole treatment, earthworms selectively increased the abundances of Sphingomonadaceae, Xanthomonadaceae, and ppo, with Xanthomonadaceae and ppo levels being 23.1% and 25.1% higher, respectively, than those in the S-hexaconazole treatment, thereby shifting the community-level degradation preference toward R-hexaconazole. Notably, similar patterns were observed in earthworm casts. Network and metagenomic binning analyses revealed that Sphingomonadaceae and Xanthomonadaceae were potential hosts of the p450 and ppo. These findings suggest that earthworms facilitate the enrichment of specific indigenous soil bacterial families (Sphingomonadaceae and Xanthomonadaceae) to accelerate the preferential degradation of R-hexaconazole, highlighting the potential of earthworms to mitigate the risks in chiral fungicide-contaminated soil.
records.authors: Han L, Wang Y, Wang Y, Li Z, Liu M, Ju C, Nie J, Wang X.
