records.title: Genomic Exploration of CRISPR-Cas Systems in Raoultella species: Diversity and Architecture.
records.abstract: Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats and CRISPR-associated protein (CRISPR-Cas) systems are adaptive immune mechanisms that protect bacteria against invading mobile genetic elements. They can influence horizontal gene transfer, phage resistance, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) dynamics. Although these systems have been investigated in several Klebsiella species, information on historically defined Raoultella species remains limited. In this study, 103 complete genomes representing Raoultella species, currently placed within the broader Klebsiella lineage, were analyzed to characterize the distribution, architecture, and diversity of CRISPR-Cas systems. CRISPR-Cas loci were identified using CRISPRCasFinder and CRISPRone, followed by subtype classification, direct repeat and leader sequence analyses, spacer matching, Cas1-based phylogenetic analysis, and AMR determinant screening. Complete CRISPR-Cas systems were detected in 23 genomes, predominantly in R. ornithinolytica strains. All complete systems were chromosomally located, whereas plasmid-associated orphan CRISPR arrays were observed in selected R. ornithinolytica strains. Two major architectures were identified, with Type I-E being dominant and Type I-F restricted to fewer strains. Direct repeat analysis revealed six consensus sequences, while leader regions displayed conserved AT-rich motifs and strain-specific divergence. Spacer analyses suggested historical interactions with phages and plasmids, particularly mobile genetic elements associated with Klebsiella and other Enterobacteriaceae. Cas1 phylogeny showed subtype-dependent clustering, indicating that CRISPR-Cas evolution does not strictly follow core genome phylogeny. The coexistence of predicted CRISPR-Cas loci and AMR determinants indicates that the presence of these loci does not necessarily preclude the carriage of resistance determinants. Overall, this study expands current knowledge of CRISPR-Cas diversity among the analyzed Raoultella genomes and provides a genomic framework for future functional studies.

records.title: Functional convergence despite taxonomic turnover across coral-associated microbiomes.
records.abstract: Coral-associated microbiomes are fundamental to holobiont health and resilience, yet their community structures often demonstrate high taxonomic variability across host species. Whether such variability results in functional instability or reflects pervasive metabolic redundancy remains unclear. Here, we investigated microbial taxonomic structure, functional potential, and community assembly mechanisms across 15 coral species using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. These communities exhibited extreme taxonomic heterogeneity, high beta-diversity, and the absence of a universally shared core genus, indicating strong host-specific filtering that dictates microbial membership. In contrast, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathway-based functional profiles exhibited striking convergence across hosts, revealing a conserved metabolic landscape despite extensive taxonomic turnover. Mantel and Procrustes analyses identified a weak but significant correspondence between taxonomic composition and functional potential, a pattern consistent with functional redundancy across coral-associated microbiomes. Null model-based assembly analyses further revealed a decoupling between taxonomic and functional organization. Taxonomic structure was shaped by a host-dependent balance of stochastic and deterministic processes, whereas functional profiles were predominantly assembled through stochastic processes, maintaining consistently high functional redundancy across hosts. Metagenomic profiling uncovered a two-tier functional architecture underlying this stability: a conserved, high-abundance metabolic core enriched in carbon and phosphorus cycling and stress response functions that support microbial persistence in the coral microenvironment, together with lower-abundance host-specific metabolic modules involved in nitrogen and sulfur transformations that enable niche adaptation. Thus, functional requirements primarily govern the coral-associated microbiome rather than taxonomic identity. This synergy between conserved survival traits and flexible metabolic capacities maintains holobiont homeostasis despite extensive taxonomic turnover.IMPORTANCECoral reefs rely on complex partnerships between corals and their associated microorganisms to maintain health and withstand environmental stress. However, it remains unclear whether changes in microbial communities across different coral species lead to loss of important functions. In this study, we examined microorganisms associated with 15 coral species from the South China Sea and found that coral species hosted highly different microbial communities, while maintaining similar microbial functions. Our findings reveal that different microbial groups can perform similar ecological roles, allowing coral-associated communities to remain functionally stable despite changes in microbial membership. This functional flexibility may help corals maintain biological balance under changing environmental conditions and provides new insights into how coral holobionts preserve resilience in the face of ecological disturbances.

records.title: Correlation-based analysis of gene expression in Cardinium, Wolbachia, and Tyrophagus putrescentiae reveals distinct host-symbiont interactions and parallel evolutionary expansion of infection-associated genes.
records.abstract: Cardinium and Wolbachia are phylogenetically distinct intracellular symbionts that have convergently evolved mechanisms to infect a wide range of arthropod and nematode hosts. Here, we investigated the interaction dynamics of two basal strains, Cardinium (cTPut) and Wolbachia (wTPut), in the stored-product mite Tyrophagus putrescentiae (Acari: Astigmata). The KEGG-annotated gene expression profiles of mite samples were analyzed in single infections (Cardinium or Wolbachia) and mixed infections across three time points (2, 4, and 6 months). Temporal effects on gene expression were marginal; therefore, correlation-based network analyses were used to characterize host-symbiont interactions. The symbionts exhibited distinct host-targeting strategies: Wolbachia displayed a "broad" interaction pattern characterized by numerous weak correlations with host KEGG genes, whereas Cardinium showed a "focused" strategy involving fewer but stronger correlations. These patterns were consistent across global KEGG data sets, immune and regulatory pathways (including AMPK, autophagy, endocytosis, Hippo, lysosome, MAPK, mTOR, and Notch), receptor subsets, and metabolic pathways. Consistent with these interaction patterns, orthologous analyses across Cardinium and selected Wolbachia genomes revealed that infection-associated genes are not broadly conserved but are enriched in lineage-specific, duplicated gene families, particularly in T. putrescentiae-associated symbionts. These findings indicate that infection-related traits evolve primarily through lineage-specific gene family expansion rather than conservation and suggest that basal Cardinium and Wolbachia employ fundamentally distinct host interaction strategies.IMPORTANCEThe study provides novel insight into host-symbiont interactions: Cardinium, Wolbachia infecting mite Tyrophagus putrescentiae, an important producer of allergens (i) Cardinium gene expression responds to the presence of Wolbachia, whereas Wolbachia gene expression shows no reciprocal response; (ii) the two symbionts employ contrasting host interaction strategies with the host, with Cardinium exhibiting fewer but stronger associations and Wolbachia showing widespread but weaker correlations; (iii) distinct host pathways are differentially associated with each symbiont; and (iv) we identified 40 of the most correlated bacterial genes to the host that include candidates of viral origin, suggesting a potential role of horizontally acquired elements in the host. Furthermore, evolutionary analyses demonstrate that infection-associated genes are primarily lineage expanded rather than broadly conserved across symbiont genomes. Given the allergenic relevance of T. putrescentiae, these findings suggest that symbiont-specific interaction strategies can indirectly influence host physiology and allergen production.
records.authors: Hubert J, Glowska-Patyniak E, Stara J, Green S.

records.title: A novel clonal and axenic isolation pipeline for the human gut protist  Blastocystis  reveals within-subtype strain coexistence
records.abstract: Blastocystis is the most prevalent protist in the human gut microbiome, but its study is impeded by limitations in existing cultivation methods that hinder routine axenic and clonal isolation. These barriers have left open the question of whether multiple strains of a protist species can coexist within a single host, as observed within the bacterial gut microbiota. To address this, we introduce egg-based monophasic (EBM) medium, a novel optically clear liquid medium that supports exponential growth of  Blastocystis from low inoculum densities in standard tissue-culture plates and flasks, a capability not supported by existing media formulations tested here. Using EBM medium, we established a modular axenization and clonal isolation pipeline and recovered axenic and clonally isolated cultures representing  Blastocystis subtypes 1–4 from human and non-human primate hosts. To investigate within-host strain diversity, we sequenced a subtype 1 culture before and after clonal isolation. The non-clonal culture yielded a 21 Mb assembly with gene copy distribution and allelic polymorphism patterns consistent with multiple strains, whereas its clonal derivative yielded a 15 Mb assembly with patterns consistent with a single strain. These results indicate that the original culture contained multiple closely related strains co-colonizing one host. We identified the same genomic signature in published xenic cultures established from single human donors, supporting the presence of strain-level diversity within  Blastocystis subtypes. Our pipeline provides a scalable platform for  Blastocystis cultivation, imaging, and clonal isolation, enabling investigation of strain-level diversity that may be obscured in non-clonal cultures.  Importance  Blastocystis is the most prevalent protist in the human gut, yet experimental investigation remains limited by a difficulty in obtaining single-microbe and genetically defined cultures. Existing methods make it difficult to separate the protist from associated bacteria or recover individual lineages from mixed cultures. We developed a liquid growth medium compatible with standard tissue culture plates, live-cell imaging, and a modular workflow for producing axenic and clonal isolates. We use this pipeline to create axenic and clonal isolates across four common subtypes. Applying this workflow exposed a mixture of closely related strains in a single-subtype culture, a finding supported by analyses of independent published cultures. This culturing pipeline enables controlled investigation of strain-level diversity, and provides a new experimental framework for the study of  Blastocystis biology and its interactions with the gut microbiome.
records.authors: Leon F, Shih JB, Keller LE, Palaniappan S, Degaetano L, Nine GA, Lind AL.

records.title: Spatiotemporal genomic epidemiology of Eurasian avian-like H1N1 swine influenza viruses
records.abstract: Abstract    Background  Eurasian avian-like (EA) H1N1 swine influenza viruses pose a zoonotic threat, yet their genomic evolution and dissemination across Eurasia remain incompletely understood. This study investigated genotype diversity, temporal persistence, and geographic spread, and assessed the association between live-swine trade and viral migration to inform surveillance.  Methods  We analysed 1,703 publicly available EA H1N1 genomes sampled from 19 countries between 2009 and 2025. Lineage assignments across all eight gene segments were used to identify genotypes and describe their temporal and geographic distributions. Time-scaled Bayesian phylogenetics and discrete phylogeography were used to reconstruct evolutionary relationships and migration patterns. Generalized linear modelling assessed migration predictors, including directed live-swine trade and sampling intensity. The mixed effects model of evolution was used to detect episodic diversifying selection in hemagglutinin, followed by structural mapping of candidate residues.  Results  We identified 19 genotypes. The wholly EA-derived genotype G1 accounted for 57.0% of genomes and was detected across nearly the entire study period. Many reassortant genotypes carrying A(H1N1)pdm09- or triple-reassortant-derived segments were detected over short intervals, although several showed prolonged persistence. Genotype composition differed geographically, with reassortant genotypes enriched in Asia and predominantly EA-derived constellations more common in Europe. Phylogeographic reconstruction indicated asymmetric dissemination within and between Europe and Asia, with Western Europe occupying a central position in the inferred migration network. Directed live-swine trade received the strongest support among migration predictors after accounting for sampling intensity. Sixteen candidate hemagglutinin codons showed evidence of episodic diversifying selection. Most candidate HA1 residues mapped to exposed regions of the globular head near antigenic regions.  Conclusions  EA H1N1 evolution across Eurasia was characterized by a persistent EA genomic background, regional genotype diversification through reassortment, and spread associated with live-swine trade. These findings support integrating genomic surveillance with animal movement data to guide surveillance along trade networks and improve the detection and assessment of emerging variants of zoonotic concern.
records.authors: Liu H, Zhang Y, Yi J, Zhou Z, Li C, Xu F, Ren R, Liao M, Sun H.

records.title: Bioprospecting cultivable microorganisms from the Pantanal reveals taxonomic and functional enzymatic diversity
records.abstract: Abstract    The Pantanal is one of the world’s largest tropical wetlands, yet its cultivable microbial diversity remains underexplored for biotechnological applications. We bioprospected cultivable bacteria, filamentous fungi, and yeasts from environmental samples collected across 10 Pantanal sites and screened them for seven enzymatic activities. A total of 122 isolates were recovered, comprising 73 bacteria, 46 filamentous fungi, and 3 yeasts, representing 51 taxonomic groups and 37 enzymatic profiles. Protease activity was the most frequent among bacteria (71.2%), all filamentous fungi were cellulase-positive, and chitinase activity was detected in only five bacterial isolates. Taxonomic diversity among enzyme-positive isolates varied according to activity and sample origin, with Shannon–Wiener diversity index values ranging from 0 to 2.86. Significant positive associations were observed between protease–lipase, laccase–amylase, and protease–amylase, whereas no origin–activity association remained significant after multiple-testing correction. Phylogenetic analyses identified three particularly divergent or taxonomically unresolved bacterial lineages: P_1.1_002 within  Rothia  , P_13.1_002 within  Pseudomonas  , and P_10.3_001 within the order Enterobacterales. These findings reveal broad taxonomic and functional diversity among cultivable Pantanal microorganisms and identify lineages of interest for further taxonomic and biotechnological investigation.
records.authors: Motta MLL, Martins GM, Coelho BCS, Bastos KGF, Vasconcelos DC, Conceição L, Okamura LA, Silva DS, Medina-Gallardo JC, Gomes KS.

records.title: Efficient benzo[a]pyrene bioremediation by a novel halotolerant Rhodococcus ruber TN-1 in salinity environment: Mechanical insight from whole-genome, degradation efficiency and microbial properties.
records.abstract: Benzo[a]pyrene (BaP) contamination in highly saline environments has received increasing attention; however, efficient degradation of BaP by halotolerant BaP-degrading bacteria from contaminated water and soils remains poorly understood. In this study, a novel BaP-degrading bacterium, designated Rhodococcus ruber TN-1, was isolated, and its BaP degradation performance was evaluated. Whole-genome sequencing revealed genes and gene clusters associated with benzoate and xylene transport and degradation, naphthalene degradation, and the catabolism of other aromatic compounds. Strain TN-1 exhibited high BaP degradation efficiency in water, with a degradation efficiency exceeding 95% after 3 d of cultivation. Inoculation with strain TN-1 significantly improved the BaP degradation efficiency in three types of saline soil. After 14 d of reaction, the BaP degradation rate increased from 12.08% to 26.94% in the control to 44.03-59.12%. Correlation analysis revealed that the degradation rate of soil BaP was positively correlated with soil catalase (CAT) activity and negatively correlated with salinity. Metagenomic and quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) analyses demonstrated that the addition of strain TN-1 significantly increased microbial abundance in three saline soils, with strain TN-1 becoming the dominant microorganism and accelerating the microbial degradation of BaP. These findings highlight strain TN-1 as a promising bioaugmentation agent for the remediation of BaP-contaminated saline soils.
records.authors: Yan Y, Wang YN, Wang F, Gao Y, Wang H.

records.title: Why does a gene cassette keep the company of an orphan reverse transcriptase? Pollutibacter on five continents
records.abstract: Abstract  Several bacterial reverse transcriptases (RTs) protect cells from phage, yet some fit no known family. Screening 189,630 genomes, we found an RT that none of our comparisons (known RT types, trees, predicted structures) places in a known family (nearest published-library RT at most 34.6% identical), which we call ESOL RT. It sits beside a gene cassette in 16 genomes, chosen for carrying it, from lake, river, pond and other waters in nine countries on five continents, all in one Bacteroidota genus, Pollutibacter. The cassette has a conserved upstream element and four genes at fixed positions, including a MIDAS-motif protein and a predicted metalloprotease-like one lacking H[EDQ]xxH. At 27 further Pollutibacter loci, 97 of 99 observable positions beside the RT hold a cassette part, both exceptions at one locus. No observable copy of the four neighbouring genes is disrupted, codon models suggest purifying selection, and long reads from other freshwater samples span up to six modules. In a post hoc search of 794 genomes, the element lies upstream of an RT at 18 of 19 hits, the 19th cut by a contig end. Yet relatives of the -1 and +3 genes occur as an adjacent pair with no RT detected nearby in 54 of 149 genera carrying a +3-type gene, so why does the cassette keep the RT's company? The pairing is observed; two questions remain: did the RT join an existing module, and does it work with it, as DRT10 is reported to with an RNA and a protein partner?

records.title: Comparative Metagenomic Analysis of Fungal Communities and Genomic Analysis of Yeasts from the Chilean Altiplano and Central Mountains
records.abstract: Fungal communities inhabiting high-altitude environments are exposed to multiple environmental constraints, yet their diversity and genomic characteristics remain poorly characterized. Here, we investigated fungal diversity across 10 high-altitude localities in the Chilean Altiplano and Central Mountain region using ITS amplicon sequencing, complemented by comparative genomic analyses of 11 yeast isolates. Fungal commu-nities were evaluated based on taxonomic composition, alpha diversity, co-occurrence patterns, and relationships among sampling localities. Yeast isolates were analyzed using genomic similarity, synteny, functional profiles, stress-associated proteins, enzyme homologs, and mitochondrial genome characteristics. Ascomycota was the dominant phylum, but fungal community composition and alpha diversity varied among localities, with geographic structuring evident at the genus level. Co-occurrence networks revealed highly connected fungal communities, while many ASVs remained unclassified at lower taxonomic levels. Genome-scale analyses supported the classification of three isolates as Sporobolomyces salmonicolor and eight as Naganishia spp., highlighting the value of ge-nome-based approaches for resolving taxonomic relationships. Functional profiles were broadly conserved, but differences in GPI-anchor biosynthesis, galactose metabolism, steroid biosynthesis, and mitophagy were detected between isolates. In addition, stress-related and potentially biotechnologically relevant enzyme homologs were iden-tified. Mitochondrial genomes showed a conserved core of oxidative phosphorylation genes but substantial variation in introns, ORFs, and synteny, indicating marked mi-tochondrial genomic diversity. Together, these findings demonstrate substantial eco-logical and genomic diversity among fungi from high-altitude environments in Chile and reveal functional and genomic features that may be relevant to environmental adaptation and biotechnology.

records.title: Systematic analysis of MYB transcription factors in lotus (Nelumbo nucifera) reveals NnMYB48 as a positive regulator of aporphine alkaloid biosynthesis.
records.abstract: Aporphine alkaloids in lotus (Nelumbo nucifera) are medicinally significant compounds, and their biosynthesis is orchestrated by a complex network involving various transcription factors (TFs). MYB TFs constitute one of the most critical classes, yet their specific functions in lotus aporphine alkaloid biosynthesis remained largely unexplored. Using the newly assembled lotus telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome, we systematically characterized the full complement lotus MYB genes and identified 126 R2R3-MYBs, 57 1R-MYBs, five R1R2R3-MYBs, and one 4R-MYB. Phylogenetic and gene duplication analysis revealed 63 collinear NnMYB gene pairs and 15 tandemly arrayed gene clusters, indicating that both whole-genome and local tandem duplication events collectively drove the expansion of the NnMYB family. Correlation analysis between gene expression and aporphine abundance identified 44 NnMYB candidates potentially involved in aporphine biosynthesis. Among them, NnMYB48 was predominantly expressed in the lotus leaves and showed a rapid transcriptional response to methyl jasmonate (MeJA). Transient overexpression of NnMYB48 in lotus petals markedly upregulated multiple aporphine biosynthetic genes and increased the accumulation of major aporphine alkaloids. Further dual-luciferase reporter assays, yeast one-hybrid, and electrophoretic mobility shift assays confirmed that NnMYB48 directly binds to the promoters of NnTYDC and NnCYP80G, thereby activating their transcription and promoting alkaloid biosynthesis. Collectively, these findings provide critical insights into the evolution trajectory and functional diversification of the NnMYB family in lotus.
records.authors: Zhang M, Yang Z, He R, Zhang Y, Huang Z, Liu J, Sun H, Li J, Yang M, Deng X.

records.title: EMtrace: offline nanopore metagenomics on a laptop for rapid viral diagnostics, genome recovery and 16S profiling
records.abstract: Nanopore sequencers produce reads within minutes, but metagenomic analysis remains challenging where internet access is limited, data are sensitive or computing resources are modest. EMtrace is an offline pipeline that runs on a laptop during sequencing: it classifies MinKNOW reads, estimates taxon abundance by expectation-maximization (EM) and assembles reference-based consensus genomes. We benchmarked it against five virome and four 16S rRNA tools on simulated, mock-community and clinical data. On field isolates and 16 SARS-CoV-2 clinical samples, EMtrace had the highest species-level F1 score (1.00 and 0.97) and one false-positive species, against 3-7 for the comparators. It recovered divergent viruses as completely as ViMOP, and low-titre field libraries more completely, at ≥99.7% identity. In replayed runs, it identified the target virus in the first 4,000-read batch (5-13 min). With a shared 16S reference, EMtrace reported two to three times fewer false-positive species than Emu.

records.title: Bacteriophage associated liver injury in a person with cystic fibrosis and prior liver transplantation.
records.abstract: A 27-year-old man with cystic fibrosis, prior liver transplantation for advanced cystic fibrosis related liver disease, tacrolimus immunosuppression, multidrug resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, recurrent drug induced liver injury, and intolerance to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor underwent matched bacteriophage therapy. Intravenous phages were administered at 109 plaque forming units per dose and nebulised phages at 5 × 109 plaque forming units per dose twice daily. Within two days, marked elevations in alanine transaminase, aspartate transaminase, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma glutamyl transferase developed, prompting treatment cessation. Peak alanine transaminase reached 494 U/L and alkaline phosphatase 527 U/L were observed, while bilirubin and coagulation parameters remained normal. Extensive investigation, including magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography and medication review, identified no alternative cause. Rechallenge with nebulised phage therapy alone resulted in recurrent liver enzyme elevation after eight days, again resolving following discontinuation. Temporal correlation was demonstrated between liver function test abnormalities and detection of phage DNA in serum and sputum. No bacteriophage neutralisation, bacterial DNAaemia, development of phage resistance, or significant bacterial genomic change was observed. Despite early cessation, lung function improved over the subsequent six months.

records.title: Upgrading yeast-based low-carbon biomanufacturing by harnessing a universal in vivo evolution system.
records.abstract: Non-conventional yeasts are emerging as key cell factories in low-carbon biomanufacturing, but unlocking their full potential requires optimizing complex traits, such as substrate utilization and high-level protein expression, through in vivo genome-wide evolution. To address this, we developed a universal plasmid vector deploying a DNA Helicase-Activation-Induced Cytidine Deaminase (Helicase-AID) for genome-wide base editing. This system enables cross-species mutagenesis in diverse yeasts, including Yarrowia lipolytica, Pichia pastoris, and Kluyveromyces marxianus. We demonstrated that MCM5-AID base editing efficiency in Y. lipolytica is time-dependent, achieving a cumulative mutation rate of 3.13 × 10-5 mutations per base pair (bp-1) over 432 hours. Using this system, we evolved Y. lipolytica variants exhibiting a 37.77% increase in maximum specific growth rate on acetate, alongside altered starch production ranging from -92.96% to 17.45%. Crucially, we utilized this platform to activate the silent expression of heterologous proteins, overcoming a persistent bottleneck in microbial strain engineering. Evolutionary, transcriptomic and genomic analyses showed that evolved Y. lipolytica variants exhibited enhanced accumulation of Cas13x, a naturally difficult-to-express protein, via reduced proteolytic degradation. In contrast, evolved P. pastoris variants gained the ability to express previously silent thaumatin through significant transcriptional upregulation, enhanced protein folding, and increased amino acid biosynthesis. Ultimately, this universal in vivo evolution system provides a robust platform for genome-directed evolution across diverse industrial yeast species, accelerating the systematic exploration of their potential in low-carbon biomanufacturing.

records.title: Comparative mitogenomics of Hippophae reveals conserved gene content, repeat-mediated structural variation, and limited phylogenetic resolution.
records.abstract: Plant mitochondrial genomes retain conserved coding content but evolve rapidly in structure. We assembled mitogenomes of four Hippophae taxa from long reads and compared them with four published mitogenomes. Gene content and codon usage were largely conserved, whereas the assemblies of closely related taxa differed by up to four inversions and two translocations. Long reads spanning repeats of 1.3-9.6 kb supported both assembled and recombinant arrangements, and allowing for repeat-mediated isomers removed all inversions among the seven records compared. RNA-seq identified 80-262 candidate editing sites per taxon, and mitogenome-plastome homologous fragments made up 12.54-12.77% of each assembly. A 31-gene phylogeny supported Hippophae monophyly but weakly resolved relationships within the genus (16 parsimony-informative sites). Only nad4 showed a Hippophae-specific increase in ω; its fixed C-to-T substitutions and intron loss point to retroprocessing rather than positive selection. Most structural differences among Hippophae mitogenomes can be explained by repeat-mediated isomerization.
records.authors: Zeng Z, Zhang H, He J, Nima C, Ouzhu D, Qiong B, Dolma D, Wang R, Bacuo C, Ma N, Qiong, Wang J.

records.title: Legume root nodule endophytes belonging to Agrobacterium, Bacillus, Paenibacillus, and Pseudomonas possess the nitrogen-fixing (nifH) gene similar to rhizobia.
records.abstract: BackgroundLegume root nodules, the site of biological nitrogen fixation, are inhabited by diverse microsymbionts. Consequently, as part of our ongoing work to discover the nitrogen-fixing microsymbionts, the present study aims to identify nodule endophytes possessing the nitrogen fixation (nifH) gene.Methods and resultsRoot nodules of Mucuna prurita, Vigna umbellata, and Vigna unguiculata were collected for microsymbiont isolation. Isolation resulted in fifty-one bacterial isolates; of these, initial screening detected eighteen nifH-positive isolates. To identify the species, 16 S rRNA was amplified and successfully sequenced for sixteen isolates. Analysis of the 16 S rRNA sequence revealed that ten isolates were rhizobia, including Rhizobium and Bradyrhizobium, while the other 6 isolates were identified as non-rhizobial endophytes (NRE) from the genera Agrobacterium, Bacillus, Paenibacillus, and Pseudomonas. Diversity in morphological and biochemical characteristics was observed among the nodule endophytes. All sixteen endophytes produce the phytohormones auxin and gibberellic acid, although they lack the phosphate solubilisation activity. To identify representative bacterial strains, random amplified polymorphic DNA (RAPD) was performed. The nifH gene from the selected bacterial strains was sequenced, and a phylogenetic tree was constructed. The nifH phylogenetic tree grouped the rhizobia and NRE, indicating a shared ancestry of their nifH gene.ConclusionThis study confirms that NRE are common members of the legume root nodule microbial community, and some of them carry nifH genes similar to those of rhizobia, providing molecular evidence for their potential nitrogen-fixing ability.
records.authors: Pongener B, Paul A.

records.title: Large-genome phages encode diverse proteins associated with host cell envelope functions
records.abstract: Abstract  Huge phages (or jumbo phages, > 200 kilobases) encode extensive protein repertoires, yet their functional diversity and potential roles in host physiology remain poorly understood. Using protein structure-based analyses of dominant protein families across 7,187 non-redundant genomes of huge phages, we uncovered pronounced phylogenetic and habitat-associated diversification. Notably, we identified diverse proteins associated with bacterial cell envelope functions, particularly in human gut-associated huge phages. These included previously unreported phage-encoded sortase B, whose putative substrates contain signal peptides and cell-wall sorting signals, suggesting a potential route for displaying phage proteins on bacterial surfaces. Phage-encoded phage shock protein A (PspA) was distributed across diverse lineages and frequently neighbored genes associated with membrane organization and transport, implicating potential roles in membrane physiology. We also identified 1,603 β-barrel outer membrane proteins (OMPs) across 1,303 huge phages from diverse ecosystems. These OMPs exhibited structural diversity and associations with predicted host taxonomy, habitat, and neighboring envelope-related genes. Metatranscriptomic analysis supported expression of representative phage-encoded PspA and OMP genes in natural communities including the human gut. Together, these findings reveal bacterial cell envelope processes as a previously underappreciated potential interface for huge phage–host interactions.
records.authors: Chen L, Yuan L.

records.title: Genomic and phenotypic analysis reveals taxonomic and biosynthetic diversity in desert-derived Saccharothrix
records.abstract: Abstract    Rare actinomycetes represent an underexplored source of bioactive natural products, yet their taxonomic diversity and biosynthetic potential remain incompletely characterized. Here, ten  Saccharothrix  strains isolated from the Gurbantunggut Desert in Xinjiang, northwestern China, were investigated using phylogenomics, comparative genomics, biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) mining, and antimicrobial assays. Genome-based analyses identified two lineages that may represent novel species. A total of 413 BGCs were predicted across the ten genomes. Comparative BiG-SCAPE analysis grouped 1,461 BGCs from the ten study strains, reference  Saccharothrix  genomes, and MIBiG into 735 gene cluster families (GCFs). Only three of the 19 GCFs containing MIBiG reference BGCs also included BGCs from the study strains, indicating limited overlap with characterized BGCs. Antimicrobial activity was detected in 89 of 300 strain–medium–indicator combinations, with positive results more frequent against fungal than bacterial indicators. Notably, the strain with the largest number of predicted BGCs did not exhibit the broadest antimicrobial spectrum. These findings reveal taxonomic and biosynthetic diversity among desert-derived  Saccharothrix  and provide a basis for prioritizing strains and biosynthetic pathways for further natural product discovery.
records.authors: Li S, Dong L, Wang Z, Wang X, Bobushova S, Tian C, Duixiannale A, Chen X, Zhang W, Fang B, Liu Y, Li X, Li W.

records.title: Whole genome sequencing of Curcuma xanthorrhiza Roxb. reveals ploidy-driven speciation and divergent specialized metabolite biosynthesis in the genus Curcuma.
records.abstract: Curcuma xanthorrhiza Roxb., commonly known as javanese turmeric (temulawak), is a rhizomatous herb with significant ethnobotanical and nutraceutical importance, valued for producing curcuminoids and xanthorrhizol. Despite its considerable medicinal and economic value, the genomic basis underlying these important traits has remained largely uncharacterized. This study presents its first whole-genome assembly, generated through a hybrid sequencing strategy utilizing 21.82 Gb of PacBio HiFi and 21.46 Gb of Illumina short-read data. Independent k-mer profiling and assembly-based analyses converged on a triploid genome architecture, resulting in a 579.07 Mb contig-level assembly (N50 = 1.48 Mb) with high completeness (BUSCO: 94.5-97.7%), 42,169 annotated protein-coding genes and a PSAURON score of 98.4. Comparative phylogenomic analysis across the Zingiberaceae revealed that while C. xanthorrhiza diverged from its sister taxon Curcuma caesia Roxb. recently (~ 1.76 Mya), it exhibits profound macrosynteny disruption, a net gene-family contraction, and the most compact gene complement among the sampled species. Genome-wide mining of biosynthetic gene clusters identified 26 candidates, including a paralogous pair of curcuminoid loci, though further validation by RNA-seq co-expression is needed. Additionally, genome-wide homology-search identified AC50XY_029945 as the strongest candidate (S)-β-bisabolene synthase for xanthorrhizol biosynthesis, proposed as a trans-acting, dispersed pathway architecture involving 51 candidate CYP71 cytochrome P450s, an SDR oxidoreductase, and co-located WRKY/ERF/MYB transcription factors. These results establish the first nuclear genomic resource for C. xanthorrhiza, highlighting the role of ploidy-driven genome instability in driving rapid-speciation and secondary metabolite diversification in the genus Curcuma.
records.authors: Rahmat E, Hutabarat JT, Anindita L, Sianipar NF, Assidqi K, Faizal A, Kang CH, Kang Y, Ansori ANM, Trinugroho JP.

records.title: The mammalian archaeome: diversity, function and emerging roles in health and disease.
records.abstract: Archaea are a fundamental yet historically overlooked part of the mammalian microbiome. Once thought to be limited to extreme environments, archaea, particularly methanogenic archaea, are now recognized as widespread colonizers of mammalian hosts, with key roles in gut metabolism, microbial syntrophy and host interaction. In this Review, we summarize current knowledge on the distribution, diversity and function of the mammalian archaeome, with a focus on humans and ruminants. We explore the ecological and physiological roles of Methanobrevibacter spp. as key gastrointestinal colonizers, archaeal interactions with bacterial communities and the host, and the impact of external factors such as diet, age and health status on the archaeome. We further highlight the translational potential of archaeome research, including methane mitigation strategies in cattle and emerging associations between the archaeome and human disease. By integrating insights across host species, we argue that understanding the archaeome is essential to fully comprehend mammalian microbiome function, evolution and its relevance to health and disease.
records.authors: Kumpitsch C, Bauer E, Arora B, Schmitz RA, Moissl-Eichinger C.

records.title: Bioinformatic pipeline for functional inference of  Rickettsia akari  hypothetical proteins reveals virulence-associated and effector candidates
records.abstract: Background  Rickettsia akari , the causative agent of rickettsialpox, is an obligate intracellular pathogen with a highly reduced genome encoding numerous hypothetical proteins (HPs) of unknown function. Many of these HPs are expressed during host-cell infection, yet their roles in bacterial physiology and potential contribution to virulence remain unclear.  Methodology/Principal Findings  We performed an integrative  in silico characterization of 54  R. akari HPs previously identified by mass spectrometry in purified bacterial cells. Using a benchmarked computational workflow, we predicted their physicochemical properties, subcellular localization, putative secretion signals, protein folds, potential interaction partners, and evolutionary conservation. Most HPs were predicted to be thermostable. The majority of HPs were predicted to be cytoplasmic (37.00%) or membrane-associated (29.63%). Predicted features associated with the type IV secretion system were more frequent than those associated with type I secretion. Network and structural analyses identified candidate HPs with features consistent with potential roles in outer membrane assembly, host-cell interaction, and immune modulation, including predicted peptidyl-prolyl cis/trans isomerases, oxidoreductases, methyltransferases, and putative E3 ubiquitin ligases. Several HPs were predicted to be antigenic and showed conservation across multiple rickettsial genomes. Molecular docking and normal mode analysis supported the plausibility of selected predicted protein-protein and protein-ligand interactions. Evolutionary analyses indicated predominant purifying selection among the analyzed HPs. A8GP20 showed elevated sequence divergence and warrants further investigation as a potential effector candidate.  Conclusions/Significance  Our findings prioritize A8GPG8, A8GP63, A8GNV4, A8GMM8, A8GM41, A8GMJ7, A8GMI5, A8GP20, A8GN23, A8GMB4, A8GM08, and A8GM39 as promising candidates for experimental validation of their predicted functions and potential roles in  R. akari biology and pathogenicity. This work provides an integrative and reproducible bioinformatic framework to guide functional discovery in  R. akari and related neglected intracellular pathogens, and identifies candidate proteins for future studies of rickettsial pathogenesis, antigen discovery, and therapeutic target development.  Author summary  Rickettsialpox is a neglected febrile illness caused by the bacterium  Rickettsia akari and transmitted by mouse mites. Although  R. akari has a small genome, many of its proteins remain uncharacterized and are annotated as “hypothetical proteins”. These proteins may contribute to the bacterium’s ability to infect host cells and cause disease, but their functions are poorly understood.  We used an integrative computational approach to characterize 54 uncharacterized proteins previously identified in  R. akari cells by mass spectrometry. Our analyses suggest that many of these proteins are predicted to be stable and associated with the bacterial membrane, whereas several may interact with host cells, potentially through a bacterial secretion system. We identified promising candidates that may contribute to host-cell interactions, immune modulation, outer membrane assembly, and other processes important for bacterial survival. Several proteins were predicted to be antigenic and showed conservation across multiple rickettsial genomes, suggesting potential value for future diagnostic or vaccine studies.  By prioritizing the most promising uncharacterized proteins for experimental validation, our study provides new insights into the biology and pathogenicity of  R. akari and offers a framework for studying similar proteins in other neglected intracellular pathogens.
records.authors: Kaliukanov S, Csicsay F, Skultety L, Quevedo-Diaz M.

records.title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Translatomic Profiling Reveals Noncanonical RNA Junctions and Hidden Coding Potential in Porcine Epidemic Diarrhea Virus
records.abstract: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) poses a major threat to the global swine industry. Although coronavirus discontinuous transcription is well characterized, the classical model cannot fully explain the diversity of viral RNA junctions, while conventional genome annotations may underestimate viral protein-coding capacity. To address these gaps, we integrated time-resolved RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), cycloheximide (CHX)- and harringtonine (HAR)-treated ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq), comparative genomics, and peptide mass spectrometry to investigate PEDV RNA expression and hidden coding potential. RNA-seq revealed that, at 3 hours post-infection (hpi), the 3’ genomic region exhibited strong relative coverage enrichment, whereas the relative contribution of the 5’ replicase-coding region increased rapidly between 3 and 5 hpi, suggesting a possible transition from sgRNA-dominated RNA accumulation toward enhanced genomic RNA replication. Genome-wide junction analysis identified 43,635 distinct noncanonical RNA junctions, although canonical sgRNA junctions accounted for 95.5% of all junction-supporting reads. Several abundant noncanonical sgRNAs were predicted to generate novel coding products, including N-x4, N-x2, M-x3, and M-x2, short peptides encoded within the 3’ untranslated region (UTR), and two distinct N-terminally truncated S proteins, thereby expanding the potential coding repertoire of PEDV. Genome-wide reading-frame analysis uncovered a pronounced asymmetry in hidden coding potential, identifying 68 overlapping open reading frames (ORFs) longer than 40 amino acids in the +1 reading frame, compared with only three in the +2 frame. Ribo-seq further revealed a progressive redistribution of viral ribosome occupancy toward structural protein-coding regions during the later stages of infection. By integrating HAR-associated translation initiation-site enrichment with CHX-based ORF-level translation analysis, we identified several noncanonical ORFs with strong translation-associated evidence, including N-x1, N-x2, S-x1, and ORF1b-x13. Moreover, peptide mass spectrometry detected a characteristic peptide corresponding to N-x1 in infected samples, providing independent proteomic evidence for the expression of this previously unannotated viral protein. Together, these findings uncover extensive noncanonical RNA synthesis and hidden protein-coding capacity in PEDV, establishing a foundation for understanding novel viral gene expression strategies and their potential evolutionary and pathogenic significance.

records.title: Meta-analysis of the agreement and accuracy of functional inference from 16S amplicon studies in arsenic-affected soils and aquifers
records.abstract: Abstract    Background.  Almost all archived environmental sequence data are 16S amplicon, so gene content is inferred from lineage rather than measured, yet inferred profiles are routinely read as measurements. Whether the reliability of inference differs between genes, and whether the predictor’s own confidence metric identifies the unreliable ones, has not been tested at archive scale. Here, 3,041 archived 16S amplicon runs from 78 studies of rice-paddy soil, arsenic-contaminated soil and arsenic-affected aquifers were re-analysed through one pipeline. Gene content was inferred by a curated marker-taxa bridge and by PICRUSt2, their agreement was quantified per gene and tested against candidate predictors, and both routes were checked against paired shotgun metagenomes. Compartments were compared under depth adjustment and study-level permutation.  Results.  Agreement between the routes varied widely by gene, from ρ = 0.906 (mcrA) to ρ = −0.118 (arsM), around a weak median of ρ = 0.286 across 698 gene-study comparisons in 57 studies. PICRUSt2’s confidence metric did not explain that range, whereas agreement tracked how consistently the marker taxa carried each gene in PICRUSt2’s reference genomes (ρ = +0.66). FAPROTAX, a published lookup, matched PICRUSt2 no better than the bridge, whereas Tax4Fun2, a second genome-based predictor, matched it more closely (ρ = +0.43 against ρ = +0.29). Sequencing depth lowered inferred abundance in 15 of 20 genes, while its effect on detection was positive for every gene. Against shotgun metagenomes from 267 biosamples in 16 studies, PICRUSt2 tracked measured abundance weakly (median ρ = +0.21), Tax4Fun2 no better, and the bridge barely (ρ = +0.05). Agreement between the bridge and PICRUSt2 predicted the accuracy of the bridge but not of PICRUSt2. No compartment difference was resolved after adjustment.  Conclusions.  Agreement between amplicon-based inference routes differs by gene within a single panel. Neither the predictor’s confidence metric nor phylogenetic conservation identifies the discordant genes, while carriage within the marker taxa partly anticipates them. Disagreement between independent routes flags method-dependent genes, but agreement does not certify accuracy. The routes disagree on arsM, one of only two arsenic-cycling genes both score. Compartment differences in arsenic-cycling potential cannot be resolved from public amplicon data without shotgun metagenomes.

records.title: Molecular Epidemiology and Resistance Profiling of Macrolide-Resistant Bacterial Pathogens in Egyptian Primary Healthcare Centers Using Third-Generation High-Throughput Sequencing
records.abstract: Abstract    Background:  Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global public health challenge, with particularly important consequences in settings where antibiotic use, diagnostic capacity, and antimicrobial stewardship remain heterogeneous. Macrolides are widely used for community-acquired respiratory and skin and soft-tissue infections, but increasing resistance threatens their therapeutic effectiveness. Genomic surveillance data describing the molecular basis and dissemination of macrolide resistance in Egyptian primary healthcare settings remain limited.  Methods:  A multicenter cross-sectional investigation was conducted from January to December 2023 across 15 primary healthcare facilities in three Egyptian governorates: Cairo, Alexandria, and Assiut. A total of 842 clinical specimens were collected from patients presenting with suspected bacterial respiratory or skin and soft-tissue infections. Bacterial isolates were identified using matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed according to CLSI M100-Ed34 (2024). Macrolide-resistant isolates were subjected to genomic characterization using Oxford Nanopore MinION and Pacific Biosciences Sequel IIe sequencing platforms. Resistance determinants, plasmids, integrative conjugative elements, sequence types, and phylogenetic relationships were investigated using established antimicrobial-resistance and genome-analysis databases and bioinformatic pipelines. Targeted PacBio HiFi sequencing was additionally used to characterize 23S rRNA mutations.  Results:  Among 642 confirmed bacterial pathogens, 289 (45.0%, 95% CI: 41.2–48.9%) exhibited phenotypic macrolide resistance. Resistance was highest among Staphylococcus aureus (58.2%, 114/196), followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae (45.0%, 98/218), Streptococcus pyogenes (39.7%, 62/156), and Haemophilus influenzae (20.8%, 15/72). The ermB gene predominated among resistant streptococci, occurring in 81.6% of resistant S. pneumoniae and 80.6% of resistant S. pyogenes isolates, whereas ermC predominated among resistant S. aureus isolates (87.7%, 100/114). Long-read sequencing enabled reconstruction of 45 plasmids and 12 integrative conjugative elements associated with resistance determinants. A conserved ermC-carrying plasmid, designated pEC-Egy1 (3,142 bp), was detected in 68.0% of ermC-positive S. aureus isolates across the three governorates, with 99.8% sequence identity among detected variants. PacBio HiFi sequencing identified the A2058G 23S rRNA mutation in 22/289 resistant isolates (7.6%) and revealed mixed wild-type and mutant alleles consistent with heteroresistance in 9/289 isolates (3.1%). Heteroresistant isolates exhibited lower erythromycin MICs (4–16 μg/mL) than isolates carrying predominantly homogeneous A2058G mutant populations (32–128 μg/mL; pConclusion:  Integrated third-generation sequencing provided high-resolution characterization of macrolide resistance determinants, their genomic contexts, and dissemination patterns among bacterial pathogens from Egyptian primary healthcare facilities. The findings demonstrate the coexistence of clonal dissemination and horizontal mobility of resistance determinants and highlight the value of long-read sequencing for resolving plasmid structures, mobile genetic elements, and heterogeneous 23S rRNA resistance alleles. These genomic data provide a framework for continued molecular surveillance of macrolide resistance in Egyptian primary healthcare settings.

records.title: Functional divergence within mulberry-associated Pantoea ananatis: Insights from comparative genomics and host-contact metabolomics.
records.abstract: Pantoea ananatis is a widely distributed plant-associated bacterium that can exhibit contrasting ecological functions, ranging from plant-beneficial activities to pathogenicity. However, the genomic and metabolic features associated with such functional divergence among closely related strains remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized 18 mulberry-associated P. ananatis isolates using phenotypic assays and selected Pa-6 and YSFJ as representatives of two predominant functional types for comparative genomic and host-contact metabolomic analyses. Pa-6 exhibited a beneficial-associated phenotype characterized by several plant growth-promoting and antagonistic traits, comparatively limited tissue damage, and lower disease severity during the later stages of co-inoculation with Ralstonia pseudosolanacearum XZqk. In contrast, YSFJ caused progressive wilt accompanied by bacterial aggregation, xylem occlusion, vascular disorganization, and tissue damage. Despite these contrasting phenotypes, Pa-6 and YSFJ shared approximately 98.9% average nucleotide identity. Comparative genomic analyses revealed differences in accessory-gene content, plasmid composition, and strain-specific homologous clusters. Annotation comparisons highlighted a GH19-associated locus in Pa-6 and wbpZ- and feoB-associated loci in YSFJ as putative gene-content differences. Exploratory pathway mapping of host-contact extracellular metabolomic profiles highlighted central-carbon, organic-acid, and redox-related processes in the Pa-6 treatment and carbohydrate transport and utilization, aromatic-compound metabolism, and stress-related processes in the YSFJ treatment. These results document contrasting host-associated phenotypes and provide genomic and metabolic context for further investigation, while the contributions of individual loci and phylogenetic background remain unresolved.

records.title: Microbiome-Informed Genomic Prediction of CH4:CO2 Ratio in Holstein Dairy Cattle Using 16S rRNA Profiles and SNP Markers.
records.abstract: Ruminant animals produce methane as a by-product of microbial fermentation in the rumen, with cattle being the largest contributors among ruminants. Methane emissions may be influenced directly by the host's genetics and indirectly through host-mediated effects on rumen microbiome composition. In this study, we investigated whether modelling both direct and indirect genetic effects could improve the genomic prediction of breeding values for methane emissions. We used genotype, methane CH4:CO2 ratio and 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data (16S), including 16S genus (16S-G), 16S species (16S-S) from Danish Holstein cows. A conventional genomic best linear unbiased prediction (GBLUP) model was used as a benchmark and compared with a microbiome-informed GBLUP approach based on three linked linear mixed models for the prediction of breeding values. In GMBLUP, the first model regresses methane emissions on three random animal effects (archaeal 16S, bacterial 16S and polygenic effects) using corresponding microbiome and genomic relationship matrices. The second and third models separately regress archaeal and bacterial 16S on random animal effects defined by the genomic relationship matrix. We evaluated prediction accuracy using five-fold cross-validation. The GBLUP model, which used only genomic marker information, achieved a mean accuracy of 0.20 across the five folds when evaluated in the animal subsets corresponding to the 16S-G and 16S-S datasets, while GMBLUP showed higher accuracy, particularly for the 16S-G dataset, with a mean accuracy of 0.48. These results highlight that incorporating microbiome information into genomic prediction models may improve predictive performance for the CH4:CO2 ratio, although further validation in larger and independent populations is required before practical implementation in breeding programmes.

records.authors: Saedi N, Zhang S, Lund MS, Cai Z, Karaman E.

records.title: Pan-Genomic Insights into Bradyrhizobium ottawaense: Highlighting a Strain with Unusual Host-Specific Compatibility.
records.abstract: Biological nitrogen fixation occupies a paramount position in sustainable agriculture. The present study elucidates the genomic diversity and symbiotic capabilities of Bradyrhizobium ottawaense focusing on the commercial B. ottawaense strain RCAM0104 to decipher the genetic bases of plant-bacterial interactions and the evolutionary adaptability of these microorganisms. Experimental assessments of symbiotic compatibility revealed that RCAM0104 effectively nodulates Arachis hypogaea, Glycine soja, and Vigna unguiculata, but is ineffective on Glycine max. Histological examinations confirmed successful infection processes in most host plants, with the exception of white nodules observed on cultivated soybean. Prediction of type III effectors in the RCAM0104 genome identified effector proteins potentially involved in its promiscuous symbiotic phenotype. These findings highlight the genetic flexibility of B. ottawaense and its capacity to adapt to diverse host plants. The observed host-specific nodulation patterns correlate with specific variations in the accessory genome, suggesting their potential role in determining symbiotic compatibility, potentially through gene transfer from local strains. This research contributes significantly to our understanding of the evolutionary dynamics and ecological plasticity of rhizobia in symbiosis with legumes, providing insights into the mechanisms regulating plant-microbe interactions. Based on these results, we hypothesize an evolutionary trade-off, where a loss of compatibility with one host may have occurred concurrently with the putative acquisition in compatibility with another.
records.authors: Kirichek EA, Tsyganov VE.

records.title: Genomic signatures distinguish isolates of  Salmonella  Typhimurium from humans and livestock
records.abstract: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium is a major cause of human salmonellosis and livestock represent an important reservoir for human infection through the food chain. However, it remains unclear whether isolates recovered from human disease reflect the broader livestock population or constitute a subset of livestock-associated isolates characterized by specific genetic features.  Here, we analysed 1,398  S. Typhimurium genomes from human, poultry, bovine and swine isolates to evaluate whether isolates associated with human disease can be distinguished from those circulating in livestock and to identify the genetic features underlying this discrimination.  Whole-genome multilocus sequence typing profiles were converted into a gene presence/absence matrix and analysed using four machine-learning algorithms, which showed high and consistent discriminatory performance. Model performance was influenced by the phylogenetic structure of the population and by the variable distribution of human- and livestock- associated isolates across lineages of sequence type (ST) 19, the most prevalent S. Typhimurium ST. Nevertheless, within ST19, 97 genes were significantly enriched and 36 were significantly depleted in human-associated genomes relative to genomes from each of the three livestock sources. Human-enriched genes included 14 genes required for biosynthesis of the lipopolysaccharide core, the O-antigen, the T1 antigen, and six virulence factors. These genes were consistently absent from livestock-associated genomes across ST19 lineages. Conversely, human-depleted genes included the galactitol utilisation cluster and five virulence genes, which are predominantly absent in specific ST19 lineages. Overall, our findings support the existence of host-associated genomic signatures that distinguish isolates associated with human disease from those sampled from the livestock reservoir. Data Summary  This study analysed publicly available  Salmonella Typhimurium genomes; no new sequencing data were generated. Genome assemblies, associated metadata and whole-genome multilocus sequence typing (wgMLST) allelic profiles were retrieved from EnteroBase (  https://enterobase.warwick.ac.uk ). The final dataset comprised 1,398 genomes, as detailed in Table S1. Custom analysis scripts, input datasets, intermediate files and analysis outputs are available in the GitHub repository (  https://github.com/GiovanniMerici/Typhimurium_Human_vs_Animal ). These include the train/test split membership, selected model hyperparameters and per-split SHAP matrices. Software versions and analysis parameters are described in the Methods.  Impact statement  Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium is among the leading causes of human salmonellosis, with livestock representing important reservoirs of infection. Genomic studies have primarily focused on identifying the animal reservoirs associated with human clinical isolates, while whether these isolates represent the broader bacterial populations circulating in livestock or a genetically distinguishable subset remains comparatively underexplored. Using 1,398 genomes and four machine-learning models, we demonstrate that human-associated isolates can be distinguished from poultry, bovine, and pig isolates with high accuracy and reproducibility. Although phylogenetic structure contributed to the classification, we were able to identify specific genes significantly enriched and depleted in human-associated genomes relative to genomes from each of the three livestock sources within the most prevalent S. Typhimurium ST. Importantly, these genomic differences were biologically coherent, rather than scattered across unrelated loci, involving genes associated with surface-antigen biosynthesis and virulence. These findings extend genomic source-attribution approaches by showing that human clinical isolates represent a distinguishable subset of livestock-associated  S . Typhimurium populations. This distinction provides a complementary perspective for interpreting genomic surveillance data and highlights the potential relevance of host-associated genomic variation for understanding the relationship between livestock reservoirs and human infection.
records.authors: Merici G, Scaltriti E, Pongolini S, Tambassi M.

records.title: Integrated optimization of experimental and computational workflows improves genome recovery in long-read gut metagenomics.
records.abstract: Short-read metagenomic sequencing has been widely applied in microbial research due to its high quality and decreasing cost. However, short reads are inherently fragmented, which limits assembly contiguity and the recovery of complete microbial genomes. In contrast, long-read sequencing, with significantly longer read lengths, helps overcome these limitations. Achieving complete and accurate genome recovery is the core goal of metagenomics. To address this challenge, we systematically evaluated and optimized the long-read metagenomic workflow, from sample processing to computational assembly, using the CycloneSEQ platform.IMPORTANCEOur results suggest that upstream experimental protocols are important contributors to long-read metagenomic performance within the evaluated framework. In particular, magnetic-plate DNA extraction, together with pretreatment, was associated with more favorable input and downstream sequencing-related characteristics for long-read analysis. These changes were also associated with broader microbial recovery in the evaluated data sets. Assembly benchmarking further showed that integrating matched long-read (CycloneSEQ) and short-read (DNBSEQ) data sets provided a favorable balance across multiple evaluation dimensions. In our fecal metagenomic data set, long-read-first assembly followed by short-read polishing showed strong overall performance when recovery, contiguity, and sequence accuracy were considered together, although workflow performance remained metric dependent.
records.authors: Hu Y, Sun L, Huang Y, Jiang F, Tong X, Yang J, Ju Y, Yang Z, Liufu S, Hu Y, Ma W, Guo R, Li W, Zhang T, Zhu X, Zhang Z.

records.title: Characterization of the urinary DNA virome of hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipient and healthy cynomolgus macaques.
records.abstract: BK polyomavirus (BKPyV) and chronic latent DNA virus infections frequently reactivate after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), where they contribute to major complications in humans with limited options for prevention or treatment. Mauritian cynomolgus macaques (MCMs; Macaca fascicularis) serve as an important animal model for transplantation research due to their limited major histocompatibility complex diversity. Similar viral reactivations and disease complications occur in MCMs and humans post-transplantation, including polyomavirus-associated hemorrhagic cystitis and nephropathy. To define the polyomaviruses associated with these outcomes and characterize the broader urinary DNA virome, we sequenced rolling circle-amplified urine DNA from healthy and HSCT recipient cynomolgus macaques, allowing for comprehensive genomic characterization of the detected polyomaviruses. De novo assembly and annotation identified three polyomaviruses with apparent specific host tropism to cynomolgus macaques: Macaca fascicularis polyomavirus 2 (MafaPyV2) and Macaca fascicularis polyomavirus 3 (MafaPyV3), which are closely related to human polyomaviruses, and a newly identified strain of simian virus 40 (SV40 type IIB). All three viruses were detected in both HSCT recipients and healthy animals, but were shed at significantly higher relative loads in HSCT recipients. Multiple polyomaviruses were frequently detected within individual hosts, and all three were identified in HSCT recipients that developed urologic disease. Together, these findings further characterize polyomavirus diversity, shedding, and disease associations in hematopoietic stem cell-transplanted Mauritian cynomolgus macaques.IMPORTANCEReactivation of latent viruses after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is a major cause of illness in transplant recipients, yet options for prevention and treatment remain limited. Progress has been hindered by the lack of animal models that accurately reflect human disease. In this study, we show that Mauritian cynomolgus macaques harbor multiple polyomaviruses that reactivate at high levels following transplantation and are associated with urinary tract disease, closely paralleling complications seen in humans. We define the genetic identity of these viruses and demonstrate that immunosuppression strongly enhances viral shedding and disease severity. By establishing clear similarities between viral reactivation in macaques and humans, this work validates the Mauritian cynomolgus macaque transplantation model as a powerful platform for studying virus-driven disease mechanisms and testing antiviral therapies and vaccines relevant to human transplantation.
records.authors: Vogel H, Neal TT, Wu HL, Kukula K, Kievit P, Sacha J, Starrett GJ.

records.title: Enhanced control ability against cyanobacteria through combinations of multiple algicidal bacterial strains.
records.abstract: Algicidal bacteria are promising microorganisms for controlling harmful algal blooms (HABs) because of their ability to inhibit algal growth or lyse algal cells in aquatic systems. However, our understanding of how to enhance their performance within complex microbial communities remains limited. In this study, we evaluated the algicidal activity of previously isolated bacterial strains in a constructed cyanobacterial consortium dominated by Microcystis aeruginosa and containing indigenous lake microorganisms. Our results revealed that while individual strains generally showed limited inhibitory effects, certain strain combinations exhibited pronounced algicidal activity. Notably, co-inoculation of strain Chromobacterium sp. MERYL1-35 and strain Paucibacter sp. MERXLGS1 achieved the highest algicidal efficiency among the tested treatments. Growth assays and quantitative proteomic analysis demonstrated that these two strains establish a distinct antagonistic interspecies interaction, where Chromobacterium exerts strong inhibitory effects on Paucibacter, accompanied by significant expression alterations in certain bacterial virulence and interaction-associated proteins. We propose that this collective enhancement in population survivability and antagonistic potential of Chromobacterium substantially contributes to the enhanced algicidal activity in the dual-strain system. These findings provide new insights into the ability-enhancing strategy of algicidal bacteria and their complex interactions with target cyanobacteria.IMPORTANCEEco-friendly and sustainable control methods of harmful algal blooms (HABs) have been urgently needed in recent years. In this study, we demonstrated that the removal efficiency of cyanobacteria by algicidal bacteria can be substantially enhanced through designed co-inoculation strategies. We found that the enhanced algicidal activity of the combined Chromobacterium and Paucibacter dual-strain inoculations is mediated by a unique antagonistic interaction, which differs from other consortia that more likely arise from cooperative strain interactions. These findings advance our understanding of the complex microbial interplay between algicidal bacteria and phytoplankton and may provide new insights into the development of biological control strategies targeting HABs.

records.title: Multi-omics analysis reveals microbial and metabolic signatures associated with neutral detergent fiber digestibility in dairy cattle.
records.abstract: BackgroundThe rumen microbiome is central to fiber degradation in dairy cows, yet the precise functional and metabolic networks driving variations in neutral detergent fiber (NDF) digestibility remain poorly understood. Elucidating these microbiome-host interactions is critical for improving forage utilization and advancing sustainable dairy production.ResultsEmploying an integrative metagenomics-metabolomics approach, we characterized the rumen microecology of lactating dairy cows exhibiting high and low NDF digestibility phenotypes (n = 10/group). Metagenomic profiling revealed a significant enrichment of fibrolytic taxa (Prevotella sp., Lachnospiraceae bacterium) and carbohydrate-active enzymes in the high-NDF group (HI). In addition, species-level differential abundance testing showed that Methanobrevibacter spp. was more abundant in the low-NDF group (LO) than in the HI group, whereas no archaeal differences were detected at the phylum or genus levels. Functional and metabolomic analyses indicated broader enrichment of amino acid degradation functions and higher concentrations of major volatile fatty acids (VFAs) in HI cows, consistent with stronger overall ruminal fermentation activity. Furthermore, VFAs and microbial composition explained 54.3% and 43.0% of the variation in NDF digestibility, respectively. An exploratory machine learning model based on selected annotated metabolite features showed moderate discriminatory performance, with an out-of-bag accuracy of 77.19%.ConclusionsOur findings suggest that coordinated shifts in rumen microbial composition, amino acid metabolism, and VFA production are associated with variation in NDF digestibility in dairy cattle. These results provide a basis for future studies aimed at improving fiber utilization through microbiome-informed nutritional or breeding strategies.

records.title: Evaluation of full-length 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing using Oxford Nanopore Technologies for diversity surveys of understudied microbiomes.
records.abstract: The use of long-read sequencing is becoming increasingly popular in the study of host-associated microbiomes. However, its application has not yet been optimized for characterizing understudied microbiomes, such as those in marine environments. We evaluated the accuracy and consistency of long-read sequencing of full-length 16S rRNA genes for diversity surveys of symbiotic dinoflagellate (family Symbiodiniaceae) microbiomes. When comparing long-read amplicon sequencing of the full-length bacterial 16S rRNA gene with short-read sequencing of the V4 hypervariable gene region using a known microbial community, the former recapitulated the bacterial taxonomic composition more accurately. Long-read sequencing performed using Oxford Nanopore Technologies was also highly consistent between sequencing runs and flow cells. Long-read sequencing technologies enable microbiome surveys using the full-length 16S rRNA gene, achieving higher accuracy and resolution. This work validates long-read sequencing as a robust approach for resolving microbiome composition in understudied marine systems, thereby supporting ecological and evolutionary investigations of host-microbe associations.
records.authors: Li VY, González-Pech R, Lera-Lozano D, Román-Reyna V, Medina M.

records.title: [Characterization of the caries-associated oral microbiome across age groups based on global metagenomic species-level genome bins data].
records.abstract: Objective: Based on the analysis of global multicenter metagenomic species-level genome bin (SGB), this study aims to identify core cariogenic SGBs across all age groups and provide a basis for the precise diagnosis and age-stratified prevention and treatment of dental caries. Methods: Eight published studies available in the National Center for Biotechnology Information database before August 2024 were included, with a total of 496 oral metagenomic samples enrolled. Samples were stratified into saliva and dental plaque groups across three age segments (Results: Analysis at the SGB level revealed that 652 SGBs were detected in plaque samples and 931 SGBs in saliva samples. Specific core SGB clusters were identified in each age group (50%). Differential analysis indicated that caries was accompanied by marked ecological dysbiosis. These differential patterns were highly age-and sample-specific. Saliva samples in the group agedStreptococcus enrichment versus Capnocytophaga in the healthy group. Notably, in the≥13-year-old group, the caries-associated microbiome shifted to anaerobic Prevotella species alongside Streptococcus. Heatmap analysis confirmed clear ecological turnovers across all ages, with the sharpest demarcation found in the youngest age group. Conclusions: Analysis at the SGB level unveils microbial dysbiosis patterns with greater precision than traditional species-level profiling, providing a novel theoretical basis for the precision diagnosis and age-specific management of dental caries.

records.title: BioDecryptors, a Bioinformatics Escape Game for Undergraduate and Postgraduate Learners in Clinical Microbiology: Prospective Before-and-After Study.
records.abstract: BackgroundBioinformatics is increasingly important in clinical microbiology with growing use of genomic sequencing, metagenomics, and phylogenetic analyses. However, introducing bioinformatics concepts and tools to medical learners can be challenging. Gamified educational approaches may allow introducing these concepts while supporting learner motivation.ObjectiveThis study prospectively evaluated BioDecryptors, an educational escape game to introduce bioinformatics principles and tools in clinical microbiology, by assessing short-term changes in knowledge and self-reported motivation and evaluating participant satisfaction.MethodsWe conducted a prospective before-and-after study between January and September 2025. Volunteers were recruited from undergraduate medical programs at Université Paris Cité and postgraduate programs or training activities for MDs and PharmDs at Université de Nantes, Université Paris-Saclay, and the French Society for Microbiology. Overall, 55 participants were included: 22 (40%) second-year medical students and 33 (60%) postgraduate MDs or PharmDs. Participants completed BioDecryptors in teams of 3 to 4 using versions adapted to their training level. Knowledge was assessed before and immediately after the activity using 2 distinct 10-item tests assessing the same predefined learning objectives. Motivation was assessed using a 12-item, 5-point Likert questionnaire covering 3 predefined domains, and satisfaction was assessed after the activity. Pre-post knowledge scores were compared using paired t tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, as appropriate. Motivation items were analyzed using paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Statistical significance was defined as a 2-sided PResultsPaired knowledge assessments were available for 50 participants. Mean knowledge scores increased from 7.0 (SD 2.0; 95% CI 6.4-7.5) before the activity to 7.9 (SD 2.0; 95% CI 7.4-8.5) afterward (PP=.79). Motivation increased for perceived usefulness (P=.04), willingness to learn (P=.01), understanding of bioinformatics in diseases (P=.002), and confidence in bioinformatics abilities (P=.002). Curiosity (P=.46) and interest in real-life applications (P=.33) did not significantly change. Among 50 satisfaction respondents, overall satisfaction was high (mean 4.7, SD 0.5; 95% CI 4.6-4.9); 98% (48/49) of the respondents to the corresponding item indicated an interest in other escape game modules.ConclusionsParticipation in BioDecryptors was associated with short-term increases in bioinformatics knowledge and self-reported motivation, together with high participant satisfaction. Unlike previously reported escape games focusing primarily on clinical or infection-control topics, BioDecryptors integrates hands-on bioinformatics analyses into a clinical microbiology scenario and offers versions adapted to undergraduate and postgraduate learners. Our findings provide preliminary evidence supporting the feasibility and acceptability of this approach as a complementary educational resource for introducing bioinformatics in health professions training. Controlled studies with longer-term assessments are needed to establish its comparative educational effectiveness and knowledge retention.

records.title: msDNA: the story of a unique satellite DNA molecule in bacteria.
records.abstract: msDNA, or multi-copy single-stranded DNA, is a small satellite DNA observed in DNA extracts from a bacterial cell. A genetic element, usually found on the chromosome, called a retron, is responsible for producing msDNA. This small single-stranded DNA has a unique structure and is synthesized by reverse transcription from an RNA template. Retrons and msDNA are found in a large variety of different bacterial species. The msDNA molecule has also been developed into an important tool for genetic engineering and genome editing. But the biological function of this unique DNA molecule remained a mystery for decades. Recent discoveries show that a retron element can protect bacteria from infection with a virus (phage) using an abortive infection strategy. And the msDNA molecule is required for this anti-phage property. A historical perspective on this unusual DNA molecule, recent breakthroughs into its functions, and a discussion of the current and possible future directions of study are presented herein.
