records.title: The attachment rate of Vibrio anguillarum to microplastics strongly varies with strain identity, particle characteristics, and environmental conditions.
records.abstract: Microplastics (MPs), resulting from plastic objects and waste degradation, are increasingly abundant, particularly in marine environments. They exhibit a hydrophobic surface on which biofilms form easily. Metagenomic analyses of these biofilms have revealed that they often contain bacterial species potentially pathogenic to humans or animals. For this reason, MPs are suspected to present a risk to public health by acting as a vector for pathogenic bacterial species. To better understand this hazard, we studied different factors potentially affecting the bacterial attachment rate to MPs. Focusing on the fish pathogen Vibrio anguillarum, a collection of 16 GFP-labeled strains was assembled, including isolates from infected fish. Their attachment rates were measured using fluorescence microscopy on three types of MPs (milled polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate particles, and commercially available polystyrene beads). A strong effect of the particle type was found, with higher attachment rates on milled particles, whose surface appeared qualitatively rougher based on visual examination of scanning electron microscopy images. Our results also revealed an intraspecific variation in attachment rate, highlighting the need for testing several strains of the same species to assess attachment rate and related hazards. Finally, it was observed that when a biofilm had formed by field incubation of the MPs, the differences in attachment rates between particle types were erased. The attachment of V. anguillarum depends on a combination of strain-related factors, particle characteristics, and environmental conditions, highlighting the need to combine microbiology, materials science, and environmental sciences to achieve a comprehensive risk assessment associated with MPs.IMPORTANCEMicroplastics (MPs) are increasingly abundant, particularly in marine environments. They are suspected to present a risk to public health by acting as a vector for pathogenic bacterial species. Focusing on the fish pathogen Vibrio anguillarum, we measured the attachment rates of 16 strains on three types of microplastics (milled polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate particles, and commercially available polystyrene beads). This study highlights a strong effect of the particle type, with higher attachment rates on irregular particles, as well as a strong intraspecific variation. In a second experiment, it was observed that when a natural marine biofilm had already formed on the microplastic particles, differences in attachment rates between particle types were erased. Our findings emphasize the importance of accounting for multiple factors when assessing the risks of MPs as carriers of pathogenic bacteria, with our study addressing the first step of the conceptual pathway linking attachment, persistence, transport, exposure, and ultimately infection.
records.authors: Massot M, Wimmer L, Moussawi MA, Hamet J, Parac-Vogt T, Rajkovic A, Dailey L-A, Callens M, Bedhomme S.

records.title: Specialist-generalist trade-offs in microbial growth rates across soil habitats.
records.abstract: Microbial life strategies are shaped by a fundamental ecological trade-off: specialization enables peak performance in a narrow niche, while generalization allows persistence across diverse environments, but may constrain maximal growth rates. In soils, this trade-off is particularly relevant in the rhizosphere and detritusphere-and at their interface, where co-occurring living roots and decaying residues are hypothesized to generate emergent biogeochemical conditions. Using H₂¹⁸O quantitative stable isotope probing (qSIP), we measured bacterial and fungal growth rates in the rhizosphere, the detritusphere, and in the combined presence of rhizosphere + root detritus. We classified taxa operationally as specialists (defined as microbes actively growing only within a single habitat) or generalists (defined as microbes actively growing in two or more habitats), reflecting realized growth breadth under the conditions tested. Bacterial specialists exhibited faster growth than generalists within the habitats where they grew, a pattern consistent with a trade-off between niche breadth and growth rate. Net relatedness and nearest taxon indices showed that total bacterial communities were phylogenetically clustered, while specialist and generalist communities were phylogenetically random, consistent with functional traits-rather than lineage-predicting realized growth-breadth strategy. In annual grassland soils, fast-growing specialists may dominate ecosystem processes when resources abound, and slow-growing generalists may sustain element transformations when conditions shift; understanding this interplay may inform predictions of soil-carbon trajectories.ImportanceSoil microbes play a crucial role in cycling carbon and nutrients, but their strategies for surviving and growing in different environments remain poorly understood. This study asks whether soil microbes that grow rapidly in one habitat trade off that speed against the breadth of habitats they can occupy. Using quantitative stable isotope probing of H218O -an approach that measures active growth rather than mere presence-we tracked bacterial and fungal growth rates across three root-influenced habitats: the rhizosphere, the detritusphere, and the combined rhizosphere + detritusphere. We found that microbes detected growing in only one habitat ("specialists") tended to grow faster within their habitat than microbes detected growing across multiple habitats ("generalists"), a pattern consistent with a trade-off between niche breadth and growth rate. This pattern was clearer for bacteria than for fungi. Although these classifications describe realized growth breadth under the conditions tested rather than universal organismal traits, understanding where and when specialists or generalists dominate may help inform predictions about the fate of soil carbon under changing plant inputs.
records.authors: Foley MM, Sokol NW, Stone B, Blazewicz SJ, Estera-Molina K, Greenlon A, Hayer M, Kimbrel JA, Pett-Ridge J, Hungate BA.

records.title: Architecture and Evolution of Prokaryotic Multicellularity: Common Patterns and Diversity.
records.abstract: Prokaryotes form multicellular structures under both natural and experimental conditions, through developmental processes that sometimes echo those known from eukaryotes. Recent research has increasingly focused on the mechanisms underlying bacterial multicellular organization and its evolutionary origins. In this review, we first consider the modes of group formation, that is, clonal or aggregative, and show how mixed strategies in prokaryotic systems complicate this division. We then survey bacterial and, where known, archaeal multicellular structures, focusing on common patterns and differences in developmental dynamics across species, and highlighting the "soft" similarities with eukaryotic tissues and organismal organization. Next, we discuss the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying the canonical hallmarks of multicellularity in prokaryotes. Finally, we discuss recent research on the evolution of prokaryotic multicellularity, drawing on experimental, computational, and comparative approaches. Studying the specific forms of prokaryotic multicellularity, beyond simplified descriptions (aggregative vs. clonal), is necessary for understanding its complexity, and its consequences for microbial ecology, biogeochemical cycles and the evolution of bacteria per se. The prevalence of multicellularity in bacteria and emerging evidence from archaea raise the possibility that LUCA already possessed multicellular traits, suggesting that multicellularity may be an ancestral feature of life. The emerging picture is that bacterial multicellularity only partly matches eukaryotic models, instead reflecting multiple independent evolutionary origins and a striking capacity to regenerate and diversify developmental programs.
records.authors: Sohl G, Schubert A, Mascher T, Colizzi ES.

records.title: Genome-wide identification and integrative analysis of the cytochrome P450 superfamily in pea (Pisum sativum L.) reveals candidate genes associated with Aphanomyces root rot response.
records.abstract: Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases (P450) constitute one of the largest and most functionally diverse enzyme superfamilies in plants, underpinning the biosynthesis of a plethora of primary and specialized metabolites involved in growth and development as well as stress response. Here, we present the first integrated genome-wide analysis of the pea P450 superfamily (CYPome), combining phylogenetic, structural, evolutionary, transcriptional, and genetic approaches to identify defense-associated candidates. We identified 210 P450 genes encoding 241 proteins in pea genome, classified into 45 CYP families across 10 clans. Comparative analyses revealed both highly conserved legume P450 lineages and a substantial fraction of pea-specific expansions, reflecting dynamic CYPome evolution. Gene structure and motif analyses confirmed conservation of core catalytic features, alongside family-specific variation consistent with functional diversification. A conserved core of many PsP450 genes induced across multiple pea cultivars at a wide range of time points post Aphanomyces euteiches infection together with their expression in root tissue was discovered. Integration of aphanomyces root rot resistance-associated quantitative trait loci further refined candidate prioritization, identifying PsP450s that co-localized with resistance loci, exhibited strong co-expression with PsIFS genes, and were rapidly induced upon infection. Collectively, this integrative analysis defines the pea CYPome and identifies a focused set of high-confidence P450 candidates likely involved in defense-associated metabolic reprogramming during A. euteiches infection. These findings provide a foundational resource for functional genomics and offer promising targets for improving disease resistance in pea and related legume crops.
records.authors: Tahir MS, Dhaubhadel S.

records.title: NanoPAMDA enables rapid PAM characterization of metagenome-derived Cas9 effectors
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  CRISPR-Cas9 orthologs remain functionally underexplored despite the rapidly growing scale of publicly available metagenomic sequencing data. Here, we applied a multi-stage computational discovery pipeline to two independent sources of metagenomic sequence data, a multi-biome collection of 620,185 metagenome-assembled genomes spanning 17 public catalogs, and raw sequencing reads from human microbiome studies assembled de novo, to identify novel Cas9 orthologs. Candidates were filtered for guide RNA architectural plausibility, sequence novelty, conservation of catalytic residues, and structural integrity, yielding 14 candidates spanning both data sources for experimental characterization. To determine PAM preference at scale, we developed a cost-effective Nanopore long-read-based adaptation of the high-throughput PAM determination assay (NanoPAMDA), enabling rapid, time-resolved, kinetic PAM profiling across many candidates in parallel. One Cas9 effector, E10, showed PAM-specific activity in vitro and was catalytically active in  E. coli . Together, these findings demonstrate a scalable, long-read sequencing-based framework for discovering and biochemically characterizing novel Cas9 orthologs from metagenomic data.

records.title: Bayesian phylogenetic inference accounting for recombination in whole bacterial genomes
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Recombination is a major evolutionary force in bacteria, and ignoring it distorts phylogenies and can invalidate downstream analyses such as dating. We present ClonalFrame2, a new software for Bayesian phylogenetic inference from whole bacterial genomes that accounts for recombination. It replaces both ClonalFrame and ClonalFrameML while using the same evolutionary model, in which both mutation and recombination events occur on the branches of the clonal genealogy. The locations of recombination events are integrated out of the likelihood using a hidden Markov model, so the algorithm targets only the clonal genealogy and three recombination parameters. Ancestral sequences are recomputed whenever the tree changes and are used to propose efficient topology updates. We validated the method by analysing data-free datasets, which recovered the prior, and by comparing the approximated likelihood with the exact one on simulated data. Across 100 simulated datasets of 100 genomes each, the recombination parameters were accurately recovered, and trees inferred while accounting for recombination were many times more accurate than when ignoring it. In  Staphylococcus aureus ST239, we showed that accounting for recombination gave a stronger temporal signal and a more robust dated phylogeny. In  Neisseria gonorrhoeae , we identified interesting patterns of clustered recombination events happening repeatedly across the branches of the tree.
records.authors: Didelot X, Falush D, Wilson DJ.

records.title: Bacterial and fungal community dynamics in black pepper (Piper nigrum) across different processing plants using culture-based and amplicon sequencing approaches.
records.abstract: Black pepper (Piper nigrum) is among the most commercially relevant spices worldwide, yet its microbial ecology throughout processing remains insufficiently understood, particularly in relation to food safety. Despite being a low-water-activity product, black pepper may harbor diverse bacterial and fungal communities, including spoilage microorganisms, mycotoxigenic fungi, and foodborne pathogens. In this study, we investigated the dynamics of bacterial and fungal communities along the black pepper processing chain in three distinct processing plants. A total of 154 samples were collected from processing plants A, B, and C in São Mateus, Espírito Santo, Brazil. Culture-dependent analyses included enumeration of aerobic mesophilic bacteria, Enterobacteriaceae, lactic acid bacteria, total fungi, and xerophilic fungi; fungal isolation and identification; and Salmonella detection and confirmation. Culture-independent profiling was performed by amplicon sequencing targeting the V3-V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene and the V9 region of the 18S rRNA gene. Microbial counts increased throughout processing, indicating that post-drying operations represent critical contamination points. Fungal isolation revealed genera of hygienic and toxicological relevance, including Aspergillus, Fusarium, Penicillium, and Cladosporium. Salmonella was detected in 14.3% of the samples, comprising nine serotypes, with the highest occurrence after drying. Amplicon sequencing identified 5 phyla and 85 genera in the fungal community, whereas for the bacterial community, 24 phyla and 475 genera were identified, with Ascomycota, Proteobacteria and Firmicutes predominating across samples. Alpha and beta diversity analyses demonstrated significant differences among processing plants and confirmed processing as a major driver of microbial community assembly. Collectively, these findings reveal processing-associated microbial shifts and underscore the urgent need for improved hygienic practices, targeted monitoring, and effective decontamination strategies for black pepper.
records.authors: Furtado MM, Margalho LP, Amorim-Neto DP, Lemos Junior WJF, Duarte VS, Garcia MV, Santos AFM, Rodrigues DP, Copetti MV, Sant'Ana AS.

records.title: COSMOS: integrated vector-pathogen metagenomics for mosquito-borne disease
records.abstract: By 2050, almost half of the global population will be at risk of mosquito-borne disease. Effective response requires monitoring both pathogen transmission and vector abundance, yet these are typically assessed using separate assays with limited taxonomic breadth. Here we present COSMOS (COmprehensive Sequencing for MOSquito-borne disease), a targeted metagenomics workflow designed to reconstruct pathogen genomes and mosquito community composition directly from mixed field-collected samples. Over three annual rounds of a major Australian surveillance program, we evaluated >120,000 mosquitoes in 219 traps, with 98.7% agreement with surveillance data across seven monitored arboviruses, and additional detections of Sindbis virus and the state’s first detection of encephalitic Little Sussex virus. Of 137 viral detections, 101 yielded near-complete genomes (>90% coverage) at median 95x depth. Using an accompanying computational workflow, COSMOS quantified mosquito composition, matching entomological estimates of reported vector species (CCC 0.78–0.89). Joint analysis of virus and vector composition identified structured mosquito communities associated with spatial and temporal environmental variation, allowing the ecological context of arbovirus detections to be characterised. Detections during the Murray Valley encephalitis virus outbreak in 2023 were concentrated within a narrowly defined mosquito-community space corresponding to rural communities dominated by the inland S-AUS sub-lineage of  Culex annulirostris . Integrated vector-pathogen metagenomics provides ecological and evolutionary context for arbovirus activity within a single scalable workflow for surveillance and outbreak response.
records.authors: Forster AJ, Khan AA, Garrett E, Toi C, Suster CJ, Haniotis J, Dang K, Watson J, Doggett S, Chen SC, Watts MR, Kok J, Sintchenko V, Payne M, NSW Arbovirus Surveillance and Mosquito Monitoring Program (NSW ASMMP), Webb C, Rockett RJ, Rockett RJ, Golubchik T.

records.title: Rhizobia transform legume nodules via native T-DNA transfer systems
records.abstract: Summary  Agrobacteria can deliver transfer DNA (T-DNA) into plant cells, causing tumorous growth. This process, agrobacteria-mediated transformation (AMT), underlies plant genetic engineering and has been regarded as an evolutionary innovation specific to these pathogens. By screening 63,759 alphaproteobacterial genomes for T-DNA border sequences, we identify mini-T-DNAs in diverse rhizobial genera. Each typically encodes a single cargo, a RolB/RolC family protein or a distant rhizobial homologue. We show that native rhizobia-mediated transformation (RMT) systems deliver these mini-T-DNAs into the root nodules of common bean, pea, and chickpea, where the cargo genes are expressed, with no signal in adjacent root tissue. RMT systems share VirG-dependent activation of the core virulence regulon but respond to distinct upstream signals. Our genome screen identifies many additional candidate T-DNA transfer systems, and phylogenetic analysis places their genes into two of the many type IV secretion system (T4SS) clades. RMT systems occur in both clades, together with other systems unrelated to T-DNA transfer, and typically have an ancestral-like T4SS configuration. In contrast, AMT systems occupy a single subclade, consistent with later acquisition of their T4SS module. AMT and RMT thus represent two specialized outcomes of an older, more widespread capability for bacteria-to-plant DNA transfer.
records.authors: Hsieh S, Lai E, Kuo C.

records.title: Functional genomic characterization of anti-phage defense systems in vancomycin-resistant  Enterococcus faecium
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Vancomycin-resistant  Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) is a significant public health threat, demonstrating high rates of antibiotic resistance and frequently causing hospital-acquired infections. Bacteriophages (phages) are a promising adjunctive therapy to reduce bacterial load and manage VREfm infections. Many bacteria encode anti-phage defense systems—groups of genes that can counteract phage infection—but these systems have not been characterized in VREfm. Here we explored the diversity of anti-phage defense systems within clinical VREfm isolate genomes and examined their impact on phage susceptibility. We first used two available bioinformatic tools (DefenseFinder and PADLOC) to identify putative anti-phage defense systems in 21 hybrid-assembled VREfm clinical isolate genomes, and observed that most anti-phage defense systems were located on plasmids, defense islands, and prophages. Combining this information with functional testing of phage susceptibility did not reveal robust associations between specific defense systems and resistance to four VREfm-targeting lytic phages. Due to inherent limitations of phage susceptibility testing, we next developed an assay to assess phage survival after co-incubation with bacteria, and identified over two dozen genes associated with phage killing, including a potentially novel defense island. Lastly, we attempted to functionally validate 10 candidate anti-phage defense systems, only four of which were ultimately tested in enterococci. Expression of one of these candidates, AbiE, decreased bacterial susceptibility to two  Enterococcus -targeting phages. As VREfm- targeting phage therapy becomes more widely available, identification of genes contributing to phage resistance can aid in streamlining the provision of phages to patients who could benefit from this new therapeutic modality.  IMPORTANCE  VREfm is a significant public health threat, acquiring resistance to last-line antibiotics and becoming endemic in healthcare systems. There is a clear need for alternative therapies to treat VREfm infections. In this study we identified and characterized genes that are predicted to cause resistance to bacteriophages, an adjunctive therapeutic approach for treating antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections, among VREfm collected from infected patients. Our findings reveal a wide diversity of anti-phage defense systems in clinical VREfm isolates, and identify several possible drivers of phage resistance in this organism. The knowledge gained will inform the development of phage therapy for patients with difficult-to-treat VREfm infections.
records.authors: Evans E, Tapia L, Van Tyne D.

records.title: Mycobacteriophage Cluster A Immunity Repressors: A Conserved Protein Fold Adapted for Diverse Biological Functions
records.abstract: Abstract    Mycobacteriophage cluster A immunity repressors are unusual in that they silence lytic gene expression by binding numerous DNA binding sites located throughout the viral genome. They can also provide immunity to infection by genetically similar phages that contain the same or similar DNA binding sites. Despite containing similar DNA binding sites and repressor proteins, cluster A viruses often display heteroimmune phenotypes, the molecular details of which are currently unclear. Using a combination of small-angle X-ray scattering, protein crystallography, bioinformatics, and DNA binding and  in vivo  immunity assays, we show that cluster A repressors conserve a common protein fold yet appear to provide DNA specificity through a narrow region of the novel stoperator DNA binding domain. Additionally, both viral and bacterial genomes contain cluster A-like repressor proteins fused to diverse protein domains, which suggest that these repressors have evolved to do more than just silence viral lytic gene expression.
records.authors: Wallen J, McKinney R, Park S, Bonogafsky H, Tuhro A, Turner M, Hollis T, Gainey M.

records.title: Rumen metagenomics of Tan sheep with divergent growth rate: functional gene and MAG profiles do not distinguish the groups
records.abstract: Abstract    Background  Feed conversion ratio (FCR) is a key economic trait in lamb production, and the rumen microbiome governs the energy the host obtains from feed. Because genus-level biomarkers are inconsistent across studies, we examined whether efficient and inefficient Tan sheep differ at the level of metabolic genes and metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). Sixteen Tan sheep, drawn from a finishing cohort of 100 animals, were ranked by average daily gain (ADG) and split into a high-growth/low-FCR group (n = 10) and a low-growth/high-FCR group (n = 6); individual feed intake was not recorded, so ADG, not measured FCR, defined the groups. Rumen contents were deep-shotgun sequenced, assembled and binned. Of 3,283 retained KEGG orthologues (KOs), a candidate required both a Wilcoxon between-group difference (P Results  Global community structure did not differ (ANOSIM taxonomy R = -0.139, P = 0.95; function R = -0.064, P = 0.682). The two-layer screen yielded 36 direction-concordant KOs (54 between-group and 94 ADG-correlated; union 112), enriched for sugar-transport (ABC/PTS) and energy genes, whereas canonical VFA genes showed no detectable difference (buk, pct, acs; all P > 0.7; absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence). However, 36 double-evidence KOs did not exceed the label-permutation null expectation (null mean 67, 95th percentile 195; P = 0.59), and the same was true for each single layer (between-group: 54 observed versus null mean 131, P = 0.83; ADG-correlated: 94 observed versus null mean 167, P = 0.67). A classifier built on the 36 KOs and evaluated with the feature set fixed in advance reached AUC = 1.000 and 87.5% accuracy, but under nested cross-validation the same pipeline gave AUC = 0.767 and 56.2% accuracy (9/16), which did not differ significantly from the permutation null (null mean AUC = 0.525, 95th percentile 0.883; P = 0.190). Initial body weight was confounded with group (Spearman rho with ADG = 0.67, P = 0.005). Only three MAGs were double-evidence, all inefficient-enriched and negatively correlated with ADG, representing unnamed novel genera (two Firmicutes-affiliated and one Bacteroidota-affiliated).  Conclusions  In this cohort of 16 Tan sheep, growth-efficiency divergence was not accompanied by any statistically detectable remodelling of rumen functional genes: the carbohydrate-uptake and energy-metabolism candidate panel did not exceed permutation-based null expectations, no KO approached FDR significance, and no classifier generalised under nested validation. The 591 MAGs recovered here provide a breed-specific genome resource for Tan sheep, and the contrast between the non-nested (AUC = 1.000) and nested (AUC = 0.767) estimates quantifies how much apparent signal feature selection performed outside cross-validation can manufacture at this sample size.

records.title: Codfishes survived essential gene loss by functionally co-opting freshwater ovulatory pathways to marine egg hydration.
records.abstract: Adaptive evolution associated with dispensable gene loss is widespread in the animal kingdom. However, loss of genes essential for embryonic survival and the mechanisms that evolved to bypass negative selection and extinction are less well known. Here, we show that all Gadiformes, an ecologically dominant order of codfishes, lost the aqp1ab-type genes that are essential for the formation of hydrated pelagic eggs and embryonic survival of marine teleosts in oceanic environments. Despite such gene loss, codfishes produce some of the most highly hydrated pelagic eggs of all marine teleosts. To resolve this apparent paradox, we initially confirmed that the mechanisms of osmotic drive are conserved with other pelagic-egg-producing marine teleosts, and then conducted comparative transcript analyses of aquaporin water channels in distantly-related freshwater and marine teleosts. This uncovered Aqp4-type channels that have been chromosomally linked to the Aqp1-type channels in jawed vertebrate genomes for >450 million years as the primary candidates. Using immunolocalization, functional assays, and inhibition experiments with zebrafish and Atlantic cod as model organisms, we show that short isoforms of Aqp4 are required for egg ovulation in more ancestral lineages of freshwater teleosts and were recruited to the oocyte hydration pathway of codfishes. By contrast, the oldest and most modern lineages of marine teleosts producing pelagic eggs still utilize the aqp1ab genes for egg hydration. Our data thus reveal that codfishes survived essential gene loss by functionally co-opting freshwater ovulatory pathways to marine egg hydration.
records.authors: Rey-Alfonso Á, Yilmaz O, Chauvigné F, Finn RN, Cerdà J.

records.title: Identification and Expression Analysis of MLO Genes in Poa pratensis in Response to Powdery Mildew Caused by Blumeria graminis f. sp. poae.
records.abstract: Poa pratensis L. is an important perennial grass that is widely used in seed and sod production for turfgrass establishment. However, its health and aesthetic value are frequently threatened by powdery mildew infection. In this study, the Mildew Locus O (MLO) genes of P. pratensis were identified through transcriptome analysis of Kentucky bluegrass in response to Blumeria graminis f. sp. poae. A comprehensive bioinformatics analysis, including physicochemical characterization, protein interaction prediction, EggNOG annotation, domain identification, and phylogenetic reconstruction, was conducted. Expression profiling revealed distinct patterns of PpMLO gene expression among varieties with different resistance levels. In this study, 33 PpMLO genes were identified from transcriptome data of plants under powdery mildew stress. Transmembrane domain analysis revealed that seven PpMLO proteins contain seven transmembrane domains, with leucine being the most abundant amino acid. The protein interaction network suggested a coordinated signaling system involving seven PpMLO proteins and functional proteins from Oryza sativa L. GO analysis revealed that the core members of the PpMLO gene family regulate immune and stress response biological processes by targeting the membrane and endomembrane systems and through molecular functions such as enzyme activities and ubiquitination. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the PpMLO gene family members of P. pratensis clustered in the same group as the homologous MLO genes of Arabidopsis thaliana and O. sativa, suggesting that they may have conserved biological functions in the response to powdery mildew stress. Expression profiling revealed that three key candidate genes, PpMLO2, PpMLO13, and PpMLO14, exhibited distinct expression patterns across cultivars with varying resistance levels. In the moderately resistant cultivar 'Taihang', PpMLO2 and PpMLO13 were significantly upregulated (Log2 fold change = 6.31 and 6.21, respectively). In the highly susceptible cultivar 'Explorer', PpMLO13 was moderately upregulated (Log2 fold change = 3.85). In contrast, PpMLO14 was strongly downregulated in the susceptible cultivar 'Black Jack' (Log2 fold change = -6.82). These differential expression patterns indicate that the MLO signaling pathway may adopt distinct regulatory strategies depending on the genetic background of the host. The identification of PpMLO2, PpMLO13, and PpMLO14 as key susceptibility candidates provides clear targets for precision molecular breeding. Targeting these genes through gene silencing or genome editing represents a promising strategy for reducing reliance on chemical fungicides and promoting sustainable green management of powdery mildew in P. pratensis.
records.authors: Liang Y, Zhang Y, Guo Z, Zhu H, Han L, Zhao X, Gao P.

records.title: Roots through time: dynamics of the rhizosphere microbiome and its nutrient-cycling potential in Zostera marina meadows with implications for microbiome-based restoration.
records.abstract: The seagrass rhizosphere microbiome is critical for sedimentary nutrient turnover, yet the spatiotemporal dynamics of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur cycling across Zostera marina developmental stages remain poorly understood. Leveraging metagenomic sequencing and 147 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), we resolved functional gene profiles in rhizosphere and bulk sediments across three discrete developmental stage (vegetative, reproductive and dormant). Temporal variation (i.e., sampling period) explained 48.1-57.4% of the variance in nutrient-cycling-associated microbial community composition, whereas spatial partitioning between rhizosphere and bulk compartments accounted for 11.6-20.0%. Carbon fixation genes were significantly enriched in the rhizosphere during reproduction but reached peak abundance in bulk sediments during dormancy. Nitrogen fixation and dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA) genes were enriched in the rhizosphere during both vegetative and dormant stages. Phosphorus mobilization-associated genes displayed parallel enrichment patterns, with the regulatory two-component system gene phoR broadly conserved across MAGs. Sulfur oxidation genes were enriched in the rhizosphere during vegetative and dormant stages, yet exhibited higher relative abundance in bulk sediments during reproduction. Critically, multiple Desulfobacterota MAGs co-occurred with nitrogen fixation and sulfate reduction genes, and the alkaline phosphatase gene phoD was identified in several of these genomes. Together, these findings reveal developmentally orchestrated shifts in microbial nutrient-cycling potential, underscoring the importance of protecting the native rhizosphere microbiome in eelgrass restoration, while considering site-specific biogeochemical constraints, particularly nutrient availability and sulfide conditions.
records.authors: Sun J, Zhao X, Yan WJ, Li WT, Sun WL, Zhang PD.

records.title: Viral potential to modulate antibiotic resistance gene succession through host interactions during food waste composting.
records.abstract: Composting can mitigate antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) risks, yet viral contributions to their dynamics remain unclear. Using time-series metagenomics, we investigated viral roles in ARG succession during composting of two food waste types. In both composts, ARGs followed an enrichment-decline-rebound trajectory accompanied by substrate-specific ARG-host turnover. Particularly, the maturation rebound involved the re-enrichment of high-risk ARGs, including tet(L) and lnu(G). Procrustes analysis showed significant associations of viral communities with bacterial and ARG profiles. Meanwhile, virus-host networks were organized predominantly around Firmicutes, with both temperate and lytic viral abundances correlated with ARG-host dynamics during the heating-to-thermophilic transition. Viral auxiliary metabolic genes (AMGs), annotated for central carbon metabolism, nutrient acquisition, and stress responses, may aid environmental adaptation in key ARG hosts, including Bacillus spp. Although mobile genetic elements (MGEs) provided important genetic contexts for ARG mobility, only four putative virus-mediated ARG horizontal transfer records were detected. Structural equation modelling suggested potential viral involvement through host interactions, while highlighting the importance of ARG hosts and MGEs in resistome succession. Further viral perturbation experiments are needed to clarify causal contributions in future. Overall, this study provides new insights into viral roles in resistome succession, informing resistance risk management during composting.
records.authors: Zhang L, Luo D, Yang J, Yang M, Yang Y, Yao R, Zhan M, Zhang Y, Su Y, Wang B, Xie B.

records.title: Progress and disparities in fungal genomics in the long-read era.
records.abstract: Fungal genomics has expanded rapidly over the past three decades, yet this growth has been phylogenetically uneven and many taxonomic gaps persist. Here we review the field from early efforts such as the Fungal Genome Initiative to the current era of third-generation long-read sequencing and compile publicly available assemblies to quantify trends in contiguity, completeness, long-read adoption and taxonomic representation. We argue that fungal genomics has moved from a period of data scarcity to one in which the principal constraints are taxonomic bias, inconsistent annotation, sparse metadata and the interpretation of complex genome structure. Substantial phylogenetic gaps remain, particularly outside Dikarya and among unculturable taxa, and only a minority of assemblies are annotated. We therefore identify priorities for the fungal community, including coordinated efforts to close major taxonomic gaps, improved repository metrics to facilitate the identification of high-quality assemblies and standardized genome annotation, which is lacking for most assemblies.
records.authors: Kroll E, Zoclanclounon YAB, Urban M, Hill R, Hammond-Kosack KE.

records.title: Genomic rearrangement of the capsule operon in a phylogenetically distinct cluster of the multi-drug-resistant Escherichia coli lineage ST131.
records.abstract: Escherichia coli ST131 is a dominant cause of multi-drug-resistant extraintestinal infections in humans. The lineage has a three-clade phylogenetic structure, of which clade C has gained resistance to multiple classes of antibiotics and is globally disseminated. As well as antimicrobial resistance, a number of virulence factors contribute to the success of ST131 clade C, including the production of capsule. Previous work on a limited number of strains has shown that the capsule operon in ST131 is highly variable. In this study, we analyzed the capsule genetics of E. coli ST131 by interrogating 3,033 genomes. Our data show a clonal distribution of capsule types and identify a monophyletic group of ST131 clade C strains that are characterized by an atypical capsule operon with highly divergent alleles of the key kpsM and kpsT genes. Our analysis suggests there is ongoing evolution within clade C of ST131, which looks to be driven not by the continuing evolution of antimicrobial resistance but by host-pathogen interactions.IMPORTANCEMulti-drug-resistant (MDR) Escherichia coli is a problematic cause of invasive disease in humans and animals. Resistance to multiple classes of antibiotics is severely limiting treatment options. ST131-C is a highly successful, MDR clone of E. coli that is a major cause of extraintestinal infections. Capsule is a key virulence factor in contributing to this clone's success, with capsule switching allowing the bacteria flexibility to thrive in different niches. We present evidence that suggests continual evolution of this proliferant clone influenced by host-pathogen interaction. Small genetic changes can define the success of a clone; therefore, it is important to monitor this continual evolution in pathogens.
records.authors: Potterill I, Hall RJ, Moran RA, Cummins EA, McNally A.

records.title: Tandem repeats in methanogenic archaea and their viruses reveal a shared potential for rapid genomic diversification
records.abstract: Methanogenic archaea drive global methane emissions, yet the molecular basis of their physiological flexibility is unclear. Archaeal adaptation is typically attributed to horizontal gene transfer, which is episodic and cannot explain rapid, reversible change. Here we show that direct tandem repeats (TRs) offer an intrinsic alternative. By screening 50,567 prokaryotic genomes, we find TR densities in Methanosarcina more than 30-fold above the prokaryotic average, paralleling Borg extrachromosomal elements. These TRs recur at conserved loci while sharing almost no sequence identity between strains, indicating independent origin, and evolve during routine cultivation. Methanogen TRs are transcribed, show ribosome occupancy, and lie near regulatory and cofactor-related genes, whilst being depleted around core energy-conserving and translational machinery. Genic TRs generate intrinsically disordered regions in proteins carrying nucleotide-binding, protein-protein interaction and cell-surface domains, and occur in structural and surface proteins of methanogen-infecting viruses. TRs are therefore an overlooked source of variability and adaptation potential in methanogens and their viruses.
records.authors: Haiss S, Skoog EJ, Herbert J, Ding C, Weidenbach K, Tufail MA, Schlaich S, Molitor B, Schmitz RA, Schoelmerich MC.

records.title: A comparison of two culture and three sequencing methods for detection of the urobiome
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Standard urine culture (SUC), the clinical reference method, is optimized for fast-growing aerobes and misses much of the urinary microbiota. Enhanced culture and sequencing methods have rarely been compared on the same specimens. We compared five methods (SUC, expanded quantitative urine culture [EQUC], short-read V4 16S rRNA gene sequencing, long-read near full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and PCR-free long-read shotgun metagenomic sequencing) on parallel aliquots of urine from pregnant participants screened for asymptomatic bacteriuria. Of 98 cultured samples, 98 (100.0%) were EQUC-positive while 85 (86.7%) SUC-positive. EQUC detected 102 species, but SUC only detected 41. Short-read 16S rRNA gene sequencing, long-read 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and shotgun sequencing were positive for 188/188, 186/188 and 139/139 samples, detecting 195, 69 and 528 species, respectively. In the 79 samples positive by EQUC and all three sequencing methods, sequencing profiles resembled each other more than culture profiles, and SUC captured only a subset of taxa detected by every other method. Shotgun sequencing gave the broadest taxonomic coverage and was the only sequencing method to identify  Escherichia coli to the species level. With EQUC, it outperformed both 16S sequencing methods in detecting  Gardnerella vaginalis and distinguishing  Lactobacillus species, and it resolved six  Gardnerella species, three detected by no other method. Long-read 16S rRNA gene sequencing gave the most confident amplicon-based species assignments, whereas culture better recovered  Corynebacterium and  Staphylococcus species. No single method was best across all endpoints, but long-read shotgun metagenomics provided the broadest species-level view. Method choice should match the research or clinical question; outcome-based studies are needed to establish clinical utility.  IMPORTANCE  The microbes reported in a urine sample depend heavily on how that sample is analyzed. Standard urine culture, the test most clinical laboratories rely on, detected only a fraction of the bacteria found by enhanced culture or by DNA sequencing of the same specimens. Sequencing methods also differed from each other: short-read 16S rRNA gene sequencing captured broad diversity but often could not name species, whereas long-read methods distinguished clinically and ecologically important species. PCR-free long-read shotgun metagenomics detected the widest range of taxa and resolved species, such as  Escherichia coli and multiple  Gardnerella species, that amplicon methods could not. Because each method has distinct strengths and blind spots, detection methods should be chosen according to the question being asked, and sequencing-based diagnostics must be validated against patient outcomes before they can replace culture.
records.authors: Khemmani M, Noronha MF, Pham TT, Ferneyhough B, Roddis MJ, Parkinson NJ, Wolfe AJ.

records.title: The differential effects of dupilumab and Janus kinase 1-selective inhibitors on the skin microbiome in adult patients with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis using metagenomic sequencing: results from the BioDay registry
records.abstract: Abstract    Background  The skin microbiome in atopic dermatitis (AD) is characterized by decreased bacterial diversity and increased  Staphylococcus aureus  colonization. Although dupilumab has been shown to improve the skin microbiome in adult AD patients, little is known about the effects of Janus kinase 1-selective inhibitors (JAK1-i). Therefore, the aim of this study was to evaluate the differential effects of dupilumab and JAK1-i on the skin microbiome of adult AD patients. Skin swabs were collected from dupilumab-treated patients (N = 10) lesional/facial at baseline (T0) and week 16 (T16), from JAK1-i-treated patients (N = 15) lesional/facial at T0, week 4 (T4) and week 28 (T28), and from healthy controls (HCs; N = 17) at a single time point. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was used to assess microbial composition and diversity. Results  During both treatments, the Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) scores significantly decreased over time (both p S. aureus  abundance significantly decreased after 16 weeks of dupilumab, whereas a nonsignificant decrease was observed after 28 weeks of JAK1-i. Microbial diversity increased in dupilumab-treated patients, approaching levels observed in HCs, while no such shift occurred during JAK1-i treatment. In both groups, commensal bacteria and fungi remained less abundant than in HCs. Conclusions  Despite comparable clinical improvements, dupilumab induced a more pronounced shift in the skin microbiome towards healthy skin compared with JAK1-i.

records.title: Pangenome and transcriptomics reveal the genomic basis associated with interspecific variation of sexually dimorphic nuptial spines in moustache toads.
records.abstract: Sexual dimorphism is a widespread phenotypic innovation that plays a crucial role in species diversification, yet its genetic origins and evolutionary trajectories remain poorly understood in vertebrates. Leptobrachium provides a tractable system in which male moustache toads develop maxillary nuptial spines used in male-male combat, whereas closely related pseudo-moustache toads lack this trait. To investigate the evolutionary genomics of these sexually dimorphic nuptial spines, we construct a pangenome from chromosome-level assemblies of six Leptobrachium species and integrate trans-species transcriptomic analyses. We find that keratin gene expansion predated the origin of nuptial spines, potentially providing genetic material for keratinized skin innovation. Recently duplicated hair keratin genes acquired putative Hoxc13 binding sites, and promoter reporter assays confirm that Hoxc13 can activate these genes in both moustache toads and pseudo-moustache toads. Differential hoxc13 expression may therefore be more important for affecting whether duplicated hair keratin genes are recruited to develop nuptial spines. Transcriptomic comparisons further reveal maxillary skin-specific expression of genes involved in keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation, as well as melanogenesis during the formation of nuptial spines. In Leptobrachium tengchongense, which has undergone secondary loss of nuptial spines, igfbp2, a conserved gene highly expressed in keratinized skin appendages across amphibians, shows positive selection and represents a candidate associated with this evolutionary transition. Our study provides amphibian pangenome resources and highlights how gene duplication coupled with regulatory recruitment may shape the evolution of novel sexually dimorphic traits in vertebrates.
records.authors: Li J, Feng Y, Huang S, Xie S, Ai Q, Huang C, Xiong R, Zhao M, Wu H.

records.title: Comparative genomics of canonical antifungal dsRNA target genes across fungal plant pathogens: conserved siRNA-length windows define the scope for broad-spectrum spray-induced gene silencing
records.abstract: Background  Spray-induced gene silencing (SIGS), in which double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) sprayed onto a crop is taken up by a fungal pathogen and silences an essential gene, is advancing as a biopesticide strategy. A recurring ambition is a broad-spectrum dsRNA: a single construct, directed at a conserved housekeeping gene, that controls several pathogens at once. Because silencing is driven by Dicer-processed small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) of roughly 21 nucleotides, the feasibility of this ambition depends on whether the target gene is conserved between pathogens at siRNA-length resolution, not merely at the level of overall gene identity. That resolution has not been mapped across the fungal plant-pathogen tree. Results  We screened eleven canonical antifungal dsRNA target genes of  Fusarium graminearum (three CYP51 sterol 14α-demethylases, six chitin synthases and two β-tubulins) for perfect 21-nucleotide identity against the transcriptomes of twelve fungal plant pathogens spanning four taxonomic classes (Sordariomycetes, Leotiomycetes, Dothideomycetes and Basidiomycota). Of 27,116 candidate siRNA start positions across the eleven genes, only 2,108 (7.8%) were conserved as a perfect 21-mer in even one other pathogen, 148 in at least three, twelve in at least seven, and none in eight or more. Conservation decayed steeply with phylogenetic distance: the congeneric  F. oxysporum shared 1,209 sites, other Sordariomycetes 262–313, Leotiomycetes and Dothideomycetes 62–204, Basidiomycota 41–48, and the reduced-genome obligate biotroph  Blumeria graminis just one. The β-tubulins carried the most broadly conserved individual sites (shared by up to seven pathogens), whereas CYP51C was the least conserved (shared by at most one). Even for the congener, perfect-match conservation covered only 4.5% of target positions and was concentrated in discrete windows rather than spread along the gene.  Conclusions  At the siRNA-length resolution that governs silencing, perfect-match conservation of canonical antifungal targets is scarce and strongly clade-limited. A perfect-match broad-spectrum dsRNA is therefore realistic only within a narrow clade, in practice around the genus level; genus- and class-spanning broad-spectrum SIGS cannot rely on perfect siRNA identity and would require mismatch-tolerant design or pathogen-specific constructs. The conserved windows mapped here identify where clade-level broad-spectrum constructs can be placed, and the gene ranking (β-tubulins most cross-targetable, CYP51C most pathogen-specific) provides a genome-guided basis for choosing antifungal dsRNA targets.
records.authors: Wasif M, Khan MA, Azmat MA, Tarcali G, Saleem H.

records.title: Fungal suppression by bacterial metabolite-activated human intestinal γδT-cells is disrupted in Crohn's disease.
records.abstract: Gut symbionts condition mucosal immunity to resist infection by enteropathogens, but the specific microbes and mechanisms involved differ significantly between host species. In higher primates, bacterial metabolite HMB-PP is sensed by a specialized population of Vγ9Vδ2+T-cells, which we now report can potently suppress growth of endogenous fungi in human intestinal organ cultures. In healthy intestine, HMB-PP-stimulated Vδ2+ T-cells restricted outgrowth of keystone fungus Candida albicans via a mechanism that required IL-22. In Crohn's disease (CD), Vδ2+ T-cells were poorly responsive to HMB-PP and permitted outgrowth of C. albicans strains that formed toxin-producing filaments, triggered neutrophil extracellular traps, and induced macrophage IL-1β release ex vivo. Genomic and proteomic analysis of the Candida isolates suggested increased tissue adhesion of CD-derived strains, which rapidly invaded the gut barrier in an 'intestine-on-a-chip' model. These data reveal that bacterial activation of Vδ2+ T-cells suppresses fungal pathobionts in human gut via an IL-22-dependent mechanism that is dysregulated in CD.

records.title: Phage N4 uses a SAR endolysin-holin system for host cell lysis.
records.abstract: Bacteriophages (phages) cause active host cell lysis to terminate their infection and release progeny into the environment. However, some phages have systems to delay their lysis, and thereby increase progeny yield, in specific conditions: a phenomenon called lysis inhibition (LIN). Two dissimilar phages of Escherichia coli are known to exhibit LIN: T4 and N4. In T4, a multi-protein mechanism stalls lysis and maintains the LIN state in response to superinfection in a high phage population density. However, the lysis proteins responsible for T4 lysis and LIN are not conserved with phage N4. In this study, we characterize the phage N4 proteins involved in lysis by molecular and genetic means. We define the functions of the minimal gene set required for lysis through heterologous expression and complementation. Furthermore, by sequence comparison with a selected mutant library that does not induce LIN, we have identified genomic regions both within and outside the lysis cassette involved in N4 LIN. We propose a model where N4 lysis proteins that execute rapid N4 lysis can be regulated to induce LIN. Despite the lack of conservation with T4 components, our study suggests that direct modulation of lysis initiation may be common and provides a springboard for identifying similar mechanisms in other phages.IMPORTANCEPhages are viruses that kill only bacteria. To do so, they use lysis proteins to disrupt the structural components of the bacterial envelope. There are commonalities between the phages that infect bacteria with similar structures, but there are also interesting differences we can exploit to learn more about specific phages or their bacterial hosts. In this study, we characterize the lysis proteins of the E. coli phage N4. Our results suggest that lysis regulation controls phage yield in N4 differently than in the well-studied phage T4. Future studies on the relationship between lysis proteins and phage yield could provide handles to use this information for optimal large-scale phage production for clinical or industrial applications.
records.authors: Awuah MB, Martin C, Chamblee JS, Tomaszewski AJ, Sullivan TE, Emilia Q, Tran S, Snowden JH, Niemiec KA, Zhu J, Ramsey J.

records.title: Genome-resolved taxonomy, global distribution, and EPS potential of Zoogloea, the canonical floc-former in wastewater treatment systems.
records.abstract: The bacterial genus Zoogloea is the fourth most abundant genus in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) globally, where it plays key roles in floc formation and nutrient removal but can also contribute to viscous bulking when highly abundant. The taxonomic assignment of Zoogloea has historically been inconsistent, as several taxa were classified based on phenotypic characteristics and later reassigned to other families or orders. This has obscured both the identity and distribution of Zoogloea and hindered interpretation of its floc-forming mechanisms, which have been attributed to polysaccharides that may not originate from phylogenetically defined Zoogloea. Using our collection of more than 22,000 high-quality genomes from global activated sludge systems (MiDAS global genome catalog), we identified 47 genomes affiliated with the phylogenetically defined Zoogloea. In combination with abundance data, this enabled resolution of the genus' taxonomy, biogeographical distribution, and metabolic diversity. Building on this framework, we mapped the phylogenetic distribution of a recently identified Zoogloea-associated floc-forming polysaccharide biosynthesis gene cluster by screening the MiDAS global genome catalog and GTDB. The gene cluster was identified across multiple genera within the Burkholderiales order, including Zoogloea, Thauera, Azoarcus, and Ca. Accumulibacter, as well as several previously undescribed taxa. The gene cluster is broadly conserved, with minor variations in gene composition and synteny, suggesting corresponding differences in polysaccharide structure. Genomes encoding this cluster also consistently contained co-occurring floc-regulating genes, indicating a common and widespread mechanism underlying floc formation in activated sludge systems.IMPORTANCEOperation of activated sludge systems depends on stable microbial floc formation for the separation of biomass from treated effluent. Floc formation is mediated by extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) produced by microorganisms, yet the identity, distribution, and biosynthesis of these polymers remain poorly characterized. Zoogloea is widely regarded as a canonical and model floc-forming genus associated with EPS production in wastewater treatment systems. However, its taxonomic classification has historically been problematic, as organisms were often assigned to Zoogloea based on morphology, leading to widespread misclassifications. This has blurred the true origin of polysaccharides attributed to the genus as well as their wider phylogenetic distribution, which has not been systematically resolved. Here, we map the distribution of the Zoogloea-associated polysaccharide biosynthesis gene cluster across a global genome data set, providing a framework to link phylogenetically defined taxa with floc-forming potential. This improves our understanding of EPS production in activated sludge systems and may support strategies for enhanced resource recovery.
records.authors: Vestergaard SZ, Liu L, Dueholm MKD, Nielsen PH.

records.title: Clavispora mexcalensis sp. nov.: a novel Mexican yeast species isolated from mezcal must with promising polyol and ethanol production from lignocellulose hydrolysates.
records.abstract: Yeasts are micro-organisms with high biotechnological potential for various industrial processes. Non-conventional yeasts offer advantages over classic Saccharomyces yeasts, such as the ability to assimilate pentoses natively. This project aimed to describe and characterize a new yeast species isolated from mezcal must in Oaxaca, México. For its identification, whole-genome sequencing was performed. Phylogenomic analyses (BUSCO, OrthoFinder and IQ-TREE) indicated 99.0% genome completeness of included 2,319 orthologs. Comparative genomic analyses were performed using average nucleotide identity (ANI), calculated with FastANI and core-proteome phylogenomics, complemented by average amino acid identity (AAI) comparisons. Additionally, macro- and micro-morphological analyses (the latter by scanning electron microscopy) were performed. l-arabinose assimilation and thermotolerance were also assessed. The uptake of various sugars, including xylose and arabinose, was evaluated, and the corresponding metabolic pathways were confirmed through experimental and genomic analyses. Phylogenomic analysis, together with FastANI and complementary AAI values, confirmed that, despite its close relationship to Clavispora lusitaniae and Clavispora paralusitaniae, this strain represents a novel species, for which the name Clavispora mexcalensis sp. nov. is proposed. The strain exhibits marked thermotolerance, maintaining substantial growth at 48 °C. It assimilates glucose, d-xylose, l-arabinose and cellobiose as sole carbon sources, and produces xylitol, ethanol and arabitol. Macro- and micro-morphological characteristics are consistent with those of other members of the genus Clavispora, although some cells exhibit numerous bud scars. These results expand the known diversity of yeasts associated with mezcal and indicate that Cl. mexcalensis sp. nov. is a potential candidate for biotechnological applications requiring high-temperature tolerance or the bioconversion of unconventional sugars.

records.authors: Lara-Meléndez A, Hernández-García JA, Ponce-Noyola T, Villa-Tanaca L, Ramos-Valdivia AC, Barrera-Cortés J, Salgado LM.

records.title: Genome-Wide Analysis of C2H2 Transcription Factors in Phoebe bournei and Functional Characterization of PnC2H2-14 in Cold Tolerance.
records.abstract: Low temperature is a major abiotic stress that severely restricts plant growth, development, and geographical distribution. Although C2H2 zinc finger proteins have been widely implicated in regulating plant growth and responses to environmental stresses, their biological functions in Phoebe bournei remain largely unexplored. In this study, a total of 61 C2H2 genes were identified from the P. bournei genome and grouped into five phylogenetic clades. Comparative analyses of conserved motifs and exon-intron organization demonstrated that members within each clade share highly similar structural characteristics. Promoter analysis indicated that PnC2H2 genes are associated with stress- and hormone-responsive elements. PnC2H2-14 was strongly induced by cold stress and predominantly expressed in leaves. Subcellular localization confirmed that PnC2H2-14 is a nuclear protein, while yeast assays demonstrated that it possesses no intrinsic transcriptional activation activity. Functional characterization revealed that ectopic expression of PnC2H2-14 in tobacco markedly improved cold tolerance by limiting reactive oxygen species accumulation, enhancing antioxidant enzyme activities, and alleviating membrane injury during cold exposure. In addition, several antioxidant-related genes were significantly upregulated in transgenic plants. These results suggest that PnC2H2-14 positively regulates cold tolerance by enhancing antioxidant defense and maintaining ROS homeostasis. This study provides insights into the evolution and function of the C2H2 gene family in P. bournei and identifies candidate genes for improving cold resistance.
records.authors: Yang Y, Zhou S, Zhu Y, Fei Y, Hu D, Yang Y, Cheng Z.

records.title: Outer Membrane Vesicles as a Potential Pathway for Antibiotic Resistance Transfer between Cyanobacteria and Bacteria.
records.abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) have profoundly exacerbated environmental risks to public health, evolving into a pressing ecological dilemma. Distinct from traditional pathways, outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) are emerging as important vectors for horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in aquatic environments, yet their role in inter-phylum ARG dissemination remains unclear. In this study, we demonstrate that OMVs mediate bidirectional HGT of ARGs between the cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 and Escherichia coli DH5α. Co-incubation experiments confirmed that OMVs derived from either strain could associate with the other, accompanied by successful functional expression of transferred resistance genes. In simulated aquatic environmental conditions, OMVs supplementation increased HGT frequency by 1.49-2.27 folds compared to the control group on day 5. Metagenomic analysis further revealed that OMVs carrying resistance genes induced subtle shifts in coastal microbial community composition. Our findings establish OMVs as mobile genetic packages that enable ARGs exchange between cyanobacteria and heterotrophic bacteria, highlighting a previously overlooked pathway for environmental dissemination of ARGs and providing a theoretical basis for mitigating antibiotic resistance risks in aquatic ecosystems.
records.authors: Yang Y, Zhang W, Ma Y, Zhang Y, Liu J, Niu Z.

records.title: A Sargassum-associated phage slows Vibrio alginolyticus persistence on macroalgal surfaces.
records.abstract: Macroalgal surfaces harbour dense and metabolically active microbial consortia in which Vibrio alginolyticus exhibits marked ecological plasticity, spanning from mutualistic to opportunistic lifestyles. In these structured biofilm habitats, phages play a central role in shaping bacterial population structure and metabolic interactions. Here, a lytic phage vB_ValP-R39Z (R39Z) and its V. alginolyticus host were isolated from the surface of Sargassum hemiphyllum. Phage R39Z displays a podovirus morphotype, with a latent period of ~50 min and a burst size of 109 p.f.u. per cell, a narrow host range restricted to its original host, and stability across environmentally relevant conditions (pH 7-9 and 4-35 °C). R39Z harbours a 71.8 kb dsDNA genome (37.7 mol% G+C), encoding 83 ORFs, and is distinct from established genera, representing a previously unclassified genus. Functionally, R39Z significantly reduced biofilm biomass in vitro, and in an ex vivo assay using Sargassum blades, it reduced the viable cell abundance of V. alginolyticus ZS10 on blade surfaces by ~99%, as determined by c.f.u. enumeration. These findings demonstrate that R39Z efficiently disrupts biofilm formation and suppresses Vibrio colonization on macroalgal surfaces, underscoring its ecological relevance and potential for targeted biocontrol in algal-associated microbiomes.
records.authors: Zuo Z, Jiang H, Zhu P, Zhang Q, Li M, Zou L, Zhang R, Yang Y, Yang Y.

records.title: Cell-free expression and NGS-powered substrate profiling reveal a thermostable metagenomic meganuclease from an extreme environment with novel specificity.
records.abstract: As an alternative to historical enzyme isolation, metagenomic databases (e.g. MGnify) provide information on vast unculturable microbial diversity, including extreme environments, and constitute an enormous source of functional proteins. Conservative mining of these data by close sequence homology alone tends to identify merely different versions of known enzymes. Here we present a discovery strategy for meganucleases based on wider capture of less homologous enzymes in metagenomic databases, and incorporating metadata with their homology. We use cell-free expression to bypass host incompatibility and the need for purification, along with deep sequencing for experimental assessment of substrate specificity and cleavage pattern, thereby circumventing classical gel-based profiling. Specifically, we discovered the temperature-stable (>55°C), intron-encoded LAGLIDADG meganuclease I-MG11 that recognizes a GC-rich 17 base pair sequence to generate 4-nt palindromic 3'-overhangs-the first monomeric meganuclease to produce such overhangs. Co-folding models of I-MG11 bound to DNA provide a structural context for enzyme-DNA interactions, highlighting differences from other monomeric LAGLIDADG meganucleases (e.g. I-SceI) shaped by InDels (insertion-deletions) in the DNA-binding region that may cause specificity changes. Our strategy streamlines general bona fide identification and annotation of meganucleases, while the unique properties of I-MG11 expand the toolbox of molecular genome engineering.
records.authors: Dorrazehi GM, Penner M, Athanasiou C, Boursinhac L, Mobarec JC, Webster CI, Papworth M, Hollfelder F.

records.title: Estuarine Biofilm Communities Adapt to Changing Conditions While Retaining Crucial Pollutant-Combatting Functions.
records.abstract: Industrialization has increased the influx of toxicants into intertidal and estuarine ecosystems. Intertidal sediments are exposed to heavy metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, pesticides, and other xenobiotics through effluents, shipping, spillages, battery disposal, and agricultural run-off. Pollutants accumulate in sediments, disrupting nutrient cycling and impairing primary productivity, thereby threatening coastal food webs. Sediment-bound biofilms or microphytobenthos are complex assemblages of microorganisms embedded in extracellular polymeric substances and play vital roles in biogeochemical cycling, sediment stabilization, and pollutant remediation. Their functional responses to contaminant exposure remain poorly understood, particularly in tropical estuaries. Biofilms from contaminated estuarine sediments were analysed using metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) and genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) in a paired field-laboratory approach. Greater metabolic diversity of field biofilms indicated broader functional capacities to sustain pollutant exposure. Conserved genes linked to organic compound degradation and metal transport co-occurred across MAGs, suggesting integrated detoxification strategies. GEM-based simulations revealed metabolic cross-feeding underlying contaminant transformation. Culture conditions shaped microbial succession and ecological roles, yet core pollutant degradation and nutrient processing functions persisted, operated by dominant taxa. Microphytobenthic experimental studies rely on laboratory-cultured communities derived from field-collected samples. Contrasting community dynamics and altered metabolism due to 'bottle effect' are foundational for correctly interpreting laboratory-based experimental outcomes.
records.authors: Mukherjee M, Roy AR, Seal P, Islam KH, Sarkar A, Karmakar S, Mukherjee J, Das R.

records.title: An integrated gut phage catalogue of nonhuman primates reveals functional adaptation to host ecology and evolutionary link to humans.
records.abstract: Nonhuman primates (NHPs), the closest evolutionary relatives of humans, are pivotal models for biomedical and ecological research. Gut phage are recognized as critical modulators of gut microbial communities; however, comprehensive insight into gut phage of NHPs is lacking. We used gut metagenomes spanning 25 NHP species and constructed an integrated gut phage catalogue (IGPC) comprising 11 389 nonredundant phage genomes. Our results revealed that the composition and function of NHP gut phage were significantly influenced by host clade, dietary niche and lifestyle. Host clade exerted a stronger influence than dietary niche on gut phage diversity. The lifestyle of NHPs influenced gut phage diversity and altered auxiliary metabolic gene profiles for different NHP species. Comparatively, 78.5% of IGPC phages were detected in human guts, with higher prevalence in nonindustrialized human guts. crAss-like phage-the most prevalent human-associated phage-were abundant in NHP guts, while exhibiting distinct evolutionary differences from crAss-like phage of humans. These findings comprehensively characterize the gut phageome of NHPs, revealing NHP host-driven and environment-driven functional adaptations, and provide an evolutionary understanding of the gut phageome between NHPs and humans.
records.authors: Yang S, Jin L, Deng W, Xiao H, Yao Y, Xie M, Xu H, Zou L.

records.title: Ecological Roles of Bacillus Lipopeptides in Mediating Plant-Microbe Interactions and Rhizosphere Community Dynamics.
records.abstract: The plant-beneficial bacterium Bacillus velezensis and related Bacillus species are increasingly recognized as important contributors to plant growth and health, yet the ecological functions of their secondary metabolites in situ remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how lipopeptides produced by Bacillus species influence plant performance and root-associated microbial communities. Using Arabidopsis thaliana as a model host, we show that bacterial lipopeptides produced during root colonization promote plant growth by enhancing the uptake of essential mineral elements, including magnesium, calcium, iron, and zinc. Transcriptomic analyses revealed that lipopeptides upregulated host genes involved in metal transport and homeostasis in roots, while downregulating negative regulators of metal uptake. The lipopeptide production reshaped the composition of root-associated bacterial communities by increasing the relative abundance of putatively beneficial taxa and altering overall rhizosphere community structure. Functional genes indicated that lipopeptide enrichment was associated with microbial pathways related to metal transport, nutrient acquisition, and stress adaptation, suggesting that lipopeptides modulate both plant and microbial traits relevant to nutrient cycling. These results provide new insight into the ecological roles of B. velezensis-derived metabolites in plant-associated microbiomes and highlight lipopeptides as promising targets for harnessing beneficial plant-microbe interactions in sustainable agriculture.
records.authors: Li H, Zeng X, Xi Y, Li Q, Li Z, Huang Z, Peng Z, Liu S, Cui S, Li C, Wei H, Wang S, Jia Y.

records.title: Social Behaviour Drives Gut Microbiome Community Assembly Among Wild Long-Tailed Macaques (Macaca fascicularis) in Thailand.
records.abstract: The 'social microbiome' conceptualises gut microbial communities as 'islands' of host social organisation. Yet, in comparison to broader aspects of social organisation such as animals' group membership and composition, the impact of inter-individual differences in sociality on microbiome community ecology remains less well studied. Among a wild but human-provisioned group of long-tailed macaques (Macaca fascicularis), we assessed the relative effects of individuals' sociality, compared to their demographic characteristics, anthropogenic and abiotic environmental factors, and microbe-microbe associations, on the relative abundance and co-occurrence of bacterial taxa. Bipartite network analysis showed that bacterial communities among macaques were nested rather than segregated or modular structures. Several 'core' bacterial genera were found across all macaques, but other 'non-core' bacteria were found only in a few macaques suggesting that their occurrence/abundance may be influenced by transient environmental factors. Joint Species Distributions Models showed that macaques' sociality, particularly their dominance rank and their connectedness or centrality within their social grooming network, had the strongest impact on taxa abundance, followed by their demographic characteristics, and finally their exposure to both anthropogenic and abiotic environmental factors. Phylogenetically distant taxa were more likely to co-occur within the same macaque hosts than phylogenetically related taxa. These findings confirm that microbiome communities are strongly influenced by the social status and connectedness of individual hosts. Nevertheless, the finding that some taxa were more prevalent among high-ranking or well-connected macaques, while others were more prevalent among low-ranking or socially peripheral macaques, warrants further investigation into how individual differences in social microbiomes might affect their health and fitness. Future studies, through the collection of behavioural and microbial data on additional macaque groups, may provide further insights into the relative effects of animals' social organisation and social behaviours on microbiomes.
records.authors: Balasubramaniam K, Kesh J, Aiempichitkijkarn N, Atwill R, Malaivijitnond S, McCowan B, Nimnual J, Sawaswong V, Visedthorn S, Payungporn S.

records.title: Genome architecture shapes the appropriate unit of comparison in small plant DNA viruses.
records.abstract: Comparative viral genomics often assumes that a single unit of analysis can be applied across datasets. However, this assumption becomes difficult to justify when viral genomes may be monopartite or multicomponent, and when multicomponent genomes differ in whether their components are co-packaged or separately encapsidated. Here, we developed an architecture-aware, alignment-free framework to compare five plant DNA virus systems spanning monopartite and separately encapsidated multipartite architectures, including two-component and six-component systems: cacao swollen shoot virus complex (CSSV), banana streak viruses (BSV), Dioscorea bacilliform viruses, cassava mosaic begomoviruses (CMB) and banana bunchy top virus (BBTV). After curation of public GenBank records, 1,342 sequences were resolved into three analytical panels, including a 130-genome monopartite panel comprising CSSV and BSV and a 1,206-record componentized panel. In the monopartite panel, whole-genome compositional geometry robustly separated CSSV and BSV. A sliding-window mosaicity analysis further prioritized a subset of CSSV genomes with elevated internal discordance, consistent with mosaic-like compositional heterogeneity. The principal panel-level results were retained with canonical 5-mers, and mosaicity rankings were stable across 300-, 400- and 500-nt windows and concordant with an independent alignment-based similarity-profile benchmark. In the componentized systems, component identity formed a strong and reproducible axis of sequence organization in both CMB and BBTV. However, their isolate-level configurations differed: the complete CMB pairs examined here consistently selected different nearest external isolates, whereas complete BBTV sets showed more heterogeneous neighbour configurations and higher component-configuration tension. These results suggest that, within the systems examined here, the biologically informative unit of viral comparison may shift with genome architecture, from whole genomes in the monopartite panel to paired or distributed component configurations in CMB and BBTV. We therefore propose architecture-aware, alignment-free comparison as a cautious screening framework for identifying cases in which deeper phylogenetic or recombination-focused follow-up is most warranted.
records.authors: Ahn E, Baek I, Oh S, Kandpal L, Kim MS, Meinhardt LW.

records.title: Nuclear Functional Divergence and Genetic Basis of Cap Colour Variation Revealed by T2T Genomes of Two Compatible Monokaryons in Pholiota adiposa.
records.abstract: Basidiomycete fungi maintain a dikaryotic state throughout their life cycle, in which two genetically distinct haploid nuclei coexist within the same cytoplasm. However, the extent and functional significance of inter-nuclear genomic divergence remain poorly understood. Here, we present the first telomere-to-telomere assemblies of two compatible monokaryons (D1 and D11) from a wild isolate of Pholiota adiposa, achieving 13 complete chromosomes with zero gaps and Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs completeness of 98.6% and 98.3%, substantially outperforming the previous fragmented assembly. The two nuclei exhibit only 75% collinear genes, with 570 (D1) and 668 (D11) strain-specific genes. D1-specific genes are enriched in energy metabolism, consistent with faster mycelial growth, while D11-specific genes are enriched in genetic information processing and mitogen-activated protein kinase signalling, revealing functional complementarity between the two haploid nuclei. Resequencing of 18 wild accessions identified two candidate regions associated with red pileus colour on chromosomes 6 and 12, the former as a major-effect locus and the latter harbouring multiple pigment-associated genes. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment implicated phenylalanine metabolism, tyrosine metabolism, and terpenoid biosynthesis in colour formation, suggesting coordinated regulation across metabolic networks. This framework facilitates dissection of nuclear functional divergence and provides candidate targets for understanding fungal phenotypic variation.
records.authors: Liu T, Fan Y, Liu Y, Yan D, Liu Y, Song S, Lu C, Guo Y, Zhang D, Sun S, Wang S, Gao Q.

records.title: From expression profiling to functional validation: evidence hierarchy and biomarker readiness of circular RNAs in aquatic animals.
records.abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are covalently closed non-coding RNA molecules that are mainly generated from precursor mRNAs through back-splicing. Owing to the lack of free 5' and 3' ends, circRNAs exhibit high stability and pronounced spatiotemporal expression specificity. In aquatic animals, recent advances in high-throughput sequencing and bioinformatic analysis have greatly expanded the catalog of circRNAs and uncovered their regulatory roles in growth, gonadal development, tissue regeneration, immune defense, and environmental stress responses. This review provides a systematic overview of circRNA biogenesis, representative molecular functions, identification strategies, and bioinformatic resources in aquatic animals, with particular emphasis on circRNA-mediated regulation during bacterial and viral infection, antiparasitic defense, trained immunity, and responses to physicochemical stressors. We further summarize the current evidence supporting the potential of circRNAs as candidate biomarkers for economically important traits, infectious disease monitoring, and ecotoxicological assessment. Importantly, we highlight the major bottlenecks that currently limit progress in this field, including incomplete genome annotation, algorithm-dependent identification bias, and the lack of robust in vivo functional validation. Overall, aquatic animals provide valuable non-model systems for expanding our understanding of circRNA biology, although many proposed regulatory mechanisms and translational applications remain to be further validated.
records.authors: Song KS, Guo M, Li CH.
