records.title: From environmental gradients to putative intrinsic resistance: Deciphering the soil resistome across Mongolian Plateau grasslands.
records.abstract: Soils are important reservoirs of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), yet the ecological differentiation and host associations of grassland resistomes remain poorly understood. We investigated topsoil resistomes across desert steppe, typical steppe, and meadow steppe of the Mongolian Plateau using short- and long-read metagenomics. The resistome comprised 28 ARG types and 819 subtypes, dominated by rifamycin, vancomycin, and multidrug resistance genes. ARG abundance increased from desert steppe to meadow steppe. Soil pH, total organic carbon, total nitrogen, and climatic variables were strongly associated with resistome turnover, whereas grazing showed weaker associations. Mobile genetic element (MGE) abundance correlated positively with ARG abundance, but only 3.37% of ARG-carrying contigs contained detectable MGEs. An operational multi-indicator framework distinguished putative intrinsic and putative acquired ARGs with contrasting host and environmental associations. Both fractions were dominated by Actinomycetota, although Pseudomonadota contributed relatively more to putative acquired ARGs. Putative intrinsic ARGs were associated mainly with nutrient-related soil variables, whereas putative acquired ARGs showed stronger climatic and edaphic associations. Long-read assemblies markedly reduced the unclassified fraction. Among 195 ARG-carrying metagenome-assembled genomes, 65.6% represented reference-poor or previously uncultured lineages. These findings reveal spatially structured and heterogeneous grassland resistomes linked to ARG composition, host affiliation, and genomic context.
records.authors: Luo J, Dong S, Yuan M, Wen W, Li YA, Li Y, Zhao R.

records.title: Perturbation-based propagation of bacterial composition uncertainty improves robustness and reproducibility of microbiome differential abundance analysis
records.abstract: Differential abundance (DA) analysis remains the analytical bottleneck of microbiome science; despite dozens of available methods, results remain poorly reproducible across tools, datasets, and study designs. Three intertwined challenges drive this failure: compositional data structure, stochastic count uncertainty, and complex experimental design; yet no existing method addresses all three simultaneously. Here, we introduce PARALLAX (Perturbation-based Assessment of Robustness Across Latent Logical Axes), a unified DA framework that resolves this gap by propagating compositional uncertainty through per-replicate linear mixed modeling across a structured scale perturbation grid, then summarizes inference through two stability-based metrics: P  post (effect consistency across Monte Carlo replicates) and R  scale (robustness to scale perturbation). PARALLAX retains uncertainty through the complete inferential pipeline while natively supporting repeated measures and multifactorial designs. Under repeated subsampling, PARALLAX identified fully stable DA taxa in 14.4% of cases, versus 1.7% and 0% for comparators. We applied PARALLAX to two independent longitudinal shotgun metagenomic datasets from mechanistically distinct mouse models: Gulf War toxicant exposure and repetitive head trauma. In both, PARALLAX resolved robust, sex-specific, and time-dependent genus-level shifts while accommodating repeated measures and multifactorial design, tasks that challenged both comparator frameworks. PARALLAX is released as an open-source, AI-compatible R workflow, lowering the barrier to rigorous microbiome DA analysis across complex study designs.  Importance  Microbiome studies link gut microbes to immune, metabolic, and neurological health, but identifying microbes that truly change with disease or treatment remains difficult. Differential abundance results often vary across computational tools because microbiome data are noisy, sparse, and compositional, especially in longitudinal or multifactorial studies. This instability limits reproducibility and creates difficulty in prioritizing microbes for biological interpretation. PARALLAX addresses this gap by focusing on consistency rather than relying on a single model fit. It analyzes data under multiple plausible representations that capture uncertainty in counts and composition, then identifies bacteria with consistent effects using stability and robustness metrics. Using ground-truth simulations and two mechanistically distinct mouse models, Gulf War toxicant exposure and traumatic brain injury, PARALLAX recovers microbial signals that remain reliable across complex study designs. This open-source R workflow provides a more reproducible path from microbiome sequencing to biological insight.

records.title: Construction of a synthetic bacterial-fungal consortium for cephalexin biodegradation: transformation pathways and ecotoxicological assessment.
records.abstract: Cephalexin (CPX), a widely used β-lactam antibiotic, is frequently detected in aquatic environments and poses risks to ecological and human health, yet the biodegradation pathways underlying its microbial removal remain incompletely characterized. In this study, a synthetic bacterial-fungal consortium (CPXS), comprising Achromobacter aegrifaciens, Citrobacter amalonaticus, Elizabethkingia anophelis, Bacillus wiedmannii, and Geotrichum pandrosion, was constructed and evaluated for CPX biodegradation. Following systematic single-factor and multivariable optimization (pH 8, 30 °C, 85 mg/L CPX), the consortium achieved 98.5% CPX removal within 48 h, and degradation was further accelerated to 30 h with sodium acetate as a co-substrate. LC-MS-based accurate mass profiling was used to identify 19 transformation products, from which five plausible degradation pathways were predicted, proposed to be initiated by ring-opening hydrolysis of the β-lactam moiety and proceeding through key intermediates, including 2-amino-2-phenylacetamide, toward simple terminal metabolites such as N-methylacetamide and (Z)-but-2-enal, consistent with substantial progression toward mineralization. The consortium also degraded amoxicillin and ampicillin in synthetic and real municipal wastewater, indicating broad-spectrum activity and applicability under complex matrix conditions. Toxicity assays using Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, and HEK-293 cells showed that degraded samples retained negligible antibacterial activity and exhibited low cytotoxicity, confirming effective detoxification of CPX and its byproducts. Overall, this study proposes a detailed, multi-pathway degradation network for CPX mediated by a bacterial-fungal consortium, culminating in simple bioassimilable end products, and identifies CPXS as a promising candidate for the bioremediation of β-lactam antibiotic-contaminated wastewater.
records.authors: Moridshahi R, Etemadifar Z, Biria D.

records.title: Viral metagenomics reveals heterogeneity in mammalian virus hosting, sharing, and spillover.
records.abstract: Zoonotic viruses originating from mammals pose a persistent threat to global health. While rodents and bats are often considered "special reservoirs," it is debated if spillover risk is driven by specific taxa or merely reflects mammalian species richness. However, most tests have focused on published host-virus association datasets, which can reflect systematic biases in host and virus sampling effort. To address this limitation, we analyzed a comprehensive repository of 4,685 metagenomic datasets, minimizing bias toward any one viral taxon and spanning 296 species across 14 mammalian orders. We characterized the global mammalian virome and found substantial heterogeneity in the capacity of different mammalian orders to harbor and share human-associated viruses. Counter to conventional wisdom, carnivores exhibited significantly higher propensities to carry human-associated viruses, with bats ranked lower in this metric of zoonotic risk. Network analyses of viral sharing further revealed higher cross-order virus sharing among specific mammalian orders (e.g., carnivores and artiodactyls). Phylogenetic comparative analyses revealed that host life-history traits (e.g., longevity) and anthropogenic factors (e.g., urban land use) were key ecological drivers of both virus richness and transmission centrality. Our study provides a data-driven framework that challenges prevailing narratives of zoonotic risk and offers a refined strategy for prioritizing surveillance and mitigating emerging zoonotic threats.
records.authors: Wang Y, Qu G, Huang ZYX, Zhang X, Li H, Wei X, Hu L, Xu S, Becker DJ, Wei F, Xu Y.

records.title: Multi-Virus Surveillance Across Diverse Freshwater Systems in Tehran, Iran.
records.abstract: Environmental surveillance of viral contaminants in water systems is an essential tool for assessing exposure risk and supporting early-warning frameworks for emerging infectious diseases. In this study, a comprehensive one-year surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 and six enteric viruses was conducted across diverse freshwater systems in Tehran, Iran - including rivers, wells, and traditional qanat (underground aqueduct) infrastructures. Water quality parameters (turbidity, pH, Total Dissolved Solids, nitrate) and fecal bacterial indicators (total coliforms, fecal coliforms, and E. coli) were also measured to contextualize viral contamination within a broader environmental risk framework. Between September 2020 and August 2021, a total of 118 water samples were collected and analyzed using quantitative molecular detection methods. Overall, 61 of 118 samples (51.7%) tested positive for at least one virus. Surface water (rivers) showed substantially higher contamination rates (80.3%; 53/66 samples) compared to groundwater (15.4%; 8/52 samples). Among groundwater sources, qanat systems were markedly more vulnerable than conventional wells, with 25.0% (6/24) of qanat samples testing positive versus only 7.1% (2/28) of well samples. This elevated contamination in qanats was dominated by rotavirus (5/6 positive qanat samples, detection rate 20.8%) and was associated with higher fecal bacterial loads (total coliform geometric mean: 245 MPN/100 mL in qanats vs. 28 MPN/100 mL in wells), consistent with the susceptibility of shallow horizontal collection channels to fecal infiltration. SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected in 34.8% of river samples and 3.9% of groundwater samples, with concentrations reaching 1.28 × 10⁴ genome copies per liter (GC/L) in surface waters, demonstrating sustained fecal contamination across all seasons. The most prevalent viruses in river water were norovirus GII (45.5%), adenovirus (43.9%), rotavirus (42.4%), and norovirus GI (40.9%), with mean concentrations ranging from 1.26 × 10² to 3.76 × 10³ GC/L. Hepatitis A and E viruses were not detected in any sample. Seasonal variation in viral detection was observed for enteric viruses, while SARS-CoV-2 and adenovirus showed year-round persistence. Strong correlations between fecal indicators and viral contamination (Spearman r = 0.61-0.63) support the use of bacterial monitoring as a cost-effective screening proxy. The results highlight the particular vulnerability of qanat systems and underscore the value of integrated environmental surveillance for water safety management in arid, water-stressed urban environments.

records.title: Metagenome sequences of unintended bacterial communities from a Pseudomonas fluorescens experimental evolution study.
records.abstract: We report 16 metagenome sequences from unintended contaminant communities that invaded an evolution experiment initiated with Pseudomonas fluorescens SBW25. Low-diversity bacterial assemblies from center and edge locations across eight populations in contrasting uniform or heterogeneous glucose agar plate environments feature four primary genera: Pseudomonas, Chryseobacterium, Delftia, and Moraxella.

records.title: Current research status of risk assessment models for oral squamous cell carcinoma based on microbiome databases.
records.abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is one of the most common oral malignancies. Due to insidious early symptoms, high invasiveness, and frequent cervical lymph node metastasis, patient survival remains poor. Recent studies demonstrate significant associations between oral dysbiosis and OSCC. To address limited early screening and suboptimal survival rates, this review systematically summarizes OSCC microbiome research and disease risk assessment applications. Studies reveal marked oral dysbiosis in patients with OSCC, characterized by enrichment of Fusobacterium and Porphyromonas, reduced Neisseria abundance, and altered community stability. These promote tumorigenesis through chronic pro-inflammatory signaling, the production of carcinogenic metabolites, and direct oncogenic pathway interference. Consequently, the oral microbiome offers non-invasive, sensitive biomarkers for early detection. We identify and distinguish four categories of predictive models in the current literature: (1) detection/discrimination of prevalent OSCC, (2) prediction of malignant transformation from oral potentially malignant disorders, (3) prediction of recurrence or metastasis after treatment, and (4) prognostic models for survival prediction. Existing databases include comprehensive and OSCC-specific collections with multi-omics integration. Risk assessment models encompass traditional statistics, machine learning, deep learning, and multimodal fusion, and have shown promising performance in retrospective cohorts. However, standardized databases are lacking, and existing models face confounding interference, limited generalizability, and insufficient interpretability. Furthermore, current predictive models are predominantly based on 16S rRNA sequencing (bacteriome-centric), whereas comprehensive risk assessment requires integrating interkingdom entities, including fungi, viruses, and archaea, through metagenomic and virome profiling. Critically, the distinction between promising retrospective discrimination and validated prospective clinical utility remains a major translational barrier. Future directions include developing standardized longitudinal databases, integrating multi-omics, using explainable artificial intelligence, and conducting prospective validation studies to achieve personalized precision treatment.
records.authors: Li GL, Zhang ZC, Lyu XM, Li MX, Lin PY, Yu HS, Zhu YY, Zhang GH, Duan CG, Cheung Y, Li W, Zhang ZJ, Xu TS, Chen F, Huang MW.

records.title: Diversity and distribution of Bartonella spp. in domestic animals, wildlife, and ectoparasites in Brazil: a comprehensive review.
records.abstract: Bartonella are intracellular Gram-negative blood-borne bacteria capable of infecting a wide range of hosts, primarily mammals and birds. They are responsible for emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases characterized by persistent intraerythrocytic bacteremia in mammals. Out of 49 species described, 13 presents zoonotic potential. This review aimed to update the current knowledge on the occurrence, distribution, and genetic diversity of Bartonella in domestic animals, wild mammals and birds, and ectoparasites in Brazil. A total of 72 scientific articles published between 2007 and 2026 were included. The available information indicates that the Southeastern and Central-Western regions of Brazil account for most reports of Bartonella in animals and ectoparasites, whereas the Northern and Northeastern regions remain comparatively understudied. Overall, studies investigating Bartonella in Brazil have become increasingly frequent and geographically widespread over the years. Although some investigations rely on single-gene analyses, most employ multi-locus sequence analysis and phylogenetic reconstruction, providing stronger evidence for species identification and diversity. In contrast, relatively few studies have incorporated whole-genome sequencing or comprehensive phenotypic and biochemical characterization through bacterial isolation and blood culture. Future research should prioritize advanced genomic approaches and bacterial isolation to improve our understanding of the diversity, evolution, and epidemiology of Bartonella circulating in Brazil.

records.title: CNTN4: A Possible Candidate Gene for Microbiota-Gut-Brain Axis in Autism Spectrum Disorders and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder.
records.abstract: The gut microbiota plays a significant role in autism spectrum disorders (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), though findings vary substantially across studies. Using gut microbiome data from a genome-wide association study of 5,959 participants and summary statistics from 46,351 ASD and 55,374 ADHD cases, we conducted bidirectional Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses with inverse variance weighting as the primary method. Reverse MR analysis assessed potential reverse causality. We annotated single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) with SNP-nexus to identify associated genes, followed by Gene Ontology (﻿GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses to characterize their functional roles. Seventeen gut microbial taxa showed causal associations with ASD risk, while 27 were linked to ADHD. Reverse MR analysis revealed associations between aSD and species Desulfovibrio piger as well as species Bacillus U, but no reverse causality was detected for ADHD. Biological annotation identified five novel conserved genes in host-microbiome interactions shared by ASD and ADHD, with CNTN4 emerging as a common candidate gene. These findings support a potential causal relationship between gut microbiota and ASD/ADHD risk while uncovering novel conserved genes implicated in host-microbiome interactions for both disorders.Lay AbstractDistinct gut microbiota profiles were observed in individuals with ADHD and ASD. Seventeen microbial species showed significant associations with ASD, while 27 were linked to ADHD. CNTN4 emerged as a potential candidate gene shared across both neurodevelopmental conditions and host-microbiome interactions.
records.journal: Autism : the international journal of research and practice
records.authors: Li Y, Wang W, Liu W.

records.title: Whole-genome analysis of avian orthoreovirus isolated in Japan reveals genetic divergence from vaccine strains.
records.abstract: Avian orthoreovirus (ARV) is an important pathogen associated with viral arthritis in chickens and causes substantial economic losses in the poultry industry. In recent years, ARVs belonging to clusters 2 and 6, which have rarely been reported in Japan, have been isolated from broiler chickens derived from breeder flocks vaccinated with the ARV vaccine strains 1733 and 2408. In this study, whole-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analyses were performed on ARV isolates circulating in Japan to clarify their genetic differences from the vaccine strains. Comparative analyses revealed considerable genomic diversity even among virus strains isolated from the same geographic region, suggesting frequent genetic reassortment among circulating ARVs. None of the genomic segments of our isolates showed high-sequence identity to the currently used vaccine strains. In particular, the σC protein showed low amino acid identities (49.39-56.48%) to strain 1733. These findings suggest substantial genetic divergence between recent Japanese ARVs and the vaccine strains. This study provide the first whole-genome characterization of recent Japanese ARVs. Continuous surveillance will contribute to a better understanding of ARV evolution and to the evaluation of the effectiveness of current vaccines against circulating field strains.
records.authors: Fujimoto Y, Tsunekuni R, Ikeda T, Nakagara K, Chuma T.

records.title: Examining microbial assemblage differences on plants preferred and avoided by threatened Hawaiian land snails to identify important food resources.
records.abstract: The Hawaiian Islands, an isolated oceanic archipelago in the Pacific, had one of the world's most spectacular land snail radiations. Unfortunately, only 35% of the 759 Hawaiian snail species remain, with >100 species threatened with imminent extinction. Though many extant Hawaiian snails are arboreal and are known to eat microbes on the surface of plants, our current understanding of which microbes compose arboreal Hawaiian snails' diets remains rudimentary. Here, we examined microbial assemblages (bacterial and fungal) on plants previously identified as preferred and avoided by a diverse assemblage of arboreal snails at three sites in wet and mesic forests on O'ahu, Hawai'i, USA, to identify microbes that may form the foundation of Hawaiian arboreal snails' diets. At Mt. Ka'ala, we also investigated if microbial assemblages change across years. Across sites, microbial assemblages differed on preferred and avoided plants. While differences across sites can complicate the process of identifying key microbes, microbes with elevated abundances on preferred plants across sites are likely important food resources. Using this approach, we identified bacterial and fungal OTUs that we hypothesize form important components of Hawaiian arboreal snails' diets. While we found that microbial assemblages differed among years at Mt. Ka'ala, differences between preferred and avoided plants remained consistent across years. Expanding a snail plant preference-microbiome framework across multiple forest types is a crucial step in understanding arboreal snail diets as microbial taxa enriched on preferred plants across sites may be meaningful components of snail-associated microbial resources. Microbial taxa enriched on preferred plants are not presented here as confirmed dietary components, but as experimentally tractable candidates that should be further evaluated in laboratory trials. This information is foundational to improving captive rearing of critically endangered snails and informing habitat quality assessments for the many threatened Hawaiian snails.

records.title: Core microbiota recruited by Salvia miltiorrhiza enhance resistance against Fusarium root rot disease
records.abstract: Abstract    Fusarium  root rot, caused by the soilborne pathogen  Fusarium oxysporum  , leads to substantial yield losses across multiple agriculturally crucial crops. While rhizosphere microbiota have been extensively studied in model species, a deeper understanding of the rhizosphere microbiome assembly associated with herb health is still needed. Given its economic importance in traditional medicine, we used  Salvia miltiorrhiza  and  Fusarium  root rot as a model to elucidate the rhizosphere microbiome assembly associated with plant health. Here, we employed 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing to profile the soil microbiome across three geographically distinct cultivation regions. Comparative analysis revealed marked divergence in bacterial community structures between healthy and diseased plants, identifying  Lysobacter  spp. as keystone bacterial taxa within the core microbiome enriched in healthy rhizospheres. Functional validation demonstrated potent antifungal activity of isolated  Lysobacter  strains against  F. oxysporum  , with  Lysobacter enzymogenes  strain Ly-1 exhibiting consistent biocontrol efficacy in both greenhouse and field experiments. Genomic and transcriptomic analyses further revealed that Ly-1 encodes specialized iron acquisition systems, including siderophore synthesis and transport machinery, with its antifungal activity being significantly amplified under iron-limited conditions, consistent with a model where iron competition cooperates with other biocontrol traits. Collectively, this study establishes a novel biocontrol paradigm and highlights the translational potential of core rhizobacterial enrichment for sustainable management of soilborne diseases in medicinal plants.
records.authors: You C, Gao Y, Ren P, Zhang W, Gong K, Zhang Q, Wang X, Zhou W, Kümmerli R, Xu Y, Shen Q, Wei Z, Wang X.

records.title: Genomic and experimental evidence from Antarctic geothermal sites indicates diverse thermophiles are globally cosmopolitan
records.abstract: Abstract  Mt. Erebus, the world’s southernmost active volcano, is highly isolated, yet a previous study found its heated soils contain prokaryotes found elsewhere globally. This was unexpected, as non-sporulating thermophilic microorganisms are thought to be dispersal limited. We searched for the presence of metagenome assembled genomes (MAGs) from Antarctic geothermal sites outside Antarctica, finding that 62% of MAGs had matching species globally. Three of these cosmopolitan thermophiles isolated from Mt. Erebus could survive atmospheric-like conditions, with UV being the strongest selective pressure. Moreover, hot soils from Hawaiʻi sampled four years after a lava flow hosted many thermophilic MAGs with identical strains elsewhere globally, indicating that dispersal/recolonisation by thermophiles can be rapid. Finally, ice core sections from Fang Glacier (Mt. Erebus) associated with volcanic events were enriched in thermophiles, implying that thermophiles could disperse via volcanic events. Our findings dispel the common conception of thermophilic microorganisms as being inherently dispersal limited.

records.title: Mechanistic insights into atmospheric and room-temperature plasma (ARTP)-induced genomic alterations and phenotypic evolution in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
records.abstract: Atmospheric and room-temperature plasma (ARTP) is a potent tool for microbial strain engineering; however, the mechanistic basis of its genome-wide mutagenic effects remains poorly understood. Utilizing Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a model, we performed a comprehensive characterization of the mutational landscape and DNA repair pathways elicited by ARTP. Under high-lethality conditions (~99% mortality), ARTP treatment induced a substantial mutational burden, with SNVs and InDels rates increasing 25.2- and 36.7-fold relative to untreated controls, respectively. These mutations exhibited a pronounced bias toward C-T/G-A and A-T/T-A substitutions and InDels within AT-rich regions. Remarkably, the frequency of loss of heterozygosity (LOH) surged 57.4-fold, suggesting a potent capacity for inducing DNA breaks. Through sectored colony assays, we demonstrate that ARTP primarily inflicts pre-replicative double-strand breaks (DSBs), with reciprocal crossovers serving as the predominant driver of terminal LOH. The distribution and pattern of LOH were also altered in ARTP-treated cells. Mechanistically, our study establishes that the translesion synthesis polymerases Rev1 and Pol ζ are indispensable for converting ARTP-induced lesions-likely pyrimidine dimers-into fixed point mutations. In contrast, Rad30 facilitates high-fidelity bypass across these dimers. The base excision repair pathway appears largely dispensable for the processing of these lesions. In contrast, the nucleotide excision repair pathway plays a predominant role in mitigating ARTP-induced mutations. Finally, the strategic application of iterative ARTP mutagenesis facilitated the rapid evolution of acetate-tolerant strains. Our findings provide fundamental insights into the molecular signatures of ARTP mutagenesis, offering a framework for its optimized application in directed evolution.ImportanceWhile ARTP is a cornerstone of non-thermal mutagenesis in industrial biotechnology, its genetic impact has long been treated as a "black box." This study provides a high-resolution molecular dissection of ARTP-induced genomic alterations using a diploid yeast model. We demonstrate that ARTP is not merely a source of point mutations but a potent catalyst for pre-replicative double-strand breaks and extensive mitotic recombination. By elucidating the pivotal roles of specific DNA repair pathways in mutation fixation, we transition ARTP from a purely empirical screening tool to a mechanistically grounded platform for directed evolution. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical utility of this platform by evolving acetate-tolerant strains and identifying the underlying genetic drivers of their resilience.
records.authors: Sheng H, Yao J, Liu Y, Li K-J, Zhang J-Z, Zheng D-Q, Zhang K.

records.title: Complete Chloroplast Genome of Nepeta griffithii and Comparative Genomics of 10 Nepeta Species.
records.abstract: Nepeta L. (Lamiaceae) is an ecologically and medicinally important genus, yet complete cp genome resources are available for fewer than 10 of the approximately 300 accepted species, with western Himalayan taxa almost entirely unrepresented. Here, we sequenced, assembled, and annotated the complete cp genome of Nepeta griffithii and compared it with nine previously published Nepeta cp genomes. The 10 cp genomes exhibited a highly conserved quadripartite structure, with genome sizes ranging from 151,254 to 152,348 bp, and contained 113 unique genes (79 protein-coding, 30 tRNA, 4 rRNA). Gene content, guanine-cytosine content, intron features, and inverted repeat contraction and expansion were highly conserved. SSR analysis identified 387 repeats across the 10 cp genomes, predominantly mononucleotide A/T motifs in intergenic spacers, yielding candidate cpSSR markers for population-level studies. Codon usage analysis revealed a strong bias toward A/T-ending codons, with leucine as the most frequent amino acid. Nucleotide diversity analysis showed intergenic spacers were more variable than both introns and genic regions. Highly polymorphic loci, including ccsA-ndhD, rpl32-trnL-UAG, and ndhG-ndhI, were identified as candidate markers for phylogenetic and population studies. Maximum likelihood phylogeny based on 79 concatenated protein-coding genes recovered a well-resolved topology within Nepeta and placed N. griffithii as sister to N. nuda with maximal bootstrap support of 100%. This study provides the first complete cp genome for N. griffithii, improves plastome sampling within the genus, and offers genomic markers for species identification, systematics, and evolutionary studies.
records.authors: Li X, Sammad A, Shah SA, Sun J, Karim A, Yir-Erong B, Tian X, Abdullah.

records.title: Genome-wide identification and expression profiling of IQM family genes in Chrysanthemum nankingense in response to abiotic stresses.
records.abstract: IQM proteins are plant-specific central modulators of calcium signaling, coordinating plant growth, development, and stress adaptation via calmodulin binding, yet no systematic characterization of the IQM family has been reported in Chrysanthemum nankingense. Here, we performed a genome-wide identification of the CnIQM gene family and conducted systematic bioinformatic analyses of their physicochemical traits, chromosomal distribution and phylogenetic relationships. RT-qPCR was used to detect transcriptional responses of CnIQM genes to exogenous phytohormones and major abiotic stresses, and yeast heterologous expression assays validated the stress tolerance of key CnIQM candidates. A total of nine CnIQM genes were identified. Most encode alkaline proteins predominantly localized to the nucleus or cytoplasm. Tandem duplication appears to be a major contributor to CnIQM family expansion, and all duplicated gene pairs are under strong purifying selection; high syntenic conservation of IQM loci is observed between C. nankingense and its congener Chrysanthemum lavandulifolium. All CnIQM proteins contain the canonical conserved IQ motif, whereas several paralogs exhibit structural variation with truncated UTR regions. Transcriptional profiling revealed differential induction under phytohormone, salt, drought, and cold treatments, with most genes rapidly upregulated by salinity and drought stress. Yeast heterologous expression assays showed that CnIQM5, CnIQM6, and CnIQM9 significantly improve salt and drought tolerance in yeast, while none enhances cold resistance in this heterologous system. This study clarifies the evolutionary and functional features of the CnIQM family and provides theoretical references and promising candidate genes for future functional research and stress-resistant molecular breeding of chrysanthemum.
records.authors: Wang T, Xie Z, Li S, Liu L, Lu N, Li C, Fan X, Han Q, Wang W, Pu S.

records.title: Large-genome phages encode diverse proteins associated with host cell envelope functions
records.abstract: Huge phages (or jumbo phages, >200 kilobases) encode extensive protein repertoires, yet their functional diversity and potential roles in host physiology remain poorly understood. Using protein structure-based analyses of dominant protein families across 7,187 non-redundant genomes of huge phages, we uncovered pronounced phylogenetic and habitat-associated diversification. Notably, we identified diverse proteins associated with bacterial cell envelope functions, particularly in human gut-associated huge phages. These included previously unreported phage-encoded sortase B, whose putative substrates contain signal peptides and cell-wall sorting signals, suggesting a potential route for displaying phage proteins on bacterial surfaces. Phage-encoded phage shock protein A (PspA) was distributed across diverse lineages and frequently neighbored genes associated with membrane organization and transport, implicating potential roles in membrane physiology. We also identified 1,603 β-barrel outer membrane proteins (OMPs) across 1,303 huge phages from diverse ecosystems. These OMPs exhibited structural diversity and associations with predicted host taxonomy, habitat, and neighboring envelope-related genes. Metatranscriptomic analysis supported expression of representative phage-encoded PspA and OMP genes in natural communities including the human gut. Together, these findings reveal bacterial cell envelope processes as a previously underappreciated potential interface for huge phage–host interactions.

records.title: Newcastle disease virus research: pioneering scientists, landmark discoveries, and virological innovations.
records.abstract: Newcastle disease (ND) has been recognized for a century as one of the most consequential viral diseases of poultry, and its scientific history provides a distinctive example of how sustained investigation of a single pathogen can drive advances across veterinary medicine, virology, immunology, epidemiology, molecular biology, vaccinology, and biotechnology. The severe outbreaks reported in Java, Indonesia, and Newcastle-upon-Tyne, England, during 1926 marked the beginning of the recognized scientific history of ND and initiated an international research effort that progressed from disease recognition and experimental characterization to diagnostics, vaccination, molecular pathogenesis, and genomic epidemiology. During the 1940s and 1950s, investigations of viral propagation, antigenicity, pathogenicity, and attenuation established the foundations of live and inactivated vaccination. From the 1960s onward, molecular investigations progressively elucidated the determinants of ND virus (NDV) replication, protein processing, and virulence, particularly the role of the fusion-protein cleavage site. The emergence of nucleotide sequencing and phylogenetic analysis during the 1980s and 1990s subsequently transformed strain characterization and provided the foundations for molecular epidemiology and genotype classification. Complete-genome sequencing and the establishment of reverse-genetics systems in the late 1990s further transformed NDV from an organism studied primarily through observation and isolation into a genetically tractable experimental system. Subsequent international efforts standardized NDV genotype nomenclature and enabled increasingly detailed analyses of viral evolution and geographic dissemination. In parallel, NDV research expanded beyond conventional disease control into recombinant vaccine development, systems-level host-virus studies, molecular diagnostics, and oncolytic virotherapy. This historical perspective traces these major scientific transitions from 1926 to 2026, emphasizing the investigators, experimental systems, conceptual advances, and technological innovations that collectively transformed NDV research from disease recognition into a multidisciplinary molecular and translational fields.

records.title: Modeling association networks from metagenome time series - a proof-of-concept from two contrasting estuaries.
records.abstract: Understanding microbial responses to environmental gradients is important for ecosystem assessment in estuarine environments. Here, we integrated time-series samples and shotgun metagenomics with association network inference, to examine patterns of taxonomic and functional co-variation. We collected and sequenced eDNA from two sediment time series from neighbouring but environmentally contrasting Basque estuaries, and compared the resulting taxonomic and functional association networks, based on Metagenome Assembled Genomes (MAGs) and KEGG Orthologous Groups (KOs), respectively. Networks inferred using 16S rRNA gene metabarcoding data were also included in this comparison. Several topology-based network properties differed strongly between the two sites, although differences were not always consistent when comparing the networks based on MAGs, KOs and metabarcoding. KO-based networks revealed distinct sets of associated Ortholog groups between sites, consistent with known environmental differences. Contrary to our expectations, metabolically related genes rarely formed complete pathway modules in gene networks, likely due to functional redundancy, gene copy number variation, synchronized pathway dynamics, or algorithmic constraints of correlation-based inference. Overall, the results illustrate both the potential and interpretative limitations of metagenome-based time association networks for functional ecosystem assessment, and support their use as hypothesis-generating tools that require further validation across a larger range of sites following environmental gradients.

records.title: Evaluation of whole genome sequencing protocols and target-capture panels for detection of respiratory viruses in clinical specimens.
records.abstract: Respiratory viruses are major contributors to global morbidity and mortality. When viral mutations compromise detection by conventional diagnostic assays, identifying cases and tracing transmission becomes challenging. Whole genome sequencing (WGS) improves on conventional diagnostics as it can detect viruses with novel mutations. This study evaluated the performance of the ePlex, a rapid multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay (RMPA), an in-house real-time reverse transcription PCR assay (RT-qPCR) and WGS for detecting respiratory virus infections in clinical specimens. Sixty-one sequence libraries were prepared, and bait enriched from nasopharyngeal swabs, collected in 2021, which were negative for SARS-CoV-2 but positive for co-infections of respiratory viruses detected by the ePlex. An in-house bioinformatics pipeline enabled a metagenomic analysis approach to be compared with the ePlex and RT-qPCR. In most swabs, respiratory viruses were detected by WGS (average genome recovery: 85.9%) or RT-qPCR which concurred with the ePlex result, but as single viruses rather than co-infections. WGS recovered respiratory syncytial viruses (80%) and metapneumoviruses (70%) most often. This study demonstrates the power of WGS and bait capture in resolving the genomes of respiratory pathogens from limited clinical material. Detection of a single virus, rather than co-infections, in this instance could highlight the targeted nature of bait capture technology or competition between viruses during bait hybridization. The number of respiratory syncytial viruses detected (16/20) could be due to a spike in activity detected after the alleviation of non-pharmaceutical interventions in the COVID-19 pandemic.
records.authors: Kelly D, Yogananthan K, Subramaniam P, Talts T, Manso CF, Kele B, Bibby DF, Zuckerman M, Mbisa JL.

records.title: Harnessing metatranscriptomics to unveil the metabolic landscape of microbiota in traditional fermented foods.
records.abstract: Traditional fermented foods are widely consumed and valued for their distinctive sensory properties and potential health benefits. These foods contain complex microbiota whose interactions and metabolic activities shape biochemical transformations relevant to product quality, safety, and functionality. Metatranscriptomics provides a culture-independent means of profiling community RNA and examining changes in microbial gene expression during fermentation. However, most fermented-food microbiome studies continue to infer function from community composition or genomic potential rather than from in situ gene expression. Existing metatranscriptomic applications also differ substantially in sampling, RNA processing, sequencing, and data analysis, limiting comparisons across food systems. This review examines the metatranscriptomic workflows applied to fermented foods, including sample preparation, sequencing strategies, and bioinformatic analysis. It identifies practical requirements for reproducible RNA-based studies in complex food matrices and compares transcriptionally represented taxa and pathways across fermentation systems. The review also distinguishes gene expression from realized metabolic activity, an important boundary when interpreting transcript annotations and reconstructed pathways. We further assess the strengths and limitations of metatranscriptomics, both alone and in combination with complementary omics, for resolving microbiota structure-function relationships. Key challenges include data integration, evidence interpretation, and the recovery of biologically meaningful information from complex transcriptomic datasets. When combined with complementary omics and experimental validation, metatranscriptomics can help relate expressed genes and pathways to fermentation phenotypes. These insights may guide the experimental evaluation of starter cultures and the development of more precise fermentation-control strategies.
records.authors: Li R, Fan X, Kang J, Huang X, Shi Y, Chen X.

records.title: Topoisomerase I participates in chromosome segregation of the polyploid bacterium Thermus thermophilus through its decatenation activity.
records.abstract: Thermus thermophilus, a polyploid thermophilic bacterium, lacks the canonical decatenases Topo III and Topo IV, posing a challenge for faithful chromosome segregation. This study aims to determine whether T. thermophilus topoisomerase I (TopoITth) has acquired decatenation activity and participates in chromosome segregation. Through gene deletion, we found that topA is essential; only a heterozygous ΔtopA::blm/WT-topA mutant could be obtained. Partial depletion of TopoITth caused severe Par- phenotypes, including cell filamentation, unsegregated nucleoids, anucleate cells, and DNA fragmentation, all of which were rescued by ectopic expression of wild-type topA, confirming the specificity of the defects. TopoITth localized to cell poles, mirroring the localization of classical segregation proteins SMC and XerD, and bacterial two-hybrid assays revealed physical interactions with both proteins. Truncation analysis mapped the interaction interfaces to the C-terminal domain of SMC and the N-terminal domain of XerD. In vitro, TopoITth exhibited decatenation and catenation activities, contrasting with Escherichia coli TopoI. SMC stimulated its decatenation in a dose-dependent manner, whereas XerD did not. Collectively, our results indicate that TopoITth acts as a decatenase integrated with the chromosome segregation machinery to compensate for the absence of Topo III and Topo IV. This study uncovers a functional expansion of type IA topoisomerases and offers a paradigm for how genome streamlining can drive the evolution of novel enzyme functions.ImportanceThis work refines the canonical view that bacterial topoisomerase I functions solely as a relaxase. By demonstrating that Thermus thermophilus Topo I has evolved robust decatenation activity and physically interacts with SMC to drive chromosome segregation, we uncover a functional expansion of type IA topoisomerases. This provides a paradigm for understanding how genome streamlining drives the acquisition of new functions by an existing enzyme. Beyond evolutionary significance, our findings may have translational relevance. Certain pathogens, such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium smegmatis, similarly lack canonical decatenases and depend on Topo I for survival. Although further studies are needed to validate whether this decatenase activity is widely conserved and essential in these pathogens, our work suggests that Topo I could be explored as a potential target for developing novel antibiotics against multidrug-resistant bacteria.
records.authors: Li H, He Y, Xu J, Zhang Y, Liu Y, Xiao W, Cao Z, Shen Y, Xu L, Liu X, Li X, Zhao Y.

records.title: Ocean depth modifies host-microbiome ecology and evolution
records.abstract: A major unsolved question in ecology and evolution is how similar free-living and symbiotic microbial communities are. In marine systems, depth homogenises free-living communities due to stronger dispersal and weaker environmental filtering compared to surface waters. We show that symbiotic communities of marine sponges follow a different pattern, with a subset of sponge species mirroring the increased similarity with depth seen in their free-living counterparts, while others remain highly host-specific both in shallow and deep waters. Moreover, in deep waters, more phylogenetically similar hosts harbor more similar microbiomes, yet host-symbiont cophylogeny nearly vanishes. This reveals two contrasting eco-evolutionary assembly rules: in more constant environments like the deep sea, community assembly is driven by host and environmental filtering with minimal signature of coevolution, whereas in variable environments, like shallow waters, host-symbiont coevolution is strong and key to maintain host-specific microbiomes.
records.authors: Díez-Vives C, Turon M, Lurgi M, Pita L, Nielsen S, Álvarez Fernández A, Thomas T, Riesgo A, Montoya JM.

records.title: GBactPro: cross-species bacterial promoter prediction using element-resolved promoter definitions
records.abstract: Accurate bacterial promoter prediction supports genome annotation, but many models use fixed-length promoter windows anchored to transcription start sites (TSSs) rather than promoter-element boundaries. We developed the  G eneral  Bact erial  Pro moter Predictor (GBactPro), a convolutional neural network–bidirectional long short-term memory (CNN–BiLSTM) framework using promoter sequences resolved by the Promoter Architecture Scanner. Using  Escherichia coli -trained models evaluated across 43 bacterial species, we compared eight input designs and identified the contiguous −35/spacer/−10 core as optimal (mean AUROC = 0.9859). Species-specific models showed broad transfer in a 43 × 43 evaluation. Joint training on all 43 species achieved a mean AUROC of 0.9943 across their held-out test sets and outperformed four established predictors under matched-length benchmarks. In genome-wide  E. coli scanning, GBactPro achieved AUROC and AUPRC values of 0.979 and 0.160 under stringent full-containment matching (0-bp tolerance), increasing to 0.997 and 0.323 under a 100-bp tolerance. False-positive predictions overlapped H-NS binding regions more frequently than true positives (24.4% versus 18.8%), and predictions also overlapped promoters derepressed in an H-NS-knockout dataset. Prediction precision varied across four TSS classes. These findings demonstrate that element-resolved promoter definitions improve cross-species prediction and support genome-wide identification of candidate bacterial promoters.
records.authors: Han HB, Kao YV, Kuo SA, Chou HD, Chang J.

records.title: Scalable phylodynamic inference of mutational and epistatic fitness effects with multi-feature birth-death models
records.abstract: Fitness is a complex phenotype determined by many different genomic features, their interactions with each other and the environment. For rapidly evolving microbes like viruses and bacteria, phylodynamic multi-feature birth-death (MFBD) models provide a way to infer the fitness of lineages with different genotypes from reconstructed phylogenies. However, existing phylodynamic methods assume very simple additive or multiplicative genotype-to-fitness (G-to-F) mappings that typically ignore epistatic interactions among features. We developed a gradient-based Bayesian MFBD framework for estimating the fitness effects of multiple features while allowing for both additive and epistatic G-to-F maps. The framework uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for posterior inference and incorporates shrinkage priors to regularize weakly supported fitness effects without cross-validation. In simulations, Bayesian inference performs well at recovering additive fitness effects, with accuracy and precision improving consistently with increasing tree size. While epistatic effects are more difficult to estimate because they depend on the co-occurrence of mutations, shrinkage improves estimation when interaction effects are weak or sparsely supported. Simulations with misspecified additive models show that ignoring moderate or strong epistasis can bias estimates of individual mutational effects. We applied the framework to a time-calibrated  Escherichia coli ST131 phylogeny with 1763 samples and estimated fitness effects for several mutations in the quinolone resistance-determining region (QRDR). These results show that Bayesian phylodynamic inference can be used to learn the genomic determinants of fitness while quantifying uncertainty in mutational and epistatic fitness effects.
records.authors: Cen S, Kepler LM, Lanzas C, Reich BJ, Rasmussen DA.

records.title: Isolation of polyethylene‑modifying soil bacteria from Egypt and Genome-based functional characterization of Sphingobacterium spiritivorum ASb3.
records.abstract: Polyethylene (PE) has been widely utilized, resulting in its accumulation in the environment due to its recalcitrant nature. In this study, seven bacterial isolates from garden soil and garbage dumps in Cairo and Giza, Egypt, grew on PE films as the sole carbon source, reduced PE weight, and formed biofilms. Scanning electron microscopy revealed surface perforations, while Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy detected new carbonyl and hydroxyl groups. Based on 16 S rRNA gene sequencing and phylogeny, the isolates exhibited high similarity to Sphingobacterium spiritivorum, Rhodococcus pyridinivorans, Pseudomonas putida, Ectopseudomonas mendocina, Zobellella taiwanensis, Achromobacter mucicolens, and Pseudomonas sp. To the best of our knowledge, S. spiritivorum, E. mendocina, Z. taiwanensis, and A. mucicolens have not previously been reported in PE biodeterioration studies. S. spiritivorum was selected for whole-genome sequencing. Comparative functional genomics revealed variation in enzyme families potentially associated with oxidation, hydrolysis, and β-oxidation. CAZy profiling identified carbohydrate-active enzymes, including proteins carrying predicted signal peptides. KEGG reconstruction supported alcohol- and aldehyde-to-fatty-acid conversion, fatty-acid activation, and β-oxidation-related metabolism. SignalP predicted secretion signals in selected proteins, while local synteny analysis showed conserved organization of these loci in Sphingobacterium strains. Overall, these findings suggest the potential of these isolates for PE biodeterioration.
records.authors: Elsayed AF, Amin DH, Gebreel HM, Mahasneh I, Youssef HI.

records.title: Prospecting for efflux pump and repressor genes in rivers of the Amazon region of Brazil.
records.abstract: BackgroundThe spread of multidrug-resistant bacteria in water bodies poses a significant public health concern. Efflux pumps represent critical mechanisms of antimicrobial resistance, regulated by genetic repressors that aid bacterial adaptation to environmental stress. This study profiles the diversity of efflux pump genes and genetic repressors in the surface waters of the Cereja (Bragança) and Uraim (Paragominas) rivers in the Amazon region of Brazil.Methods and resultsSurface water samples were collected along a gradient of anthropogenic impact, and environmental DNA was sequenced on the Illumina platform. The resulting sequencing data were subsequently subjected to metagenomic analysis, which identified a higher abundance of efflux pump genes in the Cereja River compared to the Uraim River, dominated by the RND and SMR families. Additionally, two-component system (TCS) repressor genes, particularly cbrB, were successfully recovered and modeled using Swiss-Model homology modeling.ConclusionsThe higher coverage of the cbrB repressor gene in anthropogenically impacted sites underscores its regulatory role in bacterial stress responses, suggesting its potential application as a novel biomarker of environmental pollution and antibiotic resistance spread in aquatic ecosystems.
records.authors: Chaves VA, Martins DT, Dantas CWD, da Silva SM, da Silva JAG, Queiroz Cavalcante AL, Macedo DB, Fernandes ALL, Tiwari S, Ramos RTJ, Cardenas-Alegria OV.

records.title: Elucidating changes in gene expression driving nuclear dynamics across a foraminiferal life cycle with Pheno2Seq
records.abstract: In many microeukaryotes, conserved morphology masks transitions between haploid and diploid phases of the life cycle, making it difficult to link gene expression to development. Hence, insights on such transitions come largely from ‘model’ lineages of animals, plants and fungi. To address this gap, we developed a method, Pheno2Seq, that enables visualization of fluorescently-stained individuals followed by identification of candidate genes through single-cell transcriptome analyses. We applied this method in  Allogromia laticollaris , a foraminifera with a complex life cycle that alternates between haploid and diploid phases and includes endoreplication to ∼11,000N. As this taxon lacks a reference genome, we used a conservative phylogenomic approach to identify gene families present across diverse foraminifera. We identified >800 differentially expressed genes underlying life cycle transitions along with a similar number of constitutively-expressed genes. During  Zerfall , a phase of extreme endoreplication, the transcriptome is largely silenced with the exception of gene families involved in genome processes and stability. Intriguingly, these gene families include chromatin modifiers, spliceosomal components and histone paralogs, some of which are known to contribute to cell type differentiation in multicellular eukaryotes. We also find numerous genes involved in DNA repair (e.g. DNA damage response and R-loop regulating genes). We speculate that these genes are part of an ancient eukaryotic toolkit, likely present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) and that regulates genomes during life cycle transitions. Our method, Pheno2Seq, can be adapted to diverse lineages to enable the study of life cycle regulation in microeukaryotes that lack morphologically distinguishable life cycle stages.  Significance  Unicellular eukaryotes represent most of the diversity across the eukaryotic tree of life, but life cycle transitions in many of these species can be cryptic (i.e. multiple stages share identical morphology despite changing nuclear phenotypes). We develop Pheno2Seq (Phenotype to Sequence), which characterizes nuclear phenotype by fluorescence microscopy, then elucidates gene expression underlying nuclear stage transitions. Changes in nuclear phenotype in the foraminifera sampled here demonstrates a central role of the reprogramming of histones and other genes involved in chromatin regulation, suggesting that the diverse life cycles observed across the eukaryotic tree of life emerged from a shared toolkit present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA).
records.authors: Sterner EG, Ribeiro GM, Leleu M, Katz LA.

records.title: Integrated multi-omics analysis reveals coordinated root and rhizosphere responses underlying AMF-mediated drought tolerance in kiwifruit.
records.abstract: Drought stress substantially restricts kiwifruit (Actinidia spp.) growth and productivity, yet the mechanisms through which arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) promote drought tolerance remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, root physiological and molecular analyses were integrated with multi-omics profiling of the rhizosphere microbiome to investigate AMF-mediated drought responses under well-watered and drought-stress conditions. Under drought stress, AMF inoculation improved plant growth, root development, cellular ultrastructure, and physiological performance. More importantly, root omics analysis revealed coordinated regulation of drought-responsive pathways involving glutathione metabolism, amino acid biosynthesis, phytohormone regulation, and energy metabolism. Beyond these plant responses, AMF inoculation altered bacterial and fungal community composition, enriched potentially beneficial taxa, and increased rhizosphere network connectivity under drought stress. Within the restructured microbiome, we identified an AMF-specific drought-responsive amplicon sequence variant (ASV) module composed primarily of bacterial taxa and associated with cross-kingdom microbial interactions. Integrated microbial-metabolite network analysis further identified a metabolite feature annotated as 1-piperideine as a candidate associated with selective microbial recruitment in AMF-colonized rhizospheres. Together, these findings suggest that AMF-associated drought tolerance in kiwifruit involves complementary changes in plant physiology, root molecular responses, and rhizosphere microbiome assembly. A mechanistic basis is thereby provided for developing AMF-based strategies to improve kiwifruit production under increasing water limitation.
records.authors: Shah OU, Shuchen F, Jia W, Hongfei S, Luyao C, Wenjie Z, Wenping X.

records.title: Molecular surveillance of adenovirus and coronavirus in Procellariiformes, Brazil: Detection of new divergent adenoviruses.
records.abstract: Adenoviruses are widespread DNA viruses that infect a broad range of vertebrate hosts and are recognized for their long-term host coevolution, remarkable genetic diversity, and broad pathogenic potential. Coronaviruses circulate among wild birds due to their evolutionary potential and are relevant to animal and public health. However, the diversity and ecological role of these viruses in pelagic seabirds remain poorly understood. This study provides the first molecular survey of adenoviruses and coronaviruses in Procellariiformes from the South Atlantic. Fifty stranded individuals representing 12 Procellariiformes species were collected along the southeastern Brazilian coast, between 2017 and 2023. Adenovirus and coronavirus survey were performed using nested PCR protocols, followed by sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and histopathology of positive cases. Adenovirus was detected in seven individuals (14%; 95% CI: 5.8-26.7%) from three species: Southern Giant Petrels (Macronectes giganteus), Cory's Shearwaters (Calonectris borealis), and Black-browed Albatrosses (Thalassarche melanophris). Five sequence types were identified, including similar variants in Southern Giant Petrels and distinct adenoviruses in Cory's Shearwaters and Black-browed Albatrosses. All viruses clustered within a divergent lineage with adenoviruses previously detected in New Zealand seabirds and a Chimney Swift from the USA. No intranuclear inclusion bodies were found in histopathological analysis. All specimens were coronavirus-negative. This first molecular detection of adenoviruses in Procellariiformes expands the known diversity and host range of seabird adenoviruses and suggests circulation of genetically distinct viruses across oceanic regions, highlighting the need for genomic and epidemiological studies of their evolution, transmission, and health impacts.
records.journal: Comparative immunology, microbiology and infectious diseases
records.authors: Baes L, Reigada C, Duarte-Benvenuto A, Zamana RR, Sacristán C, Guerra JM, Schreiner TM, Murro RS, Catão-Dias JL, Ewbank AC.

records.title: Clonal integration drives divergent assembly of rhizosphere bacteria and fungi in Hydrocotyle vulgaris under cadmium heterogeneity.
records.abstract: Clonal plants enhance their fitness in heterogeneous environments through clonal integration, which enables resource sharing among interconnected ramets. However, how clonal integration shapes rhizosphere microbiome assembly and function remains poorly understood. In this study, we constructed patchy heterogeneous soils with cadmium-polluted and unpolluted substrates to simulate fragmented polluted habitats. Apical ramets were grown in cadmium-polluted soil and basal positions were cultivated in unpolluted soil, with stolons left either intact or severed. Rhizosphere and root-zone soils were sampled, and bacterial and fungal communities were characterized via 16 S rRNA and ITS amplicon sequencing. Our results demonstrated that stolon integration significantly altered rhizosphere microbial composition, with elevated relative abundances of Acidobacteriota, Actinobacteriota and Ascomycota and a reduction in Firmicutes. Beneficial genera Streptomyces and Savoryella were enriched under intact stolon treatments. Bacterial α-richness (Chao1) was significantly higher in the rhizosphere of stolon-intact plants, especially at the basal positions, whereas fungal α- richness showed no significant difference among treatments. Beta-diversity analysis revealed that bacterial communities were more sensitive to stolon integration than fungal communities, with fungal community structural shifts observed only in the basal rhizosphere. Amplicon sequence variant (ASV) analysis showed that intact stolons increased unique bacterial ASVs but reduced unique fungal ASVs in the basal rhizosphere. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that clonal integration differentially regulates the assembly of bacterial and fungal communities in the rhizosphere. This study highlights the distinct ecological roles of bacteria and fungi in plant-soil feedback and emphasizes multi-kingdom assessments of clonal integration under heterogeneous Cd condition.
records.authors: Wang XG, Liu B, Wang XX, Jing H, Zhao BN, Yan J, Li D, Zhang R, Si C.

records.title: A Gap-Free Telomere-to-Telomere Genome Assembly of Talaromyces marneffei Strain B33c Provides Insights into Chromosomal Architecture and Comparative Genomics.
records.abstract: Talaromyces marneffei is a thermally dimorphic fungal pathogen endemic to Southeast Asia and southern China, yet chromosome-scale genomic resources from early clinical isolates remain limited. Here, we combined PacBio HiFi sequencing with Oxford Nanopore and Hi-C validation to generate a gap-free, telomere-to-telomere genome assembly of strain B33c, a 1984 clinical isolate from China. The 28.1-Mb assembly comprises eight chromosomes and enabled detailed characterization of chromosomal architecture, including chromosome termini, the repeat landscape, and putative centromeric regions. Using 3314 single-copy orthologs, we reconstructed a time-calibrated phylogeny that recovered two major lineages among the sampled T. marneffei isolates, with B33c clustering closely with the Vietnamese isolates. Comparative synteny analyses showed a largely conserved chromosome-scale backbone within T. marneffei, alongside isolate-specific rearrangement-like patterns. Orthogroup profiling revealed a widely shared gene-family repertoire with isolate-specific variation, as illustrated by differences in the functional enrichment profiles of the ATCC 18224- and B33c-specific orthogroup sets. Overall, the B33c T2T assembly expands genomic resources for T. marneffei and provides additional strain-specific information for comparative studies of genome organization and evolution.

records.title: Chemical diversity analysis identifies inhibitory compounds in the secretomes of citrus-associated Bacillus spp. to the Huanglongbing pathogen, "Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus," and citrus root pathogens.
records.abstract: Huanglongbing (HLB) is a devastating and incurable citrus disease associated with the gram-negative, phloem-limited, and unculturable bacterium "Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus" (CLas), transmitted by the psyllid Diaphorina citri. Our goal was to identify high-performing microbial candidates from a previously established citrus-associated microbial collection for the management of HLB and associated root pathogens. Candidate selection was based on bioactivity, genomic, and metabolomic profiles. Eighteen Bacillus isolates were screened for antagonistic activity against Liberibacter crescens, CLas, and citrus-associated Phytophthora and Fusarium spp. Phylogenetic analysis grouped the isolates into four species groups: Bacillus velezensis, B. subtilis, B. pumilus, and B. cereus. Among these, B. velezensis exhibited the strongest and broadest inhibitory activity, followed by B. subtilis. This enhanced antagonistic potential is likely associated with the greater number and diversity of biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) identified. Notably, CLas-inhibitory isolates included B. velezensis (CB0021 and CB0909) and B. altitudinis (CB0086). Bacilysin and surfactin BGCs were conserved across all CLas-inhibitory isolates, suggesting a potential role in CLas suppression. Accordingly, surfactins were detected in bioactive fractions of B. velezensis (CB0027 and CB0909) and B. subtilis (CB0893), supporting their likely contribution to bioactivity and inhibiting L. crescens growth in vitro, highlighting their potential as candidate compounds for CLas management. Overall, this study underscores the importance of microbial discovery, screening, and characterization as an effective strategy for identifying sustainable solutions to manage HLB.IMPORTANCEHuanglongbing (HLB) is a severe disease of citrus that has altered the citrus landscape worldwide and currently has no cure. It is caused by the bacterium "Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus" (CLas) and transmitted by the psyllid Diaphorina citri. Currently, the most effective control strategy for this disease relies on trunk injection of antibiotics oxytetracycline and streptomycin, and there is a need to find alternative solutions to complement or replace chemical control. Here, we aimed to select high-performing candidates from our previously established citrus-associated microbial collection to manage HLB and root-associated pathogens. We screened 18 Bacillus isolates for antagonistic activity against Liberibacter crescens, CLas, and citrus-associated Phytophthora and Fusarium spp., and we generated their genomic and metabolomic profiles. Our research centers on selecting microbial candidates for their bioactivity and antimicrobial metabolite production, aiming to develop effective plant-protective bioinoculants for mitigation of HLB.
records.authors: Vieira FC, Ramasamy M, Mandadi K, Esteves MB, de Souza A, Allen M, Ruiz Rivera C, Yang C, Maloney KN, Roper MC.

records.title: The e14 cryptic prophage belongs to a temperate phage lineage distributed across Escherichia and retains genes with potential anti-phage defence functions
records.abstract: The e14 region of Escherichia coli str. K-12 is a cryptic prophage that retains functional excision and integration machinery despite extensive loss of phage reproductive functions. However, its evolutionary relationship to other bacteriophages remains poorly resolved. Here, we identify related prophages across four Escherichia species, alongside related, independently isolated bacteriophages. The putative prophages were 34.7–43.5 kb, more than twice the size of e14 (15.2 kb), and retained much of the genomic architecture required for phage reproduction. Comparative genomic and phylogenetic analyses support e14 as a highly reduced member of a broader lineage of temperate bacteriophages. The retention of genes with established or putative anti-phage functions further raises the possibility that e14 represents a form of ‘defence flotsam’, potentially protecting its host against subsequent phage infections. More broadly, cryptic prophages may provide reservoirs of anti-phage defence functions long after losing their capacity for phage reproduction.

records.title: Ecological structuring of biosynthetic potential across terrestrial soil-associated Streptomyces genomes.
records.abstract: Streptomyces populations represent one of the richest reservoirs of microbial specialized metabolites, although the ecological organization of their biosynthetic diversity remains insufficiently resolved at large genomic scales. In the present study, 14,597 publicly available genome assemblies were initially screened. Environmental metadata associated with each genome were subsequently retrieved from the corresponding NCBI BioSample records and systematically curated to retain genomes originating from terrestrial soil-associated environments while excluding marine, freshwater, clinical, laboratory, industrial, and other non-terrestrial sources. Standardized climatic and edaphic variables were examined using principal component analysis (PCA), K-means clustering, and Kruskal-Wallis tests to evaluate ecological differentiation across terrestrial soil-associated Streptomyces populations, with false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment applied to inter-cluster comparisons. PCA revealed pronounced environmental structuring, with Principal Component 1 (PC1) explaining 44.3% of the total variance and Principal Component 2 (PC2) contributing 31.1%, together accounting for 75.4%. K-means clustering resolved three environmentally coherent groups with distinct soil and climatic profiles. Significant differentiation was detected for soil pH, rainfall, temperature, soil organic carbon, and clay content, with adjusted p-values below 0.001. Genome mining using GECCO (GEne Cluster prediction with COnditional Random Fields) revealed extensive biosynthetic diversity dominated by polyketide- and non-ribosomal peptide-associated gene clusters. Total biosynthetic richness also differed significantly among ecological groups (Kruskal-Wallis statistic = 7.28, p Streptomyces populations, advancing understanding of soil microbial and metabolic diversity.

records.title: Symbiont-dependent sexual reproduction in Rhizopus microsporus involves transcriptional reprogramming and RNAi-associated small-RNA responses.
records.abstract: Symbioses play a central role in shaping host development and physiology, yet how multiple symbiotic partners collectively influence complex biological processes remains poorly understood. In the fungal holobiont Rhizopus microsporus, bacterial (Mycetohabitans) and viral (narnaviruses) endosymbionts contribute to the formation of zygospores between compatible sexual partners, although their influence on early sexual reproduction remains largely unexplored. Here, we used mRNA sequencing data to evaluate the impact of bacterial and viral symbionts on the fungal transcriptional landscape at the onset of sexual development, revealing a substantial transcriptional reprogramming. Through network analysis, we identified candidate hub genes, including transcription factors, protein kinases, and signal transduction components, that may contribute to this developmental transition. By integrating sRNA-sequencing data, we found small-RNA signals correlating with early sexual success. Furthermore, we uncovered distinct processing patterns for the RmNV-20S and RmNV-23S viral symbionts, revealing that RmNV-23S processing shifted during the initiation of fungal sexual reproduction in the absence of the bacterial partner. Target prediction analyses further suggest that viral-derived sRNAs could influence distinct functional signatures in the fungal genome. Moreover, predicted interactions between endogenous or viral sRNAs and fungal transcripts suggest a potential role for sRNAs in fine-tuning the host transcriptional profile. Altogether, our findings provide a novel framework for understanding how multi-kingdom symbioses modulate host development and identify potential molecular factors that may contribute to the onset of sexual reproduction in R. microsporus.

records.title: Marine microbial steroids: structural diversity, biosynthetic implications, and functional relevance.
records.abstract: Marine microbial steroids represent a chemically diverse group of natural products arising from sterol metabolism and extensive scaffold tailoring. This critical narrative review synthesises steroids reported from marine fungi, microalgae, bacteria and actinomycetes, with emphasis on source-dependent structural diversification, stereochemical organisation, biosynthetic implications and biological relevance. Fungal metabolites are dominated by oxygenated, epidioxy, lactonised, rearranged and hybrid steroids, whereas microalgae exhibit distinctive sterol-profile diversification and bacteria and actinomycetes contribute transformation products, catabolites and nitrogen-containing derivatives. Across these groups, structural variation is concentrated at oxygenated centres, side chains, ring junctions and hybrid attachment sites. Reported activities include cytotoxic, anti-inflammatory, anti-infective, enzyme-inhibitory and tissue-repair effects, although mechanistic and in vivo validation remains limited. Future progress will depend on integrating genome mining, isotope tracing, enzymatic validation, metabolomics and matched-pair stereochemical studies to connect structure, biosynthesis and function.
records.authors: Liu Y, Zhang D, Yang Y, Zhao X, Zhu T, Chen N, Chu J, Liu B.

records.title: Gene conversion is a key driver of diversity hotspots in Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens and virulence-associated loci.
records.abstract: Despite the long-held view of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) as a genetically conserved pathogen, many genomic regions remain poorly resolved due to high sequence homology and repetitive content. Using complete genome assemblies generated from long-read sequencing of 151 globally representative clinical isolates, we comprehensively analyzed genome-wide patterns of genetic diversity and evolution across the Mtb genome. Our analysis uncovers pronounced diversity hotspots within paralogous regions (PRs) generated by recurrent gene conversion between homologous genes. In many cases, these hotspots exhibit more than an order of magnitude greater genetic diversity than the rest of the Mtb genome, which is otherwise characterized by remarkably low variation. Mutations within these regions display clustered substitution patterns, excess paralog-matching variants, and distinct mutational spectra consistent with ongoing gene conversion. Our analysis identifies over 300 individual gene conversion events (GCEs) distributed throughout the Mtb phylogeny. These GCEs occur predominantly within gene families associated with virulence and host-pathogen interactions, including the PE, PPE, and ESX families. Several of the most pronounced diversity hotspots occur in antigens encoded within PRs. Among these, the vaccine candidate PPE18 harbors mutations in validated epitope sequences and predicted alterations in HLA-II binding. Together, these findings demonstrate that gene conversion actively shapes antigenic and virulence-associated diversity in Mtb.
records.authors: Marin MG, Quinones-Olvera N, Jin H, Harris MA, Jeffrey BM, Rosenthal A, Murphy KC, Sassetti CM, Li H, Farhat MR.

records.title: Multivariate Genome-Wide Analysis Delineates Shared Genetic Determinants Across Periodontal and Oral Microbial Phenotypes.
records.abstract: BackgroundPeriodontitis affects approximately 10% of the global population, posing a serious threat to tooth retention and quality of life. The disease emerges from bidirectional host-microbiome interactions that can shift from homeostasis to dysbiosis and chronic inflammation, yet conventional single-phenotype analyses cannot resolve pleiotropic loci acting across interrelated periodontal and microbial traits. We aimed to jointly model the shared genetic structure of six periodontitis-related phenotypes and to prioritise pleiotropic loci with translational relevance.Methods and materialsWe harmonised European-ancestry genome-wide association studies (GWAS) summary statistics for six traits representing host periodontal phenotypes (gingivitis, chronic periodontitis, periapical abscess, dental calculus) and oral microbial composition (genus Porphyromonas, order Bacteroidales). A common genetic factor was estimated using genomic structural equation modelling (genomic SEM), and factor-level genome-wide association analysis was conducted on 4,899,781 SNPs. The resulting signals were annotated through locus discovery and novelty assessment (FUMA), fine-mapping (SuSiE and FINEMAP), gene-level testing (MAGMA), and transcriptome-wide association with Bayesian gene prioritisation (FUSION and FOCUS). Heritability was partitioned across functional annotations (stratified LD score regression), and cell types (CELLECT); spatial enrichment was assessed using gsMap, and a polygenic risk score was constructed with PRS-CS.ResultsA single-factor model provided adequate fit (CFI = 1.0). Factor-level GWAS identified 127 genome-wide significant SNPs consolidating into 56 independent lead variants, all uniquely identified at the factor level. MAGMA prioritised RASAL2 and C5orf27. Fine-mapping yielded 56 variants with posterior inclusion probabilities exceeding 0.95. Transcriptome-wide association and FOCUS converged on the long non-coding RNA RP11-563N4.1 (PIP = 1). Cell-type enrichment highlighted a vascular-stromal axis led by hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells, with additional signals in pericytes, cardiac and smooth muscle cells, endocardium, and lung stroma. Spatial mapping localised the strongest aggregate signal to lung tissue, consistent with an oral-lung mucosal axis. Polygenic risk was distributed unevenly across chromosomes.ConclusionsThese analyses delineate a vascular-matrix-centred genetic architecture shared across periodontal and oral microbial traits. The prioritised loci and effector genes provide genetically informed candidates for risk stratification and for targeted investigation of periodontal pathobiology. Clinically, these genetically informed candidates may aid in identifying individuals at elevated risk and in guiding mechanism-based preventive and therapeutic strategies for periodontitis.
records.authors: Zhang Y, Chen M, Zhang F.
