records.title: Molecular and functional characterization of interleukin-11b in large yellow croaker (Larimichthys crocea) during pathogen-induced immune responses.
records.abstract: Interleukin-11 (IL-11) is an important cytokine involved in immune regulation in vertebrates. However, the specific functions of the IL-11b paralog in marine fish, particularly in mucosal responses to parasitic infection, remain poorly understood. In this study, an IL-11b homolog, named LcIL-11b, was identified from large yellow croaker (Larimichthys crocea), and its potential role in pathogen-induced immune responses was investigated. The open reading frame of Lcil-11b was 600 bp, encoding a protein of 199 amino acids with a predicted signal peptide and a conserved IL-11 domain. Multiple sequence alignment and phylogenetic analysis showed that LcIL-11b clustered with teleost IL-11b homologs and was distinct from the previously reported IL-11a homolog in large yellow croaker. Tissue distribution analysis showed that Lcil-11b was constitutively expressed in all examined tissues, with relatively high expression levels in the skin and gill. After Cryptocaryon irritans infection, Lcil-11b was significantly induced in mucosal and immune-related tissues, especially at 24 h post-challenge. In head kidney cell line from large yellow croaker (LYCK), inactivated Vibrio alginolyticus stimulation markedly increased Lcil-11b expression at 72 h. Transcriptome and WGCNA analyses further showed that Lcil-11b was located in an infection-responsive module associated with immune receptor signaling, phagocytosis, endocytosis, chemokine signaling, and epithelial responses. Functional assays showed that LcIL-11b overexpression increased SOD and GSH-Px activities, reduced MDA accumulation and apoptosis under bacterial stimulation, and was accompanied by increased transcript levels of jak1, stat3, and bcl2. These results suggest that LcIL-11b is a pathogen-responsive IL-11b homolog and may participate in immune responses and cellular protection in large yellow croaker.

records.title: Unraveling genetic diversity and selection signatures in rice: insights from whole-genome resequencing for precision breeding.
records.abstract: Rice breeding faces numerous challenges in selecting potential materials that combine high grain yield with enhanced adaptability to diverse conditions and stress-prone environments. We sequenced the genomes of 70 conventional japonica rice varieties from Zhejiang Province to assess their genetic diversity and provide genomic support for future rice breeding efforts. Whole-genome resequencing technology serves as an effective tool for elucidating genetic diversity, deciphering population structure, and exploring adaptive evolution of rice germplasm, providing valuable insights for advancing molecular breeding efforts. To enhance the utilization of japonica genetic resources and facilitate the breeding of new varieties, a study utilizing whole-genome resequencing analysis was performed on genetic data from 70 japonica rice accessions originating in Zhejiang Province, China. We systematically investigated genetic diversity, population structure, and selection signatures through phylogenetic tree construction, principal component analysis (PCA), and select elimination analysis. Our findings revealed that the conventional japonica rice varieties in this region exhibit substantial genetic diversity, with distinct population stratification into two genetically divergent subgroups. Through select elimination analysis, 112 genomic regions that had undergone selection pressure during the breeding process were identified. Subsequent KEGG and GO enrichment analyses of candidate genes within these selected genomic regions provided a foundation for future research on gene function. Additionally, haplotype analysis further revealed significant allelic variations correlated with agronomic traits, providing valuable genetic information for improving rice varieties. This research establishes a robust genomic foundation for precision breeding and provides actionable insights to optimize the development of improved japonica rice varieties. Our findings reveal two genetically distinct subgroups among Zhejiang japonica rice varieties, with different levels of diversity reflecting their breeding histories. We identified multiple genomic regions and candidate genes that likely experienced selection. These results provide a genomic basis for more targeted use of Zhejiang japonica germplasm in future breeding efforts.
records.authors: Huang F, Lv Y, Ye J, Miao T, Wu M, Zhai R, Yu F, Zhu G, Zhang X, Zhu J, Ye S.

records.title: Species-level Torque teno virus abundance is associated with immune impairment, epigenetic aging markers, and clinical vulnerability in hospitalized older adults: the VIROMA study.
records.abstract: Torque teno viruses (TTVs) are ubiquitous components of the human virome whose replication is tightly regulated by host immunity. While elevated total TTV load has been associated with increased mortality in older adults, the clinical relevance of species-level virome composition remains unclear. We profiled the circulating anellovirome in 251 hospitalized older adults using amplicon-based whole-genome sequencing and investigated associations with frailty, cognitive impairment, mortality, immune remodeling, and epigenetic aging. Reduced TTV species evenness was associated with 1-year mortality (p = 0.013, FDR = 0.052); however, differences in species composition accounted for less than 1% of the total variance (PERMANOVA: Ružička R2 = 0.0079, p = 0.021, FDR = 0.035; Bray-Curtis R2 = 0.0082, p = 0.035, FDR = 0.035), indicating that host-related factors rather than distinct clinical phenotypes primarily shaped the virome. Following multivariable adjustment, differential abundance analyses identified TTV19 enrichment in patients with 1- and 3-year mortality, frailty, and cognitive impairment, alongside TTV9 enrichment in frail patients. Bootstrap resampling confirmed a stable association between TTV19 and cognitive impairment (logFC = 2.39, 95% CI 0.59-5.43) and between TTV9 and frailty (logFC = 2.26, 95% CI 0.11-9.86). Conversely, multivariable Cox models showed no significant association between TTV19 abundance and 1-year or 3-year mortality, and only a nominal association with seven-year mortality (HR 1.10, 95% CI 1.01-1.19) that did not pass multiple testing correction. Species-specific associations with DNA methylation-estimated immune cell subsets further supported links between selected TTV species and immune remodeling. TTV19 log-abundance showed a positive nominal association with Age Acceleration GrimAge (p = 0.024, FDR = 0.072), and with DNAm-estimated inflammatory and vascular markers. Overall, these findings suggest that the circulating anellovirome primarily reflects systemic vulnerability rather than disease-specific signatures in late life. A limited subset of viral species may represent candidate correlates of immune dysregulation and biological aging requiring further validation.

records.title: L-carnitine conjugation: a previously unrecognized pathway proposed for anaerobic benzo(a)pyrene biodegradation by Alicycliphilus sp. T452 under nitrate‑reducing conditions.
records.abstract: Anaerobic respiration of microorganisms is a key process driving the degradation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in contaminated environments. However, the mechanism underlying the anaerobic breakdown of benzo(a)pyrene remains poorly understood, limiting our knowledge of the fate and natural attenuation potential of this hazardous compound. Here, we report a novel nitrate‑reducing bacterium, Alicycliphilus sp. T452, isolated from PAH‑contaminated river sediment, which degrades benzo(a)pyrene under anaerobic conditions with a degradation ratio of 40.6% ± 2.9% over 100 h. Using UHPLC‑QTOF/MS‑based metabolite profiling, 18 potential intermediates were putatively identified, including four L‑carnitine‑conjugated intermediates, of which two were supported by deuterium labeling. Genomic and transcriptomic analyses revealed that specific clusters containing genes encoding Pfam L-carnitine dehydratase bile acid/inducible protein were specifically upregulated during benzo(a)pyrene degradation, providing multi-omics evidence supporting the proposal of a L‑carnitine‑conjugated pathway. This L‑carnitine conjugation likely enhances the solubility and intracellular transport of hydrophobic benzo(a)pyrene‑derived metabolites, representing a proposed microbial strategy to overcome bioavailability constraints. In addition, L‑carnitine is naturally present in anoxic environments, and its conjugation may represent a general microbial adaptation to hydrophobic organic contaminants. Our findings thus expand our understanding of the anaerobic fate of PAHs and offer mechanistic insights into their natural attenuation in contaminated environments.

records.title: Structure of the Chimalliviridae bacteriophage Goslar reveals host recognition and infection machinery.
records.abstract: Large-genome bacteriophages (phages) of the Chimalliviridae family have a distinctive life cycle, building compartments inside infected bacterial cells that broadly protect their genomes from host defenses. Here, we use cryo-electron microscopy to determine a structure of the Escherichia coli-infecting Chimalliviridae phage Goslar. We combine manual modeling of 25 structural proteins with AlphaFold structure predictions of an additional three proteins to generate a composite model with 2888 protein chains from 28 different structural proteins, totaling more than 1.4 million amino acid residues. Our structure reveals the architecture of the Goslar capsid, portal, tail, and baseplate, highlighting structural similarities and differences with other tailed phages. Combining our structural data with quantitative mass spectrometry of Goslar virions, we identify several high-copy virion-associated proteins that likely play key roles when injected into host cells upon infection. We also identify a Chimalliviridae-specific family of proteins that form long, flexible filaments anchored at the phage baseplate and which incorporate carbohydrate-binding domains, suggesting a key role in host recognition.
records.authors: Basu D, Gu Y, Li YX, Forman T, Ghassemian M, Min RK, Pogliano J, Corbett KD.

records.title: kinGEMs: A robust and scalable framework for resource-constraint models through stochastic tuning of deep learning-predicted kinetic parameters.
records.abstract: The construction of accurate enzyme-constrained genome-scale models (ecGEMs) remains a critical challenge in systems biology, limited by sparse kinetic data and the need for biologically meaningful representations. This work presents an integrated framework combining CPI-Pred, a deep learning model to predict kinetic parameters (kcat) from sequence and compound embeddings, with kinGEMs, a pipeline to incorporate these uncertainty-aware parameters into ecGEMs for metabolic optimization. By leveraging representations at multiple scales, the approach captures sequence, structure, and kinetic data to enhance model generalizability and accuracy. Rigorous benchmarking demonstrates the framework's capability to predict growth rates and fluxes that are consistent with experimental observations and measured proteome fractions, reduce median flux variability by several folds, and yield better-constrained metabolic models by explicitly accounting for the uncertainty inherent in ML-predicted kinetic parameters. kinGEMs successfully generated ecGEMs for 93 models spanning a phylogenetically diverse set of organisms including Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, mycobacteria, parasitic protists, fungi, and mammalian cell lines. These innovations breakdown the barrier to application of ecGEMs to non-model organisms and open new avenues for metabolic engineering and synthetic biology in more industrially relevant hosts.
records.authors: A Barghout R, Chiñas Serrano L, Sanchez-Lengeling B, Mahadevan R.

records.title: Sexing carnivores from faecal metagenomes: calibrating  R    x    for stone marten and red fox
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Knowing the sex of the animal that deposited a scat adds value to non-invasive monitoring, but read-ratio sexing methods were developed for human ancient DNA. We examined their use in shotgun metagenomes of seven stone marten (  Martes foina ) and red fox (  Vulpes vulpes ) scats. Human DNA, present in every library, was removed by competitive mapping against the host assembly and the human reference. Applying the Skoglund  R y metric to the marten samples yielded 0 to 25 Y-mapping reads per sample and failed to identify either of the two animals that  R x places firmly in the male range, so we adopted the X-to-autosome ratio  R x of Mittnik et al. instead, reimplemented as an open-source, species-agnostic Python tool. To test whether its human-derived thresholds transfer, we simulated female and male genomes of both species and drew 200 replicate subsamples at each of fourteen depths from 1,000 to 100,000 mapped reads. Nine of 11,200 replicates were assigned to the wrong sex, all of them below 2,000 mapped reads; above that depth the only failure was non-assignment, in under 5% of replicates above 7,500 reads and under 1% above 15,000. Applied to the scats,  R x identified four females and two males; one sample with 596 host-assigned reads was left unassigned. With competitive removal of human reads,  R x and its original thresholds are usable in these carnivores.
records.authors: Vujić V, Mayer C, Helyes G, Maróti-Agóts Á, Maróti G, Csabai I, Solymosi N.

records.title: Widespread  Saccharomyces  hybridization in agave fermentations arises repeatedly from asymmetric parental diversity
records.abstract: Interspecific hybridization can profoundly reshape genomes by bringing together divergent genetic backgrounds, yet its ecological and evolutionary dynamics remain poorly understood at the population level. Here, we identify an extensive hybridization system in traditional agave fermentations across Mexico involving  Saccharomyces cerevisiae , a species frequently associated with human-managed environments, and its predominantly wild relative  S. paradoxus . A genomic survey reveals unexpectedly high hybrid frequencies in geographically distant regions with contrasting environments. Targeted sampling of distilleries and surrounding natural sites reveals a strong ecological bias, with hybrids recovered almost exclusively from distilleries, although both parental species occur in anthropogenic and natural habitats. Hybrid genomes show extensive architectural diversity, including distinct ploidies, variable parental genome contributions, variable patterns of heterozygosity, and contrasting mitochondrial ancestries. Phylogenomic and population-structure analyses of hybrid subgenomes demonstrate multiple independent origins. These recurrent events show pronounced asymmetry in parental genetic diversity. Hybrids derive from several  S. cerevisiae populations, already shaped by extensive introgression, whereas every  S. paradoxus subgenome traces to a single genetically differentiated  S. paradoxus lineage found exclusively in distilleries, an unexpected association for a predominantly wild species. These findings establish agave fermentations as an exceptional system for studying recurrent interspecific hybridization and reveal how pronounced asymmetry in parental ancestry can shape hybrid formation.  Impact statement  Interspecific hybridization is a powerful source of evolutionary novelty, but its dynamics are rarely resolved at the population level outside experimental systems. We uncover a widespread system of recurrent  Saccharomyces hybridization associated with agave fermentations, revealing multiple independent origins and a striking asymmetry in the parental lineages that contribute to hybrid formation, with diverse  S. cerevisiae backgrounds repeatedly mating with a single, human-associated  S. paradoxus lineage.
records.authors: Avelar-Rivas JA, Aguirre-Dugua X, López-Gallegos C, Sedeño I, Echavarría-Solana R, Santiago-Garduño E, Arias M, Kirchmayr MR, Liti G, DeLuna A, Morales L, Mancera E.

records.title: Hybrid RY-mers increase aDNA alignment sensitivity
records.abstract: One of the key steps in ancient DNA data analysis is the accurate identification of endogenous short reads that originate from the ancient genome. Currently, this step is performed using general-purpose sequence aligners, such as BWA-aln, with parameter settings optimized for sensitivity. This approach results in increased runtime, even relative to standard DNA alignment workflows, and is not sufficient for aligning samples that are highly divergent from a reference database. We introduce hybrid RY-mers, a seed construct designed to incorporate aDNA-specific sequence damage. We adapt hybrid RY-mers to the existing concept of multi-context seeds and implement them in the read aligner strobealign. On simulated genomic and metagenomic datasets, we show that hybrid RY-mers result in higher mapping accuracy, while also reducing runtime by 4-6 times compared to the state-of-the-art aDNA alignment method BWA-aln. Furthermore, substituting aDNA aligner MALT in the metagenomic tool-suite aMeta with our new alignment approach demonstrated that aMeta gave a faster and less memory consuming detection of ancient taxa present in the samples.
records.authors: Tolstoganov I, Sahlin K.

records.title: Coarse-graining genome-scale metabolic models for dynamic, multi-scale simulations of  Pseudomonas aeruginosa  in gel environments
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Microbial communities are shaped by coupled interactions between microenvironment conditions and the intracellular adaptations that emerge in response external metabolic cues. For pathogenic microbes such as  Pseudomonas aeruginosa , these interactions can rapidly generate heterogeneous sub-populations that exhibit adaptations for sustaining host infection and resisting antibiotic treatment. Technological strides in -omics data collection, combined with robust computational tools like genome-scale metabolic models (GEM) for predicting cellular metabolism, have yielded promising multi-scale depictions of microbial population development in simulated spatial environments. These multi-scale model simulations help establish and evaluate mechanistic contexts for how infection-enhancing behaviors might emerge in the population or be influenced by variable perturbations in the biological system. However, the number and rigorous tuning of parameters influencing the connections between intracellular-extracellular events pose barriers when shaping simulations to different  in vitro systems of interest. In this work, we present a genome-scale, metabolism-informed continuum model (GEM-CM), a computational framework for coupling a reaction-diffusion model to a surrogate GEM representation that generates metabolic rate predictions informed by flux balance analysis outputs. A key feature of GEM-CM is its application of random forest regression, or ensembles, to coarse-grain the interface connecting the GEM and reaction-diffusion models down to a small set of input metabolites methodically chosen through the random forest’s evaluation of feature importance.  To demonstrate GEM-CM’s utility, we evaluated simulation predictions against  P. aeruginosa PA14 populations radially propagating in low weight percentage agar gels. In addition to biomass growth, we simulated PA14 populations producing the cytotoxic secondary metabolite pyocyanin (PCN). GEM-CM could capture PA14 growth dynamics in agar gels when ensembles were provided with three carbon source inputs describing the simulated growth media. Bacterial motility parameters and the random forest ensemble allowed GEM-CM simulations to accurately predict spatial biomass distributions for PA14 populations over time and probe their PCN production dynamics. Ensembles also demonstrated robust performance for single gene knockout conditions with GEM-CM simulation accurately capturing the partial or total biomass and PCN inhibition observed in transposon mutant screenings. When evaluating transposon mutant population development, the GEM-CM framework additionally suggested that  metH may be a promising target to inhibit the spatial propagation of PA14. This work’s proof-of-concept applications illustrated GEM-CM utility as an early stage multi-scale modeling tool for interrogating  in vitro metabolic behavior in microbial populations.  1. AUTHOR SUMMARY  Pathogenic microbial communities alter their environmental conditions as they grow and propagate, which in turn drives the development of heterogenous metabolic behaviors across different spatial regions in the population. Computational simulations using genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) can offer insights into how bacteria metabolic behaviors can influence larger population-level outcomes. Many of these simulation platforms however involve extensive parameter optimization to situate the GEM to its simulated environment making their application a challenge at the early investigation stages. To address this, we developed a computational approach that innovatively utilizes a random forest regression model to perform metabolic predictions in place of the GEM. This random forest surrogate approach reduces the number of parameters required to connect it to a simulated environment while still providing valuable, informed predictions for bacterial metabolism. We tested this computational approach to simulate  Pseudomonas aeruginosa propagation and their production of cytotoxic pyocyanin in low weight percentage agar gels. Simulations demonstrated their robustness for capturing biomass and pyocyanin perturbations in  P. aeruginosa gene knockouts and revealed potential intracellular mechanisms that may inhibit the pathogenic community’s spatial expansion. We believe this multi-scale computational approach provides population models valuable connections to metabolic behaviors, which can inform early stage investigations of crucial variables driving  in vitro bacterial population development.
records.authors: Kim MS, Papin JA, Ford RM.

records.title: Taxonomic validation of Saccharomycotina yeast genome assemblies through type-material-anchored BLAST-based average nucleotide identity analysis at the NCBI.
records.abstract: The extensive genomic resources available for Saccharomycotina yeasts, including assemblies derived from type material, make this group well suited for genome-based taxonomic verification. This study evaluates the effectiveness of type-material-informed Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI) analysis for verifying the taxonomic assignments of Saccharomycotina genome assemblies. Public yeast genome assemblies were compared against type material assemblies using an alignment-based ANI workflow. Operational thresholds were established, and results were compared with DNA-DNA hybridization and FastANI analyses. Assemblies were evaluated by best-match status and coverage, and problematic type assemblies were flagged for further review. A 95% ANI threshold yielded high concordance with declared species assignments among query-to-type comparisons. Cases of high similarity between different species and hybrid genomes were identified, highlighting the need for expert taxonomic review in certain instances. The alignment-based ANI showed a strong correlation with traditional DNA-DNA reassociation values and agreed closely with FastANI for highly alignable assemblies. Type-material-informed ANI is a reliable tool for automated taxonomic verification of yeast genome assemblies, but its effectiveness depends on the availability and quality of type assemblies and accurate metadata. The approach enables continuous quality control and supports broader application in fungal taxonomy, with recommendations for improving reference coverage and data submission practices.
records.authors: Robbertse B, Kannan S, DiCuccio M, Hoffman J, Schoch CL, Kimchi A.

records.title: Allelic Homogenization of Detoxification Genes RsCYP3A24 and RsGSTF5 Is Associated with Metabolic Resistance to SYP-14288 in Rhizoctonia solani.
records.abstract: Fungicide resistance in multinucleate fungi, such as Rhizoctonia solani, poses a growing challenge for effective disease management. This study explores the molecular mechanisms underlying resistance to the fungicide SYP-14288 in R. solani, focusing on the role of two detoxification genes (RsCYP3A24 and RsGSTF5) and fungal nuclear heterogeneity. Genotyping analysis revealed that the parental R. solani strain harbors mixed allelic variants. Under fungicide stress, continuous subculturing reduced nuclear heterogeneity in resistant mutants, which progressively showed apparent allelic fixation of selected sequence variants, a genotypic shift toward homokaryotization. Transcriptomic and genomic analyses revealed significant upregulation and optimized gene composition of these detoxification genes in the resistant mutants. Functional validation through enzymatic activity assays confirmed that RsCYP3A24 participates in phase I oxidation, whereas RsGSTF5 mediates phase II glutathione-conjugation detoxification. Heterologous expression in Escherichia coli demonstrated that the detoxification proteins of resistant strains with fixed resistance-associated alleles possessed greater detoxification efficiency for SYP-14288. These genes were coordinately upregulated and functionally enhanced under fungicide selection pressure. This selective pressure altered the nuclear composition of heterokaryotic populations and promoted adaptive evolution characterized by allelic homogenization. Overall, this study provides new insights into the relationship between allelic variation and metabolic resistance in multinucleate fungi and offers valuable guidance for the sustainable management of fungicide resistance.
records.authors: Liang Z, Zhou R, Zhang J, Wu Z, Deng W, Zhu L, Zhang B, Yu C, Hao J, Liu X, Liu P.

records.title: Bacterial Soft Rot of Oncidium Orchids Caused by Dickeya fangzhongdai, Dickeya zeae, and Pectobacterium aroidearum: Pathogen Characterization and Screening of Resistant Germplasm.
records.abstract: Dickeya and Pectobacterium species are globally important soft rot pathogens causing significant crop losses. From 2024 to 2025, 120 Oncidium plants with soft rot symptoms were collected from six areas in Fujian Province, China, yielding 91 bacterial isolates. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that 69 isolates (75.82%) belonged to Dickeya and Pectobacterium. Subsequent gapA phylogenetic analysis identified these as three species: 61 Dickeya fangzhongdai (88.41%), 6 D. zeae (8.70%), and 2 Pectobacterium aroidearum (2.90%). Multilocus sequence analysis based on 16 housekeeping genes, together with whole-genome sequencing and in silico analyses (average nucleotide identity and in silico DNA-DNA hybridization), confirmed the species-level identification, with all values exceeding established thresholds. This is the first report of D. fangzhongdai, D. zeae, and P. aroidearum causing soft rot in Oncidium orchids. Pathogenicity assays on 137 accessions (comprising commercial cultivars, breeding lines, and wild accessions) showed that Dickeya strains exhibited strong virulence (mean lesion: 21.63 to 23.34 mm), while P. aroidearum was significantly weaker (8.83 mm). Wild accessions displayed the highest resistance (7.62 to 16.91 mm), followed by commercial cultivars (8.75 to 24.47 mm), with breeding lines most susceptible (10.22 to 31.13 mm). Five resistant accessions were identified, including two broad-spectrum resistant wild accessions (86 and 130) with stable resistance to all five tested strains (lesion: 2.36 to 3.48 mm). Host range assays showed that the pathogens could infect eight additional orchid genera, indicating broad pathogenic potential. This study provides the first comprehensive characterization of these three pathogens in Oncidium soft rot and identifies valuable resistant germplasm for breeding programs.
records.authors: Fang N, Fan R, Ling B, Luo Y, Chen Y, Chen Y, Zhong S, Kong L, Lin R, Lai N, He J, Zhong H, Ye X.

records.title: Computational functional annotation and structural modelling of hypothetical proteins in Stenotrophomonas maltophilia NCTC10958.
records.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance represents a significant global health challenge, specifically concerning the escalation of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia has emerged as a prevalent pathogen affecting immunocompromised patients in intensive care units. Its incidence has notably increased, particularly during the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic, complicated by resistance mechanisms such as enzymatic degradation and biofilm formation. Despite its clinical importance, the functional roles of many genomic regions remain obscure. This study aimed to characterize 61 hypothetical proteins from S. maltophilia NCTC10958 to elucidate their involvement in virulence and adaptation. Functional annotation revealed that a significant proportion of these proteins are membrane-associated enzymes and transporters essential for environmental adaptation. Key findings include the identification of putative virulence factors involved in biofilm formation and motility, such as phosphoglycerate mutase and type IV pilus assembly proteins. Crucially, the analysis uncovered key functional determinants, including a ComEC/Rec2 family competence protein involved in DNA uptake and a mycobacterial membrane protein large family transporter linked to cell envelope processes and transport. Structural modelling validated high-confidence tertiary structures for these targets, confirming their biological feasibility. These insights provide a foundation for understanding the pathogenicity of S. maltophilia NCTC10958 and highlight specific HPs as promising candidates for therapeutic intervention.
records.authors: Alnaqshabandy IHF.

records.title: Impact of organic carbon on biogas valorization consortium: shift of intracellular storage and microbial succession.
records.abstract: Methanotroph-microalgae consortia can convert CH4 and CO2 into biomass, but the responses of the consortia to external organic carbon remain insufficiently characterized. This study investigated the effects of stepwise addition of acetate, which was used as a model organic carbon source, on a continuously operated biogas fed methanotroph-microalgae consortium. Reactor performance, carbon transformation, biomass composition, microbial succession, and metagenomic functional-gene profiles were examined. During operation with 50 mg acetate C/L, biomass concentration increased from the acetate-free baseline of 1.25 to 1.88 g/L, alongside improved ammonium removal and without compromising the efficiency of biogas conversion. Across the acetate-fed stages, the proportion of prokaryotic sequences increased, accompanied by changes in biomass composition. The glycogen-equivalent carbohydrate fraction increased from 25% to 52% of biomass dry weight. This enrichment coincided with higher abundances of glgM, glgE, and glgB, whereas protein content decreased from 44% to 30% and lipids dropped to below 10%. These synthetic model-system findings provide a basis for investigating integrated wastewater treatment and biogas conversion, with practical applicability requiring validation using real waste streams.
records.authors: Zhang B, Liu J, Zhuo M, Cai C, Zhou Y.

records.title: Development of a Four-Strain Rhizobacterial Consortium: Detection in the Field by Strain-Specific qPCR and Impact on the Wheat Rhizosphere Microbiome
records.abstract: Multi-strain consortia are expected to protect plants more reliably than single strains, yet this is rarely tested directly, and the behavior of introduced strains in the field is difficult to follow. We assembled a consortium of Stenotrophomonas rhizophila MGMM118, Bacillus halotolerans MGMM119, Pseudomonas grimontii MGMM120 and Pseudomonas viciae MGMM121 strains isolated from the winter wheat rhizosphere and characterized their hydrolytic activities, auxin production, and analyzed their genomes. The consortium increased shoot and root length of wheat. In biocontrol experiments on barley, the consortium reduced the root rot disease index caused by Fusarium culmorum by approximately ten-fold (5.6% vs. 59.7%), outperforming each individual strain (11.9–17.9%). The consortium also reduced Fusarium root rot in tomato by two-fold. In a field experiment on wheat, strain-specific qPCR detected all introduced microorganisms in the wheat rhizosphere at up to 106 CFU per gram of soil, demonstrating different dynamics for each individual strain. Metabarcoding showed that community structure depended on plant developmental stage rather than on the consortium application. Since metabarcoding could not reliably identify the introduced strains, we suppose that strain-specific qPCR is a more appropriate tool for monitoring of inoculants, particularly in complex soil microbial communities.

records.title: Opposing microbiome-mediated axes link modifiable lifestyles to health and chronic diseases.
records.abstract: Analyses disentangling the role of the gut microbiome in linking lifestyle factors to health outcomes remain limited. Here, using fecal shotgun metagenomics from 6,803 adults in the Japanese 4D cohort, we identified two opposing microbiome-mediated axes linking lifestyle to health and 15 diseases. A health-associated axis enriched in microbial metabolism of dietary components was linked to plant-based, soy and dairy intake. In contrast, a disease-associated axis, enriched in oral-derived bacteria and pathobionts, was linked to refined carbohydrates and sedentary behavior. Starter culture microorganisms used to ferment foods did not show statistically significant mediation of the observed health effects. Alcohol was associated with both health- and disease-oriented mediation patterns involving microbial host-glycan utilization. Microbiome-defined health- and disease-oriented mediator axes were supported by fecal short-chain fatty acids and plasma cytokines from >1,700 individuals, revealing butyrate-associated anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory host profiles, respectively. Microbiome-based prediction (MADE) scores captured lifestyle-microbiome-disease mediation patterns and distinguished individual diseases across 13 independent external cohorts from the United States, China, Sweden, Russia and Australia. We identify the gut microbiome as a key mediator linking lifestyle to health and disease, providing a framework for microbiome-based assessment to guide lifestyle interventions for health promotion and disease prevention.

records.title: Epidemics by beneficial microorganisms drive evolution.
records.abstract: Epidemics of beneficial microorganisms (beneficial to the host) generally go unobserved; a few recent advantageous epidemics have been reported, including an epidemic of corals by a Vibrio species that made them resistant to bleaching and epidemics of stinkbugs by Burkholderia spp. that conferred resistance of the insect to the insecticide fenitrothion. There are similarities and differences between epidemics caused by pathogenic and by beneficial microbes. Both contain genomic islands (GIs) involved in epidemics. GIs of pathogenic bacteria contain virulence genes, such as those encoding specific toxins that damage eukaryotic cells, in addition to fitness genes that assist colonization. GIs of beneficial bacteria lack virulence genes, but contain similar fitness genes. Pathogenic epidemics are detected almost immediately through symptoms and have a finite time, whereas beneficial epidemics mostly go undetected and can persist for long periods, possibly leading to genetic and thus evolutionary changes. The key to epidemics (beneficial or pathogenic) is rapid horizontal transmission of the causative agent from one host to another via contaminated surfaces, water, air, and by direct contact. Vertical transmission can also occur. Pathogenic bacteria elicit an immune response, while beneficial bacteria usually do not, since they are recognized by the host as "self". There are many examples of important evolutionary events that were driven by the acquisition of microbes by animals and plants. However, acquisition of a microbe, leading to evolution, can be considered an epidemic only if the infection spreads rapidly. We suggest that beneficial epidemics can help explain at least the initial steps of punctuated evolution.
records.journal: Infection, genetics and evolution : journal of molecular epidemiology and evolutionary genetics in infectious diseases
records.authors: Rosenberg E.

records.title: Chloroplast genome engineering: Recent advances, pathways towards commercialization and future directions.
records.abstract: Chloroplasts are ideal biofactories because thousands of transgene copies integrated into each plant cell to produce high levels of recombinant proteins and enzymes. Because chloroplast genomes are predominantly maternally inherited, transgenes are generally not transmitted via pollen. Nuclear genome engineering ushered in the GMO revolution for crop protection that mostly required lower levels of transgene expression. Higher level expression and biosafety through gene containment facilitate new applications of GM crops, including production of high-value biopharmaceuticals and enzymes. This review focuses on recent advances in this field, including the first FDA approval of biopharmaceuticals made in plant cells for evaluation in human clinical trials, topical or oral drug delivery, marker free edible plants by removal of antibiotic resistance genes and novel post-translational modifications required to produce functional human proteins. In addition, new tools are discussed to improve DNA delivery, vector free assembly, episomal or integration methods, enhancement of transgene expression through optimization of regulatory sequences, codons, targeted genome editing and other innovations in biomanufacturing. Topical drug delivery using plant cells incorporated into chewing gums to control oral viruses, pathogenic bacteria, or yeast and oral drug delivery with therapeutic proteins made in plant cells to treat diabetes, obesity and cardiopulmonary diseases currently advanced to human clinical trials are discussed. In addition, high-value industrial enzymes for launching new products or to confer valuable agronomic traits or enhance photosynthesis are discussed. Future perspectives section provides examples of biotechnology products anticipated to be launched in the next 3-5 years, with opportunities and anticipated challenges.
records.authors: Fatima I, Daniell H.

records.title: Mucosal transcriptomic and fecal microbiome signatures associated with persistent symptoms in quiescent Crohn's disease.
records.abstract: BackgroundPersistent symptoms in quiescent Crohn's disease (qCD + S) lack clear mechanistic explanations. Building on prior evidence linking qCD + S to sulfidogenic microbial metabolism, this study characterizes the underlying site-specific mucosal transcriptional programs and host-microbe interactions associated with qCD + S.MethodsWe integrated paired metagenomic and transcriptomic data from a cross-sectional cohort of patients with qCD. Host-microbe interactions in the ileum and rectosigmoid colon were analyzed using differential expression, penalized regression, and sparse canonical correlation analysis.ResultsqCD + S was associated with transcriptional differences in separate analyses of ileal and rectosigmoid samples. The ileum showed reduced expression of genes related to immune surveillance, whereas the rectosigmoid colon exhibited reduced chemokine-related and increased ribosomal gene expression. Multi-omic integration identified associations between previously identified sulfidogenic microbes and mucosal genes related to mitochondrial metabolism, epithelial homeostasis, and neurosensory signaling. Exploratory sparse canonical correlation analysis identified multivariate patterns involving oral-associated taxa and mucosal genes related to B-cell receptor signaling and RNA-processing.ConclusionsPersistent symptoms in qCD are mucosal transcriptional differences and fecal microbial features. These findings suggest a model in which altered immune regulation, microbial sulfur metabolism, and downstream epithelial and metabolic stress pathways contribute to symptom persistence despite quiescent inflammation, but this model requires mechanistic validation.
records.authors: Guo K, Golob J, Berinstein J, Sheehan J, Chey WD, Higgins PDR, Young V, Rao K, Singh P, Bishu S, Lee A.

records.title: The Isolation and Characterisation of Antimicrobial Core Histone from Chondrus crispus species.
records.abstract: Histones are classical DNA-binding proteins, rich in cationic amino acids, and recently also reported as effective antimicrobial agents against a range of Gram-negative and Gram-positive pathogens. While histones with antimicrobial functions have been identified in various marine organisms, little is known regarding the identification and characterisation of innate antimicrobial proteins and peptides, including histones, from macroalgae species. This study aimed to develop an isolation and purification protocol for histones by combining in-silico analyses with wet-laboratory techniques to identify and isolate core histones from the red macroalga Chondrus crispus. The antimicrobial properties of the purified core histone were examined against a variety of pathogenic bacteria using both minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and disk diffusion assays. The purification of the core histone fraction was assessed using SDS-PAGE analysis. The findings indicated that the core histone extracted from C. crispus displayed antimicrobial properties against a range of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, including Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, and the marine pathogens Vibrio anguillarum and Yersinia ruckeri. Furthermore, the purified core histone was digested by trypsin into peptides. The resulting peptides exhibited enhanced bacterial inhibition against both E. coli and S. aureus. These results indicate, for the first time, that C. crispus histone proteins and peptides possess antimicrobial activity. In addition to its antimicrobial properties, the purified core histone showed minimal cytotoxic effects when tested in mammalian cells. As a result, the core histone obtained from C. crispus shows potential as a novel antimicrobial candidate, supporting further evaluation across additional mammalian cell types.
records.authors: Caprani M, O'Keeffe J, Healy J, Slattery O.

records.title: Microbiota-driven of chromosomal instability in colorectal cancer.
records.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common malignancy worldwide and the second leading cause of cancer-related death, and chromosomal instability (CIN) underlies 65-70% of sporadic cases. Here we review the evidence that the gut microbiota acts as an environmental instigator of CIN through three mechanistically intertwined routes. The first is direct genotoxicity: pks+ Escherichia coli produce colibactin, which alkylates deoxyadenosine to form DNA interstrand cross-links whose repair generates double-strand break intermediates and the mutational signatures SBS88 and ID18; transient exposure of primary colon epithelial cells suffices to provoke chromosomal aberrations and malignant transformation. The second is community-level dysbiosis: the oncomicrobial community subtypes OCS2 and OCS3 are enriched in CIN-positive tumours and carry the reactive oxygen species-related signature SBS18, while at strain-level resolution Fusobacterium nucleatum subspecies animalis clade C2 shows the strongest association with the tumour niche, and Parvimonas micra and Peptostreptococcus stomatis contribute through WNT/β-catenin activation and Th17-skewed immunity. The third, advanced here as a working framework rather than an established mechanism, is the microbiota-induced bystander effect (MIBE), in which microbiota-driven para-inflammation creates a milieu rich in reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and inflammatory cytokines that damages DNA in neighbouring epithelial cells and establishes a field of cancerization. We integrate these routes into a three-stage model (initiation, propagation, perpetuation) linking microbial exposure to APC, KRAS and TP53 alterations, discuss translation towards risk stratification, faecal metagenomic diagnosis, OCS-based prognostication and targeted prevention, and delineate the limitations of the current evidence.

records.title: Phage-encoded protein PhiP targets HemA to block heme biosynthesis, suppressing bacterial growth and promoting phage propagation.
records.abstract: Bacteriophages encode diverse proteins that subvert host metabolism to promote viral propagation. Elucidating the functions and mechanisms of these proteins not only deepens our understanding of phage-host interactions but also offers new avenues for antibacterial development. Here, we identify PhiP, a protein encoded by the Pseudomonas aeruginosa phage PaoP5, as a potent inhibitor of bacterial growth. Ectopic expression of PhiP leads to impaired cell proliferation and elongation. Co-immunoprecipitation assays identify HemA, the glutamyl-tRNA reductase that catalyzes the first committed step of heme biosynthesis, as a direct interacting target of PhiP. Mechanistically, PhiP-mediated inhibition of HemA disrupts heme production, leading to accumulation of intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), heightened sensitivity to hydrogen peroxide, and subsequent growth suppression. Finally, transcriptomic analysis reveals global dysregulation of genes involved in iron uptake and redox homeostasis. Furthermore, infection-based experiments demonstrate that PhiP plays an important role in efficient phage propagation. Collectively, our findings uncover a mechanism by which a phage-encoded protein targets heme biosynthesis to perturb ROS homeostasis, suppress bacterial growth, and promote efficient phage propagation. This work expands our understanding of phage-mediated metabolic manipulation of host bacteria and may inspire novel strategies for antibacterial therapy.IMPORTANCEMultidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a leading cause of hospital-acquired infections with limited treatment options. Bacteriophages represent a promising alternative to antibiotics, but the molecular mechanisms by which their proteins inhibit bacterial growth remain largely unexplored. This study identifies PhiP, a phage protein that targets heme biosynthesis, to exert antibacterial activity against P. aeruginosa. This blockade triggers toxic oxygen compound accumulation inside the cell to inhibit cell growth and promote efficient phage propagation. This mechanism is distinct from previously described phage inhibitors, which typically target essential structural and functional components of the bacterial cell. Importantly, PhiP targets HemA, a conserved enzyme in Pseudomonas, highlighting its potential as a scaffold for new anti-infective agents. Our findings expand the known repertoire of phage-host interactions and offer a new blueprint for antimicrobial drug discovery.
records.authors: Yan W, Liu Q, Zhu J, Zhang Y, Cao J, Jing Q, Wang W, Wang Y, Wang C, Chen L, Li M, Zhang Y, Zhao X, Liang H, Wang T.

records.title: Phage-meropenem synergy against multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae biofilms: phenotypic and genomic characterisation of vB_KpnS_Tech.
records.abstract: The increasing prevalence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) Klebsiella pneumoniae and its capacity to form persistent biofilms highlight the need for alternative antimicrobial strategies. This study characterised the lytic bacteriophage vB_KpnS_Tech (PQ859379.1) and evaluated its activity in combination with meropenem against established MDR K. pneumoniae biofilms of different maturities. vB_KpnS_Tech exhibited rapid adsorption, with 98.8% of phage particles adsorbed within 7.5 min, a latent period of approximately 30 min and a mean burst size of approximately 165 PFU per infected cell. The 49,562-bp genome had a GC content of 51.1% and contained 86 predicted coding sequences, including putative holin, endolysin and Rz-like spanin-associated lysis proteins. No recognised antimicrobial-resistance, virulence or lysogeny-associated determinants were detected by the applied genomic screens, and comparative analyses placed vB_KpnS_Tech within the family Drexlerviridae and genus Webervirus, within an existing species-level genomic cluster. Phage-meropenem checkerboard assays demonstrated a clear effect of biofilm maturity on treatment response. Maximum relative biomass reduction reached 66.0% in 24 h biofilms, while the selected combination of 1 × 10⁹ PFU/ml phage and 256 µg/ml meropenem produced reductions of 62.2% and 42.7% in 24 h and 48 h biofilms, respectively. Independent Bliss analysis of biological replicate checkerboards demonstrated synergy in 24 h biofilms, with a mean global score of 10.53 ± 0.53, whereas the interaction in 48 h biofilms was attenuated and remained within the additive/independent range (3.37 ± 0.88). The selected combination reduced recoverable viable bacterial burden by 2.60 and 1.70 log₁₀ CFU/ml relative to untreated endpoints in 24 h and 48 h biofilms, respectively, and reduced viable counts below corresponding pre-treatment baselines. Combination treatment was also associated with the greatest reductions in recoverable EPS-associated carbohydrate, extracellular protein and extracellular nucleic-acid material and retained activity against five additional phage-susceptible MDR K.pneumoniae isolates. Collectively, these findings demonstrate a concentration- and maturity-dependent phage-meropenem interaction and support further evaluation of vB_KpnS_Tech-meropenem combinations against established MDR K.pneumoniae biofilms.

records.title: Isolation and Probiotic Characterization of Bacillus stercoris VR19 from the polyherbal Ayurvedic fermented formulation Madhookasavam
records.abstract: Abstract    Probiotics are live microorganisms that provide health benefits to the host when administered in adequate amounts. In this study, bacterial isolates from Madhookasavam, a polyherbal Ayurvedic fermented formulation, were screened to identify potential probiotic candidates. Preliminary safety assessment included Gram staining, hemolysis testing, and antibiotic susceptibility profiling. Among the isolates, VR19 was the only strain to exhibit γ-hemolysis, indicating a non-hemolytic phenotype, and was susceptible to several clinically relevant antibiotics, including Chloramphenicol and azithromycin. The isolate VR19 demonstrated tolerance to acidic conditions and simulated gastrointestinal stresses, including pepsin (0.1–1%), bile salts (0.1–3%), and NaCl (1–10%). Functional characterization revealed cellulase activity of up to 1.95 U/mL, corresponding to the release of 0.959 mg/mL reducing sugars. The isolate also exhibited concentration-dependent antioxidant activity, reaching a maximum DPPH radical-scavenging activity of 72.9%. Probiotic performance was further evaluated using  Caenorhabditis elegans  as an in vivo model. VR19 showed effective intestinal colonization and persistence, as demonstrated by bacterial enumeration and Gram staining of colonies recovered from the nematode intestine. Molecular identification based on, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and phylogenetic analysis identified VR19 as  Bacillus stercoris  . Collectively, these findings show that  Bacillus stercoris  VR19 possesses promising probiotic properties, including a non-hemolytic phenotype, gastrointestinal stress tolerance, cellulolytic and antioxidant activities, and effective intestinal colonization. The strain therefore warrants further safety and efficacy evaluation for potential therapeutic and functional-food applications.
records.authors: Rathi V, Babu KR, Chauhan N.

records.title: Post-Transplant Gut Dysbiosis is a Targetable Axis
records.abstract: Abstract    Long-term graft attrition remains a critical challenge despite maintenance immunosuppression, which perturbs intestinal immune homeostasis and microbial communities, which may contribute to vascular inflammation and chronic graft injury. We previously identified  Muribaculaceae  expansion as a shared feature of long-term exposure to multiple distinct immunosuppressant classes in the murine gut microbiome. In this study, using a fully MHC-mismatched mouse heart transplant model under chronic tacrolimus treatment, we tested whether oral administration of the protolerogenic  Bifidobacterium pseudolongum subsp. globosum  (  Bifido  ) or pro-inflammatory  Desulfovibrio desulfuricans  (  Desulfo  ) could redirect this dysbiotic state and affect graft fate. Longitudinal metagenomic and metabolomic profiling showed an ordered tacrolimus-associated microbial succession that culminated in sustained  Muribaculaceae  enrichment with coordinated luminal and circulating metabolic remodeling.  Bifido  , but not  Desulfo  , redirected the community trajectory by reducing  Muribaculaceae  enrichment, increasing selected fermentative commensals, and establishing metabolites linked to epithelial and immune regulation, including kynurenic acid and N-acetylspermine. Spatial transcriptomics showed that  Bifido  partially attenuated early tacrolimus-induced colonic metabolic, stress, and epithelial-remodeling programs while later selectively reprogramming ileal antimicrobial defense, crypt-proximal metabolic adaptation, and mucosal humoral immunity. These changes were accompanied by minimal graft vasculitis and fibrosis, increased Foxp3⁺ regulatory T-cell localization in mesenteric and peripheral lymph nodes (LNs), and partial preservation of tolerogenic stromal laminin α4:α5 organization. In contrast,  Desulfo  -treated mice retained  Muribaculaceae  enrichment and developed progressive vascular injury. In an exploratory human-to-mouse fecal microbiota transfer (FMT) experiment, chronic allograft vasculopathy (CAV)-associated donor stool promoted expansion of endogenous murine  Muribaculaceae  and a distinct microbial functional state, together with increased graft fibrosis, T cell infiltration, LNs remodeling, and vasculitis. Whereas non-CAV donor stool favored  Bifido  enrichment and was associated with lessened graft pathology. Together, these findings provide proof of principle that the immunosuppressant-perturbed gut ecosystem is a targetable axis, supporting novel adjunct therapies that complement immunosuppression and mitigate chronic graft injury.

records.title: Simplified Synergistic Rhizosphere Bacterial Consortia Enhance the Antagonistic Activities Against Ralstonia solanacearum and Improve Plant Health.
records.abstract: The rhizosphere microbiota plays a vital role in plant stress resistance and pathogen suppression. Bacterial wilt, caused by Ralstonia solanacearum, leads to significant economic losses in a wide variety of crops. The utilization of native microbial consortia has emerged as a promising strategy for combating this disease. In this study, we assembled a synthetic microbial consortium (Co-4) from rhizosphere bacteria with demonstrated antagonistic activity, comprising four strains of Bacillus sp., Heyndrickxia sp., Franconibacter sp., and Pseudomonas sp. Transcriptome analysis of tomato plants treated with Co-4 revealed significant alterations in gene expression, particularly in carbohydrate and energy metabolism, as well as translation processes. These changes correlated with enhancements in various plant growth traits, including height, stem thickness, biomass, leaf area, photosynthetic rate, and root development. Furthermore, two simplified consortia, SynCom1 (Bacillus, Heyndrickxia, and Franconibacter) and SynCom2 (Franconibacter and Pseudomonas), exhibited augmented antagonistic properties against R. solanacearum compared with their individual constituent strains. Using SynCom2 as a model, we demonstrated that its synergistic interactions resulted in increased biofilm formation, motility, biomass production, cross-feeding interactions, and volatile organic compound emissions, all of which likely contribute to disease suppression and enhanced plant defense. This study highlights the potential of simplified synthetic consortia for managing bacterial wilt through cooperative microbial functions, presenting an effective and environmentally sustainable biocontrol strategy.
records.authors: Liu X, Chen T, Qin X, Han M, Zhang X, Zhou J, Li P.

records.title: Characterization of Ralstonia pseudosolanacearum Phylotype I Isolates Causing Bacterial Wilt in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
records.abstract: Ralstonia pseudosolanacearum is a soilborne bacterial pathogen responsible for bacterial wilt disease in a wide range of host plants, including solanaceous crops. In this study, we collected 22 bacterial wilt isolates from solanaceous crops in seven sampling plots across the Kongo Central region of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The genomic characterization of these isolates identified a single haplotype belonging to the R. pseudosolanacearum phylotype I sequevar 31 genetic lineage. We assembled the genome sequence of one representative strain, RUN6904, placed it in a phylogenetic context, and identified its type III effector repertoire. We demonstrated the virulence of the DRC isolates on tomato and showed the resistance of the AG91-25 eggplant accession likely triggered by the recognition of the RipAX2 type III effector from these isolates.[Formula: see text] Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). records.title: Genome annotation and population genomics reveal adaptive signatures in the Japanese seahorse (Hippocampus mohnikei) based on whole-genome resequencing.
records.abstract: The Japanese seahorse (Hippocampus mohnikei) is a fish species of significant commercial and ecological value in East Asia. However, its genomic structure and adaptive mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, we performed structural annotation of the available genome and conducted a systematic population genomic survey of four geographic populations (WH, LZ, QD and XM) from coastal waters of China. The results show that the Japanese seahorse has 24,595 annotated protein-coding genes, and evaluations combining BUSCO (83.05%-92.92%), OMArk (91.95%), and transcriptomic validation (base-level precision of 77.40%) suggest a moderate-to-high completeness and structural accuracy of this gene set. A total of 5,569,533 SNPs were initially identified, and 604,542 high-quality SNPs were retained after stringent filtering and LD pruning for downstream population genomic analyses. Population genomic analysis revealed that the observed heterozygosity (Ho) was moderate (0.2419-0.2756), but nucleotide diversity (π) remained consistently low (~ 0.0030), suggesting that a putative population expansion or bottleneck event may have occurred recently. Adaptive scanning analysis identified 118 candidate adaptive loci, primarily concentrated on two contig-level genomic regions (331 and 557). Functional analysis of the 515 associated candidate genes revealed an enrichment in cell adhesion molecules (CAMs) pathways, MAPK signaling, and neurodevelopmental genes, which are putatively associated with environmental stress responses. These findings suggest that the local adaptation of the Japanese seahorse may potentially involve stress-responsive pathways. This research offers fundamental genomic insights for elucidating the adaptive evolution of seahorses.

records.title: A new species in the Magnaporthiopsis genus from wild rice enhances rice yield and disease resistance by restructuring the microbiome.
records.abstract: Wild rice serves as a rich reservoir of beneficial endophytic fungi. However, the diversity and functional potential of these endophytes remain largely unexplored, limiting their utilization in sustainable rice production. In this work, we isolated and identified a novel endophytic fungus, Magnaporthiopsis oryzae (coded MB-9-27), from wild rice, Oryza granulata, and demonstrated that it directly promotes rice growth (yield increased by 12.66%) and enhances resistance to rice blast (disease rate decreased by 45.51%) in the field. Furthermore, MB-9-27 inoculation reshaped the rice microbiome, simplifying microbial interaction networks while significantly enriching beneficial bacteria (Methylobacterium sp., Sphingomonas sp.) and fungi (Mortierella sp., Rhizophagus sp., Mollisia sp., and Coniothyrium sp.). Among 75 fungi isolated from MB-9-27-treated rice plants, five representative strains (F14: Mortierella sp., F25: Trichoderma sp., F27: Clonostachys sp., F29: Podospora sp., and F30: Pseudeurotium sp.) corresponded to taxa ranked among the top 150 dominant fungal members identified through microbiome analysis. Functional screening revealed that Mortierella sp. (coded F14) markedly promoted rice growth, increasing shoot and root development by 55.8% and 51.6%, respectively, and reducing rice blast severity by 18.2%, indicating its dual role in promoting growth and suppressing disease. Metabolomic profiling of the rice-F14 holobiont identified significant accumulation of several metabolites, including Indole-3-glycerol phosphate (IGP), Adenine, and S-lactoylglutathione (SLG), suggesting alterations in pathways related to tryptophan metabolism, cellular metabolism, and redox homeostasis. Targeted LC-MS analysis further confirmed the production of IGP by F14. Bioassays demonstrated that IGP significantly promoted rice growth, supporting a potential role of tryptophan-derived metabolites in the plant growth-promoting activity of F14. Collectively, our findings demonstrated that MB-9-27 functions not only as a growth-promoting and disease-suppressive endophyte but also as a driver of beneficial microbiota assembly. Our results highlighted the potential of wild rice-derived endophytic fungi and their associated microbiota as valuable resources for microbial-assisted sustainable rice production.

records.title: Biofilm-Controlled Molecular Crosstalk: Nitrogen Fixation, Arsenic Transformation and Antibiotic Resistance.
records.abstract: Biological nitrogen fixation, arsenic biotransformation and antibiotic resistance are conventionally studied separately, yet the environmental biofilm-bacteria's dominant organisational state in soils, sediments and rhizospheres-supplies a shared physicochemical and genetic context in which the three can intersect. The extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix imposes steep oxygen, redox and metabolite gradients across micrometre scales and demonstrably shelters oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase, retains arsenic-transforming enzymes (ArsC, ArsM and AioA) and elevates horizontal gene transfer (HGT) frequencies orders of magnitude above planktonic conditions. Individual circuits are genetically established in single organisms-RpoN coactivates pslA and nifA and the non-coding RNA NfiS stabilises nifK and katB transcripts, in Pseudomonas stutzeri A1501-but their assembly into one programme linking surface commitment, diazotrophic activation and oxidative stress defence, with additional c-di-GMP and ArsR stimulon input under arsenic stress, is proposed, not demonstrated. Arsenic-driven coselection of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) is the best-supported limb, operating through cross-resistance (RND efflux), co-resistance (ars-ARG colocation on Tn21, Class 1 integrons, IncP/IncQ plasmids) and coregulation (ArsR stimulon, SOS-derepressed intI1), whereas the proposal that diazotrophy-derived ammonium supports S-adenosyl-l-methionine supply for ArsM-mediated methylation rests on gene coenrichment and rate correlation rather than direct flux measurement. This review integrates these processes into a single biofilm framework, classifies each proposed linkage by the evidence behind it, identifies candidate trifunctional mobile elements carrying ars, nif and ARG cassettes in hyperaccumulator rhizospheres and paddy soils and specifies the minimum spatially resolved single-cell dataset (bacterial-MERFISH, par-seqFISH and SIP-NanoSIMS) needed to test the proposed couplings.
records.authors: Bagchi D, Majumdar A, Kotta-Loizou I, Buck M.

records.title: VENAS2: Bidirectional Mutation Modeling for Genomic Surveillance Reveals Reversions and Hidden Transmission Links in Pathogens.
records.abstract: Accurately resolving pathogen evolution is essential for genomic surveillance, yet existing approaches often assume unidirectional mutation accumulation and fail to capture reversions that obscure lineage classification and transmission dynamics. Here we present VENAS2, a scalable framework that integrates genomic, temporal and geographic information to construct spatiotemporal evolutionary networks while explicitly modeling bidirectional mutational processes. Applied to 7.25 million SARS-CoV-2 genomes from GISAID between December 2019 and June 2024, VENAS2 reconstructed the evolutionary history of SARS-CoV-2 and precisely inferred the temporal dynamics of major variants of concern. Further application to the Viridian dataset revealed 4,654 distinct genomic sites with at least one potential reversion event, providing a systematic view of potential reversion signals during viral evolution. Extending to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, VENAS2 delineated major lineages and identified over threefold additional transmission clusters beyond conventional genomic distance-based methods, uncovering hidden links enriched for drug-resistant strains. These results demonstrate VENAS2's capacity to uncover cryptic evolutionary processes across viruses and bacteria, providing a generalizable platform that bridges genomic surveillance with actionable public health response.
records.authors: Zhang P, Cao R, Ling Y, Xu M, Qian J, Ma L, Zhao G, Li Y, Zhang G.

records.title: Identification of highly specific bacterial L-asparaginase through genome-wide computational screening and experimental validation.
records.abstract: BackgroundBacterial L-asparaginases are key therapeutics for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), but their clinical efficacy is limited by off-target L-glutaminase co-activity, which contributes to severe side effects. This study aimed to identify highly specific bacterial L-asparaginases with minimal L-glutaminase co-activity.MethodsWe screened ~ 85,000 prokaryotic genomes using a workflow integrating AlphaFold2 structure prediction, molecular docking, binding-energy estimation, and molecular dynamics simulations. Six top-ranked enzymes were selected for experimental validation.ResultsRhAII protein from Acidobacteriota sp. showed high specificity toward L-asparagine (L-Asn), with a Michaelis constant (KM) of 12 ± 2 µM and turnover number (kcat) of 34 ± 2 s⁻¹, and negligible L-glutaminase activity. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations revealed a relationship between enzyme activity and the conformational dynamics of the flexible gating element (FGE), characterized by residue-level root mean square fluctuation (RMSF), and L-Asn positional fluctuations, evaluated by ligand root mean square deviation (RMSD) relative to the protein. High L-asparaginase activity was associated with optimal FGE dynamics and low L-Asn RMSD, consistent with stable substrate positioning within the active site. In contrast, enzymes with altered FGE dynamics relative to the reference EcAII enzyme from Escherichia coli, such as PoAII from Planctomycetota sp., showed poor L-asparaginase performance (KM 5797 ± 1143 µM; kcat 1.2 ± 0.1 s⁻¹).ConclusionsGenome- and structure-guided screening identified RhAII as a promising antileukemic candidate for further validation in biological models. A key limitation of the computational workflow was the lack of correlation between predicted substrate binding energies and catalytic efficiency, highlighting the importance of active-site dynamics in enzyme kinetics.

records.title: Endolysin potentiates depolymerase efficacy against Klebsiella pneumoniae under low-serum conditions.
records.abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a Gram-negative opportunistic pathogen responsible for severe healthcare-associated infections. The increasing prevalence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) strains, particularly those resistant to carbapenems, poses a significant clinical challenge. In this study, we isolated Jasmi2, a lytic bacteriophage targeting K2-type K. pneumoniae strains. Jasmi2 was classified within the genus Webervirus and contained a linear double-stranded DNA genome of 45,811 bp with 67 predicted open reading frames. ORF67 was identified as a K2-targeting tail depolymerase and designated DpoJ2. Recombinant DpoJ2 efficiently degraded the surface polysaccharide of K2-type K. pneumoniae and reduced biofilm biomass without significantly affecting viable cell counts. While DpoJ2 sensitized K. pneumoniae to serum-mediated killing, achieving an approximately 3.7-log reduction in bacterial counts in 25% human serum, its bactericidal activity diminished at lower serum concentrations. We successfully overcame this threshold by developing a novel combinatorial approach with the endolysin LysTS6. The DpoJ2-LysTS6 combination demonstrated superior efficacy compared to individual treatment, significantly enhancing bacterial eradication under low-serum conditions. DpoJ2 and LysTS6 exhibited no detectable cytotoxicity or hemolytic activity at the tested concentrations. The enhanced efficacy of the combination was further validated in vivo Galleria mellonella infection models, where the combination of DpoJ2 and LysTS6 increased larval survival to 20% at 72 h, whereas no larvae survived following either individual treatment. These findings establish a novel antibiotic-independent strategy combining a phage-derived depolymerase with an endolysin to enhance antibacterial activity against MDR K. pneumoniae, particularly under conditions where serum-mediated killing is limited.

records.title: Phenotypic and genomic characterization of five novel Klebsiella bacteriophages: Exploring the relationship between spot-lysis patterns and host defense systems.
records.abstract: BackgroundIndividual Klebsiella phages typically exhibit narrow host ranges; novel phages must therefore continue to be isolated and characterized to assemble phage therapy cocktails. However, the determinants governing host range remain unclear.ObjectivesTo characterize five novel Klebsiella phages and examine relationships between their spot-lysis profiles and strain genotypes or host defense repertoires.MethodsFive sewage-derived phages were morphologically characterized, and their complete genomes were determined. Spot lysis was assessed against 249 clinical isolates of the Klebsiella pneumoniae species complex (KpSC). Genotypes, virulence and resistance determinants, and anti-phage defense systems were identified from draft genomes using Kleborate and DefenseFinder.ResultsTwo phages were Myovirus-like and three Siphovirus-like, representing novel species within Jiaodavirus and Sugarlandvirus, and the known species Slopekvirus matisse. Overall, 160 of 249 isolates (64.3%) showed spot lysis with at least one phage; ΦKpT256 produced spot lysis in 137 isolates (55.0%), comparatively broad for a single phage. Spot lysis extended across diverse K/O loci, sequence types, and virulence/resistance profiles. Although 2619 defense systems of 156 types were identified, descriptive comparison revealed no obvious one-to-one correspondence between spot-lysis patterns and individual defense systems.ConclusionsSpot-lysis patterns were not readily explained by the bacterial characteristics examined or by any single defense system, suggesting that additional host and phage factors may contribute. ΦKpT256 and the three Siphovirus-like phages showed differing species-level spot-lysis profiles and warrant evaluation as potential components of a KpSC-targeted phage cocktail.

records.title: Tn-Seq-based identification of genes that play a role in antimicrobial tolerance of  Pseudomonas aeruginosa  aggregates
records.abstract: Microbial biofilms, whether surface-associated or in the form of aggregated microbes, cause a variety of persistent infections due to their inherent tolerance to antibiotic treatment. Current knowledge of the mechanistic basis of biofilm-associated antibiotic tolerance is fragmented, and the relative importance of previously identified factors remains unknown. We developed a Tn-Seq-based workflow that enables simultaneous assessment of the relative antibiotic tolerance of thousands of individual clonal bacterial aggregates, each established by a single transposon mutant. Using this genome-wide Tn-Seq analysis approach, we identified several factors and pathways that play a role in antimicrobial tolerance o  f Pseudomonas aeruginosa aggregates. The majority of these factors are important for aggregate-associated tolerance to specific antibiotics, whereas some factors play a role in aggregate-associated tolerance regardless of the class of antibiotic. This methodology provides a framework that can be adapted to investigate aggregate-associated tolerance for other bacterial species and in response to different antimicrobial agents and stressors.
records.authors: Goltermann L, Gualdi S, Rybtke M, Shahryari S, Liang Z, Lin S, Kragh KN, Eberl L, Tolker-Nielsen T.

records.title: Competence repression by the SPβ prophage in Bacillus subtilis revealed by transcriptomics across culture conditions
records.abstract: Prophages are near-ubiquitous in bacterial genomes, yet their effects on host physiology are typically assayed under a narrow range of laboratory conditions, mostly involving DNA-damaging agents or physical and chemical stress. This leaves open the question of which ecological and physiological conditions trigger prophage-host interaction, and whether the outcome benefits the host or the prophage. Here, we used publicly available transcriptomic data to investigate conditions promoting prophage-host interaction in Bacillus subtilis. This analysis identified that competence strongly induces prophage gene expression. To further investigate the role of competence, we used two sets of B. subtilis strains: a natural SPβ lysogen strain and its cured counterpart, and a natural non-lysogenic strain and the same strain lysogenised with SPβ. Under competence-inducing conditions, both lysogen strains showed lower expression of the competence genes compared with their non-lysogenic counterparts. This result was corroborated by transformation assays that showed consistently lower transformation efficiency in the lysogen strains, and by fluorescence microscopy using a transcriptional reporter for the late competence gene. Because competence is a principal route for horizontal gene transfer in B. subtilis, prophage repression of the competence programme constrains host DNA uptake and evolvability. More broadly, these results show that mining public transcriptomes for condition effects can guide experimental effort towards prophage-host phenotypes that conventional laboratory conditions would miss.
records.authors: Grosboillot V, Gnidovec L, Baebler Š, Ule J, Dragos A.

records.title: Life on leaves left a lasting mark on the  Methylobacterium  core genome
records.abstract: The extent to which core genomes reflect strictly vertical inheritance remains debated, particularly in ecologically diverse bacterial lineages. Here, we investigate the evolution of the core genome of  Methylobacterium , a major leaf-associated bacterial genus, to assess how evolutionary signals vary across genes and whether they relate to functions involved in adaptation to life at the surface of plant leaves (the phyllosphere). Identifying 1,099 protein-coding core genes across 293 genomes, we combined gene tree comparisons, phylogenetic network reconstruction, nucleotide polymorphism patterns, and functional enrichment analyses. We found that most core genes show some deviation from the consensus phylogenetic tree. However, this discordance is not randomly distributed. Across all analytical approaches, genes showing the strongest deviations are consistently associated with functions linked to life in the phyllosphere, including anoxygenic photosynthesis, protection against UV and osmotic stress. These genes are often grouped into conserved clusters in the genome. In particular, a large cluster involved in anoxygenic photosynthesis, including bacteriochlorophyll and carotenoid biosynthesis, shows strong variation in its evolutionary history and organization across lineages, despite maintaining a conserved core structure. Similar patterns of phylogenetic incongruence and gene organization are observed across related Hyphomicrobiales inhabiting the phyllosphere, suggesting that these functions extend beyond  Methylobacterium . Together, these results indicate that evolutionary heterogeneity within the core genome is concentrated in genes involved in key ecological functions. While alternative explanations cannot be excluded, these patterns are consistent with horizontal gene transfer contributing to the diversification of traits important for survival and adaptation in phyllosphere bacterial communities.
records.authors: Leducq J, Sneddon D, Alleman AB, Sanjenbam P, Sullivan JM, Agashe D, Marx CJ.

records.title: The origin of the MV Hondius Andes outbreak
records.abstract: In April-July 2026, Andes virus (ANDV) caused an outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship resulting in 12 confirmed cases and three deaths. Before symptom onset, the index case had travelled through hantavirus-endemic regions of Chile and Argentina, leaving the geographic origin of infection unresolved. We conducted phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses using newly generated ANDV genomes from human cases and rodent reservoirs to investigate the likely origin of the outbreak. Through phylogenetic analyses, we show that the outbreak genome falls within a geographically structured lineage spanning southern Chile and Argentine Andean Patagonia. Using phylogeographic reconstructions across all three segments, integrated with the index case’s travel itinerary, we identified the Toltén-Lanco area of southern Chile as the most likely geographic origin of the outbreak genome, with two candidate locations accounting for >98% of the posterior support. However, the index case visited this area 62-66 days before symptom onset, exceeding the conventionally reported ANDV incubation period of 7-42 days. Thus, while genomic evidence supports a southern Chilean origin of the outbreak genome, the timing and circumstances of transmission to the index case remain unresolved.
