records.title: PLATE: a global atlas of food metaplasmidomes
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Plasmids play a central role in the acquisition and spread of genes underlying important traits in food-associated microorganisms. Although shotgun metagenomics has greatly expanded opportunities to study food microbiomes, their plasmid diversity remains largely uncharacterized. Here, we present the Plasmid Atlas of Food Ecosystems (PLATE), a curated global resource of food metaplasmidomes. Built from 4,690 food metagenomes spanning 55 countries and 17 categories, PLATE comprises a broad catalog (bPLATE) of 3,904,895 putative plasmid contigs (PPCs) and a refined catalog (rPLATE) of 213,474 PPCs, corresponding to 181,871 unique sequences. Both catalogs are complemented by curated sample metadata, host predictions, taxonomic assignments, and functional annotations covering antimicrobial resistance (AMR), protein families and KEGG orthologs, CRISPR-Cas systems, carbohydrate-active enzymes, and bioactive peptides. We demonstrate PLATE’s utility through a case study of AMR genes detected on PPCs from food microbiomes. PLATE is freely accessible and enables users to interactively search for and download sequences, annotations, and associated metadata. By organizing plasmid-associated sequence diversity and functional potential across food ecosystems, PLATE provides a foundation for analyses of food metaplasmidomes.
records.authors: Aslan MU, Kayacan RA, Söğütdelen SA, Sağıroğlu Ö, Arıkan M.

records.title: Characterization of lactic and acetic acid bacteria and their phages from a California winery
records.abstract: Abstract    Spoilage of wine from volatile acidity or off flavors caused by uncontrolled growth of lactic acid bacteria (LAB) and acetic acid bacteria (AAB) results in significant economic losses. We aim to survey the persistence of LAB and AAB throughout the wine processing stages, and to evaluate the potential of phages as targeted microbial control. Cabernet Sauvignon samples were collected from a winery in Livermore, California during 2025 harvest season, covering grape rinse, juice/must, the end of primary fermentation and malolactic fermentation steps. Bacterial 16S amplicon sequencing of these samples identified key species that persist through the wine processing steps, including  Lactiplantibacillus plantarum  and  Levilactobacillus lactis  among LAB, and  Acetobacter oryzoeni  and  Acetobacter pasteurianus  among AAB. Phages targeting  L. brevis  ,  A. pasteurianus  and  A. fabarum  were isolated.  L. brevis  phages Indaco_L1 and Indaco_L2 (genome size of 135,623 bp and 141,184 bp, respectively) are related to phages in the  Tybeckvirus  genus of the  Herelleviridae  family, but distinct enough to form two novel species. The two novel  Acetobacter  phages, a first reported  Acetobacter  jumbo phage Vinphasol_A1 (genome size 397,952 bp) and Vinphasol_A2 (genome size 56,636 bp), share little DNA sequence similarity to phages in the current NCBI database. These isolated phages were able to inhibit the growth of  L. brevis, A. pasteurianus  and  A. fabarum  for up to 7 days in conditions simulating wine fermentation, suggests their potential application in controlling microbial spoilage during wine making processes.
records.authors: Boeckman J, Gill J, Jafri A.

records.title: Current Evidence Does Not Support Substantial DNA Cytosine Methylation in Myxosporean Genomes.
records.abstract: Some invertebrate lineages are known to have lost their ability to methylate DNA cytosines. These lineages have often lost the enzymes responsible for cytosine methylation (DNMT1 and 3), as well as other enzymes that interact with methylated cytosines. Previous studies showed that myxosporeans, a group of parasitic cnidarians, lack recognisable DNMTs and other canonical methylation enzymes, and observed a lack of cytosine methylation in two myxosporeans using whole genome bisulfite sequencing. Recently, a study of five myxosporean samples using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing reported high levels of methylation in two samples and low levels in the others and the presence of methylation-related genes in their assemblies. Here, we provide evidence that the two assemblies for which high levels of methylation were reported are heavily contaminated with fish-host sequences. In the other three samples, the lower apparent methylation signal resembles that observed in unmethylated negative controls and can be explained by ONT-background noise. Moreover, the CpG observed-to-expected ratios of the five assemblies differ from those of well-curated myxosporean assemblies. Additionally, the reported methylation profiles do not exhibit the typical distribution seen in invertebrates, possibly reflecting the presence of host contaminants. Finally, we found that most of the genes analysed are not canonical components of cytosine methylation pathways, and that the few candidate methylation-related genes reported in myxosporeans are more consistent with bacterial contamination than with genuine myxosporean genes. Together, these observations underscore important caveats in inferring the presence or absence of cytosine methylation in parasite genomes, particularly when using emerging technologies, and suggest that there is currently no robust evidence for substantial cytosine methylation in myxosporeans.
records.authors: Huchon D, Son DR, Protic IA, Sandberg TOM, Yi SV, Alvarez-Ponce D.

records.title: Identification and Genomic Analysis of Lelliottia nimipressuralis JS203 and Its Production of 2-Phenylethanol with Broad-Spectrum Activity against Phytopathogens.
records.abstract: Colletotrichum dematium, a causal agent of anthracnose, poses an escalating threat to global agriculture, exacerbated by the emergence of resistance to conventional fungicides. In this study, we employed a "one strain-many compounds" (OSMAC) approach to screen 724 environmental bacterial isolates under varied media and temperature conditions to maximize secondary metabolite diversity. Isolate JS203, identified as Lelliottia nimipressuralis through whole-genome sequencing, demonstrated robust, broad-spectrum inhibition against C. dematium and several other major phytopathogens. Bioactivity-guided fractionation of JS203 extracts, followed by NMR and GC-MS analysis, identified the volatile aromatic alcohol 2-phenylethanol (2-PE) as the primary antifungal metabolite. Genomic analysis revealed that JS203 harbors Ehrlich pathway genes, including idpC and gpr_2, which share 100% amino acid identity with validated 2-PE biosynthetic enzymes from Enterobacter sp. CGMCC 5087. These results suggest a conserved metabolic route for 2-PE production in this understudied genus. Collectively, our findings highlight L. nimipressuralis JS203 and its production of 2-PE as a promising natural strategy for the sustainable management of anthracnose and other fungal diseases.
records.authors: Srok J, Wei SY, Yang CH.

records.title: Monitoring single-cell metabolic phenotyping changes of Daqu microbiota during fermentation by Raman spectroscopy.
records.abstract: Monitoring microbial community dynamics during natural food fermentation is essential for stabilizing fermentation processes and improving product flavor profiles. This study employed single-cell Raman spectroscopy to monitor the metabolic change of Daqu microbiota during fermentation. First, we developed an operational phenotypic unit (OPU)-based clustering method to process Raman spectral data of a nine-member microbial community. The clustering was validated by sorting out representative single cells from different OPUs and performing 16S/ITS region sequencing. Second, single-cell Raman spectroscopy was applied to the mixed Daqu sample throughout fermentation, identifying 10 OPUs and 54 sub-OPUs. Single cells from different OPUs were sorted and sequenced to obtain taxonomic annotation, which were correlated with the Raman spectral characteristics of each OPU. The OPU-based Raman spectroscopy method was successfully used to monitor the single-cell metabolic phenotypes of Daqu microbiota during fermentation, and taxonomic annotations revealed the succession of microbial community structure. This study presents a novel approach for monitoring the dynamics of metabolic phenotypes within Daqu microbial communities, offering a data-driven decision-making approach for subsequent production operations in multi-species fermentation processes.IMPORTANCEMicrobial communities play pivotal roles in diverse industrial processes, yet monitoring their metabolic dynamics remains challenging. Current omics approaches, including metagenomics, transcriptomics, and mass spectrometry-based metabolomics, fail to establish direct genotype-phenotype linkages at the single-cell level and often require destructive sampling. This study introduces operational phenotypic units (OPUs) as a novel framework to bridge this gap by integrating single-cell Raman spectroscopy with sequencing technologies. Our method enables non-destructive, rapid monitoring of metabolic phenotypes while preserving cells for downstream analysis. By applying this approach to solid-state Daqu fermentation, we demonstrate its capability to track microbial community succession and identify functionally distinct populations in real time. This data-driven strategy offers significant potential for optimizing multi-species fermentation processes across food, environmental, and biotechnological industries, providing a powerful tool for microbial community management and process control.
records.authors: Xu L, Liang P, Wang Y, Zhang X-J, Chai L-J, Xu H-Y, Wang S-T, Zhang S-Y, Shen C-H, Lu Z-M, Huang WE, Xu Z-H.

records.title: Scaffold-level validation is needed for phage-host inference from metagenome-assembled genomes.
records.abstract: Accurate phage-host prediction underpins ecological interpretation and experimental validation of uncultivated phages, yet most current approaches rely heavily on metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). This reliance implicitly assumes that MAG-level quality metrics, such as completeness and contamination, ensure scaffold-level correctness. Here, we demonstrate that this assumption can be violated under particular challenging conditions. Tetranucleotide frequency (TNF) analyses reveal that CRISPR-associated regions often diverge compositionally from their host genomes, increasing the risk of misbinning, while experimentally validated phage-host genome pairs show consistent TNF separation between phages and their hosts, challenging compositional binning assumptions. Through controlled simulations, we further show that the incorporation of substantial amounts of TNF-matched, non-host phage sequences into high-quality MAGs does not substantially alter standard completeness and contamination estimates, rendering such errors largely undetectable. Together, these results expose a systematic and underappreciated source of bias in MAG-based phage-host inference and highlight the need for explicit scaffold-level validation beyond conventional genome-quality metrics. We further propose a practical scaffold-level validation framework that integrates structural linkage and taxonomic consistency to improve the reliability of phage-host inference from MAGs.
records.authors: Yuan L, Anantharaman K, Ma B, Camargo AP, Chen L.

records.title: Metatranscriptomic profiling of active endophytic microbiome functions across diverse Musa cultivars.
records.abstract: Plant-endophyte symbioses play important roles in plant health and resilience, but the active functions of endophytic microbiomes remain less characterized than those of soil and rhizosphere microbiomes. We used metatranscriptomic profiling of culture-free enriched endophytic microbiomes from seven Musa cultivars grown under shared environmental conditions to characterize active microbial taxa and functional annotations across sampled tissues. Because each genotype and tissue combination had only one metatranscriptomic sample, this pilot study focuses on the microbial transcripts and functions detected in each sample rather than testing for cultivar or tissue differences. Culture-free enrichment produced metatranscriptomic profiles across samples, including 5,434 taxonomic annotations, and 32,694 gene annotations from expressed microbial transcripts. Functional annotations included pathways involved in secondary metabolism, energy production, environmental information processing, transport systems, oxidative phosphorylation, nitrogen metabolism, quorum sensing, biofilm formation, and xenobiotic biodegradation. Several taxa, including Bradyrhizobium sp., were detected across multiple samples and linked to diverse functional annotations. Approximately 30-35% of sequence reads were annotated as hypothetical proteins, showing that the functions of many detected transcripts are still unknown. Correlation analysis also showed sample-level associations among detected pathway profiles. Overall, this pilot metatranscriptomic data set provides a resource for banana endophyte research and identifies candidate microbial taxa and functional pathways for future studies of plant-microbiome interactions and microbe-microbe relationships.IMPORTANCEEndophytic microbiomes can influence plant health, but their active roles inside banana tissues remain poorly characterized. Here, we used metatranscriptomic profiling of culture-free enriched endophytic microbiomes from seven Musa cultivars to identify microbial taxa and functional pathways detected across sampled tissues. Metatranscriptomic data characterized pathways related to metabolism, transport, microbial signaling, biofilm formation, nutrient cycling, and secondary metabolism, suggesting potential variation in active microbiome profiles among sampled plants. This work provides a pilot resource for banana endophyte research and may help guide future studies on how plant-associated microbiomes interact with their hosts, how microbes function together inside plant tissues, and how these relationships could be used for microbiome-based crop improvement.
records.authors: Aghdam SA, De Souza R, Brown AMV.

records.title: Transposon mutagenesis identifies lon, csgF, and rfbF as critical genetic determinants of biofilm architecture and adhesion in multidrug-resistant Salmonella Typhimurium.
records.abstract: Salmonella Typhimurium relies on biofilm formation to withstand environmental stressors, resist antimicrobials, and establish persistent host infections. However, the genetic networks governing biofilm development remain poorly understood. Here, we assessed the biofilm-forming capacity of 708 S. Typhimurium isolates. Among them, 88.56% formed biofilms, with 3.81% classified as strong producers associated with extensive multidrug resistance. To elucidate underlying genetic determinants, we performed EZ-Tn5 transposon mutagenesis on a strong biofilm-producing clinical isolate (15E341), generating ~ 5000 mutants. Phenotypic screening and whole-genome sequencing identified three distinct loci-lon, csgF, and rfbF-whose disruption significantly impaired biofilm formation without affecting planktonic growth. Confocal and electron microscopy (LSCM and FESEM) revealed severely compromised 3D biofilm architecture and defective surface colonization. Furthermore, these mutants exhibited significantly reduced adhesion to Caco-2 epithelial cells, glass, and silicone. Transcriptomic analysis revealed a distinct regulatory shift, characterized by marked upregulation of flagellar assembly pathways and downregulation of fimbrial genes. In a murine model, the mutants exhibited attenuated virulence, evidenced by increased host survival and significantly reduced bacterial colonization in the cecum, liver, and spleen. Notably, whereas CsgF is an established curli-assembly factor and Lon is a well-characterized stress and virulence regulator, RfbF, an O-antigen biosynthesis enzyme, emerged as a previously undercharacterized determinant of biofilm capacity in S. Typhimurium. Collectively, these findings highlight multi-gene coordination in biofilm development and identify pathways that warrant further investigation for disrupting persistent Salmonella infections.
records.authors: Ge Q, Ye T, Ma S, Jiang L.

records.title: Environmental media-based microbial source tracking enables source identification of antimicrobial resistance in urban rivers.
records.abstract: Urban rivers receiving treated wastewater remain hotspots for antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs), yet quantitative source attribution remains challenging. Conventional microbial source tracking (MST) cannot distinguish ARG contributions from treated effluent, untreated sewage, and environmental reservoirs such as sediments. Here, we developed an environmental media-based MST (EM-MST) framework integrating source-enriched microbial markers to quantify ARG sources in an urban river impacted by two wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) and combined sewer overflow (CSO). From fifteen screened markers, NOB-16S (effluent-enriched nitrite-oxidizing bacteria), dsrA (sediment-enriched sulfate-reducing bacteria), and crAssphage (sewage-associated) were selected using qPCR validation and multivariate analysis. Combined with shotgun metagenomic profiling of 676 ARGs and a non-negative least squares mixing model, these markers enabled source attribution. During dry weather, WWTP effluent accounted for the largest source proportion (81.5-93.1%), with efflux pump, sulfonamide, macrolide, and aminoglycoside ARGs. During the sampled CSO event, untreated sewage accounted for 91%-100% of the estimated source contribution, delivering β-lactam, macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin, and tetracycline ARGs associated with gut microbiota. River sediments showed greater resistome similarity to WWTP effluent, consistent with an effluent-associated ARG reservoir, while the estimated sediment contribution remained minor (3.0 ± 5.3%). The EM-MST enables quantitative differentiation of ARG sources in wastewater-impacted urban rivers.
records.authors: Sabar MA, Than VH, Sugie Y, Wada H, Zhao B, Matsuura N, Ihara M, Watanabe T, Tanaka H, Honda R.

records.title: Description of  Alternaria kierstenii  sp. nov. from invasive garlic mustard highlights agricultural biosecurity risks of foreign weeds as pathogen reservoirs
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Invasive weeds can increase agricultural biosecurity risks by serving as reservoirs for emerging or undercharacterized plant pathogens. Garlic mustard (  Alliaria petiolata ), an invasive brassicaceous weed in North America, occurs near agricultural landscapes and is susceptible to multiple crop pathogens. A previously undescribed  Alternaria species was isolated from a diseased garlic mustard population in Maryland, USA, prompting investigation of its taxonomy, origins, and host range.  De novo genome sequencing produced a near-chromosome scale assembly of 35.8 Mb comprising 17 contigs. Comparative genomic analyses with other crucifer-infecting  Alternaria species revealed expanded repertoires of predicted CAZymes and peptidases, as well as unique effectors and biosynthetic gene clusters. Phylogenetic and comparative analyses supported recognition of this fungus as  Alternaria kierstenii sp. nov., representing a distinct lineage within section  Sonchi. Host range assays demonstrated that  A. kierstenii was highly aggressive on diverse hosts in the Brassicaceae, including vegetable, ornamental, cover crop, and invasive species. The disease caused by this new pathogen manifested as foliar and stem lesions, chlorosis, necrosis, leaf death, and, in several hosts, rapid plant mortality. Amplicon sequence data from a nationwide garlic mustard microbiome study detected closely related taxa only in the plants from the eastern states of Maryland, Pennsylvania, and New York, suggesting a geographically restricted population consistent with expectations for a potentially emerging pathogen. The description of this phylogenetically unique, broad host range pathogen demonstrates the potential for widespread invasive weeds to harbor pathogens and pathogen genomic diversity with agricultural relevance, underscoring the hidden biosecurity risk of understudied invasive weeds.
records.authors: Sawyer C, Thomas JL, Groben G, Fulcher MR, Tancos MA.

records.title: GENOME ASSEMBLIES FOR 28 PHAEOSPHAERIACEAE ISOLATES FROM CANADA
records.abstract: Glume blotch and Septoria Tritici Blotch (STB) are destructive crop diseases caused by fungal pathogens formerly classified under the genus  Septoria . Recent taxonomical revisions have led to the reclassification and renaming of these fungi, some of which are now under the genus  Parastagonospora , family Phaeosphaeriaceae, order Pleosporales, and class Dothideomycetes. In this study, we performed whole genome sequencing and assembly for 28 Phaeosphaeriaceae isolates from Canada. Sequencing was performed using a combination of Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read and Illumina short-read sequencing platforms. Most of the genomes were very complete, BUSCO >99%, with the genomes assemblies derived from ONT sequencing having very few contigs that likely encompass entire chromosomes or chromosome arms. To determine the relationship between these isolates and similar fungi that have been previously characterized, we performed whole genome alignments to 2,668 other Dothidiomycete genomes obtained from NCBI using NUCmer. Comparative genomic analysis revealed that 27 of the isolates clustered discretely with either  Parastagonospora nodorum, or Parastagonospora pseudonodorum (Parastagonospora avenae f. sp. tritici ), with one genome having no other similar genome in NCBI which we hypothesize to be the first genome assembly of  Phaeosphaeria pontiformis . Both  P. nodorum and  P. pseudonodorum species were isolated from wheat and barley and only the latter was isolated from durum, while the  P. pontiformis was isolated from wheat. In summary, we sequenced and assembled the genomes of 28 isolates of Phaeosphaeriaceae spp. from Canada and the genomes add to our foundational knowledge of these plant pathogens and efforts to better understand their diversity.
records.authors: Bamforth J, Abdel-Fattah M, Gourlie R, Aboukhaddour R, Walkowiak S.

records.title: Metagenomic Next-Generation Sequencing of Mycoplasma hominis Infection in an Immunocompromised Patient: A Case Report.
records.abstract: Mycoplasma hominis is an underrecognized opportunistic pathogen that can cause extra-genitourinary infections, particularly in immunocompromised hosts. This case report describes a persistent soft tissue infection following a wooden splinter injury in a 52-year-old immunocompromised man, in whom M. hominis was identified by blood mNGS after conventional microbiological investigations were inconclusive. The patient developed recurrent fever, wound pain, swelling, and exudation. Empirical treatment with ertapenem and subsequent surgical intervention did not provide sustained clinical improvement, while conventional microbiological investigations remained inconclusive. Peripheral blood was therefore analyzed by mNGS, which detected M. hominis, human betaherpesvirus 5, and GB virus C. For M. hominis, nine species-specific reads were identified, with a relative abundance of 21.5% for the genus Mycoplasma and 99% confidence for species-level identification. The mNGS finding was interpreted together with the refractory clinical course and the absence of a convincing alternative bacterial pathogen. Following further surgical management and multidisciplinary evaluation, targeted antimicrobial therapy with intravenous moxifloxacin plus omadacycline was administered, followed by oral omadacycline after discharge. The patient subsequently became afebrile, pain improved, and inflammatory markers progressively declined. This case demonstrates the potential utility of blood mNGS for identifying an atypical pathogen in an immunocompromised patient with culture-negative, treatment-refractory infection. The findings also emphasize that low-read mNGS results should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings, conventional microbiological investigations, and treatment response.
records.authors: Li J, Zhou W, Cai L, Shen H, Lu H, Fan J.

records.title: Folding without glutamine: Proteome-scale removal of a canonical amino acid.
records.abstract: All known life uses a canonical alphabet of 20 amino acids, yet which residues are structurally essential remains untested at proteome scale. Isoleucine was recently eliminated from ribosomal proteins in Escherichia coli, establishing that amino acid alphabet reduction is feasible. Here we ask whether an entire amino acid can be eliminated from a proteome, and develop a computational framework to identify the best target. Using two independent approaches - ProteinMPNN structure-based probabilities and multiple sequence alignment conservation - we define "keep-score" as the fraction of positions where the native residue is optimal. Both methods converge on an unexpected candidate: glutamine has the lowest keep-score, with proline and glycine the highest - counter to substitution-matrix intuition. Glutamine's low keep-score is not explained by a single obvious substitute; glutamate is preferred in only 14% of replacements. Removing this target proteome-wide, we replaced every glutamine across 4,148 proteins with ProteinMPNN-optimal alternatives and modeled the resulting sequences with AlphaFold2. The recoded proteome maintained native-like structures: 85.5% of models exceeded a TMscore of 0.8, indistinguishable from the 85.9% baseline for rebuilt native sequences. Orthogonal validation - ESMFold predictions, Rosetta energy calculations, and conformational ensemble comparisons - revealed no evidence of systematic misfolding attributable to glutamine removal. As a consistency check, a glutamine-free TEM-1 β-lactamase designed with ProteinMPNN conferred ampicillin resistance in E. coli, indicating fold preservation can extend to biological function. Evolutionary evidence further supports these findings: 24% of E. coli proteins have glutamine-free orthologs in prokaryotic genomes, and glutamine ranks lowest in keep-score in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. These results show that an entire amino acid can be removed from a proteome with folds broadly preserved, establishing keep-score as a general framework and glutamine as the primary candidate for recoding. Crucially, this reflects a computational analysis of structural replaceability, not a demonstration of biological dispensability.

records.title: A Baltic Sea microbiome-derived Type III polyketide synthase produces host-protective alkylresorcinols in E. coli.
records.abstract: Marine microorganisms are a prolific source of novel polyketide synthases (PKSs) that generate structurally diverse and functional polyketides. Here, we identify a novel type III PKS, ArsMB, from Pontimonas sp. via metagenomic mining of a Baltic Sea microbiome. Heterologous expression of arsMB synthetic gene in an Escherichia coli host that lacks a native type III PKS, combined with a two-step strategy to boost acyl-CoA precursor availability in a glucose-mineral medium, enabled the in vivo synthesis of two cell-associated alkylresorcinols, identified by GC-MS as 5-pentadecyl-1,3-benzenediol (ars1) and 5-tridecyl-1,3-benzenediol (ars2). The product profile is consistent with a tetraketide alkylresorcinol biosynthetic pathway utilizing C16 and C14 acyl starter units, drawn from the host acyl-CoA pool. In agreement, AlphaFold2-based structural modeling predicts a Cys139/His275/Asn308 catalytic triad and a long hydrophobic substrate tunnel compatible with long-chain acyl starter units. E. coli producing the amphipathic cell-associated alkylresorcinols ars1/ars2 exhibited increased resistance to muralytic digestion by endolysins and to hydrogen peroxide. These findings expand the known repertoire of marine-derived type III PKSs and highlight the biotechnological potential of ArsMB-derived alkylresorcinols.

records.title: Multi-Parameter In Vitro and Genomic Characterization of Bovine-Derived Bacteria with Probiotic Potential.
records.abstract: Raw milk and bovine feces represent important sources of microorganisms with probiotic potential. This study aimed to identify potential probiotic candidates from bovine-derived samples and to comprehensively characterize their functional and safety-related features by integrating multi-parameter in vitro evaluation with whole-genome analysis. Acid-producing bacteria were isolated from 12 raw milk and 15 bovine fecal samples using bromocresol green agar. Following PCR-based exclusion of Escherichia coli and RAPD-PCR dereplication, the isolates were evaluated for acid and bile tolerance, survival under simulated gastrointestinal conditions, and autoaggregation, leading to the selection of five candidate strains: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum MX13, Lacticaseibacillus paracasei MX165, Enterococcus faecalis MX179, Enterococcus faecium MX125, and Enterococcus durans FX198. Further in vitro characterization revealed marked strain-specific differences in gastrointestinal stress tolerance, autoaggregation, cell-surface hydrophobicity, and antibacterial activity, with the two lactobacilli displaying broader antibacterial spectra than the Enterococcus strains. Multivariate analysis further revealed distinct overall phenotypic profiles among the candidates, with MX13 exhibiting a relatively balanced functional profile across the traits evaluated. Whole-genome analysis revealed clear differences between MX13 and MX125 in antimicrobial resistance-associated, putative virulence-associated, and other functional genomic features, providing additional information for candidate prioritization. Overall, this study identified and characterized five bovine-derived potential probiotic candidates with distinct functional properties through integrated phenotypic and genomic evaluation, providing a basis for their further functional validation and application-oriented assessment.

records.title: Family-specific structure in infant gut viromes enables closed-set mother-child matching
records.abstract: Abstract  The early-life gut virome differs so strongly between individuals that the variation is usually treated as noise. We show it is structured by family, specifically enough that a child's virus set points to their own mother. Across 2,664 catalogue metagenomes, 142 twin libraries and 284 shotgun metagenomes re-quantified from raw reads, we ranked 32 candidate mothers by viral overlap with each of 125 child samples from 32 families. Using all detected vOTUs, the true mother ranked first for 67 of 125 samples (53.6%; median rank 1), against a median sample-level accuracy of 2.4% after permuting maternal labels across families. The mean within-family accuracy was 52.0% (family bootstrap 95% confidence interval 37.2% to 66.6%), and the true mother ranked first at least once in 22 of 32 families. Specificity comes from where the background is empty, not where the signal is large: the own-mother excess is largest for viruses of intermediate prevalence (+ 0.64) and small for the rarest (+ 0.09), yet rare viruses discriminate best because unrelated pairs share almost none. The same asymmetry appears independently in the twin cohort, where rare-virus sharing separates co-twins from unrelated pairs at AUC 0.997. Matching is not merely taxonomic: median agreement across cohort-variable consensus positions in shared vOTUs was 1.000 for mother-child pairs against 0.768 for unrelated pairs, positive in all 24 evaluable families. These findings support family structure in infant viromes, with additional within-vOTU consensus-sequence concordance in the evaluable subset of shared viruses. The comparisons are closed-set and do not resolve transmission direction or separate maternal acquisition from continued shared exposure.

records.title: AI-driven structural informatics reveals diverse glycosylation machinery across double-stranded DNA viruses
records.abstract: Abstract  Glycosylation is widespread in biology and shapes molecular recognition, yet the diversity and biosynthetic organization of viral glycosyltransferases (GTs) remain poorly understood. Here we integrate structural-alphabet-guided searches and structure similarity networks with genomic-neighbourhood and biosynthetic gene cluster embedding analyses to examine viral GT-A proteins. This approach reveals extensive structural diversity overlooked by sequence-based annotation, including previously uncharacterized viral GT lineages. Most strikingly, we identified a jumbo-phage locus encoding five tandem glycosyltransferases alongside hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine biosynthetic and sulfation-associated enzymes, suggesting a previously unrecognized form of viral DNA modification involving a sulfated pentasaccharide. Beyond these examples, predicted saccharide-associated loci span divergent double-stranded DNA viruses, from giant viruses to tailed phages, and occupy multiple regions of the reference biosynthetic landscape. Together, our findings uncover an underappreciated repertoire of virus-encoded glycosylation machinery and suggest that viral glycan biosynthesis encompasses diverse molecular contexts and potential biological functions.

records.title: Potential of foaming events in reshaping vertical distribution of waterborne antibiotic-resistant human pathogens and signaling public health risks in surface waters.
records.abstract: While pathogens in surface waters frequently cause epidemic outbreaks and millions of annual deaths worldwide, their association with natural aqueous foaming, a common yet overlooked phenomenon, remains unexplored. This study investigated whether foaming is associated with changes in the distribution and potential risk of antibiotic-resistant human pathogens (ARHPB) in surface waters, challenging the traditional view that sediments are the primary sink for waterborne pathogens. The surface foam layer was found to coincide with selective transport of bacteria (particularly, the potential priority multidrug-resistant genera like Acinetobacter and Enterobacter) from benthic sediments into the water column via bubble adhesion, a mechanism linked to the bacterial virulence trait of motility. Meanwhile, bacteriophages were predominantly distributed in the water column, where genes associated with immune modulation were more abundant. Metagenomic analysis reveals that the relative abundance of potential human-pathogenic bacteria harboring co-localized antibiotic resistance genes and mobile genetic elements was greater in the water column during foaming (from near-zero to markedly higher levels) than under unfoamed conditions, suggesting enhanced potential for horizontal gene transfer. However, foamed and unfoamed samples were collected in July and October, respectively, and the temporal confound prevented causal attribution to foaming alone. Nevertheless, consistent patterns across four independent water bodies indicate that foaming events are among the covarying factors for the elevated potential ARHPB relative abundance and deserve further exploration as potential sentinels for public health risks. Inclusion of foam monitoring in aquatic risk assessment frameworks warrants consideration, pending prospective validation.
records.authors: Zhang M, Liu J, Shen Y, Chen J, Li J, Fang Q, Huang J, Zhang S, Shao Z, Yang J, Luo Y, Zhang D, Imanmadi D, Pan X.

records.title: Genome-wide analysis of the TAF gene family reveals a role for GhTAF8 in cottonseed oil accumulation.
records.abstract: TATA-box binding protein (TBP) associated factors (TAFs), together with TBP, com-pose transcription factor IID (TFIID), which is an essential complex for transcription initiation and regulation. TAFs are involved in regulating plant development. However, genome-wide identification and expression pattern analysis of TAFs in cotton remain unreported. In this study, a total of 124 TAF genes were identified in four Gossypium species. TAFs were divided into six subgroups based on the phylogenetic tree analysis. Analysis of collinearity and selection pressure indicated that TAF gene pairs have undergone strong purifying selection during evolution. Gene expression analysis of GhTAFs revealed that TAFs are expressed at all stages of cotton ovule development. Furthermore, a set of key GhTAF genes was identified, which are specifically or constitutively highly expressed across multiple stages of cotton ovule development. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis prioritized GhTAF8 (Ghir_D11G035840) from the blue module associated with 20 days post anthesis, a critical stage of rapid oil accumulation. GhTAF8 exhibited the highest module membership among the nine GhTAFs in this module. Overexpression of GhTAF8 in Arabidopsis thaliana increased seed oil content, whereas virus-induced gene silencing in cotton reduced seed oil content. A GhTAF8-centered co-expression network also identified genes potentially associated with seed development and lipid metabolism. These findings support a functional association between GhTAF8 and seed oil accumulation and provide a foundation for investigating its underlying regulatory mechanisms.
records.authors: Song J, Gao J, Feng P, Chen S, Jia B, Zhao W, Zhang B, Pei W, Wang L, Wu M, Zheng K, Yu J, Shu J, Liang Y, Ma J.

records.title: Genome-wide CRISPRi-seq maps essential-gene contributions to aminoglycoside susceptibility in  Pseudomonas aeruginosa
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic ESKAPE pathogen whose multiple intrinsic and acquired antibiotic resistance mechanisms restrict treatment options. Essential genes offer potential antimicrobial targets, but their vulnerability to partial inhibition and contribution to antibiotic susceptibility remain incompletely characterized. Here, we developed a rhamnose-inducible CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) platform and an 83,078-guide library for genome-wide screening in PAO1, with mismatch guides enabling graded repression. Fitness profiling in antibiotic-free Mueller–Hinton medium identified 743 genes whose repression reduced competitive fitness and revealed sequence features associated with guide performance. Combining full-match and mismatch-guide responses revealed substantial variation in essential-gene fitness effects across predicted repression strengths, while comparison of fitness profiles between Mueller–Hinton medium and fetal bovine serum identified condition-dependent effects alongside a conserved fitness landscape.  Under aminoglycoside exposure, we identified 118 recurrent sensitizing and 120 recurrent protective gene knockdowns, including many targeting essential and fitness-associated functions. Growth and killing assays with individual strains confirmed that CRISPRi targeting of  atpI ,  accC ,  secA and  ftsZ enhanced tobramycin activity. Finally, transcriptome analysis of these knockdowns confirmed target silencing, captured polar effects on neighboring genes and revealed distinct but overlapping transcriptional responses. Together, these findings quantify the variable fitness costs of essential-gene repression and identify candidate targets for potentiating aminoglycoside activity.  IMPORTANCE  Essential bacterial genes are difficult to study because their complete disruption prevents growth. Yet knowing that a gene is essential does not reveal how strongly its activity must be reduced to impair growth. Here, we developed a method to examine how reduced gene expression affects fitness across the genome of  Pseudomonas aeruginosa , a major cause of difficult-to-treat infections. This approach identified essential functions particularly vulnerable to partial depletion and mapped how gene repression alters aminoglycoside susceptibility. Repressing selected genes impaired growth and disproportionately increased killing by tobramycin. These tools and datasets provide a resource for prioritizing candidate antibacterial targets and investigating whether partial inhibition of essential functions can enhance the activity of existing antibiotics.

records.title: GraphExperiment: infrastructure for high-dimensional quantitative data and associated networks in R/Bioconductor
records.abstract: Networks are widely used to represent relationships among features (e.g. genes, proteins, and microbial taxa) and among observations (e.g. cells, samples, and species) in omics data, as well as their neighborhoods. The Bioconductor ecosystem provides users and developers with modular and interoperable software tools by relying on standard data structures that are reused across packages. However, Bioconductor lacks a standard data structure to store such networks together with the quantitative data from which they are inferred. Here, we present  GraphExperiment , an R/Bioconductor package that provides an S4 class extending  SingleCellExperiment with containers for feature-level (  rowGraphs ) and observation-level (  colGraphs ) networks stored as  igraph objects. Networks are kept in sync with assays, row and column metadata, allowing the simultaneous manipulation of quantitative data and graphs. We demonstrate  GraphExperiment in seven use cases covering bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, single-cell proteomics, microbiome, and comparative genomics data, with networks ranging from gene coexpression and protein co-abundance networks to cell-cell communication and phylogenetic networks.  GraphExperiment is available on Bioconductor (  https://bioconductor.org/packages/GraphExperiment ).

records.title: Host-microbiome asynchronous decoupling reveals systemic metabolic allostatic overload mediated by gut genomic potential degradation.
records.abstract: Background & aimsMetagenomic aging clocks predict chronological age but lose explanatory power during midlife (35-65 years). We hypothesized that cumulative allostatic load drives microenvironmental alterations, leading to asynchronous decoupling of metagenomic and metabolomic profiles.MethodsA metagenomic clock was trained on a lifespan cohort (N = 4551) and evaluated in a midlife sub-cohort (N = 1868). Independent metagenomic (N = 843) and fecal metabolomic (N = 106) cohorts assessed functional and phenotypic trajectories. Within a paired multi-omics cohort (N = 99), Procrustes and spatial dispersion analyses quantified topological decoupling. Metabolic biological age gap (metBAG) and metabolome-wide association studies (MWAS) characterized allostatic load signatures.ResultsThe lifespan model achieved R2 = 0.444 (MAE = 13.09 years). In midlife, model fit decreased (R2 = 0.187), whereas MAE narrowed to 6.73 years, indicating greater phenotypic stability. Concurrently, core taxa (e.g., Bifidobacterium breve) exhibited age-related declines. Paired analysis revealed significant spatial decoupling; microbial dispersion exceeded metabolic dispersion, suggesting host metabolic remodeling buffers microbial divergence. Elevated metBAG correlated with clinical parameters. Under high allostatic load, 1,3,7-trimethyluric acid enrichment and all-trans retinoic acid depletion were associated with the systemic aging transition.ConclusionsWe identified an asynchronous decoupling during midlife: basal microbial decline precedes systemic aging and is initially buffered by host metabolic remodeling. When allostatic load exceeds compensatory capacity, specific metabolite enrichment may accelerate systemic aging. This framework facilitates sub-health quantification and informs microbiome-targeted interventions.

records.title: Resistance mutation supply modulates the benefit of CRISPR immunity against virulent phages in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
records.abstract: Only a fraction of bacterial genomes encode CRISPR-Cas systems, but the selective causes of this variation are unexplained. How naturally virulent bacteriophages (phages) select for CRISPR immunity has rarely been tested experimentally. Here, we show against a panel of genetically and functionally diverse virulent phages that CRISPR immunity was not universally beneficial to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and its fitness effect varied strongly between phages in predictable ways. In addition to mechanisms known to alter the effectiveness of CRISPR immunity, such as encoding a matching spacer or a protective nuclear shell, we show that the fitness effect of CRISPR immunity negatively associated with the probability of evolving receptor-based resistance to the phage via spontaneous mutation. The supply of resistance mutations differed strongly between very closely related lipopolysaccharide-binding phages and was associated with variation at the C-terminus of the tail fibre protein altering residues involved in hydrogen bonding and the predicted binding site. Our results show that CRISPR immunity is more beneficial against virulent phages that are harder to evolve resistance to via receptor mutations, suggesting that virulent phage community composition and diversity will be important drivers of the prevalence of CRISPR immunity.
records.authors: Wright RCT, Lovell SC, Richmond A, Harrison C, Ashworth E, Kadioglu A, Fothergill JL, Friman VP, Westra ER, Brockhurst MA.

records.title: Australian isolates of cell fusing agent virus and Culex flavivirus provide new tools to study insect-specific flaviviruses
records.abstract: Abstract    Cell fusing agent virus (CFAV) and  Culex  Flavivirus virus (CxFV) represent the prototype insect-specific flaviviruses (ISFs) found in  Aedes  and  Culex  species, respectively. While these viruses have been isolated from mosquitoes on several different continents, no isolates have been reported from Australian mosquitoes. In this study we successfully isolated CFAV from  Aedes aegypti  originating from Cairns in North Queensland, Australia and CxFV from  Culex quinquefasciatus  collected from Brisbane in South-East Queensland, representing the first field isolates for both viruses from Australia. Phylogenetic analysis of these isolates revealed that the new CFAV isolates were closely related to CFAV sequences previously detected by deep sequencing of pools of  Aedes aegypti  collected in North Queensland, while the genome sequences of the Brisbane CxFV isolates were most closely related to isolates of CxFV from  Culex quinquefasciatus  collected from Mexico in 2008. Using these Australian isolates, we report the first infectious clone created for CFAV, and the first infectious clone of the Australian strain of CxFV. Growth kinetics revealed that infectious clones of CFAV and CxFV replicated more efficiently than their wild-type counterparts, reaching titres more than 10  8  TCID  50  /ml. Deep-sequencing of these isolates indicated that differences in replication were due to co-infections of mosquito-derived native viruses with other viruses absent in infectious clone stocks. Using a panel of novel monoclonal antibodies raised against the CFAV virion proteins, we demonstrated antigenic relatedness between CFAV and CxFV and other lineage I ISFs, particularly those carrying the conserved FKW motif at positions 106–108 in the fusion loop region of the viral envelope protein. All generated mAbs bound CFAV with one mAb additionally recognising the ISFs CxFV, Palm Creek virus (PCV), Parramatta River virus (PaRV) and Niénokoué virus (NIEV). While these mAbs did not bind CxFV and CFAV proteins in mosquitoes injected with the infectious clones, the first immunofluorescence analysis of disseminated of CFAV in  Aedes  mosquitoes was visualised through anti-dsRNA staining, showing widespread infection across multiple mosquito tissues, including the midgut and ovaries. These advancements in the development of elementary tools provide opportunity to further our understanding of ISFs and pave the way for their potential application in laboratory research, as well as innovative mosquito-borne disease control strategies.
records.authors: Peterson AJ, McMahon IE, Hall LD, Johnston RA, Argent MS, Potter JR, Paramitha D, Parry RH, Newton ND, Ang CC, Rawle DJ, Darbro J, Hall RA, Hugo LE, Hobson-Peters J, Harrison JJ.

records.title: Replicon-resolved pangenomics reveals functional specialisation and genome evolution in Vibrio coralliilyticus
records.abstract: Abstract  Multipartite genomes define the genus Vibrio, yet replicon specialisation remains poorly understood, particularly in environmental species. We developed a machine-learning classifier to assign draft contigs to putative replicons with high accuracy, integrating complete and draft genomes in comparative analyses. Independent implementation in Vibrio cholerae yielded similar performance, supporting broader applicability. Analysis of 41 Vibrio coralliilyticus genomes revealed functional specialisation between chromosomes despite similar proportions of core and flexible gene families. Chromosome I was enriched in essential cellular processes, central metabolism, motility and regulation, whereas chromosome II was enriched in environmental sensing, signal transduction, transport and interaction-associated functions. Chromosome I also exhibited greater plasticity, with more extensive homologous recombination and higher densities of mobile genetic elements and defence systems. Two previously undescribed conjugative megaplasmid lineages (254–628 kb) displayed contrasting adaptive repertoires. One was broadly distributed across hosts and geographic regions, encoding a conserved accessory repertoire including a giant multidomain putative effector predicted to mediate host interactions. The other was restricted to Mediterranean coral isolates, with an expanded mobilome and a conserved Sofic-like anti-phage defence system. Together, these findings show that functional specialisation can coexist with similar gene conservation patterns, while chromosomes and megaplasmids make complementary contributions to adaptation and genome evolution.
records.authors: Rubio-Portillo E, Nadal-Molero F, Martin-Cuadrado A.

records.title: The Global Landscape of Publicly Available Norovirus Sequences: Genotype Annotations, Genome Completeness, and Geographic Representation
records.abstract: Background:  and Objectives: In the present work, we assessed genotype annotations, genome completeness, and geographic representation of norovirus in the National Center for Biotechnology Information Virus database. Methods: We analyzed metadata for 70,632 complete and partial norovirus sequence records retrieved on 17 August 2026. Major capsid protein (VP1) genotypes and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) types were extracted from deposited annotations. Genome completeness and geographic distribution were summarized descriptively, and 55 selected complete genomes underwent phylogenetic analysis. Results: GII.4 was the most frequently annotated specific VP1 genotype (18,503 records). Specific VP1 and RdRp assignments were unavailable in the analyzed annotations for 24,804 (35.12%) and 51,892 (73.47%) records, respectively. Only 1,859 records (2.63%) were annotated as complete genomes. Country metadata were available for 65,915 records (93.32%), of which Asia contributed 56.15%. The selected phylogeny showed broad genogroup clustering, with three animal-associated genomes belonging to GIV and GVI. Conclusion: This repository snapshot identified limited complete-genome representation, incomplete typing annotations, and uneven geographic representation. These findings describe deposited records rather than population prevalence. Improved genome coverage, annotation consistency, and metadata availability could support more informative comparative analyses.
records.authors: Vargas D, Godoy M, Gaggero A, Kibenge M, Kibenge F.

records.title: Molecular mimicry arrests the phage packaging AppA-ratus.
records.abstract: Among characterized phage defenses, those that interfere with phage genome packaging and virion assembly remain comparatively underexplored. Wang et al. show that a small Salmonella Gifsy-1 prophage protein, AppA, disrupts late-stage virion assembly by mimicking the terminase assembly interface and arresting phage DNA packaging, supporting bacterial fitness during intestinal infection.
records.authors: Uppalapati S, Sbardellati D, Vázquez-Torres A.

records.title: Unveiling Microbial Gene Functions in Maize Cultivars With Varying Drought Resistance.
records.abstract: The rhizosphere microbiome is recognized as a "biological tool" for mitigating drought stress on plant development. However, the functional genes involved in plant-microbe interactions, particularly in drought-sensitive and drought-tolerant cultivars, remain poorly understood. This study comparatively evaluated the functional gene set of the maize rhizosphere microbiome in Monsanto DKC 72-70 (drought-tolerant) and CRN-3505 (drought-sensitive) maize genotypes at water holding capacity (WHC) values of 60, 80, and 100% via shotgun metagenomics. The findings revealed that both cultivars contained a variety of microbial taxa, such as Actinobacteria, Alphaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, and Bacilli, with plant stress tolerance genes. The analysis of beta diversity indicated significant differences between drought-stressed (60% WHC) and well-watered (100% WHC) conditions in both cultivars (R ≈ 0.57, 0.58; p < 0.01), which implies that the functional gene composition is different and that there are intermediate patterns at 80% WHC. In terms of functional responses, drought-sensitive maize presented increased expression of genes related to sulfur oxidation (soxA, soxB, soxD) and osmoprotectant synthesis (BetI, betC, CHCH), indicating a reactive stress response. Conversely, drought- tolerant maize presented regulated expression of the nitrogen metabolism (glnA) and iron homeostasis (FUR) genes in all the WHCs, thus indicating efficient adaptation. In addition, the drought-tolerant maize cultivar selectively expressed stress-response genes (SigB, AhpC) and protein protection genes (dnaJ, dnaK), whereas the drought-sensitive maize cultivar constitutively expressed these genes across conditions. This study provides novel evidence of cultivar-specific functional microbial signatures and demonstrates how microbial gene functions underpin drought tolerance in maize under varying water availability conditions.
records.authors: Molefe-Madlaliso RR, Amoo AE, Babalola OO.

records.title: Parasites of parasites: Herbaria as archives of hidden ecological interactions.
records.abstract: Hyperparasitism, the infection of parasites by other parasites, is among the least explored ecological interaction types. Ampelomyces, intracellular fungi that infect the plant diseases causing powdery mildews, form a naturally occurring parasite-on-parasite system that is both widespread and poorly understood. This tripartite association among plants, pathogens and hyperparasites provides a powerful model for studying multi-trophic interactions and the evolution of host specialization. Using DNA from herbarium specimens collected across 28 countries over the past 150 years as well as those available in NCBI GenBank, we revealed previously hidden ecological and evolutionary patterns in the Ampelomyces-powdery mildew system. Historical collections allowed us to detect hyperparasites that cannot be easily observed, uncovering multiple novel lineages and global patterns of host association. A global reassessment of all publicly available sequences showed that 13% of entries labelled as Ampelomyces are misidentified, revealing a major issue with uncurated, public databases. To resolve this, we developed a curated, voucher-linked phylogenetic framework in T-BAS to serve as a reference for future ecological, genomic and biocontrol studies. Together, our results demonstrate that herbaria function as large-scale ecological observatories, capable of revealing cryptic interactions across continents and providing a strengthened framework for future ecological and evolutionary research on hyperparasitism.
records.authors: Thomas J, Paul A, Crouch U, Braun U, Takamatsu S, Németh MZ, Kiss L, Carbone I, Mitchell J, Cotter HVT, Bradshaw M.

records.title: The anti-phage defense system GAPS4 is a double-edged sword that sensitizes bacteria to DNA-damaging agents.
records.abstract: The arms race between bacteria and bacteriophages (phages) gave rise to multiple layers of antagonistic mechanisms, many of which remain unexplored. Here, we investigated the widespread anti-phage defense system GAPS4. We found that GAPS4 forms a heterotetrameric complex containing active PD-(D/E)xK phosphodiesterase domains. It is triggered upon sensing DNA damage, leading to genomic DNA degradation and cell suicide. We further demonstrated that this activation mechanism renders GAPS4 a double-edged sword, sensitizing bacteria to various DNA-targeting antibacterial agents. Collectively, our findings reveal a possible evolutionary trade-off between anti-phage defense and immunity against interbacterial antagonism.
records.authors: Mahata T, Kanarek K, Haldar A, Ragavan RM, Shur G, Yehia R, Burstein D, Haitin Y, Qimron U, Salomon D.

records.title: Discovery of New Quinoxaline, Tetracyclic-Quinoxaline, and Imidazo[2,1-a]isoindole Derivatives as Potent Antibacterial Candidates Targeting DNA Gyrase and Topoisomerase IV With Molecular Modeling Simulations.
records.abstract: Developing new antibacterial agents is crucial for combating antibiotic resistance, which has predominantly emerged due to the overuse and misuse of antimicrobial agents. In this study, a new series of quinoxaline-based compounds and imidazo[2,1-a]isoindole derivatives were synthesized through the reaction of 1,2-diaminobenzene with carbonyl-rich compounds. The structures of these derivatives were confirmed through various spectroscopic analyses (IR, mass spectra, and 1H/13C NMR) and elemental analysis. Furthermore, their antibacterial activities were evaluated in vitro. Antibacterial efficacy was assessed against three gram-positive (Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus pneumoniae, and Bacillus subtilis) and three gram-negative bacterial isolates (Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa); compounds 3, 9, and 14 demonstrated significant inhibitory activity against all tested isolates, with comparable MIC and MBC values. To further explore their antimicrobial potential, these three active synthesized compounds were assessed for their antibiofilm activity as anti-infective agents against S. aureus (MDR224) and P. aeruginosa (MDR225). Notably, three compounds demonstrated superior bactericidal activity compared to ciprofloxacin (CIP), with undetectable resistance frequencies. Additionally, their potency for inhibiting DNA gyrase and DNA topoisomerase IV was found to be significantly promising, with low IC50 values ranging from 6.75 ± 0.82 to 8.27 ± 1.2 µM and from 8.79 ± 0.24 to 10.33 ± 0.81 µM, respectively, in contrast to CIP, which exhibited IC50 values of 47.68 ± 0.17 and 35.4 ± 0.55 µM. The in silico ADME, pharmacokinetic properties, docking simulations, and DFT calculations of the most promising candidates, 3, 9, and 14, demonstrate significant antibacterial activity and considerable potential for future development.
records.authors: Ragab A, Basseem M, Aboul-Magd DS, Kronek J, Kroneková Z.

records.title: Divergent Responses of Bacterial and Microeukaryotic Diversity to Water-Level Fluctuations in a Lake-Floodplain System.
records.abstract: Water-level fluctuations (WLF) are widely accepted as key drivers of aquatic species diversity in lake-floodplain systems, with diversity increasing as water levels rise. However, microorganisms may challenge this pattern that their richness does not necessarily increase with water levels. To resolve this inconsistency, we applied 16S and 18S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing to bacterial and microeukaryotic assemblages in Dongting Lake, China, during the low-water (LWP; January 2024) and high-water periods (HWP; August 2024). Microeukaryotic richness was higher during HWP than LWP (p  0.3), consistent with their divergent fates in the water column: soil microeukaryotes are more likely to persist after flooding than soil bacteria. Co-occurrence networks evidenced substantially stronger bacteria-microeukaryote associations at high water and partial least squares path modelling resolved a DOC-to-bacteria-to-microeukaryotes pathway activated only during the HWP. These signals suggest that enhanced hydrological connectivity promoted community coalescence, possibly through intensified trophic coupling, although this interpretation requires experimental verification. This study highlights that natural WLFs reshape microbial richness by intermittently reconnecting terrestrial and aquatic microbial species pools.
records.authors: Tan C, Wantzen KM, Wu R, Li W, Lu L, Mbao E, Zhang L, Xie Z, Wang C, Lin W, Li Y, Zhou C, Zhu Z, Li X, Liang J.

records.title: Proteomics-Guided Discovery of Candidate Enzymes for Degradation of a Rare Pyruvylated Glycosaminogalactan by a Newly Isolated Luteolibacter Strain.
records.abstract: Bacterial exopolysaccharides (EPS) display extensive structural diversity arising from variation in monosaccharide composition, glycosidic linkages, and non-carbohydrate modifications. However, the enzymes responsible for degrading many EPS structures remain unknown, reflecting the limited coverage of current carbohydrate-active enzyme (CAZyme) families. Here, we investigated the microbial degradation of EPSLp, a high-molecular-mass glycosaminogalactan from Lactiplantibacillus pentosus KW1 containing the uncommon GalNAcβ1 → 2(4,6-O-R-pyruvyl)Gal motif. Enrichment cultivation with EPSLp as the main carbon source led to the isolation of Luteolibacter sp. VK1, a novel strain capable of utilizing this biopolymer. Size-exclusion chromatography and MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry showed that VK1 depolymerizes EPSLp into defined oligosaccharides, consistent with endo-acting cleavage followed by further processing. By combining genomics, AlphaFold-based structural annotation and comparative proteomics, we identified candidate CAZymes potentially involved in EPSLp catabolism. Notably, a secreted GH123 protein and a distantly related GH123-like protein were strongly associated with EPSLp-dependent growth, suggesting that this enzyme family, or related structural homologues, may contribute to extracellular EPSLp depolymerization. Together, these findings support a candidate pathway for degradation of a structurally complex, pyruvylated bacterial glycan and highlight potentially novel EPS-active enzymes whose proposed roles, predicted through bioinformatic analyses, await experimental validation.

records.title: The Promise and Limitations of Metabolic Trait Prediction Across Diverse Bacteria.
records.abstract: Metabolic traits mediate microbial interactions and underpin mechanistic models of community assembly. With the rapid expansion of genomic data and bioinformatic tools, it is widely assumed that metabolic traits such as substrate utilization can be reliably inferred from genomes alone. Here, we systematically evaluate this assumption by comparing genome-based predictions from four commonly used tools to high-throughput growth phenotypes of 186 marine bacteria. For simple substrates, prediction accuracy was limited and highly variable across taxa and substrates, with many strains predicted at or near chance levels. For three of four tools, most errors were false positives, indicating that apparent pathway completeness frequently fails to translate into growth under laboratory conditions. In contrast, genomic prediction of polysaccharide utilization based on carbohydrate-active enzyme content performed substantially better, suggesting that traits that depend on a few highly specific enzymes are easier to predict. While genome-based approaches can recover broad statistical patterns in metabolic strategies, their limited strain-level reliability constrains ecological inference and modelling. For the foreseeable future, large-scale experimental phenotypic characterization will remain an indispensable component of microbial ecology, both to reveal trait distributions and to ground-truth and improve genomic predictions.
records.authors: Gralka M.

records.title: FASTOP─Fast Editing Toolkit for Top Expression Sites in Yeast.
records.abstract: Budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a widely used chassis for producing food- and agriculture-related compounds, but construction of multienzyme pathways often requires repeated genomic integration. We developed FASTOP, a genome-editing toolkit for rapid engineering of eight transcriptionally active genomic hot-spot loci. FASTOP combines selectable markers, extended homology arms, and Cas9/gRNA-assisted integration, and enables PCR-free release of donor cassettes by restriction digestion to reduce sequence errors introduced during amplification. After characterizing the sites, we integrated a five-gene naringenin biosynthetic pathway into the hot spots as a proof of concept. Our results demonstrated that, upon expressing the five essential genes in simple shake-flask culture, naringenin production reached 505.7 mg/L, 6-fold higher than an episomal control expressing the same pathway genes and 4.5-fold higher than the previously reported strain using additional precursor engineering and controlled bioreactor cultivation. FASTOP therefore provides a practical platform for the rapid assembly of multienzyme pathways in yeast for stable heterologous gene expression.

records.title: Integrated Microbial Profiling Identifies Bacterial and Fungal Communities in Pseudomyxoma Peritonei Mucin.
records.abstract: Pseudomyxoma peritonei (PMP) is a rare mucinous malignancy in which tumour-associated microbial communities remain poorly characterised, particularly, their fungal component and spatial organisation. We applied an integrated workflow combining 16S and 18S rRNA gene sequencing, microbial culture, histochemical staining, chromogenic RNAscope in situ hybridisation and a patient-derived xenograft model to investigate bacterial and fungal communities in control tissues and low- and high-grade PMP mucin. Bacterial and fungal DNA was detected in PMP-associated mucin, with grade-associated differences in bacterial composition and predicted functional potential. Viable bacteria were recovered from human PMP samples and xenograft-derived mucin. Fungal structures were independently supported by periodic acid-Schiff and Calcofluor White staining, while RNAscope localised bacterial 16S and fungal 18S rRNA signals within epithelial and mucin-rich tumour regions. Comparable microbial signals were observed in the xenograft model. Together, these complementary approaches identify PMP mucin as a multi-kingdom microbial niche and provide the first characterisation of its associated mycobiome. This integrated analytical framework may facilitate the investigation of microorganisms in other low-biomass, mucin-rich tumour environments and provides a basis for future mechanistic studies of microbe-host interactions in PMP.

records.title: The Arms Race Between Bacteria and Their Viruses: Update on Phage Countermeasures Against Bacterial Defence Systems.
records.abstract: In this editorial, I summarize recent progress on phage-encoded anti-defence against bacterial anti-phage systems (APS). Computational approaches based on structural predictions of co-folding bacterial and phage proteins identified many new PAD sponge proteins. New anti-CRISPR-Cas systems were characterized that destroy cas12a mRNA, inactivate Cas12a by acetylation, engage the seed region of the crRNA, or prevent Cas3 from cleaving DNA. The phage defence protein Gad1 forms an octamer web that wraps around the complex of the Gabija APS. Tad1 and 2 are phage sponge proteins that sequester signalling nucleotides of the Thoeris APS. Tad3 to 7 interact directly with the ThsB sensor and Tad8 with the ThsA effector of the Thoeris APS. Phage sponge proteins were also described inactivating the CBASS and Pycsar APS. Still other phages use phosphodiesterases that cleave cyclic nucleotide signals to inactivate APS. Many bacterial APS effectors are NADase, destroying the essential metabolite NAD+. Phages evolved enzymes that resynthesize NAD+ from its cleavage products or proteins directly inactivating the NADase. Many phages degrade the bacterial genome which creates signals activating the Metis or the Kongming APS. Phages counteracted these APS by suppressing pathways leading to the creation of particular mononucleotides degradation products detected by these APS. Several APS cleave specific tRNA, phages responded by mutating cleavage sites in tRNA (anti-PARIS) or increasing tRNA expression to compensate for their destruction (anti-Septu). Phages counteract toxin-antitoxin APS by evolving their own antitoxin or by blocking the toxin protein. Researchers described cases where phages escaped detection by mutating phage proteins detected by bacterial sensors. Against the stringent response phages responded by destroying alarmones or inactivating enzymes producing these stress signals. The arms race between bacteria and phages can involve complicated layers of defence and anti-defences and both bacteria and phages encode multiple defence systems.
records.authors: Brüssow H.

records.title: The Hna Phage Defence Protein: A DNA-Stimulated Helicase With Cryptic Nuclease Activity.
records.abstract: The Hna phage defence system consists of a single protein containing helicase and nuclease motifs. Hna provides defence through abortive infection, meaning that it prevents production of new phages without saving the infected cell, but its specific mechanism of action is currently unknown. We previously observed that Hna causes cell death when phage 5A single-stranded DNA binding protein (SSB) is expressed in Sinorhizobium meliloti. Here, we recreated this response by expressing Hna and phage SSB in the heterologous host Escherichia coli, indicating that no other host-specific proteins are required for Hna-mediated cell death. We also find that increased expression of Hna is lethal in E. coli even in the absence of phage SSB. We tagged and purified the Hna protein from S. meliloti, as well as helicase and nuclease motif mutants, and show that wildtype Hna binds ssDNA, performs DNA-stimulated ATP hydrolysis and unwinds short DNA duplexes. The nuclease mutant exhibits increased DNA-dependent stimulation of ATPase activity. Hna demonstrates cryptic nuclease activity: we do not observe nuclease activity in vivo, but the purified protein showed inefficient degradation of phage and bacterial genomic DNA and a ssDNA oligonucleotide in vitro. Further research should elucidate how these activities contribute to cell death.
records.authors: Sather LM, Zamani M, Andres SN, Finan TM.

records.title: Genomic and phenotypic characterization of a honey-derived Enterococcus faecium isolate from the Brazilian semiarid region.
records.abstract: BackgroundEnterococcus faecium has attracted considerable scientific interest. While some strains are recognized as opportunistic nosocomial pathogens, several non-pathogenic isolates have demonstrated beneficial properties associated with food fermentation and probiotic potential. Therefore, this study aimed to perform a functional genomic characterization of the native E. faecium strain EFBI58, isolated from honey in the Brazilian semiarid region.Materials and methodsEnterococcus faecium strain EFBI58 was sequenced using Illumina MiSeq. Bioinformatic tools were employed for comparative genomics, phylogeny, and detection of resistance, virulence, prophage, CAZyme, and bacteriocin genes. Additionally, in vitro tests assessed antimicrobial susceptibility and survival under simulated gastrointestinal conditions.ResultsThe EFBI58 genome presented 2,457,210 base pairs, containing 2,330 coding sequences. Phylogenomic analyses demonstrated that honey-derived isolates formed a genetically distinct group. The ANI showing belonging to clade A2 of animal-associated species. Antimicrobial resistance assessment revealed the absence of acquired genes related to clinical resistance, which was confirmed by the phenotypic susceptibility profile to the evaluated antibiotics. In addition, genes associated with important virulence factors were not identified. A prophage was 21 kb also identified in the genome. The strain EFBI58 showed survival capacity under simulated gastrointestinal conditions and the presence of stress-response proteins, demonstrating mechanisms of adaptation to adverse environments. The profile of carbohydrate-active enzymes and growth in prebiotics sugars revealed a conserved metabolic repertoire associated with the utilization of different substrates.ConclusionsHoney- and bee-associated E. faecium isolates possess genomic characteristics that provide a basis for future investigations involving natural antimicrobial compounds, microbial interactions, and biotechnological applications.

records.title: Phylogenetic Correlation Between the Type IV Secretion System and HIP1 Suggest an Adaptation for Horizontal Gene Transfer Conserved at the Phylum Level.
records.abstract: Most cyanobacterial genomes are rich in the GCGATCGC octamer, also known as Highly Iterated Palindrome 1 (HIP1). Despite its description over three decades ago, the biological function of this highly abundant sequence is only beginning to be elucidated. HIP1 is recognized by two DNA methylases, DmtA and DmtC, and is characterized by its evolutionary conservation and a quasi-periodic distribution within genomes. However, whether the phylogenetic distribution of HIP1 correlates with the presence of functional categories of protein families remains unknown. Here we investigated whether certain protein families share a phylogenetic distribution with this abundant palindromic sequence across cyanobacterial genomes. Our analysis revealed a strong phylogenetic correlation between several proteins of the Type IV secretion system (T4SS) and the abundance of HIP1. This finding aligns with recent discoveries demonstrating that HIP1 enhances DNA transformation in a methylation-dependent manner in two distinct cyanobacterial species. Consequently, we hypothesize that HIP1 function as a conserved adaptation for horizontal gene transfer (HGT) at the phylum level, potentially by serving as a DNA-uptake recognition sequence in cyanobacteria.
records.authors: Rodriguez-Cruz U, Moreno-Hagelsieb G, Abreu-Goodger C, Martínez-Guerrero C, Delaye L.

records.title: Productive or Transforming? How Epithelial Compartmentalization of HPV DNA and E6/E7 Transcripts Shapes Cervical Screening Assay Performance.
records.abstract: The human papillomavirus (HPV) life cycle is linked to epithelial cell differentiation, with viral genome amplification, E6/E7 transcription, and virion assembly spatially compartmentalized within the cervical epithelium. This organization is disrupted in transforming lesions. These fundamental observations determine what 'bulk' nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) of cervical exfoliates allow us to establish. DNA-based assays sensitively report high-risk HPV genome presence, which includes transient infections and virus particles. RNA-based assays target the E6/E7 transcripts in transcriptionally active disease, which accounts for their slightly higher clinical specificity for high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions. No single assay defines both viral presence and disease significance, however. Cytology, p16/Ki-67 dual stain, extended genotyping and host-cell methylation interrogate complementary axes of risk with strong biological rationale. The loss of spatial information that limits bulk NAAT approaches matters most in mixed-grade lesions and immunocompromised populations. Emerging spatial methods, AI-assisted cytology and cervical cell-lifts offer recovery of biological resolution.
records.authors: Schichl K, Doorbar J.

records.title: Duplication, Loss, and Feeding Ecology of Lysozyme Gene Copy Number in Insects.
records.abstract: Lysozymes are ubiquitous enzymes traditionally associated with immune defense via bacterial cell wall degradation. In some insect lineages, particularly Diptera with bacteria-rich diets, these enzymes have been secondarily recruited for digestion, but how widespread this shift is across other insect groups remains unclear. Here, we investigate the evolutionary dynamics and functional roles of C-type and I-type lysozymes across 275 insect genomes, inferring patterns of gene duplication and loss and testing associations between lysozyme copy number and dietary habits. Phylogenetic Generalized Least Squares method revealed few significant associations: a weak link between larval detritivory and C-type copy number, and a more consistent one between an omnivorous diet and I-type copy number across life stages. Duplication analysis revealed multiple independent expansions of C-type lysozymes within Brachycera. In Muscoidea, C-type lysozymes were highly expressed in the Musca domestica larval midgut, consistent with digestion, whereas in Blattodea, moderate C-type copy numbers and salivary gland-biased expression in Periplaneta americana adults instead suggest a primarily antiseptic role. I-type lysozymes lack the catalytic residues required for canonical muramidase activity, yet remain conserved throughout Insecta, including in lineages that lost C-type lysozymes, suggesting alternative, non-canonical functions. Together, these findings are more consistent with a predominantly lineage-specific pattern of gene family evolution, largely uncoupled from a single ecological driver, than with a broad, diet-driven adaptive signal. Digestive recruitment of C-type lysozymes may extend beyond the well-characterized cases of Musca domestica and Drosophila melanogaster to additional expanded lineages across Brachycera, although direct functional evidence remains lacking.
