records.title: Deciphering Polyomavirus-Mediated Carcinogenesis in the Genitourinary Tract.
records.abstract: Human polyomaviruses, particularly BK polyomavirus (BKPyV) and JC polyomavirus (JCPyV), establish persistent infections within the genitourinary tract and undergo reactivation under conditions of immunosuppression. Although their clinical relevance is well established in transplant-associated nephropathy and haemorrhagic cystitis, accumulating molecular, pathological, and epidemiological evidence suggests that these viruses may also contribute to genitourinary carcinogenesis. This review examines the emerging role of BKPyV and JCPyV in urothelial, upper urinary tract, renal, and prostate malignancies, with particular emphasis on the molecular mechanisms underlying viral oncogenicity. Polyomavirus large and small T antigens disrupt the p53 and pRb tumour-suppressor pathways, activate MAPK and PI3K/Akt signalling, interfere with DNA damage responses, and promote genomic instability. Viral genome integration and a potential hit-and-run mechanism involving APOBEC3-mediated mutagenesis provide complementary models for persistent or transient oncogenic effects. The review further explores viral microRNAs as regulators of viral persistence, immune evasion, and inter-polyomavirus competition, including JCPyV-mediated suppression of BKPyV replication. Clinically, polyomavirus-associated urothelial carcinomas demonstrate aggressive pathological features and are particularly relevant in kidney transplant recipients. Current diagnostic strategies integrating viral DNA quantification, urinary cytology, viral microRNA detection, immunohistochemistry, and RNA in situ hybridisation may facilitate risk stratification and tissue-level confirmation. Finally, therapeutic management remains challenging because effective oncological control must be balanced against preservation of graft function and restoration of antiviral immunity. Collectively, these findings position BKPyV and JCPyV as important, but mechanistically heterogeneous, candidates in genitourinary tumourigenesis and highlight critical priorities for establishing causal relationships and clinically actionable biomarkers.

records.title: Reflections on the early days of the DNA damage response pathway in eukaryotes.
records.abstract: The DNA damage response (DDR) pathway has emerged as the central signaling network that preserves genome stability by using sensors to monitor the genome for aberrant structures and establishing signaling centers that promote organismal homeostasis. This review revisits the formative years of DDR research, focusing on the genetic dissection of the pathway in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and its evolution into a broadly conserved eukaryotic signaling system. Early studies of ribonucleotide reductase regulation, replication stress-induced transcription, and cell cycle control identified key regulators, including MEC1, DDC2, TEL1, MRC1, RAD53, DUN1, and RAD9, providing the first evidence that DNA damage signaling is propagated through a protein kinase cascade. This cascade is initiated when RPA binds to ssDNA generated by replication blocks and double-strand DNA breaks, thereby activating the apical MEC1/ATR kinase. These discoveries integrate the contemporaneous cell cycle checkpoint literature into a more comprehensive framework in which the DDR coordinates replication fork stability, replication origin firing, nucleotide metabolism, DNA repair, genome maintenance, and cell cycle control to maintain genomic stability. Parallel studies in Schizosaccharomyces pombe, Xenopus, and mammalian systems revealed the remarkable evolutionary conservation of the pathway and linked DDR dysfunction to a wide spectrum of human diseases, including cancer. In retrospect, the emergence of the DDR field highlights the extraordinary power of classical genetics combined with molecular biology to uncover a complex signaling network that now occupies a central position in chromosome biology, cancer research, aging, immunity, and therapeutic responses.

records.title: Morphological, Molecular Phylogenetic, and Mitochondrial Genome Characterization of a Deep-Branching Marine Flagellate, Katablepharis ulleungensis sp. nov. (Cryptista).
records.abstract: Katablepharids (or kathablepharids) are plastid-less, biflagellate protists widely distributed in marine and freshwater environments. Here, we report a new katablepharid species, Katablepharis ulleungensis sp. nov., isolated from a black sandy beach in Ulleung-do, South Korea. The stock strain was co-cultured with a small bicosoecid flagellate, serving as its prey. Cells were oblong, displayed two rows of Type I ejectisomes, and possessed two subapically inserted flagella with the posterior flagellum slightly longer than the anterior one. Rather than exhibiting linear or spiral locomotion, cells rotated in place using both flagella. Transmission and scanning electron microscopy revealed two types of ejectisomes, each consisting of two coiled ribbons. The feeding apparatus, situated at the cell apex, comprised a cytostome, 9-10 cytopharyngeal rings, numerous putative enzymatic vesicles, and inner microtubular arrays. Phylogenetic analyses using 18S rRNA gene placed the isolate within the genus Katablepharis; the phylogenetic placement together with distinct morphological characteristics supports its recognition as a new species. Using Illumina data, the complete mitochondrial genome (35,191 bp) was assembled and annotated to contain 60 genes, including 33 protein-coding genes, 25 tRNAs, and 2 rRNAs. This study expands our understanding of katablepharid diversity and contributes to mitochondrial genome resources for marine protists.

records.title: Identification of novel inhibitors of Mycobacterium smegmatis growth through genome-wide overexpression of Cluster P3 mycobacteriophage Xavia genes.
records.abstract: Bacteriophages encode numerous genes with no known function, many of which can affect essential cellular processes when expressed in the bacterial host. For mycobacteriophages, genome-wide overexpression in Mycobacterium smegmatis can be used to identify proteins that impair growth. To evaluate the cytotoxic potential of the Cluster P3 phage Xavia, we constructed a plasmid library containing 71 predicted Xavia genes under the anhydrotetracycline-inducible promoter pTet and screened this library in a plate-based cytotoxicity assay to measure impacts on M. smegmatis growth. Two genes prevented transformant recovery, consistent with toxicity under basal promoter leakiness, and inducible expression of 18 additional genes impaired growth. These inhibitory proteins include structural components; factors involved in DNA metabolism, lysogeny, and lysis; and several proteins with no known function. These results extend functional screening into a lineage of actinobacteriophages that has not previously been characterized, and identify new proteins that warrant further mechanistic analysis.

records.title: Gene expression is stable despite widespread cis and trans regulatory divergence in Saccharomyces yeasts.
records.abstract: Regulatory evolution can alter phenotypes, but cis- and trans-regulatory mechanisms may also diverge extensively while total transcript abundance remains stable. Comparisons of parental expression with allele-specific expression in F1 hybrids provide a framework for separating cis- and trans-regulatory effects because both parental alleles are measured in a shared trans-regulatory environment. Here, we analyzed RNA sequencing data from Saccharomyces cerevisiae, S. paradoxus, and their F1 hybrid. Among the 4,164 genes with sufficient allele-specific support for strict classification, 2,134 (51.2%) showed detectable cis- and/or trans-regulatory divergence. However, hybrid expression remained largely conserved, with 81.5% of genes not significantly different from either parent. Compensatory cis-trans divergence predominated over reinforcing divergence; cross-replicate estimation reduced the apparent magnitude of this excess, but opposite-sign effects remained predominant in all 20 nonoverlapping replicate comparisons. To connect gene expression to genome sequence, we analyzed the strongly cis-diverged locus LYS2 and found species differences in promoter architecture, including an S. cerevisiae-specific AT-rich insertion, altered spacing among candidate regulatory features, and a promoter-proximal TATA-like element unique to S. cerevisiae. Sequence-based nucleosome prediction suggests that these differences create a broader promoter-proximal nucleosome-depleted region in S. cerevisiae than in S. paradoxus. We also quantified allele-resolved intron retention and found that it was broadly conserved, with only rare locus-specific hybrid-associated shifts. Together, these results show that regulatory divergence is widespread but often buffered in the hybrid, whereas intron-retention divergence is comparatively limited.
records.authors: Rojas DS, Lang GI.

records.title: Antiviral agent modulates freshwater methanogenesis at the nanotrace level.
records.abstract: Antiviral drugs (ATVs), such as oseltamivir carboxylate (OTC), are widely used to treat viral infections. Although environmental levels are in the ng/L to µg/L range, knowledge on risks posed by this substance class is hindered by limited assessments. Evidence on effects on microbially-driven ecosystem processes is especially scarce, which is concerning because viruses are omnipresent in the microbiome and likely to influence microbial functioning. We assessed the influence of OTC on anaerobic methane production, a greenhouse gas largely emitted from natural systems and responsible for around one third of greenhouse gas-driven warming, as a proxy for microbial ecosystem function. Oseltamivir carboxylate inhibited initial methanogenesis between 15% and 40% even at nanotrace levels (i.e., 0.006-600 µg/L). Given that in most treatments methane levels returned to those of the control, the initial inhibition is potentially attributed to a temporally limited OTC-induced shift from a neutral/temperate viral infection of prokaryotes toward a lytic viral replication. Mostly unaffected 16S rRNA metabarcoding community data indicate that this effect might be uniform throughout the community. This study points to ecosystem-level effects at the ng/L range of ATVs, suggesting a significant knowledge gap, which warrants further attention to this group of chemicals.
records.authors: Bollinger E, Feckler A, Filker S, Bourassi H, Maccagnan A, McArdell CS, Bundschuh M.

records.title: Longitudinal associations of the gut microbiome with arterial stiffness in US adults: findings from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging.
records.abstract: The gut microbiome affects arterial stiffness in experimental murine models; however, evidence in human longitudinal studies is lacking. In this study, we investigated longitudinal between-person (average) and within-person (change) associations of microbiome features with arterial stiffness. We assessed the fecal microbiome using whole genome metagenomic sequencing, and arterial stiffness using carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (cfPWV). Our analytic sample consisted of 349 adults from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, who contributed 915 visits between 2013 and 2019. Using linear mixed models, we found higher microbiome evenness and butyrate-producing bacteria were associated with lower cfPWV on average (between-person), but changes in diversity were not associated with changes in cfPWV (within-person). Several potentially pathogenic bacteria were positively associated with cfPWV, both between- and within-person. Butyrate-production pathways were inversely associated with cfPWV between-person and borderline within-person. Trimethylamine-production genes were positively associated with cfPWV between-person and borderline within-person. In addition, changes in other functional pathways including peptidoglycan biosynthesis and L-arginine biosynthesis were associated with changes in cfPWV. In conclusion, cfPWV was associated with both between-person and within-person differences in gut microbiome features, with strength and consistency depending on the feature. These results can inform which microbiome features to target in interventions to improve arterial stiffness.
records.authors: Tilves C, Xiao S, Tanaka T, Differding MK, Spira AP, Ferrucci L, Mueller NT.

records.title: Effect of TiO<sub>2</sub>-coupled 405 nm LED light on hatching performance, production performance and environmental microbial in laying hens.
records.abstract: Intensive poultry production has led to biosecurity challenges, such as vertical pathogen transmission, disinfectant residues, and antimicrobial resistance. In this study, a two-strain incubation trial and a 62-week production trial were conducted, and the effects of TiO₂-coupled 405 nm LED treatment were evaluated throughout the entire layer production cycle. During incubation, eggs received either continuous darkness or a 12L:12D photoperiod (20 lx) of the 405 nm LED light from days 8 to 21. During production trial, hens were reared under conventional or TiO₂-coupled 405 nm LED light. Production performance, microbial loads, and community structures were measured. Light treatment significantly shortened the time to 90% hatch without impairing hatchability or chick quality. Under this treatment, hens reached 50% egg production significantly earlier than those in the control group. No significant differences were observed in the growth performance, egg quality, carcass, and eye health under the light treatment. Importantly, the treatment reduced the abundance of microbes on the eggshell surface by 26.47-27.78% and the concentration of incubator airborne bacteria by 58.37-66.68% (P < 0.05). During production, microbial counts on feed trough surface decreased by 36.11-40.00%, airborne bacterial counts by 35.58-54.75%, and Staphylococcus aureus counts by 29.39%, with evident biofilm disruption. Metagenomic sequencing revealed that the light treatment reduced the abundances of Chlamydia abortus, Chlamydia psittaci, and Klebsiella pneumoniae on eggshells by 94.64%, 95.15%, and 70.09%, respectively. Correspondingly, translocation of hepatic Klebsiella in chicks decreased and the liver microbial ecosystem stabilized. Furthermore, 16S/ITS sequencing of feed trough samples showed a 13.78% reduction in the abundance of the pathogenic phyla Firmicutes, with lower abundance of Basidiomycota allergens and enrichment of beneficial Ascomycota. In conclusion, light treatment did not adversely affect hatchability or production performance in this study. Instead, it significantly reduced environmental microbial loads, suppressed the growth of key pathogens, and optimized microbial ecology, thereby demonstrating its potential as a safe and environment-friendly auxiliary biosecurity strategy during the incubation and poultry production periods.
records.authors: Wu X, Su B, Su D, Ye R, Xu J, Li X, Zhang S, Fan Y, Wang S, Yao Y, Zhang R, Li H, Sun E, Zhao X, Chen Y, Hao E, Wang D, Chen H, Shi L.

records.title: Pre-existing genome architecture partitions viral takeover in the smallest free-living eukaryote
records.abstract: Nuclear DNA viruses colonize host genomes already structured into complex spatial domains, yet whether established spatial boundaries dictate viral progression remains unresolved—in part because sequence composition and transcriptional output are intertwined in animal models. Here, we tracked productive lytic infection of the marine picoeukaryote  Ostreococcus tauri by the giant double-stranded DNA prasinovirus OtV5, recording transcription, accessibility, and 3D contact dynamics across parallel time courses. Although total cellular transcript pools collapsed 18-fold by 10 h post-infection, the host transcriptional shutdown, decay of insulation, early chromatin opening, and viral DNA positioning were all bounded by architectural coordinates defined prior to viral arrival. Across two low-GC outlier domains, chromatin accessibility spiked rapidly, spatial insulation eroded, and loci exhibited relative upregulation by 6 hpi, with the smaller outlier region retaining elevated transcript levels per cell compared to the rest of the genome. Unexpectedly, viral DNA was preferentially depleted from these accessible outlier cores, contacting instead the standard-GC telomeric flanks situated immediately beyond the pre-existing spatial boundaries. Domain identity, rather than local accessibility or active host expression, thus governs viral positioning, demonstrating that pre-existing nuclear architecture partitions the physical and transcriptional takeover of the host cell.
records.authors: Harrison K, Valiadi M, Kilias ES, Loe-Mie Y, Ragheb R, Kimmance S, Monier A.

records.title: Organisms associated with siphonophores revealed by short-read whole-genome sequencing
records.abstract: Siphonophores are associated with prey, parasites, microbes, and other organisms in the open ocean, but little is known about these siphonophore cobionts. To learn more about them, we investigated molecular bycatch: their DNA captured during siphonophore genome sequencing. We reanalysed 213 specimens of  Physalia, Nanomia, Bargmannia and other siphonophores sequenced in four previously published studies. We recovered 104 bacterial genomes forming 32 genome clusters, including recurrent Metamycoplasmataceae and diverse proteobacteria, groups also found with other cnidarians. Bacterial communities differed among  Physalia species sampled in the southwestern Pacific. We identified non-siphonophore eukaryotes from ribosomal markers in 38 specimens, including fish and copepods consistent with prey, parasitic flatworms, and  Perkinsela -like relatives of amoeba endosymbionts. Alfonsino (  Beryx ) sequences in one Hawaiian  P. utriculus specimen are consistent with capture of pelagic young of deepwater fishes. Molecular bycatch reveals the diversity of siphonophore associates from specimens already collected for genome research.
records.authors: Dunn CW, Ahuja N, Destanović D, Mańko MK, Dal Bello M, Church SH.

records.title: Metagenomic insights into microbial adaptation and resilience of single-stage partial nitritation-anammox systems assisted by graphene oxide sponges under increasing salinity.
records.abstract: Salinity is an increasingly important challenge limiting the application of single-stage partial nitritation-Anammox (PN/A) processes for treating saline nitrogen-rich wastewaters due to osmotic stress and microbial activity inhibition. In this study, a graphene oxide sponge (GOS)-assisted PN/A system was operated for 164 days under progressively increasing salinity from 2,000 to 12,000 mg/L NaCl to investigate the long-term performance and the associated physiological, ecological, and functional responses to salinity stress. Despite transient performance deterioration following each salinity increment, the reactor rapidly acclimated and maintained stable nitrogen removal, achieving ammonia removal efficiencies above 98%. Salinity acclimation promoted extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) production, particularly tightly bound EPS, and enhanced the activities of ammonia-oxidizing bacteria and anammox bacteria. Scanning electron microscopy confirmed dense biofilm formation on the GOS, while elemental analysis indicated a lower surface-associated sodium signal in the attached biomass compared with suspended sludge. Microbial community analysis revealed the enrichment of salt-tolerant functional microorganisms, particularly Candidatus Kuenenia and Nitrosomonas. Metagenomic analysis further demonstrated that microbial adaptation was primarily associated with the enrichment of genes involved in two-component systems, ABC transporters, and quorum sensing pathways, suggesting increased functional potential for environmental sensing, transport regulation, and microbial communication, while the nitrogen transformation pathways remained relatively stable. These findings characterize the long-term performance and associated microbial responses of a GOS-assisted PN/A system under progressive salinity stress, providing new mechanistic insights into the salinity resilience of PN/A systems treating saline nitrogen-rich wastewaters.
records.authors: Wu S, Quan Y, Gao F, Shi L, Liu Z, Shen Z, Elsayed Ali EA, Veeramuthu A, Chen H.

records.title: The stimulative effect of Cordyceps sinensis functionalized selenium nanoparticles on bone development in growing mice: involvement of the gut microbiota-bone axis.
records.abstract: IntroductionAchieving optimal peak bone mass (PBM) during adolescence through adequate intake of trace element such as selenium is crucial for reducing osteoporosis risk in later life. We previously developed novel functionalized selenium nanoparticles (Cs4-SeNPs) utilizing polysaccharide-protein complex isolated from Cordyceps sinensis for prevention of osteoporosis. The gut microbiota, functioning as the "second gene pool", plays a crucial role in maintaining bone homeostasis. However, how Cs4-SeNPs regulate bone metabolism via the gut microbiota-bone axis remains unclear.ObjectivesTo elucidate how the gut microbiota and microbial metabolites mediate the bone-promoting effect of Cs4-SeNPs.MethodsGrowing mice model was used to assess the effect of Cs4-SeNPs on bone development. Metagenomics, metabolomics, and proteomics analyses were conducted to uncover the mechanism of action of Cs4-SeNPs. In vitro osteoblast and osteoclast models were employed to validate the effects of key gut microbial metabolites regulated by Cs4-SeNPs on osteogenesis and osteoclastogenesis. Pseudo-germ-free mice model treated with antibiotics was employed to determine the role of gut microbiota in bone-promoting effects of Cs4-SeNPs.ResultsWe found that Cs4-SeNPs significantly enhanced bone mass in growing mice, as evidenced by improved bone microarchitecture and increased expression of bone extracellular matrix-related markers. Notably, antibiotic treatment-induced microbial depletion abolished the effects of Cs4-SeNPs on bone development in growing mice. Increased abundance of beneficial gut bacterial genera, notably Adlercreutzia and Parvibacter, were observed following Cs4-SeNPs administration. Proteomics analysis and subsequent verification experiments demonstrated that Cs4-SeNPs inhibited the TNF-R1/TAB2/NF-κB inflammatory pathway and upregulated the expression of antioxidant proteins including SERPINA3K, GPX1, and SOD in the bone tissue. Metabolomic analysis revealed that Cs4-SeNPs treatment significantly elevated fecal and serum levels of two key metabolites: kynurenic acid and trehalose. Further in vitro studies confirmed that kynurenic acid and trehalose could reproduce the effects of Cs4-SeNPs on osteoblastic and osteoclastic differentiation.ConclusionsOur findings suggest that Cs4-SeNPs optimize PBM and promote bone development in growing mice by improving the osteoblast/osteoclast balance via the modulation of the inflammatory TNF-R1/TAB2/NF-κB axis and the enhancement of antioxidant activity through the elevated levels of gut microbial metabolites kynurenic acid and trehalose in a gut microbiota-dependent manner.
records.authors: Liu ZW, Lai CH, Gan RY, Chen L, Zhang BB, Cheng WY, Dong XL, Wong KH.

records.title: Nitrogen availability modulates soil microbial carbon fixation in wetland through community and metabolic remodelling.
records.abstract: Excess agricultural nitrogen (N) from farm drainage and runoff causes wetland water N pollution and destabilizes soil carbon (C) sinks, however, how this N enrichment regulates wetland soil microbial autotrophic C fixation remains unclear. Here, we combined field experiments, 13CO2 continuous pulse labeling, DNA-stable isotope probing and metagenomics to investigate the dose-dependent effects of N input on soil microbial community assembly, co-occurrence networks, C-fixation pathways, and soil physicochemical properties in Songnen Plain saline-alkali wetlands of China. The results indicate that N input exerts a threshold regulation on microbial C fixation, with distinct depth-dependent responses. Intermediate N input (N2, 10 g N m-2 yr-1) alleviates soil microbial N limitation, elevates RubisCO and hydrolase activities, optimizes soil CN-phosphorus stoichiometry, and promotes the accumulation of mineral-associated organic C. Such intermediate N input remodels microbial community structure, increases microbial diversity and network stability, and enriches key C-fixing taxa including Cyanobacteriota and Alphaproteobacteria, thereby upregulating six core autotrophic C-fixation pathways. In contrast, excessive N (N4, 24 g N m-2 yr-1) input induces soil acidification and nutrient imbalance, disrupts microbial network stability, declines functional C-fixing microbiota and suppresses C-fixation gene expression, ultimately reducing soil CO2 assimilation and organic C accumulation. Structural equation modelling and random forest analyses further reveal soil microbial biomass N and RubisCO activity are the primary drivers of microbial C fixation, mediated by soil microbial C metabolic pathways and community diversity. This work reveals mechanisms of wetland soil C fixation under agricultural N pollution and informs wetland nutrient management and C-sink conservation.
records.authors: Luo S, Song Y, Zhao Y, Zhang H, Ren J, Zhang J, Song C.

records.title: Nucleic acid amplification testing for obligate intracellular and cell wall-deficient bacteria: from assay performance to clinical interpretation, a structured narrative review.
records.abstract: Obligate intracellular bacteria (Rickettsia, Orientia, Ehrlichia, Anaplasma, Coxiella, Chlamydia) and cell wall-deficient Mycoplasma species present profound diagnostic challenges due to their fastidious growth, low circulating burden, and genomic instability. Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests (NAATs) have revolutionized detection, yet critical gaps persist in distinguishing active infection from persistent DNA, standardizing cycle threshold interpretation, and integrating host-response biomarkers. This structured narrative review provides a comprehensive analysis of the complete diagnostic armamentarium for these pathogens. It is based on a reproducible, non-systematic literature survey and is not a PRISMA-compliant systematic review. We cover conventional methods (culture, serology), NAAT platforms (qPCR, digital PCR, isothermal amplification), and emerging technologies including CRISPR-Cas diagnostics, metagenomic sequencing, nanopore sequencing, biosensors, and host-response biomarker profiling. We introduce four conceptual frameworks: the "biological noise" paradigm reframing low-copy detection as a signal-to-noise challenge; a temporal-dynamic algorithm accounting for pathogen-specific detection windows; the "detection-disease disconnect" emphasizing clinical contextualization of NAAT positivity; and multi-analyte integration combining NAAT with viability markers and host inflammatory signatures. We also position these frameworks relative to prior diagnostic-interpretation theories, including STARD, QUADAS-2, MIQE, Bayesian pretest-posttest reasoning, Ct-value interpretation guidance, and host-response classifier frameworks. We compare ten clinically significant pathogens across technical and biological parameters, evaluate point-of-care deployment strategies, and address antimicrobial resistance testing. Performance metrics are presented as context-dependent estimates rather than fixed constants. The next frontier lies not in incremental assay improvements but in system-level integration of pathogen detection, viability assessment, host-response profiling, and clinical phenotyping, supported by artificial intelligence-enhanced interpretation and global standardization efforts.
records.authors: Naderi M, Sadidi R, Besharati R, Kebriae A, Azimian A.

records.title: Evaluation of the Safety and Efficacy of Fecal Microbiota Transplantations with Oral Capsules in Alzheimer’s Disease Patients Using Metagenomic Sequencing
records.abstract: Background:  Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease. Numerous studies have shown that the gut microbiota is closely related to the occurrence and development of Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that alterations in gut microbiota may represent a therapeutic strategy. However, the role and mechanisms of the gut microbiota in AD remain unclear, and standard research protocols for the gut microbiota are not uniform. The clinical safety and efficacy of oral capsule fecal microbiota transplantation, ( FMT) in patients with AD are not yet established, and related clinical studies are lacking. Objective: This study aimed to investigate the safety and effects of FMT capsule on cognitive im-pairment in patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease and to explore the re-lationship between cognition and gut microbiota by evaluating changes in gut microbial gene expression after FMT. Methods: In this study, 18 patients with clinically and radiologically confirmed mild to moderate AD aged 60-80years old were enrolled in this prospective single-arm clinical observation study. All subjects received allograft FMT (intestinal bacteria capsules with strict do-norscreening and in line with international FMT donor standards) three times at 0, 30 and 60 days. Serum and fecal samples were collected at 0, 30, 60 and 90 days, and MoCA, MMSE scores, HAMD, HAMA, ADL and fecal metagenomics sequencing were evalu-ated.During FMT and follow-up, safety was assessed by recording adverse events (AEs), vital signs, and laboratory parameters. Results After the intervention of FMT capsule, various cognitive and behavioral scores in FMT1 and FMT2 groups were not significantly changed, MMSE and MoCA scores in FMT3 group were significantly higher than those in FMT0 group (P Conclusion: In this study, FMT capsules can alter the intestinal microbiome structure and achieve intestinal microbiome remodeling, which may be a potential mechanism for microbiome capsules to improve AD related phenotypes.It is well tolerated and safe in the treatment of patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease.Despite the limited sample size and lack of control group, the results still provide clinical evidence for targeted inter-vention of the gut-brain axis in AD, but larger, randomized, double-blind place-bo-controlled trials are needed to further verify its efficacy and mechanism.
records.authors: Wu J, Cui D, Si Z.

records.title: PloidyPeaks: R package for automated flow cytometry cell cycle analysis and visualization in fungal microbes
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Karyotypic variation in fungal populations from ecological, clinical, and industrial environments and is also a hallmark of many cancers. The evolutionary dynamics of karyotypic vriants (i.e., changes in the number of chromosomes, either as complete sets or single chromosomes) are the same as any  de novo mutation. To quantify karyotypic subpopulations within evolving populations, an unbiased computational method is required to identify subpopulations and quantify their abundance. Flow cytometry is the standard method to measure the genome size from large populations of individual cells. Cell populations typically include cells in all stages of the cell cycle (G0/G1 before DNA replication, S phase during replication, and G2/M after DNA replication but before cell division). Existing mathematical models can be fit to genome-size distributions to determine the base ploidy of a population, but existing algorithms assume a single base ploidy. Mixed-karyotype populations therefore require manual gating to subdivide the flow cytometry data before analysis, which introduces bias, as it is not always clear where or when gates should be drawn. To overcome this, we developed an new method that identifies and quantifies karyotypic subpopulations from flow cytometry data. The open-source R package  ploidyPeaks builds on existing Bioconductor tools to import and manipulate standard  .fcs flow cytometry files. Using reference populations of known ploidy, we established thresholds to distinguish single-genome size populations and identify candidate mixed-karyotype samples. We then developed a peak-detection algorithm to identify G0/G1 and G2/M peaks, resolve karyotypic subpopulations within mixed populations, and apply nonlinear least-squares fitting of the Dean-Jett-Fox cell-cycle model to each subpopulation, providing a confidence measure for model fit. Compared with existing methods, our approach quantifies genome size in mixed-karyotype populations without manual intervention while providing an objective measure of model fit. We demonstrate the utility of this method on 240 replicate populations initiated from 20  Candida albicans genetic backgrounds evolving for 100 generations to the antifungal drug fluconazole.
records.authors: Henry M, Kostna C, von Giese L, Gerstein A.

records.title: Genomic insights into environmental adaptation and metabolic versatility of Acinetobacter junii IK2 isolated from marine biofilm.
records.abstract: Biofilm formation is ubiquitous in the marine environment, driven by microbial colonization on submerged surfaces, and poses ongoing challenges to maritime industries. In this study, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was carried out for Acinetobacter junii IK2, a strain isolated from the biofilm formed on stainless steel coupons immersed in a seawater microcosm setup to elucidate its genomic features and biofilm-forming potential. The genome consists of 3,215,808 bp with a GC content of 38.63%, assembled from Illumina-generated sequencing data. A total of 2990 protein-coding sequences (CDS), 10 rRNA genes, and 63 tRNA genes were predicted. Functional annotation through COG, GO, and KEGG databases resulted in the classification of 2909, 2389, and 2960 unigenes, respectively. Genome analysis identified the presence of thirteen genes associated with biofilm development, including the pgaABC operon, two-component systems (barA, ompR), and global regulators (crp, csrA, dksA), suggesting potential for biofilm formation. Genes such as oxyR, yfiB, yiaD, and pal further support oxidative stress resistance, adhesion, and envelope stability. The biofilm-forming ability of Acinetobacter junii IK2 was further validated using a crystal violet microtiter plate assay, confirming its ability to form biofilms. Additionally, 35 virulence genes, 6 multidrug resistance genes and 25 insertion sequences suggest enhanced survival, pathogenicity and genetic plasticity, reinforcing biofilm-mediated persistence. These genomic features provide insights into potential adaptive mechanisms that may contribute to the environmental adaptation of A. junii IK2 and offer insights into its role in the marine environment.
records.authors: Rajendran T, Dhinakarasamy I, Amith V, Kumar R, Bhoopathy S, Chandrasekar A, Varadharajan RK, Louis SA, Sivaraj A, Viswanathan J, Baskaran S, Chandrasekaran K.

records.title: Equipositioning of chromosomes in the polyploid archaeon Haloferax volcanii by HpaAB.
records.abstract: Proper genome segregation is essential for cellular survival, yet this process is poorly understood in archaea. Archaea show considerable variability in genome ploidy and organization. Haloferax volcanii DS2 is a polyploid archaeon with a fragmented genome consisting of a main chromosome, three secondary chromosomes and a plasmid. Due to high ploidy, genomic segregation in H. volcanii is typically considered random. However, we identified four two-gene operons encoding ParA-like proteins and uncharacterized partners. Here we characterized HpaA and HpaB, encoded on the secondary chromosome pHV3. HpaA contains conserved ATPase walker motifs and is a ParA protein with a bacterial origin. Mutation of key residues in HpaA alters its localization, while HpaA is necessary for proper HpaB spatial distribution. HpaB forms cytosolic foci and functions as a centromere-binding protein, analogous to bacterial ParB. Deletion of the genes hpaA and hpaB results in severe growth defects when xylose is the sole carbon source, consistent with the location of xylose degradation genes on pHV3. It also reduces the pHV3 to main chromosome ratio. Single-particle tracking suggests that HpaB influences HpaA dynamics. Together, these findings demonstrate an equipositioning of pHV3, likely supporting maintenance in the different cell morphologies observed in H. volcanii.
records.authors: Premrajka K, Johnsen U, Preidel H, Wienberg J, Corleis C, Ortjohann M, Giacomelli G, Bramkamp M.

records.title: Advancing microbial pangenomics through human pangenomics.
records.abstract: Although the term pangenome originated in the study of microbial species, recent advances in eukaryotic pangenomics have been driven largely by the need to manage the substantial computational challenges posed by population-scale eukaryotic datasets. This review evaluates the extent to which existing eukaryotic pangenome tools and methods can be extended to microbial species. We first survey current eukaryotic and microbial pangenomic approaches and then examine opportunities and challenges in adapting eukaryotic methods to microbial genomes, with particular emphasis on scalability, data quality, evolutionary complexity, and benchmarking. Finally, we highlight areas where existing approaches generalize well and where substantive redesign and redevelopment are needed.
records.authors: Bravo JE, Sapoval N, Han Y, Kokroko N, Nakhleh L, Noyes NR, Treangen TJ, Boucher C.

records.title: Exploring sex- and captivity-associated gut microbial diversity in Bengal Tigers (Panthera tigris tigris).
records.abstract: BACKGRO​UND: The gut microbiome plays a critical role in host nutrition, immune regulation, metabolic stability, and overall physiological health in wildlife. However, gut microbiome data from large carnivores remain limited, particularly for endangered tiger populations. This study conducted a comparative analysis of fecal microbiomes from captive and wild Bengal tigers, integrated with publicly avai​lable datasets from Amur, Malayan, and South China tigers, to understand how captivity and host factors influence microbial assembly. ME​THOD​S AND RESULTS: Across all tiger subspecies, Firmicutes and Proteobacteria dominated as core bacterial phyla, with Actinobacteriota, Bacteroidota, and Fusob​acteriota forming a conserved microbial backbone. Wild Bengal tigers exhibited higher microbial richness and diversity than captive tigers​. Beta diversity analyses demonstrated clear clustering by habitat (captive versus wild), but substantial overlap between male and female captive Bengal tigers, indicating that captivity-associated conditions exert influences on gut microbiome structure than sex. Comparative analyses among tiger subspecies revealed broad overlap in microbial community composition, suggesting limited phylogenetic influence. South China and Amur tigers displayed the lowest richness compared to Bengal and Malayan tigers. Furthermore, analysis identified an enrichment of protein fermentation-associated taxa in captive tigers, whereas wild tigers showed a greater abundance of environmentally associated taxa. CONCLUSIONS: The study provides evidences that captivity promotes reduction in gut microbial diversity in Bengal tigers, and highlights the potential utility of microbiome-informed captive management. Integrating gut microbiome monitoring into conservation breeding, zoo exchange and reintroduction programmes may improve adaptive fitness in endangered tiger populations.
records.authors: Dolker S, Ghosh A, Singh VK, Joshi BD, Sharma LK, Thakur M.

records.title: Genomic characterization of greenhouse-associated Aspergillus fumigatus from China reveals population structure, antifungal resistance, and relationships with global lineages.
records.abstract: Aspergillus fumigatus is a globally distributed saprophyte and a major opportunistic pathogen causing invasive aspergillosis. The emergence of azole-resistant A. fumigatus in agricultural environments poses a growing threat to human health, yet the genetic basis of resistance and the role of agricultural hotspots remain poorly understood. Here, we analyzed 226 greenhouse-derived isolates from Yunnan, China, within a global genomic framework. Although Yunnan isolates shared overall diversity patterns with worldwide populations, they exhibited pronounced population structure, with one well-supported clade (Clade B) enriched in greenhouse environments. To investigate cross-environment relationships, we further analyzed an expanded collection of isolates from greenhouse soils, air, agricultural markets, and clinical sources using multilocus genotyping. Identical or highly similar genotypes were detected across environments, including resistant strains carrying the TR₃₄/L98H allele, demonstrating that greenhouse and clinical isolates are genetically connected. Genome-wide association analyses identified candidate loci associated with antifungal resistance and stress tolerance beyond canonical cyp51A mutations, including genes involved in cell wall remodeling and mitochondrial dynamics. Together, these results reveal the genomic landscape of greenhouse-associated A. fumigatus in China and provide evidence for genetic connectivity between agricultural and clinical settings, underscoring the importance of surveillance at agricultural-clinical interfaces.ImportanceAzole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus is an increasing global health concern because resistant infections are difficult to treat and often fatal. Agricultural environments have been implicated as important sources of resistance, yet the mechanisms underlying the emergence, persistence, and transfer of resistance to human patients remain unclear. By integrating genomic and phenotypic analyses of greenhouse-derived isolates from Yunnan, China, we identified a distinct clade that is enriched in greenhouse environments and exhibits stable antifungal resistance. Resistant genotypes were repeatedly detected across greenhouses, local markets, and patients; notably, identical multilocus genotypes and cyp51A mutations were shared between market air samples and a patient with invasive aspergillosis, demonstrating genetic connectivity between agricultural and clinical settings. Beyond the well-known cyp51A mutations, genome-wide association analyses highlighted several candidate loci associated with antifungal resistance-including a dynamin-related GTPase and a strongly induced cell-wall peptidase-that may represent non-canonical resistance mechanisms. These findings provide insights into fungal adaptation and resistance evolution in agricultural contexts. They underscore the urgent need for integrated surveillance and stewardship across agricultural and medical sectors to mitigate the spread of antifungal resistance.
records.authors: Duan C, Wang Y, Gong J, Huang J, Zhou D, Zhang Y.

records.title: Acute lethality and stress-responsive phenotypes differ among three Acinetobacter baumannii strains: phenotypic, genomic and transcriptomic analyses
records.abstract: Abstract    Background  Acinetobacter baumannii  exhibits substantial strain-level heterogeneity in antimicrobial resistance, virulence-associated phenotypes and responses to environmental stress. Whether acute lethality covaries with surface-associated and stress-responsive phenotypes across different strain backgrounds remains unclear. We compared three clinically distinct  A. baumannii  strains, LS01, AB5075 and XH386, using phenotypic assays, comparative genome annotation and transcriptomic profiling. Results  The three strains displayed distinct phenotypic profiles. Following inoculation with 5 × 10^4 CFU in  Galleria mellonella  , 96-h survival was 20% for LS01, 45% for AB5075 and 60% for XH386. In immunocompetent C57BL/6J mice challenged by oropharyngeal aspiration with a common inoculum of 5 × 10^6 CFU, 120-h survival was 25% after LS01 infection, whereas all AB5075- and XH386-infected mice survived. XH386 yielded the highest HBE-cell-associated bacterial recovery in both independent experiments. OD600 trajectories during exposure to non-heat-inactivated human serum varied with serum concentration and donor; at 10% serum, XH386 showed a higher late-phase OD600 than LS01 in both donor experiments. Transmission electron microscopy showed the most prominent capsule-associated extracellular layer in AB5075, whereas LS01 showed a thinner layer and XH386 markedly attenuated capsule-associated material. Attached biomass varied with strain and environmental condition, with XH386 showing the highest biomass under 10% heat-inactivated serum in repeated experiments. Comparative genome annotation showed extensive overlap in major pathogenicity-, biofilm-, iron-acquisition-, secretion- and stress-associated systems despite these phenotypic differences. In XH386, DIP-mediated iron restriction produced the largest transcriptional response, with 1,059 genes meeting adjusted  P

records.title: Autonomous Hypothesis Testing Against Public Biomedical Data with Literature-Grounded Calibration
records.abstract: Public biomedical repositories contain petabytes of data, yet testing hypotheses against those resources still requires expert effort. I present a four-phase blinded workflow for autonomous computational hypothesis testing: an agent receives a natural-language hypothesis, discovers public datasets with academic publisher domains blocked, executes an analysis pipeline and validates findings against the literature. Published studies serve as calibration rulers, measuring how closely an autonomous workflow approaches known answers before it is trusted on unknown ones. Across five biomedical tasks spanning bacterial genomics, single-cell multiomics, metagenomics, cancer genomics and GWAS functional genomics, the agent scored 5–9 out of 10 on pre-specified rubrics in 20–188 minutes (the single-cell multiomics score was corrected from an initial 8 to 5 after blinded judge review identified over-credited criteria; see Methods). An exploratory comparison across three successive model generations found scores directionally higher for the first generation (claude-opus-4-6) on all five tasks (one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.031, rank-biserial r = 1.0; n = 5 studies), with newer models completing tasks faster; the benchmark also exposed generation-specific safety policy and schema differences that silently confound cross-generation comparisons if not corrected. Failures fell into three categories, tool-version sensitivity, data-scope limitation and analytical completeness, all self-diagnosed by the validation phase in all five cases examined here without human prompting. These results introduce a calibration framework and failure taxonomy for characterising when autonomous computational science workflows should and should not be trusted.

records.title: Population Genetic Evolution Analysis of Tsaoko Stripe Mosaic Virus and Development of RT-PCR and Real-Time RT-PCR Detection Methods for Strain Discrimination.
records.abstract: Tsaoko stripe mosaic virus (TkSMV) has been identified as the predominant viral pathogen of Amomum tsaoko in Yunnan Province of China. This virus induced various foliar symptoms, including chlorosis, stripe mosaic, and necrosis, while some infected A. tsaoko plants remain asymptomatic. Comprehensive investigation of the population genetic structure and molecular detection protocols for TkSMV is crucial for elucidating its evolutionary dynamics, epidemiology, and disease control strategies. Phylogenetic analysis based on 15 full-length genomic sequences and 29 coat protein (CP) gene fragments revealed three distinct evolutionary lineages (S1, S2, and S3) within the TkSMV population. Neutrality test analysis indicates that the genetic polymorphism of the TkSMV population is consistent with a neutral evolution model (Tajima's D > 0, not significant). The comparative evolutionary analysis demonstrated significant selective pressures across viral proteins: codon usage bias analysis revealed strong purifying selection (dN/dS A. tsaoko cultivation.

records.title: Molecular detection of Waddlia chondrophila in aborted bovine placental and vaginal mucus samples in Japan.
records.abstract: Chlamydia-related bacteria have recently raised medical and veterinary concerns as emerging causes of abortion and pneumonia in ruminants and humans in Europe and Africa. However, these bacteria have not yet been investigated in ruminants in Japan. In this study, two species, Waddlia chondrophila and Parachlamydia acanthamoebae, were examined as potential pathogens of ruminant abortion. Vaginal mucus and placental samples were collected from 29 cows that had experienced abortion or stillbirth in Japan between August 2023 and December 2023. In real-time PCR analysis, W. chondrophila DNA was detected in both the vaginal mucus and placenta from one cow, whereas P. acanthamoebae was not detected in any individual. An 856 bp 16S rRNA sequence was obtained and identified as W. chondrophila through phylogenetic analysis. The bacterial genomic copy numbers were 3.47 × 10⁴ copies/mL in vaginal mucus and 2.36 × 10⁶ copies/g in placenta, indicating that the placental load was 30- to 130-times higher. This study represents the first report of W. chondrophila detection in a bovine abortion case in Japan and highlights the need for further investigation of Chlamydia-related bacteria and other pathogens affecting animal and human health.
records.authors: Nagamine S, Endo N, Wu CF, Fukushi H, Sassa-O'Brien Y.

records.title: Assessing field-scale effects of treated wastewater on riverine biofilms: Community composition, functional genes, and micropollutant biotransformation.
records.abstract: Treated wastewater (WW) released from wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) leads to the influx of microorganisms and micropollutants (MPs) into receiving waters, and hence presents a continuous anthropogenic pressure on downstream riverine microbial communities; however, its impact on their composition and function remains insufficiently understood, particularly under environmentally realistic field conditions spanning multiple rivers, seasons, and wastewater treatment technologies. In this study, we investigated the effects of treated WW effluent on microbial community composition, functional profiles, the prevalence of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), and the fate of 189 MPs in riverine biofilms, including detailed biotransformation analyses for 122 reliably quantifiable MPs. Biofilms were grown under well-characterized field conditions across six Swiss rivers receiving effluent from WWTPs that varied in treatment technology, wastewater dilution, and season. At each river, pairs of biofilms were grown and collected at two sites upstream (up) and three sites downstream (dw) of the WWTP discharge point, resulting in a total of 60 biofilm communities. At the level of overall community composition and general functional profiles, differences between up- and downstream sites were inconsistent. However, clearer differences emerged when analyses focused on non-dominant taxa and specific functional traits, such as ARGs and MP biotransformation, indicating subtle but ecologically relevant impacts of treated WW that may be masked by broader trends. Approximately half of the analyzable MPs were measurably biotransformed, with the majority of these transformations likely occurring via co-metabolic processes, as suggested by MP structures and overall low variance in biotransformation rate constants. For a few MPs, which had previously been associated with catabolic biodegradation, enhanced biotransformation potential was detected in 8 out of 36 downstream biofilms. These observations of increased downstream biotransformation were predominantly associated with moving bed biofilm reactor (MBBR)-based WWTPs, suggesting that WW effects were highly technology-specific rather than ubiquitous. Fine-grained metagenomic analysis revealed an association between the abundance of relevant Enzyme Commission (EC) classes and enhanced saccharin biotransformation in downstream biofilms. While increased downstream biotransformation was heterogeneous and infrequent, multiple lines of evidence suggest that microbes transferred from the WWTP via treated WW effluent endowed these functions to downstream biofilms. Overall, our findings show that WWTP impacts on riverine biofilms are generally subtle at the level of overall community structure but become apparent when focusing on non-dominant taxa and specialized functional traits, which play a disproportionate role in shaping MP biotransformation potential.

records.title: Crossfeeding interactions in a minimal marine chitin-degrading community
records.abstract: Communities of heterotrophic particle-associated marine bacteria contribute to oceanic carbon cycling through interspecies interactions that can influence polysaccharide degradation. While these interactions have been extensively studied using single natural isolates or pairwise combinations thereof, their mechanistic relevance within multispecies communities remains unclear. To address this gap, we developed MCC4, a minimal chitin-degrading bacterial community consisting of two chitin degraders and two non-degrading isolates that represent globally prevalent marine bacterial taxa. We show that the community remains stable across ten growth-dilution cycles, establishing a reproducible model for controlled multi-isolate experiments. Using transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses combined with metabolite supplementation assays, we uncovered the underlying crossfeeding network. While one degrader drives chitin degradation, the other exploits chitin monomers and chitooligomers generated by the main degrader. The two non-degraders are sustained by consuming deacetylated chitin monomers, 2-carbon compounds, nucleotides, and branched-chain amino acids, likely released by degraders. Community assembly is driven by competitive scavenging abilities, potentially complemented by specific survival strategies such as increased motility and deployment of type VI secretion systems. Despite its simplicity, MCC4 captures dynamic microbial interactions characteristic of natural marine ecosystems. It offers a tractable, reproducible framework for investigating how environmental perturbations impact community function and testing ecological theories in particle-associated marine environments. records.title: Tailocin as an alternative weapon to type VI secretion system in bee gut symbionts
records.abstract: Antagonistic interactions often shape microbial communities, as co-residents compete for resources. One system of interbacterial antagonism involves tailocins: phage tail-like particles produced by some bacteria to kill close relatives. Their roles in natural communities are poorly studied. Here, we identified putative tailocin loci ubiquitously present in genomes of  Snodgrassella species, core members of the bee gut microbiota. We purified tailocins from culture supernatants of different  Snodgrassella strains and found that these inhibited growth of multiple  Snodgrassella strains but not of strains of other species that cooccur in bee guts. Proteomic analyses corroborated the production of tailocins, and cryogenic electron microscopy imaging revealed their morphology and killing activity via membrane disruption. We generated single- and double-gene knockout mutants of a predator  Snodgrassella strain that naturally possesses both tailocin and a type VI secretion system (T6SS) that was previously shown to function in intraspecies competition in bee guts. These mutants were used in tests for antagonism against a prey  Snodgrassella strain in vivo. Co-inoculations within gnotobiotic honeybees including visualization within guts showed that both tailocin and T6SS are important for  Snodgrassella in intraspecies competition. Each of these two antagonism mechanisms inhibits the establishment of susceptible strains within the ileum. Outcomes depend on the timing of colonization by competing strains, with both tailocin and T6SS giving a stronger advantage when the producing strain colonizes first. Thus, tailocin production can underlie priority effects that have been widely observed in the bee gut community and other host-associated bacterial communities.  Significance Statement  Interbacterial competition plays a pivotal role in determining bacterial colonization success in natural habitats, including guts of animals. Tailocins are phage tail-like bacteriocins that are widely encoded in bacterial genomes and that function in intraspecies killing. They have been little studied in natural communities, including those in gut environments. Here, we show that bee gut bacteria produce tailocins that kill close relatives within the gut. Tailocins function as phage-derived antagonism mechanisms together with T6SS, which are also phage-derived. The possession of both weapons provides a double safeguard, supporting that intense competition happens in bee gut environments. Our findings bring new insights into roles of antagonistic weapons in natural communities.
records.authors: Song Y, Nikaeen N, Kambar N, Jones KR, Wade M, Leal C, Moran NA.

records.title: Unexplained Febrile Syndromes in Sub-Saharan Africa: Etiological Diversity, Diagnostic Challenges and Emerging Diagnostic Approaches—A Narrative Review
records.abstract: Unexplained febrile syndromes represent a major diagnostic and public health challenge in Sub-Saharan Africa. Although malaria remains an important cause of fever, an increasing proportion of febrile episodes is attributable to nonmalarial etiologies, encompassing a wide range of bacterial, viral, parasitic, and fungal infections, as well as noninfectious causes. Their etiological characterization remains limited by the low specificity of clinical manifestations, the heterogeneity of definitions and diagnostic algorithms, and insufficient laboratory capacity. Microscopy, rapid diagnostic tests, cultures, and serology remain essential in resource-limited settings, but their targeted nature and variable performance may lead to diagnostic dead ends. Emerging approaches, particularly multiplex PCR, next-generation sequencing, and clinical metagenomics, offer new opportunities to broaden the diagnostic spectrum, identify neglected or emerging pathogens, and strengthen surveillance. However, their integration requires strengthening laboratory networks, quality systems, and human resources, as well as evaluating their relevance and cost-effectiveness. An integrated approach based on the “One Health” concept appears essential to improve the diagnosis and surveillance of febrile illnesses in Sub-Saharan Africa.
records.authors: Keita AK, Gnimadi TAC, Kande A, Diallo H, Soumah AK, Kaba D, Toure A, Fenollar F, Mediannikov O, Keita AK.

records.title: Microbes as Key Players During Evolution Part II- From Unicellular to Multicellular Organisms
records.abstract: Microbes and thereof derived structures (plasmids, plastids, transposible elements, retrotransposons) are described as key drivers in the evolution of genes, genomes and new species in metazoa. This is a change of paradigm compared to the mechanisms of mutation and selection, and Mendelian genetics. The review first describes early metazoan developments and early symbiotic interactions. It presents examples of microbial influences on medusazoans, corals and sea anemones and then continues with microbial impacts on terrestrial ecosystems: Mutualistic associations of fungi, bacteroids and bacteria with lower plants (lichens, bryophytes) and higher plants (gymnosperms, angiosperms) and the exchange of reduced carbon for reduced nitrogen. The review goes on with animals, starting with the most recent common ancestor of vertebrates about 560 million years ago. Microbial impacts are described on insects, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals including homo sapiens. A further chapter deals with impacts of transposible elements. Special emphasis is directed towards the creation of new species. Chapter 6 describes bipartite and tripartite host-microbe cooperations which led to new holobiont species in metazoa. Defense systems and reticulate evolution are further topics of this review. The discussion points out that evolution is driven by net formation including multiple nods of primary, secondary or tertiary endosymbiogenesis events.

records.title: Widespread selection of antibiotic resistance within hospital sewers.
records.abstract: Environmental microbiomes are sources of diverse antibiotic resistance determinants that can be mobilized and transferred to human pathogens under a selection pressure from antibiotics. Hospital sewers contain more antibiotics than most environments and are thus increasingly recognised as potential arenas for resistance evolution. However, it is unknown if resistance selection occurs there and what the drivers are. Here we show selection of antibiotic-resistant bacteria within Swedish hospital sewers. Evidence include; consistent selection of multiple resistances in Escherichia coli exposed to filtered wastewater from ten hospitals, but not to corresponding municipal wastewaters; in-situ enrichment of resistant over sensitive E. coli from wastewater to sewer biofilms at hospitals, but not at municipal sites; and higher resistance in bacteria collected from hospital sewers than from municipal sites as assessed by culturing and metagenomics. Evidence for drivers includes complete rescue of sensitive E. coli by addition of resistance genes to fluoroquinolones and β-lactams, and cellular effects typical for β-lactams. Measured concentrations by liquid-chromatography-tandem-mass-spectrometry compared to selective thresholds identify ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime as principal selective agents. Antibiotic concentrations and use data allow extrapolation of risks beyond Sweden. Given the absence of detectable selection at municipal sites, mitigations of risks in hospital sewers should be prioritized.

records.title: Intracity-scale study reveals spatiotemporal variation of urban airborne microbiota and dynamics of antibiotic resistance/virulence genes.
records.abstract: Airborne microbiota are critical to urban air quality and public health, yet their spatiotemporal differentiation, community assembly, and profiles of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and virulence factor genes (VFGs) across urban functional zones remain poorly characterized. In this study, monthly 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing was combined with seasonal metagenomic profiling of 12 composite samples and environmental data to investigate airborne microbiota at three sites representing commercial, industrial, and recreational zones in Changsha, China. Airborne communities showed similar spatial patterns among the investigated functional zones but strong seasonal variation, with Shannon diversity below 2.0 in July and above 6.0 in January. Proteobacteria dominated most samples, while key seasonal taxa shifted among Delftia, Cupriavidus, and Achromobacter. Neutral community modeling supported stochastic dominance (R2 = 0.664, Nm = 1200), with 92.6% of operational taxonomic units within the 95% confidence interval. However, βNTI and RCbray analyses indicated increased deterministic selection in autumn-winter, coinciding with high pressure and pollutant accumulation. Metagenomics identified 25 ARG, 14 VFG, and 6 mobile genetic element (MGE) categories, with season explaining 53.9% of VFG compositional differences. Exploratory structural equation modeling identified associations between MGE abundance and ARG/VFG abundances (β = 0.75 and 1.09, respectively; both P < 0.001). Binning and contig co-localization showed that ARG-VFG-MGE co-harboring fragments were potentially affiliated with opportunistic pathogens such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Klebsiella pneumoniae, indicating potential biosafety concerns. These findings identify season as a key driver of urban airborne microbiota and genetic risk factors, providing a basis for atmospheric biosafety monitoring and assessment.

records.title: Hydrogen nanobubbles overcome metabolic bottlenecks and remodel transcriptional networks for high-rate methanogenesis in the anaerobic digestion of Paulownia leaf litter.
records.abstract: Volatile fatty acid (VFA) accumulation limits anaerobic digestion (AD) of lignocellulosic biomass by causing acidification and microbial metabolic imbalance. Paulownia leaf litter (PLL), an underutilized lignocellulosic residue with potential for renewable energy recovery, was selected as the substrate. This study evaluated hydrogen nanobubble water (H2-NBW) as a strategy to alleviate VFA inhibition and investigated associated microbial responses using integrated multi-omics analyses. H2-NBW increased cumulative methane yields by 26.4-34.5% compared with controls, accelerated VFA turnover, improved acid-base stability and buffering capacity, and enhanced extracellular hydrolytic enzyme activities by 12.7-42.4%. Coenzyme F420 fluorescence intensity increased by 11.5-30.7%, indicating enhanced methanogenic activity. Amplicon sequencing suggested that H2-NBW enriched microorganisms associated with carbohydrate degradation and fermentation, while overall community restructuring remained limited. Metagenomic analysis revealed increased functional potential for lignocellulose degradation, reflected in carbohydrate-active enzyme and H2 metabolism genes. Meta-transcriptomic analysis further showed increased transcription of genes associated with hydrolysis, acetate-forming metabolism, the Frh/Mvh-Hdr hydrogenase system, and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis. These responses suggest that H2-NBW may support carbon conversion and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis, accompanied by enhanced transcription of genes involved in substrate degradation, H2 metabolism, and methane formation. The observed improvements may be associated with exogenous H2 availability, microbial metabolic responses, and potential nanobubble-associated physicochemical effects. Overall, this study links improved AD performance with coordinated microbial functional and transcriptional responses, highlighting the potential of H2-NBW to improve lignocellulosic biomass conversion and methane recovery.

records.title: Strain-dependent carbon partitioning and community-level functional responses during microalgae-based dairy wastewater treatment under CO<sub>2</sub> enrichment.
records.abstract: BackgroundMicroalgae-bacteria consortia offer a route for coupling dairy-wastewater treatment with carbon conversion, yet strain-dependent differences in carbon partitioning and microbial functional responses remain insufficiently resolved.MethodsChlorella vulgaris, Tetradesmus obliquus, and Synechocystis sp. were cultivated in dairy wastewater under air or a one-time 4% CO2 gas charge followed by closed-loop recirculation. Biomass production, nutrient removal, liquid-solid-gas carbon inventories, biochemical composition, bacterial succession, metagenomic profiles, and entropy-weighted TOPSIS were integrated.ResultsSynechocystis sp. treatment S1 showed the greatest liquid-phase total-carbon drawdown (72.1%), as carbon transferred to the suspended-solid pool, the proportion of liquid inorganic carbon within the instantaneous carbon inventory declined from 54.18% to 8.85%. T. obliquus treatment T1 achieved the highest biomass concentration (0.99 ± 0.01 g·L-1), NH4+-N removal (84.89%), and comparatively high carbohydrate and lipid accumulation, yielding the highest integrated TOPSIS score. Metagenomic analyses revealed treatment-associated shifts in CBB/TCA-related functions in C. vulgaris communities and late enrichment of glycogen-associated genes in Synechocystis sp. communities. RDA further linked central-carbon gene profiles with TC, TN, TP, EPS, and biochemical pools, while bacterial succession showed marked strain- and gas-condition dependence.ConclusionsThis divergence shows that maximizing biomass recovery and maximizing liquid-carbon drawdown represent different operational objectives rather than a single strain-independent response. The results identify distinct operational advantages among the tested phototrophs: T. obliquus favored biomass and resource recovery, whereas Synechocystis sp. promoted stronger short-term inorganic-carbon conversion. Together, carbon partitioning and community functional patterns indicate that tested-strains identity, carbon availability, nutrient demand, extracellular-carbon exchange, and phycosphere succession jointly shape system performance.

records.title: Establishing Potosi Virus as a Human Pathogen: Fatal Neuroinvasive Disease in a B-Cell-Depleted Patient.
records.abstract: ObjectivesTo establish Potosi virus, a mosquito-borne member of the family Peribunyaviridae, as a neuroinvasive human pathogen.MethodsCase report.ResultsA 37-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis on long-term rituximab developed rapidly progressive dementia. Serial MRI demonstrated progressive generalized atrophy. CSF showed transient, minimal lymphocytic pleocytosis. Extensive infectious, autoimmune, and prion evaluations were unrevealing, but CSF metagenomic sequencing detected all 3 genome segments for Potosi virus. Postmortem examination revealed diffuse meningoencephalitis with T-cell-predominant leptomeningeal and perivascular inflammation. Molecular analyses confirmed multiple nucleotide sequences with >99+% concordance with a known Potosi strain, with widespread viral infection confirmed by immunohistochemistry demonstrating intracellular and extracellular viral antigen. Electron microscopy demonstrated particles of a size consistent with the Peribunyaviridae family. Metagenomic sequencing of RNA extracted from frozen brain tissue identified all 3 Potosi virus gene segments without other infectious entities. Findings were concordant across multiple laboratories and institutions.DiscussionPotosi virus can cause fatal neuroinvasive disease in humans, as evidenced by convergent postmortem neuropathologic, molecular, and ultrastructural evidence. Chronic B-cell depletion may increase susceptibility to severe disease with arboviral infections, which may present without conventional CNS inflammatory markers. CSF metagenomic sequencing should be considered in immunocompromised patients with unexplained progressive neurologic decline.

records.title: Three new species in Lentistoma, Neolindgomyces, and Ophiocreas from freshwater habitats.
records.abstract: During a survey of saprobic fungi in Jiangxi and Zhejiang provinces, China, three fungal species were collected from decaying wood samples in freshwater habitats. We selected the internal transcribed spacers (ITS1-5.8S-ITS2), large subunit (28S ribosomal RNA), small subunit (18S ribosomal RNA), translation elongation factor 1-alpha (tef1), RNA polymerase II largest subunit (rpb1), and RNA polymerase II second-largest subunit (rpb2) genes for phylogenetic analyses. Maximum likelihood and Bayesian analyses were performed to clarify the phylogenetic affinities of the species. These species are separated from the other species in respective genera based on dimensions in ascomata, asci, and ascospores and DNA sequence data. Based on morphology and multilocus phylogenetic analysis, these species were confirmed as three new species and were named Lentistoma multiseptata, Neolindgomyces aquaticus, and Ophioceras jiangshanense. Newly added species are compared with other similar species, and comprehensive descriptions and micrographs are provided.

records.title: A candidate genetic trigger of female sex determination in Marsabit clawed frogs (Xenopus borealis).
records.abstract: A central question in biology asks why the genetic basis of sex determination evolves quickly in some groups even though disruption of this process carries severe risks such as sterility. A challenge to understanding mechanisms of this rapid evolution is a lack of functionally verified genetic triggers of sex determination. To begin to remedy this, we set out to identify, characterize, and functionally test the genetic trigger of female sex determination in Marsabit clawed frogs (Xenopus borealis), which has a species-specific and probably newly evolved W chromosome. Genomic and transcriptomic data identify a candidate that was expressed specifically in female gonads during sex determination. We knocked out this gene, which is a female-specific duplicate of wnt3.L - hereafter wnt3-W - and induced complete female-to-male sex reversal in 35 of 36 individuals. These sex-reversed individuals had male-typical external and internal morphology, mating behavior, mating calls, testis histology, and are fertile. This demonstrates that wnt3-W is generally necessary for feminization of X. borealis, and adds to only one other functionally verified candidate trigger of sex determination in amphibians. Phylogenetic and cytogenetic analysis indicates that wnt3-W originated recently on the tip of the X. borealis W chromosome, after this species diverged from all other extant Xenopus. Wnt3-W is the first known candidate genetic trigger of sex determination in the Wnt gene family, which is surprising because wnt3 is more generally involved with vital, but not sex-specific functions. Similarities in protein structure are consistent with the possibility that Wnt3-W is a genetic surrogate that utilizes the feminizing genetic network of Wnt4. The discovery of wnt3-W adds to a handful of other secreted peptides that trigger sex determination in animals; its proposed function as a positively acting female-determining gene - if confirmed - would further be distinguished from other known genetic triggers in vertebrates.

records.title: Microbial bioherbicides: Integrating bioprocessing, mechanisms of action and protein engineering for sustainable weed management.
records.abstract: The widespread use of synthetic herbicides in agriculture has intensified concerns regarding environmental sustainability and human health, while the evolution of herbicide resistance has outpaced the discovery of new modes of action. Bioherbicides have consequently emerged as a viable alternative, comprising biologically derived compounds capable of suppressing weed growth. This review adopts an integrated perspective on microbially derived bioherbicides, following the active biomolecules from the producing strain and its fermentation conditions to their physiological targets in the plant and to the molecular strategies available for their optimization. Unlike previous reviews, which address these dimensions separately and focus mainly on secondary metabolites, particular emphasis is placed here on enzymes with herbicidal activity and on protein engineering approaches. Based on a structured literature search, 39 original studies were analyzed. Phytopathogenic fungi, mainly Fusarium, Diaporthe, Phoma, Alternaria and Trichoderma, predominate as producing organisms, followed by bacteria of the genera Streptomyces, Pseudomonas and Bacillus, and submerged fermentation using low-cost agro-industrial substrates is the prevailing production strategy. Enzymatic classes such as cutinases, lipases, cellulases, pectinases and proteases act primarily by degrading the cuticle and the cell wall, whereas secondary metabolites frequently target the photosynthetic apparatus, particularly photosystem II; most of these compounds, however, still lack a defined mode of action within established herbicide classification systems. Molecular approaches, including heterologous expression, molecular docking and metabolic engineering, remain comparatively underexplored despite their potential to enhance activity, stability and specificity. Advances in formulation stability, bioprocess scalability, mechanistic characterization and regulatory harmonization are identified as the key requirements to translate these biomolecules into commercially viable products for sustainable weed management.
records.authors: Krein DDC, Conterato AAM, Plucinski R, Dotto GL, Dettmer A.

records.title: Pseudomonas spp.-based synthetic microbial community effects on nutrient dynamics in citrus plants under induced dysbiosis.
records.abstract: Main conclusionA targeted Pseudomonas-based synthetic microbial community reshaped rhizosphere bacterial communities and altered potassium partitioning under stress conditions, suggesting a potential role in mitigating antibiotic-induced dysbiosis. Sustainable agriculture primarily relies on biological practices to improve crop yield and resilience. Synthetic bacterial communities (SynComs) are a promising approach to promote plant growth; however, their effectiveness in situ is influenced by interactions with native microbial ecosystems and by environmental stressors, such as low pH and antibiotic use. In this context, beneficial microorganisms like Pseudomonas may enhance nutrient availability and mitigate antibiotic-induced dysbiosis by supporting microbial community reassembly and functional stability, thereby improving plant health. This study evaluated the effects of a Pseudomonas-based SynCom on nutrient accumulation and rhizosphere microbial dynamics in citrus plants subjected to streptomycin-induced dysbiosis and low-pH conditions. Selected Pseudomonas strains, chosen for their compatibility and adaptability to low-pH conditions, and through whole-genome sequencing, were applied at equal concentrations (OD600 = 0.1). SynCom treatment increased Chloroflexota abundance in the rhizosphere while reducing Actinomycetota and Pseudomonadota after 24 days. By Day 45, the abundance of Actinomycetota decreased, with slight increases in the other two phyla. At the genus level, SynCom application reduced the abundance of Pseudomonas and Agrobacterium, while enriching the Klebsiella community. Plants treated with SynCom under stress exhibited a 25% increase in leaf potassium levels, accompanied by a 29% decrease in root potassium (essential for stomatal regulation, osmotic adjustment, and photosynthetic efficiency, which are fundamental to tree growth and stress resilience) levels. Overall, our findings demonstrate that a targeted Pseudomonas-based SynCom can reshape rhizosphere communities and improve nutrient dynamics under abiotic stress, highlighting its potential as a sustainable strategy to mitigate antibiotic-induced dysbiosis and enhance citrus resilience.
records.authors: Ketehouli T, Trub MR, Goss EM, Martins SJ.
