records.title: Human milk oligosaccharides are distinctly processed by early life gut microbial sialidases.
records.abstract: The infant gut microbiome in early life is shaped by numerous factors, including feeding method. Exclusively breastfed and formula-fed infants exhibit distinct microbiome compositions. While these effects are well-established, the underlying mechanisms that drive these differences are not fully understood. Here, we examine the removal of sialic acid from human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) influenced by human microbial sialidases in early life. We identify 351 and 214 unique sialidase sequences from adult and infant microbiome metagenomes, respectively, and characterize a diverse, representative set in vitro using sialylated HMOs normally present in human breastmilk. We find these proteins exhibit distinct abilities to metabolize 3'- and 6'-sialyllactose, which are the most abundant sialylated HMOs in breastmilk, and distinctly process other more complex substrates, as well. We provide structural insights into these functional differences by pinpointing active site features uniquely present in efficient enzymes and show that these results extend to activities on complex mixtures of sialylated HMOs purified from human breastmilk. Finally, we demonstrate in human clinical data that distinct profiles of sialidase-encoding bacterial taxa are observed in breastfed and formula-fed infants at 1 and 4 months of age, prior to the introduction of solid foods. Together, these findings show that specific bacterial sialidases are influential in shaping the early gut microbiome, data that may improve the supplementation of infant formulas for enhanced developmental outcomes.
records.authors: Plisko OL, Chapel VS, Sekela JJ, Talbert JA, Townsend SD, Zemel BS, Wu GD, R Redinbo M.

records.title: Identification of a novel equine rotavirus B from Missouri in 2025, which is distantly related to group B rotaviruses.
records.abstract: Despite the wide circulation of group B rotaviruses in animals and humans, rotavirus B was not found in horses until 2021 in Kentucky, USA. Little is known about the genetic diversity and evolution of rotavirus B in this new host. Here, we described a divergent equine rotavirus B (ERVB) from a foal with idiopathic diarrhea in Missouri (designated MO-ERVB-25). Full-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analysis revealed that MO-ERVB-25 is distantly related to all previously known group B rotaviruses, including ERVB strains identified in 2021 in Kentucky (KY-ERVB-21). The mean nucleotide substitution rate of the VP4 segment was estimated as 1.44 × 10-3 substitutions/site/year, which is a magnitude higher than the VP7 segment. We further demonstrated that MO-ERVB-25, like human RVB, binds chemically neutral LacNAc-containing complex N-linked glycans, while KY-ERVB-21 recognizes negatively charged polysialic acid (polySia) with α-2,8-linkage, which is a functional receptor for unrelated enteric human adenovirus 52. Using the AlphaFold-enabled structure prediction, we showed that both MO-ERVB-25 and human RVB VP8* lack a novel C-terminal α2 helix that is only observed in the KY-ERVB-21 VP8*, which may help explain the difference in glycan binding specificities. Finally, screening of foal samples by the reverse transcription quantitative PCR assay identified 4.2% of idiopathic foal diarrhea samples (6 out of 140) positive for MO-ERVB-25. These results suggest that MO-ERVB-25 represents a new rotavirus B subgroup that circulates in foals. Its circulation, together with KY-ERVB-25 subgroup, raises the possibility of reassortment and antigenic shift as mechanisms of rotavirus B evolution in equines.ImportanceEquine RVB (ERVB) has emerged as a significant cause of foal diarrhea since 2021. Our study describes a highly divergent RVB strain identified in a foal with severe diarrhea in 2025. This ERVB variant exhibited low amino acid identity compared with previously reported ERVB strains. The novel ERVB strain escaped routine diagnostic detection. Sequence analysis demonstrated that this new strain grouped with bovine, porcine, caprine, and equine RVB but formed a distinct, independent branch. In addition, glycan array studies revealed the substantial difference in glycan recognition between new and previously described ERVB strains, which is likely determined by the presence or absence of a novel C-terminal α2 helix in the VP8* receptor-binding domain. These results suggest that this novel ERVB variant may co-circulate with existing ERVB strains in horses, which may facilitate rapid viral evolution through antigenic diversity, a property previously reported in rotaviruses from other hosts.

records.title: Genomic and environmental determinants of circular single-stranded DNA production in engineered  E. coli
records.abstract: Single-stranded DNA with hundreds to thousands of bases is a critical reagent in biotechnology. While traditional chemical synthesis is not suitable for efficient production of such long oligonucleotides, M13 bacteriophage offers a scalable pathway towards custom, long, single-stranded DNA production. However, conventional helper plasmid-phagemid systems suffer from batch-to-batch variability and off-target packaging. To address these limitations, we previously engineered eScaf, an E. coli strain with the M13 genome stably integrated into its chromosome. eScaf produces circular, single-stranded DNA with high purity, but yields of only 100 and 200 µg of DNA per liter of culture, too low for cost-effective scale-up. Here, we systematically investigate the genomic and environmental determinants of cssDNA yield in eScaf, revealing that cssDNA yield depends on both the number and chromosomal loci of integrated M13 genomes. Combining these insights with optimized media, we achieve ∼4 mg/L of cssDNA in shake flasks, a 40-fold improvement. We also evaluate fed-batch bioreactor feeding strategies for cssDNA production using eScaf. Our new strain, eScaf-IS3, enables cost-effective production of cssDNA for high-throughput therapeutic screening, operon-length knock-in donor production, and large-scale DNA origami assembly.

records.title: Continent-wide Multi-Segment Phylogenomic Study of Host and Geographic Structuring of African Hantaviruses
records.abstract: Abstract    Background:  African hantaviruses remain among the least characterized members of the family  Hantaviridae  , with fragmented genomic data limiting our understanding of their evolutionary relationships, host associations, and geographic structuring. Here, we investigated the integrated continent-wide phylogenomic structure of African hantaviruses using all three coding genomic segments. Methods: We compiled and curated 281 full-length and partial coding sequences representing the L segment (  n   = 166), M segment (  n   = 48), and S segment (  n   = 67) from 13 African countries, alongside representative global reference strains. Temporal signal was evaluated using root-to-tip regression analysis. Segment-specific phylogenetic reconstructions were performed to characterize host-associated and geographic structuring. Additionally, pairwise tanglegram comparisons of the L, M, and S phylogenies were constructed to evaluate topological congruence and identify potential signals of genetic reassortment. Results  Root-to-tip regressions revealed weak temporal signal across the L (  R  ² = 0.069), M (  R  ² = 0.021), and S (  R  ² = 0.046) datasets, precluding reliable molecular-clock inference. Phylogenetic analyses demonstrated pronounced host-associated and geographic structuring across all three segments. Rodent, shrew, and bat-associated hantaviruses formed distinct evolutionary clades, with bat and shrew-borne lineages occupying basal, divergent positions relative to rodent-associated viruses. Endemic African hantaviruses exhibited marked regional clustering, forming distinct Malagasy, East African, and West African assemblages, whereas Senegalese, Beninese, and Malian sequences clustered within globally distributed,  Rattus  -associated Seoul orthohantavirus lineages. Comparative analyses highlighted complementary phylogenetic signals: the L segment provided a robust framework for resolving deep evolutionary relationships, the M segment offered clear discrimination among closely related host and geographic groups, and the S segment consistently recovered primary lineage boundaries. Pairwise tanglegrams demonstrated substantial topological concordance among segments highest between L and M with localized incongruences primarily in the L–S comparison restricted to closely related terminal taxa, consistent with but not definitive evidence of reassortment Conclusions  African hantaviruses display strong host-associated and geographic structuring, with major evolutionary relationships broadly conserved across all three genomic segments. These findings provide an integrated continent-wide phylogenomic framework, establishing a foundation for future genomic surveillance, evolutionary studies, and One Health strategies across Africa.
records.authors: Nicodemus M, Olumuyiwa O, Lanre I, Edet UO, Adeyinka AJ, Clement MA.

records.title: cgMLST typing reproducibility is maintained across diverse whole-genome sequencing workflows in a multi-country HERA2 surveillance pilot.
records.abstract: IntroductionWhole-genome sequencing (WGS) has become indispensable in infectious disease surveillance, yet its implementation across laboratories remains heterogeneous. Six laboratories from four European countries participated in 2023 in a pilot ring trial as part of the HERA2 project, using a standardized panel of 25 bacterial isolates representing five public health-relevant species. The aim was to assess the comparability and reproducibility of laboratory-specific WGS workflows and to determine whether workflow-related variability affected cgMLST-based interpretations relevant for routine surveillance and outbreak investigations.MethodsParticipating laboratories applied their established wet-laboratory workflows, including different sample-processing, DNA-extraction and library-preparation methods and sequencing platforms. Illumina sequencing was performed by all laboratories, while Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing was available in two. To specifically evaluate variability introduced by wet-laboratory procedures, all raw sequencing data were centrally processed using the same bioinformatic pipeline. Reproducibility was primarily assessed using cgMLST allelic distances to the Lab 1 Illumina comparator assembly and concordance of cluster assignments, complemented by analyses of sequencing and assembly variability.ResultsDespite substantial differences in wet-laboratory workflows and technical sequencing characteristics, retained Illumina records showed only small cgMLST allelic differences across laboratories (0-2 alleles) and concordant cluster assignments. Sequencing and assembly metrics varied according to laboratory, species, and technical factors, but this variability did not prevent concordant Illumina-based cluster interpretation among records meeting predefined minimum quality requirements. ONT results were more species-dependent, and several records, particularly for Salmonella enterica, did not achieve the required cgMLST target completeness. These ONT findings should be interpreted in the context of the technology available at the time of the 2023 ring trial.ConclusionsOur results suggest that complete standardization of wet-laboratory workflows may not be required to achieve comparable Illumina-based cgMLST results across laboratories. Rather, laboratories may retain validated local workflows provided that the resulting sequencing data meet appropriate minimum quality requirements. This supports a pragmatic approach to multi-laboratory genomic surveillance that prioritizes data quality and fitness-for-purpose over uniformity of individual wet-laboratory procedures.

records.title: The molecular epidemiology of human respiratory syncytial virus in a tertiary paediatric hospital between 2020 and 2024.
records.abstract: BackgroundRespiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of respiratory illness in young children, contributing significantly to morbidity and mortality and placing a substantial burden on resource-limited healthcare systems. Molecular epidemiological data from sub-Saharan Africa remain limited. This study aimed to investigate the genetic diversity and evolution of RSV in a paediatric population in Cape Town, South Africa, from September 2020 to June 2024.MethodsRespiratory syncytial virus-positive respiratory samples with a cycle threshold (Ct) ResultsOf the 100 selected samples, 42 were sequenced, and 40 had sufficient coverage for analysis. Sequencing failure was associated with higher Ct values, older sample age and suboptimal storage at -20°C. Respiratory syncytial virus-A predominated (78.6%), with A.D.5.1 as the dominant lineage; RSV-B strains (16.7%) clustered within B.D.E.1 and B.D.4.1. Genotypes GA2.3.5 (RSV-A) and GB5.0.5a (RSV-B) were observed, consistent with post-pandemic global trends. G-gene analysis revealed multiple substitutions (G224E, I134K, K262E) suggestive of immune pressure. The F-gene remained more conserved; substitutions such as T122A, S211N and S389P were detected but were not linked to reduced susceptibility to monoclonals.ConclusionThis study demonstrated the co-circulation of genetically diverse RSV-A and RSV-B lineages in children between 2020 and 2024. No established resistance-associated substitutions to currently licensed RSV monoclonal antibodies were identified. Continued genomic surveillance is warranted to monitor RSV evolution.ContributionContinued genomic surveillance is essential to strengthen molecular epidemiology and guide public health preparedness.
records.journal: Journal of the colleges of medicine of South Africa
records.authors: Maseko MJ, Joseph R, Korsman SNJ, Valley-Omar Z, Hsiao NY.

records.title: A genomic resource for a hidden endemic: the complete chloroplast genome of Allium aktauense from Uzbekistan.
records.abstract: Allium aktauense is a narrow endemic species from the Aktau Range in the Nurotau Mountains, Western Pamir-Alay, Uzbekistan, where it grows in rocky limestone crevices. Genomic resources for this species have previously been limited, restricting molecular assessment of its phylogenetic placement. In this study, we sequenced, assembled and characterized the complete chloroplast genome of A. aktauense and evaluated its phylogenetic position within Allium using comparative plastome data. The plastome is 152,443 bp long and has the typical quadripartite organization, comprising a large single-copy region of 81,522 bp, a small single-copy region of 17,907 bp and two inverted repeat regions of 26,507 bp each. Annotation identified 131 gene copies, including 85 protein-coding genes, 38 tRNA genes and 8 rRNA genes. Across the broad comparative dataset, the highest nucleotide diversity was observed in the ndhF-rpl32 region (Pi approximately 0.044), followed by ycf1 (Pi approaching 0.030); these regions are treated here as candidate variable loci requiring further validation within closely related taxa. Maximum-likelihood analysis of complete plastome sequences placed A. aktauense within subgenus Allium, with A. ophiophyllum as its closest sampled plastome lineage (bootstrap support 100%). The plastome provides a genomic resource for future phylogenetic, taxonomic and conservation-related research on endemic Central Asian Allium.

records.title: Calibrating public genome archives for AMR surveillance: Four decades of redundancy-aware phylogenomics of pandemic Escherichia coli ST131.
records.abstract: AimsEscherichia coli sequence type (ST)131 is a globally disseminated multidrug-resistant pathogen, yet public genome collections are skewed by uneven sampling and repeated sequencing of genetically near-identical isolates. Rather than another reconstruction of ST131 evolution, we quantified redundancy, reassessed population structure, and tested how sampling bias affects estimates of phylogenetic diversity, clade-specific dating, and fluoroquinolone-resistance-associated diversification.MethodsEnteroBase core-genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST) hierarchical clustering was used to reduce redundancy among 16,713 public ST131 complex genomes. Representative public genomes were combined with 390 unpublished New Zealand ST131 surveillance genomes from 1999 to 2019. Clade-specific phylogenetic and temporal analyses were performed for Clades A, B, and C, with sensitivity analyses using stricter cgMLST clustering and phylogenetic-diversity-guided subsampling.ResultsPublic genomes were highly redundant: just 2/409 cgMLST groups contained 85.2% of public genomes. After redundancy reduction, dated Clades A, B, and C phylogenies spanning 1999-2023 (n = 113), 1982-2025 (n = 240), and 1999-2025 (n = 614), respectively, were constructed. Clades A and B showed distinct temporal histories and evolutionary rates. Date-randomization supported temporal information in Clade C, although incomplete convergence of the observed-date relaxed-clock and Bayesian Skyline analyses means that exact Clade C molecular-date and demographic estimates should be interpreted cautiously. The broad Clade C reconstruction nevertheless indicated expansion of the dominant fluoroquinolone-resistant lineage in the late 1990s/early 2000s and again in the mid-2000s.ConclusionsPublic ST131 datasets reflect sampling distribution as well as number of available genomes. Redundancy in dominant cgMLST groups can obscure uncommon lineages and blur emergence with later expansion. In Clade C, redundancy-aware analysis was broadly consistent with previous estimates placing major fluoroquinolone-resistant diversification in the early 1990s, while indicating that early resistance diversification preceded later amplification of resistant sublineages.
records.journal: Drug resistance updates : reviews and commentaries in antimicrobial and anticancer chemotherapy
records.authors: White RT, Biggs PJ, Burgess SA, Collis RM, Cookson AL, Downing T, Elvy J, Featherstone LA, French NP, Pattis I, Price EP, Sarovich DS, Tiong A, Ussher JE, Winter DJ, Yang Z, Dyet K.

records.title: Does the mouth seed the small bowel? Mechanisms and hypothesis-generating framework via the oral-gut axis.
records.abstract: BackgroundAs the starting segment of the digestive tract, the oral cavity harbors a complex microbial community that closely interacts with the distal gut microbiota. Recent evidence suggests that oral hygiene status and oral dysbiosis may correlate with gut microbial homeostasis and play a potential role in the initiation or exacerbation of small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO).ObjectiveThis review aims to integrate existing evidence, outline a hypothesis-generating framework, identify critical knowledge gaps, and provide new perspectives for future interdisciplinary mechanistic research and clinical translation in SIBO and related gastrointestinal disorders.DesignThis narrative review synthesizes and evaluates preliminary clinical correlations, metagenomic surveys, and animal models that support the oral microbiota as a potentially modifiable factor associated with SIBO, and discusses the proposed underlying molecular pathways.ResultsExisting evidence supports the oral microbiota as a potentially modifiable factor associated with SIBO. However, direct high-level evidence testing oral hygiene interventions against definitive SIBO outcomes is currently lacking.ConclusionsThe oral-gut axis may play a critical role in SIBO pathogenesis. Future research requires high-quality clinical trials to validate the impact of oral hygiene interventions on SIBO outcomes, bridging the current critical knowledge gaps.
records.authors: He L, Wang J, Bai T, Hou X, Ran D, Yang J.

records.title: Genome-based identification of hydrocarbon-metabolism-associated genes with putative relevance to polyethylene modification in Rhodococcus pyridinivorans AAa3.
records.abstract: Polyethylene (PE) is a highly recalcitrant plastic that accumulates extensively in the environment. In this study, Rhodococcus pyridinivorans AAa3 was analysed using hybrid WGS to investigate its genomic features and identify candidate metabolic functions with putative relevance to PE modification. The assembled genome (5,078,411 bp) exhibited high completeness and continuity. Phylogenetic, phylogenomic, and ANI analyses confirmed the strain's classification, with 98.96 % ANI to R. pyridinivorans DSM 44555T. Genome mining identified diverse oxidative enzymes, including alkane monooxygenases, cytochrome P450s, Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenases, and multicopper oxidases. Analysis of AlkB proteins showed conserved motifs, transmembrane domains, and phylogenetic conservation. Orthology and synteny analyses showed conservation of AlkB proteins and their genomic neighbourhoods, with strain-specific variation. AAa3 contained five MCO genes, placing it toward the upper end of the copy-number distribution across 41 R. pyridinivorans genomes. Molecular docking showed accommodation of n-octane, n-decane, and n-dodecane within the targeted regions of AlkB1 and AlkB2. An AlkX-like TetR-family regulator was identified near alkB2, while targeted motif analysis detected an AlkX-like motif upstream of cytochrome P450 gene ACU6L1_03615. To the best of our knowledge, no previous genome-based study has specifically investigated R. pyridinivorans in the context of PE modification. These findings warrant further experimental investigation.
records.authors: Elsayed AF, Youssef HI, Gebreel HM, Mahasneh I, Amin DH.

records.title: Integrated assessment of mercury-tolerant plant-associated bacteria from a chlor-alkali site identifies candidates for bioaugmentation.
records.abstract: Mercury (Hg)-contaminated environments harbour microorganisms with traits that may be useful for plant-assisted remediation, but high Hg tolerance alone may not identify the most suitable strains for inoculation. In this study, plant-associated bacteria isolated from a chlor-alkali site were evaluated through phenotypic screening, whole-genome analysis, genome-scale metabolic modelling, and willow inoculation assays. Fifty-one Hg-tolerant isolates were recovered, of which 16 were selected for detailed characterization. All selected isolates displayed at least one plant growth-promoting trait, including indole-3-acetic acid production, siderophore production, or phosphate solubilization. Pseudomonas canadensis UFC_B020 and Pseudomonas umsongensis UFC_B021 grew at 200 µM Hg, the highest concentration tested. Genome-based analyses identified putative functions related to metal transport, membrane efflux, oxidative stress responses and plant-beneficial metabolism, while community-scale modelling predicted potential metabolite exchanges within three selected bacterial consortia. In willow inoculation assays, consortium 1 increased root projected area by 5.7% relative to the uninoculated control. The strongest root response was therefore associated with a different consortium from that containing the two isolates with the highest Hg tolerance, highlighting the value of considering both Hg tolerance and plant responses in candidate selection. Together, these results support an integrated strategy combining Hg tolerance, plant growth-promoting traits, genome-based functional information and consortium performance to prioritize site-derived bacteria for subsequent bioaugmentation studies.

records.title: Microbiome plasticity during the early life-stage of the angelshark (Squatina squatina) in Las Teresitas (Canary Islands).
records.abstract: Shark microbiome studies offer acute insights into host health, immunity, and ecological interactions, yet remain poorly studied compared to other marine vertebrates. Shark-associated microbial communities, despite being species-specific, are influenced by environmental conditions and feeding ecology. In this study, we aimed to characterize shifts in the microbiome of the Critically Endangered angelshark (Squatina squatina) during the early stages of development and to assess how environmental factors contribute to the shaping of a specific microbiota. Samples from thirty-nine juvenile angelsharks were collected from Las Teresitas nursery area in the Canary Islands over one year. Skin, oral and cloacal microbiomes were analysed using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing. The sizes of individuals ranged between 24 and 42 cm in length. The shark microbiome was clearly distinct from the surrounding environment, indicating a unique composition from early life stages. Dominant bacteria present in the shark microbiomes included Vibrionaceae (up to 96%), Pseudoalteromonas (up to 63%), Rhodobacteraceae (up to 57%) and Alteromonadaceae (up to 20%). Seawater had a greater influence than sediment on the external skin microbiome, especially in younger individuals. This was not expected due to the burial behaviour of the species. Notably, the abundance of Pseudoalteromonadaceae (assessed by qPCR) was positively correlated with shark growth but was independent of the skin mucus. This suggests a protective role of this phylotype in younger individuals and may help in the adaptation to habitat conditions. This is the first comprehensive microbiome study in angelsharks, highlighting the importance of environmental preservation for microbial integrity and juvenile fitness.

records.title: Phylogenetic position and expanded host range of the photosymbiont Brandtodinium nutricula (Peridiniales, Dinophyceae)
records.abstract: Brandtodinium nutricula is a dinoflagellate species commonly reported in symbiosis with the marine protist host lineage, Collodaria (Rhizaria). Despite the widespread abundance of this symbiosis throughout the open ocean, and clear indications that the alga should be capable of existing outside of the symbiosis, there are no reports to date of the alga in free-living form in the environment. Even though B. nutricula molecular data are publicly available, the phylogenetic position of B. nutricula remains unclear. Our taxon-rich 18S rRNA gene phylogenetic analysis revealed a close association between B. nutricula and the copepod parasite lineage, Blastodinium. We next analyzed Tara Oceans metabarcode data to assess B. nutricula abundance outside of the Collodaria symbiosis and found that B. nutricula is common in free-living form throughout the sunlit ocean. Similarly, B. nutricula does not significantly correlate with Collodaria in terms of read depth in Tara Oceans samples, despite their tight association. We also determined that B. nutricula can live symbiotically within planktonic Foraminifera using fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy in combination with fluorescence in situ hybridization. These findings indicate that the radiolarian-B. nutricula symbiosis is less specific than previously suggested, highlighting the complexity of open ocean symbioses and the importance of weighing both host and symbiont perspectives when considering who benefits from the relationship.
records.authors: Coots NL, Blanco Bercial L, Gile GH, Keeling PJ.

records.title: An Integrated One-Click Python Pipeline for Bacterial Codon-Usage Analysis and Proteome-Wide Characterization
records.abstract: Abstract    Background:  Codon-usage analysis provides insights into synonymous codon preferences, nucleotide composition, and potential evolutionary constraints, while protein physicochemical indices offer complementary information about proteome characteristics. Together, these sequence- and protein-level measures can provide a broader computational view of genomic and proteomic variation across bacterial genomes providing insights into crucial functional mechanisms like pathogenicity and antibiotic resistance. However, integrating these analyses into a streamlined and reproducible workflow can be challenging.  Methods:  We developed an integrated one-click Python pipeline for bacterial codon-usage analysis and proteome-wide characterization. The workflow processes FASTA sequences, applies sequence-quality filters, calculates codon-usage and nucleotide-composition indices, performs parity analysis, and conducts principal component analysis (PCA) using relative synonymous codon usage (RSCU) and relative amino-acid usage (RAAU). It also estimates protein-level characteristics, including theoretical isoelectric point, molecular weight, grand average of hydropathicity, aromaticity, and sequence-length measures. Results are organized into two worksheets within a single Excel output.  Results:  The pipeline was applied to coding sequences from  Acinetobacter baumannii  ,  Pseudomonas aeruginosa  , and  Elizabethkingia anophelis  . Comparisons with previously reported values showed broadly similar estimates for selected indices, including GC content, GC3s, GRAVY, and aromaticity. However, differences were observed in third-position nucleotide composition, codon adaptation index (CAI), frequency of optimal codons (Fop), and sequence-length-related measures. These discrepancies highlight the influence of computational definitions, reference sets, and sequence-processing criteria on the resulting estimates.  Conclusion:  The pipeline integrates codon-level and protein-level analyses into an accessible workflow that generates structured outputs. Further benchmarking against established tools using matched sequences and standardized definitions is needed to establish its numerical agreement, robustness, and broader applicability. Future development could expand reference-set customization and validation across diverse bacterial genomes.

records.title: Construction and Evaluation of a Reference Strain System for Brucella melitensis Biovar 2 and Genomic Characteristic Analysis
records.abstract: Abstract    Objective  To establish a candidate national reference strain of  Brucella melitensis  biovar 2 according to relevant technical standards using a  Brucella  strain preserved in the local biological sample repository in Zhuhai City.  Methods  In accordance with the Technical Evaluation Standard for National Pathogenic Microorganism Strains (WS/T 812–2022), morphological identification of the candidate Brucella strain was performed via colony observation, Gram-staining and transmission electron microscopy. Species-level identification was carried out using matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF-MS), biochemical assays, serum agglutination tests and phage lysis assays. Whole-genome sequencing was applied for biovar typing, virulence- and resistance-associated gene profiling. Physiological characteristics were further characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing and strain stability assessment.  Results  Strain ZH25-Bru-002 (abbreviated as ZH25 throughout the text) was a Gram-negative bacillus. It grew well on modified Brucella agar and blood agar at 37°C, with cell dimensions of (0.3–0.4) µm × (0.6–0.8) µm. MALDI-TOF-MS identified it as  B. melitensis  with a score of 2.366. The strain was positive for oxidase, catalase and urease, and negative for hydrogen sulphide production. Plaque formation was observed in the Bk-phage lysis test. Agglutination titer for serum A was higher than that for serum M. Among the 12 tested antibiotics, the strain was resistant only to erythromycin (MIC > 32 µg/mL). Whole-genome sequencing together with 16S rRNA and  rpoB  gene typing confirmed its identity as  B. melitensis  biovar 2. Following serial in-vitro passaging to obtain the 1st-generation (G1), 5th-generation (G5), and 10th-generation (G10) derivatives of ZH25, colony morphology, biochemical profiles and biovar features remained stable. The strain has been deposited in the Pathogenic Microorganism Repository of Guangdong Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention and assigned a national preservation accession number.  Conclusion  The  B. melitensis  biovar 2 strain obtained in this study exhibits typical phenotypic and genotypic features of the pathogen. It qualifies as a reference strain for brucellosis surveillance, vaccine evaluation and diagnostic reagent development. The strain has passed review by the national repository and obtained the official preservation number NPRC(S) 01.0114.

records.title: Biocontrol of postharvest Fusarium oxysporum on fruits and vegetables: mechanisms and efficacy of antagonistic microorganisms.
records.abstract: Fusarium oxysporum is a major postharvest pathogen causing significant losses in stored fruits, vegetables, tubers, and bulbs. Understanding its infection mechanisms is essential for developing effective biological control strategies. This review synthesizes current knowledge on postharvest infection by F. oxysporum, including wound-dependent penetration, production of toxins (beauvericin, fusaric acid) and cell wall-degrading enzymes (polygalacturonases, cellulases), and tissue colonization leading to rot and mycotoxin accumulation. It critically evaluates biological control agents (BCAs) from three major groups bacteria (Bacillus, Pseudomonas), yeasts (Metschnikowia, Wickerhamomyces), and filamentous fungi (Trichoderma) with emphasis on their modes of action: nutrient competition (iron chelation via siderophores or pulcherrimin), antimicrobial production (lipopeptides, volatile organic compounds, hydrolytic enzymes), and mycoparasitism (unique to Trichoderma). The interactions between the pathogen and BCAs are examined within the postharvest wound microenvironment, highlighting the competitive dynamics that determine infection outcomes. Based on published storage trials, the review identifies critical knowledge gaps limiting commercial translation: most BCA efficacy studies have been conducted at 25-28 °C, and in vivo data under cold storage (4-10 °C) remain scarce; direct quantification of pathogen virulence factors in infected fruit tissues is lacking; and transcriptomic analyses of F. oxysporum during biocontrol challenge are still unavailable. A research roadmap is proposed, including cold storage screening, in situ metabolomics, RNA-seq of the pathogen during BCA exposure, multi-strain efficacy testing, and LAMP diagnostics integration.

records.title: Dynamic transcriptomic analysis of CCR4-NOT complex subunits identifies Cnot7 as an oogenesis-associated factor in Crassostrea gigas.
records.abstract: The CCR4-NOT complex is a conserved eukaryotic deadenylation machinery that plays essential roles in post-transcriptional regulation of mRNA metabolism, embryonic development, and reproduction. However, the composition and expression dynamics of the CCR4-NOT complex subunits in marine mollusks remain unexplored. Here, we systematically identified nine CCR4-NOT complex subunits in the Pacific oyster Crassostrea gigas. Phylogenetic and domain analyses revealed all CNOT proteins retained subtype-specific structural features in C. gigas. Notably, the oyster genome encodes CNOT7 but lacks CNOT8, consistent with the distribution observed in the analyzed invertebrates. Developmental expression profiling revealed typical maternal transcript expression patterns for six Cnot genes. Tissue-specificity analysis identified Cnot7 as the only Cnot gene meeting the predefined criterion for gonad-specific expression. Single-nucleus transcriptomic analysis further showed it was preferentially expressed in the oocyte lineage, with the highest expression in mature oocytes. These findings provide a molecular characterization of the CCR4-NOT subunits in a marine bivalve, and identify Cnot7 as a germline-associated candidate subunit potentially involved in reproductive development and early embryogenesis in C. gigas.
records.journal: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Part D, Genomics & proteomics
records.authors: Zhou Y, Yu H, Li Q.

records.title: From substrate composition to microbial metabolism: performance, molecular, taxonomic and functional insights into sludge-derived hydrothermal carbon sources for denitrification.
records.abstract: Liquid recovered from hydrothermal sludge treatment is an attractive denitrification carbon source, but it carries nitrogen that raises effluent total nitrogen and recalcitrant organics that leave residual chemical oxygen demand (COD). Thermal hydrolysis (TH), wet air oxidation (WAO) and two-stage WAO with catalytic WAO (WAO-CWAO) liquids were compared with sodium acetate in sequencing batch reactors, and the mechanisms were resolved by Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomics. TH and WAO liquids failed as carbon sources, with effluent COD and nitrogen above the Chinese discharge standard, whereas the WAO-CWAO liquid converted the recalcitrant organics into volatile fatty acids (VFAs), removed ammonia, and approached, but did not match, the sodium acetate control. An apparent nitrogen balance showed that residual nitrogen reflected the load introduced with the carbon source, and residual COD was traced to a CHON-rich pool unique to these effluents. Community composition followed carbon source quality, shifting from a diverse consortium sustained by slowly biodegradable organics to a streamlined assemblage of VFAs-utilizing denitrifiers. Genome-resolved analysis of the recovered metagenome-assembled genomes indicated a substrate-based division of labor: the dominant Saprospiraceae carried an expanded hydrolytic arsenal but no nitrate reductase, whereas Thauera carried complete denitrification and VFA-utilization gene sets but no polysaccharide hydrolases. A second, catalytic stage at higher temperature and oxygen pressure therefore alleviates the trade-off between nitrogen release and incomplete oxidation, yielding a sludge-derived carbon source that approaches sodium acetate.
records.authors: Fang K, Zhu Q, Zhu Y, Yao G, Zhao J, Xia S.

records.title: Genomic and In Vitro Characterization of the Candidate Probiotic Yeast Pichia kluyveri PK88™
records.abstract: Non-Saccharomyces yeasts are of growing interest as probiotic candidates, but strain-level charac-terization remains limited. We characterized Pichia kluyveri PK88™, isolated from coffee beans (NRRL deposit # 68561), using phenotypic assays, whole-genome sequencing, and in silico screen-ing. PK88™ was non-hemolytic and produced no detectable patulin, ochratoxin A, or aflatoxins. Genome analysis confirmed species identity (98.5–98.8% average nucleotide identity) and identi-fied no acquired antimicrobial-resistance genes, canonical virulence factors, or decarboxylases for harmful biogenic amines. By high-inoculum broth microdilution, MICs were low for echi-nocandins and amphotericin B and higher for fluconazole and posaconazole. Measured survival after acid, bile and anaerobic exposure was retained (93% at pH 2; 82–84% in bile), although sur-vival at pH 1 and under anaerobiosis was lower; hydrophobicity fell from 91% to 73–77% and auto-aggregation rose to 98–100%. PK88 supernatant inhibited Escherichia coli and Candida albi-cans in preliminary assays. In two independent experiments, Caco-2 cells exposed to PK88™ showed cytotoxicity ≤20% in every replicate up to 6 × 104 organisms/well and variable increases at higher doses. These preliminary data support further evaluation.
records.authors: Ahmed S, Fnu S, Valentin ES, Eltokhy A, Khater S, Goodwin E, Deaton J, McCormick TS, Ghannoum MA.

records.title: Advect, retain, sense: cilia-driven vortices deliver symbiont bacteria and flowborne cues to a mucociliary olfactory organ
records.abstract: Animals that acquire a microbial symbiont from the environment must find it against an overwhelming background of other bacteria. The bobtail squid  Euprymna recruits its luminous symbiont  Vibrio fischeri from seawater in which the symbiont occurs at fewer than ten cells per millilitre, and the host is transcriptionally primed for colonisation as soon as the first handful of symbionts become detectable at the light organ, too few to signal directly and implying a detection event upstream of it. We hypothesised that the paired olfactory organs, which sit at the entrance to the mantle cavity and hence in the path of all inhaled water, are that site. Here we characterise cilia-driven flow, particle capture and neuronal activity at the olfactory organ in hatchlings of  Euprymna scolopes and  E. berryi and in three non-symbiotic cuttlefish and squid species, i.e. species with no known light-organ symbiosis. In  Euprymna the organ is a densely ciliated, mucus-coated epithelium packed with putative chemosensory cells and expressing the peptidoglycan-recognition receptor EsPGRP4, and its motile cilia drive a vortical flow that converges head-on onto the sensory face and persists to at least 96 h after hatching in colonised as well as aposymbiotic animals. Suspended beads accumulate there more strongly than at the light organ, and swimming symbionts follow the same flow yet are retained an order of magnitude more strongly than inert beads of the same size. Cells within the organ show spontaneous calcium transients, and the subset of cells and the firing rate change in response to waterborne stimuli, including live  V. fischeri . In the three non-symbiotic species the equivalent organ sweeps water past its face rather than onto it, confining capture to the margins. Taken together, these findings suggest that in  Euprymna the olfactory organ may concentrate, hold and detect arriving bacteria at a chemosensory surface before they reach the light organ.  Significance  Animals that acquire microbial partners from the environment must select them against an overwhelming background of other microbes. The bobtail squid, which recruits a single luminous symbiont from seawater, already exhibits colonization-specific changes in gene expression before meaningful numbers of symbiont cells have reached the target organ, suggesting a potential detection event upstream of it. Here we show that the squid’s paired olfactory organs, which lie in the path of all inhaled water and express receptors for bacterial wall components, are mucociliary sensory surfaces that draw water onto the organ’s center, where bacteria and bacteria-sized particles accumulate. Putative sensory cells in the  Euprymna organ exhibit spontaneous calcium spikes and this activity rises with waterborne stimuli including bacteria, so the surface that captures the bacteria is also a surface that may sense them. In three non-symbiotic cephalopods the equivalent organ sweeps water past its surface and limits capture of flow-borne matter to the edges, suggesting a potential specialization of  Euprymna ’s organ in bacterial capture and detection compared to the other species. Mucociliary surfaces host microbial associations throughout the animal kingdom, and these findings suggest a general mechanism: motile cilia advect microbes to the surface, mucus immobilises them, and sensory cells embedded in that surface detect them.

records.title: Microbial-mediated degradation of aflatoxin B1 in agricultural soil.
records.abstract: Aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) is commonly present in agricultural soil and poses severe threats to soil ecosystems due to its high toxicity, yet its environmental fate and microbial-mediated degradation mechanisms remain insufficiently studied. In this study, the environmental behavior of AFB1 in an agricultural soil was investigated. Metagenomic analysis showed that exposure to a higher concentration of AFB1 (5.0 mg kg-1) altered soil bacterial community structure and reduced community diversity. After 30 days of incubation, AFB1 was slowly removed from natural soil microcosms but persisted in sterilized soil microcosms, indicating that indigenous soil microorganisms make a major contribution to AFB1 dissipation. Exposure to high-concentration AFB1 significantly enriched the genus Nocardioides, and a novel AFB1-degrading strain, Nocardioides sp. N13 (phylum Actinomycetota), was isolated from the agricultural soil. Strain N13 harbors three genes encoding putative F420H2-dependent reductase (FDR) homologs, which are hypothesized to be involved in the initial degradation of AFB1. Bioinformatics analysis revealed that putative FDR homolog-carrying bacteria are mostly assigned to the phylum Actinomycetota and are widely distributed across diverse soil environments worldwide. These findings provide a theoretical basis and potential microbial resources for mitigating AFB1 contamination in soil ecosystems.
records.authors: Lu P, Chen A, Feng Y, He S, Han G, Hu S.

records.title: Revitalizing simultaneous nitrification, endogenous denitrification and phosphorus removal under carbon starvation: Redox mediator-modulated electron transfer and metabolic coordination.
records.abstract: The simultaneous nitrification, endogenous denitrification and phosphorus removal (SNEDPR) process provides a resource-efficient paradigm for synergistic nutrient removal. However, its efficacy can be severely constrained by limited electron-donor availability and inefficient intracellular electron transfer under low carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) ratios. Herein, we demonstrate that anthraquinone-2-sulfonate (AQS) serves as an effective redox mediator to alleviate these electron-transfer limitations. Under severe carbon-limited conditions, with an influent C/N ratio of 3.24±0.11, supplementation with 0.3 mmol/L AQS successfully restored the deteriorated system, recovering total inorganic nitrogen (TIN) removal efficiency to 96.57±0.87% while sustaining robust phosphorus removal (96.47±2.68%). Batch kinetic assays showed that AQS increased electron transfer system activity (ETSA) by over 100%, accompanied by enhanced nitrification-related activity, endogenous denitrification and phosphorus uptake. Integrated metagenomic and metatranscriptomic analyses further revealed transcriptional responses consistent with an electron-shuttling role of AQS, including enhanced ETC-associated electron-transfer potential and increased transcription of downstream denitrification enzymes. ATP synthase-related transcription was also enhanced, indicating an increased potential for PMF-coupled cellular energy conservation. Consequently, increased transcription was observed for key functional genes involved in nitrification (amoABC, nxrAB), denitrification (narGHI, napAB, nirKS, nosZ), and polyphosphate synthesis (ppk). Furthermore, AQS-amended operation was associated with microbial community succession toward a more specialized consortium, in which comammox, Thauera and Candidatus Accumulibacter clade ⅡC were associated with nitrification, endogenous denitrification, and denitrifying phosphorus removal, respectively. Although practical translation will require effective retention or recovery of soluble AQS, these findings demonstrate the potential of AQS-enhanced SNEDPR under carbon-limited conditions and provide multi-omics evidence linking improved nutrient removal with increased electron-transfer activity and coordinated microbial metabolic responses.

records.title: GhHDZ-87, a cotton HD-Zip transcription factor, involved in regulating salt stress tolerance in G. hirsutum.
records.abstract: Salt stress severely constrains cotton seedling establishment, yield, and fiber quality. Although HD‑Zip transcription factors are known to play essential roles in abiotic stress adaptation in various plant species, their functions in cotton remain largely unexplored. In this study, we performed a comprehensive genome‑wide analysis of HD‑Zip genes in Gossypium hirsutum to uncover their evolutionary history and identify stress‑responsive regulatory components. Genome‑wide screening identified 90 HDZ members that were unevenly distributed across the 26 chromosomes of upland cotton. Phylogenetic analysis showed that the upland cotton HDZs were divided into six groups, with clade B absent from the seven clades identified across species. Analyses of gene structure and conserved domains provided strong evidence for the evolutionary conservation of HDZ members. The expansion of the GhHDZ family was primarily driven by duplication events, particularly whole‑genome duplication (WGD) and allotetraploidization, with purifying selection acting on these genes. The expression of GhHDZ-87 was upreglated under salt, drought, and ABA treatments. β-Glucuronidase (GUS) staining indicated that GhHDZ-87 was expressed in the roots, stems and leaves of ProGhHDZ-87::GUS transgenic Arabidopsis thaliana. VIGS(Virus-induced gene silencing) assays suggested that knockdown of GhHDZ‑87 reduced salt tolerance in cotton, potentially via ABA signaling and ion‑homeostasis pathways. Taken together, this study comprehensively characterized the GhHDZ gene family in cotton and identified GhHDZ-87 as a positive regulator of salt tolerance. This study not only provides genetic resources and theoretical support for improving salt tolerance in cotton, but also improves our understanding of the regulatory pathways underlying salt tolerance.

records.title: Non-canonical nucleic acid structures in viruses: Regulatory modules and emerging antiviral targets.
records.abstract: Beyond their primary sequence, viral genomes contain structural information encoded in the ability of DNA and RNA to fold into alternative conformations. These dynamic non-canonical nucleic acid structures include G-quadruplexes (G4s), i-Motifs (iMs), R-loops, G4-associated R-loops and left-handed Z-conformations. Among them, G4s have been most extensively investigated in viruses and have been reported to modulate transcription, replication, translation, latency and immune evasion. However, the functional interpretation of these structures remains highly context-dependent: similar topologies can either promote or restrict infection depending on genomic location, folding dynamics, protein interactors and the stage of the viral life cycle. Here, we discuss recent advances in viral non-canonical nucleic acid structures, emphasizing the level of evidence supporting their formation and function. We also assess emerging antiviral strategies based on structure-targeting ligands, highlighting both their translational potential and the unresolved challenges of selectivity, target engagement and pharmacological validation in infected cells.
records.authors: Ruggiero E, Zanin I, Mattellone F, Richter SN.

records.title: Pervasive short hairpin folding in non-encapsidated RNA viruses
records.abstract: Genome-wide RNA secondary structure can influence viral replication, stability, translation, and interactions with host defenses, yet its distribution and significance across RNA viruses remain poorly understood. We developed the pervasive hairpin (peHaPi) metric to quantify densely distributed stem-loop structures and applied it to 817,234 GenBank virus sequences. This revealed a distinctive RNA architecture characterized by numerous short, highly uniform hairpins spanning most of the genome. The structure was strongly enriched in capsidless RNA viruses, encompassing nearly all ormycoviruses and a substantial fraction of narnaviruses, although it also occurred in several other RNA and DNA virus groups. Comparative analyses showed that increasing peHaPi scores appeared associated with more stable and constrained predicted RNA structures and altered codon base-pairing patterns, indicating selective constraints imposed by pervasive folding. Relationships between peHaPi and RdRp sequence similarity differed among virus groups, consistent with independent evolutionary origins of this structural phenotype. Analysis of virus-derived small RNAs provided no evidence that peHaPi(+) viruses elicit a reduced siRNA response, arguing against siRNA evasion as its primary function. Finally, combining peHaPi classification with DNA-read subtraction identified candidate RNA virus contigs lacking detectable protein homology or recognizable RdRp signatures across multiple independent datasets. These findings reveal pervasive short-hairpin organization as a novel feature of predominantly capsidless viruses and establish genome-wide RNA structure as a complementary signature for discovering highly divergent ormyco-and narnaviruses. Repositories  The raw sequence reads have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive under BioProject accession number  PRJNA1549704 .

records.title: Plant Organellar Homologous Recombination Depends on Accessory Factors for Recombinase Activity
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Plant mitochondrial and plastid genomes rely on homologous recombination (HR) for error-free DNA repair of double strand breaks. Here, we reconstructed the homologous recombination pathway of plant organelles from Arabidopsis, aiming to understand how proteins of diverse evolutionary origins assemble into a functional repair pathway. We found that the three bacterial-derived recombinases, AtRecAs assemble D-loop intermediates, but only chloroplast AtRecA1 independently execute end-joining recombination on large DNA substrates. AtRecA1-mediated end-joining recombination is enhanced by plant-unique single-stranded DNA-binding proteins of the Whirly and Organellar Single-Stranded Binding (OSB) families, in contrast these proteins are mandatory for the recombination activities of the dual-targeted AtRecA2 and mitochondrial AtRecA3. Recombinational intermediates generated by AtRecAs are resolved by a bacterial-like RadA helicase but not bacterial-like RecG. Finally, AtRecX inhibits the recombinase activities of AtRecA2, while the activities of AtRecA1 and AtRecA3 remains largely insensitive. Collectively, our results provide an integrative reconstitution of the plant organellar homologous recombination machinery, revealing that homologous recombination arises from a complex system of bacterial, phage-derived, plant-specific, and eukaryotic components. Plant-specific ssDNA-binding proteins emerge as key regulators of this process, promoting recombination efficiency and genome stability, that supports the essential functions of homologous recombination in DNA repair and DNA replication maintenance. GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT  DNA repair pathways mediated by homologous recombination in plant organelles
records.authors: Mora-Garduño J, Peralta-Castro A, Aguilar-Granados A, Raygoza CD, Díaz-Quezada C, Brieba LG.

records.title: Phagocytosis without mitochondria is a lineage trait of planctomycetal bacteria of prey
records.abstract: Phagocytosis is considered energetically out of reach for prokaryotes. Mitochondria-first models of eukaryogenesis therefore suggest a non-phagocytic archaeal host. Yet two recently described planctomycetes lack mitochondria and engulf entire bacteria. Whether this mode of predation is an oddity of two isolates or the hallmark of a bacterial lineage remained unresolved. Here, we report eight additional predatory  Planctomycetota from three aquatic habitats. The ten cultured strains now span two classes of the phylum  Planctomycetota , ‘  Candidatus Uabimicrobiia’ and one newly proposed class. Using engineered fluorescent prey, we show that nine strains internalize prey into fully sealed compartments whereas one digests its prey externally, a non-engulfing predator for comparison. The strains additionally divide by two distinct modes, however, not correlating with their feeding behavior. Sequence- and structure-based searches detect no eukaryotic phagocytosis protein conserved across the engulfing strains. The actin homologue previously proposed to mediate uptake occurs only in three engulfing strains. Routine engulfment by aerobic bacteria without mitochondria thus unsettles a premise of mitochondria-first models and reopens the question of which cell plans could have hosted the mitochondrial endosymbiont.

records.title: NMR metabolome and stool consistency in IBS: a layer-wise multi-omics comparison
records.abstract: Abstract    Background  Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is markedly heterogeneous [1], and existing biological subtyping based on taxonomy (16S/metagenomic species) has limited predictive ability under subject-level validation. Using real clinical labels (IBS subtype, IBS-SSS severity, and Bristol stool consistency), this study performs a unified, subject-grouped cross-validated comparison across multiple omics layers and completes held-out zero-shot validation and label-blind transductive cross-cohort stability selection in an external cohort (zero contact with target-domain labels). The core comparison task is Bristol stool consistency regression; the three-class task serves only as an auxiliary control.  Methods  We used the Cell 2020 longitudinal multi-omics cohort [2] (75 subjects, 464 clinically labeled stool samples: IBS-D 169, IBS-C 142, healthy 153; layer-specific availability differed: genus/species 457, KO/KEGG 459, NMR 445). The Bristol score constructed from stool diaries (441 samples, 67 subjects; IBS-D 4.92 > healthy 3.94 > IBS-C 2.93, direction validated) served as the core quantitative phenotype. Eight feature layers were compared: genus/species taxonomy, SHOGUN KEGG Orthology (KO) genes, KEGG pathways (375 aggregated), NMR metabolome (19), bile acids (12), tryptophan metabolites (12), and NMR+taxonomy combined (163 dimensions). All modeling used subject-grouped 5-fold cross-validation (StratifiedGroupKFold/GroupKFold) with nested tuning; Ridge/ElasticNet for regression (evaluated by OOF R² and Spearman  ρ  ) and L2 logistic regression for classification. Cross-layer consistency was assessed by Spearman correlation between functional potential and metabolite pools (n = 423). Cell 2020-trained models were frozen and blindly tested zero-shot on the Jacobs 2023 cohort [3] (368 samples × 601 metabolites). Finally, source-domain closed-loop stability selection was performed (  π  _uni_cell using only source-domain grouped bootstrap, B = 300; platform-shift KS using only target-domain unlabeled features; two sensitivity levels, pre-screening nested and fully nested, with gates recomputed within resampling). After freezing the selector, a fully held-out zero-shot evaluation was performed on Jacobs (2000× paired bootstrap) to define the cross-platform stable core (Iron-Core). Two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) was used to test potential causal effects of 27 candidate genera on IBS risk between the MiBioGen microbiome GWAS [4] and the IBS GWAS (GCST90016564) [5] (IVW/weighted median/MR-Egger plus Cochran Q and leave-one-out sensitivity, with global BH-FDR correction).  Results  ① The taxonomic layer showed limited signal for the IBS-D/C/healthy three-class task in the  full sample  (genus 0.506 ± 0.077, 95% CI [0.421, 0.595], permutation p = 0.005; species 0.520 ± 0.134, 95% CI [0.434, 0.611]; chance = 0.333), rising to 0.556/0.559 on the common complete subset and clustering with NMR (see ②); no reliable signal for IBS-SSS severity (genus balanced accuracy = 0.500, 95% CI [0.420, 0.578], permutation p = 0.458; only 2/70 features q ρ   = 0.468 (16/19 significant), and it remained highest on the common complete subset (0.193 vs 0.196). Its OOF R² point estimate exceeded those of taxonomy (genus 0.089/subset 0.037; species 0.043/subset − 0.023), bile acids (0.053/0.073), tryptophan (0.023/0.015), and functional gene layers (KO 0.005/−0.039; KEGG 0.036/−0.008); the unfiltered NMR+genus combined model was 0.171/0.165, lower than NMR; after filtering at the same prevalence = 0.10, the combined model was 0.204 (19 NMR + 68 genera, n = 424), not significantly different from NMR alone (  Δ  R²=+0.006, 95% CI − 0.081–+0.095, p = 0.454)—the earlier “combined dilution” was mainly caused by unfiltered low-prevalence genera. The ordering of mid-tier layers (genus, species, bile acids, tryptophan) was sensitive to sample composition (genus and bile acids swapped on the subset) and does not constitute a strong ranking claim. In the auxiliary three-class task, full-sample NMR balanced accuracy = 0.558 ± 0.085, but on the common subset NMR (0.556) clustered with genus (0.556), species (0.559), and combined (0.565), indistinguishable from one another—layer ordering in the classification task is sensitive to sample composition and does not provide evidence that “NMR is optimal for classification.” Within-NMR Shapley decomposition showed that  the SCFA group's marginal contribution was  φ     = 0.106, 2.4 times the amino-acid group's  φ     = 0.045  (remove SCFA  Δ  R²=0.076, p = 0.002; remove AA  Δ  R²=0.016, p = 0.085, not significant)—upgrading “SCFA dominance” from a qualitative ordering to a reproducible decomposition conclusion. ③ The markers most strongly positively correlated with Bristol were acetate (  ρ   = 0.414), butyrate (0.379), lysine (0.374), tyrosine (0.311), propionate (0.297), succinate (0.273), and branched-chain amino acids (0.19–0.23); the branched short-chain fatty acid 2-methylbutyrate was the only significant negative correlate (− 0.185). ④ Within subtypes (exploratory): NMR retained signal within IBS-C (  ρ   = 0.288, subject-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [+ 0.074, + 0.483]; R² CI crossed zero); no robust signal was detected within IBS-D (  ρ  =−0.263, 95% CI [− 0.573, + 0.128] crossing zero, P(  ρ   ≥ 0) = 0.083; R²=−0.048, 95% CI [− 0.226, − 0.001] on the negative side, indicating no predictive ability)—under the power constraint of n ≈ 150, this is only an exploratory hypothesis and is insufficient to support unsupervised subgrouping within subtypes. ⑤ Cross-layer validation: functional potential and metabolite pools were generally weakly coupled, but  the butyrate-producing community genomic abundance marker bcd (K00248, butyryl-CoA dehydrogenase gene, non-rate-limiting enzyme) was significantly positively correlated with the fecal butyrate pool (  ρ     = 0.265, q = 8×10⁻⁶)  ; BSH/bai showed no association with the bile acid pool—“potential ≠ activity.” ⑥ Zero-shot cross-cohort validation (Cell 2020 → Jacobs 2023): the 11 shared-metabolite model achieved Diarrhea vs Constipation+Mixed AUC = 0.647 (D vs C sensitivity 0.676),  ρ  =+0.278, with directional replication in 11/11 (one-sided sign test p = 4.9×10⁻⁴; features are not independent, so this p value is descriptive only); the random 11-feature baseline AUC = 0.506 (95% CI 0.434–0.589, p = 0.005), but a demographics-only (age/BMI/sex) baseline already reached AUC = 0.593 (95% CI 0.509–0.675), and R11's increment over demographics was + 0.053 (95% CI − 0.045–+0.153, p = 0.148), not significant; the full-feature model including unmeasurable SCFAs collapsed to AUC = 0.558—feature transferability is the first constraint on cross-cohort generalization. ⑦  Source-domain closed-loop stability selection (label-blind transductive  :  π  _uni_cell ≥ 0.8 + platform-shift KS   ; after freezing, zero-shot AUC on the fully held-out target cohort was 0.634 (95% CI 0.559–0.705),  ρ  =+0.243—not significantly different from the 11-shared-feature set (R11, 0.647; paired  Δ  AUC = − 0.013, p = 0.805), and significantly better than the full 16-feature set including imputed SCFAs (F16, 0.558;  Δ  AUC = + 0.075, p = 0.013). ⑧ Two-sample MR (genus→IBS causal test independent of the metabolite layer; 313 pruned SNPs → 259 harmonized SNPs): under the current instrumental-variable power and approximate distance-pruning framework,  no robust potential causal effect was detected  (minimum FDR = 0.835); the strongest nominal signals were Bifidobacterium (OR = 1.070 [1.004–1.141], p = 0.039) and Eubacterium hallii group (OR = 1.074, p = 0.062), both with low heterogeneity (Cochran Q p > 0.7), no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy (Egger intercept p > 0.85), and stable leave-one-out estimates, but observational and causal directions did not converge; Roseburia showed a nominal protective trend (OR = 0.930, p = 0.219), opposite to its positive observational correlation (  ρ  =+0.284).  Conclusions  Under subject-grouped cross-validation,  the layer with the highest point-estimate OOF R² for the Bristol continuous-trait regression task  was the metabolome (within NMR, dominated by the SCFA group: Shapley  φ   = 0.106, 2.4 times  φ  _AA = 0.045), not taxonomy or functional gene potential. The cross-cohort platform-robust core was data-driven and conditionally stable at 5 metabolites (lysine, tyrosine, uracil, glucose, leucine), achieving discrimination on the fully held-out target cohort that was not significantly different from the 11-shared-feature set with fewer features (0.634 vs 0.647), and significantly better than the 16-feature full model (0.558). The results support three mechanistic axes in terms of directional consistency, but with different levels of evidence:  SCFA→serotonin→intestinal motility  is supported mainly by within-NMR evidence (Shapley  φ   = 0.106, consistent marker direction spectrum); the  proteolytic fermentation fingerprint  is supported by the directional consistency of BCAAs/aromatic amino acids; and the  bile acid–TGR5 secretomotor  axis is supported only by the directional positive correlation of the bile-acid layer Top6 with loose stools, lacking functional/causal validation (“potential ≠ activity”). In the single-layer comparison, the feature-layer ranking was direct metabolic measurement > taxonomy > functional potential—this ranking applies only to the single-layer comparison for the Bristol regression task and should not be extrapolated to subtype classification (in the three-class task, NMR and taxonomic layers were indistinguishable on the common subset and the ordering was not robust), nor to combined models (after the same filtering, the combined model was not significantly different from NMR). It also shows that predictive magnitude and cross-domain transferability are not equivalent—the cross-cohort stable core is not the strongest within-domain feature. Two-sample MR further indicates that, under the current instrumental-variable power and approximate LD-pruning framework, no robust potential causal evidence was detected between mainstream candidate genera and IBS risk (none significant after FDR correction), and causal interpretation of observational microbiome–phenotype associations requires larger samples, bidirectional designs, and stronger instruments.

records.title: Detection and molecular characterization of Tomato yellow leaf curl virus in Ukraine
records.abstract: Abstract    Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (  Begomovirus flavisolanum  , TYLCV) is one of the most economically important viral pathogens of tomato worldwide, yet information regarding its molecular diversity in Ukraine has been limited. This study aimed to investigate the occurrence, molecular characteristics, and phylogenetic relationships of TYLCV isolates circulating in Ukrainian vegetable production systems. A total of 34 symptomatic tomato plants representing different cultivars were collected from several regions of Ukraine and analyzed by conventional PCR targeting the coat protein gene. Eighteen samples (52.9%) tested positive for TYLCV, while all healthy control plants were negative. In addition, TYLCV was detected in chili pepper (  Capsicum frutescens  ) and zucchini (  Cucurbita pepo  var.  giraumontia  ) growing adjacent to infected tomato plants, indicating a broader cultivated host range under field conditions. Partial genome sequencing of eight representative isolates generated GenBank accessions PX234052–PX234057, PX234062, and PX234063. Phylogenetic analyses based on Neighbor-Joining, Minimal Evolution, and Maximum Likelihood methods consistently demonstrated that Ukrainian isolates constitute a genetically homogeneous population with nucleotide identities exceeding 99%. Most isolates clustered tightly together, whereas isolate PX234052 represented the most divergent variant and the zucchini isolate (PX234057) formed a slightly differentiated branch while remaining within the TYLCV clade. Comparison with representative international sequences showed that all Ukrainian isolates grouped within the TYLCV-Israel (TYLCV-IL) lineage, exhibiting the closest relationship to isolates from Israel and Mediterranean countries, suggesting a common evolutionary origin. The limited genetic diversity observed among Ukrainian isolates indicates either a relatively recent introduction of TYLCV or the continued spread of a restricted number of closely related viral genotypes. These findings provide the first comprehensive molecular characterization of TYLCV populations in Ukraine and establish a baseline for future epidemiological surveillance, vector monitoring, and phytosanitary management. The detection of TYLCV in tomato, pepper, and zucchini further emphasizes the importance of integrated disease management and continuous monitoring of alternative cultivated hosts to reduce virus dissemination.
records.authors: Gerilovych A, Shevchenko N, Bashtan N, Miroshnichenko T, Chaiuk O, Ivchenko T.

records.title: Aquifer geochemistry shapes microbial diversity and carbon and nitrogen cycling potential
records.abstract: Abstract    Despite the importance of groundwater and its ecosystem functions, including nitrogen cycling, subsurface microbial biodiversity and ecology remain poorly understood globally. We investigated how aquifer geochemistry shapes microbial diversity and metabolic potential across Aotearoa New Zealand using shotgun metagenomics of 39 groundwater samples from 11 regions. We recovered 494 high- and medium-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), which clustered into four groups (A, B, C1 and C2), based on hydrochemistry, and differed significantly in taxonomy and metabolic pathways. Cluster A had the highest microbial diversity and was dominated by uncultured taxa, particularly  Patescibacteria  . Carbon fixation pathways, predominantly the Calvin-Benson-Bassham and reductive tricarboxylic acid cycles, varied among clusters and were associated with different redox metabolisms. Aerobic respiration pathways also differed, particularly the microaerophilic  cbb  3  cytochrome  c  oxidase. Differences were also observed in nitrogen, sulfur, carbohydrate and organic acid metabolism, with several MAGs strongly correlated with nitrate, sulfate and potassium. Our findings demonstrate that aquifer geochemistry is a major determinant of microbial community structure and metabolic potential across Aotearoa New Zealand groundwater ecosystems.
records.authors: Houghton KM, Moreau M, Tschritter C.

records.title: KEGG for characterizing genomes and pathways in the biosphere.
records.abstract: The KEGG database (https://www.kegg.jp) has been developed as a model of the biological systems. By organizing knowledge of cellular and organism-level functions in the form of molecular wiring diagrams, the model enables generating new knowledge and finding practical applications. The KO (KEGG Orthology) dataset plays the basic role of organizing knowledge. KO is an ortholog with functional relevance, generalizing experimental evidence in specific organisms to other organisms. KEGG molecular networks, including pathway maps and modules, are generic networks with KOs as network nodes, and thus KEGG mapping from genomes to pathways can be applied to any organism. As the number of KOs increases and the KO annotation rate improves, KEGG mapping is further expanded. A set of KOs in the genome and a set of modules in the metabolic pathways are now used to characterize various data objects in the biosphere, including organisms, organism groups, microbiomes, viruses, and their combinations, such as endosymbiont-host, microbiome-host, and virus-host relationships. Furthermore, a simple measure of similarity either by KO compositions or module compositions is introduced to compare organism groups. The resulting similarity dendrograms possibly reflect similarity of cellular functions or, more specifically, metabolic functions, which can be compared with phylogenetic trees.
records.authors: Kanehisa M, Furumichi M, Sato Y, Matsuura Y, Ishiguro-Watanabe M.

records.title: Feed additives as systems-level modulators of the ruminant host-microbiome interaction: a multi-omics perspective on efficiency, resistance, and reproduction.
records.abstract: Ruminant livestock face converging pressures from climatic variation, antimicrobial agents, and the imperative for sustainable intensification. However, the molecular imprints through which nutritional interventions modulate host-microbiome interactions across physiological contexts remain fragmented across disciplinary themes. Here, we synthesize evidence from metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metabolomics, and host transcriptomics to propose that feed additives operate as systems-level modulators of a functionally integrated rumen-liver-immune-reproductive axis, rather than acting on isolated metabolic pathways. Prevotella, Butyrivibrio, Ruminococcus, and Fibrobacter recurrently emerged across studies to be associated with feed efficiency, immune modulation, resistome dynamics, and reproductive fitness. However, their relationship is context dependent and not causal. Furthermore, hepatic transcriptomic and microRNA (miRNA)-mediated regulatory networks could serve as a molecular bridge connecting ruminal fermentation events to systemic phenotypic outcomes. The ruminant resistome may also represent a potential interface with public health rather than an isolated ecological phenomenon, given the capacity for horizontal gene transfer through mobile genetic elements, although the extent of transmission to humans remains to be quantified. Early-life microbial programming and reproductive tract microbiome composition also represent tractable intervention windows for precision management. This integrated framework could reframe feed additive research from a single pathway to a systems-level perspective, offering a basis for precision ruminant production.
records.authors: Fijabi O, Morenikeji OB, Ivey SL, Loest C, Idowu M, Ashley R, Ogunade IM, Taiwo G.

records.title: Isolation and characterization of novel Klebsiella phages from Benin and their antibiofilm activities on multidrug resistant and hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae strains.
records.abstract: Hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae represents a growing clinical threat, particularly where multidrug resistance limits treatment options. This study aims to characterize Klebsiella phages isolated in Benin and evaluate their efficacy in reducing bacterial cell growth, biofilm inhibition and biofilm disruption. To achieve this objective, we isolated Klebsiella phages by enriching samples of hospital effluent, pig droppings, and stool, using clinical multidrug resistant and hypervirulent K. pneumoniae strains as hosts. These phages were characterized using transmission electron microscopy, whole-genome sequencing, and biological assays. Then, we evaluated their antibiofilm activity and stability under harsh conditions (pH and temperature) in vitro. So, we report the isolation and characterization of three novel lytic phages from Benin (Kp1Bj_HH11_M23, Kp2Bj_LN294_M23, and Kp10Bj_LN54_14). These Myoviruses, belonging to the genera Marfavirus and Jiaodavirus, display broad host range activity against multidrug resistant and hypervirulent K. pneumoniae strains with various capsular serotypes including KL114, KL53, KL8, KL62, KL64, KL124, KL102, KL57, KL39, KL48, KL17, KL20, KL2, KL30, KL51, KL105, KL146, KL28, KL122, KL38, KL3, and KL163. Genomic analysis confirmed the absence of virulence and antimicrobial resistance genes. The phages exhibit rapid adsorption, short latency periods (5-10 min), and high burst sizes (119-2208 PFU/cell). All three phages have significantly biofilm disruption effect in vitro (Kp1Bj_HH11_M23, biofilm disruption rate of 98.46 %, p-value = 0.0170; Kp2Bj_LN294_M23, biofilm disruption rate of 65.56%, p-value p-value = 0.003). Their stability across a wide range of temperatures and pH further supports their potential for therapeutic development. Together, these data highlight the value of locally sourced phages as candidates for tackling region-specific antimicrobial resistance challenges.

records.title: The impact of OsASR5 on rice microbiome: Implications for nutrient cycling and stress response.
records.abstract: Plant-microorganism interactions contribute to plant health by enhancing nutrient acquisition. The transcription factor OsASR5 regulates detoxification gene expression under aluminum stress in rice and is implicated as a positive regulator of responses to iron and phosphorus deficiency. Given its role in nutrient regulation, we investigated whether OsASR5 influences the assembly of the rice microbiome. In this study, we characterized the bacteria communities associated with the leaves and roots of OsASR5-RNAi rice plants compared to wild-type Oryza sativa cv. Nipponbare. Notably, OsASR5-RNAi plants showed altered bacterial beta diversity compared with wild type. The bacterial composition of OsASR5-RNAi plants differed in both organs, with decreased Desulfobacteriota and increased in Acidobacteria abundance in leaves. At the genus level, Methylobacterium, a known plant growth promoter, was less prevalent in leaves, while Magnetospirillum, associated with iron cycling, was less abundant in roots. Conversely, several bacteria were more abundant in OsASR5-RNAi plants, including Aneurinibacillus, Anaeromyxobacter, and Methylobacter, which are associated with nitrogen cycling and phosphorus solubilization. Additionally, Geobacter and Geothrix, both known for their role in metal reduction, particularly iron, were more abundant in OsASR5-RNAi plants. These suggest that OsASR5 affects plant-microbe interactions, potentially influencing nutrient cycling and plant stress responses through microbiome modulation.
records.authors: Sánchez ICC, Margis-Pinheiro M, Dias-Oliveira M, Ponte LR, Ricachenevsky FK, Margis R.
