records.title: Influenza A virus H5Nx genotypes assigned by genetic similarity are incongruent with global phylogenies
records.abstract: Influenza A virus H5N1 and related subtypes (H5Nx) have broad host ranges and pose a pandemic risk. Since early 2022, H5 clade 2.3.4.4b has predominated globally, causing unprecedented mortality in wild birds, poultry, and mammals, with spillovers to humans. Accurate viral classification is essential for tracking H5Nx variant emergence and spread, but reassortment among genome segments with distinct evolutionary histories complicates genotyping. H5Nx genotype assignment tools, GenoFlu in North America and Genin2 in Europe, assign segments to clusters by genetic similarity to reference sequences and define genotypes as constellations of segment clusters. However, genetic similarity does not necessarily imply recent shared ancestry due to independently re-occurring mutations and variability in the evolutionary rate. Furthermore, similarity is defined relative to references that may inadequately represent diversity. We evaluated the congruence of genetic similarity-based H5Nx clusters and genotypes with phylogenies of global sequences across eight segments. H5Nx genomes from 41,366 samples were assigned GenoFlu and Genin2 genotypes, and maximum likelihood phylogenies were inferred for each segment. CD-HIT and phylogenetic TreeCluster clusters were also generated for a range of distance thresholds. Clustering methods were evaluated based on phylogenetic purity, monophyly, and diversity. Reassortment within predominant GenoFlu and Genin2 genotypes was evaluated based on their phylogenetic cluster spans. Expectedly, GenoFlu was largely unable to assign genomes from outside of North America, South America, and Antarctica from 2022 to 2025, whereas Genin2 assignments struggled outside of Europe, Africa, and Western Asia. Only 14.2% of GenoFlu clusters were monophyletic, while Genin2 clusters were more variable across segments (overall 49.3% monophyletic). Despite CD-HIT yielding genetic distance clusters of similar size to TreeCluster, they were less monophyletic (44%) and encompassed greater phylogenetic diversity. We identified several genotypes, such as GenoFlu B3.13, D1.1, and D1.3, with segments that had diversified into separate subclusters. Similarly, GenoFlu genotypes B3.5 and A3, and Genin2 genotypes EA-2020-C, EA-2021-AB, and EA-2022-CH may erroneously combine multiple distinct reassortants. Genetic similarity-based H5Nx genotyping tools are rapid, stable, and sufficient for broad categorization, but may group viruses with distinct evolutionary histories and fail to assign divergent viruses, risking biased surveillance, modeling, and risk assessment.
records.authors: McLaughlin A, Tran H, Tait D, Nguyen H, Rudar J, Giacinti JA, Signore AV, Lung OA, Berhane Y, Poljak Z, Maguire F.

records.title: In Silico Validation of Contemporary East African Rift Valley Fever Virus Genomes Confirms the Enduring Robustness of the Bird et al. (2007) RT-qPCR Assay
records.abstract: Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV) is a zoonotic pathogen causing recurrent epizootics and epi-demics in East Africa. The quantitative reverse transcription PCR (RT-qPCR) assay devel-oped by Bird et al. (2007), targeting the large (L) genome segment, remains a global diag-nostic standard. However, continuous viral evolution raises concerns regarding diagnostic drift and potential assay failure. This study evaluated the contemporary robustness of this assay against East African RVFV genomes collected between 2005 and 2026. A total of 647 nucleotide records were retrieved from NCBI GenBank, from which a dataset of 193 L-segment sequences was curated based on geography, collection date, and segment an-notation. A custom sliding-window alignment algorithm quantified mismatches between the assay oligonucleotides and all valid sequences in both genomic orientations. Five se-quences initially exhibited high mismatch counts but were excluded after genomic coor-dinate mapping revealed they were partial fragments mapping outside the assay’s target region (nucleotides 4229–4723). Among the remaining 188 valid, target-spanning se-quences, 181 (96.3%) exhibited a perfect match to the forward primer, reverse primer, and TaqMan probe. Six sequences (3.2%) contained minor, biologically tolerable mismatches, and one (0.5%) showed probe-specific mismatches with intact primer binding sites. These findings confirm the enduring robustness of the Bird et al. (2007) assay against contempo-rary East African RVFV lineages, while simultaneously highlighting a critical genomic surveillance gap in Tanzania that warrants targeted infrastructural investment.
records.authors: Msoka KM.

records.title: Entamoeba invadens infection contributes to juvenile mortality in captive sea turtles.
records.abstract: Sea turtles are globally threatened marine reptiles, and infectious diseases are increasingly recognized as important causes of juvenile mortality. However, the etiology and pathogenesis of many diseases, including amoebiasis, remain poorly understood. Systemic amoebic lesions have been reported in sea turtles, yet the causative Entamoeba species has never been identified at the species level using molecular methods. We therefore investigated the etiology and pathogenesis of fatal amoebiasis using carcasses of 15 captive juvenile sea turtles (three loggerhead, Caretta caretta, and 12 green turtles, Chelonia mydas), integrating histopathological and molecular approaches. Histopathology revealed severe necrotizing enteritis, hepatitis, and pneumonia with abundant amoebic trophozoites and cysts. Polymerase chain reaction, Sanger sequencing, and in situ hybridization identified Entamoeba invadens in the intestine, liver, and lungs; 18S rRNA amplicon sequencing also detected E. invadens in fecal and intestinal samples. Phylogenetic analysis showed that the sea turtle-derived sequence clustered with E. invadens sequences from other reptile hosts. Bacterial and fungal aggregates were also observed within necrotic lesions, and 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing detected diverse bacterial communities without a consistently dominant taxon, consistent with secondary microbial translocation following intestinal barrier disruption rather than primary bacterial infection. These findings provide the first evidence that E. invadens causes fatal systemic amoebiasis in juvenile sea turtles and are consistent with polymicrobial invasion following parasite-induced intestinal damage. This study establishes a pathological and molecular basis for diagnosing systemic amoebiasis in sea turtles and has important implications for wildlife disease ecology and sea turtle conservation.

records.title: Hydroxyproline Enhances Branched-Chain Amino Acid Effects on Lifespan and Healthspan in Caenorhabditis elegans.
records.abstract: Food-derived protein hydrolysates frequently contain both collagen-associated hydroxyproline (Hyp) and branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), but the biological consequences of their combination remain unclear. This study tested whether Hyp changes the effects of leucine (Leu), isoleucine, and valine on lifespan and healthspan-related phenotypes in Caenorhabditis elegans and whether these treatment effects are accompanied by coordinated microbial and metabolic remodeling. Amino acid concentrations that did not strongly disrupt bacterial food clearance were selected for lifespan, stress resistance, motility, muscle-integrity, biochemical, microbiome, metabolomic, and transcriptomic analyses. Hyp+BCAA combinations improved lifespan- and healthspan-related phenotypes in a BCAA- and dose-dependent manner. The strongest combined treatments enhanced resistance to thermal and oxidative stress, preserved age-associated motility and muscle structure, reduced oxidative and lipofuscin-associated markers, and increased adenosine 5'-triphosphate-related readouts. Multimomics profiling showed that these direct treatment effects were accompanied by distinct C. elegans-associated microbiota signatures, altered nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) precursor-related metabolites, including nicotinic acid ribonucleoside (NaR), and a Leu+Hyp transcriptional response enriched for energy metabolism, proteostasis, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Integrated microbiome-metabolome analysis identified a positive association between Rhodococcus abundance and NaR levels. These findings demonstrate that, under the tested culture conditions, Hyp+BCAA exposure improves longevity-related phenotypes and identifies microbial composition, NAD precursor metabolism, and host energy homeostasis as candidate, testable mediators.

records.title: Extensive mobilome heterogeneity in a widespread endosymbiont: A candidate dimeric plasmid and highly fragmented prophages in Wolbachia from Culex pipiens.
records.abstract: The obligate, intracellular bacteria Wolbachia have gained increasing interest due to their selfish modifications of host arthropod reproduction, impacts on host evolution, and utility in vector control efforts to reduce arbovirus transmission worldwide. Despite their highly reduced genomes, Wolbachia harbor a rich mobilome that includes phages, insertion sequences and plasmids in mosquito vectors. However, these repeat-rich mobile genetic elements are notoriously difficult to assemble and can generate artificial, chimeric sequences that obscure their true diversity. As a result, conventional genome sequencing and assembly approaches often fail to resolve the complexity, leaving critical gaps of knowledge on how these elements evolve, mobilize, and shape both symbiont and host genomes. To address these challenges, we established a novel Oxford Nanopore long-read sequencing strategy that avoids prior PCR amplification and leverages single-dissected, female ovaries. Using this approach, we report and characterize-directly from native long-read molecules-the first near-complete Wolbachia genome and its mobile elements from individual ovaries of the mosquito vector Culex pipiens molestus. Additional short reads from individuals of the same strain were used to assess and validate candidate mutations, particularly in repetitive regions. We report a new dimeric structure of the pWCP plasmid, suggesting the existence of multimeric plasmid forms potentially associated with active replication. We also observed extensive fragmentation of prophage WO regions despite long read sequencing, underscoring their structural complexity. Raw long read analyses recovered multiple alternative gene syntenies within WO regions, pointing to heterogeneous prophage architectures missed by the assembly and marked diversity of WO elements in Wolbachia of Culex pipiens (wPip) group strains. Taken together, our results illuminate the structural heterogeneity of the endosymbiont genome that is shaped by integrated and episomal mobile elements.
records.authors: Brunner A, Mahout M, Amoros J, Rahmoun M, Jarry M, Bordenstein SR, Bordenstein SR, Trouche B, Reveillaud J.

records.title: Distinct core minor pilin complexes prime specialized type IV filaments in cyanobacteria.
records.abstract: The model cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 encodes, in addition to the major pilin of the Type IV pilus filament, an extensive, partially uncharacterized repertoire of minor pilins. For those cyanobacterial minor pilins that have been characterized, their roles span a surprisingly diverse range of functions. To elucidate the roles of uncharacterized minor pilins in a systematic way, we applied structural phylogenomics across 90 genomes, classifying cyanobacterial pilins into six conserved families that form two distinct putative core priming complexes. We demonstrate that these complexes initiate the assembly of two morphologically distinct Type IV pilus filaments: short, hyper-dynamic pili for natural competence, and long, adhesive pili for motility and phototaxis. Structural analysis revealed a conserved β-solenoid domain in PilX subunits, which we propose fulfills the capping function of PilY1 homologs. Proteomic data indicate that the minor pilin PilX2 facilitates the assembly of motility pili, which is required to maintain DnaJ3 co-chaperone levels and trigger cAMP-dependent surface sensing. These findings challenge the concept of a single multipurpose pilus, establishing that cyanobacteria utilize a shared machinery to assemble two specialized filaments, each primed by distinct core minor pilin complexes to meet the conflicting biophysical requirements of DNA uptake and surface motility.

records.title: Genetic characterization of rabies virus circulating in crab-eating fox (Cerdocyon thous) in the State of Paraiba, Northeastern Brazil.
records.abstract: Rabies is a fatal viral zoonosis that remains endemic in more than two-thirds of all countries worldwide, causing approximately 70,000 human deaths annually-equivalent to one death every ten minutes. The rabies virus (RABV), a member of the genus Lyssavirus (family Rhabdoviridae), has bats and canids as its primary reservoirs, although infections have also been reported in other wild species, including Cerdocyon thous (crab-eating fox) and Pseudalopex vetulus (hoary fox). In this study, we performed a comprehensive genomic and biological characterization of a RABV variant circulating in wild foxes from the Northeastern region of Brazil. Using Next Generation Sequencing (NGS), phylogenetic analysis, and in vitro and in vivo assays, we identified genetic similarities between these isolates and previously described RABV strains from wild and domestic canids in Brazil. However, the presence of escape mutants indicates a heterogeneous viral population, suggesting ongoing adaptive evolution in wildlife reservoirs. These findings reinforce the importance of genomic surveillance to detect emerging variants that may compromise current vaccination or control strategies. Overall, our results provide new insights into the molecular diversity, pathogenicity, and ecological dynamics of RABV circulating among wild canids in Brazil, contributing to improved understanding and prevention of rabies in endemic regions.

records.title: Culture-free  Helicobacter pylori  genomics reveals within-host virulence heterogeneity and antibiotic resistance
records.abstract: Helicobacter pylori (Hp) infects over 40% of the world’s population and causes most cases of gastric cancer worldwide, yet fundamental questions about its within-host genetic diversity remain unresolved. Decades of work on Hp genomics depends on culturing clinical isolates, which can distort within-host genetic heterogeneity that informs Hp virulence and antimicrobial resistance. Culture-free alternatives have been limited by the extremely low Hp abundance in gastric tissue (usually 10  −3 to 10  −7 of total genomic DNA), making direct metagenomics prohibitively expensive and existing enrichment strategies insufficient for whole-genome recovery. Here we develop ultra-sensitive Hp sequencing (uHp-seq) for reconstructing Hp genomes directly from gastric biopsies. uHp-seq achieves a thousand-fold Hp DNA enrichment and recovers near-complete genomes across samples spanning orders of magnitude in Hp abundance. Notably, individual hosts may harbor multiple co-existing Hp strains or cagA EPIYA variants with different oncogenic potential. Resistance-associated variants for six commonly used antibiotics are resolved with greater accuracy than PCR-based and probe-based commercial panels. Applied to minimally invasive gastric string samples, uHp-seq delivers reliable resistance profiles without endoscopy, opening a path to genome-guided Hp eradication.

records.title: Genetic diversity, spatiotemporal dynamics and evolution of porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus 2 (PRRSV-2) lineage 1 in China
records.abstract: Abstract  Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus 2 (PRRSV-2) lineage 1 (L1) has become the dominant epidemic lineage worldwide, posing a serious threat to the swine industry. However, the fine-scale evolutionary history, spatiotemporal transmission dynamics, and molecular drivers of L1 in China remain poorly understood. In this study, 32,215 global PRRSV-2 ORF5 sequences including 1,213 ORF5 sequences from Chinese L1 strains were systemically analyzed. Phylogenetic analysis revealed a unipolar dominance of the L1C sublineage (NADC30-like strains), accounting for 86.12% of Chinese L1 strains and forming a well-supported monophyletic clade. Transmission network analysis identified Henan Province as the primary hub for cross-regional spread of L1C, with Shandong Province as the secondary hub and Fujian, Guangdong and Sichuan Provinces serving as tertiary transmission nodes. Positive selection analysis of ORF5 revealed that L1C accumulated a broader set of positively selected sites, highly enriched in B-cell epitopes and glycosylation sites, indicating a strong selective advantage in immune evasion. Furthermore, whole-genome recombination analysis of L1 identified major recombination hotspots concentrated in certain viral non-structural protein genes (nsp2, nsp9) and structural protein genes (ORF5, ORF6). Together, these findings demonstrate that the unipolar dominance of L1C in China is sustained by a synergistic cycle of transmission, antigenic evolution, and recombination, providing an important basis for precision molecular surveillance and region-specific control of PRRSV-2.
records.authors: Chi C, Yang N, Zhang P, Jiang S, Zheng W, Chen N, Zhu J.

records.title: Isolation and comparative genomic characterization of Ralstonia pickettii from bronchoalveolar lavage fluid of a cat with pneumonia
records.abstract: Abstract    The clinical significance of  Ralstonia pickettii  recovered from the feline lower respiratory tract remains poorly characterized. A 1.5-year-old neutered male cat presented with recurrent respiratory signs for approximately four months and pulmonary radiographic abnormalities. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid culture yielded a  Ralstonia  isolate, whereas concurrent lavage-fluid and instrument controls showed no bacterial growth. Identification as  R. pickettii  was supported by 16S rRNA sequencing and a digital DNA–DNA hybridization value of 77.2% with the type strain. Whole-genome sequencing yielded a 5.46-Mb draft assembly comprising 70 contigs. Broth microdilution testing identified susceptibility to levofloxacin, doxycycline and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and resistance to eight tested agents, including imipenem and meropenem. Marbofloxacin susceptibility was reported separately by the commercial laboratory. Clinical improvement occurred during ongoing marbofloxacin treatment and adjunctive nebulization. Comparison with 37 public reference genomes identified 3,389 core gene clusters. The feline isolate shared 99.9727% orthologous average nucleotide identity with the reference having the shortest estimated pairwise genetic distance, an International Space Station-associated isolate. Low support for the adjacent internal branch and unequal source representation limited interpretation of fine-scale relationships and acquisition source. This case documents a species-confirmed feline lower respiratory tract isolate and its genomic context. The single-case design, absence of concurrent lavage-fluid cytology and improvement during continuing combined treatment preclude firm conclusions about causation or treatment efficacy.
records.authors: Ma Y, Wang Y, Li B, Zhang S, Pan Z, Yao H.

records.title: Chinese fir-Phoebe mixture increases microbial diversity and functional potential by accelerating SOM decomposition and increasing nutrient availability.
records.abstract: Near-natural silviculture practices have gained prominence as sustainable forestry strategies for optimizing stand site conditions and enhancing forest productivity. The performance of these ecosystem processes is closely related to soil microorganisms. However, there is still a lack of systematic characterization of how microorganisms respond to such silvicultural interventions, and this critical knowledge gap limits our ability to predict long-term forest ecosystem trajectories. Moreover, the specific functions of microbial communities in mixed plantations remain largely unknown. Here, we analyzed the compositional and functional profiles of bacterial and fungal communities across a gradient of stand types, including nine near-natural mixed Cunninghamia lanceolata and Phoebe bournei plantations (a 3 × 3 factorial design with three densities per species) and one pure C. lanceolata stand. The results showed that mixed planting enhanced bacterial and fungal diversity and altered their community structures by accelerating soil organic matter decomposition and total nitrogen mineralization, while increasing soil pH, available phosphorus, and available potassium. Notably, mixed planting increased the relative abundance of bacteria involved in carbon and nitrogen metabolism, along with saprophytic and symbiotic fungi, while reducing that of pathogenic fungi. Moreover, microbial community variation was stronger among mixed planting treatments than between soil depths, with reduced C. lanceolata density exerting a greater influence than increased P. bournei density. These findings underscore that tree diversity and planting density collectively determine soil microbial assembly. Consequently, this study provides empirical evidence to predict the impact of near-natural silviculture on microbial communities and offers insights for optimizing the management of C. lanceolata plantations.ImportanceDriven by western forest management concepts of "Nature-Approximating Forestry," near-natural afforestation has emerged as a key strategy for improving forest quality and productivity, especially in mixed conifer-broadleaf afforestation. Soil microorganisms constitute a vital component of forest ecosystems, serving as a primary driver of ecosystem functioning. Our research demonstrated that mixed conifer-broadleaf forests (Chinese fir-Phoebe) can increase soil bacterial and fungal diversity and functional potential in pure C. lanceolata plantations by accelerating organic matter decomposition and increasing soil pH, available phosphorus, and available potassium levels.
records.authors: Li K, Wang D, Zhang X, Lin F, Liu Z.

records.title: Gut Clostridium aminophilum as a protective microbe in never-smoker lung cancer: insights from metagenomics and machine learning.
records.abstract: Lung cancer in never-smoking patients (LCINS) has gradually gained attention in recent years, and emerging evidence points to a potential role of the gut microbiota in LCINS by modulating host immunity and metabolism. In this study, metagenomics was performed on stool samples from 24 LCINS patients and 18 healthy individuals. LCINS patients exhibited reduced microbial richness in α-diversity compared with healthy controls, and differences in principal component distribution were observed. Pathway enrichment analyses revealed that LPS biosynthesis capacity was significantly increased, whereas the fatty acid biosynthesis pathway was significantly decreased in LCINS. A total of 317 differentially abundant species were identified, including 29 assigned to the module most strongly associated with LCINS based on weighted gene co-expression network (WGCNA). Then, 36 machine learning-based diagnostic models were constructed based on these 29 species, with the glmBoost + Ridge model showing the best performance for LCINS discrimination (AUC = 0.855). SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) identified Clostridium aminophilum as a protective factor and the top contributor to model performance (SHAP value = 0.068), with a single-species AUC of 0.743. In vitro, the culture supernatant of Clostridium aminophilum markedly suppressed A549 cell proliferation and migration. In vivo, oral administration of Clostridium aminophilum (5 × 106 CFU) for 21 days significantly suppressed tumor growth in subcutaneous A549-derived xenograft models. These findings suggest a significant association between LCINS and the gut microbiota, characterized by a marked depletion of Clostridium aminophilum. Notably, metabolites derived from Clostridium aminophilum were shown to inhibit lung cancer progression.IMPORTANCELung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer incidence and mortality worldwide, and the proportion of lung cancer in patients who have never smoked (LCINS) has been steadily increasing. However, the potential role of the gut microbiota in this disease has not been fully explored. In this study, we characterized the gut microbial spectrum of LCINS patients using metagenomic sequencing and developed a lung cancer predictive model with translational potential. Importantly, we identified a beneficial bacterium, Clostridium aminophilum, which may be developed as a probiotic to support conventional lung cancer treatments. These findings offer promising avenues for early diagnosis, adjunctive therapy, and personalized management of gut microbiota in LCINS patients.
records.authors: Zhang J, Fang L, Ma C, Hu Z, Chen C, Zhu T, Ying J, Zhu W, Huang G, Ni J, Zhang C, Yu G.

records.title: Isolation and characterization of humic acid-degrading microorganisms from natural environments.
records.abstract: Humic acid (HA) is an important component of natural organic matter and is widely present in soils, sediments, and wastewater. Due to its complex aromatic structure and high chemical stability, HA exhibits poor biodegradability and increases the difficulty of wastewater treatment. Microbial degradation has attracted increasing attention as an environmentally friendly approach for HA removal. However, functional HA-degrading microorganisms from natural organic matter-rich environments remain insufficiently explored. In this study, artificial lake sediment and humified soil beneath decayed ginkgo wood were selected as microbial sources for screening HA-degrading microorganisms. A total of 33 microbial isolates were obtained through enrichment culture, acclimation, and screening procedures. Among them, three representative strains, designated as HA-X1, HA-X4, and HA-Z3, exhibited relatively higher HA removal efficiencies. Based on morphological characteristics and molecular identification, HA-X1 and HA-X4 were assigned to Bacillus-related taxa, while HA-Z3 was affiliated with the genus Phoma. The growth characteristics and HA removal performances of the selected strains under different initial HA concentrations, pH conditions, and inoculum dosages were further investigated. The results showed that all selected strains could grow in HA-containing media and exhibited HA removal capability under the tested conditions. Among the three strains, HA-X4 showed the highest overall removal performance. The selected strains displayed different responses to environmental factors, indicating variations in their HA transformation characteristics. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis revealed the morphological characteristics of bacterial cells and fungal mycelial structures. This study provides functional microbial resources for further investigation of HA biodegradation and the development of biological treatment technologies for HA-containing wastewater.
records.authors: Cao Y, Lei Z, He Q, Wei S, Chen W, Pang T.

records.title: A Pilot Study Investigating the Impact of Oral Probiotic Supplementation on the Vaginal Microbiota and Aspects of Well-being
records.abstract: This double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled pilot study investigated the effects of a six-strain probiotic formulation containing  Lactobacillus crispatus CUL40 and  L. gasseri CUL09 on vaginal microbiota composition and well-being in 40 women with recurrent vaginal discomfort. Participants received either the probiotic (20 billion colony-forming units/day) or placebo for 20 days. Vaginal samples collected at baseline, midpoint and endpoint were analysed using shotgun metagenomic sequencing, microbial culture and species- and strain-specific quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Vaginal symptoms and broader well-being were recorded daily. At endpoint, vaginal detection of CUL40 and CUL09 was significantly higher in the probiotic group, with neither strain detected in the placebo group. Viable  L. crispatus CUL40 was recovered from vaginal cultures, whereas viable CUL09 was not recovered.  L. gasseri relative abundance was significantly higher in the probiotic group at midpoint and endpoint, while Gardnerella counts were significantly lower at endpoint. Probiotic supplementation significantly influenced beta diversity over time between groups, although community state types remained broadly stable. During the second half of the intervention, rates of vaginal itchiness, burning sensation and anxiousness were significantly lower in the probiotic group. Bloating was also less frequent throughout the intervention. These findings demonstrate increased vaginal detection of orally administered probiotic strains, including recovery of viable CUL40, alongside changes in vaginal microbiota composition and reduced vaginal discomfort. Larger studies are warranted to confirm these exploratory findings and establish longer-term effects. This trial was registered at  ClinicalTrials.gov (  NCT07364383 ).  Importance  Evidence that probiotic bacteria taken orally can subsequently be detected alive in the vagina remains limited. In this pilot trial, we combined genetic testing with bacterial culture to investigate vaginal detection of  Lactobacillus crispatus CUL40 and  Lactobacillus gasseri CUL09 following oral supplementation. Both strains were detected, and viable CUL40 bacteria were recovered. These findings were accompanied by changes in vaginal bacterial communities and reduced reporting of some symptoms. The study provides evidence to guide further research into oral probiotics and vaginal health.
records.authors: Hulme E, John DA, Michael DR, Coates N, Smith JM, Sośniak E, Gimblett E, Dabcheva M, Wang D, Plummer SF.

records.title: Rhizospheric Bacteria From Artocarpus heterophyllus Exhibit Antimicrobial Traits and Antagonistic Activity Against Pantoea stewartii subsp. stewartii, Causal Agent of Jackfruit Bronzing Disease.
records.abstract: The Jackfruit bronzing disease represents a significant phytosanitary constraint affecting Artocarpus heterophyllus production. In this context, the exploration of plant-associated microorganisms as a source of potential biological control agents aligns with sustainable agricultural strategies. This study is aimed at isolating, characterizing, and evaluating the in vitro antagonistic interactions, and antimicrobial potential of indigenous rhizospheric and endophytic bacteria with the potential to be developed as biocontrol agents for the control jackfruit bronzing causal agent Pantoea stewartii subsp. stewartii. A total of 138 bacterial isolates were obtained from rhizospheric soils and internal plant tissues, with a predominance of rhizospheric bacteria (78.3%). In vitro antagonism assays revealed that only rhizospheric isolates exhibited inhibitory activity against the phytopathogen, identifying 12 strains with consistent antagonistic capacity. These isolates were further characterized to elucidate the potential mechanisms involved in microbial antagonism. Functional analyses demonstrated that the antagonistic isolates possessed multiple extracellular enzymatic activities, predominantly lipase, followed by amylase and cellulase activities, whereas protease activity was absent. Additionally, selected isolates exhibited biosurfactant production, suggesting their role in pathogen inhibition. Antibiosis was confirmed through the production of diffusible antimicrobial compounds. Furthermore, molecular screening revealed the presence of nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) gene fragments in several strains, supporting their genetic potential to synthesize bioactive secondary metabolites. Phylogenetic identification based on 16S rDNA gene sequencing assigned the isolates to bacterial taxa known for their ecological versatility and functional attributes. Overall, this study provides evidence that rhizospheric bacteria associated with jackfruit harbor significant antagonistic and antimicrobial capabilities against jackfruit bronzing causal agent. These findings contribute to the understanding of microbial interactions and functional traits associated with plant microbiota. This study provides the first assessment of microorganisms associated with jackfruit.
records.authors: Arvizu-Gómez JL, Hernández-Morales A, González-Reyes C, Cervantes-Díaz CN, Campos-Guillén J, Pacheco-Aguilar JR.

records.title: Source apportionment and resistome signatures of community and hospital effluents in urban sewer networks.
records.abstract: Antibiotic resistance surveillance has traditionally focused on clinical settings, potentially overlooking broader microbial reservoirs in the community. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) provides a powerful tool for capturing these population-level signals. This study aimed to identify source-specific resistome characteristics and estimate the relative compositional contributions of hospital and residential wastewater to the downstream wastewater treatment plant (WWTP). By integrating droplet digital polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR) with metagenomic sequencing, spatiotemporal dynamics across an urban sewer network were characterized. Bacterial 16S rRNA gene concentrations did not differ significantly between hospital and residential wastewater. Under the specified flow scenarios, hospital wastewater represented a small fraction of the estimated total influent volume. Bayesian source tracking further indicated that residential sources collectively accounted for nearly 80% of the inferred source contribution to the influent antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) profile and 70.9% of the influent microbial community composition, whereas hospital wastewater accounted for only 5.5% of the inferred resistome contribution. These findings show that hospital wastewater contained clinically important resistance genes (e.g., blaKPC-2), whereas the sampled residential references accounted for the largest combined inferred contribution to the influent microbiome and resistome. Together, these results highlight the importance of incorporating community surveillance through wastewater-based approaches within the One Health framework.
records.authors: Li X, Liu H, Wu J, Xi C.

records.title: The Palatine Tonsil Bacterial Microbiota in Pigs: Diverse, Underexplored, Yet Functionally Relevant.
records.abstract: The palatine tonsils play a pivotal role in porcine upper respiratory tract immunity by acting as an interface between the host and the external environment. As such, the tonsillar microbiota represents a critical yet insufficiently characterized microbial ecosystem. This review provides an overview of current knowledge on the porcine tonsillar microbiota, beginning with a description of sampling strategies and laboratory approaches, including metabarcoding, shotgun metagenomics, and culturomics. The development of the tonsillar microbiota over time and the main environmental, host-related, and management factors shaping its composition are examined. Particular emphasis is placed on the core bacterial communities commonly identified in the palatine tonsils, which are largely dominated by members of the Pasteurellaceae, Streptococcaceae, and Moraxellaceae families. The review further discusses how infectious and non-infectious diseases can disrupt tonsillar microbial homeostasis, as well as the effects of antimicrobial treatments, vaccination, and other prophylactic interventions on microbial structure and function. Finally, methodological biases inherent to current studies are highlighted, key knowledge gaps are identified, and future research directions are proposed to advance metagenomic investigations and better elucidate the role of the tonsillar microbiota in swine health and disease.
records.authors: Hercouët K, Tardy F, Marois-Créhan C.

records.title: Agent_K: An Agent-Orchestrated Pipeline for Mapping Genes to Biosynthetic Pathway towards Metabolite Discovery
records.abstract: The identification of biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) and their associated metabolic pathways is central to genome-guided natural product discovery. However, existing computational tools depend on fragmented workflows for data processing, annotation, and analysis, which require substantial manual intervention and lack seamless integration across heterogeneous platforms and tools. Here, we present, Agent_K, an agent-orchestrated framework that automates the end-to-end process from bacterial whole genome sequence analysis to biosynthetic pathway mapping and metabolite discovery as candidate gene products for functional insights. The system employs a large-language-model (LLM) agent to coordinate multiple bioinformatics tools, enabling dynamic execution, data integration, result interpretation, and flexible and intuitive visualization. By integrating genomic sequences to functional annotations and pathway-level reconstructions, the framework facilitates the identification of candidate gene products, their biosynthetic pathways associated with individual BGCs, and the putative metabolites produced by those pathways. The developed novel agentic framework provides a user-friendly scalable and extensible solution for automated high-throughput analysis and mapping of bacterial secondary metabolism pathways for interactive exploration of candidate potential.
records.authors: Roy RS, Han JJ, Narayana JL, Zhou A, de Figueiredo P, Han A, Qian X.

records.title: Camptothecin transformation in plant-associated Sphingobium lineages is linked to a plasmid accessory region.
records.abstract: Specialized plant metabolites impose strong chemical constraints on plant-associated microorganisms; however, the bacterial pathways that enable transformation of complex alkaloid scaffolds remain poorly understood. Here, we show that plant-associated Sphingobium lineages transform camptothecin (CPT) and that this phenotype is associated with a plasmid accessory region. Strain OP1, isolated from the rhizosphere of the CPT-producing plant Ophiorrhiza pumila, transformed CPT into a transient product, M1, which retained the E-ring lactone and subsequently decreased during incubation. OP1 also transformed 10-hydroxycamptothecin, whereas transformation of 7-ethyl-10-hydroxycamptothecin was delayed or limited, indicating substrate selectivity. Genome-based taxonomic analyses placed OP1, NN19, and KJ09 in one putative novel Sphingobium species-level lineage and IROP2 in a related but distinct lineage. Comparison of NN19 with its non-transforming derivative NTG18 resulted in the identification of GAP2, a 97.8-kb region of plasmid pNN19-1 absent from NTG18 and enriched in redox, hydrolase, transport, regulatory, oxygenation, and ring-cleavage functions. A rearranged pIROP2 module retained homologs of the core GAP2 oxygenation and ring-cleavage candidates, whereas IROP2 generated oxygenated products from CPT analogs. RNA sequencing during growth of NN19 with CPT as the sole added carbon source prioritized the same early module, including monooxygenase and dioxygenase candidates. The collective phenotypic, chemical, genetic, comparative-genomic, and expression evidence supports a model in which a plasmid accessory module contributes to CPT transformation.
records.authors: Takeda H, Takahashi N, Kakiura KSI, Suzuki H, Kijinami T, Horiuchi M, Wakana D, Sudoh H, Hosoe T.

records.title: Microecological-metabolic links along the brain-gut-muscle axis in Tuina analgesia from the perspectives of gut metagenomics and untargeted metabolomics.
records.abstract: Chronic pain involves multilevel processes including central sensitization, peripheral tissue abnormalities, neuroimmune responses, metabolic alterations, and changes in gut microecology. Tuina and related manual therapies can influence local soft-tissue status, peripheral sensory input, autonomic activity, inflammatory responses, and muscle metabolism, whereas the links between their distal systemic effects and gut microecology remain insufficiently characterized. The brain, gut, and skeletal muscle can interact through autonomic pathways, immune-inflammatory signaling, circulating metabolites, myokines, and other distal signals, providing a biological context for analyzing cross-organ changes related to Tuina analgesia. A limited number of studies have reported changes in gut microbiota after Tuina, massage, or combined manual interventions; however, direct evidence continuously linking mechanical stimulation, microbial function, metabolic signaling, and pain improvement remains limited. Gut metagenomics extends analysis beyond species composition to strains, functional genes, and metabolic pathway potential, whereas untargeted metabolomics captures metabolic changes jointly shaped by the host and microbiota. Short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, tryptophan derivatives, and molecules related to lipid and energy metabolism have shown functional associations with neuroimmune regulation, sensory neural activity, and pain sensitization in different pain models. Myokines, metabolites, and extracellular vesicle signals derived from skeletal muscle also provide a possible biological basis for bidirectional gut-muscle communication. Nevertheless, most of these mechanisms originate from studies of pain, the microbiome, or exercise physiology and cannot be directly equated with mechanisms of Tuina analgesia. Integrated metagenomic and metabolomic analyses can identify candidate links involving microbial functions, metabolic alterations, host responses, and pain phenotypes, thereby narrowing the scope of subsequent functional validation. Their interpretation remains influenced by Tuina stimulation parameters, diet, gut transit, medication use, circadian rhythms, and other host factors. Standardization of the intervention, longitudinal multi-omics observation, targeted quantification, functional experiments, and cross-center replication will help clarify the temporal relationships and functional significance of these changes. Microecological-metabolic links across the brain, gut, and skeletal muscle can therefore serve as a cross-organ framework for investigating the systemic effects of Tuina analgesia, although specific pathways and their clinical predictive value still require direct experimental and prospective validation.
records.authors: Zhang X, Wang H, Xing J, Zhao H, Liu Y, Jiao J.

records.title: Detection of nodularin in a benthic Planktothrix strain isolated from a tychoplanktonic microbial mat.
records.abstract: Cyanobacterial blooms can disrupt aquatic ecosystems and threaten human and animal health through the production of potent toxins. Early detection of toxic cyanobacterial blooms using gene-based methods is predicated on the accurate detection of biosynthetic genes responsible for toxin production. Here, we report the isolation of a nodularin-producing freshwater benthic cyanobacterium from a tychoplanktonic microbial mat potentially linked to donkey deaths at a natural watering hole in Northeast Italy. Morphometric and genomic analyses identified the strain as a member of the genus Planktothrix. The isolated strain produced the demethylated nodularin variant [D-Asp¹]NOD at a high intracellular concentration, with levels reaching up to 556.90 ± 38.34 µg g-1 (dry weight) and extracellular concentrations reaching 97.93 ± 2.95 µg L⁻¹ in spent culture medium. This is the first report of a Planktothrix strain capable of producing nodularin. We identified a complete 47-kb nodularin biosynthetic gene cluster in a complete genome sequence, which shares up to 98-100% sequence identity with microcystin biosynthetic gene clusters from microcystin-producing Planktothrix. A mechanism for how the nodularin biosynthetic gene cluster arose in this strain is presented. Detection of microcystin and nodularin biosynthetic genes over the last two decades has enabled early prediction of toxic blooms. However, especially in benthic communities with co-occurring nodularin- and microcystin-producing strains, such methods cannot discriminate whether one or both toxin classes are produced. These findings underscore the need to refine molecular monitoring strategies and develop more precise genomic or metabolomic tools to accurately predict and manage cyanobacterial toxin risks in freshwater ecosystems worldwide.

records.title: Metagenomic Next-Generation Sequencing Enhances Pathogen Detection and Prognostic Stratification in Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation Recipients.
records.abstract: BackgroundAs an emerging detection technique, metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) provides superior genomic resolution and enhances detection precision relative to conventional pathogen detection methods. Patients with malignant hematological disorders are susceptible to infections following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). mNGS demonstrates a significantly higher positivity rate compared with conventional testing.MethodsA total of 100 patients who had undergone HSCT were retrospectively enrolled in this study. The detection rates and patient mortality rates associated with conventional diagnostic methods and mNGS were analyzed and compared. Additionally, the impact of mNGS results on the adjustment of antibacterial therapy was investigated, and the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve was utilized to assess the predictive value of mNGS for mortality.ResultsmNGS detected pathogens in 81% of patients (viruses 71.0%, with herpes simplex virus type 1 [HSV-1] at 26.7%; bacteria 25.0%, predominantly Enterobacteriaceae at 61.5%), outperforming conventional testing ( P P ConclusionCompared with conventional methods, mNGS has a broader pathogen detection spectrum, which may improve the overall detection rate of unknown, uncommon, and mixed infectious pathogens. The selection of diagnostic modalities may be guided by patient-specific factors including CRP levels, age, length of hospital stay, transplantation modality, and granulocyte reconstitution time. mNGS informs antibiotic adjustment, while combined biomarkers (AUC = 0.812) provide prognostic value.

records.title: Chiral antibiotics amplify the phage-associated antibiotic resistome in salinized soil.
records.abstract: Anthropogenic global change is intensifying antibiotic pollution and soil salinization, yet how salinity shapes bacteria-phage interactions to drive the dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) under chiral antibiotic pressure remains poorly understood. Using viral metagenomic analyses and laboratory validation, we show that salinity amplifies the enrichment of total and high-risk ARGs along gradients of racemic ofloxacin and its S-enantiomer levofloxacin, concomitant with the parallel accumulation of mobile genetic elements and virulence factors. High-concentration antibiotic treatment in saline soils selected for stress-tolerant, fast-growing antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARBs) carrying abundant prophages and diverse defense systems, thereby promoting tight ARB-phage interactions. Under these dual extreme stresses, lysogenic phages were enriched, enhancing their carriage of ARGs, auxiliary metabolic genes (AMGs) that bolster host survival, and antidefense genes via a "piggyback-the-winner" strategy, thereby increasing ARG dissemination potential. Notably, high-concentration levofloxacin exerted stronger selective pressure than ofloxacin, increasing virus-to-host ratios and phage-associated ARG accumulation, as supported by incubation assays. Collectively, our findings support a mechanistic framework in which soil salinization interacts with chiral antibiotic exposure, particularly levofloxacin, to increase phage-associated ARG dissemination potential. This highlights a long-underappreciated, Anthropocene-driven pathway intensifying environmental resistance risks and posing new challenges for the One Health framework.
records.authors: Xie T, Lin D, Tong SQ, Wang Q, Ni N, Wang N, Yang Z, Liu XH, Zhu D.

records.title: Artificial intelligence in the diagnosis and identification of bacterial pathogens: Current advances and future perspectives.
records.abstract: Bacterial infections remain a major global health challenge, which are responsible for significant morbidity, mortality, and increasing antimicrobial resistance worldwide. Rapid and accurate identification of bacterial pathogens is therefore essential for guiding appropriate antimicrobial therapy, improving patient outcomes, and supporting effective infection control strategies. However, conventional microbiological diagnostic methods such as culture, microscopy, and biochemical testing are often time-consuming, labor-intensive, and dependent on expert interpretation. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly emerged as a powerful tool capable of transforming clinical microbiology by enabling rapid analysis of complex biomedical data. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the role of AI in the diagnosis and identification of bacterial pathogens and to discuss its current applications, advantages, limitations, and future perspectives. Key AI-assisted technologies, including machine learning and deep learning algorithms such as Random Forest, Support Vector Machines, Artificial Neural Networks, and Convolutional Neural Networks, are increasingly applied to diagnostic platforms, including automated microscopy, next-generation genomic sequencing, MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, and clinical data analysis systems. Current evidence indicates that AI-assisted diagnostic approaches can substantially improve the speed, accuracy, and automation of microbial pathogen detection while enabling large-scale analysis of microbiological and clinical datasets. In the future, AI-integrated microbiology laboratories, rapid diagnostic platforms, genomic surveillance systems, and AI-assisted clinical decision support tools are expected to further enhance infectious disease diagnostics and contribute to improved antimicrobial stewardship and global infection management.

records.title: Plasmid-mediated copper resistance in Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans: determination of plasmid copy number and stability.
records.abstract: The management of bacterial spot of tomato is challenged by the widespread occurrence of copper resistance among its causal pathogens. In Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans, a major causal agent, copper resistance is conferred by cop genes organized in an operon located on either the chromosome or plasmid. In the United States, copper resistance is predominantly chromosomally encoded. Plasmid-borne resistance is limited to a few phylogenetic groups but is prevalent in other bacterial spot pathogens. We hypothesized that plasmid-encoded copper resistance genes exhibit higher expression than chromosomally encoded genes but may be unstable in the absence of selective pressure for resistance. To test this hypothesis, we examined how the chromosomal versus plasmid-borne cop operon influences gene copy number and expression, as well as plasmid stability. Relative to strains with only chromosomal resistance, strains carrying plasmid-encoded resistance exhibited an increased copy number of copB, a key gene in the operon, while strains carrying both chromosomal and plasmid-encoded resistance showed an even greater increase in gene copy number. Correspondingly, copB expression was elevated in both groups. During in vitro growth without copper, partial or complete plasmid loss occurred in a subset of strains, and genome sequencing of colonies with reduced plasmid size revealed transposase-mediated plasmid rearrangements. These findings demonstrate that plasmid-borne copper resistance increases gene copy number and expression of copper resistance genes but can be unstable without copper selection in some strain backgrounds, highlighting the role of mobile genetic elements in shaping Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans adaptation to changing copper environments.IMPORTANCEPlasmids are key players in the dissemination of antimicrobial resistance. Although copper resistance is widespread among Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans strains, copper-based bactericides remain at the forefront of disease management. We previously demonstrated that distinct genetic elements, including plasmid- and chromosomally encoded genomic islands, contribute to the acquisition of copper resistance and the occurrence of multicopy resistance in X. euvesicatoria pv. perforans. Here, we show that the localization of copper resistance genes on a plasmid, chromosome, or both influences gene copy number and expression of copper resistance genes. Furthermore, rearrangements between co-resident plasmids affect plasmid stability, leading to the loss of copper resistance in X. euvesicatoria pv. perforans. These findings highlight how plasmid dynamics can shape bacterial evolvability and adaptation to selective environments.

records.title: Lineage II Escherichia coli O157:H7: genomes, prophages, colicins, and the absence of detectable Stx2.
records.abstract: The genomes of three lineage II strains of E. coli O157:H7 (FRIK2069, FRIK2455, and FRIK2533) with different pulsed-field gel electrophoresis patterns were sequenced, assembled, and compared. The genomes were closely related, with overall synteny, with the exception of a 302 kbp inversion in FRIK2069. FRIK2533 lacked pO157, which may account for its limited isolation. FRIK2455 was the dominant strain isolated over several years and was selected for comparison with lineage I (Sakai) and lineage I/II (EC4115) strains. Distinct polymorphisms were identified in prophages and MGEs among the three lineages. All lineages contained stx1 prophages and the locus of enterocyte effacement. The stx2a prophage was present in Sakai and EC4115, while the stx2c prophage was found in EC4115 and FRIK2455. Eleven geographically disparate LII strains from the United States were tested for functional phage and Stx2. Three of the 11 LII strains underwent delayed lysis after 24 h post-mitomycin C treatment. stx2 transcription was observed in two of the three lytic strains, but Stx2 was not detected in the lytic or non-lytic LII strains by Western blot. The supernatant of lysates from eight lineage II strains inhibited growth of the phage host (E. coli strain MG1655) due to the production of a colicin (D, B, or M). These findings add to the body of evidence that LII EHEC do not produce functional phage or a detectable level of Stx2. Additionally, colicin production and pO157 may be key characteristics to the persistence of EHEC strains in the bovine host and farm environment.IMPORTANCEEscherichia coli O157:H7 is a human pathogen that is phylogenetically separated into three lineages. Strains belonging to lineages I and I/II are isolated from both clinical and bovine samples, whereas lineage II strains are only isolated from bovine and environments they occupy. This study sequenced, assembled, and compared the genomes of three lineage II strains. The genomes were closely related and syntenic, with differences in plasmid content and a chromosomal inversion. Comparison of the genome from FRIK2455 (lineage II strain) with the genomes of lineage I and I/II strains found distinct polymorphisms in prophages and mobile genetic elements. None of the lineage II strains examined produced functional phage or Stx2, but eight strains produced a colicin. Results from this study support previous reports that lineage II strains do not produce a detectable level of Stx2. Additionally, colicin production and pO157 may contribute to the persistence of EHEC in bovine.
records.authors: Stanton E, Teng L, Lee C, Wahlig TA, Park D, Jeong KC, Kaspar CW.

records.title: Integrated epidemiological and genomic characterization of respiratory bovine coronavirus in U.S. cattle 2020-2025.
records.abstract: Bovine coronavirus (BCoV) is an important contributor to the respiratory disease complex in cattle; however, integrated genomic and epidemiological data describing currently circulating respiratory BCoV strains in the United States remain limited. The objective of this study was to monitor respiratory BCoV at the genomic level and analyze its epidemiological patterns over five years, in addition to assess the pathological findings of the currently circulating BCoV in cattle. A total of 4,505 respiratory samples submitted to a diagnostic laboratory between January 2020 and November 2025 were analyzed, of which 693 (15.38%) tested positive for BCoV. Positivity was highest in young calves (0-40 days; 20.0%) and declined significantly with increasing age based on logistic regression analysis. Temporal trend analysis using locally estimated scatterplot smoothing and the Mann-Kendall test showed no significant monotonic change in BCoV detection during the study period. Co-infections were commonly detected between BCoV and other viral respiratory pathogens, while bacterial pathogens predominated in many samples. Lung tissues submitted from bovine respiratory cases were screened by qRT-PCR, and selected samples with high viral loads were subjected to next-generation sequencing. Complete genome sequencing identified four respiratory BCoV isolates (~31 kb), all clustering within genotype GIIb with recent U.S. strains. Comparative genomic analysis revealed amino acid substitutions in structural and non-structural proteins that may influence viral attachment, replication, and tissue tropism. These findings provide updated epidemiological and genomic insights into respiratory BCoV circulating in U.S. cattle.IMPORTANCEThis study demonstrates continued detection and genetic evolution of respiratory bovine coronavirus (BCoV) among diagnostic respiratory samples submitted from U.S. cattle, with 15.38% positivity observed among 4,505 submitted samples and a higher proportion of positive submissions from young calves. Whole-genome sequencing of lung-derived isolates revealed consistent clustering within genotype GIIb alongside ongoing molecular diversification, including amino acid substitutions in spike, hemagglutinin-esterase, nucleocapsid, and membrane proteins, and the emergence of a previously unrecognized putative alternative ORF near 4.8-kDa NSP. These findings highlight that respiratory BCoV is continuously evolving at the site of disease. The observed genetic changes provide critical targets to refine diagnostic assays, support updating of vaccine strains, inform antiviral development, and enable more effective, evidence-based management strategies for controlling respiratory BCoV in cattle, requiring potential experimental validation.
records.authors: Shah AU, Varga C, Gauger P, Hemida MG.

records.title: Adaptive landscape and genetic divergence of Karnah sheep revealed by selection scans across multiple ovine breeds.
records.abstract: Indigenous sheep constitute vital reservoirs of adaptive genetic diversity, yet their genomic signatures of adaptation are poorly understood. The present study provides a comprehensive genomic characterization of the endangered Karnah sheep (Ovis aries) native to North Kashmir, India. A total of 41,812 high-confidence SNPs were used across 266 individuals representing nine geographically and functionally diverse breeds (i.e., Karnah, Garole, Deccani, Changthangi, Tibetan, Australian Merino, Rambouillet, Suffolk, and Texel). Population structure analyses revealed pronounced genetic stratification with PC1-PC3 explaining 13.81% variance, separating Asian indigenous clusters (high-altitude vs. lowland) from European-derived wool and mutton populations. This pattern was consistently supported by ADMIXTURE (optimal K value of 8) and neighbor-joining phylogenetic analysis, identifying two deeply rooted clades. Genome-wide nucleotide diversity (π) estimates indicated relatively uniform diversity across populations, with Australian Merino exhibiting the highest diversity (106% of the mean), followed by Karnah (102%), while Garole showed the lowest (93%). Pairwise FST values ranged from 0.03 to 0.188, reflecting moderate genetic differentiation, with the lowest differentiation observed between Changthangi and Tibetan breeds and the highest between Garole and European breeds. Selection signature analyses revealed strong adaptive signals in Karnah sheep. Intra-population iHS analysis (|iHS| > 3) identified key candidate genes such as RELN, ADIPOQ, and RAP1B associated with environmental resilience, metabolism, and reproduction. Cross-population XP-EHH and FST analysis further highlighted genes involved in lipid metabolism (ATP8B2, ELOVL1), calcium signaling (CACNA1C), and immune response (NFKB2, HS6ST3), indicating adaptive divergence driven by climatic and ecological pressures. Functional enrichment supported pathways related to immunity, metabolism, and reproduction. Collectively, these findings provide a robust genomic framework for understanding adaptive evolution in Karnah sheep and offer valuable insights for conservation and climate-resilient breeding strategies.
records.journal: Mammalian genome : official journal of the International Mammalian Genome Society

records.title: Strong habitat-associated differentiation of microbial communities across a fine-scale land-water interface
records.abstract: Microbial communities can remain strongly differentiated across environmental boundaries despite their potential for widespread dispersal. However, the extent to which habitat differences structure microbial communities at fine spatial scales remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated bacterial and fungal communities across a 350-m land-water interface in Lake Vänern, Sweden, including mainland soil, two small terrestrial islands and lake water. Using 16S and ITS amplicon sequencing, we compared microbial diversity and community composition across habitats and with increasing distance from the shoreline. Both bacterial and fungal communities showed pronounced habitat-associated differentiation, with the strongest contrasts between terrestrial and aquatic samples. Despite being surrounded by lake water, island communities were compositionally more similar to mainland soil communities, suggesting that geographic proximity alone does not necessarily lead to microbial community homogenization. Fungal, but not bacterial community composition varied significantly with shoreline position within both terrestrial and aquatic habitats, indicating contrasting spatial patterns between the two groups. Fungal genera also showed greater taxonomic overlap between terrestrial and aquatic habitats than bacterial genera, although overall community composition remained distinct. Taxonomically inferred functional profiles and ecological guilds further reflected habitat-associated differences. Together, our findings reveal strong microbial community differentiation across a fine-scale land-water interface and highlight how habitat identity and spatial context are associated with distinct patterns of bacterial and fungal community assembly.
records.authors: Haberkorn C, Oporto CI, Pinto J, Stelkens R.

records.title: Rapid and convergent evolution of Wolbachia genomes in mosquito cell culture.
records.abstract: Wolbachia are widespread bacterial symbionts of arthropods that manipulate host reproduction and can confer fitness benefits, such as protection against viral pathogens. Their self-spreading ability coupled with their antiviral effect has been harnessed in health programmes to curb the transmission of dengue virus by Aedes mosquitoes. In this context, a better understanding of evolutionary dynamics over short timescales is critical to inform and improve the efficacy of Wolbachia-based disease control interventions. Moreover, experimental evolution of Wolbachia may provide a powerful approach for generating novel symbiont strains with improved properties for disease control. Here we generated new mosquito cell lines by introducing five Wolbachia strains from Drosophila into the symbiont-free Aedes albopictus Aa23 cell line. Following transinfection, long-read whole-genome sequencing revealed multiple mutations, including structural changes, some of them being associated with major shifts in bacterial density. Signs of convergent evolution, an excess of non-synonymous mutations and comparisons with previous studies, indicate that Wolbachia evolution in cell culture is predominantly driven by selection and occurs faster than in insect hosts. Altogether, our study demonstrates that cell culture is a valuable tool to investigate short-term symbiont evolution, explore the genetic basis of bacterial density regulation and generate higher-density symbiont strains suitable for disease control.
records.authors: Martinez J, Wairimu AW, Sinkins SP.

records.title: A stratified human colon model reveals SCFA cross-feeding-driven host-microbe dynamics associated with epithelial and immune responses.
records.abstract: Host-microbe interactions are essential for maintaining intestinal homeostasis, yet most in vitro models lack physiological oxygen gradients, mucosal architecture, and reproducibility. We developed the Mucosal Mimetic 3D-Host Aerobic Microbiota Anaerobic Co-culture (Mm 3D-HaeMan) system, a colon-mimetic, oxygen-stratified platform enabling stable co-culture of colonic epithelial cells, human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (hPBMCs), and obligate anaerobes. Oxygen profiling confirmed a stable gradient consistent with human colonic stratification. Using a canonical short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) cross-feeding pair (Anaerostipes caccae and Bifidobacterium bifidum, AcBb consortium), we performed integrated, multilayered analyzes of the host-microbe interface. Co-culture with the SCFA-producing AcBb consortium was associated with enhanced epithelial-mitochondrial respiration, maintenance of transepithelial resistance, tight junction protein expression without barrier disruption, and rebalanced cytokine profiles. Host transcriptomics identified 41 differentially expressed genes (15 upregulated, 26 downregulated) associated with homeostatic-relevant epithelial responses. Simultaneously, bacterial metatranscriptomics revealed 29 differentially expressed gene families; notably, glaK was enriched in bacteria-only cultures; SORD, nuoG, and nuoE were specifically induced during co-culture, indicating host-associated bacterial transcriptional changes. The compartmentalized design permits independent sampling for layer-resolved multi-omics and functional readouts. These findings establish Mm 3D-HaeMan as a physiologically grounded platform for dissecting bidirectional host-microbe responses and immune-associated interactions. This model offers broad applicability for mechanistic research and translational screening of probiotics and microbiome-based therapeutics.
records.authors: Kim T, Park JY, Kim M, Kim NY, Jang SA, Park HG, Lee DW, Lee K, Kim BS, Kang NJ.

records.title: Cordyceps as a multitarget therapeutic platform: biology, bioactive metabolites, and translational challenges.
records.abstract: Cordyceps-related fungi have garnered global attention as multifunctional therapeutic resources owing to their exclusive entomopathogenic biology, remarkable metabolic diversity, and expanding pharmaceutical bearing. Recent taxonomic revisions determined by molecular phylogenetics have redefined the traditional notion of Cordyceps, revealing distinct evolutionary lineages with species-specific metabolite profiles and biological functions. This review provides a complete and evidence-based synthesis of the taxonomy, ecology, host interactions, chemical composition, biosynthetic pathways, pharmacological activities, and translational prospects of chief medicinal species, including Ophiocordyceps sinensis, Cordyceps militaris, Cordyceps cicadae, and related taxa. Particular emphasis is placed on cordycepin, the signature bioactive nucleoside, and its integration with broader metabolite networks encompassing polysaccharides, sterols, peptides, and secondary metabolites. Current evidence demonstrates that Cordyceps-derived compounds influence multiple interconnected signaling pathways, including AMPK, PI3K/Akt/mTOR, NF-κB, MAPK, and oxidative stress-response networks, thereby contributing to immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, anticancer, neuroprotective, and metabolic regulatory effects. The review further reviews recent advances in genomics, transcriptomics, metabolomics, biosynthetic gene-cluster analysis, synthetic biology, metabolic engineering, and exactness fermentation technologies that are redesigning Cordyceps research and industrial production. Critical challenges including species authentication, chemical standardization, pharmacokinetic limitations, product reproducibility, safety evaluation, regulatory requirements, and inadequate clinical validation are also discussed. By integrating biological identity, metabolite biosynthesis, molecular mechanisms, and technological innovation within a translational framework, this review positions Cordyceps as a promising systems-level platform for future therapeutics, functional foods, and precision mycotherapy.
records.authors: Chaudhary A, Maurya S, Ehsan S, Choure K, Singh MP.

records.title: Most metagenomic vanT calls are not vancomycin resistance genes
records.abstract: Metagenomic resistome surveys frequently report  vanT G as the dominant glycopeptide resistance gene, but these calls rely on homology without verifying catalytic residues or operon context. By analyzing 107,008 metagenome-assembled genomes, we demonstrate that only 3.7% of predicted  vanT G genes possess the required active-site substitution, with the vast majority being misannotated alanine racemases. Incorporating structural and genomic context corrections reveals a novel split-architecture lineage in gut-associated Erysipelotrichales missed by current profiling tools.
records.authors: Shetty P, Maroti G, Wirth R.

records.title: Genomic insights into population structure, resistome, virulome, and mobilome of multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
records.abstract: BackgroundPseudomonas aeruginosa is a leading opportunistic Gram-negative pathogen causing severe healthcare-associated infections. The aim of the present study was to assess the interplay between population structure, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants, virulence factors (VFs), and mobile genetic elements (MGEs) of P. aeruginosa genomes retrieved from public databases.MethodsWe performed genomic profiling of 301 human-associated MDR P. aeruginosa genomes from clinical sources. The comprehensive genomic analyses primarily focused on characterization of sequence types (STs), antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs), VFs, plasmids, insertion sequences (ISs), integrons, prophages, and pangenome using established bioinformatics tools.ResultsThe dataset exhibited diverse population structure dominated by internationally recognized high-risk STs, particularly ST621, ST277, and ST235 among the MDR genomes. The MDR P. aeruginosa genomes contained a greater ARG burden (mostly acquired aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, β-lactamase genes, sulfonamide resistance genes, and disinfectant resistance determinants). Additionally, higher numbers of ISs, complete class 1 integrons, plasmid contigs, and prophage sequences, were identified supporting the pivotal role of MGEs in genome evolution and AMR dissemination. Pangenome analysis revealed an extensive accessory genome, highlighting substantial genomic diversity. In contrast, the intrinsic resistome and virulome remained highly conserved.ConclusionMDR genomes exhibited greater burden of acquired ARGs against a conserved intrinsic resistance background. The integrated genomic framework provides insights into genomic characteristics associated with MDR P. aeruginosa and supports genomic surveillance of emerging MDR lineages and their associated mobile resistance elements.
records.authors: Pearl S, George EA, Ramaiah S, Anbarasu A.

records.title: Transcriptional silencing of a conjugative Sinorhizobium megaplasmid upon transfer to different rhizobial species.
records.abstract: Horizontal gene transfer of large conjugative megaplasmids drives bacterial evolution, however, it forces new hosts to rapidly adapt to a massive influx of exogenous DNA; even the acquisition of small plasmids can have variable effects on host genome activity and fitness. In Sinorhizobium fredii GR64 (symbiont of the common bean) the megaplasmid pSfr64a (191 kb) displays a high conjugative transfer rate. Interestingly, when pSfr64a is transferred to Rhizobium etli (another bean symbiont) conjugative transfer from this host became nearly undetectable, whereas in Agrobacterium tumefaciens it is maintained at a high rate. To unravel the host-plasmid dynamics driving this host-specific response, we undertook a transcriptome analysis of pSfr64a in different hosts. The results reveal that in its original host, pSfr64a transcriptional activity is centered in four zones, including the conjugative zone. Expression of these zones is markedly quelled when pSfr64a resides in R. etli, explaining the reduction in conjugative activity. Crucially, this silencing ensures minimal effects on the host's transcriptional activity, allowing R. etli to adapt to the megaplasmid with zero fitness cost. In contrast, a weak silencing in A. tumefaciens allows conjugation, but triggers a widespread transcriptional reorganization across both linear and circular chromosomes, severely penalizing host fitness. Although inactivation of the xenogeneic silencer MucR in R. etli leads to a partial recovery of plasmid expression, it does not restore conjugation. These results highlight a fundamental evolutionary conflict: the successful adaptation to a newly acquired megaplasmid depends on a hierarchical, host-specific silencing architecture that must tame the biological cost of the plasmid's "selfish mode."
records.authors: de la Cruz C, Cervantes L, Torres-Tejerizo G, Romero D.

records.title: Contrasting stage-associated succession and ecological assembly of bacterial and fungal communities during industrial sauce-flavor Baijiu heap fermentation.
records.abstract: Whether stage-associated community differentiation corresponds to inferred assembly processes and profile dissimilarities remains unclear in industrial sauce-flavor Baijiu heap fermentation. Pre-turn and post-turn samples from rounds R3-R7 of two consecutive production cycles were examined by integrating bacterial and fungal community profiles, βNTI-RCbray assembly assignments, PICRUSt2-predicted MetaCyc profiles, FUNGuild annotations, physicochemical measurements, GC-MS volatile profiles, and matched local temperatures. Exploratory pair-aligned models related each pair's assembly-process family (ProcessFamily) to annotation-profile or measured volatile-profile dissimilarity calculated from the same samples. After adjustment for Round and Position, Stage accounted for 1.85-2.01% of bacterial and 12.69-14.24% of fungal Bray-Curtis variation, while Round had the largest conditional share. Fungal Stage shares remained larger after temperature adjustment and across corresponding leave-one-round-out comparisons, without a greater prevalence of selection-related assignments. Adding round-specific time trends reduced Stage shares to 0.18-0.56% for bacteria and 0.62-1.44% for fungi, indicating substantial sensitivity to fermentation progression. In Cycle II, ProcessFamily associations with bacterial MetaCyc and fungal guild-profile dissimilarities had partial R2 values of 2.30% and 5.97%, respectively, with little change after physicochemical adjustment. Neither cross-cycle reproducibility nor a general correspondence with measured volatile-profile dissimilarity was established. These findings distinguish compositional differentiation from inferred assembly structure and ecological-annotation correspondence from measured chemical relationships. They identify fungal composition and pair-level annotation associations as candidates for further validation, without establishing an independent turning effect.
records.authors: Zhang N, Huang X, Zhang S, Shen C, Wang S, Li J, Li Z, Zou X.

records.title: Streptococcus bovipulmonis sp. nov., a pathogenic bacterium isolated from a dead dairy cow with hemorrhagic pneumonia.
records.abstract: A strain of Gram-stain-positive, oxidase- and catalase-negative, facultative anaerobic coccus-shaped bacterium, designated as ZY171113T, was isolated from lung of a dead dairy cow with hemorrhagic pneumonia in Yunnan Province, southwest China. The pairwise comparisons of 16S rRNA gene sequences indicated that the strain share the highest similarities to Streptococcus suis CCUG 7984T and S. gallinaceus CCUG 42692T with 96.2 and 96.0 %, respectively, suggesting the strain belongs to the genus Streptococcus. The phylogenetic analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequences and phylogenomic analysis of 113 single-copy gene sequences placed the strain as a distinct clade within the genus Streptococcus. The genomic orthologous average nucleotide identity and digital DNA-DNA hybridization values between strain ZY171113T and its close relatives within the genus Streptococcus were ≤ 72.9 % and ≤ 28.7 %, which were below the cut-off values for species delineation. The optimal growth of strain ZY171113T occurred at 37 °C, at pH 7.0 and in the presence of 1.0 % (w/v) NaCl. The genomic DNA G+C content of strain ZY171113T was 48.8 mol%, which was higher than the upper limit of the range 33.1-44.6 mol% of the type strains within the genus Streptococcus. The strain ZY171113T shared the major fatty acids C14:0, C16:0, C18:0 and C18:1 ω9c, and the major polar lipids phosphatidylglycerol, monogalactosyldiacylglycerol, ether-linked phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylinositol with its closest relatives S. gallinaceus CCUG 42692T and S. suis CCUG 7984T. The strain harbored the sole Lancefield group D antigen. Based on the phenotypic, genotypic and chemotaxonomic features, strain ZY171113T represents a novel species within the genus Streptococcus, for which the name Streptococcus bovipulmonis sp. nov. is proposed, with strain ZY171113T (=NBRC 116579T=CCTCC AB 2023267T) as the type strain. The pathogenicity test indicated that strain S. bovipulmonis ZY171113T could induce respiratory disease in mice. These results confirmed that the novel species S. bovipulmonis is a pathogenic bacterium, and suggested that it may be a new pathogen of the respiratory disease in cattle.
records.authors: Li F, Zhao W, Gao H, Song J.
