records.title: Antimicrobial Resistance at Slaughterhouse and Meat-Processing Interfaces in East Africa: A One Health Review of Contamination Pathways, Occupational Exposure and Control Strategies
records.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major One Health challenge because resistant microorganisms and resistance determinants can circulate among humans, animals and the environment. Slaughterhouses and meat-processing facilities represent important interfaces within this interconnected system. Animals carrying resistant bacteria may introduce them into slaughter environments, where contamination can occur through gastrointestinal contents, hides, carcasses, workers’ hands, knives, equipment, water and processing surfaces. These pathways may expose workers and consumers while contributing to the wider environmental dissemination of resistant microorganisms. This review examines evidence concerning AMR at slaughterhouse and meat-processing interfaces in East Africa, with emphasis on contamination pathways, occupational exposure, bacterial resistance patterns, genomic evidence and feasible control strategies. A targeted narrative literature search was conducted using PubMed-indexed records, PubMed Central, publisher platforms, institutional repositories and international policy sources. Relevant evidence was identified from Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda and Ethiopia. Studies from western Kenya have demonstrated resistant bacteria in slaughterhouse environments, carcasses and workers, while investigations in Tanzania have identified antimicrobial-resistant Escherichia coli in goat meat and meat-handler-associated isolates. Evidence from Ethiopia has documented Salmonella and Staphylococcus aureus contamination across carcasses, workers and processing environments. A 2026 investigation in southwestern Uganda additionally reported antimicrobial residues and resistant bacteria in beef samples. Genomic investigations from Tanzania have identified extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing E. coli, including isolates carrying blaCTX-M-15 and multidrug-resistance-associated plasmids. However, the available evidence is geographically uneven, methodologically heterogeneous and insufficient to establish the direction or frequency of transmission between animals, workers, meat and environmental compartments. Important limitations include inconsistent sampling designs, variable antimicrobial susceptibility testing, limited genomic surveillance and a lack of longitudinal studies linking antimicrobial use, slaughterhouse contamination and human colonization. A coordinated One Health response should combine antimicrobial stewardship in livestock production, ante-mortem and post-mortem inspection, hygienic slaughter practices, worker protection, water and waste management, food-chain surveillance and genomic epidemiology. Strengthening these measures through regional collaboration could improve food safety and reduce opportunities for the dissemination of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria in East Africa.

records.title: Human cognitive performance-associated gut microbiota influences learning and memory in mice through arginine and pterin metabolism.
records.abstract: The human gut microbiome undergoes changes across the lifespan and has been implicated in age-related decline. The symbol digit modalities test (SDMT) is a measure of information processing speed and is sensitive to mild cognitive impairment. Here, we assessed SDMT scores and fecal shotgun metagenomics in older individuals from the Imageomics cohort (n = 867) and performed fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from human donors to male C57BL/6 mouse recipients. In mice, we evaluated cognitive performance using the Morris water maze (MWM) and measured neurone density, fecal shotgun metagenomics, hippocampal metabolomics, and cortical gene expression to identify microbial-derived functional properties related to cognitive performance. In humans, both microbial species composition and functional profiles were associated with cognitive performance. FMT from high-SDMT donors improved cognitive performance and increased neuronal density in recipient mice compared with FMT from low-SDMT donors. In both humans and mice, higher cognitive performance was associated with arginine and proline metabolism and pterin-related pathways. In mice receiving microbiota from high-SDMT donors, cortical gene expression showed enrichment of dopamine receptor pathways and reduced dopamine reuptake and catecholamine biosynthesis. Our findings highlight the potential role of the gut microbiome in cognitive performance among older individuals, particularly information processing speed, and identify potential mechanisms involving alterations in arginine and pterin metabolism. Integrating human and mouse data supports a model in which microbiota-associated metabolic remodeling influences cognitive performance.
records.authors: Tracey H, Antolín A, Teichenne J, Jones OAH, Van TTH, Puig J, Ramos R, Garre-Olmo J, Fernández-Real JM, Mayneris-Perxachs J, Del Bas JM.

records.title: Orf virus early genes ORFV113 and ORFV114 are individually dispensable for replication in vitro but required for full virulence in vivo.
records.abstract: Orf is a highly contagious zoonotic disease caused by Orf virus (ORFV), resulting in significant economic losses to the livestock industry. ORFV113 and ORFV114, located in the terminal variable region of the ORFV genome, are putative virulence-associated genes. To elucidate their biological functions, we characterized the transcription kinetics of both genes and generated single-gene deletion mutants by homologous recombination, using transfer plasmids carrying flanking homology arms and an enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) reporter cassette. Lamb testis (LT) cells transfected with the recombinant plasmids were infected with the parental ORFV-JS strain; recombinant viruses were enriched by limiting dilution, purified by consecutive rounds of plaque isolation, and verified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Both genes are highly conserved among ORFV isolates (92-100% nucleotide identity) and are transcribed with early kinetics. The genetically stable deletion mutants, designated ORFV-Δ113 and ORFV-Δ114, were successfully generated. Deletion of either gene did not significantly alter viral growth kinetics or cytopathic effects (CPE) in LT cells. In a rabbit skin scarification model (n = 4 per group), however, both mutants induced markedly milder macroscopic lesions with lower cumulative clinical scores (P < 0.05), and viral loads in scab tissue were reduced 17-fold (ORFV-Δ113) and 10-fold (ORFV-Δ114) relative to the wild-type strain (P < 0.01). Thus, ORFV113 and ORFV114 are dispensable for viral replication in vitro but are required for full virulence in vivo. The resulting deletion mutants provide valuable tools for dissecting virus-host interactions and are promising candidates for the rational design of live-attenuated ORFV vaccines.
records.authors: Zhou W, Hu J, Wang X, Wang N, Cheng Z, Cheng A, Pang F.

records.title: Coordinating substrate accessibility with indigenous microorganisms functionality to enhance medium-chain fatty acid production from waste activated sludge.
records.abstract: Efficient medium-chain fatty acid (MCFA) production from waste activated sludge (WAS) depends on both substrate accessibility and microbial conversion. To clarify their roles in chain elongation (CE), three pretreatments were evaluated in a two-stage fermentation system with indigenous microorganisms retained or inactivated. Thermal-alkaline pretreatment achieved the highest MCFA production (4973.9 ± 274.2 mg COD/L) by improving substrate accessibility, although its relatively low selectivity indicated that greater precursor availability did not necessarily favor carbon allocation to MCFA. Retaining indigenous microorganisms increased MCFA production by 35.8-76.9% compared with corresponding autoclaved reactors and altered ethanol consumption and short-chain fatty acid dynamics, suggesting their involvement in intermediate utilization. Community analysis associated effective CE with complementary hydrolytic, acidogenic, and chain-elongating populations, including Macellibacteroides, Romboutsia, Clostridium, and Caproiciproducens, rather than the enrichment of chain-elongating bacteria alone. Metagenomic analysis of the thermal-alkaline system indicated differences in genetic potential for substrate degradation, glycolysis, electron transfer, acetyl-CoA formation, and reverse β-oxidation. These results suggest that coordinating pretreatment-driven substrate supply with indigenous microbial conversion capacity is essential for improving sludge-derived MCFA production.
records.authors: Tan L, Mei J, Song X, Bai X, Chen B, Wang Y, Shi J, Xu X, Jiang Z, Liu Z, Liu W, Yue X, Zhou A.

records.title: Genomic epidemiology and transmission dynamics of Acinetobacter baumannii: Comparison of clinical and wastewater isolates.
records.abstract: This study characterized the epidemiological, phenotypic, and genomic dynamics of Acinetobacter baumannii across inpatient, outpatient, hospital environmental, and diverse wastewater habitats from January to December 2025. Bacterial detection exhibited pronounced seasonal variations and habitat heterogeneity, with wastewater showing the highest prevalence and summer marking the peak period. High-touch surfaces represented the core hospital contamination nodes, and healthcare workers faced potential risks of carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii (CRAB) colonization. Notably, CRAB and multidrug-resistant strains appeared confined to clinical niches, where the dominant ST2Pas and ST164Pas clones stably harbored abundant carbapenemases, disinfectant resistance genes, and virulence factors. Anthropogenic antibiotic and sanitizer selective pressures likely drive their high multiple antibiotic resistance index (MARI) phenotypes. Conversely, wastewater strains were predominantly pan-susceptible (MARI < 0.2) but enriched with novel sequence types (STs) and rare resistance genes, suggesting their role as a natural reservoir for genetic diversification. Core-genome SNP transmission networks indicated high-density intra-hospital cross-transmission and occult inter-hospital dissemination, while capturing potential bidirectional cross-habitat spillover events. Mechanistically, conjugative plasmids, insertion sequences (IS256/IS3/IS66), and active prophages mediated resistance and virulence recombination in clinical strains. Meanwhile, wastewater strains might utilize the ISNCY family to undergo environmental adaptation, with integrons playing a minor role in resistance spread. This study uncovers the divergent evolutionary pathways of A. baumannii, providing critical genomic evidence for integrated clinical-environmental management to mitigate the cross-niche dissemination of antimicrobial resistance.
records.authors: Wang X, Zhang Y, Liang Y, You S, Xu T, Xu Y, Qiu Y, Wang Y, Feng J, Zhao B, Shen Y, Ren L.

records.title: SNAT2-mediated amino acid import maintains osmotic balance to restrain macrophage metabolic reprogramming and inflammasome activation.
records.abstract: Macrophages undergo metabolic reprogramming during inflammatory responses to microbial infection, in part because of activation of the transcription factor HIF-1α (hypoxia-inducible factor 1α). Here, we identified regulators of HIF-1α-dependent gene expression during immune activation induced by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and during the hypoxic response using genome-wide CRISPR screens in cultured mouse macrophages. The small neutral amino acid transporter SNAT2 (encoded by Slc38a2) was a key inhibitor of HIF-1α activation and metabolic reprogramming in cultured and bone marrow-derived mouse macrophages in response to LPS but not to hypoxia. Inflammatory stimulation increased SNAT2 protein abundance and dynamically expanded intracellular amino acid pools in a largely SNAT2-dependent manner. Consistent with the role of intracellular amino acids as osmolytes, SNAT2 deficiency resulted in osmotic imbalance and aberrant activation of NFAT5, a central transcriptional regulator of osmotic stress responses. In turn, NFAT5 promoted nitric oxide- and HIF-1α-dependent metabolic reprogramming and augmented NLRP3 inflammasome activation under hyperosmotic conditions. Supplementation with organic osmolytes mitigated both the excessive metabolic reprogramming and hyperosmotic inflammasome activation in SNAT2-deficient macrophages. Consistent with the heightened inflammatory phenotype in vitro, myeloid-specific deletion of SNAT2 reduced bacterial burden in mice infected with Listeria monocytogenes. Together, these findings identify SNAT2 as a negative feedback regulator that restrains macrophage metabolic reprogramming and inflammatory activation by maintaining amino acid availability that supports osmotic homeostasis.

records.title: Microbial hydrocarbonoclastic responses to extreme marine environments: adaptive strategies of psychrophilic and halophilic microorganisms.
records.abstract: The biological remediation of complex petroleum waste streams suffers from severe performance bottlenecks in industrial and marine settings due to the simultaneous thermal, osmotic and mechanical stress. In these hypersaline and multi-extreme matrices, such as produced water, coastal oil spills, and refinery lagoons, conventional mesophiles succumb to rapid plasmolysis, catalytic deceleration, and metabolic uncoupling. Halophilic microorganisms offer indispensable advantages for remediating these hostile environments; their specialized adaptations including acidic proteomes that resist salting-out, compatible solute accumulation that maintains cellular turgor, and cell-bound biosurfactant secretion preserve biocatalytic integrity where conventional degraders fail. This review provides a detailed overview of recent advances in the structural biology of extremophilic enzymes, biosurfactant-mediated interfacial bioavailability changes and genome-scale regulatory networks regulating hydrocarbonoclastic psychrophiles and halophiles. This article integrates structural insights, e.g. localized molecular flexibility of cold-active oxygenases and surface acidity stabilizing salt-tolerant biocatalysts, with functional multi-omics workflows that trace carbon flux from dynamic stress-sensing mechanisms to complete hydrocarbon mineralization. In addition, this paper discusses particular eco-physiological challenges of oil spills in the open ocean, such as the spatial compartmentalization of deep-water plumes, the dynamics of marine oil snow formation, and the metabolic trade-offs imposed by synthetic chemical dispersants. Also, this review discusses how the integration of high-throughput multi-omics data with artificial intelligence pipelines and predictive machine learning algorithms can accelerate strain engineering and bioprocess optimization. Finally, it offers a strong data-driven systems biology approach to move next-generation extremophilic bioprocesses from exploratory laboratory concepts to scalable, field-reproducible industrial realities.

records.title: Satellite DNA landscape in the alpaca genome and comparison with other camelids.
records.abstract: Satellite DNAs (satDNAs) are among the least resolved components of telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome assemblies despite recent advances in long-read sequencing. Among mammals, camelids provide an excellent system to study satDNA evolution because of their exceptional karyotypic conservation despite more than 11 million years of independent evolution. Here, we systematically characterize the satDNA landscape of the chromosome-level alpaca reference genome VicPac4 by combining bioinformatic reference-guided repeat identification, PCR validation, and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). Cross-species PCR analysis of 13 candidate satDNAs revealed two major conservation patterns: six families amplified across all camelids, whereas seven were restricted to South American camelids (SACs). FISH further demonstrated distinct chromosomal organization of nine satDNA families: four showed widespread chromosomal distribution; three localized near centromeres of a subset of chromosomes; one was primarily associated with chromosome 26 but had lower copy number on additional chromosomes, and one exclusively mapped to chromosomes 27 and 36 in all SACs. The latter displayed consistent and prominent copy number differences between species, individuals and homologous chromosomes, suggesting naturally occurring variation in satellite array expansion. This satellite amplified by PCR across Camelidae, whereas FISH detected expanded arrays only in SACs, suggesting differences in satellite organization between SAC and Camels. Beyond satDNA identification, the proposed workflow facilitated the discovery and comparative analysis of pseudogene-rich repetitive blocks in the alpaca genome and their absence in Camels' genome assemblies. These findings substantially expand the alpaca satDNAs catalogue and provide a cytogenetic framework for future T2T genome refinement and comparative studies across Camelidae.

records.title: CRISPR interference-based gene silencing in insects: from functional genomics to prospective insect-pest management applications.
records.abstract: Insect-pests remain a major constraint to global agriculture, causing yield losses through direct feeding and transmission of phytopathogens. Chemical pesticides and transgenic crops expressing Bacillus thuringiensis toxins have shown initial success; however, their use is increasingly constrained by resistance, non-target effects, environmental contamination and regulatory restrictions. Although RNA interference (RNAi) presents a targeted and eco-friendly alternative, it is limited by species variability, rapid double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) degradation, inconsistent silencing and off-target effects. Nuclease-active Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9) enables genetic editing, but its irreversible genome modifications raise ethical, ecological and regulatory concerns. CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) offers a programmable approach for sequence-specific, reversible transcriptional suppression without inducing double-strand DNA breaks. Using catalytically inactive Cas9 (dead Cas9 or dCas9) -guided by single-guide RNA (sgRNA), CRISPRi inhibits transcription initiation or elongation while maintaining genomic integrity. Experimental studies in insect models, including disease-vector mosquitoes, have demonstrated effective suppression of coding and non-coding genes, supporting CRISPRi as a functional genomics tool. This review discusses CRISPRi mechanisms, applications, advantages and limitations in insects, comparing it with RNAi and CRISPR/Cas9. Overall, current evidences indicate that CRISPRi is a precise and non-mutagenic platform for insect-pest management, particularly where controlled, reversible and species-specific gene regulation is desirable. However, its application in agricultural pest management remains an extrapolation from functional-genomics studies and requires validation in pest species under whole-organism and field-relevant conditions.
records.authors: Saini A, Sharma N, Sharma N, Kumari N, Singh B, Thakur AK.

records.title: Catabolite activator protein and quorum sensing cross-control group behaviors in Vibrio campbellii.
records.abstract: Vibrio species adapt to different niches by sensing and responding to environmental signals such as nutrients, host cues, and quorum sensing autoinducers. Vibrio campbellii uses the master quorum sensing transcription factor LuxR to control the expression of hundreds of genes at high cell density. Furthermore, many gamma-proteobacteria use the global transcription factor catabolite activator protein (CAP) to control numerous physiologically relevant pathways, many of which are also modulated by quorum sensing, such as competence, biofilm formation, and carbon metabolism. However, the extent to which these two global transcription factors overlap to co-regulate gene expression and bacterial behaviors is understudied. In this work, we used chromatin immunoprecipitation coupled with high-throughput Illumina sequencing (ChIP-seq) and RNA-seq to determine the individual and combined regulons of CAP and LuxR in V. campbellii. We found that CAP and LuxR co-occupied 11 promoters to synergistically or antagonistically co-regulate genes involved with metabolism, respiration, and virulence. It was previously proposed that CAP and LuxR both bound the bioluminescence (luxCDABE) promoter to co-regulate these genes, and our RNA-seq data showed that these were indeed the most strongly co-regulated genes. However, our ChIP-seq data revealed that only LuxR bound the luxCDABE promoter in vivo. This pattern of co-regulation-where both CAP and LuxR strongly impact transcription, but only LuxR binds the promoter-was the most common mechanism observed. Our model for bioluminescence regulation is that CAP indirectly activates luxCDABE expression through the regulation of an intermediate factor. This study established new connections between the global gene regulatory networks underpinning nutrient sensing and population sensing.ImportanceVibrio bacteria (vibrios) colonize and infect diverse marine hosts, including corals, fish, oysters, and shrimp, and can also cause life-threatening human infections, all of which are rising annually due to increasing ocean temperatures. To develop effective treatments against Vibrio infections, it is critical to understand the global gene regulation mechanisms vibrios use that enable pathogenic lifestyles. Signal transduction systems in bacteria are well-characterized; however, how vibrios coordinate global gene expression changes in response to multiple environmental inputs is understudied. Here, we determined how the aquaculture pathogen Vibrio campbellii regulates global gene expression in response to bacterial population signals and nutrient availability signals. Our findings help contextualize how vibrios respond to their fluctuating environments in nature.
records.authors: Mullins CM, Ball AS, Geyman LJ, Lukich LK, Hermann LK, Podicheti R, Ren Z, Wang X, Rusch DB, van Kessel JC.

records.title: PlantPAN 5.0: updated database for integrating multiomics evidence and exploring multilayered transcriptional regulatory networks in plants.
records.abstract: Plant Promoter Analysis Navigator (PlantPAN) 5.0 (https://plantpan.itps.ncku.edu.tw/) is an integrated multiomics resource for investigating plant cis-regulatory elements and transcriptional regulatory networks. This release expands genome annotations and promoter sequences to 240 species and provides 71 040 transcription factor (TF) annotations and 7762 nonredundant binding matrices. Its companion database, PCBase 3.0, substantially expands ChIP-seq data and newly incorporates ATAC-seq, bisulfite-sequencing, and four Hi-C-based chromatin interaction datasets for Arabidopsis thaliana. The new Differential Analysis function enables comparison of TF binding, chromatin accessibility, and DNA methylation across conditions. The redesigned Promoter Analysis interface provides TF family-level statistics, with a Pattern Overview panel integrating TF-binding site (TFBS) densities, plant DNA large language model-predicted open-chromatin regions, CpG-rich regions, and tandem repeats. Two new modules are introduced: (i) Transcriptome Regulatory Analysis and Coexpression, where candidate regulatory TFs and shared cis-elements in gene sets are prioritized through differential expression and coexpression analysis, and (ii) Interaction Topology Analysis for Chromatin and TFs, where chromatin interaction regions are integrated to reveal potentially coregulated genes and their shared TFs and predicted TFBSs. A Dockerized package enables large-scale local promoter analyses, with data privacy. Therefore, PlantPAN 5.0 is a comprehensive framework for discovering plant transcriptional regulatory mechanisms.
records.authors: Yang CW, Wang WL, Chow CN, Tseng KC, Shen YL, Tsao TW, Chien YH, Lee TY, Chang WC.

records.title: Melanoidins Suppress Cucumber and Tomato Diseases Incited by Pathogens that are Oomycetes, Bacteria and a Virus
records.abstract: We recently reported that solutions of the nitrogenous compounds melanoidins (M), that are formed during the final stages of the Maillard Reaction, are inducers of plant resistance (Elad et al. 2026). M promoted immunity and induced disease resistance through an effect on the transcriptome, primarily through the salicylic acid pathway. Here we tested the effect of M on plant diseases that are caused by Oomycetes, bacteria and a tobamovirus. Drench and spray of M suppressed Pythium aphanidermatum damping off in cucumber, cucumber downy mildew (Pseudoperonospera cubensis), tomato late blight (Phytophthora infestans), bacterial speck (Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato), bacterial canker (Clavibacter michiganensis subsp. michiganensis) and the Tobamovirus Tomato brown rugose fruit virus (ToBRFV) in tomato. In various experiments control was achieved by concentrations of 0.03 and 0.1% and on older and younger leaves and even in long term experiments where the M was applied for ca 11 weeks. It can be concluded that the disease resistance inducer M can suppress soilborne and foliar diseases that are caused by Oomycetes, bacteria and a virus of the genus Tobamovirus, in addition to the fungal pathogen Botrytis cinerea reported earlier.
records.authors: Elad Y, Rav-David D, Tsechansky L, Graber ER.

records.title: Epidemiological Investigation and Genetic Evolution Analysis of Feline Calicivirus during 2025–2026 in Shandong Province
records.abstract: Abstract  Feline calicivirus (FCV) is a major viral pathogen associated with feline respiratory diseases. To characterize the epidemiological and evolutionary features of FCV in Shandong Province, China, 656 clinical feline specimens were collected during 2025–2026. RT-PCR was used to screen for common feline viral pathogens, and FCV-positive samples were subjected to virus isolation, purification and whole-genome sequencing. The overall FCV-positive rate was 1.67% (11/656). Co-infections predominated among FCV-positive specimens, with feline parvovirus (FPV) as the most frequent co-infecting agent. Eleven local FCV strains were isolated; genogroup analysis showed that both GI (six strains) and GII (five strains) were circulating. Four high-confidence recombination events were identified. Notably, strain F1481 (genogroup GI) originated from inter-genogroup recombination between a GII-type isolate (F1506) and a GI-type isolate (F1498), providing bioinformatic evidence for natural inter-genogroup recombination between GI and GII FCV strains. These findings indicate that recombination and antigenic drift are important evolutionary forces shaping local FCV populations and provide empirical evidence for regional disease control and the development of geographically matched vaccine candidates.
records.authors: Wang Y, Tian A, Wei K, Yang S, Zhao L, Qi L, Lin X, Sun W, Ma F, Fang L, Zhang L, Wu J.

records.title: PlasmidCall: predicting whether resistance genes in short-read assemblies lie on plasmids or chromosomes, tested in 432 carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales
records.abstract: Abstract  Antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) can lie on the bacterial chromosome, where they are passed on mainly with the host strain, or on plasmids, which can move them between bacteria. Most bacterial genomes are sequenced with short reads, which assemble into many fragments (contigs), so whether a contig, and any ARG on it, comes from a plasmid or from the chromosome usually has to be predicted. Plasmid classifiers are software tools that make this prediction for each contig from different kinds of evidence, and each tends to fail on different contigs. PlasmidCall v1.2-General is a logistic-regression model that combines the plasmid or chromosome calls of twelve such classifiers into one decision. Four gradient-boosting models, fitted on a larger training set, combine some or all of these calls with features of the contig, its neighbours in the assembly graph and its isolate. The five models were tested without refitting on 432 carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales isolates from one hospital, none used in model development. For each isolate, a hybrid assembly built from long and short reads provided reference labels (plasmid or chromosome) for 30,986 of its 35,805 short-read contigs of at least 1 kb, whether or not they carried an ARG. PlasmidCall v1.2-General gave a decision on every contig: 94.9% of its plasmid calls were correct (precision 0.9491; 95% CI 0.8915-0.9642, resampling clusters of closely related isolates), and it found 91.8% of plasmid contigs (recall 0.9184). Its precision was 0.028 lower than a previously reported estimate; the two 95% intervals overlapped when clusters of related isolates were resampled, but not when single isolates were. The gradient-boosting models found 98.9-99.2% of plasmid contigs at precision 0.887-0.922. On contigs carrying ARGs, v1.2-General had precision 0.935 and recall 0.969, and on the 383 contigs carrying the carbapenemase gene blaKPC (post hoc), 0.994 and 0.970. PlasmidCall can therefore place resistance genes, including blaKPC, on a plasmid or the chromosome from short-read data alone, with a choice between higher precision and higher recall.

records.title: Soil nitrogen availability reveals contrasting and genotype-dependent microbiome assembly strategies in eggplant ​
records.abstract: Abstract    Aims  Plant genotype and nutrient availability are key drivers of root microbiome assembly, yet their relative contribution remains poorly understood in eggplant (  Solanum melongena  L.). Methods  In this study, root-associated bacterial communities from four eggplant genotypes, grown under contrasting nitrogen regimes, were characterized using a combined culture-dependent and 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing approach. Results  Across all genotypes, Proteobacteria dominated the root microbiome, while host genotype emerged as the primary determinant of bacterial diversity and community structure. Nitrogen availability acted as a secondary but consistent environmental driver, reshaping community composition and promoting the enrichment of Actinobacteriota under fertilized conditions. Genotypes did not differ in whether their microbiomes responded to nitrogen, but rather in the magnitude of community restructuring, revealing a continuum from highly constrained to more plastic microbial assemblages. Notably, one genotype maintained a stable Bacillus-dominated microbiome regardless of nitrogen availability, suggesting strong host-mediated filtering. Predicted functional profiles mirrored taxonomic differences, particularly for nitrogen-cycling and organic matter degradation functions. The integration of culture-dependent isolation generated a representative collection of dominant bacterial taxa, providing a valuable resource for future functional studies. Conclusions  Overall, these findings demonstrate that eggplant genotype plays a central role in shaping root microbiome assembly and its responsiveness to nutrient availability, highlighting the potential of microbiome-informed approaches for improving nutrient-use efficiency and crop performance.
records.authors: Guaschino M, Toppino L, Tassone MR, Rotino GL, Salamone F, Narduzzo A, Cacco G, Chitarra W, Nerva L.

records.title: Cell-Level Auditing of an Orthology-Database-Derived Gene Presence/Absence Matrix Reveals Lineage-Specific Gene Gain, Duplication, and Pseudogenization
records.abstract: Abstract  Cross-species gene presence/absence (PA) matrices are widely used to infer metabolic-pathway evolution, but orthology database clusters may contain deeply diverged homologs, lineage-specific duplicates, or pseudogenes, leading to erroneous assignments. Using OrthoDB v12 as the initial data source, we constructed a PA matrix comprising 34 human genes involved in nitrogen waste excretion and ammonia metabolism across 60 species, totaling 2,040 gene-by-species cells. Cells with uncertain assignments or distributions inconsistent with biological expectations were iteratively audited using NCBI/RefSeq searches, whole-genome tblastn, competitive paralog discrimination, locus-level clustering, phylogenetic priors, and published evidence. The final matrix contained 412 cells without support for the focal ortholog, 1,578 OrthoDB-only presence calls, 38 presence calls additionally supported by RefSeq or tblastn, 6 ancestral or unresolved homolog calls, 5 known pseudogenes, and 1 cluster bleed-through call. Sequence-level assessment of 20 randomly sampled OrthoDB-only presence cells yielded confirmation rates of 75% under a strict single-HSP criterion and 85% under a locus-aggregate criterion. Direct sequence evidence supported all four highest-risk absence assignments. All six candidate GLUD loci examined in non-ape vertebrates favored GLUD1 over GLUD2, with five exceeding the 2σ discrimination threshold, supporting the ape-specific retrocopy origin of GLUD2. Two loci on different chromosomes in Anolis carolinensis showed GLUD1-favored signals, suggesting a candidate GLUD1 duplication in this lineage. UOX sequences from four great apes shared a codon 33 stop mutation, supporting UOX pseudogenization in the Hominidae ancestor. These findings demonstrate that database cluster membership cannot be equated directly with focal-ortholog or functional-gene presence. Cell-level auditing provides a transparent and traceable framework for interpreting orthology-database-derived PA matrices and lineage-specific gene gain, duplication, and pseudogenization.
records.authors: Ling Y, Fu H.

records.title: High-Throughput Sequencing-Assisted Microbial Profiling and Koch's Postulates Validation Identify Fusarium pernambucanum as the Causal Agent of Fruit Rot in Idesia polycarpa.
records.abstract: Idesia polycarpa is an economically important tree species valued for urban greening and oil production owing to its oil-rich fruits and high levels of unsaturated fatty acids. The increasing incidence of fruit diseases has become a major constraint on its cultivation; however, the microbial dynamics during disease progression and the primary causal agent remain unclear. In this study, diseased fruits were collected from Sichuan Province, China, a region with frequent disease outbreaks, and categorized into five disease stages based on symptom severity, including initial infection (S1), advancing infection (S2), severe infection (S3), blackening (S4), and necrosis (S5). High-throughput sequencing (HTS) of bacterial 16S rRNA gene and fungal internal transcribed spacer regions from S1, S3, and S5 samples revealed limited variation in bacterial communities across disease stages, whereas fungal communities exhibited pronounced compositional shifts, including a progressive enrichment of Fusarium spp., a well-known group of plant pathogens. Subsequent fungal isolation, morphological characterization, molecular phylogenetics analyses, and pathogenicity assays identified F. pernambucanum as the causal agent of fruit rot. This study elucidates HTS-based microbial profiling during fruit rot, and the results guided pathogen identification based on Koch's postulates, providing insights into disease diagnosis and management in I. polycarpa.
records.authors: Luo Y, Feng A, Li Y, Ren Y, Ma T, Jiang Y.

records.title: Salicornia: a halophyte with unique salt-tolerant genes for developing future climate-resilient crops, high-value bioproducts and saline land utilization.
records.abstract: Salicornia, a stem-succulent halophyte, grows naturally in coastal areas with high salinity and can complete its life cycle in extreme environmental conditions due to its high adaptability to salt, drought, and temperature stress. It survives in saline environments through morpho-anatomical modifications, ion homeostasis, biochemical changes, osmolyte accumulation, and antioxidant defense mechanisms. Its growth and adaptation to salinity are further supported by a variety of rhizospheric and endophytic microbes. Salicornia is a valuable source of herbal salt, food, feed, medicines, and biofuel due to its high content of essential fatty acids, minerals, and bioactive compounds. Its large-scale cultivation on coastal and saline wastelands contributes to sustainable blue and green economies by aiding in soil reclamation and carbon sequestration. The Salicornia derived genes and biomass offer significant potential for developing climate-resilient crops and value-added bioproducts. Recent genomic and transcriptomic advances, including chromosome-scale and telomere-to-telomere genome assemblies, have provided valuable resources for understanding molecular adaptation to salinity. Several transcription factors (TFs), transporters, and stress-responsive genes have been identified and studied to understand the molecular mechanisms underlying salinity tolerance across different Salicornia species, and few of these genes have been functionally validated using transgenic techniques demonstrating enhanced salinity, drought, or osmotic stress tolerance. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of current knowledge on the distribution, genetic diversity, cultivation, economic importance, and multi-level mechanisms underlying salinity tolerance in Salicornia, while highlighting recent genomic resources, functional validation studies, plant-microbe interactions, and their potential application in developing salinity-resilient crops.

records.title: Butyrate Deficiency due to Microbial Dysbiosis Promotes Anxiety.
records.abstract: Individuals with diabetes frequently suffer from anxiety; however, the mechanism for this association remains incompletely understood. Diabetes-associated genes have been implicated in the control of central nervous system (CNS) disorders. In the current study, we observed a marked down-regulation of secretagogin (SCGN) across multiple organs in diabetic mouse models, and Scgn knockout (Scgn -/-) mice developed diabetes, confirming SCGN as a diabetes-associated gene. Behavioral analyses revealed that Scgn -/- mice exhibited anxiety-like phenotypes compared to wild-type (WT) mice. Notably, germ-free (GF) Scgn -/- mice did not manifest these behavioral abnormalities, suggesting that SCGN influences anxiety through gut microbiota-dependent mechanisms. Subsequent shotgun metagenomic sequencing confirmed gut microbiota dysbiosis in Scgn -/- mice. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from Scgn -/- donors into GF mice recapitulated the anxiety-like phenotypes. Given the established roles of microbial metabolites in gut-brain axis signaling, we identified a substantial depletion of butyrate, a key neuroactive metabolite, in fecal and plasma samples from Scgn -/- mice. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed neural overactivation, as reflected by c-Fos expression in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of Scgn -/- mice, which was corroborated by metabolomic profiling indicating dysregulated tryptophan metabolism in this region. Mechanistically, up-regulation of indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1) and kynureninase (KYNU) led to excessive production of quinolinic acid, an NMDA receptor agonist that increased pyramidal neuron excitability in the mPFC, thereby promoting anxiety-like behaviors in Scgn -/- mice. Supplementation with Odoribacter splanchnicus, a butyrate-producing bacterium, could reverse this abnormal signaling pathway and alleviate anxiety-like behaviors. Critically, butyrate administration mitigated this anxiogenic cascade in vivo and in vitro, as validated by electrophysiological recordings. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that SCGN deficiency induces gut dysbiosis, reduces butyrate availability, and promotes excitotoxicity in the mPFC, at least in part, through disrupted tryptophan metabolism, ultimately leading to anxiety. This SCGN-modulated gut-brain axis highlights potential new therapeutic targets for the treatment of diabetes-associated anxiety.

records.title: Advances in the microbiological characteristics of peri-implant health and peri-implant diseases. A systematic review.
records.abstract: BackgroundPeri-implant diseases represent a major and increasingly prevalent clinical challenge. Peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis are inflammatory conditions associated with dysbiotic biofilms, yet the specific microbial features that distinguish peri-implant health from disease have still to be conclusively demonstrated. The present systematic review compared microbiological profiles across peri-implant health, peri-implant mucositis, and peri-implantitis, with particular emphasis on how conventional and next-generation sequencing (NGS)-based detection methods influence reported microbial findings.Materials and methodsThis review was registered in the PROSPERO registry (CRD42020182626) and conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. Electronic searches of MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were conducted up to December 31st 2025. Comparative experimental or observational studies reporting microbiological outcomes for at least two peri-implant conditions (health, mucositis, peri-implantitis) were eligible. Study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment (adapted Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, evaluated across four domains: selection, comparability, outcome assessment, and statistical analysis) were performed independently by three reviewers. Twenty-eight studies were included, using either conventional methods (culture, checkerboard DNA-DNA hybridization, and PCR-based techniques) or next-generation sequencing (16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics).ResultsAcross studies using conventional detection methods, classical periodontal pathobionts-including Porphyromonas gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, Treponema denticola, Prevotella intermedia, and Fusobacterium nucleatum-were detected more frequently at diseased than at healthy implant sites, while healthy sites were characterized by higher proportions of commensal taxa such as Streptococcus sp. NGS-based studies similarly reported a higher relative abundance of periodontal pathobionts at diseased sites, but findings on microbial diversity were inconsistent: some studies reported higher alpha diversity at healthy implant sites, whereas others reported the opposite, suggesting that abundance and diversity shifts do not necessarily follow the same pattern across studies. The risk of bias assessment identified comparability and confounder control as the most frequent methodological limitations. Substantial heterogeneity in disease definitions, patient characteristics, sampling strategies, and microbiological methodologies limited direct comparisons across studies and detection methods.ConclusionAcross both conventional and NGS-based detection methods, mucositis and peri-implantitis are consistently associated with enrichment of periodontal pathobionts and depletion of health-associated commensals, supporting a dysbiotic shift in peri-implant diseases. However, findings on microbial diversity are inconsistent, and methodological heterogeneity, including variable risk of bias across studies, limits the strength of cross-study conclusions. Standardization of disease definitions and sampling protocols, along with comparison of methodological approaches (including sequencing targets, platforms, and reference databases), is needed before microbiological profiles can inform clinical predictions or treatment implications.

records.title: Integrating PCR and sequencing for the identification of pathogenic fungi on formalin-fixed tissues: a systematic review toward a pragmatic histomolecular solution.
records.abstract: Although histopathology is a gold standard for the diagnosis of invasive fungal infections, the morphological analysis does not provide an accurate genus and/or species identification. Because this specific identification is required for antifungal therapy prescription, the implementation of molecular techniques to identify fungi on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue in practice is crucial, especially when specimen has not been simultaneously sent to the mycology laboratory. However, such approaches/procedures remain heterogenous. The objective of this systematic review (PROSPERO: CRD420261420594) was to gather data from the literature to support future efforts toward the standardisation of diagnostic practices for fungal identification on FFPE tissue. Among the 1,550 records found on MEDLINE-PubMed and Google Scholar, 57 studies were included. Thirty-two, 27, and 10 studies investigated the use on FFPE tissue of taxon-specific fungal PCR (n = 1421 FFPE samples tested), panfungal PCR followed by Sanger sequencing (n = 1647 FFPE samples tested), and targeted next-generation sequencing/massive parallel sequencing (NGS/MPS) or untargeted metagenomics (n = 408 FFPE samples tested; some studies reported several techniques), respectively. The sensitivity and specificity of the techniques, according to pre-analytical, histopathological, and molecular criteria were reported and discussed. Advantages and limitations of each technique are presented. While taxon-specific fungal PCR are widely available and highly sensitive, sequencing-based techniques have a broader spectrum for identification purpose. Finally, because of the contamination of tissue sections and the presence of fungi belonging to microbiota on samples, the molecular identification should always be correlated to the pathogenic fungi's morphology, to ensure an accurate and reliable integrated histomolecular diagnosis.

records.title: Mining and engineering novel staphylococcal lysostaphins as species-specific antibacterial agents.
records.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) presents a serious global healthcare challenge, with staphylococci, especially Staphylococcus aureus, being the main cause of deadly infections. Peptidoglycan hydrolases, particularly lysostaphins, are highly promising alternatives to traditional antibiotics, collectively termed enzybiotics, due to their specific lytic action against the bacterial cell wall. To thoroughly explore their therapeutic potential, we performed comprehensive genome mining of 118,127 staphylococcal and 500 closely related mammaliicoccal genomes. Ultimately, we discovered 19 unique lysostaphin sequences, divided into four distinct evolutionary clusters. By characterizing five novel lysostaphins alongside known references, we observed diverse lytic activities and species-specificities. Notably, we identified a novel lysostaphin variant from Staphylococcus simulans, Lys-Ssim, representing a previously unknown evolutionary cluster, which exhibits unmatched substrate promiscuity and an unprecedented lytic activity that extends beyond staphylococci. Additionally, structural modeling and site-directed mutagenesis revealed that peptidoglycan hydrolysis by these M23 metalloproteases depends on highly flexible conformations of the binding cleft. Using these structural insights, we successfully engineered lysostaphins with significantly improved enzyme selectivity for S. aureus while nearly eliminating activity against the skin commensal S. epidermidis. We also demonstrated the potential to engineer lysostaphins active against species other than staphylococci. Our findings show that natural staphylococcal lysostaphins are a rich, highly specialized resource for developing rationally engineered, microbiota-friendly antibacterial agents.

records.title: Free-living autotrophs drive a carbon fixation peak within the Orca Basin chemocline while heterotrophs dominate total activity from seawater to brine.
records.abstract: Deep hypersaline anoxic basins (DHABs) are stratified, polyextreme environments found within enclosed and semi-enclosed seas worldwide. Here, we quantified microbial activity in Orca Basin, the largest known DHAB, to investigate carbon cycling across its steep chemical and salinity gradients. We measured total anabolic activity and dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) fixation as a function of metabolic lifestyle (autotroph or heterotroph) and spatial niche (free-living or particle-associated) using dual-isotope labeling experiments and single-cell analysis by nanoscale secondary ion mass spectrometry (nanoSIMS). Activity was detected within all ten depths investigated from seawater to hypersaline brine, including by most cells within the brine. DIC fixation and total anabolic activity peaked within the oxic-anoxic interface, notably separate from the peak in cell and particle density deeper in the halocline. Autotrophs drove the peak in DIC fixation, but heterotrophs drove that of total activity; autotrophs were more abundant than heterotrophs at this depth but on average smaller and slower growing. Particle-associated heterotrophs, but not autotrophs, were significantly more active than their free-living counterparts within the interface. Heterotrophic communities derived an average of 4% to 10% of their biomass from DIC across the vertical transect, contributing just 2% of total DIC fixation within the peak but the majority within overlying seawater. Metagenomic analysis of catabolically active, sorted cells indicated members of at least five phyla were active within the oxic-anoxic interface, including putatively autotrophic Thermoproteota. These data provide high-sensitivity microbial activity measurements in Orca Basin and highlight the widespread viability of the resident microbiome.

records.title: Alternative sigma factor σ54 (RpoN) of Vibrio fischeri is required during initial squid light organ colonization but its continued induction is not required for maintenance.
records.abstract: Animals depend on bacterial symbionts that provide functions essential for host physiology and fitness. The marine bacterium Vibrio fischeri establishes a mutualistic association within the light organ of the Hawaiian bobtail squid Euprymna scolopes, where bacterial bioluminescence enables a host camouflage behavior. Successful colonization of the light organ requires the alternative sigma factor σ54 (RpoN), which activates genes involved in biofilm formation and motility that are essential for bacterial entry into the host. However, whether σ54 remains important after the initial stages of colonization has been unclear. Here, using an IPTG-inducible rpoN expression system, we demonstrate that induction of rpoN is required for initial entry into the light organ, but continued inducer exposure is not required for subsequent maintenance of colonization and bioluminescence production. Transcriptomic analysis of RNA-sequencing of low-cell-density cultures identified σ54-dependent expression of genes involved in flagellar motility, chemotaxis, nitrogen assimilation, molybdenum cofactor (Moco) biosynthesis, and formate metabolism. We further show that the bacterial enhancer-binding protein VF_1401 activates genes required for Moco biosynthesis and formate metabolism but is not required for light organ colonization. Together, these findings define the temporal requirement for σ54 during symbiosis establishment and reveal a previously unrecognized role for σ54 in regulating molybdenum-dependent metabolism in V. fischeri.IMPORTANCEMany bacteria encode the alternative sigma factor σ54 (RpoN), which enables selective activation of specific cellular processes in response to environmental signals. Our findings refine the conditions under which σ54 contributes to host colonization by a bacterial symbiont, providing new insight into the context-dependent roles of this conserved regulator. In addition, our transcriptomic analysis identifies a previously unrecognized link between σ54 and molybdenum assimilation, revealing a potential mechanism by which σ54 coordinates trace element homeostasis with bacterial physiology. These findings broaden our understanding of σ54 regulatory networks and may inform future strategies to manipulate the physiology of beneficial bacterial symbionts.
records.authors: Muriel-Mundo CA, Miyashiro TI.

records.title: PCB-Exposed Gut Microbiota Recapitulate Neurobehavioral Deficits and Reprogram Hippocampal Transcriptomic Signatures
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) are persistent environmental pollutants associated with developmental neurotoxicity and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, whether PCB-induced alterations in gut microbiota contribute to neurodevelopmental toxicity independently of direct chemical exposure remains unclear. Here, we investigated whether transplantation of PCB-associated gut microbiota produces early neurobehavioral alterations and disrupts brain molecular pathways in offspring. Gut microbiota from conventional dams exposed to the Fox River PCB mixture (FRM; 6.0 mg/kg/day) or vehicle were transplanted into germ-free recipient females without direct PCB administration. At postnatal day 7 (P7), offspring underwent ultrasonic vocalization (USV) testing, whole-brain RNA sequencing (n = 4/sex/group), and untargeted serum metabolomics. Untargeted serum metabolomics were also performed in donor dams. PCB-associated fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) significantly reduced offspring USVs, reproducing effects observed following direct maternal PCB exposure. Brain transcriptomics in offspring identified substantially more differentially expressed genes in males (9,339) than females (1,082), including 512 shared genes. Concordantly regulated genes revealed downregulation of neurotransmitter signaling and ion channel pathways alongside upregulation of RNA processing pathways. Male-associated responses involved altered protein synthesis and neuronal signaling, whereas female-associated responses involved DNA repair and extracellular matrix remodeling. Despite these molecular differences, behavioral responses showed no significant sex-dependent effect. Maternal metabolomics revealed increased bile acids and decreased indole-3-propionic acid, highlighting potential AhR-NFκB and bile acid-associated signaling mechanisms. Offspring metabolomics further identified alterations in lipid-associated metabolites and metabolic profiles. Collectively, these findings show that transferring PCB-exposed microbiota reproduces early neurobehavioral alterations and induces shared and sex-biased molecular responses, identifying the maternal gut microbiome as a candidate mediator linking PCB exposure to developmental neurotoxicity.
records.authors: Suh YP, Wilson RJ, Breese NM, Lein PJ, Lehmler H, Cui JY.

records.title: PP271, a novel bacteriophage primase-polymerase, enables Primer-Free DNA Amplification
records.abstract: Primases are essential enzymes that initiate DNA replication by synthesizing  de novo primers for replicative DNA polymerases, which ensure accurate genome duplication owing to their high specificity, fidelity, and processivity. PrimPols have emerged as versatile DNA-initiating enzymes that are widely distributed across diverse replication systems, from bacteriophages to humans.  In this work, a novel PrimPol enzyme, PP271, encoded by bacteriophage vB_EfaS-271, was characterized. PP271 belongs to the archaeal–eukaryotic primase (AEP) superfamily and contains the conserved catalytic core, together with a C-terminal PriCT domain. Enzymatic analysis demonstrated that PP271 functions as a  bona fide PrimPol, i.e. a DNA primase capable of synthetizing short DNA primers. PP271 priming activity is strongly stimulated by  ADP , which serves as the preferred initiating nucleotide. Additionally, PP271 exhibits relaxed specificity for selecting the priming site, compared to other PrimPols with more restricted template preferences.  TruePrime™ amplification technology combines the  Thermus thermophilus PrimPol and the highly processive Phi29 DNA polymerase to achieve primer-free DNA amplification. While highly efficient, further improvements in amplification yield, fidelity and product complexity remain possible. Here, we show that DNA primers synthesized by PP271 are efficiently extended by Phi29 DNA polymerase, enabling their coordinated action. Moreover, the short primers generated by PP271 are expected to minimize the contribution of primase-derived errors to the final amplification product while allowing efficient DNA synthesis across a broader range of sequence contexts. Altogether, these findings identify PP271 as a promising alternative for improving primase-dependent DNA amplification.  Key points  Bacteriophage EFAS271 encodes PP271, a DNA-dependent DNA primase-polymerase PP271 preferentially uses  ADP as the initiating nucleotide during primer synthesis  PP271 enables primer-free isothermal DNA amplification with Phi29 DNApol
records.authors: Jiménez-Mejías A, Guerra-González S, Olmos R, Lázaro I, Blanco L, Martínez-Jiménez MI.

records.title: Integrating bacterial genomics and host transcriptomics links  Burkholderia pseudomallei  variation to melioidosis mortality and neutrophil responses
records.abstract: Bacterial genetic variation contributes to the outcome of infection, but its relationship with host immune responses is rarely investigated in the same patients, limiting the biological interpretation of pathogen-associated disease severity. Here, we integrated pathogen genomics, clinical outcomes and host transcriptomics to investigate host-pathogen interactions in melioidosis, a frequently fatal infection caused by  Burkholderia pseudomallei . We analysed prospective clinical data from 2,142 patients, whole-genome sequences from 2,101 infecting isolates and 646 paired host blood transcriptomes across five cohorts collected between 2012 and 2023. Infections were typically dominated by a single strain, with limited within-host diversification, supporting the use of an infecting isolate genome to investigate pathogen- associated clinical outcomes. Bacterial genome-wide association studies identified one locus associated with binary mortality at genome-wide significance. Incorporating patient age, sex, body mass index and Charlson Comorbidity Index increased this to four, while modelling time to death as a continuous phenotype identified seven loci. Integration with paired host transcriptomes linked mortality-associated bacterial genetic variation to imputed signatures of increased immature neutrophils and reduced neutrophil degranulation. An intergenic region upstream of the polyketide synthesis locus  BPSS1006 -  BPSS1011 was additionally associated with downregulation of host genes involved in myeloid-cell signalling and cell proliferation pathways. These findings connect naturally occurring  B. pseudomallei genomic variation associated with mortality to distinct host immune signatures, providing insight into pathogen- host interactions underlying severe melioidosis and a framework for investigating the contribution of pathogen genetic diversity to clinical outcomes.
records.authors: Wongprommoon A, Boonklang P, Burnham KL, Chomkatekaew C, Angchagun K, Wongsuvan G, Ngernseng T, Limmathurotsakul D, Boonchalermvichien T, Coston TD, Phunpang R, Yimthin T, Rongkard P, Lee W, Kronsteiner B, Knight J, Corander J, Peacock SJ, Parkhill J, Day NPJ, Dunachie SJ, West TE, Chantratita N, Thomson NR, Davenport EE, Chewapreecha C.

records.title: Molecular evolution of Andes virus lineages leading to recent human outbreaks
records.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to-person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.
records.authors: Sharma C, Översti S, Stass R, Lucaci AG, Audet J, Safronetz D, Zhao L, Lythgoe K, Katzourakis A, Bowden TA, Lytras S, Ghafari M.

records.title: Plant Growth–Promoting Potential of Endophytic Bacteria Isolated from Asparagus racemosus Willd and their role in improving Chickpea (Cicer arietinum L.) Germination
records.abstract: Abstract    Endophytic bacteria inhabiting internal plant tissues are increasingly recognized for their role in enhancing plant growth and stress tolerance. The present study investigated the plant growth-promoting potential of root-associated endophytic bacteria isolated from the medicinal plant  Asparagus racemosus  Willd. and evaluated their effect on seed germination of desi chickpea (  Cicer arietinum  L.). Healthy tuberous roots were surface sterilized, and endophytic bacteria were isolated using standard microbiological techniques. Seven morphologically distinct bacterial isolates were obtained and characterized through morphological, biochemical, and molecular approaches. The isolates were screened for important plant growth-promoting traits including indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) production, phosphate solubilization, nitrogen fixation, siderophore production, ammonia production, hydrogen cyanide production, ACC deaminase activity, and extracellular hydrolytic enzymes. Among the isolates, strain AR1 exhibited the most comprehensive PGP profile, showing positive responses for IAA production, phosphate solubilization, nitrogen fixation, siderophore production, ACC deaminase activity, and multiple hydrolytic enzymes. Molecular identification based on 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that AR1 belonged to  Enterobacter wuhouensis  , while amplification of the nifH gene confirmed its nitrogen-fixing potential. Seed inoculation experiments demonstrated a substantial enhancement in chickpea germination, with inoculated seeds achieving 85.19% germination compared to 29.63% in uninoculated controls. Enhanced radicle growth and seedling vigor were also observed. These findings highlight  A. racemosus  as a valuable reservoir of beneficial endophytic bacteria and demonstrate the potential of strain AR1 as a bioinoculant for sustainable crop production. Further investigations involving whole-genome sequencing, transcriptomic analyses, and multilocation field evaluations are warranted to validate its agricultural applicability under diverse environmental conditions.
records.authors: Dhali S, Pradhan M, Swain CK, Das A, Pradhan C.

records.title: CRISPR-Based Metabolic Engineering of Microbial Cell Factories for Sustainable Bio manufacturing: A Systematic analysis of 1,000 Studies (2012–2026)
records.abstract: Abstract  CRISPR genome editing and microbial metabolic engineering now work hand in hand. That pairing has changed sustainable bio manufacturing in real ways. This review pulls together 1,000 peer-reviewed articles from 2012 to 2026. They come from 201 journals. We mapped how the field evolved, how the technology diversified, which host chassis researchers prefer, what product classes they target, and where in the world the work gets done. Our approach mixed bibliometric, feature engineering, and multivariate statistics. That includes principal component analysis, hierarchical clustering, co-occurrence network analysis, and correlation mapping. We tracked the CRISPR variant landscape, host chassis distribution, product class priorities, and geographic concentration of research output. The temporal analysis shows a shift. Early work explored many CRISPR variants. Recent work focuses on applications. Mean CRISPR variants per article dropped from 2.42 in 2018 to 1.40 in 2026. Our findings give a quantitative roadmap of where the field is heading. They also point to emerging opportunities in non-conventional yeast, filamentous fungi, and cyanobacterial chassis for sustainable bio manufacturing.
records.authors: Zeeshan N, Afzal T, Ahmed Z, Abid I.

records.title: Genome-Informed Development of a Highly Specific Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification Assay for Detection of the Laurel Wilt Pathogen in Avocado.
records.abstract: Laurel wilt, caused by the ambrosia fungus Harringtonia lauricola (HL), threatens Lauraceae forests and avocado production. Rapid and accurate diagnosis is critical for disease management, but current methods are often slow or difficult to implement directly from field-collected wood samples. A published loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay targeting the HL β-tubulin (β-tub) gene enables rapid detection but lacks extensive validation for avocado tissues and may produce ambiguous amplification products when applied to non-target fungi and crude plant extracts. This study evaluated the specificity, sensitivity, and inclusivity of the β-tub assay and developed a novel HL-specific LAMP marker (HL_0354) through comparative genomic analyses. Both assays were validated using fungal isolates, diverse HL strains, and naturally and artificially infected avocado wood samples. The β-tub assay produced late nonspecific amplification products with several non-HL species and consistently detected HL at 5 pg DNA. In contrast, HL_0354 showed no reproducible amplification from non-target fungi and reproducibly detected 0.5 pg of HL DNA in crude avocado DNA matrices (0.05 ng/µl), with amplifications typically occurring within 5-12 min. Inclusivity testing confirmed detection of all HL strains evaluated despite minor annealing-temperature variation among Southeast Asian isolates. When applied to field samples, HL_0354 achieved a true-positive rate of 97% and an overall diagnostic accuracy of 98%, outperforming the β-tub assay (90% and 94%, respectively), without false-positive detections. Coupled with a simple Chelex-based extraction protocol, HL_0354 provides a rapid, sensitive, and field-deployable approach for detection of H. lauricola in avocado wood samples, supporting laurel wilt surveillance and management.
records.authors: Díaz-Valderrama JR, Navia-Urrutia M, Weber S, Padmanabhan C, Cano LM, Cárdenas DE, Manosalva P, Gazis R.

records.title: Isolation, identification and whole genome sequence analysis of influenza B virus from Shanghai during 2023-2024.
records.abstract: Influenza B virus, a member of the Orthomyxoviridae family, is a significant contributor to global respiratory infections alongside influenza A virus. This study investigated the prevalence and genomic characteristics of influenza B virus during the 2023-2024 season in Shanghai, China. Among 174 clinical samples collected from the Nanxiang Branch of Ruijin Hospital, the positivity rate for influenza B virus was 62.36%. Genomic analysis revealed that all characterized isolates belonged to the B/Victoria lineage and were classified within subclade C.5.7, corresponding to the legacy designation V1A.3a.2. No B/Yamagata lineage strains were detected. Comparative genomic analysis further revealed close genetic similarity between the Shanghai isolates and strains from Shanxi Province, suggesting a potential geographical or evolutionary relationship. These findings highlight the substantial activity of influenza B virus in Shanghai during the study period and underscore the importance of continued genomic surveillance to monitor viral evolution and inform public health strategies.

records.title: Longitudinal Taxonomic and Predicted Functional Gut Microbiome Responses to Tirzepatide and Semaglutide: An Exploratory Secondary Analysis of the OMDOT-1 Randomized Controlled Trial.
records.abstract: AimsGlucagon-like peptide-1-based therapies improve metabolic outcomes, but longitudinal gut microbiome dynamics remain poorly characterized. We compared taxonomic and predicted functional microbiome responses to tirzepatide and semaglutide in Type 2 diabetes.Materials and methodsThis exploratory secondary analysis included 36 participants from a randomized controlled trial comparing tirzepatide, semaglutide and conventional treatment. Faecal samples were collected at five time points over 16 weeks and analyzed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Genus-level features were screened using MaAsLin2, and candidate genera were further evaluated using longitudinal mixed-effects models. Predicted microbial functions were inferred using PICRUSt2 and analyzed using MaAsLin2. Primary analyses were adjusted for baseline body mass index, with exploratory sensitivity analyses additionally adjusted for changes in body weight and haemoglobin A1c.ResultsNo significant between-group differences in beta diversity were observed. Alpha diversity increased predominantly in the tirzepatide group, with a significant time-by-treatment interaction versus control. Longitudinal trajectories relative to the control group differed for several genera, including Romboutsia_B, Barnesiella and Ruminococcus_E with both treatments and Vescimonas with tirzepatide (q ConclusionsTirzepatide and semaglutide were associated with partially distinct taxonomic changes, accompanied by broadly similar predicted functional patterns. These longitudinal findings complement, while remaining distinct from, Week-16 shotgun metagenomic endpoint analyses.Trial registrationJapan Registry of Clinical Trials (jRCT), jRCT1051240017.

records.title: A multi-scale cell-type resolved map of  trans  -regulatory architecture in the aging human brain
records.abstract: Mapping genetic effects on distal genes and regulatory programs is essential for understanding how genetic variation influences complex diseases; yet  trans -QTL discovery remains limited by weak effect sizes, extensive multiple testing and poor reproducibility. Here, we introduce  TransMap , a generalizable computational framework that combines multi-scale  trans -QTL mapping with multi-phenotype genetic colocalization to improve the discovery and interpretation of distal regulatory variants. Beyond individual  trans -eGenes,  TransMap constructs local co-regulatory program phenotypes that account for background expression variation to improve the detection of weak, coordinated distal genetic effects. Across a broad range of simulation settings,  TransMap achieved 9.2-36.7% higher  trans -QTL discovery power than existing methods while maintaining well-controlled type I error rates. We applied  TransMap to bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomic profiles from the aging human brain in the ADSP Functional Genomics Consortium (FunGen-AD), further integrating proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic biomarker measurements (average  N= 476 donors). Genome-wide fine-mapping of  TransMap single-gene and program-level QTL yielded variant annotations with 2.75-2.88x heritability enrichment across 57 complex diseases and traits (average  N= 307K), with complementary heritability information captured across regulatory scales. Multi-phenotype colocalization identified 49,532  trans -regulatory events supported by shared genetic signals with  cis -eQTL or biomarker-QTL, including 1,825 candidate  cis–trans–biomarker regulatory configurations.  TransMap further revealed an asymmetric cross-cell-type regulatory architecture in which neuronal  cis -regulatory signals preferentially associate with coordinated glial  trans -regulatory responses, supported by co-culture experiments and spatial transcriptomics. Alzheimer’s disease (AD) GWAS-prioritized colocalization identified  trans -regulatory associations in 115 AD-associated loci, including a  KNOP1 cis -eQTL associated in  trans with a microglial regulatory program containing  MS4A4E , with additional support from statistical mediation analysis.  TransMap provides a multi-scale, cell-type-resolved atlas of  trans -regulatory variation and a generalizable framework for elucidating the regulatory architecture of complex diseases.

records.title: Root exudate flux as a quantitative language of phytobiome assembly and stress resilience.
records.abstract: Climate change threatens crop productivity and soil function, increasing reliance on rhizosphere microbiomes that support plant nutrition, stress tolerance and disease suppression. Plants shape these communities through root exudation, which transfers an estimated 13.4 Pg C yr-1, about 9% of global gross primary productivity, belowground. Yet most studies report exudate composition rather than the concentrations and rates microorganisms perceive. This review synthesises the literature, with particular emphasis on studies published between 2015 and 2026, especially those from 2020 onwards, while incorporating foundational earlier studies. It proposes a quantitative signalling framework in which absolute concentration, release flux and spatial gradient influence microbial responses at defined activation thresholds. Exudate chemistry, biosynthesis, transport and uptake are first examined, distinguishing passive diffusion sustained by the microbial sink from transporter-mediated release, root re-uptake and phytosiderophore-mediated iron acquisition. Sampling and analytical approaches, including HRMS-based metabolomics, stable isotope tracing, imaging and kinetic modelling, are then evaluated, separating relative from absolute quantification. Because most high-precision flux data derive from hydroponic or sterile systems, where wheat phytosiderophore release exceeds that in soil by about 50-fold, in situ microdialysis, corrections for sorption and degradation, and minimum reporting standards are proposed. Signal-response modules and allelochemical signalling at the root-microbe-soil interface are discussed, followed by multi-omics integration, where static metabolite pools and transcripts cannot resolve flux unless anchored by pulse labelling with LC-MS, stable isotope probing and NanoSIMS. Stress-induced quantitative reprogramming of exudation is interpreted within this framework. Exudation measured in soil is concluded to be a net flux, and unresolved compound-specific thresholds remain the principal barrier to predictive rhizosphere manipulation.
records.authors: Elias EM, Benny CM, Thomas T.

records.title: Identification and characterization of new  P. aeruginosa  phages using a surface receptor platform
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Bacteriophages are of increasing interest for their potential use as alternatives to antibiotics for treating drug-resistant infections. Phage steering, specifically receptor-based steering, involves use of phages that bias the development of resistance in bacteria towards phenotypes such as reduced fitness. Phage therapy typically involves administering cocktails of phages with different targets to reduce the likelihood of resistance emerging. To ensure effective steering and cocktail design, there is a need to identify the receptors used by phages of interest, and to isolate phages that use diverse receptors. Here we describe a SURFAce Receptor (SURFAR) platform consisting of a set of defined  Pseudomonas aeruginosa strains and mutants for rapid characterization of phage receptors. This platform can also be used to enrich for and isolate diverse phages from environmental samples, yielding novel phage genomes from wastewater. Using the SURFAR platform, two new phages were isolated and characterized: Dalewood, which targets both flagella and the conserved LPS outer core, and Bowman, a biofilm targeting phage capable of supressing growth of a subset of carbapenem-resistant clinical isolates. This tool helps to standardize the laborious but important task of phage receptor characterization, with the goal of expanding the known repertoire of  P. aeruginosa phage receptors and phages.  SIGNFICANCE  Partially guided by increasing interest in phage therapy and technological advances, novel phages are regularly being discovered. Identification of phage receptors is an important aspect of initial characterization, but this step can be difficult due to lack of standardized strains and methodology. Most  P. aeruginosa phages target the type IV pilus, LPS O-antigen, or flagella, thus there is a need to find phages with more diverse receptors. SURFAR was successfully used to identify the host ranges of phages with known receptors, data that can act as a reference during future characterization of new phages. Many SURFAR strains lack those canonical structures to bias for selection of phages that recognize new  P. aeruginosa receptors. We showed that enrichment of wastewater filtrates using SURFAR strains yielded novel phage genomes, including new phages with therapeutic potential. Receptor-led characterization and isolation strategies with the SURFAR platform is a promising approach for finding new phages that can be combined into therapeutic cocktails of phages that target different receptors to mitigate resistance.
records.authors: Tran VN, Lahane TS, Qaderi I, Harvey H, Burrows LL.

records.title: cpr0186 contributes to promoting sporulation in Clostridium perfringens SM101.
records.abstract: ObjectivesAlthough the precise mechanism underlying activation of Spo0A needs to be clarified to fully understand C. perfringens sporulation, the molecules directly interacting with Spo0A have not been fully elucidated. This study aimed to identify proteins interacting with Spo0A during C. perfringens sporulation by a yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) assay.MethodsPrey libraries constructed using the genomes of C. perfringens SM101 and str. 13 and a bait plasmid encoding the receiver domain of Spo0A in C. perfringens SM101 were used for Y2H assay. The deletion mutant and its complemented strain were constructed by homologous recombination. Phenotypic analyses included measurements of bacterial growth, sporulation efficiency, cell morphology, mRNA expression of sporulation-related genes, and the amount of phosphorylated Spo0A. Potential protein interactions were evaluated using AlphaFold 3.ResultsY2H screening identified CPR0186, a hypothetical protein in C. perfringens SM101, as a Spo0A-interacting candidate, and AlphaFold 3 modeling supported the possibility of the direct interaction with the receiver domain of Spo0A. The cpr0186-null mutant exhibited growth comparable to that of the wild-type strain, but showed significantly reduced sporulation. The mutant also showed significantly decreased mRNA expression of spo0A, sigF, sigE, sigG, and sigK. No apparent difference in the ratio of Spo0A∼P to unphosphorylated Spo0A was observed among the strains under the conditions tested.Conclusioncpr0186 promotes sporulation in C. perfringens SM101 and is suggested to contribute to the expression of Spo0A-regulated genes. CPR0186 may interact directly with Spo0A although the functional significance of this interaction remains to be determined.
records.authors: Yasugi M, Sugimoto M, Kusakabe S, Miyake M, Nariya H.
