records.title: Aniline Biodegradation and Nitrogen Removal by Salt-Tolerant Pseudomonas sp. H1: Performance and Potential Mechanisms of Catechol-Mediated Enhancement.
records.abstract: Industrial wastewater containing salts, nitrogen, and aromatic pollutants presents challenges for biological treatment. Although salt-tolerant microorganisms have shown potential for nitrogen removal and aromatic pollutant degradation, their functional versatility and the effects of co-substrates on pollutant biodegradation remain insufficiently understood. Here, we investigated the aniline degradation and nitrogen removal capabilities of salt-tolerant Pseudomonas sp. H1, with particular emphasis on catechol-mediated enhancement of aniline biodegradation. Strain H1 degraded only 9.11% of aniline (200 mg⋅L-1) within 60 h as sole substrate, but the degradation rate approached 100% within 24 h with catechol as co-substrate. Moreover, the strain tolerated high salinity (20-60 g⋅L-1 NaCl), achieving a maximum average NH4+-N removal rate of 10.98 mg⋅L-1⋅h-1. Whole-genome sequencing, nitrogen balance analysis, and enzyme activity assays supported ammonium assimilation as an important nitrogen removal pathway. Transcriptomic analysis revealed differential expression of genes associated with antioxidant defense, carbon metabolism, and aromatic compound degradation under catechol-supplemented conditions, suggesting potential transcriptional responses associated with enhanced aniline biodegradation. These findings demonstrate that catechol supplementation can substantially improve aniline biodegradation by a salt-tolerant bacterium with nitrogen removal capability, providing a basis for the potential application of strain H1 in saline wastewater treatment.
records.authors: Zha Z, Ren Y, Chen F, Yu C, Lei L, Li Z, Chen H.

records.title: Efficacy of Two Antimicrobial Peptides Against Pseudomonas syringae pv. actinidiae in Kiwifruit.
records.abstract: Kiwifruit bacterial canker caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. actinidiae (Psa), has led to substantial economic losses worldwide and represents a major challenge to kiwifruit cultivation. Due to the inadequate effectiveness and environmental safety of current treatments, there is a pressing demand for novel antimicrobial compounds, such as antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). In this study, two AMPs, P255 and P256, previously designed by our group, were used to determine their efficacy against Psa in kiwifruit. P256 with a minimum inhibitory concentration of 18.75 µg/mL demonstrated stronger antimicrobial activity against Psa than did P255. P256 and P255 showed synergistic effect when combined with EDTA. In addition, they effectively inhibited the biofilm formation, and regulated the expression of genes related to Psa biofilm formation. Both peptides bound with the lipopolysaccharide of Psa, targeted the membrane and increased the permeability of Psa cell membrane, resulting in calcium leakage. P256 and P255 disrupted the cellular morphology and intracellular structure of Psa cells. They also bound to the genomic DNA of Psa and induced the accumulation of intracellular reactive oxygen species. In experiments on infected leaf discs, P256 and P255 displayed superior control of Psa compared to commercial agricultural streptomycin. Collectively, P256 and P255 efficiently controlled Psa in kiwifruit and could be further developed as a new eco-friendly bactericidal agents.
records.authors: Zhou Y, Yang Y, Wang L, Gao Y, Xu X, Ying F, Dang X.

records.title: Shinella sp. LB1 remediates acetamiprid-contaminated soil by coupling NHase- and amidase-mediated dual-pathway biodegradation with nitrogen‑cycle regulation.
records.abstract: Microbe‑mediated biodegradation offers a promising strategy for acetamiprid (ACE) removal. Although nitrile hydratase (NHase) and amidase from distinct microbes constitute the two main enzymatic routes, dual-enzyme degraders are rare, and their nitrogen-cycle modulation in soil bioremediation remains unclear. Here, we enriched a microbiota DCM (dominated by Shinella, Achromobacter, and Agrobacterium) from ACE-contaminated cowpea soil, and isolated a novel degrader Shinella sp. LB1, the first reported member of its genus capable of utilizing ACE as the sole carbon and energy source, with an exceptional degradation rate of 27.10 ± 0.55 mg·L-1·h-1. Genomic analysis, heterologous expression and LC-MS/MS analyses demonstrated that strain LB1 uniquely harbors both NHase (1635 bp, chromosome) and amidase (2713 bp, plasmid 3) gene clusters, enabling dual-pathway conversion of ACE to N-amidoamide derivative (IM 1-2) via hydration and to N-methyl-(6-chloro-3-pyridyl) methylamine (IM 1-4) via N‑deacetylation, respectively. Comparative genomics suggested that NHase may be vertically inherited across 77.19% of Shinella spp., whereas the amidase, flanked by an ISPps1 transposase, is likely exclusive to LB1 via horizontal transfer. Soil microcosm experiments revealed that ACE contamination enriched nitrifiers (e.g., Nitrosospira), depleting NH4+-N and accumulating NO3--N. Bioaugmentation with LB1, which lacks a complete nitrate‑reduction pathway, not only accelerated ACE dissipation by 54.12% but also selectively recruited indigenous nitrate reducers (e.g., f_Comamonadaceae), enhancing soil catalase, urease, and nitrate reductase activities and promoting NO3--N to NH4+-N conversion. These findings provide novel insights into the metabolic diversity and evolutionary dynamics of ACE-degrading bacteria, offering a sustainable bioaugmentation strategy for ACE-contaminated soil remediation.

records.title: First contact: biophysical insights into non-enveloped viruses from VLPs to packed virions.
records.abstract: Precise biophysical characterization of non-enveloped viruses and virus-like particles (VLPs) is essential for evaluating assembly, structural integrity, and sample heterogeneity - key parameters that influence infectivity, manufacturability, and therapeutic performance. Analytical ultracentrifugation, light scattering, and mass photometry provide complementary information on particle size distributions, empty/full ratios, and assembly quality. Native and charge-detection mass spectrometry extend this, enabling accurate mass determination and genome-loading assessment. Solution-based structural techniques, such as SAXS and spectroscopy, provide dynamics. High-resolution X-ray crystallography, cryogenic electron microscopy, and tomography reveal global architectures, quaternary arrangements, and conformational switching essential for entry and maturation. Besides these methods, atomic force microscopy also allows nanoscale visualization in conjunction with mechanical profiling, linking physical stability with functional behavior. Thermal, chemical, and mechanical stress assays offer insight into unfolding pathways, pH-dependent disassembly, and genome-driven capsid pressurization, informing both viral biology and formulation science. Finally, mass spectrometry-based methods enable site-specific mapping of post-translational modifications and conformational perturbations. Together, these approaches establish a comprehensive framework for characterizing viral particles and VLPs, supporting rational engineering of stable, homogeneous, and functional assemblies for vaccines, gene delivery, and nanobiotechnology. This review summarizes current label-free methods for assessing size, mass, structural organization, and stability of intact viral particles.
records.authors: Rothe J, Uetrecht C.

records.title: MOCHI enables systematic identification of candidate independent intronic transcriptional signals from short-read RNA-seq data
records.abstract: Standard short-read RNA-seq analysis pipelines quantify expression over annotated exons and disregard signals mapped to introns, thereby missing independently transcribed intronic RNAs. Existing strategies depend on annotation, biologically crude whole-intron quantification, or subjective, low-throughput manual genome-browser inspection. We present MOCHI (  M apping  o f  C ryptic  H idden  I ntronic Transcripts), a framework that couples reference-independent, k-mer-based signal discovery with reference-guided genomic interpretation and a custom multi-step filtering module to systematically curate potential independent intronic transcription units from strand-specific short-read RNA-seq data. On two simulated datasets, MOCHI recovered annotated sense-intronic long non-coding RNAs removed from the reference and distinguished them from intronic signal confounders. Across paired ribosomal RNA-depleted and poly(A)-selected libraries from ten cancer cell lines, MOCHI curated candidates whose host introns are strongly enriched for a transcription-initiation signal. Candidate expression is largely uncoupled from host-gene exons, and their genomic features resemble those of annotated long non-coding RNAs. In ten matched cohorts from The Cancer Genome Atlas, candidates were detected in tumor samples, and a subset was associated with overall survival after adjustment for age and host-gene expression. Consequently, MOCHI extends the transcriptomic landscape that can be mined from existing short-read RNA-seq data and provides a curated resource of candidate intronic transcripts for downstream analyses.
records.authors: Gürer-Er DC, Karakülah G, Gautheret D, Akgül B.

records.title: Foodborne Bacterial Protein Toxins: Structural Genomics, Stability, and Prospects for Enzymatic Detoxification in Food and Gut Environments.
records.abstract: Foodborne bacterial toxins remain a major global health threat, causing millions of diarrheal cases annually by disrupting ion balance, inhibiting protein synthesis, and dysregulating immune responses. Key agents include AB5 enterotoxins such as cholera toxin, heat-labile toxin, and Shiga toxins; heat-stable peptides (STa/STb); staphylococcal superantigens; and pore-forming toxins from Bacillus cereus and Clostridium perfringens. Encoded on mobile genetic elements or chromosomal loci, these structurally robust toxins often resist host proteolysis, limiting natural detoxification. Despite abundant data on individual toxins, an integrated synthesis that links high-resolution structural and genetic features with practical implications for enzymatic neutralization is lacking. This review addresses this gap by compiling the structural genomics of major toxin families and mapping toxin architecture and gene context onto stability profiles and enzymatic vulnerability. We examine their genetic organization, structural stability, and susceptibility to enzymatic neutralization by microbial proteases, probiotic-mediated modulation, and engineered biocatalysts. Enzymatic detoxification of mycotoxins is discussed only as a limited translational analogy: small-molecule conversion by lactonases, oxidoreductases, or hydrolases is biochemically distinct from proteolysis of large, conformationally complex protein toxins. Thus, mycotoxin studies inform enzyme-discovery and engineering workflows but do not constitute direct evidence that these pathways can neutralize AB5 holotoxins, superantigens, or pore-forming toxins.

records.title: Borrelia-specific cell-free DNA in plasma from adults with Lyme neuroborreliosis: an explorative study.
records.abstract: Current blood-based diagnostic modalities for LNB have significant limitations. Using Next Generation Sequencing, we investigated blood samples from patients with LNB and non-LNB controls for Borrelia burgdorferi-specific cfDNA (Bb-cfDNA). Blood-samples from 61 adults suspected for LNB were analysed with amplification-free Nanopore metagenomic sequencing and detected cfDNA was cross-referenced with human and Bb-genome databases to identify Bb-specific-cfDNA. Bb-cfDNA was detected in 3 of 45 patients with LNB (6.7%) and in none of the 16 controls. Positive samples contained low levels of Borrelia-classified reads. Bb-cfDNA is unlikely to become a relevant blood-based diagnostic test for LNB in immunocompetent adults.

records.title: Genomic Profiling of the Virulence Potential and Antimicrobial Resistance of Shiga Toxin-Producing Escherichia coli from Surface Water and Animal Sources.
records.abstract: The aim of this work was to characterize the pathogenic potential of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) circulating in environmental and animal reservoirs. To achieve this, 225 genomes were analyzed: four genomes were obtained from bovine mastitis isolates, and 221 were obtained from the NCBI Pathogen Detection database originating from surface water and animal fecal samples. All genomes were analyzed to identify virulence-associated factors and antimicrobial resistance profiles in strains collected from surface water and animal samples. Virulence analysis revealed that stx1 and stx2 were detected in 32% and 44% of isolates, respectively. Environmental genomes frequently carried adhesion and LEE-associated genes, while mastitis isolates lacked these markers but exhibited enriched iron uptake systems and hemolysins, indicating niche-specific virulence repertoires. Resistance analysis identified 105 genes that contribute to antimicrobial resistance against multiple antibiotic families, including beta-lactams, quinolones, tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, and polymyxins. Phylogenetic analysis classified the strains mainly into phylogroups B1 (63.56%) and E (28%), and serotyping identified 41 serotypes, with O157:H7 being the most common (25.33%). MLST revealed 46 STs, with ST11 being the predominant one in animal fecal isolates. Overall, the data indicate a genetically diverse STEC population, with shared lineages among water, feces, and mastitis, as well as combined virulence and multidrug resistance profiles. This supports the need to incorporate genomic surveillance in environmental and livestock reservoirs to anticipate and mitigate the risks of transmission to the human population.

records.title: The biochemical composition of coronavirus Nucleocapsid proteins drives the bicistronic properties of their sub-genomic mRNAs
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  The nucleocapsid (N) gene of coronaviruses (CoVs) encodes a structural RNA-binding protein required for viral assembly. In SARS- and MERS-CoV viruses, reading frame 2 of N contains an overlapping open reading frame (ORF) encoding an innate immune antagonist accessory protein. However, the extent of this dual coding capacity across the CoV family, and the genetic features driving overlapping ORF formation, remain unexamined. Here, we developed an  in-silico tool (ORFan) to screen structural gene sub-genomic mRNA sequences from 152 species of coronavirus for the presence of overlapping accessory gene candidates. We found that frame 2 of the N gene in Alpha-, Beta- and Delta-CoVs frequently contains a potential accessory ORF (AcORF), conserved at the subgenus level, unlike the spike, envelope and membrane genes. We also show that CoV nucleotide biases in conjunction with codon biases integral to N protein function drive the relatively high abundances of start codons in frame two and stop codons in frame three, explaining the tendency towards frame 2 AcORFs. We further suggest that viral nucleotide biases and the codon composition required for RNA-binding function facilitate overlapping ORF formation in other virus families.

records.title: Application of metagenomic sequencing to improve sessile serrated lesion detection using the faecal immunochemical test
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Most population colorectal cancer (CRC) screening programs use the faecal immunochemical test (FIT), which quantifies occult haemoglobin in faeces and has proven to be effective in detecting and reducing CRC incidence and mortality. Sessile serrated lesions (SSLs) account for up to 30% of sporadic CRC, yet FIT has low sensitivity to detect them. Faecal microbial biomarkers may improve their detection, but FIT samples have not previously been used to study the SSL microbiome. We asked whether FIT samples preserve the faecal microbiome as accurately as fresh collection, and whether they can reveal a microbial signature of SSL. We first reanalysed a published dataset of paired FIT and fresh faecal samples from the same participants. Donor identity explained 63.5% of compositional variance compared with 16.7% for collection method, indicating that FIT preserves the donor-specific signature on which biomarker discovery depends. We then generated shotgun metagenomes from FIT samples of 24 adults scheduled for diagnostic colonoscopy, twelve with at least one clinically significant SSL and twelve with no neoplasia (NN) and compared each group with a published fresh faeces cohort matched on colonoscopy outcome. Collection method explained 6.3% to 7.6% of variance, and no individual species was significantly differentially abundant between methods. Between SSL and NN FIT samples, community structure did not significantly differ, and conservative differential abundance analysis returned no results. More permissive count-based models suggested a depletion of fermentative commensals in SSL. Functionally, SSL samples encoded significantly fewer KEGG orthologs and less polyamine biosynthesis capacity, while orthologs carried by several  Bifidobacterium species were more abundant. Many depleted functions reflected  Enterobacteriaceae gene content concentrated in a few control samples. No single feature was diagnostic on its own. A multi-feature signature, confirmed in larger cohorts and applied to samples that screening programs already collect, may increase the detection rate of SSLs.
records.authors: Hart BJ, Laven-Law G, Harker CM, Doane MP, Parker R, Menberu M, Cock C, Edwards RA, Symonds EL, Winter JM, Roach MJ.

records.title: Host-Derived Lipids Sustain Membrane Biogenesis in an Obligate Endosymbiont
records.abstract: Intracellular symbionts often undergo extreme genome reduction and lose pathways considered essential in free-living bacteria, including membrane phospholipid biosynthesis. Yet how such symbionts maintain their membranes remains poorly understood. The pea aphid  Acyrthosiphon pisum harbors the obligate endosymbiont  Buchnera aphidicola within specialized host cells called bacteriocytes, providing a tractable system to address this question. Here we integrated untargeted lipidomics, transcriptomics, and functional assays to investigate lipid metabolism across the symbiosis. Although  Buchnera lacks nearly all canonical genes for phospholipid biosynthesis, purified  Buchnera contained all major phospholipid classes detected in the host, including phosphatidylcholine (PC), phosphatidylserine (PS), phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), phosphatidylglycerol (PG), and cardiolipin (CL). This repertoire differs markedly from conventional bacterial lipidomes, combining canonical bacterial phospholipids with PC, PS, and cholesterol sulfate, features more characteristic of the eukaryotic host environment. Every lipid species detected in  Buchnera was also present in aphid tissues, consistent with extensive host contribution to the symbiont lipidome. Yet the  Buchnera lipidome was compositionally distinct, with characteristic differences in the relative abundance of individual lipid species. Bacteriocytes were transcriptionally specialized for lipid precursor metabolism, including upregulation of phospholipid precursor synthesis and acetyl-CoA transport pathways. RNA interference targeting host lipid precursor genes reduced  Buchnera abundance and disrupted symbiont morphology, linking host lipid metabolism to  Buchnera maintenance. We also found that sterol availability influences  Buchnera abundance. Together, these findings support a model in which host lipid metabolism sustains membrane biogenesis in a highly reduced endosymbiont and identify membrane lipids as an important dimension of metabolic integration in obligate intracellular symbioses.  Significance Statement  Obligate intracellular symbionts often lose genes considered essential for independent life, raising the question of how basic cellular functions are maintained. Remarkably, the highly reduced aphid endosymbiont  Buchnera aphidicola , despite lacking nearly all genes for phospholipid biosynthesis, contains a diverse membrane lipid repertoire shared with its host. Host cells harboring  Buchnera are specialized for lipid precursor metabolism, and perturbing these host pathways compromises symbiont abundance and cellular integrity. These findings reveal a previously underappreciated level of metabolic integration in which host lipid metabolism supports symbiont membrane biogenesis. Because similar losses of lipid biosynthetic capacity occur widely among intracellular symbionts, host-supported membrane biogenesis may represent a general feature of endosymbiosis evolution.
records.authors: Tan KXY, Michellod D, Arita M, Hori A, Nozaki T, Matsuda N, Kondo M, Shigenobu S.

records.title: Residual barcode-like sequences and barcode-associated artifacts after Dorado and Barbell preprocessing of metagenomic reads
records.abstract: Background  Residual barcode-like sequences after preprocessing are a quality-control concern in multiplexed Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing data, particularly in low-biomass, host-dominated samples such as blood. Using blood datasets spiked with a microbial mock community and prepared with the Native Barcoding Kit 96 V14 (SQK-NBD114.96), we compared Dorado 1.1.1, Dorado 2.0.0, and Barbell 0.3.2. Results  Dorado demultiplexing reduced barcode-positive reads to approximately 2% of reads, with internal barcode-like matches in 0.17–0.19% of reads. Barbell 0.3.2 applied to untrimmed Dorado basecalls yielded an approximately 50-fold lower detector-defined internal-match rate (0.0035–0.0037%) while retaining 91.2–91.8% of input reads. In the NCBI core_nt release of 12 September 2026, the focused screen identified complete, ungapped 24 nt identity for 64 of the 96 barcodes (66.7%), comprising 505 distinct barcode-accession pairs across 482 accessions and 195 exported TaxID groups of mixed taxonomic ranks. Records annotated as rRNA genes, chromosomes/genomes, and plasmids accounted for 35.6%, 23.2%, and 22.4% of the pairs, respectively. The barcode was located within its native ligation flanks in 224 pairs (44.4%), including 170 (33.7%) with the complete Dorado barcode search window and 3 (0.6%) with the full adapter construct. Conclusion  Barbell combined 91–92% read retention with lower detected internal barcode signals. After demultiplexing, barcode-like sequences remained in sample data. Moreover, kit barcode sequences, often within their native ligation flanks, were detected in reference records. Both findings call for careful preprocessing, reference inspection, and downstream validation. Further research should determine whether barcode-associated artifacts in reads and reference records affect taxonomic classification in clinical metagenomic workflows.
records.authors: Dinse T, Engländer VR, Metz S, Schrezenmeier H, Messerer DAC.

records.title: Visual surfaceomics reveals the substrate-scavenging cell surface of Asgard archaea
records.abstract: The emergence of eukaryotes from Asgard archaeal ancestors  1–5 likely required a specialized cell envelope that enabled sustained physical and metabolic interactions with proto-mitochondrial symbionts  6–10 . While the protrusion-rich cell architecture of Asgard archaea may enable such interactions, the molecular composition of their cell surface and its role in establishing cell-cell contacts remains unknown.  Here, we developed a “visual surfaceomics” approach, integrating subtomogram averaging, predictive structural modeling, transcriptomics, proteomics, and expansion microscopy to identify surface proteins  in situ . We show that Asgard cell bodies and protrusions lack an archaea-typical paracrystalline S-layer and are instead decorated by two main classes of surface proteins: subtilisin-like serine proteases (SubSs) and oligopeptide-binding proteins (OppAs). SubSs were detected as membrane-anchored dimers and were sparsely distributed across the surface. OppAs showed near-total membrane coverage but lacked any rigid, higher order assembly. Thermal shift assays and single particle cryo-EM showed that OppA binds oligopeptides  in vitro . Comparative genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics suggest that this peptidophilic surface architecture is conserved across Asgard archaeal phyla. Finally, we discovered that the cell surface was remodeled at cell-cell contact sites.  Altogether, our integrative approach revealed a metabolically specialized and structurally flexible cell surface that couples extracellular protein degradation with peptide capture and uptake, while potentially contributing to establishing and maintaining the symbiotic interactions of Asgard archaea.
records.authors: Malit JJL, Amendola D, Xu J, Dufresne L, Kokhanovska A, Gonet A, Wiegand CP, Clavien J, Wollweber F, Pilhofer M.

records.title: Primary vitamin B  12  limitation and widespread stress in Antarctic phytoplankton
records.abstract: Iron is considered the dominant limiting or colimiting nutrient for phytoplankton growth in the Southern Ocean. However, strong competition and limited biosynthesis capabilities for vitamin B  12 (cobalamin) within the microbial community creates conditions suitable for cobalamin limitation. Through a nutrient enrichment experiment in the Amundsen Sea, we show that growth in a phytoplankton community comprising diatoms and prasinophytes was limited primarily by cobalamin and secondarily by iron. Protein biomarkers across a broad area of the Southern Ocean further indicate widespread cobalamin stress within diatoms and  Phaeocystis . As warming-induced melting of ice-shelves increases iron supplies in the coastal Southern Ocean, shifts from iron to cobalamin limitation favor mixotrophic flagellates with low cobalamin requirements, altering community composition and function.

records.title: Metabolites cross the membrane, the transcriptome does not follow: co-localization is required for the cyanobacterial response to a yeast partner
records.abstract: Interactions between phototrophs and heterotrophs are usually explained by cross-feeding, yet whether that exchange alone accounts for the phototroph’s response has rarely been tested. We grew the sucrose-secreting cyanobacterium  Synechococcus elongatus with the yeast  Rhodotorula toruloides as a synthetic community, either in mixed co-culture or in membrane-separated co-culture (0.22 µm pore size), each with a matched axenic control. Metabolite exchange occurred in both configurations: sucrose reached the yeast and was consumed, and yeast-derived metabolites reached the cyanobacterium. The yeast reached a higher final density behind the membrane, whereas the cyanobacterium gained about 9% over its axenic control only in mixed co-culture. Yet the cyanobacterial transcriptome responded only with co-localization: expression of 51 genes changed consistently across time points (day-averaged q Importance  Partnerships between light-powered microbes and the heterotrophs living alongside them move large amounts of carbon in oceans and soils, and are now built on purpose to turn carbon dioxide into fuels and chemicals. Such partnerships are usually described by the chemicals the partners trade, so we asked whether those chemicals are enough. The cyanobacterium  Synechococcus elongatus and the yeast  Rhodotorula toruloides were grown together in one vessel, or in two chambers divided by a membrane that molecules cross but cells cannot. The yeast fed on cyanobacterial sugar in both, yet the cyanobacterium changed its gene activity only when the two shared a space. Partners in nature are usually clustered rather than evenly mixed, so closeness may contribute as much as the chemicals themselves. Keeping partners apart in engineered cultures can still deliver carbon to the heterotroph, but may not deliver the benefits of partnership to the phototroph.
records.authors: Bohutskyi P, Johnson Z, Veličković M, Kim Y, Cheung MS.

records.title: Decoding the molecular cues regulating the transition of Influenza virus polymerase from transcriptase to replicase
records.abstract: Influenza virus polymerase (FluPol) dynamically transitions between distinct conformational states to coordinate viral gene transcription and genome replication. While vRNP-associated monomeric FluPol supports transcription, ANP32-dependent asymmetric and ANP32-independent symmetric polymerase dimers mediate genome and antigenome (vRNA/cRNA) replication. How FluPol coordinates these distinct functional states to maintain the transcription–replication balance remains poorly understood. Here, we identify and characterize interdomain interactions within PB2 that govern the stability of the replication-competent conformation of FluPol. Specifically, a highly conserved salt-bridge between PB2 Mid-E282 and NLS-K752 stabilizes the replicase conformation, while the charge state of residue 627 (E or K) dictates ANP32 engagement, together coordinating polymerase dimerization and replication activity. Strikingly, bat influenza A viruses H17N10 and H18N11 harbor unconventional serine substitutions at both positions, compromising polymerase dimerization, ANP32 interaction, and vRNA/cRNA replication. Remarkably, introducing these bat-signature substitutions (E282S/K627S) into human H1N1 polymerase results in phosphorylation at both positions in human cells. These findings suggest that phosphorylation can partially compensate for the loss of negative charge at these residues, revealing a phosphomimetic adaptation mechanism that modulates polymerase conformational dynamics and function. Collectively, our study reveals how a conserved interdomain interaction within PB2 regulates conformational transitions and transcription– replication balance of FluPol, which might have been driven by phosphomimetic adaptations during the course of diverse range of influenza virus evolution.
records.authors: De A, Roy A, Mondal A.

records.title: The Geography of Speciation Across Andean-Centred Clades
records.abstract: Aim:  Mountains harbour a disproportionate share of global biodiversity, yet the geographic pathways through which this diversity arises remain debated. In the Andes, diversification has been linked both to geographic isolation generated by complex topography and climatic dynamics, and to ecological divergence across steep environmental gradients. Here, we assess the predominant geographic modes of speciation across Andean-centred clades using a large-scale comparative framework, while evaluating how alternative representations of species distributions influence macroevolutionary inference. Location: Andes, South America. Taxon: A total of 102 Andean-centred genera of animals, plants, and fungi. Methods: We combined time-calibrated phylogenies with species distribution data derived from two alternative spatial representations: concave polygons and potential distribution models. For each genus, we estimated 13 summary metrics capturing range overlap, range asymmetry, and phylogenetic structure. We then used simulation-trained, likelihood-free classification approaches, including linear discriminant analysis and two approximate Bayesian computation methods, to assign each clade to its most probable geographic mode of speciation: vicariant, peripatric, parapatric, sympatric, or mixed geographic scenarios. Results: Across clades, overlap-associated scenarios, corresponding to parapatric or sympatric classifications, were inferred as predominant in 57–67% of genera, whereas strictly allopatric scenarios, that is, vicariant or peripatric speciation, accounted for 23–30%, depending on the spatial representation and classification method used. Sympatric scenarios alone were inferred in 38–52% of genera, particularly when potential distribution models were used. At least one-third of clades showed congruent classifications across both analytical methods and spatial representations. However, several genera were sensitive to how species distributions were represented, with some shifting between allopatric and sympatric classifications depending on the spatial input used. Main Conclusions: Our results suggest that Andean diversification has not followed a single dominant geographic pathway, but instead reflects a mosaic of spatial contexts involving both isolation-driven and overlap-associated scenarios. However, classifications as parapatric or sympatric should be interpreted as hypotheses of geographic overlap during lineage divergence, rather than as direct evidence of speciation with gene flow. By shifting from single-clade case studies to a broad multi-taxon comparative perspective, this study suggests that the geography of Andean speciation reflects a heterogeneous process shaped by multiple spatial pathways to lineage divergence, while identifying candidate clades for future phylogeographic, ecological, cytogenetic, and population genomic studies of mountain biodiversity.
records.authors: Ramos Torres A, Molina-Henao YF.

records.title: Acquire and rewire: mobile genetic elements co-opt the bacterial core genome
records.abstract: It is assumed that bacterial genomes are streamlined, with genes encoding core functions integrated with one another and with aligned fitness interests. Such genes can gain little from horizontal transfer, as any recipient would already carry its own copy better adapted to resident networks. These restrictions motivated the ‘complexity hypothesis’, which predicts that core genes are rarely transferred. Yet homologues of core genes are repeatedly found outside their native chromosomal context, carried by mobile genetic elements such as plasmids and phage-plasmids, and by domesticated replicons such as chromids. Explaining this pattern requires us to ask whether a copy rides a mobile, self-interested element or a domesticated, host-aligned one. On domesticated, vertically inherited carriers, a second copy plausibly serves the host, through dosage, niche-specific benefit or functional specialization. On mobile, selfish elements, it may instead serve the element, by promoting behaviors that favor onward transmission. Because they enter cells that already have a host-encoded copy, we propose that mobile variants can act through dosage or through effects disproportionate to their abundance, for example by co-assembling with the chromosomal product. Here, we discuss the evolutionary drivers and consequences of extrachromosomal core genes and argue that these overlooked copies deserve systematic study.
records.authors: Carvalho R, Hall J, Botelho J.

records.title: Discovery of Apis mellifera filamentous virus in the blue orchard bee: Characterization of impacts and interactions with an organosilicone surfactant
records.abstract: Abstract    While RNA viruses have received attention in impacts on bee health, research is limited for DNA viruses. DNA viruses, such as  Apis mellifera filamentous virus  (AmFV), have been identified in solitary bees; but infection dynamics and impacts are not well studied. We detected AmFV in diapausing  Osmia lignaria  adults and dead larvae from wild populations using metagenomic sequencing. Finding AmFV in diapausing adults in cocoons indicated an active AmFV infection. Unmodified larval provisions from nests had significant levels of AmFV, suggesting virus transmission may occur via fecal/oral routes via pollen. Using established rearing methods, we fed  O. lignaria  larvae AmFV and monitored survival, development, and adult weight metrics. Increased amounts of AmFV in larval provisions resulted in increased mortality. Co-exposure to an organosilicone surfactant (OSS) in provisions synergistically increased AmFV titers in larvae and adults, indicating that agrochemicals could affect viral infections. With increased development time from 2nd instar to pupation, bees of both sexes weighed more; however, male and female bees were impacted differently by AmFV and OSS. OSS plus AmFV exposure significantly increased the time to pupation in female bees. Male bees exposed to OSS weighed more. These results provide crucial insights into AmFV disease dynamics.
records.authors: Williams MF, Schaeffer RN, Cox-Foster DL.

records.title: Sex influences the mosquito virome in a host-specific way.
records.abstract: Mosquitoes harbor diverse eukaryotic viruses. These viral communities, or viromes, probably influence mosquito physiology, including pathogen transmission. However, the factors shaping the virome remain largely unstudied, limiting our understanding of its role in mosquito biology. Here, we assess the influence of sex on the eukaryotic virome of mosquitoes. Ecological differences between males and females, such as female-specific blood feeding, may lead to differential viral exposure and virome structure. We investigated the influence of sex in sympatric populations of Culex quinquefasciatus and Aedes aegypti, two major human pathogen vectors. A total of 5,743 mosquitoes were collected in various habitats in Burkina Faso (West Africa) over 2 years. Shotgun sequencing of 115 pools revealed 47 viral taxonomic units (VTUs) from 28 viral families. Viromes differed between the two mosquito species, enabling within-species analysis of sex effects. Significant differences in beta diversity were observed between sexes in both species, while alpha diversity differences were significant only in C. quinquefasciatus. Additionally, five indicator viruses, taxonomically diverse and including two novel species, were identified associated with sex. Most indicator VTUs were found in both sexes but with different infection rates. Their low prevalence suggests that sex-based differences are not present in all individuals but are detectable at the population level. Our findings unveil that sex can influence the mosquito virome, and that this effect depends on mosquito species. Moreover, our results provide a first model of the virome structure as a function of sex in two mosquito species of public health significance.IMPORTANCEMosquitoes carry many viruses that do not infect humans but can influence how mosquitoes interact with pathogens that threaten human health. Yet, the factors that shape these viral communities in nature remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated whether male and female mosquitoes differ in the viruses they carry. Sex could affect the virome because males and females have distinct ecological and physiological traits, such as blood feeding in females. We examined the viromes of two major disease vectors, Aedes aegypti and Culex quinquefasciatus, collected in large numbers in Burkina Faso and screened using metagenomics. We found that males and females harbor different viral communities, and that these differences vary between species. These patterns were not driven by sex-specific viruses but by viruses that differed in prevalence between sexes. Our findings show that sex influences mosquito viromes in the field and offer new insight into mosquito-virus interactions.

records.title: Bridging generalizability and reproducibility in machine learning-based antimicrobial resistance prediction.
records.abstract: The rapid growth of whole-genome sequencing and machine learning (ML) has led to a multitude of methods for predicting antimicrobial resistance (AMR) from bacterial genomic data. Despite increasingly high reported predictive performance, substantial differences in data sets, phenotype definitions, genomic preprocessing, evaluation strategies, and validation procedures make it difficult to determine whether models will perform reliably beyond the data on which they were developed. In machine learning, this problem is generally framed in terms of generalizability: the ability of a model to maintain performance when applied to previously unseen data. In microbiology, many of the same considerations ultimately manifest as a problem of reproducibility. In this review, we provide a brief overview of the fundamental concepts underlying machine learning-based AMR prediction and then examine the factors that affect model generalizability and reproducibility.
records.authors: Elseifi N, Rogers H, Ferraro M, Boucher C.

records.title: Industrialization restructures the domestic dog gut microbiome while preserving host specificity.
records.abstract: Industrialization has reshaped human gut microbiomes, but its effects on other human-associated mammals remain poorly understood. Domestic dogs provide an informative comparative system because they have shared human environments and food systems for millennia yet retain distinct host biology. However, most canine microbiome studies have focused on industrialized companion, colony, or controlled-feeding dogs, limiting our understanding of the ecological range of the domestic dog gut microbiome. We analyzed fecal 16S rRNA gene profiles from 261 dogs sampled across Nepal, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates, and the United States, spanning forager, agrarian, pastoralist, urban, and industrialized lifestyles; 257 dogs remained after excluding those with reported recent antibiotic exposure. Lifestyle was the strongest measured correlate of canine gut bacterial composition, and this association persisted in restricted analyses of mature, non-shelter dogs sampled from temperate regions. Industrialized dogs differed from non-industrialized dogs through directional genus-level shifts, prevalence-defined VANISH-like and BloSSUM-like bacterial guilds, coabundance structure, and shifts in predicted functional potential. Non-industrialized dogs were not microbiologically uniform: pastoralist dogs showed non-industrialized gut bacterial community profiles but diverged from a simple forager-to-industrialized continuum. Cross-species comparisons with humans sampled across matched lifestyle categories showed parallel lifestyle-associated restructuring in both hosts, but host species remained the dominant axis of variation, and genus-level responses were largely host specific. These findings expand the ecological baseline for canine gut bacterial communities and identify industrialization-associated lifestyle change as a major axis of gut bacterial community restructuring in a long-term human-associated mammal. More broadly, they show that shared lifestyle transitions can impose parallel ecological pressures across host species without overriding host-specific community assembly.ImportanceDomestic dogs are one of the closest animal companions of humans, yet we know surprisingly little about how their gut microbiomes vary outside industrialized pet populations. This study shows that industrialization-associated lifestyle change is not only relevant to human microbiomes but also a broader ecological force that reshapes gut microbial communities in animals living alongside us. By comparing dogs across diverse human lifestyles, we show that shared environments can impose parallel pressures on the gut bacterial communities of humans and dogs, while each host maintains a distinct microbial identity. These findings suggest that gut microbial communities are shaped by the interaction between host biology and changing ecological conditions. Expanding microbiome research beyond industrialized settings is therefore essential for understanding what microbial diversity has been retained, altered, or lost during recent lifestyle transitions.

records.title: Off-panel resistance determinants in a high-resistance setting: comparative evaluation of syndromic multiplex PCR, metagenomic sequencing, and phenotypic AST in bloodstream infections.
records.abstract: Rapid syndromic molecular panels substantially reduce turnaround time for bloodstream infection diagnosis by identifying common pathogens and selected antimicrobial resistance determinants directly from positive blood cultures. However, their fixed target repertoires may limit diagnostic coverage in settings with diverse endemic resistance mechanisms and clinically relevant off-panel organisms. This retrospective comparative diagnostic study evaluated direct-from-positive-blood-culture metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), the BioFire Blood Culture Identification 2 (BCID2) panel, and routine microbiological methods across 165 positive blood-culture episodes from 145 patients at a tertiary-care center with a high burden of antimicrobial resistance. Complete recovery of the routine-culture organism set was achieved in 155/165 episodes (93.9%) by mNGS and 142/165 (86.1%) by BCID2. Among 23 episodes with incomplete routine-set recovery by BCID2, mNGS restored complete coverage in 18 (78.3%). For meropenem resistance, sensitivity was numerically higher with mNGS than with BCID2 (90.0% versus 75.0%), whereas ceftriaxone-resistance sensitivity among Enterobacterales was numerically higher with BCID2 (97.5% versus 85.0%); neither paired difference was statistically significant. BCID2 meropenem very major errors were concentrated among non-fermenting gram-negative organisms, particularly Acinetobacter baumannii, and were frequently associated with off-panel blaOXA-23 detected by mNGS. Overall, targeted syndromic testing and mNGS demonstrated complementary diagnostic performance, with mNGS extending organism and resistance-mechanism coverage beyond predefined molecular targets, while phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing remained necessary for definitive susceptibility assessment.IMPORTANCERapid molecular blood-culture panels provide clinically actionable results, but are inherently restricted to predefined pathogen and resistance targets. This limitation is particularly relevant in regions where local antimicrobial resistance epidemiology includes mechanisms not represented within commercial panel repertoires. In this study, metagenomic sequencing improved recovery of routine-culture organisms and identified off-panel carbapenem resistance determinants underlying several false-susceptible panel results, particularly OXA-23 in Acinetobacter baumannii. However, broader genomic detection did not consistently improve phenotypic resistance prediction across antimicrobial classes. These findings illustrate that diagnostic breadth and phenotypic predictive accuracy are distinct attributes and support the use of metagenomic sequencing as a complementary approach to rapid targeted testing and conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing.

records.title: From Genomics to Diagnostics: Combating the Spread of Vascular Streak Dieback in North America.
records.abstract: Vascular streak dieback (VSD) has emerged as a major threat to woody ornamental production in the United States (U.S.), currently affecting at least 50 tree and shrub species across 25 botanical genera in at least twelve U.S. states. The putative causal agent, here termed the VSD-associated Ceratobasidiaceae lineage (Csp), presents diagnostic challenges due to its fastidious growth requirements and vascular colonization pattern. Here, we integrate genomics-guided marker discovery with multi-platform genome-anchored tools (SSR, TaqMan qPCR, and LAMP that target unique genomic regions identified through comparative genomics) to deliver a field-deployable, genome-anchored toolkit for detection and genotyping of Csp across nurseries and landscapes. We evaluated the performance of these tools using 103 samples representing DNA isolated from 64 VSD-symptomatic plants or their fungal isolates and 39 non-target Ceratobasidiaceae outgroups. Genome assembly of Illumina reads yielded ten informative microsatellite markers with an overall amplification success rate of 95.8% (91.7%-100.0% across Csp samples). These markers demonstrated strong performance in distinguishing the Csp samples from the outgroups. Among the three TaqMan probes developed, VSD048 exhibited superior performance with 100% detection across Csp samples, characterized by cycle threshold (CT) values of 26.8 ± 4.2, and no cross-reactivity with C. theobromae or other Ceratobasidiaceae species. A multi-laboratory ring trial confirmed the reproducibility of the VSD048 TaqMan assay across various testing platforms. The loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay targeting the Csp-unique region achieved a sensitivity of 0.82 [95% CI 0.68-0.968] and specificity of 1.00 [95% CI 1.00-1.00], with a practical detection threshold of approximately 25 copies of the target region. Our molecular survey of the disease revealed a surprisingly broad host range beyond Cercis canadensis (Eastern redbud), encompassing eight additional genera, and confirmed its geographical distribution across the eastern and midwestern U.S. These validated molecular tools provide rapid, sensitive, and specific detection methods for Csp surveillance and management. The field-applicable LAMP assay and laboratory-based TaqMan/SSR protocols offer complementary approaches for different diagnostic scenarios, thereby enabling early detection and supporting efforts to limit the spread of this emerging pathogen in nursery and landscape settings.

records.title: Evaluation of ITS copy number variation among Clarireedia jacksonii isolates using single-copy genetic markers cam and hsp60.
records.abstract: Molecular tools are widely used for plant pathogen detection and quantification. Recent quantitative PCR applications for the turfgrass disease causal agent Clarireedia jacksonii were developed targeting the ITS region and showed potential utility in improved disease management. However, accurate and consistent pathogen quantification is contingent on stable copy numbers of the target genes across populations. In this study, we evaluated the genomic copy number of molecular markers in C. jacksonii using in silico analyses, quantitative PCR, and digital PCR. Calmodulin (cam), elongation factor 1-alpha (ef1α), and minichromosome maintenance protein 7 (mcm7) were consistently identified as single-copy loci, whereas ITS exhibited multiple copies in two out of nine assemblies. Digital PCR confirmed that cam and heat shock protein 60 (hsp60) closely followed theoretical single-copy expectations across a genomic DNA dilution series of C. jacksonii isolate HRS10. In the analysis of 27 C. jacksonii isolates, ITS was consistently detected as a multicopy locus, with copy number estimates ranging from 33 to 48 copies per genome when normalized using cam and from 34 to 52 copies per genome when normalized using hsp60. These results demonstrate that ITS copy number variation among C. jacksonii isolates was consistently observed, independent of the single-copy reference locus used for normalization. Therefore, single-copy genetic markers, such as cam and hsp60, may represent superior choices for accurate and stable estimation of fungal genome equivalents in C. jacksonii.

records.title: First Comprehensive Characterization and Highly Sensitive Detection of Hop Stunt Viroid in Chinese Sweet Cherry.
records.abstract: Hop stunt viroid (HSVd) is an emerging threat to sweet cherry production in China, yet its geographic distribution and genomic characteristics remain poorly understood. Here, we report the first occurrence of HSVd in cherry in Hebei Province and the complete genome sequences of three local isolates: YT-HSVd-1 (PQ580329), YT-HSVd-14 (PQ580330), and YT-HSVd-15 (PQ580350). Phylogenetic analysis placed them within a distinct plum-type clade alongside the isolates SC-17, SC-13 (Shandong sweet cherry), FP2 (Japanese plum; AB098502.1), HSVd.apr9, and HSVd.apr10 (Moroccan apricot), sharing 91.45 to 97.01% nucleotide identity with other known HSVd variants. Additionally, we developed a cherry-adapted SYBR Green I-based RT-qPCR assay using optimized primer sets (HSVd-q117F/R and HSVd-q168F/R) at 10 μmol/liter with annealing temperatures of 55.0 and 56.9°C, respectively. The assay demonstrated high sensitivity, with detection limits of 12.9 and 1.29 copies/μl and excellent reproducibility (Ct value [CV] < 5%). When applied to field samples, HSVd was reliably detected (100% detection rate) across all tested tissues, showing the highest viral titer in branch bark, followed by leaves and fruit stalks, and the lowest in fruit peels. This study provides the first complete HSVd genomes from Hebei Province and establishes a rapid, sensitive detection tool to support future surveillance and etiological research.

records.title: Variety-specific interrelationships between glucosinolate-related metabolite profiles and microbial communities in fermented mustard with divergent physicochemical and volatile properties.
records.abstract: Mustard exhibits varietal diversity in glucosinolate (GSL) composition, potentially affecting fermentation microbiota and product quality. Two varieties, LM01 (Brassica juncea var. longepetiolata Yang et Chen) and LM05 (Brassica juncea var. latipa), were selected from eight varieties and analyzed using volatile profiling, widely targeted GSL metabolomics, and metagenomics. After 20 d fermentation, LM05 had lower reducing sugars content but higher total acidity than LM01 (0.71 vs. 0.53 g/100 g) and retained higher levels of differential GSLs. The relative abundance of Lactiplantibacillus reached 89% in LM05 compared with 77% in LM01, accompanied by the enrichment of glycoside hydrolase-related functions, indicating distinct microbial functional potential associated with GSL transformation. Correlation analyses revealed distinct association patterns: LM01 exhibited a relatively simplified LAB-dominated network suggestive of a "stress-adaptive" pattern, whereas LM05 showed broader associations among LAB, yeasts, and GSL-derived metabolites. These findings provide a basis for targeted inoculation to improve fermentation performance across mustard varieties.
records.authors: Mei Y, Ge L, Wang Y, Yang M, Lai H, Zhao J, Du Q, Li H, Liu S, Hu K, Liu D, Zhao N.

records.title: Genomic Features and Risk Factors of Carbapenem-Resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa Bloodstream Infections.
records.abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa (CRPA) bloodstream infection is associated with high mortality and limited treatment options. This retrospective cohort study was conducted at a single Chinese hospital from January 2020 to January 2026 and included adult patients with P. aeruginosa bloodstream infection. Clinical data were extracted from the hospital information system, and whole-genome sequencing was performed on 48 CRPA isolates to determine multilocus sequence types, carbapenemase genes, and capsular serotypes. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression were used to identify factors associated with CRPA acquisition. Among 110 patients, 48 (43.6%) had CRPA bloodstream infection. Prior ICU stay within 1 month (adjusted OR = 5.67, 95% CI: 2.81-11.45, p < 0.001) and prior carbapenem exposure within 30 days (adjusted OR = 3.89, 95% CI: 1.92-7.88, p < 0.001) were independent risk factors for CRPA acquisition. ST-3757 was the predominant sequence type (39/48, 81.3%), KPC-2 was the predominant carbapenemase gene (32/48, 66.7%), and O11 was the most frequent serotype (12/48, 25.0%). All ST-3757 isolates shared pairwise average nucleotide identity above 98.5%, and phylogenetic analysis placed them in a single well-supported clade. These findings indicate that prior healthcare exposure and carbapenem use drive CRPA bloodstream infection in this setting and that an ST-3757-O11-KPC-2 lineage is locally epidemic, supporting targeted antimicrobial stewardship and genomic surveillance.
records.authors: Fu H, Yao Y, Wang X, Chen X.

records.title: Novel halotolerant microbial system enhanced by gamma irradiation for advanced multimetal bioremediation.
records.abstract: BackgroundSaline industrial effluents are difficult to treat because elevated ionic strength can inhibit biological treatment and alter metal speciation. This study evaluated two moderately halotolerant microorganisms recovered from seawater and shark-associated samples and examined whether gamma selection altered the performance of the more radioresistant isolate.ResultsThe isolates were identified as Serratia proteamaculans PX875896 and Rhodotorula mucilaginosa PX876763 by 16 S and 18 S rRNA gene sequencing, respectively. Both grew at 3-5% (w/v) NaCl but not at 10% or higher. In synthetic saline medium, S. proteamaculans showed the highest removal after 72 h for Cd (50.71%), Mo (42.56%), Cu (34.13%), and Co (25.26%); no net Cr removal was detected. S. proteamaculans was not recovered after 0.5 kGy, whereas R. mucilaginosa survived exposure up to 4 kGy. Relative to the wild yeast, gamma-selected yeast derivatives showed higher removal for several metals, including Co (22.61% at 48 h) and Cu (12.34% at 72 h) by the 4 kGy derivative and Mo (14.73% at 72 h) by the 3 kGy derivative. The 4 kGy derivative also contained more total carotenoids (67.30 µg/mL) than the wild strain (44.40 µg/mL). In textile wastewater, the 4 kGy derivative yielded the greatest removal of Mo (93.05%), Cr (77.88%),Co ( 60.80%) and Cd (51.42%), whereas S. proteamaculans yielded the greatest removal of Mo ( 58.43 %, Cr 57. 14 %, Fe (52.17%) and V (74.68%).ConclusionsSaline-derived Serratia proteamaculans PX875896 showed greater metal removal in synthetic saline medium, while Rhodotorula mucilaginosa PX876763 exhibited broader metal tolerance and greater gamma resistance.The 4 kGy yeast derivative improved multimetal removal from textile wastewater, coinciding with a more carotenoid-rich phenotype.These findings highlight the value of moderate halotolerance, gamma-assisted selection, and complementary bacterial-yeast approaches, while showing that tolerance alone does not predict removal efficiency. l.
records.authors: Ouda SM, Yousef SA, El-Sayed ESR, Othman AM, Abdelaziz G.

records.title: Personalization and evaluation of human whole-body metabolic models and community microbiome models using Persephone.
records.abstract: Human metabolism and human gut microbiome co-metabolism can be difficult to investigate in vivo owing to the complexity of the systems involved. Genome-scale metabolic modeling with human whole-body metabolic models (WBMs) offers a computational approach to address this challenge. However, personalization and analysis of WBMs requires comprehensive knowledge of metabolic modeling, which can be daunting for beginners. To reduce the computational expertise required and to standardize the process of working with and analyzing WBMs, we present Persephone: a personalization and evaluation pipeline for human WBMs. Persephone has functionalities to create community microbiome models from raw sequencing data or taxonomy-assigned read tables, use physiological and metabolomic data to create personalized WBMs, combine community microbiome models with WBMs or personalized WBMs to create community microbiome (personalized) WBMs, optimize WBMs according to user-defined metabolic reactions, perform statistical analyses to describe the data, and visualize significant results in various figures. Persephone saves intermediate results as well as a log file with all changes made to the model, data and any warnings encountered during the various steps. Persephone is designed for use by anyone with basic research-computing experience and access to modest computer hardware. Applications include the investigation of human-microbiome co-metabolism and the evaluation of the effects of various physiological parameters, such as weight, on human metabolism. Using a dataset of 100 metagenomic samples, it can take several days to a week to run Persephone on a single computer, depending on the number of reactions optimized and whether taxonomic assignment is performed.
records.authors: Nap B, Hensen T, Barton W, Sheehy A, Widder J, Chenna S, Thiele I.

records.title: Feedstock-specific biochar attenuates brominated flame retardant transfer to cherry radish: Links to rhizosphere microbiome reassembly and dietary exposure reduction.
records.abstract: Brominated flame retardants (BFRs) are emerging contaminants in agricultural soils that threaten food safety and human health. Although biochar can remediate contaminated soils, its performance and mechanisms in soil-root vegetable systems remain unclear. Herein, the effects of biochars from pig manure (PHC), peanut shell (FSC), corn straw (STC), and bamboo (BBC) on soil-to-food transfer and dietary exposure of decabromodiphenyl ether (BDE-209) and pentabromotoluene (PBT) were investigated in a 48-day pot experiment with bacterial and fungal community analyses. PHC, FSC, and BBC reduced BDE-209 and PBT accumulation in cherry radish by 60.1-78.3% and 34.1-89.4%, respectively, relative to the control. These biochars enriched putative BFR-attenuating taxa (Pseudomonas, Sphingomonas, and Humicola); enrichment of oxygen-containing functional groups (C=O and O-C=O) and dissolved organic matter in these biochars may have provided high-affinity niches that selectively recruited these taxa, potentially contributing to lower BFR accumulation. PHC, FSC, and BBC also promoted deterministic fungal assembly and more complex, stable networks. Overall, BFR transfer to cherry radish was associated with feedstock-dependent biochar properties, plant performance, and rhizosphere community assembly, providing an integrated basis for selecting biochars for contaminated agricultural soils. These findings link soil, rhizosphere, and food exposure and support feedstock-specific biochar use to reduce contaminant transfer while improving rhizosphere ecological health.

records.title: Computational Structural Dynamics and Preliminary Heterologous Expression Suggest a "Rigid-Anchor, Flexible-Melting" RNA Chaperone Mechanism for Rice OsCSP1.
records.abstract: Cold and drought are major abiotic stresses that severely constrain rice (Oryza sativa) growth and productivity. Cold shock proteins (CSPs) act as RNA chaperones that facilitate post-transcriptional adaptation under environmental stress. In this study, we combined phylogenetic analysis, prokaryotic heterologous expression, and all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to elucidate the evolutionary features, stress-protective capacity, and working mechanism of rice OsCSP1. Promoter analysis revealed enrichment of low-temperature responsive (LTR) and MYB-binding drought-responsive (MBS) cis-elements upstream of OsCSP1. Heterologous overexpression of OsCSP1 in Escherichia coli showed no cytotoxicity at 37°C. Under 17°C cold stress, recombinant strains overcame initial metabolic burden and exhibited superior biomass accumulation (OD600) compared with empty vector controls during late log phase. Spot dilution assays indicated enhanced colony-forming ability at 10-3 dilution. Sector-plate assays further demonstrated strong induction-dependent cytoprotection against both prolonged cold (17°C) and 15% (w/v) PEG6000-induced osmotic stress in E. coli, highlighting its potential protective efficacy in heterologous systems. AlphaFold 3 modeling of the OsCSP1-U6 RNA complex yielded a moderate interface confidence (ipTM = 0.66), which is expected for proteins containing intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). Subsequent 100-ns all-atom MD simulations revealed rapid contraction in radius of gyration (Rg) and solvent-accessible surface area (SASA), forming a compact, solvent-resistant conformation. RMSF analysis showed a rigid N-terminal CSD anchor coupled with a highly dynamic C-terminal IDR. MM/PBSA binding free energy decomposition indicated that the interaction is primarily driven by van der Waals and electrostatic forces. We propose a "rigid-anchor, flexible-melting" model in which the CSD is predicted to provide stable RNA binding while the flexible IDR is hypothesized to facilitate the destabilization of misfolded RNA secondary structures. These findings provide a foundational biophysical framework that facilitates future in planta functional validation of OsCSP1 as a potential target for engineering climate-resilient rice.
records.authors: Liang Y, Zhang J, An X, Kong Y, Xu L, Liu J, Zhao F, Wu J.

records.title: Bacterial 2',3'-cGAMP signaling induces membrane splitting in antiphage CBASS immunity.
records.abstract: Bacterial cyclic-oligonucleotide-based antiphage signaling systems (CBASS) are evolutionarily related to the mammalian cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway. The bacterial CdnB-Cap14 CBASS system is notable for producing 2',3'-cyclic GMP-AMP (2',3'-cGAMP), the same second messenger used by the mammalian cGAS-STING pathway; however, its functional mechanism has remained unclear. Here, we show that CdnB-Cap14 protects against phage infection through abortive infection (Abi) by triggering cell death. Structures of apo CdnBΔC and its complexes with ATP and guanosine triphosphate (GTP), together with inactive and activated 2',3'-cGAMP-bound Cap14, reveal that CdnB is autoinhibited by its C-terminal AGS-C domain and becomes activated by DNA together with intracellular ATP/GTP depletion to synthesize 2',3'-cGAMP in vitro. This signal drives Cap14 assembly from dimers into zipper-like two-layered filaments that partition the membrane and disrupt its integrity. We further show that phage-encoded Acb2 sequesters 2',3'-cGAMP to block signaling. These findings reveal mechanistic parallels between bacterial CBASS and eukaryotic cGAS-STING immunity and provide a molecular basis for therapeutic engineering.
records.authors: Li Z, Chen W, Li Y, Xia Y, Wei XY, Yang L, Zhang JT, Wang C, Jia N.

records.title: Non-triazole agricultural fungicides indirectly select for triazole resistance in the human pathogen Aspergillus fumigatus.
records.abstract: Agricultural intensification relies on chemical fungicides to manage crop disease,1,2 driving the evolution of resistance in plant pathogens.3 Fungicides persist in the environment, allowing activity beyond their intended targets, affecting downstream ecosystems and agricultural practices. The saprophytic and ubiquitous fungus Aspergillus fumigatus is an important human pathogen causing severe invasive fungal disease.4 Selection by agricultural triazoles, or demethylase inhibitors (DMIs), has led to cross-resistance to clinical triazoles, as both target the cyp51A gene.5,6 In the Netherlands,7,8 most triazole resistance arises from two cyp51A haplotypes, TR34 and TR46.9,10 Genomic surveys show that these resistance alleles often co-occur with resistance alleles to non-DMI fungicides, including quinone outside inhibitors (QoIs) and succinate dehydrogenase inhibitors (SDHIs).11 We hypothesize that agricultural environments with non-DMI fungicides can indirectly select for triazole resistance. Using grass mesocosms to compete A. fumigatus isolates, we found that low concentrations of DMI, SDHI, and QoI fungicides, comparable to agricultural residues, independently increased the proportions of triazole-resistant alleles. Resistance alleles for each class are not intrinsically cross-resistant, indicating that their co-occurrences result from linked resistance alleles. Consistent to these findings, environmental samples from heaps with only non-DMI fungicides contained high phenotypic triazole resistance (>20%). This work provides experimental and field evidence that triazole and non-DMI resistance can increase in parallel, consistent with genomic hitchhiking. We thus predict that novel resistance alleles are likely selected in isolates that have already accumulated resistance alleles to other fungicide classes. Therefore, managing selection and spread of environmental triazole resistance will require consideration of all fungicide classes.
records.authors: Kortenbosch HH, Kanellopoulos SG, Timmermanns L, Reyes Marquez F, Zwaan BJ, Auxier B, Snelders E.

records.title: Dimeric aromatic polyketides isolated from the marine-derived fungus Didymella aeria and their antifungal activity against Candida auris.
records.abstract: An integrastatin derivative, integrastatin A methyl ether (1), was isolated from the marine-derived fungus Didymella aeria, along with the known compound integrastatin A (2). The structure of 1 was elucidated using the NMR and MS spectroscopy. Integrastatin derivatives 1-3 and their related monomers 4 and 5 were evaluated for antifungal activity against Candida auris, an emerging multidrug-resistant fungal pathogen urgently requiring novel therapeutic agents, and against C. albicans. Compounds 1 and 2 showed inhibitory activity against C. auris, with minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values of 3.12 µg/mL for both compounds, whereas 3 showed weaker activity, with an MIC value of 25 µg/mL. In contrast, compounds 4 and 5 showed no inhibitory activity at 100 µg/mL. None of the tested compounds inhibited the growth of C. albicans at 100 µg/mL. The minimum fungicidal concentrations (MFC) of compounds 1 and 2 against C. auris were 12.5 µg/mL each, resulting in a MFC/MIC ratio of 4 and suggesting fungicidal activity under these assay conditions. Genome sequence analysis of D. aeria led to the identification of the putative biosynthetic pathway, including a non-reducing polyketide synthase gene cluster and a benzaldehyde lyase-like enzyme. This suggests that a benzoin condensation-like dimerization is a key step in integrastatin biosynthesis.
records.authors: Kamauchi H, Tanaka M, Usui K, Kiba Y, Kitamura M, Hashimoto M, Ichinose K, Sugita Y.

records.title: Decolorization and detoxification of aniline blue dye by Cloacibacterium normanense Gsp-T3 newly isolated from amphipods: Novel of bacterial community composition, synthetic dye-degrading bacteria, ligninolytic potential, and biodegradation pathway.
records.abstract: Synthetic dye contamination negatively affects ecological creatures and health because of the durability and toxicity of dye molecules. This study aimed to isolate dye-degrading bacteria from three amphipod species, comprising Floresorchestia amphawaensis (FA), Quadrivisio meufong (QM), and Grandidierella sp. (Gsp), and assess the potential of natural bacterial isolates for dye decolorization and detoxification. Based on analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequences, six novel strains that decolorize a wide range of dyes were closely related to Stenotrophomonas nitritireducens (isolate FA-T13), Isoptericola nanjingensis (FA-T16), Klebsiella quasipneumoniae (QM-T13), Acidovorax temperans (QM-T15), Bacillus subtilis group (QM-T27), and Cloacibacterium normanense (Gsp-T3). Among them, the promising strain C. normanense Gsp-T3 had the highest decolorization capability of 60.51% for a harmful triphenylmethane dye, aniline blue, and demonstrated the highest activity of ligninolytic enzymes, including laccase, manganese peroxidase, and lignin peroxidase. Decolorization by Gsp-T3 was monitored using UV-Vis spectral and HPLC analyses, and the products derived from dye biodegradation were analyzed using FTIR and GC-MS analyses. Eight degradation products were identified as aromatics, short-chain aliphatic acids, and aliphatic alcohol, and a degradation pathway of aniline blue by Gsp-T3 was proposed. Moreover, alterations in bacterial cell surface morphology were detected by SEM. In detoxification assays, the biodegradation products had a reduced cytotoxicity effect on Vero cells and did not elevate phytotoxicity (mung bean, and rice). As culture-independent method, 16​S rRNA metagenomic analysis revealed diverse amphipod-associated bacterial communities, containing several genera potentially involved in pollutant biodegradation. The findings provided knowledge of amphipod-associated bacteria and their capability for synthetic dye bioremediation.

records.title: Immunomodulatory natural products via toll-like receptor 2 signalling: from agonists to inhibitors across diverse natural sources.
records.abstract: Covering: up to 2025Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) is a versatile pattern recognition receptor whose activity can be tuned in either direction-agonism or antagonism-to produce distinct therapeutic outcomes, ranging from vaccine adjuvants and cancer immunotherapeutics to anti-inflammatory agents for sepsis, neuroinflammation, and autoimmune disease. Natural products from bacteria, fungi, plants, and marine organisms have emerged as a structurally rich source of TLR2 modulators, encompassing acylated lipopeptides, glycolipids, polysaccharides, flavonoids, non-flavonoid polyphenols, an aromatic aldehyde, an aporphine alkaloid, and even large bacterial antagonist proteins. This review surveys these natural TLR2 agonists and inhibitors, highlighting how the effective allocation of hydrophobic chains between the TLR2 pocket and its partner receptor, rather than total acyl-chain number alone, combines with chain branching, stereochemical presentation and polar head-group interactions to govern TLR1/TLR6 heterodimer selectivity among bacterial and gut-commensal lipids, and how mechanistically distinct inhibitory strategies-direct receptor competition, transcriptional downregulation, and TIR-domain interference-converge on a shared druggable interface exploited independently by plant polyphenols and staphylococcal virulence factors alike. Persistent experimental challenges are also discussed, including microbial contamination of natural extracts and structural heterogeneity of isolated lipids, along with how total synthesis and chemically defined oligomers have resolved these ambiguities, underscoring natural products as a promising yet still underexploited chemical space for developing selective TLR2-targeted therapeutics.

records.title: YEASTRACT+: the 2026 update with focus on global quantitative transcription regulation data and metabolic engineering applications.
records.abstract: YEASTRACT+ (http://yeastract-plus.org/) is a tool for the analysis, prediction, and modelling of transcription regulatory data at gene and genomic levels in yeasts. It incorporates three integrated databases: YEASTRACT, PathoYeastract, and NCYeastract, focused on Saccharomyces cerevisiae, pathogenic yeasts, and non-conventional yeasts of biotechnological relevance, respectively. In this release, YEASTRACT+ offers upgraded information on transcription regulation for 13 yeast species, extending the database to two additional yeasts of the basidiomycota phylum, the pathogenic yeast Cryptococcus neoformans, and the biotechnologically relevant Rhodotorula toruloides. A dramatic upgrade in the quality of the data provided occurred, as regulatory associations between transcription factors (TFs) and target genes are now associated with quantitative assessment. Quantitative impact of TFs on gene expression levels enabled the construction and release of two additional analytical tools: quantitative rank by TF, for the prediction of the most relevant TFs underlying a given transcriptomics dataset; and metabolic engineering based on integrating the quantitative impact of TF expression into genome-scale metabolic models. Altogether, this release of YEASTRACT+ provides unparalleled access to massive, curated, quantitative data associated with gene expression control in 13 yeast species, and a set of tools to enable its full exploitation towards fundamental, biotechnological, and health-related applications.

records.title: TIGRdisco  : a tool for the discovery of TIGR arrays and TIGR-associated Tas proteins from nucleotide sequences
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Tandem Interspaced Guide RNA (TIGR)–TIGR-associated protein (Tas) systems mediate DNA targeting through a hypercompact Tas effector, guided by dual spacers within a tigRNA that is processed from TIGR arrays. TIGR-Tas loci are composed of a Tas coding sequence associated with TIGR arrays of short units in either dual-repeat or stem-loop architecture. Unlike CRISPR (Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) arrays that comprise units of near-identical direct repeats interspersed with unique spacers, the two distinct TIGR architectures only conform in extremely short box motifs and show sequence variability within an array, complicating detection. Here, we present  TIGRdisco , an integrated tool capable of discovering both the Tas protein and its associated TIGR arrays directly from unannotated nucleotide sequences.  TIGRdisco implements independent engines to detect the two array architectures through a motif-agnostic approach. We benchmarked  TIGRdisco against a reference dataset of TIGR-Tas loci, recovering more than 80% of array units within its search window for both types of TIGR array architectures. Furthermore,  TIGRdisco recovered arrays for loci within clades of Tas where associated arrays were mostly unannotated in the existing reference. We found that these arrays largely contain non-canonical box motifs or unit lengths. Lastly, as a case study, we utilized  TIGRdisco and successfully uncovered TIGR-Tas loci across metagenomic and genomic datasets.
records.authors: Gu S, Gong Z, Mortimer JC.

records.title: ACTIVATION OF THE ARYL HYDROCARBON RECEPTOR REDUCES VISCERAL HYPERSENSITIVITY IN A MOUSE MODEL OF COLITIS IN REMISSION
records.abstract: The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) is expressed on gut-projecting transient receptor potential vanilloid-1 (TRPV1)  + nociceptors, but whether it has a role in regulating abdominal pain remains to be determined. Approximately 50% of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients experience chronic abdominal pain, even when their inflammatory disease is in remission. Previous work has shown that tryptophan metabolism to indole derivatives is reduced in IBD patients. Since microbial tryptophan metabolites (indole derivatives) serve as ligands for AhR, we hypothesized that reduced AhR activation contributes to enhanced pain sensitivity. We used a post-colitis mouse model of visceral hypersensitivity to examine the role of AhR as a mediator of nociception. AhR activation using both natural and synthetic agonists reduced visceral hypersensitivity in both male and female post-colitis mice. Conversely, pharmacological inhibition of AhR blocked the antinociceptive effects of indoles. Mechanistically, AhR activation by indole-3-pyruvic acid (IPyA) increased the transcription of the inward rectifying potassium channel Kir2.2, in TRPV1  + neurons and markedly reduced neuronal activation within the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Metagenomic analysis revealed sex differences in indole-producing bacteria, with control males exhibiting enriched abundance of  Akkermansia muciniphila and  Alistipes compared to post-colitis males and female controls. These findings demonstrate that oral IPyA supplementation in post-colitis mice attenuates visceral hypersensitivity in part through activation of nociceptor AhR, providing insights that support the therapeutic targeting of AhR to treat abdominal pain in IBD patients in remission.
records.authors: Habibyan YB, Mackenzie C, Mohan A, Baggio CH, Gordon N, Mohon MAN, Shutt TE, Defaye M, Thornton CS, McDonald B, Altier C, Sharkey KA, Nasser Y.
