records.title: A symbiont-derived biosurfactant couples bacterial surface properties to host-mediated clearance
records.abstract: Abstract  Host mechanisms that regulate intestinal colonization are viewed as acting on microbes, yet microbial traits that determine susceptibility to host control remain poorly understood. Using the association between Caenorhabditis elegans and its symbiont Pseudomonas lurida MYb11, we identify the cyclic lipopeptide biosurfactant massetolide as a bacterial factor that couples microbial physiology to host-mediated clearance. An unbiased screen of >11,000 bacterial mutants coupled to a host transcriptional reporter, combined with bacterial and host genetics, chemical complementation, transcriptomics, and physiological analyses, revealed that massetolide triggers host TGF-β and serotonergic signaling to promote intestinal peristalsis, limiting colonization. Massetolide also alters bacterial surface properties and promotes swarming. Experimentally increased serotonin-dependent peristalsis selectively reduces colonization by massetolide-producing bacteria, whereas massetolide-deficient bacteria remain resistant to host-mediated expulsion. Together, our findings reveal a symbiont-derived biosurfactant that links host neuroimmune control of intestinal peristalsis with bacterial susceptibility to expulsion, coupling host and microbial physiology to regulate symbiont abundance.
records.authors: Pees B, Escudero-Hernández C, von Hoyningen-Huene A, Rosenstiel P, Schmitz R, Dierking K.

records.title: ProteoKnight: Image-Based Encoding for Phage Virion Protein Classification and Uncertainty Estimation
records.abstract: Abstract  Accurate prediction of Phage Virion Proteins (PVPs) is essential for genomic studies due to their crucial role as structural elements in bacteriophages. Machine learning has emerged as a promising approach for annotating phage protein sequences obtained via high-throughput sequencing. However, effective annotation requires informative sequence encoding. This paper introduces ProteoKnight, an image-based encoding method that adapts the classical DNA-Walk algorithm using amino-acid-specific pixel colors and adjusted walk distances. It addresses the spatial information loss inherent in the previously reported image-based representation for PVP classification, frequency chaos game representation (FCGR). Moreover, this study bridges a gap in uncertainty analysis for protein sequence classification by evaluating prediction uncertainty in binary PVP classification through the Monte Carlo Dropout technique.In this study, variance and entropy measures were used to assess prediction uncertainty across proteins of various classes and lengths, forming the foundation of this investigation into protein classification and uncertainty quantification.The experiments highlight the efficacy of our approach in binary classification, achieving approximately 89% accuracy, demonstrating competitive performance with previously reported methods. Nevertheless, multi-class classification accuracy remains suboptimal. Furthermore, the uncertainty analysis unveils variability in prediction confidence influenced by protein class and sequence length, contributing novel insights to protein classification research.Combined with parameter-efficient convolutional neural networks, ProteoKnight enables accurate PVP prediction. Moreover, our uncertainty investigation identifies data points associated with low-confidence predictions, enhancing the comprehensiveness of our analysis.
records.authors: Khan MI, Bhuiyan AA, Neha SA, Rahman MK, Noor J.

records.title: A systematic review of whole-genome sequencing studies of Mycobacterium bovis that determine the direction of transmission between badgers and cattle
records.abstract: Abstract  Background: Tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium bovis, is a bacterial disease affecting cattle and other domestic species, wild mammals, and with resilience to survive in the wider environment for many months. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) methods can distinguish closely related isolates and local transmission clusters. However, the relatively slow evolutionary rate of M. bovis, with substitutions accumulating more slowly than individual transmission events occur, results in limited genetic divergence between epidemiologically linked isolates and a weak temporal signal, greatly limiting the ability to determine precisely ‘who infected whom’ and to estimate transmission rates. Differences in surveillance, sampling intensity, geographic coverage, and detection probability between cattle and the European badger Meles meles warrants a review to examine the strength of evidence, to better inform disease control considerations. Methods: Following PRISMA guidance, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase for peer-reviewed studies using WGS data from sympatric cattle and European badgers. Studies were assessed according to their sampling design, temporal and geographic coverage, genomic diversity, analytical framework, treatment of unsampled and environmental transmission pathways, and integration of genomic and epidemiological data. Evidence was considered separately for host sharing, local persistence, maintenance, spillover, and transmission direction. Results: The reviewed studies consistently showed close genetic relationships and local sharing of M. bovis strains between cattle and badgers. However, estimates of transmission direction varied substantially between studies with large variation in sampling quality and analytical approaches. Some studies reported patterns compatible with greater badger-to-cattle transmission, while others indicated the opposite, and some emphasized within-species spread and cattle movement. Directional estimates were potentially sensitive to unequal host sampling, differences in surveillance processes, weak temporal signal, incomplete observation of infection chains, the treatment of environmental or unsampled transmission pathways, and especially model assumptions. Close genomic similarity supported shared local transmission histories but generally did not establish direct transmission or its direction. Collectively the evidence base is considered insuﬀiciently rigorous for findings to be definitive and this is recognised by most authors. Conclusions: Current WGS studies demonstrate shared local M. bovis strains and epidemiological connections, but directionality and reservoir status remain highly uncertain and particularly sensitive to sampling and modelling assumptions some of which show signs of confirmation bias. Existing caveated estimates of transmission are presently insuﬀicient to inform generalised conclusions about variation in interspecies transmission rates and their use to validate badger intervention in disease control strategy.
records.authors: Torgerson P, Ghielmetti G, Langton T.

records.title: Population genetics reveals adaptive signatures of Exidia glandulosa across diverse climates from China
records.abstract: Abstract    Background  Wood-decaying fungus  Exidia glandulosa  , as the type species of the genus  Exidia  , is widely distributed in China. However, the scarcity of genomic limits the development of subsequent resources mining and utilization. Results  Here, we firstly assembled the high-quality reference genome of  E. glandulosa  using third-generation and next-generation sequencing technologies, systematically analyzed the population structure and adaptive evolution characteristics of  E. glandulosa  across diverse climatic regions in China based on 78 samples. This assembled genome revealed an abnormally high level of genome heterozygosity, suggesting elevated ancestral genetic diversity or historical inter-lineage hybridization events. Population genetic analyses indicated that genetic differentiation among  E. glandulosa  populations, likely driven by regional climatic variations. Selection signal analysis suggested that temperate populations mainly responded to climate variations through enhancing signal transduction and stress responses, subtropical populations focused on energy metabolism, and plateau populations through multidirectional regulation of pathways including energy sensing, autophagy regulation, and DNA damage repair. Conclusions  This study elucidates the significant roles of climatic and geographic factors in driving population differentiation and local adaptation in  E. glandulosa  . The rich genetic diversity and flexible molecular regulation mechanisms identified here underpin its wide ecological distribution. Additionally, this work provides a valuable genomic resource for future  Exidia-  related omics research and contributes to birding the gap in studies on climate adaptability of wood-decaying fungi within the framework population genetics.
records.authors: Liu S, Zhao H, Li W, Ablat T, Wu F.

records.title: Qiliqiangxin Capsule ameliorates post-myocardial infarction heart failure: associations with gut microbiota remodeling, altered fecal short-chain fatty acid profiles, and myocardial HDAC3-associated histone acetylation and JNK/TGF-β-related signaling.
records.abstract: BackgroundQiliqiangxin Capsule (QLQX) is a guideline-recommended adjunctive therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, but mechanisms underlying post-myocardial infarction heart failure (post-MI HF) remain incompletely defined, particularly gut-heart microbial metabolism.PurposeThis study aimed to characterize the gut microbial and fecal short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) alterations associated with the cardioprotective effects of QLQX and to determine whether gut-associated factors contribute functionally to its therapeutic effects in post-MI HF.MethodsA rat model of post-MI HF was established by permanent ligation of the left anterior descending coronary artery. Cardiac function, ventricular remodeling, histopathological injury, and inflammatory indices were evaluated after QLQX treatment. An integrated analytical strategy comprising fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing, targeted fecal SCFA quantification, untargeted fecal and myocardial metabolomics, myocardial transcriptomics, and targeted protein analyses was used to characterize gut and cardiac responses. A publicly available human ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction transcriptomic dataset was included for exploratory pathway-level comparison. Spearman correlation analysis with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction was performed to examine associations among microbial taxa, SCFAs, inflammatory markers, and cardiac functional indices. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations were used to assess the structural plausibility of selected candidate interactions, and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) was performed to experimentally evaluate the predicted interaction between isobutyrate and JNK1. Antibiotic treatment and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) were further performed to evaluate the functional contribution and transferability of gut-associated fecal factors.ResultsQLQX improved cardiac dysfunction, adverse ventricular remodeling, myocardial injury, and inflammatory responses in post-MI HF rats. Treatment reshaped the fecal microbial community and altered the fecal SCFA profile, including restoration of butyrate and isobutyrate. Selected SCFAs and bacterial taxa were associated with inflammatory markers and cardiac functional indices. Integrated omics and protein analyses further showed that these gut-associated alterations were accompanied by coordinated changes in myocardial cAMP, nuclear HDAC3 abundance, histone H3 acetylation, AMPK/mTOR signaling, and JNK/TGF-β related molecular indices. SPR analysis further demonstrated concentration-dependent binding of isobutyrate to JNK1, with an equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) of 5.89 × 10⁻⁵ M. Antibiotic treatment attenuated the therapeutic response to QLQX, whereas FMT from QLQX-treated donors partially transferred the protective phenotype, supporting a functional contribution of fecally transferable gut-associated factors.ConclusionQLQX ameliorated post-MI HF in association with remodeling of the gut microbial ecosystem, alterations in fecal SCFA profiles, and coordinated myocardial metabolic, epigenetic, and stress-signaling responses. The antibiotic and FMT experiments suggest that gut-associated factors partly contribute to the cardioprotective effects of QLQX. Butyrate and isobutyrate emerged as prioritized candidate metabolites, with SPR providing direct binding evidence for the isobutyrate-JNK1 interaction, although their broader causal roles and myocardial exposure require further validation.

records.title: The SbNAC gene family in sorghum: Genomic characterization, functional diversity, and roles in abiotic stress responses.
records.abstract: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench) is an important cereal for water-limited environments, yet drought, salinity, and temperature extremes constrain its growth and productivity. The plant NAC transcription-factor family is named after NAM (No Apical Meristem), ATAF (Arabidopsis Transcription Activation Factor), and CUC (Cup-shaped Cotyledon). SbNAC (Sorghum bicolor NAC transcription factor genes) refers to the NAC family genes in sorghum. Genome-wide studies have characterized a diverse SbNAC family, although reported gene numbers differ among analyses using distinct genome annotations and identification criteria. Transcriptomic studies have documented SbNAC responses to drought, salinity, cold, and abscisic acid, with expression patterns varying by genotype, tissue, developmental stage, and sampling time. Functional evidence in sorghum is concentrated in a small number of genes: SbNAC2 has been linked to activation of the stress-responsive gene SbAP37, while manipulation of SbNAC9 alters drought-related traits, including photosynthetic performance, root development, and reactive oxygen species scavenging. Conversely, SbNAC56 overexpression has been associated with increased sensitivity to salt-, osmotic-, and hormone-related treatments during germination, highlighting context-dependent effects within the family. Multi-omics and network studies identify candidate pathways but do not alone establish direct SbNAC-mediated regulation. In this review, we synthesize previous genomic, expression, functional, and multi-omics studies of SbNACs, distinguish candidate responses from experimentally supported mechanisms, and identify priorities for validating their roles in sorghum stress adaptation and crop improvement.
records.authors: Seck EM, Sun R, Wang F, Rehman FU, Diack O, Kanfany G, Di P, Zhang J.

records.title: Synergy in viral-bacterial co-infection expedites algal bloom demise.
records.abstract: Algal bloom demise, often caused by viruses, is a major driver of carbon cycling in the surface ocean1,2. However, although blooms collapse synchronously, fewer than 30% of algal cells are actively infected by viruses3, indicating the involvement of additional mortality agents. Here we quantified tripartite interactions within a synthetic community composed of the abundant coccolithophore Gephyrocapsa huxleyi, bacteria and viruses isolated during a bloom. We found that bacteria significantly enhanced virus-induced algal mortality in G. huxleyi as well as in three other globally widespread microalgae. We quantified this interaction using two new metrics: the synergy index, which measures viral-bacterial interaction strength, and the benefit index, which assesses changes in bacterial fitness. We identified Alteromonas bacteria as drivers of viral-bacterial co-infection, with consistently high synergy index and benefit index. We found that during algal blooms, Alteromonas displayed high chemoattraction towards infected cell extracts, accumulated in aggregates derived from bloom demise, and increased in abundance during oceanic bloom collapse. Viral-bacterial synergy represents a previously unrecognized mortality agent that controls bloom termination, modulating the balance between the carbon-recycling viral shunt and the carbon-exporting viral shuttle pathways, which influence global carbon cycling4-6.

records.title: Alterations of fecal microbiome and metabolome in patients with diminished ovarian reserve.
records.abstract: Study questionAre there distinct variations in the gut microbiome and metabolism among infertile women diagnosed with diminished ovarian reserve (DOR), and how might the gut microbiome influence ovarian function?Summary answerIn DOR patients, Hoylesella abundance correlated with anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH)/antral follicle count (AFC), and stearic acid was identified as a key differential metabolite that was associated with activated PI3K-Akt signaling.What is known alreadyAccumulating evidence underscores the presence of a 'gut-ovary axis', highlighting a substantial interplay between the intestinal microbiome and ovarian function. However, the specific microbial and metabolic profiles characterizing infertile individuals with DOR remain largely uncharacterized.Study design, size, durationThis study was a cross-sectional observational study. We enrolled participants receiving frozen embryo transfer at the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University between 1 October 2024, and 31 December 2025. Each participant was limited to a single frozen embryo transfer within the study.Participants/materials, setting, methodsA total of 190 participants were included: 91 with DOR and 99 with normal ovarian reserve (NOR). Clinical information and stool specimens were collected from every subject. Sequencing of 16S rRNA and non-targeted metabolomics were implemented to characterize the gut microbiome and metabolome, respectively. Molecular docking analysis and network pharmacology were then implemented to screen for overlapping genetic targets among DOR-associated targets and key metabolite-targeted proteins.Main results and the role of chanceRelative to NOR controls, the DOR population exhibited significantly lower Gut Microbiota Health Index (P = 2.52 × 10-22) and higher Microbiota Dysbiosis Index (P = 8.31 × 10-10). The genus Hoylesella was significantly depleted in the DOR group (P = 0.018). Spearman analysis demonstrated that Hoylesella proportions were significantly positively correlated with AMH and AFC levels. Metabolomics analysis identified 243 differential metabolites across the study cohorts. Among these, four metabolites were associated with Hoylesella, and stearic acid exhibited high predictive performance (area under the curve = 0.89) for distinguishing DOR. Network pharmacology analysis of stearic acid and DOR identified five core targets: tumor necrosis factor, AKT serine/threonine kinase 1, SRC proto-oncogene, non-receptor tyrosine kinase (SRC), peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARG), and epidermal growth factor receptor. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathway enrichment indicated that the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway was the most significantly enriched.Large scale dataRaw 16S rRNA sequencing data have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive under BioProject accession PRJNA1444490. Untargeted metabolomics data have been deposited in MetaboLights under accession MTBLS14194.Limitations, reasons for cautionThe current investigation represents an initial effort to identify the alterations in intestinal microbes and associated metabolites in women with DOR-related infertility through 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics; however, experimental validation of the underlying mechanisms is still missing. Furthermore, the metabolomics analysis in this study did not further stratify by age.Wider implications of the findingsThrough immunological dysregulation and inflammatory reactions, aberrant alterations in key intestinal microbes and metabolic products likely participate in the underlying mechanisms of DOR. These results provide direction for further research into the causal connections between important microbial species and metabolites in patients with DOR.FundingThis research was supported by grant 32271169 from the National Natural Science Foundation of China and the Henan Province Young and Middle-aged Health Science and Technology Innovation Leading Talent Project (Grant No. LJRC2024009).DisclosuresThe authors have no conflicts of interest.Trial registration numberN/A.

records.title: On the trail of novel bacteria: time to scale up the species description process.
records.abstract: Bacterial taxonomy provides a framework for classifying, naming, and identifying microbial diversity, yet the number of formally described bacterial species remains remarkably small compared with the vast bacterial diversity estimated to exist on Earth. The reasons for this include the historical difficulty of cultivating microorganisms and the traditional polyphasic taxonomy practice. Culturomics, that is, the combination of diverse cultivation conditions with high-throughput identification methods such as MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, has demonstrated that many bacteria previously considered uncultivable can, in fact, be isolated and characterized. Coupling culturomics with whole-genome sequence analysis paves the way for scaling up the species description process.
records.authors: Vandamme P, Wieme AD, Peeters C.

records.title: An orphan LuxR regulator controls plant developmental reprogramming during interaction with  Novosphingobium resinovorum  HR1a
records.abstract: Summary  Rhizoremediation depends on productive plant/pollutant-degrading microorganism interactions, yet the bacterial regulatory mechanisms that shape host responses remain poorly understood. We investigated the role of the previously uncharacterized orphan LuxR874 from the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH)-degrading bacterium  Novosphingobium resinovorum HR1a, in the modulation of plant physiology. Bacterial transcriptomics revealed that LuxR874 controls the expression of genes associated with aromatic and sugar metabolism, and acyl-CoA-related functions. Inactivation of  luxR874 altered bacterial responses without affecting root colonization, suggesting that this regulator contributes to the physiological state required to elicit host responses. In gnotobiotic systems, HR1a induced a root phenotype characterized by reduced primary root elongation, increased root thickness, and enhanced root hair formation. These alterations were attenuated in the  luxR874 mutant and restored by complementation despite similar colonization levels among strains. Plant RNA-seq analyses revealed extensive host transcriptional reprogramming, including activation of developmental regulators, hormone-associated pathways, cell-wall remodeling genes, and oxidative stress responses. In contrast, plants inoculated with the  luxR874 mutant displayed a weaker transcriptional response resembling the non-inoculated state. Functional analyses supported LuxR874-dependent activation of reactive oxygen species-and ethylene-related pathways. Our results reveal an unexpected role for an orphan LuxR regulator in coordinating multi-level responses during a rhizoremediation-relevant plant–microbe interaction.
records.authors: Molina L, Hurtado I, Udaondo Z, Segura A.

records.title: Factors affecting microbial community composition in Split Lake, MB, Canada
records.abstract: Split Lake is a large freshwater lake in northern Manitoba, Canada, that receives major inflows from the Nelson River, Burntwood River, and Grassy River. In 1976, during the Churchill River Diversion (CRD) project, most of the water in the Churchill River was diverted into the Nelson River via the Rat River, and the Burntwood River, creating a large inflow pressure in the lower Nelson area, including Split Lake. Decades after its implementation, the Churchill River Diversion still influences ecological and environmental processes in the area. In this study, metabarcoding of the 16S rRNA gene was employed to characterize the microbial community structure of the lake. Environmental factors (temperature, pH, turbidity, dissolved oxygen) and cyanotoxin levels were also assessed. The objectives of this study were to establish a baseline for microbiota across the lake and examine how environmental variables affect microbial population dynamics. The study was conducted in the summer of 2024, encompassing 14 sites on Split Lake and 2 sites on Assean Lake, an adjacent waterbody with minimal influence from hydroelectric infrastructure. Split Lake was found to harbor six distinct microbial clusters, with turbidity and dissolved oxygen levels correlating with different aquatic regimes within the lake. The predominant taxa in Split Lake included Actinobacteria hgcI clade and  Cyanobium . Microcystin concentrations measured throughout the study were always below the Maximum Acceptable Concentration (MAC) set for Canadian federal drinking water standards.

records.title: Developing synthetic auxin-based trans-kingdom signaling
records.abstract: Synthetic trans-kingdom signaling systems with tunable transduction properties provide a unique avenue to explore how communication between organisms coordinate behaviors without the confounding complexity of natural systems. However, existing trans-kingdom signaling systems suffer from either toxic signal molecules, a need for rare precursors for signal generation, or transduction machinery which is either species-specific or cannot be easily tuned. This limits their capacity to be broadly applied across kingdoms and their utility as a model system to study trans-kingdom interactions. In this work we elucidate the design principles for a trans-kingdom signaling system based on the plant phytohormone, Indole 3-Acetic Acid (auxin), that overcomes these challenges. We demonstrate how auxin biosynthesis can be engineered into a model sender organism, the cyanobacteria  Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942, and how this signal can be tuned with low leak and high dynamic range. We also show these signals can be connected to gene expression using tunable synthetic auxin-responsive signaling systems across multiple kingdoms. We demonstrate that  S. elongatus generated auxin signals can tune gene expression in co-cultured  Saccharomyces cerevisiae via auxin-induced degradation. Additionally, we show that when the  S. elongatus are associated with the roots of the model plant,  Arabidopsis thaliana , the auxin they generate can control gene expression via auxin-responsive synthetic transcription factors expressed from the plant’s genome. Taken together, our results demonstrate the design principles for a tunable auxin-based trans-kingdom signaling system that can be broadly applied across species.

records.title: GeneFamHunter: annotation-independent recovery of divergent and tandemly arrayed gene-family members from genome assemblies
records.abstract: Motivation  Gene families expand by tandem duplication, diverge and decay, so their members are often missing, fragmented or fused in automated genome annotations, and divergent copies escape pairwise similarity searches. These challenges are particularly pronounced in non-model organisms, for which well-annotated genomes and reference proteomes are often unavailable, limiting the applicability of protein-based gene family recovery methods. Results  We developed GeneFamHunter to recover gene-family members directly from nucleotide assemblies. It searches continuous six-frame translations of overlapping genomic windows using four complementary domain- and profile-based methods, clusters hits while distinguishing tandem paralogs, predicts and validates gene models, and constructs gene trees. Across six Quest for Orthologs genomes, window-based HMMER searches recovered all 130 reference papain-like (C1A) loci, with 21 off-target hits, compared with 45 for stop-to-stop ORF searches; whole-contig HMMER searches recovered 108 (83.1%). With 11 distantly related queries, PSI-BLAST and DELTA-BLAST recovered all reference loci, whereas RPSTBLASTN recovered 98.5–99.2% and TBLASTN, as used by BITACORA, recovered 94.6– 95.4%. Across six mite genomes, GeneFamHunter recovered all 209 previously reported C1 loci and identified 37 additional candidate loci. In a separate comparison, it recovered all 128 reference UniProt C1A proteins and identified five additional loci without annotated gene models; OrthoFinder included 35 non-C1A proteins, whereas OMA recovered 98 reference proteins. Availability and implementation  GeneFamHunter is implemented in Bash for Linux and SLURM clusters and is freely available at  https://github.itap.purdue.edu/HeLab/GeneFamHunter (MIT license). Benchmark code and data:  https://github.itap.purdue.edu/HeLab/GeneFamHunter_benchmarks and Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23744704).  Supplementary information  Supplementary data are available at  Bioinformatics online.

records.title: Deterministic DNA-first discovery reveals recurrent genomic architectures
records.abstract: Genome mining typically begins with known genes or protein families, which can make systems defined primarily by genomic organization difficult to detect. We developed a DNA-first framework combining asymmetric-ovariance natural-vector representations with generic positional recurrence, joining separately calibrated signals through genomic coordinates. In benchmarks of array-associated reverse transcriptase (ART) loci, the target-free mathematical arm localized seven of eight predeclared loci, including all seven with exact-array coordinates. Dual-arm signals occurred in none of three non-array RT controls and in one of five UG27 systems, indicating selectivity within these small control sets. A separate profile-guided search of 6.12 Gb identified five candidate array-associated RT-like systems. In an independent 54.38-Gb evaluation of this profile-guided arm, structural compatibility was 24/32 under a historical-rule mirror, 12/32 after novelty-only selection, and 0/17 for architecture-selected complete ORFs; the two 32-member panels shared six exact sequences. Together, these results suggest that mathematical features of raw DNA can complement protein-directed searches in nominating genomic architectures for experimental RNA-to-DNA studies.

records.title: Phenotypic plasticity segregates antagonistic species but undermines their coexistence
records.abstract: Environmental change often induces novel phenotypes in multiple cohabiting species, yet how such common-cue-induced plasticity shapes their coexistence is largely unknown. Testing this link requires disentangling inducing-environment effects from induced-phenotype effects, which remains elusive. We address this gap using two mutually antagonistic bacterial species,  Staphylococcus aureus (  Sa ) and  Pseudomonas aeruginosa (  Pa ). In habitual salinity, where both bacteria show unicellularity,  Pa severely diminished  Sa . In contrast, high salinity induced macroscopic cell clustering that spatially segregated  Sa and  Pa (  Sa : bottom-dwelling vertical filament;  Pa : top-dwelling horizontal mat), and led to >10-fold higher coexistence than habitual salinity. Counterintuitively, physically inhibiting cell clustering (abolishing segregation) in high salinity led to a further >100-fold higher coexistence (  Sa :  Pa ∷∼1:1). This was because salinity-induced clustering was adaptive for  Pa , but not for  Sa : such adaptive plasticity enabled killer  Pa to proliferate by monopolizing oxygen, which diminished  Sa in a correlated manner, thereby weakening coexistence (mechanistically explained by diffusion-based killing). Hence, although the inducing environment promoted overall coexistence, the induced phenotype undermined it. Community-wide genomics revealed that the high level of coexistence achieved by abolishing segregation in high salinity allowed rapid coculture-specific evolution. Taken together, we uncover how plasticity can appear to promote antagonistic coexistence despite causally undermining it.
records.authors: Shaji DE, Hadi M, Chavhan Y.

records.title: Detection, Genetic Characterization, and Evolutionary Analysis of Jingmen Tick Virus in Ticks from Border Regions of Yunnan Province, China
records.abstract: Abstract    Background  Jingmen tick virus (JMTV), an emerging tick-borne arbovirus of global public health concern, is a segmented positive-sense RNA virus assigned to the genus Flavivirus of the family Flaviviridae. Although JMTV has been detected in ticks and mammals across Asia, Africa, Europe, and the Americas, epidemiological data from the border regions of southwestern China remain limited. This study investigated the prevalence and genetic characteristics of JMTV in ticks collected from border areas of Yunnan Province, China. Methods  A total of 1,035 ticks infesting cattle were collected from five border regions of Yunnan (including Ruili and Malipo) between May 2024 and August 2025. Tick species were identified by PCR amplification and sequencing of the mitochondrial  COI  and 16S rDNA genes. JMTV was detected by RT-qPCR, and genetic and phylogenetic analyses were performed on near-full-genome sequences of positive samples; attempts were made to isolate the virus in Vero, BHK-21, and C6/36 cells and in Kunming mice. Results  Three tick species were identified:  Rhipicephalus microplus  ,  Haemaphysalis longicornis  , and  Haemaphysalis bispinosa  . The overall JMTV-positive rate was 70.82% (733/1,035), with JMTV detected exclusively in  R. microplus  ; the regional positive rates were 93.90% in Ruili and 71.33% in Malipo, a statistically significant difference (P R. microplus  along the China–Myanmar and China–Vietnam borders of Yunnan, posing a potential public health risk and providing epidemiological evidence to support local JMTV prevention and control. Because sampling was uneven across regions, more balanced future surveys are needed to refine regional epidemiological estimates.

records.title: Deciphering Viral Antigenic Relationships Through Antigenic Cartography: A Narrative Review
records.abstract: Background:  Antigenic cartography is a computational approach that quantitatively visualizes antigenic relationships among viral strains using serological data, including hemagglutination inhibition and virus-neutralization assays. Since its introduction in the early 2000s, it has substantially advanced the study of viral antigenic evolution by transforming complex serological measurements into interpretable antigenic maps, thereby facilitating assessment of antigenic diversity, immune escape, cross-reactivity, and vaccine–virus relationships. Objective: This review examines the historical development, methodological principles, applications, limitations, and emerging directions of antigenic cartography across clinically relevant viruses, with particular emphasis on its relevance to viral surveillance, antigenic drift monitoring and vaccine-strain selection. Methods: The literature was synthesized comparatively across major applications of antigenic cartography, encompassing human seasonal influenza and other viruses, including dengue, lyssaviruses, foot-and-mouth disease virus, Enterovirus A71, norovirus, rotavirus, SARS-CoV-2, and HIV. Particular attention was given to real-world applications, methodological advances, sources of uncertainty, and integration with genomic, structural, evolutionary, and computational approaches. Findings: Influenza remains the most extensively studied viral pathogen, where antigenic cartography has supported recognition of epidemiologically relevant antigenic transitions and informed vaccine decisions. Examples include the emergence of A/Fujian/411/2002-like H3N2 viruses during 2004–2005 and assessment of A/California/07/2009 during 2010–2011. Applications to other viruses demonstrate broader utility for characterizing antigenic landscapes and evaluating cross-protective immunity and vaccine performance. However, map reliability is influenced by serological assay variability, serum-panel composition, measurement noise, incomplete and geographically biased datasets. Limited inter-operability among serological, genomic, and structural datasets further restricts reproducibility and cross-study comparability. Future Directions and Conclusions: The field is transitioning from retrospective visualization toward predictive and mechanistically informed antigenic surveillance. Integration of artificial intelligence, protein language models, evolutionary modelling, structural vaccinology, and real-time genomic–serological surveillance could enable earlier prediction of antigenic drift, identification of emerging vaccine mismatches, and prioritization of candidate vaccine strains. Future platforms should incorporate standardized and automated serological measurements, inter-laboratory calibration, harmonized data standards, geographically representative datasets, experimental validation, and interpretable continuously updated models. Such integration could establish antigenic cartography as a scalable predictive framework for vaccine design and for strengthening preparedness against emerging viral threats.
records.authors: Biswas D, Subaschandrabose RK, Ningombam JD.

records.title: A heat-induced HagF-HrcA regulatory loop promotes chlamydial fitness and infectious progeny yield under stress.
records.abstract: Bacterial survival under environmental stress requires precise regulation of protein homeostasis, yet how this is achieved in organisms with streamlined genomes remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify HagF as a previously unrecognized protein that antagonizes the conserved heat-inducible transcriptional repressor HrcA in Chlamydia. Using genetic and biochemical approaches, including overexpression and CRISPRi-mediated knockdown, we show that under non-stressed conditions, HrcA represses hagF along with its five known targets, including hrcA and four chaperone genes. Upon heat stress, HagF is induced and binds HrcA, attenuating its repressor activity. This negative feedback loop enhances chaperone gene induction, particularly from the hrcA-grpE-dnaK operon, and promotes infectious elementary body yield. Notably, HagF is conserved across members of the order Chlamydiales, highlighting a lineage-specific adaptation. Together, these findings define a regulatory circuit in which a specialized antagonist modulates a widely conserved repressor, enabling Chlamydia to couple heat-responsive gene expression with developmental progression and enhance fitness under restrictive conditions.

records.title: Environmental enrichment is associated with changes in the gut microbiome and resistome of captive pythons.
records.abstract: Environmental enrichment is widely used to improve the welfare of captive animals, yet its effects on reptilian gut microbiota remain poorly understood. Here, we used shotgun metagenomic sequencing to investigate the gut microbiome and resistome of two captive python species: Burmese python (Python bivittatus) and reticulated python (Malayopython reticulatus), before and after environmental enrichment. We found that environmental enrichment was associated with increased α-diversity in Burmese pythons, as indicated by significantly higher ACE and observed species indices, while NMDS ordination revealed differences in the observed patterns of community composition between the two species. Pseudomonadota and Bacteroidota were dominant phyla in the gut microbiota of both python species, but their relative abundances responded differently to enrichment between hosts. Functional analyses suggested an enhanced metabolic potential in Burmese pythons, particularly in carbohydrate metabolism and environmental information processing, accompanied by increased abundance of carbohydrate-active enzymes. In addition, enrichment may influence the gut resistome, with Pseudomonadota contributing the majority of antibiotic resistance genes. Overall, our results demonstrate that environmental enrichment measures, such as dietary changes and improvements in water and air quality, are associated with changes in the gut microbiome and resistome of captive pythons in a host-dependent manner, highlighting the combined roles of diet and environmental conditions in the observed changes in the gut microbiota. These findings provide exploratory insights into the functional responses and host-microbiome evolution of reptile gut microbiota to captivity and have important implications for the management and welfare of captive animals.

records.title: Effect of continuous application of pig manure on soil antibiotic resistance genes.
records.abstract: The large-scale application of livestock and poultry manure in protected agriculture is common; however, research on the spread of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) from this practice remains limited. Herein, 16 S and metagenomic sequencing methods were used to investigate the effects of eight consecutive years of pig manure application on tetracycline (TC) antibiotics in protected soil and to evaluate the ecological consequences. In addition, the characteristics of soil ARGs and bacterial diversity were explored, and the potential hosts of ARGs in protected soil and the influence of environmental factors on these potential hosts and ARGs were preliminarily investigated. After 8 years of applying composted pig manure, the total tetracycline residues in the protected soil was as follows: commercial organic fertilizer soil > pig manure soil > rapeseed cake fertilizer soil. Soil enzymes indirectly affect ARG abundance by influencing the microbial community structure. g__unclassified_p__Acidobacteria and g__unclassified_c__Actinomycetia may be the two most important ARG hosts, with a highly significant positive correlation with 32 ARG subtypes. Total nitrogen (TN) and soil organic matter (SOM) significantly promoted the abundance of these two important potential hosts. Nocardioides, g__unclassified_o__Solirubrobacterales, Actinoplanes, and Methyloceanibacter are potential hosts for intI1. TC, Soil urease(S-UE), Soil acid phosphatase(ACP), Soil β-glucosidase(S-β-GC), TN, total phosphorus (TP), and SOM significantly promoted the abundance of potential intI1 hosts. Soil environmental factors collectively accounted for 72.27% of ARG variation, making them the most important factor affecting ARGs. Our research will support manure management in protected agriculture to reduce ARG spread.

records.title: Identification of Vibrio cholerae proteins that bind 3',3'-cyclic guanosine adenine dinucleotide.
records.abstract: Cyclic dinucleotides are used as signaling molecules in both antiphage defense and normal cellular functions. Horizontal gene transfer can introduce antiphage defense systems that encode specific signaling molecules into a new host. Whether these new signaling molecules interact with existing host signaling proteins and whether such interactions have evolutionary implications remain unknown. Vibrio cholerae represents an organism in which a new cyclic dinucleotide signaling molecule, 3',3'-cyclic guanosine adenine dinucleotide (3',3'-cGAMP) produced by DncV, is introduced by horizontal gene transfer of an antiphage system. 3',3'-cGAMP activates CapV phospholipase activity, leading to reduced growth and swim motility. To identify additional 3',3'-cGAMP-binding proteins, we performed a 3',3'-cGAMP-binding screen of the V. cholerae El Tor ORFeome. In addition to the expected 3',3'-cGAMP-binding proteins CapV and three V-cGAP proteins, this screen identified seven additional 3',3'-cGAMP-binding proteins that were previously found to bind c-di-GMP. These seven all bind to c-di-GMP with greater affinity, suggesting that these proteins do not bind 3',3'-cGAMP specifically. We assessed the function of 3',3'-cGAMP-binding proteins by testing the expression of DncV, CapV, or both in V. cholerae. Expression of DncV alone did not affect growth or swimming motility, in contrast to co-expression with CapV. In Escherichia coli, which lacks native 3',3'-cGAMP-signaling pathways, co-expression of CapV and DncV also led to reduced growth and swimming motility. In contrast, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which also lacks endogenous 3',3'-cGAMP, is less susceptible to CapV and DncV co-expression. Signaling nucleotides from antiphage systems primarily function in phage defense but have the potential to regulate other processes when the phage pressure subsides.IMPORTANCEIn this study, we systematically identified 3',3'-cGAMP-binding proteins in V. cholerae, which also uses the similar cyclic dinucleotide c-di-GMP for signaling. In addition to previously observed 3',3'-cGAMP-binding proteins, including 3',3'-cGAMP-activated phospholipase CapV and V-cGAP proteins, this screen identified seven new 3',3'-cGAMP-binding proteins that bound c-di-GMP as well. We found that both 3',3'-cGAMP production and CapV phospholipase activity were necessary and sufficient to inhibit growth and swimming motility as previously observed. In heterologous bacteria that use c-di-GMP but lack 3',3'-cGAMP-signaling pathways, 3',3'-cGAMP activation of CapV phospholipase was similarly required to inhibit growth and swimming motility as observed in V. cholerae. These results suggest that the acquisition of signaling nucleotides from antiphage systems may evolve to regulate cellular processes.
records.authors: Kim S-K, Carter JA, Park JH, Kung WC, Jiang X, Yildiz FH, Lee VT.

records.title: Antibiotic class shapes O-antigen-dependent phage outcomes in a clinical Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate.
records.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a high-priority opportunistic pathogen characterized by significant genetic plasticity and increasing multidrug resistance. Although phage-antibiotic combinations are increasingly explored to combat antimicrobial resistance, whether these interactions are synergistic or antagonistic and how different antibiotic classes influence phage replication and the subsequent development of resistance remain unclear. In this study, we examined combinations of the O-antigen-dependent phage phipa10 with amikacin (AMK), levofloxacin (LEV), or meropenem (MEM) against P. aeruginosa ZS-PA-35. At 24 h, the combinations showed antibiotic-dependent patterns of bacterial growth suppression. High concentrations of amikacin and meropenem reduced the extracellular yield of infectious phipa10. The highest tested levofloxacin concentration also reduced the recovered phage yield. Whole-genome sequencing of phage-resistant mutants showed that meropenem treatment drove large chromosomal deletions encompassing galU and hmgA, resulting in a characteristic brown pigmentation phenotype. LEV-selected isolates carried smaller deletions involving galU, whereas AMK-selected isolates shared a galU substitution. In a Galleria mellonella infection model, phipa10-antibiotic combinations improved host survival relative to either treatment alone, although the magnitude of the benefit varied across antibiotic classes. The meropenem combination yielded the highest observed survival proportion despite reduced phage yield in vitro. These results show that bacterial suppression, infectious phage yield, and resistance outcomes can diverge among the three tested antibiotic partners.IMPORTANCEPhage-antibiotic combinations may affect bacterial suppression, phage yield, and resistance-associated phenotypes differently. We compared three antibiotic partners in a single Pseudomonas aeruginosa-phage system. The observed growth, genetic, and larval survival outcomes varied across the tested treatments. Reduced phage yield did not preclude improved survival in the infection model. These observations support evaluating multiple outcomes when assessing a phage-antibiotic combination. Their broader relevance requires validation with additional isolates, phages, and antibiotics.

records.title: Sulfite disproportionation by Desulfotomaculum from marine sediments.
records.abstract: Sulfite disproportionation is a critical pathway of global sulfur cycle since primordial Earth, yet the microbial diversity underlying this process remains incompletely explored. Here, we report an autotrophic enrichment culture from marine sediments capable of producing both sulfate and sulfide by disproportionating sulfite. This culture was dominated (>95% relative abundance) by a novel bacterial strain closely related to Desulfotomaculum profundi. Genomic analysis revealed a complete pathway for dissimilatory sulfate reduction, which likely facilitates sulfite disproportionation by operating the enzymes for sulfate reduction to sulfite in reverse. Unlike the characterized species within the Desulfotomaculum genus, this highly enriched organism apparently lacked the physiological capacity to respire sulfate when tested with acetate and formate as electron donors, suggesting a specialized metabolic adaptation for sulfite disproportionation. Our findings represent the first experimental evidence linking sulfite disproportionation to the genus Desulfotomaculum. Given the widespread occurrence of functional genes across diverse ecosystems, we propose that Desulfotomaculum-mediated sulfite disproportionation is a biogeochemically significant yet underappreciated process in sulfur-enriched modern ecosystems.IMPORTANCEBacteria within the ubiquitous genus Desulfotomaculum (known as Desulfotomaculum subcluster Ia) are key actors in the sulfur cycle across diverse terrestrial and marine anoxic environments. Historically, cultivated strains have been characterized exclusively as sulfate reducers. Here, we expand the metabolic profile of this genus by characterizing a highly enriched Desulfotomaculum population capable of autotrophic sulfite disproportionation. In contrast to known Desulfotomaculum species, the enriched population showed no detectable sulfate reduction when tested with acetate or formate. These results indicate that Desulfotomaculum lineages can actively participate in sulfate formation and autotrophic carbon fixation, suggesting an expanded role in coupling the sulfur and carbon cycles across anoxic subsurface and sedimentary ecosystems.
records.authors: Su J-Y, Wu X-T, Bao P, Ren H-Y, Li S, Chen S-C.

records.title: The Fungal Response Regulator Skn7: Domain Architecture and Multifunctional Roles in Fungal Biology.
records.abstract: The two-component phosphorelay system (TCS) is an ancient signaling module that enables fungal adaptation to changing environments. It consists of a hybrid histidine kinase (HHK), a histidine phosphotransfer protein (HPt), and downstream response regulators (RRs). Among these, the nuclear response regulator Skn7 is unique to fungi and absent from mammalian and plant cells, making it an attractive antifungal target. This review integrates structural and functional evidence to describe the multi-layered regulatory architecture of Skn7 orthologs across fungal phyla. Structurally, Skn7 combines prokaryotic signaling with eukaryotic transcriptional features through a conserved receiver (REC) domain, a central coiled-coil oligomerization motif, and a winged helix-turn-helix heat shock factor (HSF) DNA-binding domain. Functionally, Skn7 coordinates oxidative stress responses through cross-talk with the osmotic and cell wall integrity (CWI) MAPK pathways while acting as both a transcriptional activator and co-repressor. Notably, Skn7 regulates fungal development, morphogenesis, secondary metabolism-including pigments, toxins, and volatile organic compounds involved in interspecific competition-and cell fate by controlling autolysis and programmed cell death cascades. Overall, this comprehensive review highlights the evolutionary plasticity and functional versatility of Skn7, supporting its potential as a therapeutic target against fungal infections.
records.authors: Hernández-Rojas DI, Coria R.

records.title: Bacterial vaginosis as a polymicrobial biofilm ecosystem: microbial interactions, host responses and therapeutic challenges.
records.abstract: The vaginal mucosa is a hormonally responsive barrier ecosystem in which epithelial integrity, immune tone and microbial composition are interconnected. In eubiotic states, estrogen-supported, Lactobacillus-dominated communities help maintain low pH, reinforce epithelial barrier function and modulate mucosal immunity through lactic acid and antimicrobial metabolites. Disruption of this equilibrium can lead to bacterial vaginosis (BV), a polymicrobial dysbiosis characterized by depletion of lactobacilli and formation of structured biofilms adherent to the vaginal epithelium. Genomic, transcriptomic and metabolomic studies increasingly support the view that BV reflects a spatially organized, metabolically integrated biofilm network rather than simple bacterial overgrowth. Gardnerella species are considered key early colonizers, forming an epithelial scaffold that recruits secondary anaerobes. Interspecies cross-feeding, glycan degradation, amine production and density-dependent regulation contribute to biofilm maturation, antimicrobial tolerance and persistence. These biofilms degrade mucus and weaken epithelial integrity through cytolytic and enzymatic activities, triggering low-grade mucosal inflammation with limited neutrophilic infiltration, favoring recurrence and increasing susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections and adverse reproductive outcomes. This review examines the establishment and organization of BV-associated polymicrobial biofilms in bacterial vaginosis, key interspecies interactions and virulence mechanisms, experimental approaches used to study these communities and implications of biofilm persistence for recurrence and emerging therapeutic strategies.
records.authors: Bernard L, Baud D, Stojanov M.

records.title: Changes in the Gut Microbiota Composition and Metabolic Pathways in Six-Week-Old HIV Exposed Breastfed Infants Receiving Antiretroviral Prophylaxis.
records.abstract: IntroductionUnderstanding the association of HIV exposure, antiretroviral therapy (ART) prophylaxis and human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) on the gut microbiota of breastfed infants is crucial for developing strategies to promote infant health. Our study explored gut microbiota diversity and development in breastfed infants, analysing the influence of nevirapine (NVP) in HIV Exposed infants and HMOs in HIV Unexposed infants.MethodsInfants delivered vaginally and exclusively breastfed were recruited from City Council Clinics in Harare, Zimbabwe, at six weeks postpartum. A total of 110 infants were enrolled, and stool samples were collected for shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Dried blood spots from HIV-exposed infants were analyzed for nevirapine using HPLC-MS/MS, and breast milk from HIV-uninfected mothers was analyzed for human milk oligosaccharides using UPLC-MS. Of the collected samples, 93 stool specimens passed all bioinformatics quality filters. Alpha diversity and beta diversity were assessed, and associations between microbial diversity and HIV exposure, nevirapine levels, and HMO concentrations were evaluated using MaAsLin2.ResultsOur analysis showed no significant differences in microbial diversity across various NVP concentrations in HE infants or in 3'SL and 6'SL in the HU infants group (p ≥ 0.05). HIV exposure was associated with higher levels of Stenotrophomonas maltophilia and Mediterraneibacter faecis (corrected p-values 2.08×10-5 and 0.00246), respectively. Moreover, HIV exposure was linked to changes in specific metabolic pathways.ConclusionAlthough overall diversity remained stable across NVP concentrations in HE infants and HMO levels in HU infants, specific taxa and functional pathways differed by HIV exposure, highlighting that compositional and functional changes can occur independently of global diversity metrics. Therefore, HIV exposure itself may influence gut microbiota composition and metabolic functions at species level, particularly with an increased abundance of specific bacteria and altered metabolic pathways leading to disturbances in vitamin metabolism.
records.authors: Mudhluli TE, Nel Van Zyl K, Kujawska M, Mashingaidze-Mano R, Marsh CC, Chitsike I, Zia N, Manasa J, Hall LJ, Gomo E, Zhou DT.

records.title: Cross-Cohort Transcriptomic and Oral Microbiome Analyses Identify Ferroptosis-Associated Signatures in Periodontitis and Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma.
records.abstract: BackgroundPeriodontitis (PD) and oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) have been investigated in relation to inflammation, oral microbial alterations, and iron/redox biology. Whether ferroptosis-associated expression patterns overlap across independently sampled periodontal and cancer cohorts remains uncertain. We characterized these patterns without presuming that the available datasets represent matched individuals or a temporal disease sequence.MethodsWe analyzed gingival single-cell RNA-sequencing data (GSE171213), an OSCC discovery expression cohort (GSE30784), and an independent oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma validation cohort (GSE13601). Periodontal microbial functional gene profiles (GSE54290) and a cross-study OSCC 16S abundance resource were examined separately. Analyses included cell annotation, KEGG ferroptosis gene-set scoring, sample- and cell type-level comparisons, differential expression, external transcriptomic signature validation, microbial diversity and abundance analyses, and LPS-stimulated cell-line RT-qPCR and ELISA measurements. The transcriptomic and microbial cohorts were not linked at the individual-patient level.ResultsQuality control retained 34,342 cells from 12 gingival samples (four healthy controls [HCs], five PD, and three treated periodontitis [PDT]), assigned to 11 annotated cell populations. Mean sample-level ferroptosis gene-set scores were 0.081 in HC, 0.114 in PD, and 0.076 in PDT; these descriptive scores do not measure ferroptotic cell death. SAT1 showed a positive PD-versus-HC association in cell type pseudobulk analysis (log2 fold change, 0.546; false discovery rate [FDR], 0.012) and positive effects across all three transcriptomic cohorts. A discovery-derived ferroptosis-associated OSCC signature achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.933 in GSE13601. Periodontal functional profiling identified 25 advanced PD-associated annotations (FDR ConclusionsIndependently sampled periodontal and OSCC cohorts show ferroptosis-associated transcriptomic changes, with SAT1 emerging as a cross-cohort candidate. Parallel microbial datasets identify disease-associated functional gene and taxonomic differences but do not demonstrate within-patient host-microbe interactions or causal mediation. LPS-exposed cell-line measurements show expression changes in selected ferroptosis-associated markers, not ferroptotic cell death or functional resistance. The results are exploratory associations; in the absence of direct ferroptosis assays, paired longitudinal cohorts, and prospective clinical validation, they cannot establish a disease-progression mechanism, clinically deployable biomarker or therapeutic efficacy.

records.title: Knockdown of fibrillarin reveals cell- and virus-dependent restriction of henipavirus replication and enhanced antiviral immune signalling
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  The  henipavirus genus includes several highly pathogenic zoonotic viruses that lack medical countermeasures. The 2’-O-methyltransferase fibrillarin (FBL) has been identified by genome-wide functional genomics studies as a henipavirus pro-viral factor. While FBL is a potential target for host-directed antiviral therapeutics, its impact on henipavirus replication in cell types relevant to henipavirus disease has not been explored. Here we demonstrate that depleting cellular FBL using short interfering RNAs (siRNAs) has varying impacts on henipavirus replication, depending on cell type and virus. FBL depletion in small airway epithelial cells (HSAEC1-KT) significantly impaired viral gene transcription for Hendra virus (HeV) genotypes 1 and 2 (HeV-g1, HeV-g2), and Nipah virus (NiV) Bangladesh strain (NiV-B), but not NiV Malaysia (NiV-M) strain or Cedar virus (CedV). Conversely, reduced FBL expression in bronchial epithelial (NuLi-1) cells, aortic endothelial (Telo HAEC) cells or neuroblastoma (BE(2)-M17) cells did not inhibit HeV-g1 replication. Transcriptomic analyses revealed that impaired virus replication in FBL knockdown cells was associated with enhanced activation of innate immune pathways and robust upregulation of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs). Together, these findings demonstrate a virus- and cell-type dependent impact of FBL on henipavirus replication and support a role for FBL in modulation of the antiviral innate immune response.
records.authors: Sathiqu RM, Rootes CL, Brice AM, Caputo AT, Williams SM, Rodrigues CHM, Farr RJ, Alexander MR, Stewart CR.

records.title: A hidden T-DNA-linked inversion-duplication is associated with a light-dependent Arabidopsis mutant phenotype.
records.abstract: Key messageA hidden T-DNA-linked genomic rearrangement alters gene dosage and exacerbates light-dependent phenotypes in Arabidopsis, highlighting the importance of structural genome validation for reliable interpretation of mutantphenotypes. T-DNA insertion mutants are widely used to study gene function, yet associated genomic alterations can confound phenotypic interpretation. We investigated mutants affecting mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase (MDH1) and heterodimeric NAD-dependent malic enzyme (ME1/ME2) under different photoperiods and irradiance regimes. Under long-day conditions, mutant combinations showed no major phenotypic differences from wild type. Under short-day, low-light conditions, mdh1.1 me2 mutants were markedly smaller than wild type and, unexpectedly, more severely affected than mdh1.1 me1 me2 triple mutants. ME1 was undetectable in mdh1.1 me2, indicating that both genotypes effectively lack heterodimeric NAD-ME. Whole-genome analysis identified a 137-kbp inverted duplication downstream of the MDH1 insertion in mdh1.1 me2, absent from the triple mutant. The original mdh1.1 population segregated for the severe phenotype, whereas an independent mdh1.2 allele did not reproduce it, linking the defect to the mdh1.1-associated rearrangement. The duplication increased gene dosage and transcript abundance, particularly under low light. Proteomics detected only five of 38 proteins encoded within the duplicated region, including phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase 1 (PEPC1). mdh1.1 me2 accumulated oxaloacetate-derived amino acids and exhibited altered carbon/nitrogen balance. These findings suggest that the duplication contributes to the phenotype, potentially through increased PEPC1 activity and consequent perturbation of carbon-nitrogen metabolism. However, interactions with MDH1 deficiency cannot be excluded, making PEPC1 a candidate contributor rather than the sole causal determinant. Our results highlight how T-DNA-linked structural variation can confound condition-dependent phenotypes and emphasize the need for structural validation of insertion loci, particularly given the widespread use of Agrobacterium-mediated DNA transfer in plant genome editing.

records.title: Humic acid with manure promotes fungal necromass carbon accumulation in saline-alkali soils.
records.abstract: Microbial necromass carbon is increasingly recognized as a vital precursor for stable soil organic carbon (SOC). However, how diverse organic amendments regulate its accumulation and the underlying mechanisms in saline-alkali soils remains poorly understood. Based on a 4-year field experiment and an additional 13C-labeling incubation, we investigated the variation in fungal necromass carbon (FNC) and bacterial necromass carbon (BNC) under four organic amendments (organic manure (OM), organic manure plus crop straw (OM + CS), organic manure plus humic acid (OM + HA), and an unamended control). OM stimulated nitrogen mineralization through leucine aminopeptidase activity, while structural C sources in crop straw amendments (OM + CS) enhanced cellulolytic enzyme activities and biomass accumulation. In contrast, OM + HA upregulated N-acetyl-glucosaminidase at 0-20 cm and alkaline phosphatase activity at 20-40 cm, concurrently enriching K-strategist fungi (e.g., Basidiomycota) through deterministic assembly. This was accompanied by more complex, highly modular fungal networks. Glucose-derived C was preferentially retained in the FNC pool after 150 days, with 13C-labeling confirming FNC contributes 28.8%-30.4% of 13C-SOC versus merely 4.6%-4.7% for BNC. While OM + CS promoted necromass via biomass-enzyme co-enhancement, OM + HA synergizes enzyme-driven FNC/BNC co-transformation with K-strategist fungal enrichment and increased 13C-BNC efficiency by 19.0% versus OM. These findings highlight OM + HA as a promising strategy for promoting microbial necromass C accumulation in degraded saline-alkali ecosystems.

records.title: Tourmaline enhances nitrogen removal efficiency in partial Nitrification/Anammox systems via an adsorption Enrichment-Gene Regulation-Electron transfer triple mechanism.
records.abstract: The partial nitrification (PN) / anaerobic ammonium oxidation (anammox) coupled process offers distinct advantages, including reduced aeration energy consumption and elimination of organic carbon dependence. Nevertheless, its full-scale application faces several critical challenges, particularly the difficulty in sustaining a stable nitrite accumulation rate (NAR) during the PN stage, coupled with the inherently long doubling time of anaerobic ammonium oxidation bacteria (AnAOB) in the anammox stage. Natural tourmaline (Tur), a mineral distinguished by its unique physicochemical characteristics and potential for microbial regulation, provides a promising approach to overcoming these limitations. Experimental results indicated that Tur promoted the enrichment of functional microorganisms (e.g., Nitrosomonas) and the nitrogen removal efficiency (NRE) of the PN/Anammox_Tur system showed a relative increase of 14.77%. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations further demonstrated that the active sites on Tur surfaces exhibited selective adsorption affinity for key substrates-namely NH4+, NO2-, and O2-thereby providing a theoretical foundation for Tur-enhanced NRE in PN/Anammox system. Analysis of microbial community structure revealed that Tur induced a significant restructuring of the microbial consortium. Moreover, metagenomic analysis confirmed the directional reconstruction of metabolic gene networks and pathways, and elucidated the differential regulation of electron transport chains by Tur via its micro-electric field. This study proposed and refined a novel mechanistic framework-termed the "Adsorption Enrichment-Gene Regulation-Electron Transfer" triple mechanism-through which Tur enhances the NRE of the PN/Anammox system. These findings provide a theoretical basis for applying natural mineral materials, particularly tourmaline, advancing mineral-based materials for biological nitrogen removal and enhancing their engineering-scale implementation feasibility.

records.title: Facilitating efficient anammox bacteria enrichment with loofah sponge: coupled roles of physical retention, slow-release carbon supply, and metabolic synergy.
records.abstract: Anaerobic ammonium oxidation (anammox) provides an energy-efficient and sustainable strategy for nitrogen removal. However, the slow growth and challenging enrichment of anaerobic ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (AnAOB) remain key constraints on its engineering application. In this study, the biodegradable biomass material loofah sponge was introduced into the system to enrich AnAOB from nitrification-denitrification sludge and achieve a rapid commencement of the anammox process. During the AnAOB maturation period, the system achieved TIN (Total Inorganic Nitrogen) and NH4+-N removal efficiencies of 66.8% and 99.6%, respectively. Extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) analysis indicated that biofilms formed on the loofah sponge exhibited a high protein-to-polysaccharide (PN/PS) ratio, thereby enhancing microbial aggregation and facilitating AnAOB enrichment. Analysis of the microbial community structure showed that the relative abundance of the key anammox genus Candidatus Brocadia in the loofah sponge significantly increased from 0.03% in the seed sludge to 17.07%. Metagenomic analysis detected genes associated with cellulose and hemicellulose degradation, while the effluent COD profile supported gradual loofah sponge biodegradation and soluble organic matter transformation. The loofah sponge also exhibited higher abundances of genes related to central carbon metabolism, the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway, and heme biosynthesis, indicating greater metabolic potential. Overall, AnAOB enrichment on loofah sponge may have resulted from the combined effects of physical biomass retention, gradual biodegradation, and associated microbial interactions. This study offers a feasible pathway for integrating agricultural waste valorization with low-carbon nitrogen removal and steers the anammox process toward greater economic and environmental sustainability.

records.title: Engineering rhizosphere microbial consortia for soil bioremediation: Mechanisms, field constraints, and evidence-based design.
records.abstract: Soil contamination continues to threaten ecosystem health and agricultural productivity worldwide. However, rhizosphere-mediated bioremediation has emerged as a nature-inspired, sustainable approach for mitigating these impacts. This review advocates field-scale implementation of rhizosphere microbiome engineering by exploiting interactions among plants, microorganisms, and soil. Unlike previous reviews that primarily summarize rhizosphere-mediated remediation processes, it integrates mechanistic, ecological, and engineering perspectives to identify critical barriers limiting field performance. This review synthesizes recent advances in rhizosphere microbiome engineering, with an emphasis on root-exudate manipulation, synthetic microbial communities (SynComs), biochar-assisted remediation, and multi-omics technologies. The evidence reviewed indicates that root exudates are key regulators of microbial recruitment, biofilm formation, and expression of contaminant-degrading genes, while engineered microbial consortia enhance functional complementarity and pollutant transformation. A comparative analysis of laboratory and field studies reveals substantial performance gaps, with highly efficient degradation observed under controlled conditions often declining following field deployment because of microbial competition, environmental variability, and contaminant sorption dynamics. The review further shows that integration of SynComs with biochar carriers and precision root-exudate engineering can improve microbial establishment and remediation efficiency. Advances in metagenomics, metabolomics, and systems biology are enabling more predictive design and monitoring of rhizosphere processes. Collectively, this review provides a mechanistic synthesis, identifies key translational bottlenecks, and outlines practical directions for developing scalable rhizosphere-based remediation technologies.

records.title: Whole-proteome structure/function prediction in uropathogenic E. coli reveals previously missed host-microbe and microbe-phage interaction pathways.
records.abstract: The rapid advancement of high-throughput sequencing technologies has vastly increased the number of known protein sequences, but the experimental characterization of their structures and functions lags behind. This gap in knowledge impedes our understanding of biological mechanisms of these proteins, hinders the interpretation of high-throughput experiments, and exposes a significant challenge in modern biology: deducing the structural and functional information of proteins based on their sequences. Most computational approaches rely on homology with well-annotated proteins, yet many proteins lack identifiable homologues, reducing the power of this approach. Here, we integrated cutting-edge protein structure and function prediction methods to develop a complete sequence-structure-function pipeline that predicts structures and functions based on primary sequences. We applied this pipeline to predict the structure and function of all proteins in Escherichia coli UTI89, a model strain of uropathogenic E. coli. Based on the predicted functions, we performed enrichment analysis on the whole genome and revealed the possible roles and related biological mechanisms of poorly annotated proteins in this organism. Moreover, the performance of our pipeline was further validated through detailed case studies of the UTI89_C0931 and ybtS genes. Finally, we compiled the UTI89 structure and function database (https://seq2fun.dcmb.med.umich.edu/UTI89), offering it as a crucial resource to aid researchers in elucidating the roles of unannotated proteins. This database aims to bridge critical knowledge gaps in microbial pathogenicity and resistance, enhancing our capacity to tackle emerging health threats.

records.title: Soil amendments reshape alpine meadow microbial communities across degradation gradients by modulating nutrient availability.
records.abstract: Climate change and overgrazing have led to the continued degradation of alpine meadows on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, thereby severely impairing the ecosystem services provided by these grasslands. Soil amendments are an important strategy for restoring degraded grasslands; however, the regulatory effects of different amendment measures across varying degradation gradients and the underlying microbial response mechanisms remain unclear. This study systematically investigated the effects of three soil amendments (humic acid, superabsorbent polymer, and Bacillus subtilis) on soil physicochemical properties and microbial community structure in mildly, moderately, and severely degraded alpine meadows. The results indicated that the regulatory effects of soil amendments are significantly dependent on the degradation gradient: In the severe degradation stage, amendments significantly increased available nutrients, lowered pH, and alleviated alkalization, whereas their regulatory effects were limited in the mild degradation stage. Amendments selectively altered the abundance of microbial groups involved in organic matter degradation, nitrogen cycling, and stress-tolerant symbiosis. Humic acid demonstrated the optimal regulatory effect in the mild degradation stage, whereas superabsorbent polymers and Bacillus subtilis were more suitable for restoration in the moderate and severe degradation stages. Redundancy analysis indicated that bacterial communities were primarily subject to deterministic selection by soil pH, available potassium, and organic matter gradients, with the intensity of environmental selection increasing with increasing degradation severity; fungal communities exhibited significant environmental responses only in the moderate degradation stage, while stochastic processes dominated community assembly in the mild and severe degradation stages. In summary, alpine meadows at various stages of degradation require differentiated remediation strategies. Precise, stage-specific remediation tailored to degradation severity can facilitate synergistic restoration of the soil-microbial system, providing a theoretical basis and practical guidance for restoring degraded alpine meadows on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.

records.title: Core effectors of the Fusarium pan-effectome contribute to host specificity.
records.abstract: Fusarium fungi cause economically important diseases of cereal crops, including Fusarium head blight, ear blight, and root rot. Central to these interactions are secreted effector proteins that manipulate host biology to promote infection. In turn, plants have evolved to recognize effector activity to activate immune responses and restrict disease. Despite their importance, the diversity, conservation, and evolution of Fusarium effectors remain poorly understood. Here, we present the Fusarium sambucinum Species complex Effector Compendium (FUSEC), a sequence-defined pan-effectome constructed from 188 high-quality genomes representing 27 species. FUSEC comprises 4,057 sequence-defined effector families, including a conserved soft-core repertoire of 235 families present in at least 95% of isolates. Structure-guided comparisons reorganized these conserved families into 184 structure-defined groups, revealing relationships that extend beyond sequence similarity and identifying similarities to numerous experimentally characterized fungal (a)virulence factors. Despite their broad conservation, soft-core families exhibited substantial within-family sequence diversity, and analyses of diversifying selection identified 44 candidate families undergoing adaptive evolution. Functional screening revealed that the majority of these candidates altered wheat immune responses, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene deletions in Fusarium graminearum demonstrated that multiple conserved effectors contribute to cultivar-dependent Fusarium head blight severity.
records.authors: Blackman CT, Aguayo-Limon A, Lei T, Zarrouki M, Balcerzak M, Witte T, Rampitsch C, Desveaux D, Subramaniam R.
