records.title: Bacterial diversity associated with Streblidae flies parasitizing cave-dwelling bats from northeastern Brazil.
records.abstract: Bats (Chiroptera) are highly diverse mammals that play key ecological roles and harbor a wide range of microorganisms, yet the microbiome of their ectoparasitic flies remains poorly understood. This study characterized and compared the bacterial microbiomes associated with two bat-ectoparasite systems, Pteronotus gymnonotus-Trichobius johnsonae and Desmodus rotundus-Trichobius parasiticus, from cave-dwelling bat populations in northeastern Brazil using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Sixty-eight bat fly samples were successfully sequenced, and 67 were retained for downstream ecological analyses after quality filtering. Bacterial communities were dominated by members of the classes Gammaproteobacteria and Alphaproteobacteria, with Arsenophonus, Bartonella, and unresolved endosymbiont-associated taxa among the most abundant bacterial groups. Alpha-diversity patterns varied according to the metric considered: observed ASV richness was influenced by bat fly species, sex, and their interaction, Shannon diversity differed according to streblid fly species and sex, and Faith's phylogenetic diversity differed between bat fly sexes. Notably, male T. johnsonae exhibited greater observed ASV richness than females, whereas no significant sex difference was detected in T. parasiticus. Beta-diversity analyses consistently revealed differences in bacterial community composition between the two bat-ectoparasite systems, while the influence of sex was system-dependent, with significant differentiation between T. johnsonae males and females but not between sexes of T. parasiticus in phylogenetically informed analyses. Differential abundance analysis further identified Romboutsia, Bartonella, Bacteroides, and an unclassified Pseudomonadota genus as discriminatory taxa among groups. Overall, these findings reveal distinct bacterial diversity and composition patterns between the two bat-ectoparasite systems and indicate that sex-associated microbiome variation is not uniform across bat fly species.
records.journal: Comparative immunology, microbiology and infectious diseases
records.authors: de Mello VVC, Funnicelli MIG, Barbier E, Micolta LFB, Machado RZ, Barros-Battesti DM, Pinheiro DG, André MR.

records.title: Planktonic community rescue under herbicide pollution: the driving factors and ecological consequences.
records.abstract: Community rescue enables ecological communities to persist under otherwise lethal environmental stress through adaptive changes. The present study addresses what community attributes may predict the chance of rescue, and the ecological consequences associated with community rescue. Replicate aquatic microcosms were set up from each of 20 base planktonic communities, and were exposed to a gradient of concentrations of an herbicide. Planktonic respiration rate was measured as a surrogate of community activity, to infer the potential of community rescue. We found that the rescue potential depended on planktonic taxonomical composition but not diversity per se. We then studied in detail planktonic communities that rescued from a specific high concentration of herbicide pollution. Community rescue was accompanied with multiple ecological costs, including reduced taxonomical diversity and primary productivity, as well as simplified planktonic interaction networks. A shift from producer-dominated toward decomposer-dominated taxa was observed; specifically, certain heterotrophic bacteria and fungi became more abundant at the expense of microalgae. A number of taxa highly resistant to glyphosate were identified. Our results highlight that community rescue under severe herbicide pollution may be associated with unwanted ecological costs, and studies of this kind may help to search for microbial taxa capable of pollutant biodegradation.
records.authors: Zhou DH, Chu XL, Xu B, Zhang QG.

records.title: Pan-genome insights into the evolutionary dynamics and functional diversification of genes in monkeypox virus.
records.abstract: Monkeypox virus (MPXV) continues to emerge as a global health threat. While genetically diverse, its genomic structure and evolution remain undercharacterized. This study analyzed 157 non-redundant MPXV genomes (subtypes Ia, Ib, IIa, IIb), identifying 183 core and 222 non-core genes via pan-genome analysis-indicative of an open pan-genome. Over half (55.8%) of MPXV genes show gene number variation. Non-core genes exhibit a higher ratio of insertions/deletions compared to core genes. Additionally, selection pressure analysis indicated that non-core genes are more prone to positive selection. Furthermore, interaction analysis revealed that core viral proteins target immune-related human pathways, while non-core proteins engage with viral infection-associated proteins. These results deepen our understanding of MPXV evolution and inform future research directions.
records.authors: Liu Y, Tang Y, Xu Y, Long X, Zhu Z.

records.title: Genome-wide identification and functional analysis of SR proteins in wheat reveal their roles in heat stress tolerance.
records.abstract: Serine/arginine-rich (SR) proteins play critical roles in pre-mRNA splicing and stress responses in plants. Here, we identified 60 SR genes (TaSRs) in wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) through a genome-wide survey and classified them into seven subfamilies based on phylogenetic relationships. The TaSRs were unevenly distributed across the wheat genome, with the highest numbers on chromosomes 1 and 4. Gene structure and motif analyses revealed conserved exon organization and subfamily-specific motif patterns. Using Y2H, LCI, and BiFC assays, we found that 12 of 14 representative TaSR proteins physically interacted with TaU1-70K, the wheat U1-70K protein and a core component of the U1 snRNP complex essential for pre-mRNA splicing, thereby supporting their conserved association with U1 snRNP during spliceosome assembly. Expression profiling indicated tissue-preferential expression and induction of multiple TaSRs under diverse abiotic and hormone treatments. Notably, heat stress altered the splicing patterns of TaSR30 and TaSR45, and heterologous overexpression of either gene in Arabidopsis enhanced seedling thermotolerance. Collectively, our work provides a comprehensive resource for the wheat SR gene family and highlights candidate TaSR genes for improving heat stress resilience.
records.authors: Xu W, Gao Y, Ni S, Li M, Yan K, Guo Q.

records.title: Extracellular vesicle packaging of a supercluster-encoded antimicrobial combination with enhanced potency against fungal biofilms
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Bacterial specialized metabolites are bioactive compounds that have been mined extensively as antibacterials, antifungals, and other drugs. They are widely used as experimental probes of complex biological systems. Since their discovery, their functional characteristics have typically been investigated as single, soluble compounds. The discoveries in this work expand this model. First, we report the co-packaging in extracellular vesicles (EVs) of two specialized metabolite complexes, candicidin and antimycin A, the products of a supercluster of biosynthetic genes, by a  Streptomyces soil isolate. Secondly, we report that the products of this supercluster have synergistic antimicrobial activity against fungal biofilms, whereas biofilms are tolerant to the individual compounds. Finally, we show that co-packaging these compounds in EVs ensures simultaneous delivery with enhanced potency. This research advances understanding of the elegant complexity that shapes the evolution and function of bacterial specialized metabolites. In particular, the enhanced antibiofilm activity of co-packaged metabolites compared to individual soluble compounds is notable given the relevance of biofilms to microbial ecology and to pathogenesis. Our work supports the evolution of coordinated activity of specialized metabolites to counter conditional environmental challenges, and highlights co-packaging in EVs as one mechanism for secretion and co-delivery of combinations of bioactive molecules.
records.authors: Meyer KJ, Chow V, Piliouras E, Lee Y, Ostapska H, Ojeda Valencia O, Ben Makhlouf I, Robbins N, Cowen LE, Nodwell JR.

records.title: Genome-wide analysis of the annexin gene family in alfalfa (  Medicago sativa  L.) and functional characterization of  MsANN22  under drought stress
records.abstract: Annexins are a conserved family of calcium-dependent phospholipid-binding proteins that participate in diverse plant stress responses. However, the annexin gene family in Medicago sativa and the molecular mechanisms underlying annexin-mediated drought tolerance remain largely unexplored. In this study, 73  MsANN genes were identified in the alfalfa genome. Their phylogenetic relationships, synteny, conserved motifs, gene structures, and promoter cis-acting elements were systematically analyzed. Synteny analysis revealed 75 segmental/whole-genome duplication-associated gene pairs but no tandem duplications, indicating that large-scale duplication was the major driver of  MsANN family expansion. The  MsANN promoters contained ABA- and drought-responsive elements. Expression profiling identified MsANN22 as a strongly drought-responsive gene encoding a cytoplasm-localized protein.  MsANN22 overexpression enhanced drought tolerance in both Arabidopsis thaliana and alfalfa: in Arabidopsis,  MsANN22 overexpression promoted seed germination under osmotic stress, whereas in alfalfa it enhanced antioxidant capacity, with superoxide dismutase and peroxidase activities reaching 1.38- and 1.70-fold those of wild-type plants, respectively. Consistently,  MsANN22 -overexpressing alfalfa accumulated approximately 20% less malondialdehyde and exhibited reduced H O and O • accumulation, as indicated by DAB and NBT staining. Yeast two-hybrid and luciferase complementation assays further supported physical interactions of MsANN22 with MsIAA and MsPR-10. These findings provide insight into the molecular mechanism by which  MsANN22 mediates drought tolerance and offer a candidate gene for improving drought resistance in alfalfa.
records.authors: Sheng Z, Jiang G, Wang J, He H, Du P, Li H, Meng Z, Shao Q, Li H, Xie Q.

records.title: Nucleic Acid Aptamer-Based and Oligonucleotide Hybridization Biosensors for the Detection of Helicobacter pylori: Recent Advances, Transduction Mechanisms and Point-of-Care Perspectives
records.abstract: Helicobacter pylori infects about half of the world's population and is classified as a group 1 carcinogen, yet routine diagnosis still depends on methods that are invasive, instrument-heavy or insensitive at low bacterial burden. Nucleic-acid aptamers—short single-stranded DNA or RNA oligonucleotides isolated by SELEX—are chemically synthesised, thermally robust and programmable recognition elements for H. pylori biosensors, whereas sequence-complementary oligonucleotide probes detect bacterial genomic and ribosomal nucleic acids (genosensors). This review synthesises the 2019–2026 literature on both classes and keeps them explicitly separate. We examine whole-bacterium and recombinant-protein SELEX together with post-SELEX truncation and spacer engineering; the validated target spectrum, from whole cells and surface antigens to CagA, Hsp60, BabA and HpaA; electrochemical, optical, mass-sensitive and microfluidic transduction; and nucleic-acid circuitry, nanozyme and nanomaterial amplification. Six comparative tables summarise targets, platform performance, nanomaterial roles, amplification schemes, point-of-care formats and remaining barriers. Reported limits of detection reach 1 CFU mL⁻¹ for whole cells, 0.017 ng mL⁻¹ to 0.429 nM for proteins and 0.32 fM to 0.098 µM for nucleic acids, with preliminary clinical agreement against the ¹³C-urea breath test and PCR. Interface stability, standardisation, multiplexing, extension of protein-SELEX to VacA and urease, and multi-centre validation remain the main obstacles to routine deployment.
records.authors: Zhao Y, Cheng H, Zhou S, He L, Lu X.

records.title: A phage-encoded GapR nucleoid-associated protein binds a bacterial GapR to deactivate it via an inhibitory hetero-oligomer mechanism.
records.abstract: Nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) play key roles in bacterial chromosome organization and cellular processes. Recent work identified GapR as an essential NAP that is ubiquitous in α-proteobacteria. GapR structures revealed that the GapR dimer can form dimer of dimers in the presence of DNA to create a DNA-encasing clamp and data showed that GapR is required for bacterial replication as it recruits topoisomerases to regions of overtwisted DNA. Interestingly, diverse phages that infect α-proteobacteria encode GapR homologs. To gain insight into how phage GapRs may impact their cellular homologs we performed structure/function analyses on the Roseobacterial and Roseophage RDJLΦ1 GapR proteins. Crystal structures revealed that the RDJLΦ1 GapR structure differs from that of the bacterial GapR in a way that is incompatible with DNA binding. Cellular localization and fluorescence binding assays confirmed that the RDJLΦ1 phage GapR does not bind DNA. Strikingly, we show that the RDJLΦ1 GapR and Roseobacterial GapR can form heterodimers that are unable to bind DNA, suggesting the phage GapR may act as a bacterial GapR poison. This was further supported by cellular studies. Collectively these studies reveal a unique autoinhibitory mechanism by which a phage encoded NAP impacts DNA binding by the host NAP.
records.authors: Schumacher MA, Stodgell MB, Salinas R, Yadav S, Leung K, Kwiatkowski LM, Ellis PK, Zhang H, Guo MS.

records.title: A scaffold for success: The many phases of herpesvirus capsid assembly.
records.abstract: Viruses are masters of cellular reorganization and self-assembly processes, including the formation of a protein capsid that protects and traffics the viral genome throughout the cell. One example is Herpesviruses, a group of enveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses that establish lifelong, latent infections in a wide range of hosts, including humans. These large viruses assemble an ~125-nm capsid in the nucleus through a coordinated series of steps that culminates in packaging of DNA genomes up to 225 kilobases in length and nuclear egress to the cytoplasm. Despite more than three decades of study, the precise mechanisms underlying herpesvirus capsid assembly remain unclear. Central to this process is the Scaffold protein, which supports capsid growth and ensures proper capsid geometry. Here, we revisit evidence suggesting that the Scaffold functions as more than a structural support. We highlight prior observations indicating that it may promote the formation of nuclear capsid assembly sites through self-interactions. By integrating these findings with recent structural studies, we identify key gaps in our understanding of herpesvirus capsid assembly and areas that warrant renewed investigation.
records.journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Molecular basis of disease
records.authors: Gordon SA, Latifi T, Pan XA, Draganova EB.

records.title: Start‑up and functional performance assessment of electron-shuttling-driven microalgal-anammox process.
records.abstract: The anaerobic ammonium oxidation (anammox) process has received extensive attention because of its low energy consumption and high nitrogen removal efficiency. Nevertheless, its long start-up period limits practical application. In this study, a microalgae-bacteria symbiotic system (ABSS) based on Chlorella vulgaris (C. vulgaris) was established to investigate its effects on anammox start-up and nitrogen and phosphorus removal. The introduction of C. vulgaris shortened the start-up time from 68 to 46 days, corresponding to a 32 % reduction. After 210 days of operation, the nitrogen removal rate (NRR) and phosphorus removal rate (PRR) in the microalgae-bacteria symbiotic reactor (RAM) were 21 % and 25 % higher than those in the control reactor (RA), respectively. The concentration of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) derived from C. vulgaris, as quantified via total organic carbon measurement, was 297.73 ± 8.55 mg/L. Spectroscopic analyses suggested the presence of humic-like substances and quinone-related structures in the EPS, indicating a potential role in electron transfer. At 100 mg/L, EPS increased hydrazine dehydrogenase (HDH) activity by 49 % relative to the control group. After CoQ extraction, EPS restored HDH activity more effectively than exogenous coenzyme Q (CoQ). Metagenomic analysis showed higher abundances of genes associated with photosynthesis, carbon fixation, and nitrogen metabolism. These findings imply that EPS-mediated electron transfer and strengthened HDH activity may have contributed to the establishment of anammox activity and the shortened start-up period. Overall, this study highlights microalgal integration as a potential strategy for accelerating anammox startup and improving simultaneous nitrogen and phosphorus removal.

records.title: Burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance associated with modifiable human antibiotic consumption: An observational study.
records.abstract: BackgroundHuman antibiotic use is widely believed to contribute to the evolution and maintenance of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in bacterial pathogens. While antibiotic stewardship should thus discourage use in situations where AMR-related harms outweigh clinical benefit, evidence to inform this assessment of tradeoffs is lacking, most notably in low-resource settings where gaps in antibiotic access persist. Quantitative understanding of use-resistance relationships is thus necessary as countries navigate commitments from the 2024 UN General Assembly resolution to reduce AMR burden by 2030.Methods and findingsWe used global surveillance data on AMR prevalence from 2000 to 2018 representing over 30 million bacterial isolates from 114 countries, along with antibiotic consumption estimates for each country and year, to estimate elasticity relationships between AMR and antibiotic exposure. Our analyses addressed 16 bacterial pathogens and antibiotic consumption across 7 drug classes, controlling for country-level health and development indicators via weighted regression models. Across pathogens, evidence that AMR is associated with population-level antibiotic exposure is strongest for Acinetobacter spp., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Escherichia coli. In a modeled counterfactual scenario, we estimate that 10% lower levels of antibiotic use, in comparison to current levels, across classes, would be associated with 38,000 (95% confidence interval: 36,000-41,000) fewer annual deaths attributable to AMR globally. Although substantial, this total represents only 0.50% of estimated bacterial disease mortality. In sub-Saharan Africa, where risk of death due to bacterial disease is greatest, the modeled avertible burden of AMR-attributable deaths comprises only 0.34% of bacterial disease mortality. Key limitations of the study include reliance on ecological relationships to infer modifiable burden, and under-representation of low-resource settings in surveillance data on antibiotic consumption and AMR.ConclusionsOur findings suggest near-term achievable reductions in AMR-attributable deaths may be modest relative to the persisting burden of bacterial disease mortality. These estimates should inform assessments of the potential benefits and harms of restrictive versus permissive antibiotic use paradigms in epidemiologically distinct settings.

records.title: E2 displacement of CIP2A from TOPBP1 activates the DNA damage response during papillomavirus life cycles.
records.abstract: The papillomavirus life cycle is linked to epithelial differentiation, and the virus manipulates differentiation to facilitate viral production. One such manipulation is the activation of the DNA damage response (DDR), which promotes viral replication via homologous recombination. Here, we show that the papillomavirus transcription/replication/segregation factor E2 activates the DDR. During differentiation, E2 attenuates sirtuin 1 (SIRT1) activity, enhances the acetylation of DDR factors, and displaces cancerous inhibitor of protein phosphatase 2A (CIP2A) from DNA topoisomerase II-binding protein 1 (TOPBP1), resulting in CIP2A-mediated inhibition of protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) and ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM) activation. E2 associates with TOPBP1 and ATM while reducing TOPBP1-ATR complexes and ataxia-telangiectasia and Rad3-related (ATR) activation. This ATM-high, ATR-low DDR phenotype promotes viral replication and cell proliferation. We observe this DDR activation in E2-expressing keratinocytes, human papillomavirus 16 (HPV16)-positive cells, Mus musculus papillomavirus 1 (MmuPV1)-induced lesions, HPV-positive head and neck cancer cell lines, and HPV16-positive patient-derived xenografts. ATM inhibition preferentially kills E2-expressing cells, supporting ATM signaling as a potential therapeutic target in HPV-associated disease retaining E2 expression and episomal genomes.

records.title: Staphylococcus warneri MN336185 from Fermented Rice Water: a Multifunctional Probiotic with Anti-pathogenic and Longevity Benefits in C. elegans.
records.abstract: Fermented ecosystems serve as critical reservoirs for functionally diverse microorganisms with applications in food safety and nutraceuticals. This study focuses on Staphylococcus warneri MN336185 (SW), a non-traditional probiotic strain isolated from fermented rice water and evaluating its probiotic and bio-preservative properties. SW demonstrated significant gastrointestinal and oxidative stress tolerance, high epithelial cytocompatibility (> 80%), non-hemolytic safety, and an exceptional cholesterol assimilation efficiency of 85%. Moreover, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) confirmed genomic biosafety, establishing the absence of acquired enterotoxins, superantigens, ica-dependent biofilm determinants, and most transmissible antibiotic resistance elements. Studies on the host-microbe interface confirmed strong adherence of SW to HT-29 cells with proportionate competitive anti-adhesion potential against Salmonella enterica and Escherichia coli. The strain could also upregulate tight-junction proteins, claudins and zona occludens, indicating barrier-protective effects. In Caenorhabditis elegans, supplementation of SW as live feed enhanced lifespan, pharyngeal pumping, locomotory abilities, and resistance to pathogens. Further, challenge tests involving incorporation of live cells or cell-free supernatant of SW into rice-based matrices resulted in significant, time-dependent reduction of pathogens with a 4 log₁₀ CFU decrease during refrigerated storage. Collectively, these observations could establish S. warneri MN336185 as a multifunctional probiotic strain with potential application in functional food and natural biopreservation strategies.
records.authors: Prakash V, Madhavan A, Babu P, Vanuopadath M, Jayakumar A, Raveendran A, Abhinand K, Sain T, Sasidharan NB, Hely S, Alphonse J, Nair BG, Pal S.

records.title: Field Evaluation of a Low-cost, Simplified Method to Detect and Characterize Toxigenic  V. cholerae  O1 from Environmental Water in Lagos, Nigeria
records.abstract: Cholera is caused by toxigenic  Vibrio cholerae serogroups O1 or O139 and is transmitted through contaminated water or food. Conventional detection methods for  V. cholerae in environmental water samples, including membrane filtration and culture, typically require about three days, specialized equipment, and technical expertise. A simple and rapid method for detecting the  V. cholerae O1 in water could support outbreak prevention, environmental surveillance, and studies of persistence and transmission. Here, we describe a low-cost, streamlined method for detecting toxigenic  V. cholerae O1 in environmental water which can detect  V. cholerae O1 within 24 hours. We filter one liter of the water through gauze, incubate the gauze in alkaline peptone water (APW) overnight at 37 C, and test the APW sample with a serogroup O1-specific rapid diagnostic test (RDT). To preserve nucleic acid material from APW broth, we place two drops on each circle of a filter paper (Whatman 903), dry it, and later analyze the DNA using PCR and whole genome sequencing. We evaluated this method using 95 environmental samples collected from 17 sites in Lagos, Nigeria. 54 samples were RDT positive and each of these samples were confirmed by culture and by PCR targeting  ompW and  ctxA as toxigenic  V. cholerae O1. Whole-genome sequencing identified these isolates as belonging to the AFR12 lineage.  Among the RDT-negative samples, PCR detected 24 samples positive for  ompW but negative for  ctxA , consistent with non-toxigenic non-O1  V. cholerae , and 11 of these were further identified as non- toxigenic serogroup O139 by qPCR using a commercial assay (Bioperfectus). The cost for the RDT test was Author Summary  Standard methods to identify water samples contaminated with  V. cholerae serotype O1 are commonly used, but their use for public health practice has been limited due cost, time, and resource requirements. This study describes a convenient, efficient and inexpensive method to detect  V. cholerae O1 from environmental water samples and evaluates this method using water samples collected from 17 sites in Lagos, Nigeria during 2025. The method involves filtering one liter of water through a gauze pad, followed by overnight incubation of the gauze in alkaline peptone water (APW) enrichment broth. The APW is then tested for cholera using a rapid diagnostic test (RDT) specific for  V. cholerae O1. Among 95 environmental water samples, 54 were positive for  V. cholerae O1 using the RDTs. This method provides results within one day at a cost of <$2.50 USD per sample. If there is need for additional studies, RDT positive samples can be sent for culture, and nucleic acid from the APW can be saved by spotting the APW on filter paper. The filter paper can then be stored at room temperature indefinitely. All of the RDT positive samples were confirmed by culture and PCR Among the PCR negative samples, 24 samples were PCR positive for non-O1  V. cholerae, including 11 that were positive for non-toxigenic  V. cholerae O139 by qPCR. Whole genome sequencing of the samples found the RDT positive samples to be of the AFR12 lineage, and the DNA contained many genetic markers of antibiotic resistance. Identifying cholera contaminated water quickly provides information to health authorities which can facilitate interventions to reduce transmission and can also provide samples for further epidemiologic and molecular studies.

records.title: Detection and antimicrobial resistance of Campylobacter spp. from retail chicken parts in the Southeastern U.S.: A molecular approach.
records.abstract: In the United States, contaminated poultry and meat products account for more than 70% of Campylobacter-related foodborne infections in humans. To isolate Campylobacter and conduct genomic analyses, 103 chicken parts were purchased from retail grocery stores located in the Southeastern U.S. Phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility tests were performed using the National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System broth microdilution method. The antimicrobial resistance genes and virulence factors of each isolate were also identified. Data were analyzed in R with Firth's penalized logistic regression using the "logistf" package to determine the effect of chicken parts and production labels on the odds ratio of Campylobacter detection, with P Campylobacter in chicken parts was 20% (21/103), with prevalence ranging from 8% in breast meat to 54% in wings. Moreover, the odds of Campylobacter detection in wings were 11 times (95% confidence intervals [CI]; 2.36-73.56) more likely than those in breast samples (P = 0.00199). However, there were no significant differences (P > 0.05) in the odds of Campylobacter detection among production labels. Among positive samples, 71% (15/21) of the isolates were identified as C. jejuni, while 29% (6/21) were identified as C. coli. Phylogeny results suggested the presence of closely related isolates or possible clonal dissemination at the retail level, while phenotypic resistance results showed that 52% (11/21) of Campylobacter isolates were resistant to at least one antibiotic tested, with no isolate being multi-drug resistant. Therefore, intervention strategies against Campylobacter are warranted to reduce its contamination in retail chicken meat.IMPORTANCECampylobacter species commonly cause foodborne gastrointestinal infections in humans. One challenge is that these bacteria are commensal in chickens, meaning that they thrive in chicken's intestinal tracts and multiply to up to 108 cells per gram of feces without causing clinical signs, resulting in contamination of chicken carcasses or parts during processing and being carried to the retail-level. Their genomic characteristics, including phylogenetic analyses, antimicrobial resistance, and virulence factors, are not well understood. In this study, Campylobacter spp. were often detected in skin-on chicken parts, and >50% of isolates showed phenotypic resistance to at least one clinically important antibiotic tested. The detection of virulent and drug-resistant Campylobacters species in chicken parts at the retail level poses a serious food safety threat. Therefore, it is essential to cook raw chicken meat properly, avoid cross-contamination of chicken meat with other grocery items, and conduct routine food safety-related consumer awareness programs to prevent from Campylobacter-related foodborne infections in humans.

records.title: Dengue virus-2 triggers Epstein-Barr virus replication in primary B cells by co-opting the IRE1-XBP1 signaling axis.
records.abstract: The intricate interplay between co-infecting viral pathogens within a host can significantly influence disease outcomes. Dengue virus (DENV), a globally prevalent arbovirus from the Flaviviridae family, and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a ubiquitous human herpesvirus, share extensive geographical overlap, yet their potential interactions remain largely uncharacterized. This study elucidates a novel molecular mechanism whereby DENV-2 infection triggers disruption of EBV latency. We systematically demonstrate that DENV-2 infection consistently induces EBV lytic gene expression and viral replication in diverse cellular contexts, including epithelial cell lines and, critically, in primary human B lymphocytes-the principal reservoir of latent EBV. Mechanistically, we establish that the substantial burden of DENV-2 protein synthesis and replication induces profound endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, activating the unfolded protein response (UPR). Through pharmacological inhibition and genetic knockdown, we dissect the three UPR branches and identify the IRE1-XBP1 signaling axis as the indispensable pathway for this phenomenon. DENV-2 infection promotes the endoribonuclease activity of IRE1, leading to the unconventional splicing of XBP1 mRNA into its transcriptionally active isoform, XBP1s. Depletion of IRE1 or XBP1 attenuated DENV-induced BZLF1 expression, whereas ectopic XBP1s expression increased BZLF1 transcription. Our findings delineate a precise virus-host-virus signaling model in which an acute RNA virus engages a cellular stress pathway to promote entry into the EBV lytic program and viral genome amplification. This provides a new paradigm for understanding the pathobiology of dengue fever and the complex dynamics of the human virome.IMPORTANCEThis research uncovers a previously unrecognized molecular dialog between two of the world's most common viral pathogens. By demonstrating that dengue virus infection can awaken dormant Epstein-Barr virus, this study provides a mechanistic basis for the long-suspected but poorly understood complications arising from viral co-infections. We pinpoint a specific cellular stress pathway, the IRE1-XBP1 axis of the unfolded protein response (UPR), as the critical molecular switch. This discovery is significant because it not only explains how an acute viral illness can trigger the reactivation of a latent, potentially oncogenic virus but also opens new avenues for therapeutic intervention. Understanding this intricate interplay could lead to novel strategies for managing severe dengue and other diseases where viral co-infection is a contributing factor to pathogenesis.
records.authors: Deng X, Deng R, Guo X, Li J, Liao Y, Lai H, Wu J, Lin W, Liu Z, Xu P.

records.title: Genetic Parameters and Genome-Wide Association Analysis of Reproductive Traits in Egyptian Buffalo.
records.abstract: Reproductive efficiency is a crucial factor in the sustainability and profitability of buffalo production systems. However, genetic improvement of reproductive traits is challenging due to low heritability, environmental sensitivity, limited recording, and shrinking reference populations caused by crossbreeding. This study aimed to estimate genetic parameters and detect the genomic architecture of key reproductive traits in Egyptian buffalo using pedigree-based analyses and genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Over a 44-year period (1980-2024), reproductive records from five Egyptian experimental herds were analysed. The dataset comprised 2843 buffalo cows, sired by 140 bulls and out of 1328 dams. In total, 2359 records were available for age at first calving (AFC), 10,478 for gestation length (GL), 7966 for calving interval (CI), 6705 for days open (DO), and 12,909 for calving ease (CE) and stillbirth (SB). For genome-wide association analysis, 275 Egyptian buffaloes were genotyped using the Affymetrix Buffalo 90 K array, and 66,295 high-quality SNPs were retained after quality control. De-regressed proofs derived from pedigree-based genetic evaluations were used as response variables in a mixed linear model implemented in the rMVP package. Genome-wide association analysis identified putative genomic regions associated with GL, CI, CE, and SB, whereas no genome-wide significant associations were detected for AFC and DO. Functional annotation and QTL enrichment analyses were subsequently used to provide exploratory biological context for the identified genomic regions. Heritability estimates were generally low: 0.16 for AFC, 0.06 for GL, 0.02 for CI, 0.02 for DO, 0.18 for CE, and 0.06 for SB. Manhattan plots revealed that 15 genomic regions containing significant SNPs were identified on chromosomes 2, 4, 10, 12, 13, 15, 19, 20, and 25 for the reproductive traits of GL, CI, CE, and SB. These findings provide preliminary evidence of genomic regions potentially contributing to variation in reproductive traits in Egyptian buffalo, although the relatively small number of genotyped animals limits the power to detect and validate small effect loci. Seven significant genomic regions on chromosomes 10, 13, 15, 20, and 25 were associated with the GL trait. Additionally, three suggestive SNPs mapped to chromosomes 2 and 19 were associated with the CE trait, and three suggestive SNPs mapped on chromosome 12 were significantly associated with the SB trait. The results of KEGG enrichment analyses and QTL classification analyses for reproductive traits in Egyptian buffalo suggest that candidate genes within known QTL may be involved in complex biological networks involving immune competence, cellular homeostasis, and systemic physiological resilience. Among the enriched pathways, Fc gamma R-mediated phagocytosis, protein export, viral myocarditis, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) were highlighted. Most annotated genomic regions (QTL) were related to reproductive traits (63.4%), followed by 17.3% for milk production traits, 9.95% for general production traits, 3.47% for meat and carcass traits, 3.71% for body conformation and robustness exterior traits, and 2.08% for health traits.

records.title: A Modular Multilocus Engineering Platform for Iterative Prototyping of Oncolytic Adenoviruses.
records.abstract: The development of oncolytic adenovirus type 5 (Ad5) has been constrained by inefficient genome-engineering workflows and a lack of reusable backbones for iterative vector optimization. To address these limitations, we established a modular and reusable engineering workflow for constructing tumor-selective oncolytic Ad5 genomes by integrating BJ5183-mediated homologous recombination with in vitro homology-based DNA assembly. First, the BJ5183-based system enables targeted modification of multiple loci within adenoviral genomes, including the installation of locus-compatible restriction sites such as BstBI, ClaI, and SwaI. Second, an in vitro homology-based DNA assembly module enables insertion of target gene expression cassettes. Third, PacI-linearized genomes are rescued in HEK-293A cells. The resulting backbone retained viral rescue competence and replication selectivity. This platform supports engineering of therapeutic and structural loci within a retained full-length plasmid backbone while allowing the final recombinant plasmid to be sequence-verified before virus rescue. Thus, it provides a practical framework for iterative and parallelized prototyping of armed, capsid-modified, and combinatorial oncolytic Ad5 vectors.
records.authors: Dai Z, Yu H, Ye J, Zhang T, Xiong S, Si Y, Li W, Gao Q, Ma D, Li F.

records.title: Calixarene-based nanocarrier for ciprofloxacin and curcumin: evaluation of antibacterial, antibiofilm, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities.
records.abstract: Drug delivery and multidrug therapy are essential research fields in the fight against complex diseases, including infections. Here, we investigated the capability of a polyanionic nanocarrier, formed through the spontaneous self-assembly of an amphiphilic p-sulfonate-calix[4]arene derivative, to load ciprofloxacin and curcumin, both individually and in combination, using a simple and reproducible organic solvent-free method. Entrapment in the nanocarrier enhanced the aqueous solubility and stability of both ciprofloxacin and curcumin and protected them from UV light-induced photodegradation. The supramolecular nanosized assemblies exhibited antibacterial activity against Gram-positive (Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 6538) and Gram-negative (Escherichia coli ATCC 10536, Pseudomonas aeruginosa ATCC 9027) bacteria, including antibiotic-resistant strains (S. aureus (MRSA) ATCC 43300, S. aureus 1199B, Enterococcus faecium DSM 17050, Acinetobacter baumannii DSM 106838, E. coli DSM 105388, and P. aeruginosa DSM 102273). Against S. aureus 1199B, the nanoassemblies reduced biofilm formation, an effect largely attributable to the empty nanocarrier, and were effective against mature biofilms. The antioxidant activity of curcumin was preserved following its incorporation into the nanocarrier, as demonstrated by its DPPH radical scavenging activity. Additionally, the nanoassemblies loaded with ciprofloxacin and curcumin showed anti-inflammatory effects, as evidenced by the reduced TNF-α levels in LPS-stimulated eukaryotic cells. The multifunctional nature of the nanoassemblies highlights their potential for combining antimicrobial, radical-scavenging and anti-inflammatory properties, offering a promising approach to addressing the complex challenges associated with bacterial infections, including those involving biofilms.

records.title: AltORF-encoded microprotein recruits primary-ORF-encoded dehydrogenase to cell poles upon heat shock
records.abstract: Alternative open reading frames (altORFs) initiating from in-frame or out-of-frame start sites within annotated protein-coding genes represent a largely unexplored source of protein-coding potential and remain poorly understood in terms of regulation, function, and impact on physiology. Here we investigate  Escherichia coli GndA, encoded by an out-of-frame altORF within  gnd , which encodes 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase. We observe that the GndA protein is induced by heat shock, consistent with the initial identification in a quantitative membrane proteomics screen, but is unstable, while the levels of the stable Gnd dehydrogenase are unchanged. Using translational fusion assays and in vivo RNA structure probing, we show that an internal complementary sequence upstream of  gndA acts as a thermo-responsive secondary RNA structure controlling GndA translation. Mutagenesis of either  gnd or  gndA reduce heat shock survival of  E. coli indicating both gene products are important for resistance. GndA fractionates with membranes consistent with in silico predictions that the protein forms an amphipathic α-helix. In contrast, Gnd is predominantly cytoplasmic but shows GndA-dependent relocalization to cell poles upon heat shock. Together, our results demonstrate that an altORF-encoded microprotein is required for stress-dependent relocalization of its primary ORF partner, revealing a functional interplay between proteins encoded by overlapping ORFs in bacterial stress adaptation.  Significance  Alternative translation from internal translation initiation sites enables bacteria to expand their proteomic versatility without increasing genome size. Here we show that a single  Escherichia coli transcript encoding the well-characterized dehydrogenase Gnd also produces an additional microprotein from an internal alternative open reading frame (altORF), whose translation is controlled by an RNA thermometer-like structure. We further demonstrate that this heat shock-induced microprotein promotes spatial relocalization of its primary ORF-encoded partner during aerobic heat stress. Together our findings highlight how alternative translation can expand the cellular response to stress.
records.authors: Schmidt JJ, Ramos-León F, Zhang A, Zeinert R, Shabalina SA, Storz G.

records.title: A host-virus arms race over FAM134B in African swine fever virus infection.
records.abstract: Although reticulophagy, the selective autophagy of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), restricts several RNA viruses, whether this pathway constrains DNA virus infection remains unknown. Recently, we found that FAM134B (family with sequence similarity 134 member B), an ER-resident cargo receptor that mediates reticulophagy, restricts African swine fever virus (ASFV), a large cytoplasmic DNA virus, by targeting the major capsid proteins p72 and pA137R for lysosomal degradation, thereby blocking capsid assembly at perinuclear viral factories. ASFV counters this restriction through the virulence factor pMGF300-2R encoded by the MGF300-2R gene of ASFV, which binds to FAM134B, recruits LC3B (microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 beta), an ATG8 (autophagy-related protein 8) family member, via the C-terminal LC3-interacting region (LIR) motif, and directs FAM134B into autophagic degradation. Deletion of the MGF300-2R gene in the ASFV genome restores FAM134B abundance, reduces viral replication, and attenuates virulence in pigs. These findings establish reticulophagy as a previously unrecognized antiviral barrier against a large DNA virus and reveal a host-virus arms race centered on the reticulophagy receptor.Abbreviations: ASFV: African swine fever virus; ER: endoplasmic reticulum; FAM134B: family with sequence similarity 134 member B; LC3B: microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 beta; LIR: LC3-interacting region; VFs: viral factories.

records.title: Antibiotic susceptibility and antagonistic activity of candidate probiotic strains relevant to poultry production: An in vitro screening study.
records.abstract: The global pressure to reduce antibiotic use in poultry production, driven by antimicrobial resistance (AMR), highlights the need for safe and effective microbiota-based alternatives. This study performed an in vitro screening of 10 candidate probiotic strains (Lactobacillus spp., Bifidobacterium lactis, Carnobacterium divergens, and Bacillus spp.) to assess (i) antibiotic susceptibility and (ii) antagonistic activity against poultry-associated pathogens (Salmonella Typhimurium, Salmonella Enteritidis, Escherichia fergusonii, and Listeria monocytogenes). Susceptibility was first assessed using complementary agar disk diffusion screening with 14 antibiotics at different concentrations and minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) determination for seven antibiotics using Etest®. Subsequently, cell-free supernatants were evaluated using microtiter plate pathogen growth inhibition assays. The results revealed pronounced strain- and antibiotic-specific variability in observed antibiotic susceptibility profiles, underscoring the importance of strain-level assessment and cautious interpretation in the absence of standardized breakpoints for many probiotic species. All untreated cell-free supernatants produced strong, statistically significant in vitro growth inhibition of the four pathogens: Gram-negative S. Typhimurium, S. Enteritidis, and E. fergusonii, and Gram-positive L. monocytogenes. Enzyme-treatment experiments suggested that peroxide-sensitive and, in some strain-pathogen combinations, lipase-sensitive components contributed to antagonism; however, the pattern was strain- and pathogen-dependent and is therefore consistent with a multifactorial inhibitory effect rather than a single dominant mechanism. Overall, this study highlights the value of integrating antibiotic susceptibility profiling with functional antagonism assays for rational prioritization of candidate probiotic strains. The results identify candidate probiotics for further genomic, mechanistic, and in vivo validation rather than supporting stand-alone safety or efficacy claims.
records.authors: Akhavan N, Stadnicka K, Thiem D, Gardiner GE, Lawlor PG, Randazzo CL, Hrynkiewicz K.

records.title: Emergence and characterisation of bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid resistance in recurrent rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis patient: A case report.
records.abstract: BackgroundBedaquiline (BDQ), pretomanid (Pa) and linezolid (LZD)-based (BPaL) regimens have transformed rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB) treatment. However, resistance to these drugs is increasingly reported, while longitudinal data integrating clinical, phenotypic and genomic evolution remain limited.Case presentationWe report a fatal case of recurrent RR-TB in a 40-year-old South African woman with HIV infection who received BPaL therapy. Following treatment completion, recurrent disease was complicated by pregnancy, treatment interruption and loss to follow-up. She subsequently re-presented with advanced cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis and respiratory failure. Despite re-initiation of BPaL, she deteriorated and died from septic shock. Routine drug susceptibility testing, available posthumously, confirmed resistance to BDQ, Pa and LZD. Seven sequential Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates collected during treatment underwent minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) testing and whole-genome sequencing. All demonstrated phenotypic resistance to the three BPaL drugs. Serial genomic analysis identified progressive Rv0678 diversification associated with a two-fold increase in BDQ MIC, while resistance-associated rrl and fbiC mutations remained comparatively stable despite persistently elevated LZD and Pa MICs.ConclusionsThis case demonstrates the interaction of treatment interruption, delayed resistance detection and continued within-host bacterial adaptation during BPaL therapy. Longitudinal phenotypic and genomic findings revealed distinct resistance trajectories among BPaL drugs, highlighting the importance of treatment retention, timely susceptibility testing and genomic surveillance for preserving BPaL effectiveness.
records.authors: Kaapu KG, Ntsoane RV, Raphiri C, Lekalakala-Mokaba MR, Rukasha I.

records.title: A genome-wide scan for signatures of selection in two indigenous Sicilian chicken breeds.
records.abstract: Natural and artificial selection can leave distinctive genomic signatures that provide insights into the evolutionary history of populations. In this study, we used high-density SNP arrays to investigate genomic signatures of selection in two indigenous Sicilian chicken breeds: the Siciliana, also known as Coronata (SIC), and the recently recognized Cornuta di Caltanissetta, also known as Cornuta di Sicilia (COR). We combined two extended haplotype homozygosity (EHH)-based methods, iHS and Rsb, with a complementary site frequency spectrum (SFS)-based analysis using SweeD software, to identify genomic regions potentially affected by selection. Several candidate regions were identified in COR, with regions on chicken chromosomes (GGA) 1, 8, and 21. On GGA1 strong iHS signals coincided with elevated composite likelihood ratio (CLR) values from SweeD, whereas regions on GGA8 and GGA21 showed overlapping iHS and Rsb signals, supported by additional exploratory evidence from SweeD. These regions contain several genes associated with nervous system development and function, including PCDH9 on GGA1; ASTN1, TNR, and BRINP2 on GGA8; and CLSTN1, NMNAT1, UBE4B, and KIF1B on GGA21. Additional candidate genes identified within regions showing differential selection signals on GGA3, including TTBK1, SLC8A1, TTL, and VSX1, also have reported roles in neural processes. Collectively, these genes highlight potential links between the identified genomic signals and neural processes that may contribute to phenotypic differentiation between the two breeds, although their involvement in breed-specific traits remains to be established. Beyond these candidates, we identified selection signatures encompassing genes associated with gene regulation, including transcriptional co-regulation and alternative splicing. Several highly significant variants were also located within long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) regions, pointing to a possible contribution of regulatory variation to the observed genomic patterns. Overall, our results identify candidate genomic regions containing genes involved in neural function and gene regulatory processes, providing a basis for future investigations into the evolutionary history and phenotypic differentiation of these indigenous Sicilian chicken breeds.

records.title: Discrepant responses of abundant and rare taxa to polyethylene microplastic and nanoplastic perturbations in cold seep sediment.
records.abstract: Microplastics (MPs) and nanoplastics (NPs) are emerging contaminants in deep-sea ecosystems, yet their specific impacts on the internal heterogeneity of cold seep microbiomes remain poorly understood. Here, microcosm experiments with cold seep sediments exposed to polyethylene particles were conducted to investigate the response patterns of abundant and rare taxa to MP/NP-induced disturbances. The results indicated that MPs/NPs exposure reshaped bacterial community structure, with significant enrichment of Epsilonbacteraeota, a phylum associated with chemoautotrophic metabolism. In contrast, archaeal alpha diversity showed no significant response to MPs/NPs exposure. Abundant and rare taxa exhibited contrasting responses in community composition, assembly patterns, and network associations. Despite stochastic processes largely governing overall community assembly, the assembly mechanism of rare bacteria shifted toward heterogeneous selection under NPs exposure, which contrasted sharply with the homogeneous selection observed in the rare archaea. Furthermore, network analysis revealed that rare taxa constituted the majority of nodes in both co-occurrence networks. Functional predictions suggested contrasting responses, with lower relative abundances of taxa assigned to sulfate respiration in abundant bacteria under most treatments and higher relative abundances of taxa assigned to sulfur oxidation and nitrogen cycling in rare taxa under some treatments. Overall, this study highlights the contrasting responses of abundant and rare taxa to MPs/NPs exposure and provides insights for assessing the ecological risks of plastic pollution in deep-sea environments.
records.authors: Yuan Y, Ma B, Xu Z, Wang J, Tang Q, Yin Q, Zhou H, Chen C, Zhang C.

records.title: A secreted NanoLuc luciferase-expressing PRRSV for high-throughput antiviral screening identifies lithocholic acid as a post-entry inhibitor of viral replication.
records.abstract: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) is an economically important swine pathogen without effective antiviral agents. Here, we constructed recombinant PRRSV reporter viruses expressing secreted NanoLuc luciferase (Nluc) based on the PRRSV TA-12 strain and established a quantitative antiviral screening platform. The selected rGNluc reporter virus exhibited stable replication characteristics and enabled rapid evaluation of PRRSV replication. Screening of a library of 146 gut microbial metabolites identified several antiviral candidates, among which lithocholic acid (LCA) exhibited potent inhibitory activity against PRRSV replication with a favorable selectivity index. LCA exhibited antiviral activity against multiple PRRSV-1 and PRRSV-2 strains, although susceptibility varied among strains, and primarily inhibited viral replication at post-entry stages. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that LCA reduced viral genomic RNA and subgenomic RNA synthesis and early viral protein expression, while its antiviral activity was independent of the bile acid receptors FXR and TGR5. Furthermore, cholesterol supplementation almost completely rescued PRRSV replication inhibited by LCA, suggesting the involvement of host cholesterol homeostasis in its antiviral activity. These findings establish a robust high-throughput screening (HTS) platform and identify LCA as a promising host-directed antiviral candidate.
records.authors: Zhang L, Shi J, Li Q, Xu T, Li C, Li Y.

records.title: HIV-1 Integrase C-terminal Domain Mutations Regulate ALLINI Sensitivity
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  HIV-1 integrase (IN) performs two essential functions in virus replication: catalyzing the integration of reverse-transcribed viral cDNA into host DNA and promoting proper virion maturation. The latter is mediated by IN binding to the genomic RNA (gRNA) through basic residues in its C- terminal domain (CTD), thereby ensuring correct repackaging of the gRNA inside the remodeled capsid lattice. Allosteric integrase inhibitors (ALLINIs) bind within a V-shaped pocket at the interface of the catalytic core domain (CCD) of IN dimers, promote the engagement of the CTDs from adjacent dimers, and thereby occlude gRNA binding. However, virological evidence supporting a role for the IN-CTD in ALLINI mechanism of action is lacking, as mutations in CTD residues implicated in ALLINI-induced multimerization typically yield non-infectious viruses. Here we demonstrate that IN-CTD mutants bearing compensatory substitutions that restore infectivity exhibit markedly altered sensitivity to ALLINIs. Specifically, we show that R269A/K273A substitutions within the IN-CTD confer ∼100-fold enhanced sensitivity to ALLINIs. This correlates with a loss of IN-gRNA binding at low ALLINI concentrations, while exerting minimal effects on IN multimerization  in vitro and in virions. In contrast, we found that the IN I268T substitution which arose as a suppressor mutation of I268A confers partial resistance to ALLINI-induced inhibition of gRNA binding. Collectively, these findings provide the first direct genetic evidence that CTD residues, despite being distal to the primary drug binding site at the CCD dimer, modulate sensitivity to ALLINIs and highlights IN-gRNA binding as a central target of ALLINIs.  SIGNIFICANCE  In addition to its catalytic role in viral DNA integration, HIV-1 integrase (IN) is essential for virion maturation. IN binding to the viral RNA genome (gRNA) through basic residues in its C-terminal domain (CTD) ensures the proper repackaging of the gRNA inside the mature capsid lattice. Allosteric integrase inhibitors (ALLINIs) bind to a pocket within the catalytic core domain (CCD) of an IN dimer and are thought to disrupt IN-gRNA interactions by triggering aberrant IN multimerization through the engagement of the CTDs of a nearby dimer. However, direct genetic evidence supporting a role for the IN-CTD in ALLINI mechanism of action is lacking. Herein, we show that IN-CTD mutants bearing compensatory substitutions that restore infectivity have significantly altered sensitivities against ALLINIs. Our findings provide the first virological evidence that residues within the CTD, away from the primary drug binding site at the CCD dimer, can alter ALLINI sensitivity.

records.title: FapA extends the flagellar cage-dependent network into the cytoplasm to control surface-associated behaviors in  Helicobacter pylori
records.abstract: Flagellar systems enable many host-associated bacteria to colonize successfully. One such pathogen is  Helicobacter pylori , which assembles an elaborate, high-torque flagellar motor that has a wide C-ring, 18 stator complexes, and is surrounded by a cage that includes homologs of the type IV pilus proteins PilM, PilN, and PilO. PilMNO act to repress soft-agar migration while promoting cell aggregation, microcolony, and biofilm formation, but the pathway linking the flagellar cage to these behaviors is unknown. Here we identify FapA, a member of the flagellar assembly protein A (FapA) family, as a component of this pathway. Deletion of  fapA increased soft-agar migration and reduced microcolony and biofilm formation, similar to deletion of  pilMNO . Epistasis analysis placed FapA downstream of the PilMNO flagellar cage. Using fluorescent fusions and protein-protein interaction experiments, FapA was found to localize to the cell poles, the sites of flagellar motor placement, and interact with the cytoplasmic PilM component of the cage. Indeed, cryo-electron tomography experiments detected cytoplasmic density near PilM that was lost in the Δ  fapA deletion mutant. Phylogenetic analysis suggests that FapA proteins are more widespread than previously appreciated, being found in multiple bacterial phyla including Campylobacterota, Bacillota, Spirochaetota, Desulfobacterota, Thermotogota, Synergistota, and Pseudomonadota. Together, these findings support that the  H. pylori flagellar cage has additional components that reside in the cytoplasm but similarly function to limit motility and activate a sessile/biofilm lifestyle. Given the widespread nature of FapA, our results suggest that many other bacteria might employ FapA homologs for similar purposes.  Importance  The flagella of  Helicobacter pylori enable it to colonize the stomach, but its flagellar motor appears to do more than propel the bacterium. A protein cage surrounding the motor helps determine whether cells swim or settle into microcolonies and biofilms, yet the molecular components that link this structure to cellular behaviors remain poorly understood. This knowledge gap is particularly intriguing because  H. pylori lacks the cyclic-di-GMP signaling system that many bacteria use to coordinate motility and biofilm development. Our identification of FapA as a cytoplasmic component of the cage-dependent regulatory network provides a foundation for understanding how  H. pylori coordinates motility and surface-associated growth and given the widespread nature of FapA, raises the possibility that many other bacteria use similar mechanisms.
records.authors: Fong JNC, Witt CD, Huang EHL, Yue J, Liu X, Roujeinikova A, Liu J, Ottemann KM.

records.title: Weak cross-trophic coupling of multidimensional stability in plankton communities under multiple stressors.
records.abstract: Nutrient enrichment and biological invasions frequently co-occur in freshwater ecosystems, yet it remains unclear whether stability of entire planktonic groups responds uniformly to these combined stressors. To address this question, we conducted a fully factorial mesocosm experiment that crossed three nutrient regimes with two invasive species that impose distinct disturbance pathways. We quantified temporal stability, resistance, resilience, and recovery across functional and compositional facets in zooplankton, phytoplankton, and bacterioplankton communities. Our results revealed highly taxon- and dimension-specific responses. Snail bioturbation significantly reduced the functional resistance of zooplankton under high nutrient conditions. Meanwhile, the functional resistance of bacterioplankton declined with increasing nutrient levels. This suggests that functionally distinct stressors may affect different trophic guilds through distinct mechanisms. Species richness was consistently positively associated with compositional temporal stability, resistance and recovery across all trophic levels, but was negatively associated with resilience, revealing a fundamental trade-off between maintaining community robustness and enabling rapid adaptability. Functional and compositional stability were positively correlated only in the temporal stability dimension, but exhibited negative associations in the resistance and recovery dimensions. This indicates that biomass-related functions and community structure can follow divergent trajectories throughout perturbation and recovery. Most critically, the multivariate analyses and pairwise correlations among trophic levels indicated generally weak cross-trophic coupling, suggesting that, under the conditions of this mesocosm experiment, no single planktonic group provided a consistently reliable proxy for multidimensional whole-community stability. These findings highlight the value of assessing multiple dimensions of ecological stability across trophic groups. Consideration of stability indicators across multitrophic groups may provide complementary information for adaptive lake management as global pressures from nutrient loading and biological invasions continue to intensify.
records.authors: Wang Y, Li R, Sun S, Zhong M, Wang C, Chu Y, Qin Y, Zhang X, Rao Q, Chen J, Su H.

records.title: Impacts on water chemistry and the non-target microbial community following application of a novel chemical control strategy for Karenia brevis.
records.abstract: Environmental impact is a critical factor when considering potential control of Florida red tide (Karenia brevis). A combination of ammonium (50 μM) and putrescine (85 μM), hereafter "NP", was formulated to control K. brevis growth in laboratory culture. However, effects of NP on water quality and non-target organisms in complex microbial communities require investigation. To assess potential impacts, mesocosms containing non-red tide microbial communities were treated with NP and compared to Controls over seven days. Putrescine had a residence time of two days while total ammonia increased to toxic levels following NP application. Dynamics in oxygen, pH, and turbidity implicated microbial heterotrophy in the removal of putrescine and release of ammonia. Except on Day 5, chlorophyll a was not significantly different between treatments. However, accessory pigment analysis and eukaryotic metabarcode profiling revealed that NP treatment restructured phytoplankton and heterotrophic microeukaryote communities. NP-treated phytoplankton communities experienced reductions in abundance and diversity of dinoflagellates, and increases in relative abundance of other phytoplankton groups, including diatoms and chlorophytes. Metabarcoding showed that heterotrophic microeukaryotes increased over time regardless of treatment, and became the majority of metabarcode reads in NP-treated communities. Heterotroph community composition was distinguished by relatively abundant eukaryvores in Controls, and bacterivores in NP-treated mesocosms. Thus, NP had complex interconnected impacts on water quality and the microbial community, with an increase in the relative abundance and diversity of heterotrophs and beneficial phytoplankton species, while also resulting in elevated ammonium and sustained decreases in pH.
records.authors: Johnson GI, Burris DS, Miller C, Wetzel DL, Wang Y, Lovko VJ, Coyne KJ.

records.title: Community differentiation and assembly of soil nosZ-type denitrifiers across dominant plant communities in an alpine wetland of Qinghai Lake.
records.abstract: BackgroundNitrous oxide (N₂O) reduction mediated by nosZ-harboring microorganisms represents the terminal step of denitrification and an important biological sink for N₂O in wetland soils, yet how naturally occurring dominant plant communities are associated with the diversity, taxonomic differentiation, and assembly of nosZ-type communities in alpine wetlands remains poorly understood.MethodsWe investigated four dominant plant communities in wetlands surrounding Qinghai Lake on the northeastern Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, dominated by Blysmus sinocompressus (BS), Carex regescens (CR), Elymus nutans (EN), and Leymus secalinus (LS), and integrated nosZ-targeted amplicon sequencing with vegetation biomass, soil physicochemical properties, environmental-association analyses, and phylogeny-based null models to evaluate variation in community diversity, taxonomic composition, environmental correlates, and assembly processes.ResultsThe four plant communities exhibited pronounced differences in vegetation-soil conditions and supported distinct nosZ-type communities. LS-associated soils showed the highest richness and the largest pool of community-specific OTUs, whereas Proteobacteria and Bradyrhizobium dominated the overall taxonomic composition. Environmental associations differed between community diversity and taxonomic structure: diversity was more strongly associated with plant biomass, soil temperature, and carbon and nitrogen status, whereas compositional variation was more closely related to soil C ratio, pH, total carbon, moisture, and nitrate nitrogen. Phylogeny-based null-model analysis further indicated that community assembly was predominantly associated with variable selection, although the relative contributions of dispersal limitation and other stochastic processes differed among dominant plant communities.ConclusionThese findings demonstrate that dominant plant communities in the Qinghai Lake alpine wetland are associated with coordinated differentiation in vegetation-soil environments, nosZ-type community composition, and assembly processes, thereby characterizing the taxonomic differentiation and inferred assembly of the primer-defined soil nosZ community across contrasting plant-community habitats; however, the implications for realized N₂O reduction require direct validation using gene-abundance, transcriptional, enzyme-activity, and gas-flux measurements.
records.authors: Zhou S, Zhang N, Tang J, Chen K.

records.title: Sewer-relevant aging of microplastics drives plastic-class-dependent N<sub>2</sub>O emissions from denitrifying sludge.
records.abstract: Microplastics (MPs) accumulate in sewer systems and wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs), where they undergo aging processes distinct from photo-oxidation in surface waters. How such sewer-relevant aging impacts denitrification-associated nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions remains unknown. Here, we simulated sewer-relevant aging (sulfidation and mechanical abrasion) for non-biodegradable, compostable and biodegradable MPs (NMPs, CMPs, BMPs) and evaluated their effects on N2O emissions relative to pristine MPs, while linking MP-derived dissolved organic carbon (DOC) characteristics to microbial physiological and community responses. Aging increased DOC release from CMPs and BMPs by 30.0% and 115.8%, respectively, and generated plastic-dependent molecular signatures enriched in aromatic and sulfur-containing compounds. Rather than bioavailable carbon sources, aged MP-derived DOC could barely be consumed as the electron donor yet acted as a potent physiological disruptor. Correspondingly, aged CMPs and BMPs increased N2O emissions to 2.5- and 8.0-fold those of their pristine counterparts, with a stimulation order of BMPs > CMPs > NMPs under carbon-sufficient conditions (C/N = 4:1). Stronger N2O stimulation was associated with more severe membrane damage and greater impairment of electron supply. Metagenomic analysis further revealed enrichment of Paracoccus under stronger N2O stimulation, together with shifts in denitrification-related genomic potential. As a genus capable of degrading diverse plastic additives while harboring a complete denitrification pathway, Paracoccus could favor N2O accumulation under electron-limited conditions, where N2O reduction is disadvantaged relative to upstream denitrification steps. These findings showed that sewer-relevant aging reshaped MP effects on denitrification-associated N2O emissions in a plastic-dependent manner and challenged the presumed environmental benignity of compostable and biodegradable plastics, underscoring the need to incorporate MPs aging into risk assessment for WWTPs.
records.authors: Yue H, Guan X, Shen Y.

records.title: Multi-layer analysis of gut metagenomic functional potential in major depressive disorder.
records.abstract: BackgroundMajor depressive disorder (MDD) is associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis, but previous studies have mostly focused on species composition and are subject to confounding factors such as age and diet. Robust differences at the functional pathway level remain unclear.MethodsWe included 98 indigenous residents of Xinjiang, China, whose families had resided there for three or more generations (49 MDD patients and 49 healthy controls) and performed shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Functional profiles were annotated with HUMAnN3 across seven levels: GBM, GMM, KO, EC, Module, Pathway, and PathAbundance. Features were transformed using the centered log-ratio (CLR) method. After controlling for 10 covariates (age, sex, BMI, bowel movement frequency, diet, gastrointestinal symptoms, years of smoking, alcohol consumption, physical activity, and sleep), OLS regression was performed with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction (q ResultsAfter covariate adjustment, overall functional profiles did not differ significantly between groups (PERMANOVA R²=1.9%, p = 0.071; PERMDISP p = 0.98). After FDR correction, 33 significant features were detected across five levels: EC, Pathway, Module, GMM, and PathAbundance (no significant signals at the GBM or KO levels). Key biologically meaningful signals included: propionate CoA-transferase (EC 2.8.3.1, β=-1.42, q = 0.022)↓, teichoic acid biosynthesis (map00552, β=-0.34, q = 0.045)↓, vancomycin resistance module (M00651, β=-1.28, q = 0.014)↓, galacturonate degradation II (MF0023, β=+1.82, q = 0.048)↑, and heme b biosynthesis I (PathAbundance, β=+0.93, q = 0.033)↑. MaAsLin2 effect sizes were correlated with the main OLS results at the Pathway level (R²=0.84) with consistent direction. GRSA independently confirmed downregulation of the phosphotransferase system (map02060, padjConclusionsGut microbiota functional potential in MDD patients shows a mild but directionally consistent shift after controlling for confounders, involving short-chain fatty acid production, Gram-positive bacterial cell wall metabolism, and cofactor metabolism. This study measures functional potential and requires validation by metabolomics.

records.title: Bacterial community profiles of soils from the Mount Makiling Forest Reserve, Philippines.
records.abstract: The Mount Makiling Forest Reserve harbors diverse microorganisms with potential biotechnological applications, yet bacterial taxonomic profiling across its watersheds remains limited. Amplicon metagenome sequencing targeting the 16S rRNA gene revealed Proteobacteria and Acidobacteriota as dominant phyla, with Actinobacteriota, Verrucomicrobiota, Chloroflexi, Myxococcota, Methylomirabilota, Bacteroidota, Nitrospirota, and Planctomycetota present at varying abundances.
records.authors: Creencia AR, Arguelles EDLR, Tan Gana NH, Capanzana RMAD, Martinez JP, Lanceras JC, Salaan CAM, Del Castillo RAM, Cadao DFB.

records.title: The core interaction network of transcription elongation factors is broadly maintained across diverse bacteria.
records.abstract: Bacterial transcription elongation has been investigated most thoroughly for the model bacterium Escherichia coli. The E. coli elongation factor NusG associates through its N-terminal domain with the transcription elongation complex (TEC), while its C-terminal domain forms mutually exclusive interactions with either ribosomal protein S10 or Rho termination factor. The E. coli NusG:S10 complex bridges the TEC with a pioneering ribosome for coupling of transcription and translation. NusG also participates in antitermination complexes (ATC) that inhibit Rho-dependent termination and increase transcription of rRNA operons. A characteristic sequence in the nascent rrn RNA, called boxA, loads E. coli NusB:S10 onto the NusG-bound TEC, leading to the formation of the rrn ATC. However, these findings may not extend to all bacteria. Rho-dependent termination is less important in gram-positive bacteria, including some that do not encode Rho, and transcription and translation remain uncoupled in Bacillus subtilis and many other gram-positive bacteria. It is therefore unclear whether the interaction network for E. coli elongation factors is conserved in these organisms. We identified boxA-like sequences upstream of 16S and 23S genes in Bacillus species and found that they associate directly with NusB. We also found that B. subtilis S10 associates with both NusB and NusG, and that Rho can also associate with NusG. Bioinformatic analyses revealed conservation of interaction interface residues across multiple phyla. Together, these data demonstrate that the core interaction network of bacterial elongation factors is broadly conserved across diverse bacteria, despite differences in how these interactions function in individual species.ImportanceEscherichia coli is known to use several key elongation factors that promote direct coupling of transcription with translation. These factors also trigger the formation of an antitermination complex that protects the synthesis of ribosomal RNA and CRISPR transcripts from interference by the Rho termination factor. However, Bacillus subtilis is not thought to couple transcription with translation. It is also not known whether B. subtilis needs to suppress Rho, given that its Rho is dispensable. Therefore, we purified B. subtilis elongation factors and mapped their interaction network. Surprisingly, we find that the B. subtilis elongation factors form complexes that closely resemble E. coli counterparts, despite the significant mechanistic differences in how these bacteria control transcription elongation.
records.authors: Tran TNP, Peterson RE, Jiang X, Sevugan SA, Ranaweera S, Babitzke P, Fushman D, Winkler WC.

records.title: Periodontal Infectogenomics in Africa: The Biological Case for a Population-Centred Research Agenda.
records.abstract: African populations harbour the greatest human genetic diversity on earth and carry the highest global burden of severe periodontitis, yet their absence from periodontal infectogenomics represents a biological limitation of the field with profound implications for host-microbe interaction research. This Perspective builds the biological case for African populations as an urgent research priority and proposes a research roadmap integrating genomics, metagenomics and multiomics approaches.
records.authors: Kabbashi S, Chetty M.

records.title: Genomic characterization of a novel bunyavirus FsBV1 from Fusarium solani.
records.abstract: A novel bunyavirus, tentatively named Fusarium solani bunyavirus 1 (FsBV1), was identified in the phytopathogenic fungus Fusarium solani. The complete sequence of the L segment of FsBV1 is 7,186 nucleotides (nt) in length and contains a single open reading frame (ORF) encoding an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) of 316 amino acids (aa). The RdRp contains six conserved bunyaviral motifs, including the SDD tripeptide. The M segment is 1,422 nt long and contains a single ORF encoding a YwqJ-like deaminase of 81 aa. The S segment is 1,301 nt long and contains a single ORF encoding a protein containing putative multifunctional flavoprotein (SiRFP) domain. BLASTp analysis showed that the RdRp of FsBV1 shared the highest amino acid sequence identity (48.73%) with that of Cheeloo tick associated virus 2. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that FsBV1 clusters with unclassified bunyaviruses. Based on its genome organization, protein sequences, and phylogenetic position, FsBV1 is proposed as a novel virus within the class Bunyaviricetes.
records.authors: Xiao H, Peng Y, Deng Z, Chao J, Mao H, Zhang Y, Tan W, Xie Y, Cai C, Zheng L, Liu T.

records.title: Hormesis as a universal cellular strategy for growth.
records.abstract: Our review synthesizes a vast and dispersed literature to demonstrate that subtoxic doses of structurally diverse chemicals can induce a conserved growth-stimulatory (hormetic) response across bacterial, microalgal, plant, and mammalian cells. Stimulation is concentration- and exposure-time-dependent, with higher concentrations inhibiting growth. In eukaryotic models, moderate ROS signaling and activation of DNA-PKcs/Akt, ERK1/2, PI3K/AKT, mTOR, or AURKA accompany growth stimulation, with Cyclin D-CDK4 promoting G1/S transition in mammalian cells. The proliferative DNA-PKcs/Akt response is observed in human hepatic cells, while bacterial examples involve LuxR-dependent signaling and fatty acid β-oxidation. Metabolism rewires, with some microalgae enhancing glycolysis and Krebs cycling, whereas other photosynthetic microorganisms reroute photosynthetic carbon toward lipid or starch storage while downregulating selected carbohydrate-catabolic proteins. Nrf2-driven antioxidants in mammalian cells, carotenoids, and detoxifying enzymes are upregulated, establishing a preconditioned state that can attenuate apoptosis upon subsequent challenge. Within the Catabolic-Anabolic Cycling Hormesis (CACH) model, some time-dependent responses are consistent with an anabolic overshoot following a transient catabolic decline (ATP depletion). This anabolic reprogramming accompanies biofilm formation, altered motility, and, in neoplastic cells, anchorage-independent growth. Thus, cell proliferation is a metabolic strategy shaped by adversity, with functional consequences that depend on cellular context and the endpoint assessed.
records.authors: Agathokleous E, Markouizou A, Calabrese EJ, Saitanis CJ.
