records.title: Telotrons: spliceosomal introns composed of telomeric repeats
records.abstract: Spliceosomal intron numbers vary widely across eukaryotes, but the only established mechanism for large bursts of intron gain is the spread of transposable introner elements. We describe telotrons, spliceosomal introns composed predominantly of telomeric repeats. In a survey of 10,310 eukaryotic genome assemblies, we identified 7,008 introns with >85% telomeric repeat coverage and an additional 44,423 with >50% to ≤85% coverage, in 25 genomes spanning haptophytes, dinoflagellates, a cryptophyte, stramenopiles, the apicomplexan  Eimeria , and the nematode  Mesorhabditis . Most telotrons carry GT–AG or GC–AG splice boundaries, and RNA-seq supports their splicing. Their repeat orientations are consistent with telomerase extension of broken DNA ends, and intron absence at corresponding positions in orthologs supports widespread  de novo gain. In  Eimeria and  Mesorhabditis , telotrons instead occupy positions where orthologs carry ordinary introns, suggesting modification of existing introns. Telotrons thus point to telomerase as an endogenous driver of structural innovation through intron creation and remodeling.
records.authors: Kramer AM, Corbett-Detig R.

records.title: A global post-transcriptional regulator directs  Acinetobacter baumannii  carbon preference and gut colonization
records.abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a multidrug-resistant pathogen that colonizes the gut, increasing the risk of subsequent infection and transmission. Recent work showed that  A. baumannii catabolizes ornithine, a non-preferred carbon source, to colonize the gut. However, the mechanisms of carbon preference were unknown in  A. baumannii . Here, experimental evolution identified the conserved RNA-binding protein CsrA as a regulator of carbon preference in  A. baumannii , a previously unreported CsrA function. RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-Seq) revealed hundreds of CsrA-bound transcripts  . A. baumannii CsrA directly bound and repressed expression of the  ast arginine/ornithine catabolic operons. The  Pseudomonas aeruginosa CsrA homolog RsmA repressed arginine/ornithine catabolic operon expression, suggesting this CsrA function extends to other bacterial taxa. Finally, CsrA was required for competitive fitness during  A. baumannii gut colonization. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized role for a global regulator in  A. baumannii carbon preference and persistence in the gut, a critical reservoir for multidrug-resistant pathogens.
records.authors: Mason Clark R, Sava RL, Holt KJ, Gebhardt MJ, Palmer LD.

records.title: SARS-CoV-2 susceptibility and vulnerability of human blastocysts during in vitro preimplantation development.
records.abstract: Human preimplantation embryos express the SARS-CoV-2 entry factors ACE2, TMPRSS2 and BSG (CD147) on trophectoderm (TE) cells, suggesting susceptibility to infection. Likewise, SARS-CoV-2-pseudotyped reporter viruses induced cytopathic effects in blastocysts, while the zona pellucida (ZP) appeared to confer partial protection. The impact of authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection on embryonic lineage specification and developmental competence has not been established. Here, we exposed cryopreserved human embryos, donated under ethics approval and informed consent, to authentic SARS-CoV-2 (B.1.617.2, Delta variant). While embryos with an intact ZP remained uninfected, laser-assisted hatching rendered 19/21 (90.5%) of embryos susceptible to infection, as confirmed by detection of viral dsRNA. Moreover, SARS-CoV-2 infection had a pronounced effect on blastocyst development with a possibly fatal outcome. Compared to mock-treated embryos (n = 47), infected blastocysts (n = 48) showed a significantly reduced surface area (p = 0.0003), reduced total cell number (p = 0.0139), and reduced NANOG+ epiblast cell numbers (p = 0.0054) 24 hours post-exposure, while the number of GATA4+ primitive endoderm cells remained unaffected (p = 0.5255). Intriguingly, despite viral replication being largely confined to the trophectoderm (TE), this selective epiblast reduction suggests a disruption of TE-derived paracrine signaling required for epiblast specification. Finally, prolonged viral replication resulted in embryonic lysis and death. Digital transcriptomic profiling (mock, n = 29 embryos; SARS-CoV-2, n = 28 embryos; each in n = 5 minipools) revealed upregulation of innate antiviral and inflammatory genes, including IFIH1, IRF7, NOD2, and TNFRSF1A, as well as the recently identified SARS-CoV-2 entry factor TMEM106B, alongside altered developmental signatures concerning genome activation, pluripotency, and lineage-specific programs. These findings show that ZP disruption makes human blastocysts susceptible to productive SARS-CoV-2 infection, with adverse consequences for lineage allocation and direct implications for biosafety and virological counselling in medically assisted reproduction practice.
records.authors: Kumpanenko Y, Tryfonos M, Essahib W, De Munck N, Van Weyenbergh J, Alpizar YA, Dallmeier K, Van de Velde H.

records.title: Batch, Prefetch, Skip, Orient, Squeeze: Faster, Smaller k-mer dictionaries via the Spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform
records.abstract: Looking up k-mers in an index is a core operation in genomics, underlying read mapping, metagenomic classification, and many other tasks. Queries are often streaming: the k-mers come from a longer sequence such as a sequencing read, and consecutive k-mers overlap. The fastest index for such queries is currently the hashing-based SSHash; indexes based on the spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform (SBWT) are competitive in space but slower. We show how to make SBWT indexes both faster and smaller. First, we process queries in small batches and prefetch the memory each will need next, hiding the latency of the dependent random accesses that dominate a lookup; together with a new rank structure that reads one cache line per query, this makes k-mer lookups about seven times faster than unbatched SBWT search. Second, we extend batching to streaming search and show that one failed lookup can rule out many k-mers of a read at once, which removes the need for the longest common suffix array. Third, we build an SBWT that stores only one orientation of each k-mer, thereby halving its size, with a modified search that exploits how rarely the orientation changes along a read. Finally, we adapt a compact subset rank structure to batched search. On the collections of the SSHash benchmark, and on two collections up to 15 times larger, our fastest index answers streaming queries for 31-mers faster than SSHash on every read set, by up to 4.9 times, using 12 bits per canonical k-mer against SSHash's 7.4-11.1. We also show that a 6.1-bit index is still faster than SSHash on most read sets, and that our smallest index needs about 4 bits per canonical k-mer. Unlike that of SSHash, the space of our indexes barely varies across collections. Our code is available at https://github.com/anadis504/sbwt-squeeze-rs.

records.title: gyrB-BASED MOLECULAR IDENTIFICATION AND PHYLOGENETIC RELATEDNESS OF UROPATHOGENIC Klebsiella quasipneumoniae IN TWO TERTIARY HOSPITALS IN SOUTHWEST NIGERIA
records.abstract: Abstract    Background  Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most frequent bacterial infections worldwide and pose a major public health problem.  Klebsiella  species are primary causes of UTIs and are often associated with drug resistance. In this study, we sequenced and compared the  gyrB  gene of uropathogenic  Klebsiella  spp. isolates from two tertiary hospitals in southwest Nigeria with reference strains of the  Klebsiella  pneumoniae complex available in GenBank to determine their phylogenetic relatedness and bridge the knowledge gap on the genetic relatedness of uropathogenic  Klebsiella  spp. in southwest Nigeria. Methods  We collected 227 urine samples from University College Hospital Ibadan and Federal Medical Centre Abeokuta, Ogun State, Nigeria, and biochemically identified  Klebsiella  spp. Sequencing of the  gyrB  gene was conducted on 7 isolates based on resistance patterns. Phylogenetic analysis was done by NGPhylogeny.fr, and the phylogenetic tree was visualized by Interactive Tree of Life (iTOL). Results  Of the cultured samples, 96 colonies appeared morphologically as  Klebsiella  spp-like on Eosin Methylene Blue agar (EMB). Biochemical identification revealed that  K  .  pneumoniae  (42) and  Klebsiella oxytoca  22 made up the  Klebsiella-like  isolates, with the remaining (32) being  Enterobacter  spp. Seven randomly selected  Klebsiella pneumoniae  isolates were identified as  Klebsiella quasipneumoniae  using the  gyrB  gene sequence. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the isolates from the two hospitals clustered closely with reference strains, indicating shared evolutionary lineages. Conclusion  The uropathogenic  Klebsiella  spp. isolates from the two hospitals in southwest Nigeria are closely related to members of the K. pneumoniae complex. These findings underscore the importance of continued molecular surveillance and suggest that conserved transnational lineages are involved in proper taxonomic classification.
records.authors: Sadiq SO, Ike WE, Oloyede AR, Ojo OE, Adewole AI.

records.title: Bacterial Preconditioning Differentially Reshapes Neuronal Responses to Intermittent and Continuous Hypoxia-Like Stress
records.abstract: Abstract    The microbiota–gut–brain axis exposes the nervous system to microbial information, but whether such exposure becomes part of the biological history that shapes later neuronal stress responses remains unknown. Here, we tested whether transient direct exposure to live  Lactiplantibacillus plantarum  (  L. plantarum  ) alters how differentiated B35 neuronal cells subsequently respond to hypoxia-like metabolic stress. We compared two trajectories combining chemical HIF stabilization with nutrient restriction: an intermittent, sublethal condition with recovery periods (MHX), relevant to recurrent vascular insufficiency, and a continuous severe condition (SHX). These trajectories generated distinct structural, metabolic and transcriptional states. Prior  L. plantarum  exposure was associated with higher MTT-derived metabolic viability after MHX but not SHX, and induced broader transcriptional reorganization under MHX (167 versus 64 differentially expressed genes), engaging signaling and cytoskeletal programs together with pathways linked to negative regulation of apoptosis and oxidative-stress-induced cell death. Only one bacterially responsive gene was shared between the two stress trajectories. Thus,  L. plantarum  did not impose a fixed neuroprotective program. Instead, prior microbial exposure acted as a biological input whose consequences depended on the subsequent stress trajectory. These findings establish neuron–bacteria communication as history-dependent and define an adaptive range in which microbial signals can influence neuronal responses before metabolic stress becomes overwhelming—a principle relevant to preventive intervention during recurrent vascular stress.

records.title: Metagenomic assessment of airborne and surface viral signals and worker acceptability during a partial-lid intervention in a Cambodian live bird market
records.abstract: Abstract  Mechanical defeathering can disperse viral material in live poultry markets, but interventional machine modifications must fit routine work. This nonrandomized field study evaluated partial lids on defeathering machines at Orussey Market, Cambodia, across six sampling days, three with lids and three without. Targeted RT-qPCR and target-enriched metagenomics characterised viral RNA in air samples collected during a three-hour air-sampling period and in nearby surface samples collected before and after that period, while work questionnaires assessed usability. Sequencing detected 73 poultry-associated viral taxa. Influenza A virus, avian coronavirus and rotavirus G together accounted for over 80% of relative metagenomic abundance in 14 of 18 air samples. In air samples, RT-qPCR cycle thresholds correlated inversely with metagenomic relative abundance for avian influenza virus and Newcastle disease virus (Spearman’s ρ = −0.645 and − 0.684, respectively). Airborne richness was descriptively lower on days with lids, but targeted viral detections did not change consistently, and composition profiles overlapped. Surface profiles changed from before to after the air-sampling period on days with and without lids; the study did not establish a lid-associated difference in these changes. All five workers reported discomfort and perceived slower work; none wanted to use the lid in its tested form, although three would continue if it were permanently integrated into the machine. With only three sampling days per condition, the study did not establish a consistent reduction in airborne or surface viral contamination associated with lid use. Future studies should evaluate lids redesigned with workers alongside complementary measures addressing ventilation, hygiene, and clean water and waste management to reduce occupational exposure.

records.title: Structure-function analyses of the O<sub>2</sub>-dependent dimer-monomer transition in the FNR transcription factor.
records.abstract: About 2,5 billion years ago, oxygenic photosynthesis favored the evolution of gene expression regulatory strategies to respire atmospheric O2 in many anaerobic organisms. One such strategy was the evolution of the Fumarate Nitrate Reduction (FNR) regulator from a cAMP-binding transcription factor. The activity of FNR is regulated by a [Fe4S4] cluster-dependent dimer-monomer transition. The dimeric FNR responds to O2 through cluster degradation, which causes monomerization and loss of binding to its palindromic DNA receptor sites. Despite extensive structural and functional characterization, the molecular mechanism underlying signal transmission from the cluster to the DNA-binding domain and the dimer interface remains unclear. Here, we used a series of specific variants to explore this process both functionally, through stopped-flow and in vivo activity tests, and structurally, by exposing FNR crystals to O2 and three-dimensionally determining its effects. The emerging picture consists of three clearly interconnected major steps: cluster degradation, breaking of two intermolecular salt bridges, and bending and separation of the two dimerization α-helices. We also performed a preliminary analysis of FNRs belonging to different bacterial classes and concluded that their variable cysteine-based cluster coordination motifs might influence signal transmission.

records.title: The changing epidemiology of multidrug-resistant bacteria in hospitals: from high-risk clones to clinical impact.
records.abstract: Multidrug-resistant bacteria (MDRB) have become a major challenge for healthcare systems, representing a leading cause of healthcare-associated infections worldwide. The hospital environment provides ideal conditions for the emergence and dissemination of these microorganisms due to intensive antimicrobial use, the concentration of vulnerable patients, frequent invasive procedures, and opportunities for cross-transmission. The epidemiology of MDRB is dynamic and varies according to geographic region, healthcare practices, and local antimicrobial selective pressure. This review briefly summarizes the current epidemiology of MDRB in hospital settings, focusing on the ESKAPE pathogens. Special attention is given to the emergence and international dissemination of the so-called high-risk clones, which have played a central role in the global spread of antimicrobial resistance. The review also addresses the principal epidemiological risk factors, transmission routes, the role of environmental reservoirs and colonized patients, and the contribution of intensive care units as major amplification points for MDRB transmission and maintenance. Moreover, infections caused by MDRB are associated with increased mortality, prolonged hospitalization, and higher healthcare costs. Continuous surveillance, rapid microbiological diagnosis, infection prevention and control measures, and antimicrobial stewardship programs remain essential to limit their spread and clinical impact. New genomic surveillance approaches are improving our understanding of transmission dynamics and supporting more potentially effective control strategies.

records.title: Gut microbiota, immune cell traits, and infectious mononucleosis: a two-sample mendelian randomization and mediation analysis.
records.abstract: Infectious mononucleosis (IM) is an acute disease caused by the Epstein-Barr virus. This study assessed the causal association between the gut microbiota (GM) and IM and how the immune cells are mediators of this process through Mendelian randomization (MR). Two-step, two-sample MR was used to test the overall causal impact of GM on IM, the impact of GM on 731 immune cell characteristics, and the indirect effect of GM on IM. GM summary statistics (207 taxa, 7,738 Dutch participants), immune cell genome-wide association studies (GWAS, 3,757 Sardinians), and IM data (3,838 cases/486,087 controls, FinnGen R12) were used. P10 were used as the criteria in selecting instrumental variables. Bidirectionality MR and mediation MR with 1000 bootstrap replications were done to determine reverse causality and proportional mediation effects. MR analysis revealed 12 GM taxa with protective effects against IM and three taxa associated with an increased risk of IM. G__Lachnospiraceae_noname increased IM, and o__Burkholderiales.f__Oxalobacteraceae and g__Oxalobacter_formigenes had protective effects. IM had no impact on GM composition, and 22 immune cell characteristics were causally associated with IM with 10 risk-enhancing and 12 protective traits. The increased absolute count of hematopoietic stem cells (HSC AC) mediated 10.4% and the reduced percentage of CM CD8br %CD8br mediated -13.3% of the protective effect of o__Burkholderiales.f__Oxalobacteraceae. The results offer an important piece of information on microbial and immunologic targets of IM prevention.

records.title: Therapeutic and Prophylactic Agents for Viral Diseases: Current Status, Challenges, and Future Prospects.
records.abstract: Viral diseases remain a major global health challenge despite substantial advances in vaccination, antiviral therapeutics, and public-health interventions. However, current antiviral strategies are still constrained by important gaps, including rapid viral evolution, limited broad-spectrum efficacy, immune escape, antiviral resistance, incomplete durability of protection, and inequitable global access to prevention and treatment. This review provides a comprehensive and integrated overview of contemporary antiviral prevention and therapeutic strategies, spanning vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, direct-acting antivirals, host-targeted therapies, immunomodulators, RNA-based therapeutics, gene-editing technologies, and cellular immunotherapies. We discuss the mechanistic foundations, clinical applications, pharmacologic considerations, and translational challenges associated with each modality across major human viral pathogens, including HIV, HBV, HCV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, RSV, Ebola virus, arboviruses, and herpesviruses. Particular emphasis is placed on emerging innovations such as long-acting prophylaxis, Fc-engineered monoclonal antibodies, nanoparticle and mucosal vaccine platforms, CRISPR-based antiviral systems, and broadly protective host-directed approaches designed to overcome resistance and enhance pandemic preparedness. In addition, we highlight the growing importance of real-time genomic surveillance and equitable global deployment strategies in shaping future antiviral responses, collectively underscoring that the next generation of antiviral medicine will depend on the convergence of universal immunization strategies, durable therapeutics, precision immune modulation, and rapidly deployable platform technologies capable of addressing both endemic and emerging viral threats.
records.authors: Khan S, Nisar A, Li X, Yu H, Qadeer A, Mehmood SA, Lamraoui I, Liu S, Zhu L, Deng X, Kong B, Zhong K, Xia Z.

records.title: CRISPR Technology: From Bench to Bedside Applications.
records.abstract: CRISPR-Cas genome editing represents one of the most transformative advances in modern molecular biology, enabling programmable site-specific genetic modification that has revolutionized functional genomics and precision therapeutic development. Beyond canonical Cas9 nucleases, the CRISPR toolkit has diversified into precision base editors, prime editors, CRISPR-associated transposases, and Cas12/Cas13 RNA-targeting effectors, each with distinct mechanistic properties. Clinically, ex vivo CRISPR therapies for hemoglobinopathies have secured regulatory approval, while base editing, prime editing, and in vivo Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR)-T candidates are advancing through trials for a broad spectrum of hematologic, oncologic, and rare genetic disorders. However, existing reviews largely address technical innovation or clinical translation in isolation, lacking a holistic, up-to-date synthesis of the full bench-to-bedside trajectory of CRISPR technology. This review systematically dissects the molecular mechanisms, advantages, and limitations of core CRISPR editing platforms; summarizes pivotal clinical data across hemoglobinopathies, CAR-T immunotherapy, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cardiometabolic diseases and rare monogenic diseases; evaluates delivery systems including lipid nanoparticles and viral vectors; and discusses key translational barriers such as off-target genotoxicity and immunogenicity alongside emerging optimization strategies. This work provides a holistic bench-to-bedside framework for CRISPR research, offering critical insights to advance next-generation precision genetic medicine.
records.authors: Ma X, Li L, Sun Y.

records.title: The synthetic biology frontier: engineered oncolytic viruses and viral vectors for next-generation cancer therapy and gene delivery.
records.abstract: Viruses are no longer used merely as naturally occurring tools for gene transfer or as blunt cytolytic agents. Researchers are rewriting their genomes, capsids, tropisms, regulatory elements, and payloads to create therapeutic systems that sense disease, execute conditional programs, and remodel pathological tissue. In oncology, engineered oncolytic viruses (OVs) can combine tumor-selective replication with immunogenic cell death, antigen release, and local immune stimulation. In parallel, viral-vector engineering, particularly AAV and LVs, is addressing central limitations of gene delivery: the prevalence of pre-existing neutralizing antibodies, the difficulty of systemic administration and repeat dosing (AAV), and the manufacturing bottleneck of ex vivo cell therapies (LV). The clinical record is encouraging but uneven: T-VEC has shown that an engineered herpes simplex virus can improve durable responses in selected melanoma lesions, while G47Δ/teserpaturev and newer armed HSV platforms provide evidence of feasibility, safety, and occasional durable responses in difficult solid tumors. Lentiviral vector-based in vivo CAR-T cell generation, exemplified by KLN-1010/inMMyCAR and related first-in-human programs, signals a paradigm shift away from ex vivo manufacturing. However, the broader field has not converted its large preclinical literature into a proportional number of clinically meaningful, systemically deployable medicines. The main bottlenecks remain delivery, tumor heterogeneity, immune clearance, suboptimal pharmacodynamic biomarkers, manufacturing complexity, resistance, and the difficulty of proving benefit for products with delayed or immunologically mediated effects. This review examines the synthetic biology toolkit for programmable viral therapeutics through a unified engineering framework that integrates OVs, AAV, and LVs by design principle rather than by vector class. We discuss tumor-selective promoters, microRNA detargeting, retargeted capsids and ligands, attenuation, genome-scale assembly, immune-stimulatory payloads, bispecific and trispecific engagers, logic-gated circuits, safety switches, serodivergent AAV capsids, biomimetic cloaking, cell carriers, biomaterial delivery systems, and in vivo CAR-T generation. Our central thesis is that the next generation of viral medicines will be selected not by the most elaborate genome, but by the most coherent alignment of five measurable success factors: tumor selectivity, immune remodeling, delivery and biodistribution, controllable safety, and manufacturability. The emerging paradigm is therefore programmable viral therapeutics: context-sensitive biological medicines designed to operate within the constraints of human tumors and human immunity.
records.authors: Alsharedeh RH, Aljabali AAA, Obeid MA, Alqudah A, Gammoh O, Qnais E, Mishra V, Mishra Y, El-Tanani M.

records.title: Synthetic Community Driven by a Keystone Rhizosphere Bacterium Suppresses Whitefly-Mediated Begomovirus Transmission via the Jasmonate Signaling Pathway in Tomato.
records.abstract: Tomato production is threatened by the combined stress of whiteflies and the whitefly-transmitted Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV). Although the rhizosphere microbiome plays a critical role in plant defense, the rational assembly strategy and underlying mechanisms of a synthetic microbial community (SynCom) targeting this insect-virus complex remain unclear. Here, leveraging the beneficial soil legacy induced by Beauveria bassiana, we constructed an eight-strain synthetic community through multi-omics analysis, soil incubation, and root exudate chemotaxis assays. One-strain knockout experiments confirmed that strain N2 is the keystone species driving the biocontrol function. Through supernatant cross-culture assays, we further refined this consortium into an optimized synthetic community (OptSynM) consisting of the single keystone strain and four helper strains. Bioassays demonstrated that OptSynM significantly reduced whitefly fitness and suppressed TYLCV accumulation in tomato plants. Within the consortium, the helper strains enhanced the rhizosphere colonization of N2 by promoting its growth and biofilm formation. Mechanistically, OptSynM activated host systemic immunity via the jasmonic acid signaling pathway. Furthermore, OptSynM maintained robust biocontrol efficacy in pot trials conducted with natural agricultural soil. Our findings highlight the practical promise of microbiome-based interventions and provide a strategic framework for using synthetic microbial communities to facilitate sustainable agricultural practices.
records.authors: Zhao J, Wang Y, Yan G, Chen H, Xie Y, Wang W, Liu H.

records.title: Human papillomavirus 16 genomic variation in head and neck cancer: a systematic review with structural and functional annotation.
records.abstract: Human papillomavirus type 16 (HPV16)-positive head and neck cancer (HNC) is generally associated with a more favourable prognosis than HPV-negative disease. However, emerging evidence suggests that specific HPV16 genomic variants may be associated with poorer clinical outcomes. We therefore conducted a systematic review of HPV16 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) reported in HNC and mapped selected variants to viral genomic and protein regions to assess their potential relevance. We searched four major databases (PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science) for studies reporting HPV16 SNPs in HNC. Most studies focused on either E6 or E7, while only a few studies examined the entire HPV16 sequence. These SNPs were extracted and mapped to the HPV16 genome, while structural and functional characteristics were assessed using UniProt and the RCSB Protein Data Bank. Fourteen studies were analysed, identifying 30 SNPs in E6 and seven in E7. Structural mapping suggested that core HPV16 oncogenic motifs remain highly conserved, while recurrent variants tend to occur in mutationally permissive regions, such as the E6 interdomain linker. Only one study reported associations between HPV16 variants and poorer patient survival within the upstream regulatory region. However, these findings require independent validation before any clinical relevance can be established. The comprehensive mapping of HPV16 SNPs in HNC provides an important grounding for understanding how these SNPs may be associated with disease progression and patient outcomes. Although many of the identified SNPs are within important HPV16 regions, their associations with disease progression remain unclear. Further studies are required to determine which variants are associated with patient outcomes. A more comprehensive understanding of HPV16 genomic variation and its relevance could provide broader clinical insights across HPV16-associated cancers.
records.authors: Tran NH, Nguyen HG, Sais D, Lima N, Todd A, Van Nguyen T, Elliott M, Tran N.

records.title: Reduced methoxine formation by a sulfhydrylase variant identified through adaptive laboratory evolution of engineered Methylorubrum extorquens.
records.abstract: Streamlining metabolic pathways in microbes is a key strategy in metabolic engineering, often intended to channel evolution toward predictable outcomes. Here, Methylorubrum extorquens PA1 was rationally engineered by deleting redundant formate dehydrogenase operons (fdh234) to focus adaptive laboratory evolution on the remaining formate oxidation step under methanol stress. Genome sequencing identified a MetY-1 Y57D substitution in all five endpoint isolates from one evolving population, while the retained formate dehydrogenase operon carried no detected mutation. In vitro biochemical assays with purified MetY-1 showed that Y57D shifted the methoxine dose-response relative to the wild-type enzyme; at 5% (v/v) methanol the wild-type enzyme accumulated 0.386 ± 0.085 µM methoxine, whereas methoxine remained below the 0.025 µM detection limit for Y57D. A homocysteine-equivalent thiol signal, measured with Ellman reagent, remained detectable for both enzymes under the tested conditions. These results support a fine-tuning model for the product specificity of MetY-1 under methanol. The findings identify this specificity as a candidate point at which methanol toxicity may be mitigated; the contribution of the Y57D substitution to cellular growth was not tested here.
records.authors: Lee GM, Song DU, Ryu H, Kim J, Park S, Lee H, Kim D.

records.title: Characterization of EHV-1 viral genes at the respiratory tract using a tracheal explant culture model.
records.abstract: Equine herpesvirus 1 is the cause of respiratory disease, abortions, and equine herpesvirus myeloencephalopathy (EHM) in horse populations worldwide. Current vaccines do not prevent EHM. Several viral genes have been implicated in systemic dissemination and viral transfer to the CNS, but their roles during early respiratory events remain unclear. This study employed an equine tracheal explant culture model to characterize the role of selected EHV-1 genes in viral replication, infectivity, and innate immune activation during early respiratory infection. Tracheal explants were collected from respiratory healthy horses and inoculated with EHV-1 Ab4 WT or EHV-1 Ab4 recombinant viruses containing deletions or substitutions in genes involved in neuropathogenesis. Viral infection was evaluated using complementary approaches including immunohistochemistry, quantitative PCR, TCID₅₀ assays, and RT-qPCR analysis of innate immune genes. Deletion of ORF1 resulted in increased viral antigen detection, elevated viral DNA levels, enhanced production of infectious virus, and induction of innate immune markers (TLR3, IRF7, IRF9, CXCL9, CXCL10, CCL2, IL-6) supporting the role of ORF1 in modulating epithelial immune responses during early infection. Deletion of ORF2 increased antigen detection and showed limited regulation of chemokines (CXCL9, CCL5). Deletion of the gI-gE heterodimer reduced infectious virus production despite limited effects on viral genome presence, while increasing the expression of TLR3, IRF7, and CXCL9, highlighting its importance in cell-cell spread at the respiratory epithelium. Additionally, gB4, gD4, and the N752 variant exhibited WT-like replication with only subtle immune effects. Collectively, these findings provide insight into viral determinants that shape early epithelial infection and may influence downstream disease outcomes.
records.authors: Vázquez GB, Giessler KS, Sharma S, Osterrieder N, Kiupel M, Azab W, Hussey GS.

records.title: Visual Detection of Foodborne Viruses in Leafy Greens Using an AsCas12f-Split-G-Quadruplex Sensor.
records.abstract: Foodborne viruses are responsible for a substantial burden of disease worldwide, with fresh produce serving as the most abundant vehicle for transmission. However, rapid detection in solid produce, such as leafy greens, remains underdeveloped, as conventional methods often require labor-intensive sample preparation and specialized instrumentation. Herein, we present a colorimetric CRISPR-split-G4 biosensor for rapid viral surveillance in leafy greens that combines reverse transcription recombinase polymerase amplification (RT-RPA), AsCas12f-mediated trans-cleavage, and a modular split-G-quadruplex (split-G4) reporter system. In this system, target recognition activates the trans-cleavage activity of AsCas12f, resulting in degradation of a blocker strand and subsequent assembly of a catalytically active G4-hemin DNAzyme that generates a visible signal easily detectable by the naked eye. Using norovirus as a model pathogen, the platform exhibited high analytical sensitivity and specificity, enabling reliable detection of viral particles with minimal instrumentation. To evaluate practical applicability, the assay was coupled with a simplified leaf-disk extraction workflow and successfully applied to contaminated romaine lettuce and baby spinach samples without requiring viral nucleic acid purification. The platform achieved detection limits of 1000 and 5000 viral copies per 100 mg of romaine lettuce and spinach tissue, respectively. From sample processing to visual readout, the entire assay was completed in approximately 2 h. By integrating isothermal amplification, CRISPR-based target recognition, and instrument-free signal generation into a streamlined workflow, this strategy provides a promising platform for decentralized food safety monitoring and establishes a flexible framework for the on-site detection of viral pathogens in complex food matrices.
records.authors: Kasputis T, Landivar M, Yuan L, Wright RC, Zhang C, Chen J.

records.title: Host and anatomical filters prevent microbiome convergence in avian scavengers.
records.abstract: How host-associated microbiomes assemble under intense environmental microbial exposure remains a central question in microbial ecology. Vultures represent a unique natural system because these species differ markedly in feeding ecology and carcass use. We characterized bacterial communities across four anatomical niches (facial, buccal, tracheal, and cloacal) in 155 individuals spanning all four European obligate vulture species (subfamily Gypaetinae: Gypaetus barbatus, Neophron percnopterus, and Aegypiinae: Aegypius monachus and Gyps fulvus) and the facultative scavenger Milvus milvus. Microbiome composition was jointly structured by host species and anatomical niche, with host identity explaining more variation than anatomical compartment and a significant interaction indicating that interspecific differentiation depended on body site. Each niche supported distinct bacterial assemblages and core microbiomes: Cloacal communities were enriched in anaerobic gut-associated taxa, whereas facial and tracheal communities contained more environmental and respiratory-associated bacteria. Host-specific taxonomic signatures persisted within anatomical niches despite recurrent exposure to the same carrion-associated microbial pool. Age further influenced community composition, whereas sex had little detectable effect. The facultative scavenger showed the same broad anatomical compartmentalization observed in obligate scavengers, although taxonomic signatures differed among species. Thus, sustained exposure to a shared, microbially rich resource was insufficient to produce a common scavenger microbiome. Instead, microbiome assembly reflected hierarchical filtering by host identity, anatomical environment, and ontogeny. These findings distinguish microbial exposure from microbial persistence, establishing avian scavengers as a natural model for understanding how host-associated communities remain differentiated, despite recurrent exposure to shared environmental microbial reservoirs across ecological and anatomical scales in vertebrate hosts.

records.title: Beyond association: pathogenesis models reveal ecological drivers of vaginal dysbiosis.
records.abstract: Despite its critical importance to health, our understanding of the vaginal microbiome lags far behind other mucosal sites, reflecting both the distinct biology of the human vaginal microenvironment and the historic neglect of women's reproductive health in biomedical research. Recent investment in this area, coupled with the widespread use of high-throughput omics technologies, has greatly expanded our understanding of vaginal microbiota states and their associations with health and disease. However, associative studies that correlate community composition with clinical outcomes are limited in their ability to define causal, modifiable host-microbe relationships that support a protective microbiota. Consequently, broad probiotic strategies based on descriptive findings show limited success in restoring lasting homeostasis in the female reproductive tract. Murine infection models provide tractable systems for identifying evolutionarily conserved physiological processes that influence microbial growth. Here, we highlight studies across pathogenesis fields that leverage murine models to identify ecological factors controlling infection susceptibility in the vaginal microenvironment. Rather than treating pathogen colonization as an endpoint alone, we emphasize how genetically tractable microbes reveal the resources, barriers, and immune responses mediating microbial persistence, ascension, and inflammation. Where possible, we integrate these findings with clinical observations to assess their relevance to human reproductive health. Together, these studies illustrate how imperfect but tractable models reveal causal drivers of vaginal dysbiosis in women and help ground large-scale associative studies in a more clinically relevant way.
records.authors: Radlinski LC, Bäumler AJ.

records.title: Reducing bacterial resistance evolution through antimicrobial peptide modifications.
records.abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have emerged as promising alternatives to conventional antibiotics, yet bacteria can evolve resistance toward them through mechanisms that are poorly understood. Here, we selected a well-characterized antimicrobial peptide, melittin, as a model peptide that was shown to induce high levels of resistance in the human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus. We hypothesize that the physicochemical properties of AMPs might play a role in resistance development. To explore this hypothesis, we used computational approaches to design melittin derivatives with diverse physicochemical characteristics. A data set of 191 melittin-derived sequences (8-26 amino acids long) was analyzed to identify representative peptides spanning diverse physicochemical clusters. Selected peptides were synthesized and tested in an experimental evolution assay. Resistance dynamics, cross-resistance patterns, and cytotoxicity were evaluated in parallel. Full-length melittin with an amide or carboxylic acid C' terminus and highly hydrophobic derivatives [e.g., Mel(2-22)] showed high resistance occurrence, whereas Mel(5-24), a truncated variant, maintained antimicrobial activity while eliciting minimal resistance development. Whole-genome sequencing of endpoint populations revealed that melittin-evolved strains accumulated convergent mutations most prominently in pmtR, whereas Mel(5-24)-evolved populations converged only on ydbT, with no mutations in canonical resistance loci, suggesting fewer accessible adaptive pathways against the truncated peptide. Our results indicate that peptide hydrophobicity and chain length correlated with resistance fold change, whereas coil propensity showed a negative correlation. Notably, Mel(5-24) displayed reduced cross-resistance to other peptides and lower cytotoxicity toward mammalian cells than melittin, suggesting a broader therapeutic window. Overall, our findings indicate that tuning peptide hydrophobicity and chain length along with structural propensity can mitigate the evolutionary pressure driving resistance while maintaining antibacterial potency. Rational modulation of such physicochemical properties may provide a practical route for designing AMPs with improved selectivity and lower resistance potential.
records.authors: Cohen Tzemach H, Maron B, Malach E, Hayouka Z.

records.title: The protection of chronic cerebral ischemia by Hua-Feng-Dan involves the modulation of hippocampal transcriptome and gut dysbiosis.
records.abstract: The protective effects of Hua-Feng-Dan recipes against chronic cerebral hypoperfusion-induced ischemia were examined; RNA-seq and 16 S-rRNA-seq were used to explore the molecular mechanisms. Male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent unilateral common carotid artery ligation surgery to establish chronic cerebral hypoperfusion (CCH) models. Then, the CCH rats were treated with various Hua-Feng-Dan recipes in diet for 20 days. Finally, behavioral tests were performed, followed by histopathology. Hippocampal RNA was isolated for RNA-seq and RT-qPCR analyses; Colon bacterial DNA was isolated for 16 S rRNA-seq and bioinformatics. The CCH rats exhibited cognition deficits evidenced by Behavioral tests. The neurons in the hippocampus CA1 area were damaged. Hua-Feng-Dan recipes as Reduced_H (0.5 g/kg), Original, and Nonferment improved behavioral deficits and morphological changes, while Reduced_L (0.25 g/kg) was ineffective. RNA-seq revealed distinct gene expression pattern among groups. Ingenuity pathway analysis of differentially expressed genes revealed Hua-Feng-Dan recipes ameliorated Canonical pathways involved in cytosolic Ca2+ overload, disruption of IGF homeostasis and Neutrophil degranulation; attenuated CCH-activated Upstream regulators such as IL1B, IL6, TNF, IGF1, and glucose metabolism. CCH-decreased Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio were recovered by Hua-Feng-Dan recipes. CCH-increased Prevotellaceae and decreased Lachnospiraceae were attenuated; CCH-increased ASV1 and decreased ASV39 were brought to normal after Hua-Feng-Dan treatments. Similar to the efficacy against CCH, Reduced_L was ineffective in transcriptome and gut microbiota analysis. Hua-Feng-Dan recipes (Reduced_H, Original, and Nonferment) are effective against CCH-induced chronic cerebral ischemia, while Reduced_L was ineffective. The mechanisms of the protection are related to transcriptome regulation in the hippocampus, and modulation of CCH-disrupted gut dysbiosis.
records.authors: Liu B, Huang B, Xu Y, Liu J.

records.title: Diverse bacteria exhibit superadditive growth on mixed classes of carbon sources
records.abstract: Heterotrophic bacteria in nature encounter complex mixtures of functionally-distinct carbon sources, yet whether such diversity enhances growth yield across diverse taxa remains unknown. We grew dozens of strains from four phyla on defined mixtures representing five classes of carbon sources. Remarkably, many but not all strains exhibited superadditive growth on a dilute mixture of all 64 compounds—that is, yield exceeding the weighted sum of yields on more concentrated subsets of functionally-similar compounds. Using exometabolomics, pooled genetic screens, and proteomics, we find that superadditive growth is associated with enhanced carbon consumption in the mixed-class medium, combined with reduced dependence on amino acid and nucleotide biosynthesis. Moreover, superadditive growth was predictable from genomes within the tested strain panel and correlated with genomically encoded sugar-over-acid preference. These findings reveal a previously underrecognized axis of physiological variation among heterotrophs and open the door to understanding the biochemical and evolutionary basis of this divergence.

records.title: A Framework for Variant Filtering to Improve Diagnostic Outcomes in Genome Sequencing
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Rare genetic disorders frequently remain undiagnosed despite the use of exome sequencing (ES) and genome sequencing (GS). This study aimed to enhance diagnostic yield by introducing a systematic framework: SMART filtering (Systematic, Multi-step, Automated, Rare variant prioritization Tool), designed to optimize GS analysis, with a particular emphasis on non-coding regions. We retrospectively analyzed 153 cases with previously negative ES and GS results. SMART filtering was applied as a pre-annotation filtering step, integrating conservation metrics, allele frequency thresholds, and splicing prediction scores. Then followed by phenotype-based prioritization and manual review. Application of this framework identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 4.6% of cases, strong variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in 1.3%, and additional candidate variants in 5.2% of cases. Several deep-intronic variants were confirmed by RNA studies and segregation analyses. The framework enabled efficient prioritization of non-coding and regulatory variants that were overlooked by standard analyses. In conclusion, SMART filtering offers a reproducible and scalable strategy to improve diagnostic yield in GS, particularly in cases where conventional analysis methods fall short. Integrating such frameworks into clinical genomic pipelines can enhance variant interpretability and diagnostic performance, ultimately leading to better patient care outcomes.

records.title: 41% of Gram-negative bacteria encode a Type Six Secretion System
records.abstract: The type six secretion system (T6SS) is a highly studied, versatile bacterial nanoweapon that is important in bacterial pathogenesis and evolution. Despite extensive study, its prevalence remains poorly quantified. Analyzing 35,467 representative genomes, we find that approximately 41% of genomes in the average well-sampled Gram-negative genus (more than 30 sampled genomes) encode a T6SS. Further, we show that the distribution of the T6SS is patchy at all taxonomic levels. The uneven distribution we found is consistent with context-dependent selection, repeated evolutionary loss, or greater evolutionary lability. Our dataset provides a foundation for studying the drivers of T6SS distribution, and our pipeline enables similar surveys of other secretion systems, gene clusters, and multi-protein complexes across bacteria.
records.authors: Zhang C, Hassler H, Ratcliff WC, Speare L, Hammer BK.

records.title: Impacts of algal community structure on algae-derived phosphorus concentrations in Lake Taihu, China, from 2021 to 2025
records.abstract: Abstract    Phosphorus control remains a critical challenge for managing eutrophication in Lake Taihu, yet quantitative assessments of algae-derived phosphorus (ADP) and its response to community shifts remain scarce. Based on monthly data from 20 entire-lake stations during 2021–2025 and an experimentally determined cellular phosphorus content for  Microcystis  spp. (1.46×10  − 10  mg/cell), we estimated cell-specific phosphorus for 113 algal species by cell-volume conversion and quantified ADP and phylum-level contributions. Annual mean total algal density decreased from 1.2×10  8  cells/L in 2021 to 6.9×10  7  cells/L in 2025, with marked turnover:  Microcystis  spp. fell from 83.6% to 32.4% of total density, while diatoms, cryptophytes and chlorophytes rose significantly. Annual mean ADP ranged from 0.015 to 0.022 mg/L (33.4% of TP) and was dominated by cyanobacteria, diatoms and chlorophytes. Cyanobacteria supplied over 65% of ADP during 2021–2022, declining markedly after 2023, while diatom and chlorophyte contributions rose. Notably, an algal rebound in December 2024 (density up 79.3% year-on-year) coincided with a 25.0% ADP decrease, because a large gain in small-celled cyanobacteria was outweighed by a much smaller loss of large-celled diatoms containing seven to eight times more phosphorus per cell. These findings show that ADP is a key component of TP in Lake Taihu and is governed by two mechanistically distinct controls: algal biomass (quantity) and the community-weighted cell-specific phosphorus content set by the assemblage cell-size structure (quality), which can act in opposite directions. Algal community structure thus acts as an active regulator of lake phosphorus and must be considered alongside algal density in phosphorus management.
records.authors: Yang Z, Zhu B, Zhang J, Dai X, Zhang H, Xu Y, Song T, Zhuang Y.

records.title: Long-term organic fertilizer amendment improves citrus yield and quality in calcareous soil mainly by shaping the microbiome and mobilizing soil phosphorus
records.abstract: Abstract    Background and aims  Citrus, the largest fruit globally, often encounters nutritional imbalances, notably phosphorus (P) deficiency, when cultivated in calcareous soil. Although organic fertilizers outperform inorganic alternatives in citrus production, their specific impacts and the microbiome’s role in calcareous soil remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of rapeseed cakes (RC) and cow manure (CM) on citrus plant-soil performance and their correlations with microbiome composition and functional profiles. Methods  We conducted a 5-year long-term positioning field experiment on citrus under calcareous soil conditions. Field experiments combined with amplicon and metagenome sequencing were employed to analyze differences in plant-soil performance and rhizosphere microbiome traits under RC and CM treatments. Isolation-culture verification was further performed to validate the function of key differential microorganisms. Results  RC and CM supplementation enhanced fruit yield and quality while facilitating P utilization in calcareous soil, with CM showing a better improvement effect. Both organic fertilizers induced significant alterations in rhizosphere microbiome composition and function. The genus  Cupriavidus  was significantly enriched in rhizosphere under organic fertilizer treatments. Isolation-culture verification confirmed it enhanced soil P availability by secreting organic acids, alkaline phosphatases and other enzymes, serving as plant-growth-promoting rhizobacteria for citrus. Conclusion  Our findings clarify the effects of rapeseed cakes and cow manure on citrus growth and soil P activation in calcareous soil, and reveal the key role of the rhizosphere microbiome represented by  Cupriavidus  in this process. This study advances our understanding of microbiome-mediated improvement of citrus growth and P utilization via organic fertilizer application.
records.authors: gong k, wang h, you c, zheng c, Qian W, Pang Y, yang w, yin h, Li q, zeng y, peng l, wang n, Chun C.

records.title: Worldwide emergence of SARS-CoV-2 NB.1.8.1 sublineage with spike 420N and 478T dual substitution.
records.abstract: BackgroundAfter a year of quiescence, SARS-CoV-2 activity increased rapidly in Hong Kong since June 2026. We sought to characterize the genomic profile of SARS-CoV-2 driving this COVID-19 surge in Hong Kong and to examine the global dissemination of the identified circulating lineages.MethodsWe performed SARS-CoV-2 whole-genome sequencing on archived respiratory specimens collected at Queen Mary Hospital, Hong Kong, between January 2025 and July 2026. Viral lineages were assigned via Nextclade. Global SARS-CoV-2 metadata downloaded from GISAID as of July 2026 were analysed to track global evolutionary trends.ResultsAmong 615 successfully sequenced strains, the XDV descendant NB.1.8.1 was the predominant lineage. Between April and July 2026, NB.1.8.1 descendants accounted for 95.6% (108/113) of sequenced strains, dominated by PQ.16.1.1 (81.5%). Spike substitutions 420N and 478T emerged rapidly. While 478T increased gradually throughout 2025, 420N emerged in April 2026 and reached 98.0% by June-July 2026. Strains harbouring 420N-478T dual substitution arose independently across distinct NB.1.8.1 lineages, accounting for 94.4% (102/108) of NB.1.8.1 descendants in Hong Kong during this period. Globally, the prevalence of NB.1.8.1 strains with 420N-478T dual substitution increased from ConclusionThe 2026 COVID-19 surge in Hong Kong was driven by NB.1.8.1 descendants harbouring spike 420N and 478T substitutions. The rapid worldwide expansion of these dual-substitution lineages highlights their competitive growth advantage and underscores the need for continued global genomic surveillance.

records.title: Epigenetic and Post-Transcriptional Regulation of Autophagy in Inflammatory Bowel Disease.
records.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), principally comprising Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), encompasses chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disorders of the gastrointestinal tract. Genome-wide association studies have identified hundreds of susceptibility loci associated with IBD. Recent studies have highlighted the critical importance of autophagy in maintaining intestinal epithelial homeostasis, regulating host-microbiota interactions, coordinating immune responses and restricting microbial pathogens. Furthermore, emerging evidence indicates that classical epigenetic mechanisms and post-transcriptional regulators may influence autophagy-related pathways in IBD and thereby shape intestinal inflammatory responses. This review critically evaluates current evidence linking epigenetic and post-transcriptional regulation to autophagy in IBD, distinguishes established mechanisms from indirect associations and discusses their mechanistic and translational implications.
records.authors: Liu Y, Jiang W, Zhou J, Xun F, Li H, Li Y, Zhang J, Qian Y, Wang H.

records.title: Genetic mechanisms underlying feeding behaviour in silkworm larvae.
records.abstract: The silkworm, an economically important insect that feeds almost exclusively on mulberry leaves, has emerged as a pivotal model for understanding the genetic basis of feeding behaviour in herbivorous specialists. Recent advances have begun to unravel the complex molecular networks that enable efficient host plant recognition, nutrient intake and metabolic adaptation. Feeding behaviour in silkworm larvae is governed by a multi-layered regulatory system that coordinates peripheral detection, internal organ sensing and neuroendocrine regulation. Key players include gustatory and odorant receptors, odorant-binding proteins, odorant-degrading enzymes, neuropeptides and transcription factors, all functioning in a coordinated, tissue-specific manner. In this review, we synthesize current knowledge of these genetic mechanisms within an integrative framework that links peripheral chemosensation and internal organ sensing to neuropeptide regulation and ultimately to behavioural output. We further discuss how comparative and evolutionary perspectives illuminate the genomic and adaptive evolution of mulberry specialization. We also consider emerging regulatory layers, including epigenetic modifications and the microbiota-gut-brain axis, which have been implicated in feeding behaviour in other insects but remain largely unexplored in the silkworm. Finally, we highlight emerging technologies that will advance research in this field, providing a foundation for improving artificial diet-based sericulture.
records.authors: Jiang D, Tong X, Dai F, Zou Y.

records.title: Unraveling the Genetic Architecture of Sclerotinia Basal Stalk Rot Resistance in Cultivated Sunflower Through Genome-Wide Association Mapping.
records.abstract: Sclerotinia basal stalk rot (BSR), caused by the necrotrophic fungal pathogen Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, is an economically important disease of cultivated sunflower (Helianthus annuus L.). Resistance to BSR is quantitative and genetically complex, and although biparental mapping studies have identified genomic regions associated with resistance, knowledge of the broader genetic architecture of BSR resistance in diverse cultivated sunflower germplasm remains limited. In this study, genome-wide association studies were conducted to understand the genetic architecture of BSR resistance using two independent panels. The Sunflower Association Mapping (SAM) panel was evaluated under greenhouse conditions with two S. sclerotiorum isolates differing in aggressiveness, BN166 or NEB-274, using two disease traits: mean days to death and area under the mortality curve. An open-pollinated variety (OPV) panel was evaluated across four field environments after inoculation with isolate NEB-274 and scored for disease incidence. Genotyping datasets comprised 3.2 and 3.5 million single nucleotide polymorphisms for the SAM and OPV panels, respectively. The study identified 20 significant associations in the SAM panel and 7 in the OPV panel. No overlapping associations were detected between panels or isolates, indicating isolate- and environment-specific genetic architecture despite moderate positive correlations between isolates (r ≈ 0.74). Eight loci co-localized with previously reported BSR quantitative trait locus intervals. Candidate genes included a protein kinase at the strongest association, a receptor-like kinase, a glutathione S-transferase, and members of the WD40 repeat protein family detected in both panels. These findings provide genomic resources for marker-assisted selection and resistance breeding.
records.authors: Angidi S, McNellie JP, Henning S, Pasche JS, Hulke B, Underwood W.

records.title: Inferring viral variants and fitness advantages from longitudinal wastewater sequencing data
records.abstract: During the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, wastewater-based epidemiology emerged as an effective tool for monitoring infection dynamics. However, wastewater represents a pooled sample of incomplete viral genomic fragments originating from multiple individuals in the catchment area of a wastewater treatment plant, preventing the assembly of complete viral genomes. Existing computational pipelines are therefore limited in detecting new variants that are absent from clinical sequencing data. We developed FitNMF, an integrated viral dynamics and non-negative matrix factorization model that leverages the temporal structure of wastewater sequencing data and the underlying variant competition to jointly infer mutational signatures, relative abundances, and fitness advantages of circulating variants directly from wastewater next-generation sequencing data. Using simulated data as well as wastewater time-series data collected between 2021 and 2024 across six Swiss wastewater treatment plants, we demonstrate FitNMF's ability to identify and quantify emerging variants de novo, offering a powerful tool for real-time variant surveillance in settings with limited clinical sequencing.
records.authors: Rimaite A, Beerenwinkel N.

records.title: Improving Talaromycosis Infection Diagnosis and Prognosis with Metagenomic Next-Generation Sequencing.
records.abstract: BackgroundEarly diagnosis and timely initiation of appropriate antifungal treatment are critical for improving the prognosis of talaromycosis infection. We aimed to test whether metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), versus conventional microbiological testing (CMT), improves talaromycosis diagnosis and management in HIV-negative patients via higher sensitivity and faster detection.MethodsWe retrospectively investigated the clinical data of patients with Talaromyces marneffei (T. marneffei) infection in six hospitals in Fujian, China, between July 2015 and June 2024. The diagnostic performance and clinical impact of mNGS were compared with those of CMT.ResultsSeventy-four patients were included, with 38 cases in the mNGS group and 36 cases for CMT group, based on the method that established the definitive diagnosis. The median duration from hospitalization to confirmed diagnosis was significantly shorter in the mNGS group than in the CMT group (5.0 vs 12.0 days, p p p = 0.033; 26.3% vs 5.56%, p = 0.025). The mNGS group has a trend of lower mortality compared with the CMT group (18.4% vs 38.9%, p = 0.072). In addition, the length of stay was significantly shorter in the mNGS group than in the CMT group (14.5 days vs 21.0 days, p = 0.007).ConclusionmNGS facilitates rapid diagnosis and improves administration of targeted antimicrobial therapy, thus improving the prognosis of T. marneffei infection. The clinical utility of mNGS for talaromycosis in at-risk populations should be investigated in prospective and large studies.
records.authors: Zhang L, He X, Xu L, Xiao J, Lin J, Song B, Chen L, Chen G, Liu K.

records.title: An integrated analytical strategy combining UPLC-QTOF-MS-based metabolomics and 16S rRNA sequencing to explore the mechanism of Shenqi Jieyu decoction in coronary heart disease complicated by depression in ApoE<sup>-/-</sup> mice.
records.abstract: Coronary heart disease combined with depression (dual-heart disorder) exhibits high morbidity and poor prognosis, lacking safe unified therapeutic agents. Shenqi Jieyu Decoction (SQJY) relieves depressive and cardiovascular symptoms in percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) patients, yet its underlying multiple potential mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, an ApoE-/- mouse model of dual-heart disorder was induced via high-fat diet combined with chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS). Behavioral testing, aortic pathological staining, hippocampal neurochemistry, and ultra-performance liquid chromatography coupled with quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UPLC-QTOF-MS)-based untargeted metabolomics of serum and cecal contents were integrated with 16S rRNA sequencing, establishing an integrated multi-omics workflow to examine the potential modulatory effects of SQJY and to explore its possible mechanism. Behavioral and pathological assays indicated that SQJY alleviated atherosclerosis and depression-like phenotypes, elevated hippocampal 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), dopamine (DA) and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and suppressed neuroinflammatory cytokines. 16S sequencing suggested SQJY remodeled dysregulated gut microbiota toward a more balanced profile. Metabolomics identified disturbed sphingolipid and glycerophospholipid metabolism as important metabolic signatures that H-SQJY group corrected more extensively in cecal content (68 of 265 metabolites) than in serum (8 of 103). Phylogenetic Investigation of Communities by Reconstruction of Unobserved States 2 (PICRUSt2)-based prediction of microbial functions was integrated, and Spearman correlation analysis showed significant associations between predicted microbial functions, differential gut microbes and lipid metabolites. Collectively, SQJY showed concurrent potential cardioprotective and antidepressant effects, possibly through restoring gut microbial homeostasis and modulating lipid metabolic disorders. These correlative and predicted findings provide preliminary evidence for the potential application of SQJY in dual-heart disorder.
records.journal: Journal of chromatography. B, Analytical technologies in the biomedical and life sciences
records.authors: Lu W, Zhang D, Zhang H, Fu Y, Hei Z, Song L, Wang S, He F, Wang F, Cang S.

records.title: Aldehyde-dependent β-aminocarbonyl chitosan/Ag composites: Linking chemical structure, silver loading, and antibacterial performance.
records.abstract: In this study, β-aminocarbonyl chitosan (BACC) derivatives were synthesized through Mannich modification using different aldehyde precursors and subsequently incorporated with Ag to investigate the relationship between chemical structure, Ag loading, and antibacterial performance. The resulting materials were characterized by FTIR and UV-Vis spectroscopy, while Ag incorporation was quantitatively determined using atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS). Antibacterial activity was evaluated against bacteria associated with fresh chicken meat using the total plate count (TPC) method at concentrations of 1000 and 2500 ppm after 0, 3, and 7 days of refrigerated storage. FTIR analysis indicated interactions of Ag species with nitrogen- and oxygen-containing functional groups, while the evolution of surface plasmon resonance bands supported the formation and stabilization of Ag species. AAS revealed structure-dependent Ag loading, with values of 1.25%, 0.93%, 0.80%, 0.73%, and 0.53% for BACC-Sa/Ag, BACC-OV/Ag, BACC-F/Ag, Ch/Ag, and BACC-P/Ag, respectively. BACC-Sa/Ag achieved the highest bacterial reduction of 96.39 ± 0.39% at 2500 ppm after 7 days, while BACC-F/Ag reached 96.27 ± 0.59% under the same conditions. Notably, BACC-P/Ag achieved 95.40 ± 0.42% reduction after 3 days at 1000 ppm despite having the lowest Ag loading. These results demonstrate that antibacterial performance was governed by the combined effects of aldehyde-derived functionality, Ag incorporation, concentration, and storage time rather than Ag loading alone. The results demonstrated their potential to suppress microbial growth, highlighting the applicability of these materials as candidates for further development in antibacterial food-preservation systems. Nevertheless, additional investigations involving film fabrication, silver-ion release, migration, and safety assessments are necessary before their suitability for food-contact packaging applications can be established.

records.title: Cryo-EM structures of an  Acinetobacter baumannii  podovirus reveal a canonical capsid maturation
records.abstract: Phages that hunting multidrug resistant bacteria represent a promising approach in precision medicine nowadays, including these infecting  Acinetobacter baumannii . To data, a large number of  A. baumannii phages has been isolated, however, complete structural information remains not adequately released. Previously, we reported a podovirus, AbP20, that infects  A. baumannii with potent efficacy in mouse model. In the present work, we further report the high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of AbP20 and its procapsid. The near-atomic resolution reveals that AbP20 is composed of five distinct structural subunits, i.e., capsid, portal, nozzle, fiber, and adaptor. We then characterized the assembly mechanisms of molecular interactions within capsid and portal-tail complex. By co-expressing the scaffold protein and the capsid protein of AbP20, we constructed the self-assembled DNA-free procapsid of AbP20. A near-atomic resolution reconstruction reveals it a double-layered concentric spherical architecture with a nearly 1:1 ratio of these two proteins. Comparison between the mature and apo-form of the capsid of AbP20 uncovers a canonical model of conformational switch from procapsid to capsid. Altogether, the present work reports the first whole atom structure of a podovirus infecting  A. baumannii , providing a reference for structure-based phage engineering and editing.  Author summary  Multidrug-resistant bacteria, particularly  Acinetobacter baumannii , pose a severe threat to global health. As a promising alternative in precision medicine, phages, viruses that naturally infect and kill bacteria, offer a new avenue to combat these dangerous infections. Although numerous phages targeting  A. baumannii have been identified, their detailed structural information remains largely elusive. In this study, we utilized high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to determine the native virion structure of AbP20, a podovirus with potent efficacy against  A. baumannii . We revealed the detailed architecture and assembly of its distinct components. Furthermore, by reconstructing the procapsid structure of AbP20, we elucidated the role of its scaffold protein in capsid assembly and maturation. This work reports the first complete atomic structure of a podovirus infecting  A. baumannii , reveals a canonical model for virion capsid maturation, and provides a valuable reference for structure-guided phage engineering and editing.

records.title: Detection and characterization of RNA viruses in ticks of the genus Amblyomma Koch, 1844 (Arachnida: Acari: Ixodidae) from the Brazilian Amazon reveals a putative novel virus.
records.abstract: Ticks are among the major vectors of infectious agents to humans. These arthropods are known to transmit a complex of encephalitis-causing viruses responsible for severe acute and chronic neurological infections in both animals and humans. This study aimed to investigate the RNA virus of Amblyomma cajennense s.s. and Amblyomma geayi ticks collected in various municipalities within the state of Pará, in the Brazilian Amazon, using a viral RNA metagenomics approach. A total of 12 viral sequences were identified, distributed across four families: Chuviridae (n = 1), Rhabdoviridae (n = 7), Orthototiviridae (n = 1), and Partitiviridae (n = 3). Among the detected viruses, Geayi mivirus, identified in Amblyomma geayi, represents a possible new virus described in this study, thereby expanding knowledge regarding RNA viruses associated with ticks of the genus Amblyomma in the Brazilian Amazon.This study presents a comprehensive characterization of RNA viruses from Amblyomma cajennense s.s. and Amblyomma geayi in the Brazilian Amazon. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first characterization of RNA viruses from A. geayi and the first report of members of the family Partitiviridae in A. cajennense s.s. in Brazil. Furthermore, a possible new virus, named Geayi mivirus, was identified in A. geayi. We highlight the underrepresentation of RNA viruses associated with Brazilian ticks in reference databases, underscoring the importance of expanding metagenomic surveillance.

records.title: Genetic foundations of copper stress tolerance in safflower: bridging heavy metal contamination and global warming challenges.
records.abstract: Key messageIntegrated phenotyping and multi-omics approaches identified Cu-tolerant safflower genotypes and candidate genes underpinning Cu stress resilience for climate-adaptive breeding. Copper (Cu) contamination threatens agriculture, yet safflower's genetic basis for Cu tolerance remains unexplored-especially as global warming intensifies risks through night-time warming and soil acidification. We conducted a pot experiment using 94 safflower genotypes under four copper chloride (CuCl₂) concentrations, revealing substantial variation among genotypes and treatments with trait reductions ranging from 1.75% (root-shoot ratio) (RSR) to 57.14% (dry root weight) (DRW). Correlation analysis showed positive trait relationships, while principal component analysis (PCA) grouped genotypes into three clusters. Ten genotypes consistently performed better under Cu stress, indicating strong tolerance potential for climate-resilient breeding. Genome-wide association study (GWAS) detected 180 significant marker-trait associations (MTAs) across eight traits, and gene annotation linked candidate genes to brassinosteroid signaling, ion homeostasis, metal response, and transport. Co-expression analysis revealed a tightly connected tolerance module in which AT5G01610 and AT5G14640 shared the same top co-expressed partners (r > 0.8), including HMA4, CAX1, and SOS1, suggesting coordinated roles in Cu stress tolerance. Convergent protein-protein interaction (PPI) validation confirmed these candidates as distinct hubs that are physically interacting and transcriptionally co-regulated, supporting their function as Cu tolerance modules. In silico heatmap-based expression profiling showed distinct, stress-specific transcriptional responses in Arabidopsis roots, with Cu inducing, cadmium (Cd) eliciting mixed, and (Al) aluminum repressing expression. RNA-seq analysis identified seven Cu stress tolerance genes, validated by qRT-PCR. These findings highlight promising genotypes for developing Cu-resilient safflower cultivars, while further investigation of the highly expressed genes is needed to clarify their roles under Cu stress.
records.authors: Ali F, Ali A, Shah OU, Arif MAR, Nadeem MA, Baloch FS, Jan SM, Thi Ha MKT, Chung YS.

records.title: Nocardia seriolae Infection Causes Granulomatous Pathology, High Mortality and Growth Impairment in Cultured Rice Field Eel (Monopterus albus).
records.abstract: During a recent epidemiological survey of rice field eel (Monopterus albus) aquaculture farms in Jiangxi Province, China, we observed a characteristic presentation of multifocal granulomatous nodules suggestive of nocardial infection. Bacterial isolation yielded light-yellow, pigmented colonies with a granular texture and dry, wrinkled surface. Microscopy revealed branching filamentous rods characteristic of Nocardia, while histopathology demonstrated granulomatous inflammation with severe necrosis. Molecular identification, supported by whole-genome sequencing, confirmed the isolate as Nocardia seriolae, designated strain HZAU2505. Targeted sampling of clinically symptomatic fish across fifteen batches revealed a Nocardia seriolae PCR detection rate of 22.86% (8/35) among diseased animals. Notably, specific PCR surveillance targeting the Nocardia seriolae ITS gene detected Nocardia seriolae DNA in 90.9% (10/11) of frozen feed samples from affected facilities. Disk diffusion screening for aquaculture-approved drugs indicated that strain HZAU2505 was susceptible to doxycycline, neomycin, florfenicol, intermediate susceptible to ciprofloxacin, and resistant to enrofloxacin and penicillin. Complementary broth microdilution assays (CLSI M24) revealed consistent resistance patterns: isolates were susceptible to aminoglycosides (amikacin), tetracyclines (doxycycline), macrolides (clarithromycin), and oxazolidinones (linezolid), showed intermediate susceptibility to quinolones (ciprofloxacin), but exhibited strong resistance to β-lactams (amoxicillin-clavulanate), sulfonamides (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), and glycopeptides (vancomycin). Experimental infection with 106 CFU/fish of strain HZAU2505 led to 80% cumulative mortality. Infected Monopterus albus displayed perianal lesions, internal white nodules, and clinical signs consistent with natural infections. Bacterial loads reached up to 105 copies/mg sample. Infected fish also exhibited significantly reduced growth, with a 17.7% lower weight gain rate after 21 days compared to controls, alongside markedly elevated total triglyceride (TG) concentrations. This study provides evidence of Nocardia seriolae infection in Monopterus albus, which manifests as severe necrotizing lesions, significant growth impairment, and high mortality. These findings highlight a critical risk to eel aquaculture productivity and disease management.
records.authors: Tian TT, Yan B, Zhou H, Jin Y, Zeng H, Tang S, Zhang YA, Zhou Y.

records.title: Ecological commissioning links microbial succession to treatment stabilization during managed aquifer recharge.
records.abstract: Managed aquifer recharge (MAR) systems require ecological as well as hydraulic commissioning, yet when attached microbial communities become spatially organized and associated with stable treatment remains unresolved. We operated duplicate 10 m sand-column trains supplied with River Lek water for 12 months and tracked water quality and bacterial communities monthly at 1, 5, and 10 m and in the effluent. Removal trajectories for dissolved organic carbon, Fe²⁺, Mn²⁺, NH₄⁺, and NO₂⁻ and bacterial diversity showed little sustained directional change after approximately 5 months, while distance-associated communities became evident after month 6. At month 12, ASVs shared with 10 m sand accounted for 69.7% of effluent sequence abundance. Only 11.6% of shared influent-sand sequence abundance was consistent with neutral expectations, whereas sand-to-effluent neutral-model fit increased to R² = 0.60. We define this coordinated transition as ecological commissioning: a months-long process in which environmental selection organizes attached communities, spatial zones emerge, and terminal-zone dispersal increasingly shapes produced-water microbiology. Although timing is system specific, this framework identifies start-up and terminal aquifer zones as targets for MAR treatment verification and biological water-quality management.

records.title: SiTIFY9 enhances salt stress tolerance and promotes early flowering in foxtail millet.
records.abstract: Soil salinity severely limits plant growth and productivity through osmotic stress, ion toxicity, and excessive accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Although TIFY proteins regulate plant responses to environmental stresses, their roles in salt tolerance in foxtail millet (Setaria italica) remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized SiTIFY9 (Seita.9G51810) through phylogenetic analysis, expression profiling, subcellular localization, transcriptional activation assays, stable overexpression, physiological measurements, and transcriptome sequencing. SiTIFY9 clustered with rice OsTIFY11a/OsJAZ9, localized predominantly to the nucleus, and exhibited no autonomous transcriptional activation activity in yeast. Under salt stress, SiTIFY9-overexpressing plants showed reduced hydrogen peroxide and malondialdehyde accumulation, increased catalase and peroxidase activities, and enhanced proline accumulation compared with wild-type plants. Overexpression also restricted Na+ accumulation, promoted K+ retention, and increased the K+/Na+ ratio, indicating improved ionic homeostasis. Transcriptome analysis revealed extensive transcriptional changes associated with stress responses, redox regulation, ion transport, phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, carbohydrate metabolism, and secondary metabolism. RT-qPCR further confirmed altered expression of genes involved in ion transport, osmoprotection, transcriptional regulation, and stress defense. Independently, SiTIFY9-overexpressing plants flowered 14-16 days earlier than wild-type plants under non-saline conditions, suggesting an additional role in flowering-time regulation. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that SiTIFY9 overexpression enhances salt tolerance by improving antioxidant defense, osmotic adjustment, and ionic homeostasis, accompanied by transcriptional reprogramming of stress-responsive pathways. Furthermore, its association with earlier flowering suggests a potential developmental function. This study identifies SiTIFY9 as a promising candidate for further investigation of salt-stress tolerance and flowering-time regulation in foxtail millet.
