records.title: Second-site capsule-locus mutations, not Ade efflux disruption, determine phage susceptibility across an  Acinetobacter baumannii  transposon mutant panel
records.abstract: Resistance-Nodulation-Division (RND) efflux pumps have been implicated in phage adsorption in several Gram-negative bacteria, suggesting that AdeABC, AdeFGH and AdeIJK, the three characterised RND efflux systems of multidrug-resistant  Acinetobacter baumannii, could play a similar role. We tested this hypothesis using five phages (Equilibrator, Taro, AT01, BB02, and AC03) and a panel of 13  A. baumannii strains, including nine AB5075 transposon mutants affecting AdeABC, AdeFGH, or AdeIJK. Host-range testing, efficiency-of-plating assays, capsule-associated density measurements, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and whole-genome sequencing were performed to assess the relationship between genotype and phage infection. Overall, the data did not support a role for the Ade components as receptors. Phages Equilibrator, Taro and AT01 formed plaques on every strain, and the restricted host ranges of BB02 and AC03 did not correspond to disruption of a particular efflux system. Sequencing instead identified second-site mutations in the KL25 capsule locus in six of the ten AB5075 strains. These included a 1,998-bp deletion affecting  wzc , substitutions in  mnaA and  mnaB , an IS  Aba13 insertion in a putative glycosyltransferase and a subpopulation-associated frameshift in  wzx . AC03 formed plaques on all six strains with capsule-locus changes but on none of the five strains without them. Capsule dependence differed among the other phages: relative to the parental AB5075, infection by these phages, Equilibrator, Taro and BB02, was restricted on the capsule-deficient  wzc ::T26 strain, whereas AT01 efficiency was only slightly reduced. Insertion-site mapping also distinguished a near-terminal  adeK insertion that retained the parental antimicrobial phenotype from an early  adeK insertion associated with loss of AdeIJK function. Together, these findings identify capsule-locus variation as the strongest correlation with phage susceptibility in this panel and demonstrate the importance of verifying mutant genomes before assigning phenotypes to their annotated insertions.  Impact statement  Transposon mutant collections are valuable for linking bacterial genes to phenotypes, but the recorded insertion does not necessarily describe every genetic change in a strain. We investigated whether the Ade efflux systems of  A. baumannii contribute to phage susceptibility. Although the initial host-range patterns suggested differences among efflux mutants, whole-genome sequencing revealed independent capsule-locus mutations in six of ten AB5075 strains. Newly isolated phage AC03 formed plaques on every strain with a capsule-locus change and on none with wild-type capsule loci. This association explained differences between strains carrying separate insertions in the same  ade genes. The other phages we isolated also differed in their dependence on capsule: some infected the capsule-deficient mutant poorly, whereas AT01 was comparatively unaffected. These results emphasise two considerations for phage studies. The capsule state of the isolation or test host can strongly influence which phages are recovered and how efficiently they plate. Whole-genome verification is equally important when interpreting phenotypes from ordered mutant libraries, particularly when surface structures are involved.
records.authors: Tarasenko A, Papudeshi B, Hutton ALK, Zang M, Davies BJ, Bouras G, Mallawaarachchi V, Eijkelkamp BA, Edwards RA.

records.title: Wild wood mouse gut microbiota are influenced by captivity and cross-fostering
records.abstract: Background  Wild and laboratory animals harbour profoundly different gut microbiota, but how microbiomes shift between these states, and the relative roles of captivity, microbial history, and host identity in shaping that shift, remain unclear. Here, we developed a unique wood mouse (  Apodemus sylvaticus ) system comprising free-living mice (Wild:  As ), a wild-derived colony maintained in captivity for over a decade (Wild-like:  As ), and a second colony that we generated from the Wild-like:  As mice by caesarean rederivation and cross-fostering to laboratory  Mus musculus (Lab-like:  As ). We compared these three  Apodemus cohorts with conventional laboratory  Mus musculus (Lab:  Mm ) to ask how microbial diversity, community composition, and functional potential vary across a spectrum of wild-to-laboratory conditions.  Results  We found that alpha diversity varied substantially among cohorts but showed no consistent wild-to-laboratory trend: Shannon diversity was higher in Lab:  Mm and Lab-like:  As than in Wild:  As and Wild-like:  As mice, whereas phylogenetic diversity was similarly high in both the Wild:  As and Lab:Mm groups. Community composition more closely reflected cohort histories. Despite over a decade in captivity, Wild-like:  As mice remained most similar to Wild:  As conspecifics, whereas Lab-like:  As mice shifted strongly away from Wild-like:  As and toward, but remained distinct from, Lab:  Mm mice. The clearest wild-to-laboratory pattern emerged in microbiome consistency: core ASVs (present in ≥90% of individuals) increased from 9 in Wild:  As to 46 in Wild-like:  As , 72 in Lab-like:  As , and 138 in Lab:  Mm mice. Predicted functional potential revealed a further distinction between taxonomic and functional patterns: Wild:  As and Wild-like:  As microbiomes did not differ significantly, whereas Lab-like:  As shifted toward the Lab:  Mm state despite remaining taxonomically distinct.  Conclusions  Together, these results show that laboratory-associated microbiomes do not emerge through simple loss of wild microbial diversity, but through broader reorganisation of community composition, consistency, and predicted functional potential reflecting microbial history and host context. The persistent Wild-like and Lab-like microbiome states within  Apodemus provide a powerful experimental system for future timely work testing how microbiome history influences host physiology, resilience, and responses to environmental challenges.
records.authors: Bancroft RE, Wolf SE, Hall J, Sweeny A, Pedersen AB.

records.title: Analysing antimicrobial resistance mobility patterns using a diverse dataset of over 8000 bacterial species
records.abstract: Advances in genomics have enhanced surveillance of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), yet the factors governing resistance gene mobility, and therefore their risk of spread, remain poorly characterized. Here, we analyzed AMR gene distributions across thousands of bacterial genomes from NCBI RefSeq, encompassing clinical, agricultural and environmental isolates, to quantify associations with plasmids and predicted mobile genomic islands. AMR genes were identified using the Resistance Gene Identifier, and in addition to plasmid identification, mobile chromosomal elements were predicted using IslandViewer 4. Analysing both the full dataset and subsets of data with corrections for sampling bias, we show that known AMR genes are significantly enriched in mobile regions overall. However, stratification by resistance mechanism supported marked heterogeneity: certain drug classes and mechanisms are strongly associated with mobile elements, whereas others are predominantly chromosomal and non-mobile. Notably, mechanisms with specialized functions showed higher mobility, consistent with their role as “ecological public goods” that need not be present in all cells to confer community-level benefit. Differences were also observed across bacteria with distinct cell envelope structures. Together, these findings lay the groundwork for predictive models of AMR gene mobility and provide a framework for incorporating gene-level mobility into AMR risk assessment and antimicrobial stewardship policy.
records.authors: Jia B, Alcock BP, Raphenya AR, Spence J, Maguire F, Beiko RG, McArthur AG, Bertelli C, Brinkman FS.

records.title: Genomic Regions Associated with Resistance to Soybean Cyst Nematode (Heterodera glycines) Population HG Type 1.2.5.7 in Dry Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris).
records.abstract: North Dakota, the largest dry bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) producing state in the United States, faces an emerging production threat caused by the soybean cyst nematode (SCN; Heterodera glycines Ichinohe, 1952). Host resistance is an effective management strategy, yet resistance to the virulent SCN population HG type 1.2.5.7 has not been genetically characterized in dry beans. In this study, 170 dry bean genotypes (113 breeding lines/cultivars and 57 germplasm accessions) were evaluated for response to HG type 1.2.5.7 under controlled conditions using the female index (FI) as the resistance phenotype. FI values ranged from 4.1 to 78.1%, with one genotype (PI 313733) classified as resistant, 35 moderately resistant, 104 moderately susceptible, and 30 susceptible. Genome-wide association analysis using 2,044 single-nucleotide polymorphism markers from the 3.8K Bean Panel chip and the BLINK model identified four significant marker-trait associations on chromosomes Pv02, Pv05, Pv07, and Pv11. Linkage disequilibrium-defined candidate intervals spanned 108 kb (Pv02), 1.50 Mb (Pv05), 798 kb (Pv07), and 1.45 Mb (Pv11), collectively containing 126 annotated genes: 20 on Pv02, 39 on Pv05, 35 on Pv07, and 32 on Pv11. The intervals contained putative genes annotated for signaling and transcriptional regulation, cell wall and carbohydrate metabolism, transport, and secondary metabolism. Together, these findings indicate that the response to HG type 1.2.5.7 in dry bean is quantitative and associated with multiple genomic regions. The identified intervals provide candidate targets for independent validation, fine mapping, functional analysis, and future marker development to support breeding for SCN resistance.
records.authors: Poudyal P, Figueroa-Cerna J, Osorno JM, Singh G, Yan G.

records.title: Cell-Cell Communication Network Analysis of Tertiary Lymphoid Structures in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer.
records.abstract: Tertiary Lymphoid Structures (TLS) are associated with a favorable prognosis in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC). However, the mechanisms governing their formation, particularly the existence of breast cancer subtype-specific critical cell communication networks, remain unclear. This study aims to systematically decipher the specific cellular interaction networks associated with TLS in TNBC and Estrogen Receptor-positive Breast Cancer (ER+ BC). Public spatial transcriptomics (TNBC: GSE210616; ER+ BC: 10x Genomics public Visium dataset) and single-cell transcriptomics (GSE176078) data were integrated to attribute TLS-associated genes to their cell-type origins and infer intercellular communication. TLS regions were independently identified by two pathologists based on H&E images (TNBC: 7 TLS; ER+ BC: 12 TLS), followed by differential expression analysis. Using single-cell data, a dual-criterion (expression rate ≥20% and average expression level ≥ upper quartile) was employed for cell-type expression attribution, with sensitivity analysis across thresholds. Cell-cell communication network inference and quantitative analysis were performed based on an expanded ligand-receptor database (CellTalkDB, 3,398 pairs), and the core findings were cross-validated using CellChat. TLS in TNBC exhibited a far more active transcriptional state compared to ER+ Breast Cancer (ER+ BC), with 198 vs 29 differentially expressed genes. Interaction network analysis revealed that in TNBC TLS, fibroblasts (cancer-associated fibroblasts, CAFs) constituted the dominant core signaling hub (net signal output strength: +458.7), whereas endothelial cells were the predominant net signal receiver (net output: -808.6). In contrast, TLS in ER+ BC were characterized by interactions predominantly involving fibroblasts (dominant output, +261.1) and plasma cells (dominant reception, -127.0). Cell-type expression attribution further confirmed that TLS-associated signals in TNBC predominantly originated from fibroblasts (70.3% of core TLS genes). Our intercellular communication analysis reveals a stark subtype-specific landscape: TLSs in TNBC are predominantly characterized by a fibroblast (CAF)-centered signaling hub, whereas TLS in ER+ BC features a fibroblast-plasma cell axis. The association between the TLS-related transcriptional signature and immune cytolytic activity was further supported in the independent The Cancer Genome Atlas breast cancer cohort (r = 0.747, P < 0.001). However, as these inferences are drawn from transcriptional correlations in public datasets, further mechanistic studies-such as ligand-receptor functional assays or in vivo perturbation models-are essential to determine whether this TNBC-specific hub actively contributes to TLS formation or merely reflects the local immune microenvironment. This study identifies a TNBC-specific fibroblast (CAF)-centered communication hub as a prominent feature of TLS-associated intercellular networks, offering prioritized candidate axes warranting further functional validation for potential immunotherapy development.
records.authors: Meng M, Li Y.

records.title: Structure-based binding pocket conservation analysis identifies 9-OH urolithin dehydroxylase candidates across phylogenetically diverse bacteria.
records.abstract: Urolithins are polyphenolic compounds produced by gut microbiota from dietary ellagitannins and ellagic acid, with urolithin A being the most bioactive and associated with a range of pharmaceutical activities like anti-aging and anti-inflammatory effects. Despite these benefits, the number of known urolithin A-producing bacteria and their corresponding enzymes is very limited. In this study, we combined conventional sequence-based homology search with structural modeling to identify novel bacteria potentially harboring 9-OH urolithin dehydroxylases, primarily characterized in the Enterocloster genus, that catalyze a key dehydroxylation step essential for urolithin A production. Using three Enterocloster references, a sequence database search coupled with subunit co-occurrence screening was performed. AlphaFold 3 was then employed to model the three-dimensional structures of the candidate multi-subunit complexes. Based on these models, comparative analysis was conducted to screen for candidate enzymes that share closely conserved three-dimensional structural characteristics and conserved core residue architectures within their active-site pockets. The resulting non-Enterocloster candidates, including Aromatoleum sp. and Dehalobacter restrictus, exhibited high predicted functional similarity to the reference enzymes based on conserved binding pocket architectures. This study demonstrates that binding pocket structural signatures help the identification of novel potential urolithin dehydroxylases and previously unrecognized urolithin A-producing bacteria.
records.authors: Piroozmand F, Kaushik R, Kawashima H, Yamaguchi T, Mizuguchi K, Mohammadipanah F, Re S.

records.title: Seasonal variation in the spatial distribution, community assembly, and associated factors of antibiotic resistance genes in tropical drinking water reservoirs of Hainan, China.
records.abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) have been widely investigated in temperate and subtropical reservoirs but remain poorly understood in tropical drinking-water reservoirs. We sampled four drinking-water reservoirs in Hainan during both winter and summer, integrating physicochemical, heavy-metal, and metagenomic data to investigate the diversity, spatiotemporal patterns, and assembly of ARGs, mobile genetic elements (MGEs), and microbial communities. ARG composition and community structure differed significantly by season and reservoir. Contig-based analysis identified ARG-MGE arrangements in diverse putative hosts; sul1 and qacEdelta1 co-occurred with integrases and transposases, demonstrating MGE co-localization. Null-model analysis indicated reservoir-specific ARG assembly in winter but predominantly stochastic assembly in summer, whereas microbial community assembly was deterministic in both seasons. Mantel and Spearman analyses showed seasonal variation in ARG relationships: stronger correlations with environmental factors in winter and more positive correlations with MGEs in summer. Summer co-occurrence networks were larger and more connected, with more positive ARG-MGE-microbial genus associations. Partial least squares path modeling (PLS-PM) showed positive MGE-ARG associations in both seasons, whereas microbial community composition was negatively associated with ARGs only in winter. These results characterize seasonal ARG variation and its associations with MGEs and microbial communities in tropical reservoirs, providing a baseline for monitoring regional drinking-water sources.
records.authors: Huang L, Chen B, Liu X, Guo Z, Zhang G, Li J, Fu Q.

records.title: From community profiling to functional insights: bacterial populations in marine sediments from an Antarctic Specially Protected Area (Terra Nova Bay, Ross Sea, Antarctica).
records.abstract: Marine sediments remain among the least characterised components of the Antarctic microbial landscape. Here, bacterial communities were investigated in sediments from three sites within the Antarctic Specially Protected Area No. 161, in Terra Nova Bay (Ross Sea, Antarctica). Samples were collected during the XXXIII Italian Antarctic Expedition. The sites differed in their local environmental context, including proximity to the Adélie penguin colony and Mario Zucchelli Station. Bacterial communities were characterised by 16S rRNA gene sequencing (V3-V4 region), with amplicon sequence variants resolved using DADA2, and complemented by PICRUSt2 predicted functional potential, bacterial isolation, and quorum-sensing bioassays. Bacteroidota and Proteobacteria dominated all sites, but community composition and diversity differed significantly among sampling sites. AC showed the highest alpha diversity, while ASPA2 showed the lowest. Of the 5423 amplicon sequence variants detected across the nine samples (three per site), 680 were shared across all samples and defined a core microbiome dominated by Bacteroidota and Proteobacteria. Despite marked differences in community composition, broad predicted functional profiles were relatively conserved, whereas finer-scale KEGG Orthology profiles showed site-associated variation. Seventeen psychrophilic strains were isolated, predominantly Psychrobacter, and most displayed hydrolytic activity towards olive oil, tributyrin, or both substrates. Biosensor-responsive activity was detected exclusively in enrichment cultures and not in extracts from individual isolates, providing preliminary evidence of putative quorum-sensing-related activity associated with mixed microbial consortia. These findings provide a baseline for investigating environmental drivers of Antarctic sediment microbiomes and microbial interactions in future studies.

records.title: A global survey of type I secretion systems and the substrates in Gram-negative bacteria.
records.abstract: Type I secretion system (T1SS) is a special device employed by Gram-negative bacteria, which only contains three components but can mediate the transport of proteins through two cell membranes. Despite their important functions, the true distribution and diversity of T1SSs in Gram-negative bacteria remain unclear. Here, we started from annotating and clustering 50 sets of T1SSs with experimentally validated functions, followed by comprehensive screening of T1SSs from the genomes of 2996 representative bacterial strains with a homology-based detection strategy combined with gene organization analysis. In total, we found 4967 highly confident sets of T1SSs from 2037 strains, encompassing 13 phyla, 357 genera and 901 species. The T1SSs were divided into nine clusters, while Salmonella contains most of the clusters, among which many are specific to the genus. To more comprehensively and precisely identify T1SS substrate proteins (T1SPs), the evolutionary features of validated T1SPs were observed and used to expand the size of high-confidence T1SPs. We also trained multiple traditional machine-learning models, ensemblers, and protein language models to predict T1SPs. Comparisons by a cross-validation strategy and an independent testing dataset both demonstrated the superior performance of a Mamba-based model (T1SEstacker 3.0) over other machine-learning or language models, ensemblers and other state-of-the-art tools. We further applied the model to screen the T1SPs and observed their distribution across the representative bacterial genomes. In summary, the study made a systematic survey on T1SSs and their substrate proteins, providing important resources for the community studying bacterial T1SSs and other protein secretion systems, secreted proteins and virulence.
records.authors: Li J, Chen Z, Liu K, Zhang J, Kong W, Wang Y, Yu M, Wu J, Chen J, Hu X, Cao X, Liu X, Wang Y.

records.title: Global change reshapes marine microbial communities, functions and One Health outcomes.
records.abstract: Marine microorganisms underpin primary production, biogeochemical cycling and host-associated symbioses, supporting climate regulation, coastal protection, fisheries and other ecosystem services. Rapid global change, including ocean warming and marine heatwaves, acidification, deoxygenation, eutrophication, pollution and overuse reshape microbial communities and their functions across marine habitats. These changes can alter carbon, nitrogen and sulfur cycles, promote microbialization and harmful algal blooms, disrupt host-microbiome associations and modify pathogen and antimicrobial resistance dynamics, collectively amplifying the ecological and societal impacts of global change. This Review frames marine microbiomes as cross-scale mediators that translate external pressures, including climate change, pollution, eutrophication and habitat degradation, into altered microbial metabolism, biogeochemical fluxes, host-associated health outcomes, ecosystem service consequences and broader One Health risks. We synthesize shared mechanisms and cross-habitat patterns, highlight cases in which microbiome interventions and stewardship could mitigate impacts and/or accelerate recovery, and outline management options ranging from the reduction of local stressors to emerging microbiome stewardship approaches in ecosystem restoration. Building upon this, we outline pathways for embedding marine microbiome science into globally coordinated One Health strategies, operational management protocols and financing frameworks that align economic incentives with long-term ecosystem and public health outcomes.

records.title: The H5N1 avian influenza threat: a European Perspective on Research Gaps and State of Preparedness.
records.abstract: H5N1 influenza clade 2.3.4.4b has spread from South East Asia through migratory birds since 2020. The expansion seeded frequent spillovers into wild and domestic mammals including cattle in the United States. While the risk for humans not in direct contact with infected animals is low, the widespread presence and opportunities for evolution constitutes a pandemic threat. If sustained human-to-human transmission (H2H) would emerge, there is limited time to mount a public health response. Initially, non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) are needed until vaccines are available. Experience with H5N1 viruses since 1997 suggests that infections are seen mostly in people born after 1968, indicating that people under sixty may be at particular risk. Closely monitoring viral diversity and evolution in wild life, and at the human animal interface, using integrated One Health surveillance and genome-based selection of viruses for further characterization for instance receptor affinity of H5N1 to human receptors is mandatory.

records.title: Inflammatory and transcriptional profiles associated with structural and functional recovery in pre-XDR/XDR tuberculosis.
records.abstract: BackgroundIn drug-resistant TB, bacteriology-based monitoring often fails to capture recovery. We aimed to identify baseline host inflammatory and transcriptional features associated with multidomain treatment recovery in pre-XDR/XDR-TB.MethodsWe conducted an ancillary analysis of a pilot clinical trial in patients with pre-XDR/XDR-TB (NCT02781909). Participants were assessed at baseline and during treatment using clinical, radiological, microbiological, and health-related quality-of-life measures, plasma biomarkers, and whole-blood transcriptomic profiling, analyzed in relation to treatment outcomes.ResultsMicrobiological and symptomatic improvement occurred earlier than radiological and functional recovery. Baseline elevated NLR, SII, and IL-6, and an increased expression of interferon-related genes as CD274 and GBP5, were associated with poorer radiological and HRQoL outcomes. IL-8 consistently correlated with symptom severity, radiological and functional outcomes. Previously published blood transcriptomic signatures were more strongly associated with radiological and HRQoL recovery than with early bacterial clearance.ConclusionsBacteriological cure precedes but does not ensure structural and functional recovery in pre-XDR/XDR-TB. Baseline inflammation identifies patients at risk of incomplete recovery, and IL-8 emerges as a candidate cross-domain monitoring biomarker. These findings support multidimensional treatment monitoring and a biological rationale for host-directed interventions targeting persistent inflammation.

records.title: Bifunctional cytochrome P450/ferredoxin is required for fungal phytochrome assembly at mitochondria.
records.abstract: Mitochondria act as dynamic signaling hubs intertwining cellular metabolism and environmental perception in fungi. Here, we elucidate the assembly of the red-light sensing phytochrome (FphA) at the mitochondrial outer membrane in Alternaria alternata. Phytochrome photoconversion strictly relies on biliverdin biosynthesis by heme oxygenases. While mammalian and plant heme oxygenases localize to the endoplasmic reticulum or chloroplasts, the fungal system uniquely repurposes the outer mitochondrial membrane. We demonstrate that the fungal heme oxygenases HoxA and HoxB form a heteromeric complex integrated into the membrane via mitochondrial import machinery components Mim1 and Mim2. At the mitochondrial surface, only HoxA binds directly to FphA. Genomic screening identified Bifunctional Cytochrome P450 Reductase/Ferredoxin A (BcfA) as the essential physiological electron donor. Quantitative kinetics established that BcfA operates as an asymmetric hub, displaying higher affinity for HoxB than HoxA. HoxB functions as a high-affinity kinetic tether locking the donor at the membrane boundary. Consequently, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of bcfA disrupts red-light signalling. Thus, a multi-protein mitochondrial complex evolved in fungi to wire light perception through spatial compartmentalization.
records.authors: Schuhmacher L, Landmark A, Jähring T, Müller A, Streng C, Fischer R.

records.title: In Vitro Activity of Cefiderocol against Carbapenem-Resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Acinetobacter baumannii and the Cefiderocol Resistance Mechanisms.
records.abstract: BackgroundExtensively drug-resistant and pandrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria, including Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, pose a major threat due to limited treatment options and high mortality. Rising prevalence of carbapenem resistance has further complicated therapy, necessitating novel antimicrobial agents. Cefiderocol, a siderophore-conjugated cephalosporin, offers a promising therapeutic option against these multidrug-resistant pathogens.ObjectivesTo assess the in vitro activity of cefiderocol and key comparators against carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacteria from a Malaysian hospital.MethodsA total of 448 non-duplicate carbapenem-resistant bacterial strains collected from the University Malaya Medical Centre diagnostic laboratory from year 2018-2021 were included. Broth microdilution was used for susceptibility testing of cefiderocol and other agents relevant to the respective carbapenem-resistant organisms (CROs), in accordance with CLSI guidelines. Susceptibility was interpreted using CLSI breakpoints, with FDA breakpoints applied for tigecycline. Genotypic detection of antimicrobial resistance-associated genes was performed via polymerase chain reaction. Whole genome sequencing was performed on cefiderocol-resistant isolates for genetic characterisation.ResultsCefiderocol demonstrated the highest susceptibility rate for the tested CROs when compared to other antimicrobial agents. More than 90% of the carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae and carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii isolates were susceptible to cefiderocol, whereas 81.2% of carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates were susceptible. Among a total of 22 cefiderocol-resistant isolates, 17 isolates produced NDM-1 and 11 isolates produced PER or VEB ESBL.ConclusionsCefiderocol remains an effective treatment option for patients infected with CROs. Ongoing surveillance and antibiotic stewardship are essential to monitor the emergence of resistance and preserve the effectiveness of cefiderocol against multidrug-resistant pathogens.
records.authors: Wong JH, Woon JJ, Ponnampalavanar SSS, Yamashiro H, Miyagawa D, Onishi M, Takemura M, Yamano Y, Teh CSJ.

records.title: Developmental PFAS exposure impairs host resistance and is associated with immune-developmental molecular signatures in marine medaka.
records.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent environmental contaminants with recognized immunotoxic potential, yet their effects on the developing immune system remain incompletely understood. Building directly on a previously established analytical and exposure framework for developmental PFAS exposure in this species, this study examined the immunotoxicity of legacy (PFOS, PFOA) and replacement (PFHxS, PFHxA, PFBS, GenX) PFAS in marine medaka (Oryzias melastigma) during a later developmental window relevant to T-cell maturation (12-19 days post-hatch). At the organismal level, larvae were assessed for immune competence using a host resistance assay following bacterial challenge. To explore candidate molecular processes associated with these organismal responses, we additionally profiled whole-body metabolomes and transcriptomes and integrated the two through joint pathway analysis. Developmental exposure to GenX, PFBS, and PFOA significantly reduced post-challenge survival relative to challenged controls (50% survival), with survival falling to 7% (GenX), 13% (PFBS), and 0% (PFOA, 5 ng/mL), with effects that were compound-specific rather than monotonically dose-dependent, demonstrating that several replacement PFAS impair host resistance at environmentally relevant concentrations. Metabolomic and transcriptomic profiling identified candidate molecular processes associated with these exposures, with over-representation analysis of nominally responsive genes recovering, among a broader set of enriched terms, terms related to immune and hematopoietic development-including T-cell activation, T-cell differentiation, and thymus development-across multiple PFAS. Joint pathway analysis highlighted central energy metabolism, particularly the citrate (TCA) cycle, as a recurring feature across compounds. Together, these findings establish that replacement PFAS can functionally compromise host resistance during early development and provide molecular hypotheses implicating immune-developmental and metabolic processes worthy of targeted follow-up.
records.authors: DiBona ER, Lu Y, Elliott J, Labeille RO, Abdulla H, Seemann F.

records.title: Trace metal contamination, microbiological quality, and human health risk assessment of edible oyster (Crassostrea belcheri) from the Cox's Bazar Coast, Bangladesh.
records.abstract: Oysters are effective bioindicators of aquatic contamination. Their filter-feeding behavior causes them to bioaccumulate heavy metals and emerging contaminants from coastal waters. This poses both ecological and human health risks through seafood consumption. This study evaluated trace metal contamination, microbiological quality, and human health risk in Crassostrea belcheri from the Cox's Bazar coast, Bangladesh. Twelve trace metals were quantified in the soft tissue. Na, K, and Ca dominated the metal profile, followed by Zn, Mg, Fe, Cu, Mn, Ni, Cr, Pb, and Cd, which occurred at comparatively low levels. Most metals exceeded Bangladesh's national shellfish contamination guideline, except Cd. This points to a broader baseline contamination burden, even where dietary-intake indices suggested low risk. Estimated Daily Intake values for all metals stayed within permissible limits. This corresponds to negligible non-carcinogenic hazard. However, carcinogenic risk estimates for Cd, Cr, and Ni exceeded acceptable thresholds. This indicates a real long-term cancer risk from chronic consumption, despite the reassuring non-carcinogenic profile. Escherichia coli was detected in microbiological screening of collected oysters, whereas Vibrio cholerae and Salmonella spp. were not detected in any of the analyzed samples. This suggests a relatively low burden among the tested pathogens, though other microbial hazards cannot be ruled out. Trace metal contamination in C. belcheri poses a greater long-term health concern than national guidelines or acute intake thresholds alone would suggest. Regular monitoring is recommended to protect consumer health and support quality assurance for export markets that depend on this regionally important but understudied resource.
records.authors: Nasrin K, Bhattacharjee SC, Anisuzzaman M, Hasan M, Islam MA, Islam MI, Islam MT, Hasan MR, Ahmed S, Islam MSMM.

records.title: Replication-coupled maturation of readthrough late transcripts by a polyomavirus small T antigen
records.abstract: Productive polyomavirus gene expression requires the maturation of long, non-polyadenylated "wraparound" transcripts generated by late-strand readthrough of the polyadenylation signal on the circular genome, giving rise to structural protein mRNAs and microRNAs. In Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCV), small T (sT) antigen, along with large T (LT) antigen-mediated DNA replication, drives this process. Deletion of sT (MCVΔsT) attenuates late gene transcription, abolishes splicing, eliminates VP1 expression, and traps unspliced transcripts in the nucleus. Exogenous sT restored transcription and splicing in an aphidicolin-sensitive manner, requiring domains that activate DNA replication and bind chromatin. RNA sequencing revealed that sT promotes splicing and polyadenylation of wraparound transcripts, thereby increasing cytoplasmic VP1 and VP2 mRNA levels. A dual-fluorescence reporter confirmed that the leaky late poly(A) signal (LpA) was used more efficiently upon sT expression, indicating enhanced polyadenylation. Co-expression with LT abolished this effect, likely by overwhelming the capacity of the polyadenylation machinery. sT from HPyV7 and HPyV9 could similarly rescue this defect, indicating that this regulatory activity is conserved in a subset of sT proteins. Together, these findings define sT as a replication-coupled regulator of late transcript expression, splicing, and polyadenylation, revealing how a compact DNA virus converts readthrough transcription into productive gene expression.

records.title: Nutrient and Organic Matter Driven Reorganization of Phytoplankton Communities Downstream of Wastewater Discharge in the Styr River (Ukraine)
records.abstract: Abstract  The study investigated changes in the phytoplankton community of the Styr River in the area affected by wastewater discharge from a nuclear power plant. The aim was to assess the effects of nutrient loading associated with wastewater discharge on phytoplankton species composition, abundance, biomass, and community structure. Samples were collected in May - August 2024 at two river sites located upstream and downstream of the wastewater discharge point. Water samples were analyzed for dissolved organic carbon (DOC), total nitrogen (TN), and total phosphorus (TP). UV–Vis optical indices indicated a downstream shift toward more aromatic and higher-molecular-weight DOM characteristics, consistent with changes in the composition of the dissolved organic matter pool. Phytoplankton was assessed in terms of abundance, biomass, mean cell biomass, and taxonomic structure. Correlation analysis and principal component analysis (PCA) were used to examine relationships between hydrochemical and biological variables. Downstream of the discharge point, DOC, TN, and TP concentrations increased by 19.4%, 56.5%, and 72.7%, respectively, compared with the reference site. Against this background, phytoplankton abundance decreased from 3.0 × 10⁶ to 0.5 × 10⁶ cells dm⁻³, while biomass decreased from 0.70 to 0.15 mg dm⁻³. At the same time, mean cell biomass increased, indicating a shift in the size structure of the community. Bacillariophyta dominated upstream, accounting for 79% of total abundance and 85% of total biomass. Downstream, Chlorophyta and Euglenophyta became predominant, whereas the contribution of diatoms declined markedly. The saprobity index increased from 1.96 to 2.61, indicating increased organic loading. Correlation analysis showed negative relationships between nutrient concentrations and Bacillariophyta, but positive relationships with Chlorophyta and Euglenophyta. PCA confirmed clear spatial separation of the phytoplankton communities along the trophic gradient. Overall, increased organic matter and nutrient concentrations in the discharge-affected area were accompanied by a restructuring of the phytoplankton community, characterized by a reduced contribution of diatoms and an increased contribution of taxa tolerant of organic pollution.
records.authors: Biedunkova O, Kuznietsov P, Pryshchepa A, Statnyk I.

records.title: Self-organized colloidal growth of stromatolites
records.abstract: Abstract  Stromatolites have been widely regarded as key biosignatures of early life, yet the controls on their morphogenesis and diversity remain poorly constrained. Here, we investigate Mesoproterozoic ironstones from North China featuring stromatolitic structures and composed of laminated Fe(III)-oxyhydroxide colloids. Microstructural observations and colloidal stability calculations indicate that terrestrial colloids flocculated rapidly upon mixing with seawater in an estuarine environment and aggregated on the seafloor. We then numerically simulate the forming processes of stromatolites via diffusion-limited aggregation and surface diffusion (DLA–SD) mechanism and reveal that stromatolitic morphogenesis is primarily controlled by depositional and aggregation dynamics of colloids, which are related to geochemical and hydrodynamic conditions in estuaries. This DLA–SD framework also provides quantitative insights into the microbial sediment-trapping mechanisms for the formation of carbonate stromatolites and reveals that the diversification of morphologies of stromatolite were linked to the evolution of oceanic chemistry and microbial communities throughout the Earth history.
records.authors: Zhou M, Qiu W, Ballhaus C.

records.title: Photoelectrochemical biosensor using CoPP to quench PTCA for the detection of mip gene fragment.
records.abstract: Legionella pneumophila is a harmful Gram-negative aquatic pathogen that causes Legionnaires' disease, and sensitive detection of this bacterium is essential for epidemiological investigation. Herein, a photoelectrochemical (PEC) biosensor based on 3,4,9,10-perylenetetracarboxylic acid (PTCA) as the photoactive material and tetraphenylporphyrin cobalt (CoPP) as the signal quencher was constructed for the detection of the macrophage infectivity potentiator (mip) gene fragment from Legionella pneumophila. PTCA with favorable optoelectronic properties and film-forming capacity provided a strong initial photocurrent response. Gold nanoparticles (Au NPs) were electrodeposited on the electrode surface to immobilize DNA S1 through Au-S interactions. After target-induced DNA hybridization, CoPP was intercalated into the formed DNA duplex, which efficiently quenched the PEC signal of PTCA. Benefiting from the signal quenching effect of CoPP towards PTCA, the proposed biosensor achieved quantitative detection of the mip gene fragment in the range from 100 fmol/L to 1 µmol/L with a detection limit of 33.3 fmol/L. This work provides an analytical tool and shows promise for practical screening of the mip gene fragment of Legionella pneumophila in respiratory specimens with high bacterial loads.
records.journal: Analytical sciences : the international journal of the Japan Society for Analytical Chemistry
records.authors: Zhang F, Lu L, Li S, Gong L, Li M.

records.title: Synthesizing multi-omics evidence of interface-specific selection in lung adenocarcinoma metastasis: A trait-origin-interface-function framework across lymph-node and brain ecosystems.
records.abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) mortality is driven largely by metastatic progression, yet lymph-node metastasis (LNM) and parenchymal brain metastasis (BrM) arise in fundamentally different immune and anatomical ecosystems. Here, we present an integrative review that conceptually synthesizes published genomic, single-cell, spatial-transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic findings. Our trait-origin-interface-function (TOIF) framework maps individual claims to trait origin, anatomical interface, metastatic stage and functional output, with separate annotations for evidence type and study context. In LNM, lymphatic access and nodal occupation are associated with remodeling of antigen presentation, progenitor T-cell maintenance, lymphoid organization, and immune-cell export; however, evidence for individual tumor-immune communication axes remains uneven. In BrM, neurovascular entry, perivascular survival, glial-myeloid signaling, metabolic adaptation, and restricted effector access represent separable bottlenecks. Cross-platform evidence indicates that shared genomic ancestry can coexist with site-enriched transcriptional, immune, and metabolic states, while temporal and lineage-resolved measurements help distinguish their possible pre-existence, selective expansion and acquisition after tissue exposure. We therefore propose a TOIF framework that links each candidate mechanism to the omics layers that support it, the spatial context in which it operates, and the experiment needed to test causality. This framework clarifies why similar low-cytotoxicity phenotypes may reflect distinct mechanisms in nodal and brain lesions, and provides a basis for multi-omics biomarker development and stage-matched therapeutic investigation in LUAD metastasis.
records.authors: Xu Y, Zhang R, Hu Y, Yang M, Shan H, Liang T, Guo L.

records.title: L-Lysine production from glucose and chitin monomers using engineered Vibrio natriegens.
records.abstract: Despite its industrial importance, microbial L-lysine production has largely been confined to classical producer strains, leaving the fast-growing, non-pathogenic marine bacterium V. natriegens mostly unexplored as an emerging biosynthetic platform. In this work, we established an L-lysine-overproducing V. natriegens DSM759 strain through a stepwise rational engineering strategy targeting the native biosynthetic pathway. Building on our prior systems-level analysis of the strain's genetic and regulatory architecture, we identified key metabolic bottlenecks and targeted interventions to relieve them. The central intervention was relief of feedback inhibition on the two key regulatory enzymes, aspartate kinase (AK, lysC) and dihydrodipicolinate synthase (DHDPS, dapA). Transferring feedback resistance substitutions previously characterized in E. coli to conserved positions in the V. natriegens DSM759 enzymes produced L-lysine-insensitive variants with kinetic parameters comparable to the corresponding wild-type enzymes. Among the tested configurations, the strain co-expressing Vn.lysC2 and Vn.dapA1:E84T reached the highest L-lysine titer (9.0 ± 0.6 mM) and yield (0.11 ± 0.01 molLys molGlc-1), whereas overexpression of additional L-lysine pathway genes provided no further benefit. Exploiting the host's substrate range, we further demonstrated L-lysine synthesis from the chitin-derived amino sugar N-acetylglucosamine (0.09 ± 0.00 molLys molGlcNAc-1), highlighting the potential to valorize chitin-rich waste streams from the seafood industry. This work establishes a minimal rational strategy for L-lysine biosynthesis in V. natriegens DSM759 and positions it as a candidate platform for sustainable amino acid production. KEY POINTS: • E. coli-derived rational engineering strategies were transferable to V. natriegens • Native pathway deregulation was sufficient to enable L-lysine production • Chitin-derived N-acetylglucosamine supports L-lysine synthesis.
records.authors: Straube E, Tran TVA, Faber A, Ihle N, Crespo Blanco R, Le HT, Fritz G, Frazão CJR, Walther T.

records.title: RtmR is a membrane-embedded RRM family RNA-binding protein.
records.abstract: The animal symbiont Vibrio fischeri has served as a model organism for molecular processes underlying bacterial group behaviors, including quorum sensing, and biofilm development. Here, using a genetic approach to identify negative regulators of biofilm formation in V. fischeri, we identified a membrane-bound RNA-binding protein, RtmR (VF_2432), that acts as an inhibitor of the symbiosis polysaccharide (SYP) biofilm. Membrane localization of the protein seems to be required for protein stability or expression, as truncation of the transmembrane helices led to an inability to detect the protein. The conserved RNP1 and RNP2 motifs in RtmR's cytoplasmic RNA recognition motif (RRM) domain are required for function, and we demonstrate binding to RNA substrates. Identification of RtmR RNA ligands was conducted with an individual-nucleotide resolution crosslinking and immunoprecipitation sequencing (iiCLIP-seq) approach that revealed a large interactome. One transcript identified was that of the biofilm regulatory histidine kinase RscS. We found that RtmR biofilm inhibition depends on RscS activity, and that RtmR negatively regulates levels of RscS. Overall, this work characterizes a novel type of bacterial RNA-binding protein.IMPORTANCEBacterial RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) perform key functions to regulate stress responses and development. Bacterial RBPs, including the RNA chaperones Hfq and ProQ, the global regulator CsrA, and the cold shock proteins (Csps), have been extensively studied, although additional classes of RBPs have been predicted by bioinformatic methods, including those carrying an RNA recognition motif (RRM) domain. This work expands on recent studies of RRM domain proteins in bacteria to characterize a membrane-bound RRM protein that regulates bacterial biofilm development. Given our rapidly expanding knowledge regarding the role of RNA-binding proteins in bacterial molecular biology, this work contributes a new class of membrane-bound regulators with homologs in human pathogens and marine symbionts.
records.authors: Vander Griend JA, Ludvik DA, Nottage HC, Mehle A, Mandel MJ.

records.title: More than the sum of its parts: reproductive addiction in the ecology and evolution of fungal-bacterial symbioses.
records.abstract: SUMMARYReproductive control exerted by endosymbionts over their hosts is an adaptation for maintaining host-symbiont associations across generations. This strategy is particularly well-characterized in endosymbiotic bacteria (EB) associated with arthropods, in which EB of disparate species have independently evolved diverse mechanisms to manipulate host reproduction, thereby ensuring their reliable transmission across host generations. Like arthropods, fungi in the phylum Mucoromycota commonly harbor ancient and highly coevolved EB that significantly affect fungal life histories, including reproduction. In particular, the symbiosis between the mucoromycete Rhizopus microsporus and its Mycetohabitans spp. endosymbionts is significantly contingent on reproductive addiction, as removal of the symbiont results in the loss or severe impairment of host asexual and sexual reproduction. Here, we synthesize the current knowledge on sexual reproduction in mucoromycete fungi and the Rhizopus microsporus-Mycetohabitans symbiosis. We highlight current gaps in the knowledge of mucoromycete reproduction as well as present novel hypotheses for studying these interactions based on the understanding of reproductive manipulation in arthropods.
records.authors: Branine ME, Hempel N, Pawlowska TE.

records.title: Integrative structural and functional analysis of full-length hibernation-promoting factor and its association with antibiotic susceptibility in Mycobacterium smegmatis.
records.abstract: Ribosome hibernation is a critical adaptive mechanism that enables bacteria to survive stress by stabilizing inactive ribosomes and conserving cellular resources. This process is facilitated by hibernation-promoting factors (HPFs). However, structural and functional insights into the full-length architecture of Mycobacterium smegmatis HPF, particularly its C-terminal region, remain limited. Here, we combined in silico and experimental approaches to characterize HPF (MSMEG_1878) from M. smegmatis and investigate its role in ribosome-associated physiology and antibiotic response. Sequence and phylogenetic analyses revealed strong conservation of HPF among mycobacterial species, including the extended C-terminal region. A full-length 230-amino-acid structural model generated using complementary modeling approaches and molecular dynamics refinement showed close agreement with the experimentally resolved region. Structural mapping positioned HPF at the 70S ribosomal intersubunit interface, with the modeled C-terminal region extending toward the vicinity of the 16S rRNA decoding-center. Docking analyses predicted that paromomycin and neomycin localize within the h44-associated decoding-center region, near the HPF-associated surface, whereas chloramphenicol and tetracycline localize to spatially distinct ribosomal regions. Deletion of hpf impaired bacterial growth and reduced susceptibility to paromomycin and neomycin, while complementation restored susceptibility toward the wild-type phenotype. Furthermore, neomycin exposure significantly increased hpf transcript abundance, whereas paromomycin exposure showed a nonsignificant trend toward increased expression. Collectively, these findings suggest that M. smegmatis HPF contributes to ribosome-associated physiology and may influence the cellular response to selected antibiotics, providing insights into the relationship between ribosome hibernation and antibiotic response in mycobacteria.IMPORTANCEThis study provides new structural and functional insights into the full-length architecture and ribosome-associated role of HPF (MSMEG_1878) in Mycobacterium smegmatis, with particular emphasis on its C-terminal region. Using complementary structural modeling approaches, we investigated the predicted architecture of the C-terminal region and its spatial relationship with the ribosomal decoding-center region. Functional analyses further demonstrate that loss of HPF affects bacterial growth and alters susceptibility to selected aminoglycosides. Together, these findings suggest that HPF contributes to ribosome-associated physiology and may influence cellular responses to selected antibiotics. This work provides a potential structural and functional framework for further investigation of how ribosome-associated factors influence antibiotic responses in mycobacteria.
records.authors: Tiwari PK, Singh VK, Shivani, Verma D, Kushwaha AK.

records.title: Isolation, Identification, and Whole Genome Sequencing Analysis of Common Foodborne Bacteria from Fresh Fruits, Vegetables, and Their Ready-to-Eat Products in Shijiazhuang, China.
records.abstract: With evolving lifestyles, consumer demand for fresh fruits and vegetables has increased. However, these products are susceptible to contamination by foodborne bacteria from farm to table. To investigate the contamination status of foodborne bacteria in commercially available fresh fruits, vegetables, and their ready-to-eat (RTE) products in Shijiazhuang City, a total of 406 samples were collected from 2024 to 2025. Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), Clostridium perfringens (C. perfringens), diarrheagenic Escherichia coli (diarrheagenic E. coli), and Salmonella were identified and analyzed for genomic characteristics using traditional biochemical tests and whole genome sequencing (WGS). The results showed that the detection rate of S. aureus was 4.68% (19/406), of which 5 isolates were identified as methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), accounting for 1.23% (5/406). The detection rate of C. perfringens was 8.37% (34/406), and the detection rate of diarrheagenic E. coli was 0.25% (1/406). No Salmonella was detected. Genomic characterization revealed that S. aureus strains were predominantly ST59 and ST22, with the MRSA strains primarily identified as ST59-SCCmec-IVa (2B)-t437. A total of 20 enterotoxin genes were detected, with 94.74% (18/19) of the strains carrying at least one enterotoxin gene. The sea gene was the most prevalent (52.63%, 10/19), and the tsst-1 gene, which can cause toxic shock syndrome, was detected in 2 strains. C. perfringens isolates were divided into 30 STs, exhibiting high genetic diversity. All toxin types were classified as type A. The mprF gene showed the highest carriage rate of resistance genes (94.12%, 32/34), and the main resistance profile was mprF + cplR (55.88%, 19/34). The diarrheagenic E. coli isolate was identified as enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) and carried multiple antimicrobial resistance genes. This study systematically reveals the contamination levels and molecular characteristics of common foodborne bacteria in fresh fruits, vegetables, and their RTE products sold in Shijiazhuang for the first time.
records.authors: Wang Y, Chen M, Wang J, Liu S, Jiang Y, Hu X, Sun X, Wang Y, Gao Y, Xu X, Wang J.

records.title: FRET-based nanoprobes for nucleic acid sensing and disease diagnosis: materials, probe architectures, and analytical trends.
records.abstract: Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) translates nanometre-scale changes in donor-acceptor separation into ratiometric fluorescence signals, enabling homogeneous and isothermal detection of nucleic acid biomarkers. In this review, we critically survey FRET-based nanoprobes for nucleic acid sensing and disease diagnosis, spanning organic dyes and cationic conjugated polymers to metallic nanoparticles, quantum dots, upconversion nanoparticles, carbon nanostructures, MXenes and polymeric nanoantennae. We organise probe designs by architectures, including sandwich hybridisation, disassembly hairpins, molecular beacons, dynamic junction sensors and enzyme-free DNA circuits, and analyse how these platforms achieve attomolar limits of detection, single-nucleotide discrimination and multiplexing in complex matrices. Representative case studies highlight applications in viral (e.g. SARS-CoV-2), bacterial and fungal pathogens, circulating cancer-related miRNAs and mRNAs, and neurodegenerative disease markers, as well as integration of FRET readouts with PCR and isothermal amplification workflows. We then compare FRET nanoprobes with established nucleic-acid assays in terms of analytical figures of merit, instrumentation, and compatibility with point-of-care (POC) formats. Remaining challenges, including photobleaching, spectral crowding, matrix autofluorescence, nanocarrier toxicity, and inter-laboratory reproducibility, are discussed in the context of emerging solutions such as near-infrared and lifetime-based FRET, CRISPR-coupled assays, DNA-origami nanoantennas, and microfluidic or smartphone-enabled devices. Finally, we outline key trends that could drive translation of FRET-based nucleic acid nanoprobes from proof-of-concept demonstrations to clinically actionable diagnostics.
records.authors: Ammar IM, Panja SK, Geng J.

records.title: Temperature-dependent regulation of persistence and virulence genes in Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1 on oak leaf lettuce and indications for root internalization.
records.abstract: Increasing evidence of Pseudomonas aeruginosa on fresh plant-based foods raises food safety concerns, particularly under changing environmental conditions. Temperature changes may affect plant microbiota and human pathogen presence on fresh produce. This study investigates the temperature-dependent gene expression of P. aeruginosa PAO1 on oak leaf lettuce as a model system and explores the potential for root internalization by P. aeruginosa PAO1. Therefore, temperature-dependent transcriptomic changes of P. aeruginosa PAO1 were assessed by analyzing differentially expressed genes following plant inoculation and incubation at 18 and 22 °C. Moreover, oak leaf lettuce was cultivated in soil inoculated with P. aeruginosa PAO1_sfGFP_UHH07, and internalization was analyzed using confocal laser scanning microscopy. Transcriptomic analyses showed that a moderate temperature increase shifted bacterial gene expression, with virulence-associated genes upregulated at 22 °C and persistence-associated genes predominating at 18 °C. Results provide preliminary evidence that P. aeruginosa PAO1 may internalize into the roots of oak leaf lettuce, whereas no GFP signal indicative of translocation into the leaves was detected. The findings indicate that temperature changes could influence the transcriptional emphasis on virulence- and persistence-associated genes of P. aeruginosa PAO1 present on oak leaf lettuce and provide a basis for further investigation under more complex environmental conditions.
records.authors: Griese J, Hoffmann T, Peal J, Weiss A.

records.title: Extracellular amylolytic activity in marine Croceibacter sp. 23-6: Cu2+ response and optimized wheat starch hydrolysis.
records.abstract: BackgroundMarine bacteria are important sources of extracellular hydrolytic enzymes, but the amylolytic activity of many non-model marine bacterial lineages remains insufficiently characterized at the phenotype level. This study evaluated extracellular amylolytic activity in the marine isolate Croceibacter sp. 23-6 and examined its metal-ion response and wheat starch hydrolysis performance under defined laboratory conditions.MethodsStrain 23-6 was isolated from mesopelagic seawater of the western Pacific Ocean and identified at the genus level using 16S rRNA gene sequence analysis. Extracellular amylolytic activity was first screened on starch agar. A partially purified extracellular amylolytic protein preparation was then used to determine the effects of temperature, pH, thermal and pH stability, metal ions, apparent kinetic parameters and hydrolysis of different starch substrates. Wheat starch hydrolysis was further evaluated using single-factor experiments and response surface methodology based on a Box-Behnken design.ResultsStrain 23-6 produced a clear starch-hydrolysis halo and was conservatively assigned to the genus Croceibacter. The partially purified extracellular protein fraction showed maximum amylolytic activity at 50 °C and pH 7.0 and retained comparatively higher activity under near-neutral conditions. Among the tested metal ions, Cu2+ increased the measured relative activity to 119.0% at 3 mM, whereas K+, Mn2+, Zn2+ and Fe2+ decreased the measured activity. Wheat starch showed the highest relative reducing-sugar release among the tested insoluble starch substrates. Response surface optimization predicted suitable hydrolysis conditions of approximately 52 min, 50 °C, 4.0 U/mL enzyme and 1.0% wheat starch. Validation under the adjusted conditions yielded 2.43 ± 0.09 mg/mL reducing sugars, expressed as maltose equivalents, consistent with the model prediction.ConclusionsThese results provide strain-level evidence that Croceibacter sp. 23-6 exhibits extracellular amylolytic activity and indicate that its partially purified extracellular protein fraction displays a measurable Cu2+-responsive activity profile and wheat starch hydrolysis capacity. The findings define the functional properties of this marine bacterial extracellular amylolytic fraction while leaving the identity of the responsible enzyme(s), preparation homogeneity, and the mechanism of Cu2+ response for future work.
records.authors: Jiang F, Zhang Y, Zhang H, Lin X, Xu X, Feng H.

records.title: Identification of candidate host susceptibility genes for viral myocarditis through integrated transcriptomic and mendelian randomization analyses.
records.abstract: This study investigated the genetic mechanisms underlying myocardial inflammatory responses related to Coxsackievirus B3 (CVB3) infection through an integrative transcriptomic and genetic approach. Gene expression profiles from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between CVB3-infected and control myocardial tissues. These genes were subsequently evaluated using Mendelian randomization (MR) based on publicly available expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data and genome-wide association study (GWAS) data for myocarditis. MR analysis prioritized four candidate genes whose genetically predicted expression levels were significantly associated with myocarditis susceptibility. To ensure the robustness of these findings, multiple sensitivity analyses were performed to assess potential pleiotropy and heterogeneity. Functional analyses suggested that the priority candidate genes (PCGs) were associated with immune regulation, inflammatory signaling, and cellular metabolic processes. In addition, immune cell infiltration analysis suggested alterations in the myocardial immune microenvironment and associations between PCG expression and estimated immune cell proportions. An independent GEO dataset was used for external validation, and in vitro experiments further confirmed the significant upregulation of these genes following CVB3 infection. This integrative strategy combining transcriptomic profiling, human genetic analyses, and experimental validation identified four genetically prioritized candidate genes associated with myocarditis susceptibility and provided preliminary insights into the immune-regulatory mechanisms underlying cardiac inflammatory responses.
records.authors: Zhang M, Zhang Q, Shen H.

records.title: Occurrence and Toxigenic Potential of Planktonic Cyanobacterial Blooms and Benthic Mats in the Tropical Rio Grande de Comitán and Montebello Lakes National Park, Southern Mexico.
records.abstract: The tropical aquatic ecosystems of the Río Grande de Comitán and Lagunas de Montebello National Park (southern Mexico) exhibit signs of advanced eutrophication, with environmental conditions that can promote the proliferation of potentially toxic cyanobacteria. This study assessed the distribution and ecotoxicological risk of planktonic blooms and benthic mats throughout the subbasin. Using a polyphasic approach combining cultured-based analysis, molecular detection and HPLC, we found a low-diversity cyanobacterial community dominated by Planktothrix agardhii, which reached densities up to 2.2 × 105 cells/mL during the warmest months. Benthic Microcoleus sp. and localized blooms of Anabaenopsis elenkinii were documented. Molecular analyses confirmed the presence of microcystin and anatoxin synthesizing genes, with high microcystin concentrations detected (67.5-3169 μg/L). Seasonal analyses revealed significant differences in temperature in both lakes (H = 20.8, p 25 (H = 10.7, p = 0.0169). PCA explained 65% and 64% of the variance in the first two axes for lakes and rivers, respectively, separating sites according to gradients in nutrients, conductivity, and other water-quality variables. In lakes, redundancy analysis (RDA) showed that the first two axes explained 72% of the constrained variation, with total nitrogen, specific conductance, total phosphorous, catchment disturbance index, pH, and dissolved oxygen contributing to the environmental gradients structuring cyanobacterial composition. Wastewater discharges from the upper basin (Comitán) act as a continuous source of nutrients and cyanobacterial inoculant, whereas tourism and fishing activities mechanically disperse these populations across the lakes. These results demonstrate the widespread occurrence of potentially toxic cyanobacteria across the subbasin and highlight the need for early-warning and monitoring programs, particularly in areas affected by wastewater inputs and intensive human activities.
records.authors: Salas AIS, Borrero APC, Carmona-Jiménez J, Márquez-Santamaria KP.

records.title: Helicase family proteins promote antiviral ADP-ribosylation of DNA purines
records.abstract: DarTG defense systems studied to date contain a DarT1 or DarT2 toxin that blocks phage replication by ADP-ribosylating DNA and a NADAR or macrodomain antitoxin, DarG, that reverses this modification at homeostasis. Here, we identify additional DarTG subfamilies, one of which comprises a DarT3 toxin, an ADP-ribosylhydrolase (ARH)-domain antitoxin, and a helicase family protein, DarH. The  Escherichia coli DarHTG3 system confers broad phage defense, requires DarH and, unlike previously characterized DarTG systems, modifies adenine. Characterization of additional DarH-containing DarTG systems reveals that a subset also target guanine. Our data support a model in which ADP-bound DarH functions as a processivity factor by recruiting DarT to its single-stranded DNA substrate and allowing for ADP-ribosylation of multiple target sites. These findings reveal how a helicase family protein regulates an antiviral effector by promoting DNA engagement rather than unwinding and thereby expanding the functional repertoire of helicase family proteins in bacterial immunity.

records.title: Prokaryotic Community Structures in the Bering and Chukchi Seas
records.abstract: Bacteria are essential to marine ecosystems as they remineralize organic matter, cycle carbon, nitrogen, and other key elements, and support higher trophic levels through food webs. The Bering and Chukchi Seas off the coast of Alaska are among the most productive regions in the world, with intense seasonal algal blooms, yet their bacterial communities remain poorly characterized, and the region is warming rapidly as heat transport from the Pacific Ocean increases. Here, we used 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing of 181 samples collected on 0.2 µm filters at three depths (surface, middle, and bottom) across 62 stations during the Arctic Shelf Growth, Advection, Respiration and Deposition Rate Experiments (ASGARD) cruise in June 2017, when sea surface temperatures were anomalously warm. Hierarchical clustering of amplicon sequence variant (ASV) relative abundances resolved 11 sample clusters in three divisions, all dominated by Alphaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, and Bacteroidia. Community structure was related to water mass, salinity, and bloom stage, but not to depth. Clusters ranged from Gammaproteobacteria-dominant, Bacteroidia-poor assemblages in warm and cool Shelf Water (Division A) to Bacteroidia-rich assemblages spanning pre- to post-bloom conditions (Divisions B and C). In distance-based redundancy analysis, temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen, nitrate, and fluorescence together explained 14.8 % of the variation in community composition, with salinity the strongest contributor. These results indicate that water-mass origin, physicochemical conditions, and bloom stage jointly shape bacterial communities, and that changes in temperature, salinity, and the magnitude and timing of blooms could substantially alter bacterial communities of this Pacific gateway to the Arctic.

records.title: Making sense of chaos: replication and segregation defects in the yeast    mcm4  Chaos    3  mutant
records.abstract: Genome instability is a defining feature of cancer and is strongly influenced by alterations in the fidelity and timing of DNA replication. The conserved Mini-Chromosome Maintenance (MCM 2-7) helicase is a central component of the eukaryotic DNA replication machinery, playing critical roles in origin licensing and activation. Genetic screens for genome instability mutations in mice identified  mcm4  Chaos3 , a hypomorphic allele of  MCM4 associated with the formation of micronuclei and tumorigenesis, suggesting that the  mcm4  Chaos3 allele causes genome instability. To define the mechanistic basis of this instability, we examined the effects of the corresponding mutation in  Saccharomyces cerevisiae. We found that  mcm4  Chaos3 selectively compromises origin firing at a subset of early S-phase origins, with pronounced effects at many centromere-proximal origins. Chromosome V, containing the sensitive centromere-adjacent  ARS510, exhibited elevated loss rates that were rescued by replacement with the robust early-firing origin  ARS305 , restoring both origin activity and chromosome stability. Together these findings demonstrate that  mcm4  Chaos3 compromises genome stability by impairing a subset of early, centromere-proximal origins that are intrinsically sensitive to origin activation capacity. Our results establish that robust origin function near centromeres is critical for accurate chromosome segregation and reveal how subtle perturbations in helicase function can lead to chromosome instability.  Author Summary  The defining feature of cell division is the distribution of replicated chromosomes to the two daughter cells. Each chromosome contains a single centromere that is essential for their faithful inheritance. But before a cell divides, it must duplicate its DNA. DNA replication begins at sites called origins that differ in their activity and regulation. We studied a mutant version of Mcm4, a component of the molecular machinery that unwinds DNA during replication, to determine how compromised replication affects chromosome inheritance. This mutation was first discovered in mice, where it causes chromosome instability and cancer. Using Baker’s yeast, we found that the mutation reduces activity at a subset of origins, with origins near centromeres being preferentially affected. We also found an approximately three-fold increases in the rate that a test chromosome (chr V) is lost. These results suggest that the  mcm4  Chaos3 mutation can promote genome instability by compromising timely replication of centromeres. Replacing a sensitive origin near the centromere with a robust origin from elsewhere in the genome restored local replication activity and rescued chromosome loss to normal levels. This rescue depended on origin-associated binding sites and a centromere-associated protein, indicating that both origin features and chromosomal context contribute to replication activity. Our findings show that selective defects in replication initiation can compromise chromosome inheritance and that restoring activity at a single centromere-proximal origin can suppress this instability.
records.authors: Verhey JI, Moore AK, Armstrong JO, Alvino GM, Dunham MJ, Brewer BJ, Raghuraman MK.

records.title: Metabolomics-guided discovery of cytotoxic anthraquinones from the Red Sea-derived fungus Aspergillus amstelodami associated with Sargassum aquifolium.
records.abstract: Marine macroalgae-associated fungi constitute an underexplored reservoir of structurally diverse secondary metabolites with considerable pharmaceutical potential. To assess the chemical diversity and anticancer potential of fungi associated with Sargassum aquifolium, several fungal endophytes were isolated from specimens collected along the Egyptian Red Sea coast. Among the isolated fungi, Aspergillus amstelodami AUMC 16413 (Am-10) was prioritized for in-depth chemical and biological investigation based on its metabolite-rich profile in preliminary screening assays. UPLC-HRMS/MS-based metabolomics and GNPS networking enabled the annotation of 53 metabolites (anthraquinones, dihydro-isocoumarins, and prenylated benzaldehydes), revealing an anthraquinone-rich metabolome. Fractionation and spectroscopic analyses led to elucidation of seven anthraquinones, identified as danthron 1, catenarin 2, questin 3A, rubrocristin 3B, questinol 4, dermolutein 5A, and endocrocin 5B. The fungal extract exhibited cytotoxic activity toward MCF-7 cells (CC50 = 16.5 ± 1.9 µg mL-1; SI = 5.07), with a differential response observed between MCF-7 and normal cells together with alteration in cell-cycle progression and induction of apoptosis. RT-qPCR showed upregulation of Bax and p53, with downregulation of Bcl-2. Among the tested metabolites, compound 1, 3A/3B and 5A/5B mixtures displayed cytotoxic activity, with 5A/5B mixture showing the highest cytotoxic activity and selectivity index among the tested compounds (CC50 = 7.37 ± 0.38 µg mL-1, SI = 8.88). Molecular docking showed predicted interactions with apoptosis-related targets. Moreover, SwissADME and toxicity predictions indicated predicted ADME properties of the investigated compounds. These findings highlight Red Sea-derived A. amstelodami as a source of bioactive anthraquinones warranting further biological investigation.
records.authors: Badawy ET, Ragab AE, Farag MA, Finkelmeier D, Burger-Kentischer A, Abo El-Seoud KA, Zayed A.

records.title: Highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1-species-specific histopathology and viral antigen distribution in migratory and resident wild birds, South Westphalia, Germany 2025.
records.abstract: In late 2025, Germany faced a major outbreak of highly pathogenic influenza virus subtype H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, causing high mortality in migratory and resident wild birds and poultry. We examined 16 deceased birds, including Eurasian cranes, geese, a teal, and raptors found in western Germany between October and December 2025. Here, we provide a comparative analysis of light microscopic findings using histology and viral antigen distribution determined by immunohistochemistry, alongside the underlying viral phylogeny. Lesions and viral antigen distribution varied by species, with cranes showing infection in a broad organ spectrum, including the central nervous system (CNS), pancreas, spleen, liver, and kidneys, whereas other species exhibited a more targeted organ involvement. Phylogenetic analysis identified the EA-2024-DI.2.1 sublineage, with cranes forming a monophyletic cluster, which was consistent with the shared roosting/migratory behavior of cranes, although epidemiologic links were not formally demonstrated. In summary, our findings indicate species-specific lesion patterns and viral tissue tropism, which may influence transmission dynamics and environmental shedding.
records.authors: Beythien G, Gerhards H, Peters M, Kilwinski J, Pöpperl P, Nägler I, Ahrens AK, Pohlmann A, Beer M, Baumgärtner W, Wohlsein P.

records.title: Structural characterization of ZIKV M protein as a candidate viroporin: insights from molecular dynamics, evolutionary coupling and DFT.
records.abstract: Viroporins are small viral membrane proteins that facilitate ion transport and play critical role in viral pathogenicity. In this study, we investigate the Zika virus M protein viroporin to elucidate its proposed pore forming architecture using a combined computational framework of molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Sequence analysis shows 75 amino acid long Zika M protein is highly conserved across the continents and a significant variation is observed within different flaviviruses. The ab-initio model determined by AlphaFold is characterized by two hydrophobic C-terminal alpha helices and a N-terminal compact ectodomain. MD simulations in DPPC bilayers indicate that a pentameric pore-like assembly was the most structurally persistent model tested, featuring a single pore with a mixed distribution of polar and nonpolar residues. Leu12, Ile30, Trp35, Phe42, Ile49, Tyr63, Ile67, and Tyr74 provide structural rigidity and pore geometry, thereby stabilizing oligomeric packing. DFT analyses provide atomistic insights into electronic interactions and energetics that underpin conformational switching. Ca2+ displays well-defined multidentate coordination and strong structural organization, whereas Na+, K+, H+, and Cl- engage more weakly, governed mainly by long-range electrostatics and solvation effects. Virtual screening of >170 marketed ion channel modulators identified Lumacaftor and Gliquidone as the highest-scoring compounds for the Zika M oligomer pore-binding pocket, generating hypotheses for future experimental validation. Our study provides a structural and computational framework for the ZIKV M protein as a candidate viroporin, offering testable hypotheses regarding oligomeric stoichiometry, pore-lining architecture, and ion coordination that motivate future experimental validation.
records.authors: Zeba A, Mallasandra Krishnappa C, Rajendran S, Javeed N, Periyasamy G, Sekar K, Ganjiwale A.

records.title: Combinatorial Tuning of Multigene Biosynthetic Pathways based on RNA Interference.
records.abstract: Fine-tuning the expression level of multigene pathways remains a major challenge in engineering eukaryotic microbial cell factories. Modifications to individual pathway genes and CRISPR-based approaches often require repeated genome reconstruction, large regulatory components, or complex guide-array assembly. Here, we developed a lightweight, post-transcriptional RNAi-based strategy that enables fine-tuning gene expression without iterative genome editing. Size-selected small-RNA sequencing and functional testing were used to identify endogenous Pol III promoters spanning graded transcriptional strengths in Schizochytrium sp. Combining promoter strength with multiple short hairpin RNA (shRNA) target positions expanded the accessible repression range and enabled high-resolution gene-dosage tuning. The RNAi-based combined regulation strategy was applied to the three-gene carotenoid pathway of Schizochytrium sp. and the nine-gene docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) pathway of Yarrowia lipolytica, significantly enhancing the product production in both hosts. Integration of RNAi screening and dosage optimization further identified and tuned bypass pathways, increasing the ratio of DHA to docosapentaenoic acid (DPA) by 4.50-fold versus wild type. These gains were maintained during 5-L fermentation and serial passaging. This work establishes a compact and scalable regulatory framework for engineering complex biosynthetic pathways in eukaryotic microbial hosts.
records.authors: Zhang Z, Xu Y, Li Z, Du F, Ma W, Yang G, Sun X.
