records.title: Polyethylene microplastics reduce aluminum uptake but obstruct nodulation in broad bean under acidic aluminum stress.
records.abstract: Soil acidification and microplastic pollution increasingly threaten agricultural systems worldwide, yet their combined effects on crops remain largely unexplored. In this study, we subjected broad bean (Vicia faba L.) to polyethylene (PE) microplastics, aluminum (Al) stress, or their combination, and integrated physiological assays, root metabolomics, and rhizosphere metagenomics to dissect their interactive effects. PE microplastics unexpectedly lowered root Al accumulation by 41.7% compared to Al alone, which was associated with reduced exchangeable Al in the rhizosphere. Despite this reduction, the combined PE and Al treatment still significantly suppressed root (by 50.1%) and shoot (by 42.0%) biomasses and severely compromised nodulation and nitrogen (N) acquisition, with effects similar to or even stronger than those of the mono Al treatment. Metabolomic profiling revealed that combined stress extensively downregulated ten flavonoids and fundamentally rewired flavonoid-rhizobia correlation networks, shifting potential symbiotic signaling away from compatible interactions. Metagenomic analysis further showed that while combined stress increased microbial co-occurrence network connectivity by 54.8%, it simultaneously suppressed the abundance of functional genes related to metal resistance and N cycling, pointing to a systemic metabolic burden rather than a targeted stress response. These results demonstrate that PE microplastics modulate Al bioavailability but do not mitigate phytotoxicity; instead, they exacerbate symbiotic disruption through flavonoid signaling interference and microbiome functional decline. These findings highlight the vulnerability of legume-rhizobia symbiosis to multi-stressor environments and call for a reassessment of soil management practices in regions where acidification and microplastic contamination co-occur.
records.authors: Yang J, Wang R, Hu N, Li B, Li Y, Xu J, Deng Y, Li Y, Li X.

records.title: A split nozzle and two-protein chain-like fibers define the tail architecture of Pseudomonas aeruginosa podophage A1002.
records.abstract: Phage therapy offers unique advantages against antibiotic-resistant bacteria. However, high-resolution structural studies of phages targeting Pseudomonas aeruginosa-a top-seven global pathogen-particularly podophages, remain severely limited, directly impeding structure-based development of novel antimicrobials. In this study, we utilize cryo-EM to resolve the high-resolution intact structure of mature phage A1002, a podophage infecting carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa. Based on density maps combined with AlphaFold3 predictions, we identified 11 structural protein components from the head to the tail. Phage A1002 exhibits a distinctly elongated tail morphology distinct from other reported podophages. Notably, the A1002 nozzle employs a distinct assembly strategy, featuring the unique nozzle-rope protein and nozzle-base protein, which may have evolved through modular evolution and horizontal gene transfer. Furthermore, the nozzle-rope protein provides 11 adsorption sites for fiber dimers, and these dimers are assembled from two proteins, giving rise to two types of dimers: dimers 1-7 correspond to fiber I (gp40), and dimers 8-11 correspond to fiber II (gp41). The nozzle-rope protein and these dimers combine to form a chain-like fiber. The tail tube comprises a double-layered, elongated tube structure that functions to simultaneously increase tail length and provide docking sites for six chain-like fibers. These distinctive structural features provide the molecular basis for A1002's broad-spectrum infection of drug-resistant P. aeruginosa and offer a novel molecular blueprint for rational design of structure-guided phage therapeutics.
records.authors: Pang H, Chen Y, Peng Z, Xiao H, Chen W, Li X, Chen P, Zheng J, Liu H.

records.title: Whole-genome characterization of a food-derived Kurthia gibsonii isolate reveals a tet(L)-str-repUS12 resistance-associated region.
records.abstract: BackgroundThe emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in environmental and food-associated bacteria has attracted increasing attention within the One Health framework. However, genomic information regarding antimicrobial resistance determinants and mobile genetic elements in Kurthia gibsonii remains limited. This study aimed to characterize a food-derived K. gibsonii isolate (KT09) by whole-genome sequencing, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and comparative genomic analysis, with emphasis on the genetic context of a tet(L)-associated resistance region.Methods and results(KT09), recovered from phyllo dough on gentamicin-supplemented medium was sequenced using Illumina platform. The reported draft genome consisted of 2,944,613 bp in 122 contigs > 500 bp (GC content, 36.65%; N50, 72,389 bp), with 99.34% completeness and 2.87% contamination by CheckM. TYGS analysis confirmed assignment to K. gibsonii. Disk diffusion showed variable inhibition-zone diameters, with particularly small zones for tetracycline and streptomycin. Genome analysis identified tet(L), str, and aadA1, while emrB was detected by genome annotation. The tet(L)-str-repUS12 resistance-associated region was located on contig00014, which showed a mean read depth of 290.97× and 100% breadth of coverage. Comparative BLASTn and synteny analyses showed high nucleotide similarity between this localized region and homologous chromosomal and plasmid-associated sequences from Kurthia, Enterococcus, and Staphylococcus. However, the complete contig was predominantly Kurthia-like and was not resolved as an independent circular component.ConclusionsThe KT09 genome expands the limited genomic information available for food-derived K. gibsonii and documents a tet(L)-str-repUS12 resistance-associated region with close sequence similarity to plasmid-associated loci reported in other Gram-positive bacteria. These findings are consistent with a shared mobile gene pool but do not establish plasmid localization, mobility, or the source or direction of horizontal gene transfer. Long-read sequencing and experimental plasmid characterization are required to resolve the genomic location and transferability of this region.

records.title: Deletion of the Envelope gene attenuates SARS-CoV-2 infection by altered spike localization and increased cell-to-cell transmission.
records.abstract: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) causes COVID-19, a highly transmissible acute respiratory infection that can result in severe pneumonia and death. Many details of SARS-CoV-2 infection are not fully understood, including the cell biology and host-virus interactions involved in coronavirus assembly and release, in which the Envelope (E) structural protein is instrumental. Deletion of E in other coronaviruses has been shown previously to either attenuate or abrogate infection. To determine the role of E in SARS-CoV-2 virus production and infectivity, we produced a reporter SARS-CoV-2 with or without the E gene deleted using a bacterial artificial chromosome. Replication of ΔE SARS-CoV-2 was attenuated in Vero E6 cells expressing human ACE2 and TMPRSS2 and in human epithelial cell lines. Electron and immunofluorescence microscopy and virology assays showed that ΔE SARS-CoV-2 increased cell surface expression of Spike (S) glycoprotein, leading to reduced S incorporation into ΔE SARS-CoV-2 particles and promotion of increased cell-to-cell transmission that evades neutralizing antibody inhibition. Trans-complementation of E partially rescued ΔE SARS-CoV-2 S incorporation and restored cell-free transmission. In addition to validating the role of E in retention of S in the ER-Golgi intermediate complex (ERGIC), our results showed that a lack of E led to reorganization of the ERGIC and Golgi during SARS-CoV-2 infection. Improved understanding of E in SARS-CoV-2 replication and host pathogenesis may help the development of novel therapeutics.IMPORTANCENon-Spike coronavirus structural proteins, including Envelope, are conserved, making them potential pan-coronavirus therapeutic targets. Many details about these proteins and their roles in viral replication and host pathogenesis are unknown. In this study, we showed that severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) replicates without Envelope but is attenuated and impaired in virus particle formation, with less Spike incorporated into virions and more Spike expressed on the cell surface compared to wild-type virus. SARS-CoV-2 lacking Envelope transmitted primarily via cell fusion and evaded neutralizing antibodies. In addition, the absence of Envelope resulted in the reorganization of the cell secretory compartment during SARS-CoV-2 infection. A better understanding of how Envelope influences SARS-CoV-2 replication could guide directed design of novel therapeutics for treatment of COVID-19 patients, as well as the potential for pan-coronavirus protection against future coronavirus outbreaks.

records.title: Aberrant expression of HERV-K envelope in lymphoma represents an opportunity for novel treatments.
records.abstract: PurposeHuman endogenous retrovirus K (HERV-K/HML-2) is a human-specific endogenous retrovirus family that maintains intact open reading frames and is aberrantly expressed in multiple cancers. We tested whether HERV-K, specifically its envelope (Env) protein, marks clinically relevant diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) states and serves as a tractable immunotherapeutic target.Experimental designLocus-level transposable element (TE) and HERV expression was quantified in two independent DLBCL RNA-seq cohorts using curated TE annotation and a uniform alignment/counting workflow. Env transcript and protein expression (including cell-surface localization) was validated in lymphoma cell lines using RT-qPCR, immunoblotting, and flow cytometry. Functional relevance was assessed by siRNA-mediated Env knockdown. Candidate extracellular linear epitopes were predicted in silico and synthesized for serological and phage display assays. Anti-Env camelid VHHs were isolated, humanized, and tested for binding, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC), and antigen-dependent internalization.ResultsTE transcripts stratified DLBCL into clinically distinct subgroups, and high HERV-K expression associated with an interferon/viral-mimicry program. Env RNA was detected in patient tumors and cell lines, and the protein was detected on the surface of a subset of lymphoma cell lines, in which Env knockdown reduced proliferation. A humanized heavy-chain antibody (FF-01) bound surface Env, induced selective ADCC in Env-positive models (reporter and primary NK-cell assays), and underwent rapid antigen-dependent internalization.ConclusionsHERV-K activity identifies biologically meaningful DLBCL states and exposes a targetable surface antigen. FF-01 provides proof of principle for antibody-based strategies against HERV-K Env, including ADCC- and ADC-oriented approaches.

records.title: Absolute quantification of synthetic microbial communities using a simplified multiplexed ddPCR method.
records.abstract: Synthetic microbial communities provide experimentally tractable systems for studying community assembly, stability, and function and for integrating quantitative experiments with mathematical models of community dynamics. These applications require accurate and reproducible absolute quantification of individual community members, yet commonly used methods rely on relative abundance measurements or suffer from amplification bias and limited reproducibility. Here, we present a simplified and scalable multiplexed digital droplet PCR-based workflow for absolute quantification of species abundance in synthetic microbial communities. Using a four-member community composed of Bacillus subtilis, Pseudomonas fluorescens, Rhodococcus ruber, and Enterobacter asburiae, we developed an integrated experimental workflow encompassing DNA isolation, primer and probe design, and multiplex assay configuration. A hybrid targeting strategy was adopted, substituting a single-copy gyrB gene target for Bacillus subtilis to avoid 16S rRNA gene cross-reactivity, while retaining 16S rRNA gene targets for the remaining three community members. Key assay parameters were systematically optimized to enable robust discrimination and simultaneous quantification of all community members within a single reaction. The method exhibits high linearity across a broad dynamic range, resistance to amplification bias, and tolerance to common polymerase chain reaction inhibitors. This streamlined approach, intended for experimental characterization of defined synthetic microbial communities under controlled experimental conditions rather than for microbial diagnostics or clinical detection, enables reproducible absolute quantification of defined microbial consortia and provides a quantitative foundation for systems-level analyses and model-informed studies of microbial community behavior, with species specificity being defined operationally within this community and scaling to additional targets to require manual tuning.IMPORTANCEMechanistic understanding of microbial communities increasingly depends on quantitative data that can be directly compared across experiments and used to parameterize mathematical models. However, simple methods for measuring the absolute abundance of individual species in synthetic microbial communities remain limited. We describe an accessible multiplexed digital droplet polymerase chain reaction workflow that enables direct and reproducible cell quantification in a defined microbial consortium. Unlike methods developed for microbial diagnostics or clinical testing, this approach is optimized for experimental reproducibility and quantitative modeling in well-defined microbial consortia rather than for broad-spectrum detection or regulatory validation. By supporting accurate absolute quantification, this framework strengthens integration between experimental and theoretical studies aimed at explaining how microbial communities are established and maintained.

records.title: Global Metabolic Rewiring Induced by HAC1 Overexpression Facilitates Efficient Linalool Synthesis in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
records.abstract: The present study employs global transcriptional engineering (GTE) to optimize metabolic flux toward linalool synthesis by screening seven key transcription factors in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Overexpression of HAC1 in the strain SA44, the master regulator of the unfolded protein response (UPR), increased 2.9-fold in linalool titers compared to the control strain (SA49). Genome-wide transcriptomic analysis revealed that Hac1p-mediated activation induces a redirection of carbon flux into the mevalonate (MVA) pathway, the glyoxylate cycle, and gluconeogenesis, alongside the substantial repression of master sterol pathway activator (UPC2) and the hexose transporters. Multi-layer network analysis revealed GCN4- centered upregulation of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase genes (aaRS) in the HAC1- overexpressing background, associated with putative HAC1-linked transcriptional repression of ERG9. Functional validation of the Hac1p regulatory networks via co-expression of HAC1 with the succinate-fumarate transporter (SFC1) yielded a synergistic improvement in linalool titer. Furthermore, the co-expression of MAF1, a negative regulator of tRNA biogenesis, and HAC1 has been shown to reduce linalool production. Notably, the high-linalool-titer strain (SA44) exhibited a distinct metabolic profile, with higher glycerol accumulation (~5.0 g/L). SA44 demonstrated superior sterol accumulation compared to SA49, with 1.6-fold higher squalene and 1.2-fold higher ergosterol production. Additionally, qRT-PCR was used to independently confirm the differential expression of seven regulatory genes, yielding a high Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.994. This study reports the first HAC1-mediated enhancement of linalool biosynthesis, establishing a robust strategy for microbial monoterpene production.

records.title: Enterobacteriaceae and Bacteriophages: Implications Against Antimicrobial Resistance.
records.abstract: Enterobacteriaceae represent a clinically challenging bacterial family owing to the global emergence of multidrug resistance. Bacteriophages, the natural predators of these bacteria, have emerged as powerful tools for detecting, targeting, and inhibiting these pathogens. This review provides a comprehensive overview of bacteriophages targeting Enterobacteriaceae hosts, focusing on their diversity, virion architecture, and the molecular determinants of host specificity. The dynamic co-evolution between bacterial defence strategies and phage counter-defences is discussed to illustrate the complexity of the phage-Enterobacteriaceae host interactions. Translational applications of Enterobacteriaceae phages, including phage therapy, engineered phages, phage-derived lysins as antimicrobials, and phage-based diagnostics for rapid and specific pathogen detection is also explored alongside their limitations including limited large-scale clinical trials, regulatory and manufacturing hurdles, and the need for robust host-range prediction and standardization. Overall, this review elaborates implications of bacteriophage-Enterobacteriaceae interactions to combat antimicrobial resistance and support the development of next-generation antibacterial therapies and diagnostics.
records.authors: Ramadoss R, Moovarkumudalvan B, Jothimani P, Lakshmanan D.

records.title: Harnessing yeast biodiversity to identify superior chassis strains for metabolic engineering and precision fermentation.
records.abstract: Microbial cell factories are increasingly used for the sustainable production of fuels, chemicals and pharmaceuticals. Yeasts are particularly suitable as production hosts because of their metabolic flexibility, robustness, and expanding synthetic biology toolkits. Metabolic engineering of yeast historically relied on a narrow set of reference species and strains, especially Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Recent studies, however, show that applying identical pathway designs to different strain backgrounds or species can yield significant differences in titer, rate and yield (TRY). In this review, we examine how diversity within and between species in genomic features, metabolic regulation, substrate utilization and stress tolerance shapes chassis performance. We focus on eight species, including S. cerevisiae, Yarrowia lipolytica, Kluyveromyces marxianus, Komagataella phaffii, Ogataea polymorpha, Rhodotorula toruloides, Lipomyces starkeyi and Pichia kudriavzevii. We highlight that different species and strain backgrounds provide distinct advantages depending on the target product, pathway requirements, substrate, and process conditions. Finally, we discuss the transition from empirical strain screening toward diversity-informed and predictive chassis selection through multi-omics, phenotyping, metabolic modeling, and machine learning. We propose that chassis identity should be treated as a design variable, and that chassis selection should become an integral part of the Design-Build-Test-Learn cycle to develop optimal cell factories.
records.authors: Zhu Y, Voordeckers K, Steensels J, Verstrepen KJ.

records.title: Breakpoint Mapping and Disrupted Gene Identification in Azoospermic Patients With Chromosomal Balanced Translocation by Nanopore Sequencing.
records.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the utility of nanopore long-read sequencing for precise breakpoint mapping in azoospermia patients with chromosomal balanced translocations, and to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying translocation-induced spermatogenic failure.MethodsPeripheral blood specimens were collected from two azoospermic patients with balanced chromosomal translocations. G-banding karyotype analysis and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) results served as the reference standard, and whole-genome long-read sequencing of peripheral blood samples was performed on the PromethION platform. Breakpoint positions were visualized using the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV), and gene annotations were conducted using the UCSC Genome Browser.ResultsSequencing was successfully completed for both samples, yielding mean read lengths of 9713.3 bp and 8129.8 bp, respectively. Nanopore sequencing afforded superior molecular resolution of chromosomal aberrations relative to traditional cytogenetic approaches. A total of eight breakpoints were identified through IGV visualization, with four precisely mapped at single-nucleotide resolution. Annotation revealed that five breakpoints resided within intergenic regions without compromising gene integrity, whereas three breakpoints (ChrX:147,998,514-147,998,515, Chr3:65,894,036-65,899,651, and Chr16:53,815,988-53,815,992) were situated within intronic segments of the AFF2, MAGI1, and FTO genes, respectively, resulting in gene disruption.ConclusionThis study employed nanopore long-read sequencing to precisely map chromosomal breakpoints in two azoospermic patients, including cryptic breakpoints undetectable by conventional karyotyping. Disruption of AFF2, MAGI1, and FTO at three breakpoints provides novel candidate gene evidence for translocation-associated spermatogenic failure, confirming nanopore sequencing as a robust tool for structural variant characterization and the discovery of spermatogenesis-related genes.
records.authors: Zhang J, Chen XL, Chen JY, Ge YS.

records.title: Dual role of RBM3 in PEDV infection: stabilization of viral RNA and upregulation of the entry factor HSPA5
records.abstract: RBM3, a member of the cold shock protein family, functions as an RNA chaperone that stabilizes target transcripts by binding to their untranslated regions (UTRs). Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) is an enteric coronavirus that poses a serious threat to the swine industry, and its replication heavily depends on its genomic and subgenomic RNAs, making these RNAs potential targets for host RNA binding proteins. In this study, we show that RBM3 promotes PEDV replication through a dual mechanism. On one hand, RBM3 exhibits a binding preference for the viral 3’UTR, which prolongs the half-life of viral RNA and thereby promotes PEDV proliferation. RBM3 also interacts with the PEDV nucleocapsid (N) protein and replication-associated double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) signals, suggesting that RBM3 may be associated with viral replication complexes, though its contribution to their functional integrity remains to be determined. On the other hand, RBM3 increases HSPA5 promoter activity and HSPA5 mRNA levels, linking RBM3 to HSPA5, a host factor known to facilitate PEDV attachment and internalization. These two mechanisms together provide a mechanistic basis for efficient PEDV infection. Our findings identify RBM3 as a positive host regulator of PEDV and establish, for the first time, a functional link between RBM3 and HSPA5, offering new insights into coronavirus host interactions and suggesting RBM3 as a potential target for antiviral intervention.
records.authors: Li S, Zeng Y, Li J, Liu Y, Liu H, Yang X, Qin W, Li T, Chen Z, Liu J, Tong G, Cao X, Kong N, Shan T.

records.title: DarHTG is a tripartite phage defence system for purine DNA base ADP-ribosylation
records.abstract: Bacteria evolved a variety of phage defence strategies to combat the constant onslaught of viral threats. DarTG toxin-antitoxin systems provide phage defence by ADP-ribosylation of bases in single-stranded DNA which interferes with viral replication and aborts phage infection. Here, we describe DarHTG, a system widespread among bacteria, that combines DarTG with a non- processive superfamily I helicase functioning as co-toxin for DarT and thereby enabling the ADP- ribosylation of double-stranded DNA. We identified two such DarHTG subclasses which catalyse the ADP-ribosylation of adenosine and guanosine bases, respectively, and reverse these modifications with structurally unique ARH superfamily antitoxins. Thus, DarHTG antitoxins expand the known macromolecular target spectrum of the ARH enzyme class to nucleic acids. These DarHTG systems confer resistance to a broad range of bacteriophages and can be triggered by the highly charged tails of viral single-stranded DNA-binding proteins, which occlude the active site of the ARH antitoxin.

records.title: Phylogeny-Guided Global-Local Shrinkage for Microbiome Feature Selection
records.abstract: Microbiome feature selection is challenging because sequencing counts are sparseand compositional, while evolutionarily related taxa may exhibit similar associations with an exposure. We propose phylogeny-guided global--local shrinkage (PGL), a Bayesian regression method for identifying exposure-associated differences in the relative abundances of individual amplicon sequence variants (ASVs). A multinomial logit-normal working model analyzes relative abundance among ASVs detected in each sample. A zero-sum constraint gives the regression coefficients a log-ratio interpretation relative to the mean across retained ASVs. Global--local shrinkage accommodates weak and large associations, while an estimated weight controls information sharing along a supplied phylogenetic tree. Simulation ablation studies showed that phylogenetic borrowing improved detection power and estimation of nonzero coefficients when associations aligned with the tree, with little change under a tree-independent generator. Estimated borrowing decreased as the supplied tree was corrupted. Comparisons with benchmark methods revealed different trade-offs between detection power and false discovery rates across simulation settings. In an HIV oral microbiome application, ablation analysis showed that phylogenetic borrowing preserved the overall pattern of estimated associations while changing posterior uncertainty and selecting three additional ASVs. PGL provides ASV-level inference with adaptive information sharing across evolutionarily related features.
records.authors: Zhu Z, Zhang S, Tang X, Zhang L.

records.title: Severe Intracranial Hemorrhage and Intracranial Infection Caused by Ureaplasma parvum Infection in an Extremely Preterm Infant: A Case Report and Literature Review
records.abstract: Abstract  Background:Ureaplasma parvum (Up) is an under-recognized pathogen in neonatal central nervous system infections. We retrospectively analyzed the clinical data of one extremely preterm infant presenting with severe intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) and intracranial infection attributed to Up infection, and systematically reviewed the relevant literature. The analysis covered perinatal history, neurological manifestations, serial cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and imaging changes, metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) results, and treatment course. Case presentation:A male infant was born at 26⁺¹ weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 920 g. Intracranial hemorrhage, initially grade I on day 1 of life, progressed to grade IV by day 4. CSF examination showed typical features of intracranial infection: the nucleated cell count was markedly elevated, glucose was profoundly decreased (0.07 mmol/L), and protein reached 7,443 mg/L. Conventional bacterial cultures were repeatedly negative; however, mNGS of CSF identified Up (115 sequence reads; relative abundance 87.19%). Following targeted treatment with azithromycin, CSF inflammatory markers improved. Nevertheless, given the severity of the intracranial lesions, the family ultimately chose to withdraw care. Conclusion: This case suggests that Up infection may act as a synergistic factor in the development or progression of severe ICH in extremely preterm infants. Potential mechanisms include direct injury to the cerebral vascular endothelium and fragile germinal matrix vessels, as well as blood-brain barrier disruption secondary to inflammatory cytokine release. In extremely preterm infants with unusually rapid progression of ICH and poor response to conventional treatment, Up infection should be considered early, and mNGS testing should be arranged without delay. As this is a single case report, the causal relationship warrants confirmation in future studies.

records.title: Soil pH, not land-use type, predicts microbial motility and denitrification genes after rainforest conversion in Sumatra and Borneo
records.abstract: Abstract    Conversion of lowland rainforest to rubber and oil palm alters soil microbial communities, but whether functional gene responses are consistent across regions, and what drives them, is unclear. Public soil shotgun metagenomes from Jambi, Sumatra (32 plots: rainforest, jungle rubber, rubber, oil palm) and Sabah, Borneo (24 plots: unlogged forest, logged forest, oil palm) were reanalysed. The Sumatran workflow reproduced published fold changes (r = 0.998). In Sumatra, land use explained 41% of the variation in functional composition (permutation test, p = 0.0001); flagellar assembly genes declined by 27–35%, chemotaxis genes by 17–20% and secretion-system genes by 10–12% in converted systems, while denitrification genes increased in oil palm (  nirS   + 220%,  nosZ   + 164%). In Sabah, oil palm differed little from unlogged forest, and oil palm effects pooled across sites were not significant and highly heterogeneous (I² = 83–99%). In contrast, relationships with soil pH were consistent in both regions: denitrification (combined ρ = 0.69) and nitrogen-fixation genes (ρ = 0.50) increased with pH, whereas type VI secretion (ρ = −0.64), flagellar motility (ρ = −0.53) and chemotaxis genes (ρ = −0.41) decreased (all p ≤ 0.002). Plantations raised soil pH consistently in Sumatra but not in Sabah. Decimal errors in 32 published soil values and a misassigned  mcrA  gene were also corrected. Soil chemistry, particularly pH altered by liming, predicts microbial functional responses to rainforest conversion better than land-use type alone. Measuring soil pH alongside metagenomes should improve predictions of microbial denitrification potential in plantation landscapes, including in the Philippines.

records.title: RNA pol II speed controls the level of read-through mediated transcriptional interference
records.abstract: Abstract    Transcriptional interference, which can be mediated by read-through transcription, is recognized as a mechanism negatively controlling gene expression levels. Recent studies highlighted the importance of transcriptional interference mediated by read-through transcription in response to different kinds of stresses and in response to viral infections. In this study we investigated the extent of transcriptional interference mediated by read-through transcription in different human cell lines. Our results, based on the analysis of transcriptomics and genomics data, reveal that transcriptional interference is widespread in the human genome in unperturbed conditions. Furthermore, through the use of RNA pol II mutants with different velocity, we show that transcriptional interference can be controlled by RNA pol II speed. Finally, we observe that read-through transcription invading downstream genes significantly associates with decreased level of translation of downstream genes in tandem gene pairs, therefore probably affecting protein levels. Together these data indicate that transcriptional interference is a mechanism controlling gene expression in unperturbed conditions. In addition, our results uncover the importance of transcription speed in controlling the expression level of downstream genes in tandem gene pairs.  *Virginie Jouffret and Maurane Eisele contributed equally to this work.  **Didier Trouche and Lisa Muniz contributed equally to this work.

records.title: A genomic toolkit for surveillance and elimination of the principal malaria vectors in Southeast Asia.
records.abstract: While substantial progress has been made toward malaria elimination in Southeast Asia, major challenges remain. The principal mosquito vectors,  Anopheles dirus and  Anopheles minimus , inhabit diverse ecological niches and exhibit a wide range of behavioural and physiological insecticide resistance phenotypes, complicating vector control efforts. In Africa, genomic surveillance has transformed our understanding of vector evolution and resistance, supported by open-access tools and data. Comparable resources for Southeast Asian vectors remain limited. Here, we release Adir1.0, a curated, analysis-ready catalog of 540  An. dirus whole-genome sequences, accessible for interactive cloud-based analysis via the malariagen-data-python application programming interface (API). Alongside, we provide an updated Amin1.0 API to enhance functionality and usability, enabling integrated analyses across historical and new datasets. We demonstrate these resources by performing the first exploratory population genomic analysis of  An. dirus from Bangladesh, Thailand, and Cambodia, revealing population structure, candidate regions of physiological resistance, and genomic structural variation. Together, these resources provide a foundation for genomic surveillance studies to inform vector control and malaria elimination strategies in Southeast Asia.

records.title: Integrative lipidomic and genomic analysis identifies key lipids for wooden breast in chickens.
records.abstract: BackgroundWooden breast (WB) is a prevalent myopathy in broilers that substantially reduces meat quality and causes considerable economic losses. However, the genetic architecture and lipidomic alterations associated with WB remain poorly understood. This study aimed to integrate untargeted lipidomics and genomic analyses to characterize lipid alterations and their associated genetic factors in WB.ResultsTo characterize WB-related phenotypes, pectoralis major muscles from 312 broilers were evaluated for WB severity, compression force (CF), endomysium thickness, and total lipid abundance. By integrating differential abundance analysis, trend analysis, and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), we identified a core set of 25 lipid species. Further refinement using Mendelian randomization (MR) and mediation analyses prioritized nine lipids as candidate molecular traits associated with genetic variation and WB, seven of which showed consistent associations in an independent cohort (n = 119). Metabolome genome-wide association study (mGWAS) of these lipids identified a consensus genetic locus on chromosome 6 (19.55-20.15 Mb) shared by three candidate lipids. Integration of transcriptomic profiles from genes within this locus prioritized five candidate genes, with MAPK8 and NPY4R showing consistent expression patterns in the independent cohort. Based on its potential biological relevance, MAPK8 was selected for functional characterization in chicken primary myoblasts. MAPK8 overexpression and knockdown produced opposite effects on lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and fibrosis-related gene expression, suggesting that MAPK8 may participate in cellular processes involved in lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and fibrotic remodeling associated with WB.ConclusionsThis study provides an integrated overview of lipid metabolic alterations and their genetic architecture in WB-affected chickens. Collectively, these findings identify candidate lipid biomarkers and genetic loci and implicate MAPK8 as a candidate gene associated with lipid deposition and fibrotic remodeling in WB.

records.title: Toxicity of oxadiargyl to marine microalgae on competitive displacement and overlooked risk from transformation products.
records.abstract: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase (PPO) inhibitors are widely used in agriculture, yet their risks to marine ecosystems are often underestimated due to assumptions of target-site specificity and rapid environmental dissipation. Here, we demonstrated that oxadiargyl (OXA), a representative PPO herbicide, exhibits pronounced toxicity toward marine microalgae at 1-32 µg/L, highlighting the need for monitoring and risk assessment in coastal waters affected by agricultural runoff. Acute 96h-EC50 values for the keystone species Chlorella sp. and Skeletonema costatum were 6.02 and 9.35 μg/L, respectively, indicating they were highly sensitive taxa. OXA could disrupt community hierarchies through the competitive displacement of sensitive species by the tolerant diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum. Although parent OXA dissipated rapidly in seawater (half-life 0.95 d), persistent toxicity in the solution was observed as the growth of microalgae remained suppressed even after parent OXA fully degraded. Using solid phase extraction-liquid chromatography-high resolution tandem mass spectrometry (SPE-LCHRMS/MS), nine (seven new) transformation products (TPs) were identified. Computational toxicity screening predicted that four TPs retain algal toxicity comparable to that of OXA. These findings demonstrate that rapid dissipation of parent compound does not equate to risk elimination, emphasizing the necessity of integrating community-level competition endpoints and TP profiling in future pesticide risk assessments.

records.title: In silico characterisation of lysis and host-recognition modules in Staphylococcus aureus bacteriophage genomes.
records.abstract: BackgroundMethicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a leading human pathogen, and declining antibiotic efficacy has renewed interest in lytic bacteriophages, whose efficacy phenotypic assays predict poorly.ObjectivesTo characterise the lysis and host-recognition modules of lytic S. aureus bacteriophages, and to determine how far the detectability of each module depends on the annotation source rather than on the genomes.MethodsTwenty-two S. aureus phage genomes from NCBI GenBank were processed through an identical detection funnel under three annotation sources: the deposited record, Pharokka and Phold. Modules were validated by InterPro, disrupted endolysins resolved by tBLASTn, and each domain aligned separately to measure identity.FindingsThe LysK-type endolysin (CHAP-Amidase-SH3b) was conserved and detected identically under all three sources. Tail fibre/receptor-binding protein (RBP) detection was strongly source-dependent: 14 of 22 genomes from the deposited annotation, 20 of 22 after re-annotation, and 22 of 22 combined. Resolved by domain, conservation was scale-dependent: the amidase domain was invariant within species while SH3b varied by 5.7%.Main conclusionsLysis-module conservation is independent of the annotation source; the apparent variability of host recognition is largely an artefact of incomplete deposited annotation. Module-level surveys require re-annotation before comparative claims.

records.title: Nutrigenomics in Dairy Cattle: Causes and Implications.
records.abstract: Nutrigenomics is a rapidly developing interdisciplinary field that investigates the interactions between nutrients and the genome, with particular emphasis on how dietary components regulate gene expression and metabolic pathways. In dairy cattle, nutrigenomics has gained increasing attention due to its potential to improve milk production, metabolic efficiency, health, reproduction, and overall animal performance. Nutrients and bioactive dietary compounds can influence gene activity directly through transcriptional regulation or indirectly through epigenetic mechanisms such as DNA methylation, histone modification, and noncoding RNA-mediated gene regulation. These nutrigenomic interactions affect important biological processes including lipid metabolism, adipogenesis, immune response, mammary gland development, and milk synthesis. Advances in omics technologies including transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and next-generation sequencing have enhanced understanding of the molecular responses of dairy cows to nutritional interventions. Dietary fatty acids, vitamins, methyl donors, and short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate have been shown to regulate key transcription factors including peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), sterol regulatory element binding proteins (SREBPs), and liver X receptors (LXRs), thereby modulating metabolic and physiological functions. Nutritional interventions, feed restriction, and supplementation produce tissue-specific molecular responses in the liver, adipose tissue, mammary gland, and immune system, demonstrating interaction between diet, physiological state, and metabolic regulation. Despite these advances, challenges with genetic and physiological variability, tissue-specific responses, integration of multi-omics data, and translation of molecular findings into practical feeding strategies remain unresolved. Future integration of nutrigenomics with microbiome research, multi-omics, artificial intelligence, and precision livestock technologies may facilitate nutritional strategies to improve dairy cattle health, productivity, feed efficiency, and product quality.

records.title: CYP123, a sterol C4-methyl oxidase, acts with CYP51 to initiate mycobacterial lanosterol catabolism
records.abstract: Mycobacteria exploit host cholesterol, both as a carbon source and as a source of catabolites proposed to modulate host immunity, but their capacity to catabolise other host sterols has not been established. Lanosterol, the first sterol intermediate of host cholesterol biosynthesis, accumulates in the activated macrophages these bacteria infect. Here we define the initiating steps of mycobacterial lanosterol catabolism, combining genomic enzymology, transcriptional profiling, mutagenesis, biochemistry, NMR and crystallography. We identify the cytochrome P450 CYP123 as a sterol C4-methyl oxidase. It is encoded with the lanosterol 14α-demethylase CYP51 in a co-oriented region conserved across most  Mycobacteriaceae . The region carries no binding site for the cholesterol-responsive regulators KstR or KstR2, and in  M. abscessus lanosterol induces both genes while cholesterol does not. CYP123 oxidises the C4α-methyl group of C14-demethylated sterols in three steps to the carboxylic acid, yet acts on neither lanosterol nor cholesterol, because Met82 excludes the C14-methylated precursor. An M82A variant binds and oxidises lanosterol. In a single reaction containing both recombinant  M. smegmatis enzymes, CYP51 converts lanosterol to FF-MAS, which CYP123 then oxidises to the C4-carboxylic acid, so the two act in sequence.  M. smegmatis ,  M. phlei and  M. abscessus grow on lanosterol as a sole carbon source. Growth slows in  M. smegmatis cyp123 and  cyp51 mutants. Mycobacterial sterol catabolism therefore extends beyond cholesterol, and blocking the cholesterol route alone may not deprive these organisms of host sterols. Induction where lanosterol confers no growth advantage raises the possibility that the pathway also serves functions beyond carbon acquisition.  Significance  Mycobacteria feed on host cholesterol, a dependence long proposed as a drug target but never exploited therapeutically. This work shows that they also catabolise lanosterol, an early cholesterol precursor that accumulates in activated macrophages. Two cytochrome P450s encoded in a conserved, lanosterol-induced locus act in sequence: CYP51 removes the C14-methyl group, and CYP123 then oxidises the C4α-methyl group to a carboxylic acid. This explains why mycobacteria retain CYP51 despite being unable to make sterols, and identifies CYP123 as the first bacterial P450 sterol C4-methyl oxidase and a third enzymatic solution to C4-demethylation. The locus is conserved across more than 90% of  Mycobacteriaceae , spanning pathogens of humans, livestock and the environment, and contributes to fitness during infection, making both enzymes attractive, azole-binding drug targets. Because cholesterol and lanosterol run through separate routes, depriving mycobacteria of host sterols would require blocking both.

records.title: One-step glycan photoaffinity probe synthesis enables identification of human milk oligosaccharide-interacting microbiota
records.abstract: Glycans are found on the surfaces of all living cells and engage in cell signaling through the binding of various molecular targets. However, chemical probes to detect and identify carbohydrate interactions remain difficult to produce, due in large part to the challenges of late-stage, site-specific functionalization of oligosaccharides. Here, we report the synthesis and application of a minimal bifunctional diazirine/alkyne linker utilizing an  N,O -dialkylhydroxylamine (NODHA) moiety that can readily be installed on the anomeric position of unprotected sugars. Our linker functionalizes glycans with complete β-stereoselectivity, appends less mass than a single hexose unit, and maintains the closed-ring structure of the reducing end sugar. With this molecule, we generate glycan photoaffinity probes in a single step using unprotected human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs). We then validate binding selectivity of our compounds using lectins with known affinity towards our sugars. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of these glycan photoaffinity probes by performing photocrosslinking on a complex microbiota community and use cell sorting paired with metagenomic sequencing to identify potential new HMO-interacting microbes. Together, our work provides a one-step route to synthesize photoaffinity probes from unprotected, reducing glycans for interrogating carbohydrate interactions at the host-microbiota interface.

records.title: Multiple domains of Matɑ1 transcription factor contribute to binding site specificity
records.abstract: Among homologous transcription factors with the same function, DNA-binding specificity can diverge. Matɑ1 is a high mobility group (HMG) box transcription factor in budding yeast whose  Saccharomyces cerevisiae and  Candida albicans homologs regulate ɑ-specific genes but bind distinct  cis -regulatory sequences. To identify the protein features underlying this divergence, we generated structure-guided chimeras and measured their activity using species-specific reporters. Replacing any of the four Matɑ1 regions reduced activation of the  S. cerevisiae reporter, while all chimeras retained activity on the  C. albicans reporter. Thus, all four regions of Matɑ1 – not just the HMG box domain – are important for sequence specificity.
records.authors: Knisely-Durham E, Giovanetti SM, Sadhu MJ.

records.title: Potential biomarker candidates for improving diagnosis and disease treatment in adenomyosis.
records.abstract: Adenomyosis remains challenging to diagnose due to its unclear pathogenesis and clinical overlap with conditions such as endometriosis and uterine fibroids. While non-invasive imaging techniques like transvaginal ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging have improved adenomyosis detection, histopathological examination remains the gold standard. As this typically requires hysterectomy, it limits fertility-preserving diagnostic options. Therefore, the search for potential biomarkers is essential to improve the diagnosis of adenomyosis. This review summarises current evidence on genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic and microbiome biomarkers identified using conventional molecular techniques and high-throughput multi-omics approaches in eutopic endometrium, blood, urine, faeces, cervicovaginal lavage and vaginal swab samples with potential clinical applicability, enhancing diagnostic accuracy, and enabling early detection and monitoring. In addition, describing adenomyosis biomarkers may enhance the understanding of adenomyosis pathogenesis and help identify new therapeutic approaches. Although numerous candidate biomarkers have shown promising results (e.g. STEAP1, TOMM20, GLT8D2, and NME5, hsa_circ_008959/hsa-miR-124-3p/SLC15A4 + VAS score, miR-92a-3p or Weissella confusa, and Lactobacillus zeae), the current evidence remains insufficient for their implementation in routine clinical practice owing to the lack of external validation, standardised methodologies, and large multicentre studies.
records.authors: Merino-Pérez A, Albert AB, Del Mar Mascarell-López M, Pellicer A, Corachán A, Ferrero H.

records.title: Research progress in the production, purification, and applications of long single-stranded DNA.
records.abstract: Long single-stranded DNA (long ssDNA) plays important roles in cutting-edge fields such as DNA origami, gene therapy, and synthetic biology. However, the production, preparation, and purification of long ssDNA remain technically challenging. This review systematically summarizes current strategies for long ssDNA production and preparation, including phage-E. coli-based biological production, template-dependent enzymatic amplification, and viral-vector-based generation of ssDNA genomes. CRISPR-Cas-assisted approaches are discussed separately as complementary tools for post-synthetic processing, sequence-selective cleavage, enrichment, and quality control, whereas other enzymatic approaches are considered for post-synthetic strand conversion. We compare the characteristics and limitations of these production and preparation strategies, discuss purification techniques for long ssDNA, and summarize its applications in DNA origami nanotechnology and gene therapy. This review comprehensively synthesizes the bottlenecks in long ssDNA production, preparation, and purification, and outlines further development trends. We highlight template-independent de novo enzymatic DNA synthesis, automated DNA manufacturing, synthetic biology-based production systems, and AI-assisted sequence optimization. These developments are expected to accelerate the transition of long ssDNA technologies from laboratory research toward scalable manufacturing and practical applications.
records.authors: Wang X, Wu Y, Zhang X, Du Y, Liu N, Wang Z, Zhang H, Gao X, Zheng A.

records.title: Early-life enteric bacterial infection alters hippocampal cell fate and leads to cognitive deficits.
records.abstract: Early-life enteric infections are increasingly recognized as a major driver of adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes. However, the cell-type-specific mechanisms linking intestinal inflammation to persistent cognitive deficits in the developing brain remain poorly defined. Here, we demonstrate that transient Citrobacter rodentium infection in mice, which models human pathogenic Escherichia coli infection, disrupts hippocampal development and impairs cognitive function. These phenotypes were observed only during a critical postnatal window, coinciding with transient intestinal permeability. Hippocampal transcriptomics revealed persistent dysregulation of neurogenic pathways, and cellular analyses confirmed alterations in neurons, microglia, and endothelial cells. Critically, we identified accumulation of the microbial metabolite D-lactate in the hippocampus. Oral D-lactate supplementation in a gut barrier disruption model, exacerbated both behavioral deficits and hippocampal neuronal loss. Finally, in the presence of inflammatory stimuli, exposing primary neurons to D-lactate reduced the ratio of NeuN expressing neurons. Together, these findings identify age-dependent intestinal barrier dysfunction as a potential route linking early-life enteric infection with increased D-lactate exposure, hippocampal neuronal alterations, and persistent behavioural impairment.
records.authors: Tabusi MM, Serapio-Palacios A, Creus-Cuadros A, Octoman A, Lewis V, Metcalfe-Roach A, Snyder JS, Finlay BB.

records.title: Cyclotides from Clitoria ternatea: Genomic Organization, Biosynthesis, and Roles in Plant Defense.
records.abstract: Clitoria ternatea, commonly known as butterfly pea, is a perennial legume widely recognized for its ornamental and medicinal value. Beyond its characteristic anthocyanin-rich blue flowers, the plant produces cyclotides, a type of ultra-stable, cyclic cystine-knot peptide, with exceptional biological functions. Unlike other cyclotide-bearing families that carry independent cyclotide genes, C. ternatea integrates cyclotide domains into albumin-1 genes, replacing β-chain domains through divergent or convergent evolution. Genomic and transcriptomic studies reveal a large repertoire of albumin-1 loci and associated biosynthetic enzymes, including asparaginyl endopeptidases (butelase-1), protein disulphide isomerases, and peptidyl-prolyl isomerases, which orchestrate the cyclization, folding, and stabilization of cyclotides. Transcriptome analyses further demonstrate tissue-specific expression patterns, with distinct cyclotides such as cliotides T2 and T3 enriched in flowers and pods, and cliotides T8-T10 specialized in seeds, reflecting adaptive responses to localized biotic stress. Functionally, C. ternatea cyclotides exhibit broad-spectrum defense properties, including insecticidal, bactericidal, nematicidal, and antifungal activities, primarily through membrane permeabilization and disruption of lipid bilayers. Their preferential affinity for phosphatidylethanolamine-rich membranes highlights their selective toxicity toward insect and microbial targets. Recent advances in synthetic biology exploit cyclotides' structural stability as molecular scaffolds for therapeutic peptide design, with applications in immunomodulatory, antimicrobial, and anticancer drug development. This review consolidates genomic, transcriptomic, and functional insights into cyclotide biosynthesis and activity in C. ternatea, highlighting its evolutionary distinctiveness and biotechnological potential. Future research integrating multi-omics and spatial single-cell analyses can further unravel regulatory networks, defense dynamics, and translational applications of these unique plant peptides.

records.title: Molecular characterization and phylogenetic analysis of the meq gene of Marek's Disease Virus strains from Vietnamese commercial poultry flocks.
records.abstract: Marek's disease (MD) is a highly contagious lymphoproliferative disease of chickens caused by Marek's disease virus serotype 1 (MDV-1) and remains a major concern for the global poultry industry despite widespread vaccination. Although current vaccines effectively prevent clinical disease, the emergence of more virulent strains has been recorded. Molecular surveillance of field strains is essential, particularly in regions where data remain limited. This study aimed to molecularly characterize MDV-1 isolates from recent cases in Vietnamese commercial poultry flocks, focusing on the meq gene, a key virulence-associated marker, and to compare variants with vaccine strains CVI988/Rispens. A total of 12 MDV-1 positive samples from multiple regions of Vietnam were analyzed using Sanger sequencing of the full-length meq gene. Phylogenetic analysis grouped the Vietnamese isolates into three genetic clusters (G1-G3). The attenuated-like G1 isolates showed high similarity to CVI988/Rispens clones and contained four to seven proline-rich repeat (PPPP) motifs. In contrast, G2 and G3 isolates were classified as field virulent genotypes and contained two to three PPPP motifs. Comparative sequence analysis revealed multiple amino-acid substitutions in the Meq protein relative to CVI988/Rispens, including conserved mutations characteristic of Asian field strains. Vietnamese isolates clustered primarily with contemporary Asian lineages from China and India. The results demonstrate the presence of both vaccine-derived and virulent MDV-1 strains in this Vietnamese sample set and highlight the importance of continued molecular surveillance to monitor viral evolution and support vaccination strategies.

records.authors: Duy HD, Hoang PT, Soster P, Duc DN, Molnár J, Samoy C, Christiaens I, Truong VK, Hao QP, Thien NHL, Kim PDT, Bich THT, Thi TL, Gussem M.

records.title: The Journey of Newcastle Disease Virus Across the Indonesian Archipelago.
records.abstract: Newcastle disease (ND), caused by Newcastle disease virus (NDV), remains a major threat to poultry production, food security, and livelihoods worldwide. ND was first recognized in Java, Indonesia, in 1926, followed by its description in Newcastle-upon-Tyne, England, in 1927. Since then, ND has been repeatedly detected in Indonesian poultry systems, including free-range, backyard, and commercial production, with outbreaks causing substantial mortality and economic losses. Indonesia's archipelagic geography, extensive poultry movement and marketing networks, and heterogeneous production systems create complex conditions for virus persistence and dissemination. This review summarizes the century-long journey (1926-2026) of NDV in Indonesia, highlighting its historical emergence, epidemiological evolution, genetic diversity, and control strategies. Molecular epidemiological studies demonstrate substantial genetic diversity, with virulent genotype VII viruses frequently associated with contemporary outbreaks, while genotypes I, II, VI, and XIII have also been reported in Indonesian domestic and wild birds. The evidence supports repeated endemic circulation and ongoing viral evolution across Indonesia, emphasizing the importance of continuous molecular surveillance to monitor viral diversity and inform control strategies. Understanding the long-term epidemiological and evolutionary dynamics of NDV in Indonesia provides valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying viral emergence and persistence in a unique geographical location. Strengthening representative genomic surveillance, improving vaccination implementation, and enhancing regional cooperation across Southeast Asia will be critical for mitigating the future impact of ND on poultry production and food security.
records.journal: Avian pathology : journal of the W.V.P.A
records.authors: Ul-Rahman A, Untari H, Nugroho W, Munir M.

records.title: Genome characterization of a novel monopartite begomovirus infecting Capsicum annuum in Central India.
records.abstract: Complete genome sequences of two isolates of a novel begomovirus and its associated betasatellite were determined from two individual Capsicum annuum samples, exhibiting indistinguishable severe leaf curl symptoms, collected from Anuppur, Madhya Pradesh, India. The genome sequences of Anuppur-04 (GenBank accession PZ428100) and Anuppur-05 (PZ428101) isolates were 2760 nt each and contained six open reading frames, typical of the Old World monopartite begomoviruses. They shared 95.8% nucleotide sequence identity, whereas the highest identity was 89.4-89.5% with Tomato leaf curl Joydebpur virus. Phylogenetic analysis placed both isolates in a distinct monophyletic clade. Falling below the ICTV species demarcation threshold of 91% for complete genome sequence, these isolates represent a novel begomovirus species and are tentatively named chilli leaf curl Madhya Pradesh virus (ChiLCMPV). Split-decomposition analysis using a Neighbor-Net network, together with recombination analysis, provided evidence of recombination involving begomoviruses related to different species of tomato leaf curl virus. The associated betasatellite sequences from Anuppur-04 (PZ487063) and Anuppur-05 (PZ487064) were of 1320 nt each and shared 83.1% nucleotide identity, while highest 83.3-85.3% identity and clustered with Betasatellite capsi (chilli leaf curl betasatellite; ChiLCB), indicating that they represented new strains of ChiLCB. Collectively, these findings established the occurrence of the novel begomovirus species ChiLCMPV in association with ChiLCB infecting C. annuum in Central India and expanded the known genetic diversity of begomoviruses and their associated satellites.

records.title: In vitro phenotyping and genomics: a conceptual framework linking plant tissue culture with GWAS, QTL mapping, and multi-omics.
records.abstract: Main conclusionStandardized in vitro phenotypes provide genetically tractable traits that integrate GWAS, QTL mapping, and multi-omics, enabling mechanistic insight and genetics-informed improvement of plant regeneration. Plant tissue culture (PTC) has traditionally been employed as a technical tool for propagation, transformation, and germplasm conservation. This review reframes in vitro culture systems as quantitative phenotyping platforms that enable rigorous genetic dissection of complex traits, such as regeneration competence, stress tolerance, and developmental plasticity. By operating under highly standardized and reproducible conditions, in vitro systems reduce environmental noise and expose genotype-dependent variation that is often obscured in field or greenhouse experiments. When formalized as quantitative traits, culture responses, including callus induction, organogenesis, somatic embryogenesis, and stress survival, become amenable to genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping. Synthesizing evidence across diverse plant species, this review demonstrates that in vitro traits are genetically structured, polygenic, and biologically meaningful, reflecting coordinated regulation of hormonal signaling, chromatin accessibility, stress response pathways, and developmental gene networks. Numerous GWAS and QTL studies have identified loci and candidate genes underlying regeneration efficiency, embryogenic competence, and stress-responsive culture performance, confirming that tissue culture responsiveness is rooted in genomic architecture rather than protocol effects alone. The interpretive power of genetic mapping is substantially enhanced through integration with bioinformatic and multi-omics layers, including transcriptomics, epigenomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and network-based analyses, thereby refining candidate prioritization and facilitating mechanistic inference. This review further examines the dual role of somaclonal variation as both a constraint on clonal fidelity and a source of genetic and epigenetic diversity that can reveal cryptic genotype-phenotype relationships. Emphasis is placed on study design principles, phenotyping challenges, statistical modeling strategies, and integrative pipelines that connect genotype to in vitro phenotype and ultimately to breeding and biotechnology applications. This synthesis highlights in vitro culture systems as powerful, genetics-informed platforms for precision breeding, gene validation, and supporting efforts to more predictably and rationally manipulate complex traits, particularly in horticultural and clonally propagated crops.
records.authors: Isak MA, Fatima S, Haider I, Yetişir H, Şimşek Ö.

records.title: Integrated GWAS and RNA-Seq analyses identify candidate genes for drought tolerance in spring wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) from the cold and arid region of China.
records.abstract: Key messageUsing germplasm accumulated over 50 years in China's cold, arid region, 20 drought-responsive loci were identified through GWAS, and 7 key candidate genes were further revealed by integrating RNA-Seq data from drought-tolerant and sensitive lines. Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is a major staple crop central to global food security, yet yield is severely constrained by drought. To dissect the genetic basis of drought tolerance, we evaluated 257 spring wheat germplasm lines, accumulated over five decades of breeding in the cold and arid region of China, under well-watered (WW) and rain-fed water stress (WS) conditions for seven yield-related traits. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for seven agronomic traits and three drought tolerance indices, utilizing three analytical models identified 20 stable loci significantly associated with drought response. Transcriptome profiling of drought-tolerant and drought-sensitive lines under both conditions revealed 4,411 drought-responsive genes. Integrative analysis of GWAS and RNA-Seq data prioritized seven candidate genes, one of which for plant height overlapped with weighted gene co-expression network analysis hub modules, highlighting potential regulators of drought adaptation. Furthermore, genomic prediction based on the identified loci, using Bayesian ridge regression, achieved high trait-specific accuracies, with plant height reaching 85.4%. Collectively, these findings provide novel insights into the genetic architecture of drought tolerance in wheat and offer valuable molecular resources for marker-assisted selection and the development of drought-resilient cultivars.
records.journal: TAG. Theoretical and applied genetics. Theoretische und angewandte Genetik
records.authors: Lyu X, Xie X, Meng X, Cui Y, Zhang W, Ren K, Ni J, Yang F, Dai X, Zeng J, Liu W, Li J, Mu L, Ma W, Xu D.

records.title: Butyrate reverts  Chlamydia pneumoniae  -induced transcriptional suppression of macrophage polarization markers and promotes chlamydial clearance in macrophages
records.abstract: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are generated by gut microbiota through fermentation of dietary fibers. SCFAs contribute to human health through immunomodulation, metabolic regulation and other extraintestinal functions. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of SCFAs on the survival and antibiotic susceptibility of the intracellular bacteria  Chlamydia pneumoniae and  Chlamydia trachomatis , both representing prevalent human pathogens associated with chronic sequelae. Despite earlier reports on their direct antimicrobial activity, none of the three major SCFAs acetate, propionate nor butyrate affected the growth of  C. pneumoniae or  C. trachomatis in epithelial cells. However, butyrate decreased  C. pneumoniae genome copy numbers and infectious progeny production in THP-1 macrophages harbouring antibiotic-refractory infection phenotype. In addition, butyrate enhanced the chlamydiocidal efficacy of azithromycin in the macrophages. Similar results were obtained with  C. trachomatis -infected macrophages. To elucidate the underlying molecular changes, impact of chlamydial infection, butyrate treatment and the combination theirof on macrophage polarization and antimicrobial peptide expression was investigated.  C. pneumoniae suppressed the expression of macrophage polarization markers CD80, TLR4, CD64, CD204 and CD206, and the antimicrobial peptide LL-37, while butyrate treatment reverted the expression of both the polarization markers and LL-37 in the infected macrophages. These findings suggest that butyrate may play a role in modulating immune responses in macrophages during  Chlamydia infections, highlighting the role of diet-derived metabolites in shaping  Chlamydia –host interactions and antichlamydial treatment efficacy.
records.authors: Ylätalo M, Reigada I, Hanski L.

records.title: Age Associated Shifts Toward Anaerobic Taxa and Amino Acid Degradation Potential in the Canine Oral Microbiome
records.abstract: Introduction  Periodontal disease is common in dogs and is associated with changes in oral microbial community composition. How the canine oral microbiome restructures across age at both ecological and metabolic levels remains incompletely characterized. Methods  We analyzed shotgun metagenomic buccal-swab profiles from 1,125 dogs using MetaPhlAn. Functional profiles from HUMAnN were analyzed at pathway and functional-group levels. We annotated species-level taxa with oxygen preference and evaluated oxygen-tolerant and anaerobic taxa abundances across age. We also characterized community structure, metabolic potential, Shannon diversity, and age and weight prediction using nested cross-validated Elastic Net models. Results  Age was associated with substantial restructuring in the oral microbiome. Mean oxygen-tolerant taxa abundance decreased from 67.5% in puppies to 29.1% in mature dogs, whereas anaerobic abundance increased from 14.3% to 53.8%. The oxygen-tolerant: anaerobe log-ratio declined with age (Spearman ρ = −0.616). Metabolic profiles also varied with age, with higher amino-acid-degradation potential and lower glycolysis and central-carbohydrate potential, and aerobic-respiration-I abundance in older dogs. Shannon diversity increased with age (ρ = 0.537, p Discussion  Canine age was associated with coordinated changes in oral-community oxygen preference and metabolic pathways. These findings extend prior taxon-specific observations by examining a broader ecological shift and metabolic potential in the canine oral microbiome. This provides a reference for future longitudinal or clinical studies of oral maturation and periodontal disease.

records.title: The Almond Expression Atlas: A comprehensive multi-tissue transcriptomic resource for almond gene expression
records.abstract: Background  Improving crop adaptation and enhancing agronomic and quality traits requires a deeper understanding of gene expression regulation, for which expression atlases are valuable tools. Almond (  Prunus dulcis (Mill.) D.A. Webb) is one of the most economically important tree nut crops worldwide. However, an integrated transcriptomic resource for this species is still lacking. Available data remain fragmented across independent studies, limiting their comparability and reuse.  Results  Here, we present the first almond gene expression atlas: a comprehensive multi-tissue transcriptomic resource integrating publicly available RNA sequencing data. A total of 142 high-quality untreated and control samples from 17 independent projects were curated through a metadata standardization process and analyzed using a unified bioinformatics pipeline. Standardized expression profiles were generated for 25,225 annotated genes in the  Prunus dulcis ‘Texas’ v2.0 reference genome. The atlas integrates two complementary expression approaches: a median TPM approach capturing quantitative expression levels and a rank-based strategy implemented using the Bgee expression calling method, designed to improve comparability across heterogeneous datasets. This design enables the identification of tissue-specific candidate genes and the exploration of expression patterns across tissues and developmental stages. Its applicability is demonstrated through two use cases, highlighting its ability to identify biologically meaningful gene sets associated with bud dormancy transitions and to prioritize candidate reference genes for RT-qPCR normalization in almond.  Conclusions  The Almond Expression Atlas v1.0 is publicly available through FruitDBase (  fruitdbase.csic.es ), providing an interactive platform for gene expression exploration and visualization. This resource supports functional genomics studies and facilitates candidate gene discovery in almond, while ensuring data traceability and promoting data reusability.
records.authors: López-Fernández EM, Zwieniecki M, Tixier A, Botía JA, Martínez-García PJ.

records.title: Maternal progesterone signaling establishes lifelong oral homeostasis
records.abstract: Abstract  Pregnancy is accompanied by profound endocrine remodeling, yet the mechanisms by which maternal hormonal signals establish long-term tissue homeostasis remain largely unknown. Here we identify maternal progesterone signaling as a developmental cue that establishes lifelong oral homeostasis through a hormone–lipid–microbiome axis. We show that the membrane progesterone receptor mPRδ is selectively expressed in the developing and maternal submandibular glands, where it mediates non-genomic progesterone signaling to promote epithelial differentiation by driving the selective mobilization of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). Loss of this pathway disrupts salivary gland maturation, reshapes the oral microbial ecosystem through the selective expansion of Pasteurellaceae, and causes local inflammation as well as systemic metabolic dysfunction. Mechanistically, antibiotic treatment abolishes these phenotypes, whereas transfer of the oral microbiota recapitulates disease, demonstrating that developmental defects in the host are translated into long-term pathology through the oral microbiome. Remarkably, maternal—but not adult—DHA supplementation restores salivary gland development and microbial homeostasis and prevents adult disease phenotypes, identifying a critical developmental window during which oral homeostasis is durably established. Collectively, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized maternal endocrine mechanism that establishes lifelong host–microbiome homeostasis and identify developmental programming as a fundamental principle linking maternal physiology to adult health.

records.title: Nematodes as bioindicators of ecological status in midland Irish peatlands
records.abstract: Abstract  Peatlands play a critical role in global carbon sequestration, yet widespread drainage and land-use change have disrupted their hydrology and soil biological integrity, accelerating peat decomposition and greenhouse gas emissions. Rewetting is increasingly promoted as a key restoration strategy, but its effectiveness in re-establishing belowground ecological structure remains insufficiently understood. This study assessed the response of nematode-based soil food webs across a broad range of peatland habitats, including intact bogs, degraded systems, rewetted and non-rewetted managed peatlands, fens, wasted peatlands, and semi-natural sites, using a combination of morphological identification and DNA-based molecular sequencing. Nematode community composition and functional structure were evaluated using Enrichment Index (EI) and Structure Index (SI) diagnostics. Intact bog habitats consistently exhibited higher SI and lower EI values, reflecting well-structured food webs dominated by fungal-associated and higher trophic nematode families, including Dorylaimidae and Qudsianematidae. In contrast, degraded and non-rewetted peatlands showed simplified food webs characterized by elevated EI and dominance of opportunistic bacterial-feeding families such as Rhabditidae and Cephalobidae. Rewetted sites generally exhibited reduced EI relative to non-rewetted counterparts, indicating dampened nutrient enrichment and microbial pulses following hydrological restoration; however, SI values remained low in the short term, suggesting limited recovery of higher trophic complexity. Comparisons between morphological and molecular datasets revealed strong concordance at the family level for dominant taxa, while molecular sequencing detected additional rare and cryptic nematode families not consistently recovered through morphology alone, underscoring the complementarity of both approaches. Fen peatlands displayed higher EI values consistent with naturally greater nutrient availability, whereas wasted peatlands supported persistently impoverished food webs regardless of management. Overall, the results demonstrate that rewetting effectively stabilizes nutrient dynamics and initiates early recovery of soil food web functioning, but full restoration of trophic complexity requires long-term ecological recovery. Integrating hydrological restoration with biological monitoring is therefore essential for maximizing peatland carbon storage and climate mitigation potential.
records.authors: Pulavarty A, Ringholz L, Klappauf T, Cooper E, Molina PM, McMillan D, Kakouli-Duarte T.

records.title: Gut microbiota ablation depletes secondary bile acids and shifts the cytokine balance in BCG-infected mice
records.abstract: Abstract    Background.  Antibiotic ablation is the standard test of whether a host phenotype depends on the gut microbiota, but it removes the community and perturbs the host at once, so depletion alone cannot assign a metabolite shift to the community. We built a four-arm mouse model on a single BCG infection background: untreated controls (NC), BCG alone, BCG after mixed-antibiotic ablation (ABX_BCG), and BCG followed by faecal microbiota transplantation with no antibiotic exposure at any point (BCG_FMT). The ablated and transplanted arms were independent branches, not a depletion-then-restoration sequence.  Results.  Dual-polarity untargeted LC-MS (9,706 negative-mode and 11,589 positive-mode features) and shotgun metagenomics showed that ablation left a block of 726 negative-mode and 313 positive-mode features absent from all three ABX_BCG samples but detected in 88–94% of the other nine; total ion signal in the ablated arm exceeded that of the quality-control injections, excluding dilution and matrix loss. Twenty-seven block features were annotated, resolving to 17 unique InChIKeys, 21 of them microbial compound classes including secondary bile acids. Deoxycholic acid eluted at 437.93 s in negative mode and 437.28 s in positive mode; deoxycholic and lithocholic acid were undetected in the ablated samples. Both omics layers resolved the same four groups (PERMANOVA R² = 0.562 for the genus table and 0.635 for the metabolome) yet failed to couple at sample level; exhaustive within-group re-pairing excluded sample mismatch, identifying a shared treatment rather than an individual axis. Ablation accompanied higher TNF-α and IL-6 and lower IFN-γ and IL-10 in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and serum alike.  Conclusions.  The gut community contributes a set of metabolite features whose absence is specific to the ablated state rather than shared with infection or transplantation, and the same arm occupies the extreme of the cytokine readout in both compartments. Running the ablated and transplanted arms as independent branches off the infected baseline is what makes this an antibiotic-specific control, and the two omics layers carry a shared treatment structure rather than a shared individual axis.
